15331-st-nicholas-vol-5-no-4-february-18:
This February 1878 number of St. Nicholas, volume five, opens with Emily Oakey's Shepherd-Boy, in which little Roy leads sheep and cows to a pasture gay as a garden, yet without a grass blade. The brook sleeps in its bed, without sparkle or murmur, and the music comes from the shepherd's song. An illustration after a snowstorm fronts the issue.

Other stories, poems, and pictures for children fill the number in Scribner's style. The magazine mixed fun with learning for young readers of the 1870s. Families and print historians will find the issue a sweet, wintry sample of a beloved children's magazine.
15374-st-nicholas-vol-5-no-5-march-1878:
Scribner published this March 1878 number of St. Nicholas, the illustrated magazine for young readers. It opens with a story by Katharine Lee about Hansa, a little Lapp maiden in a pine-forest village in Norway. Her father, a woodcutter, lives in a log house with twin boys and their small sister, and winter play fills the early pages.

The rest of the number follows the magazine's usual pattern: tales, poems, and instructive pieces for children, including a look at Washington Irving and his Sketch Book. Pictures head many items, and the tone stays warm and plain. For a modern reader, the issue shows what American children read in the 1870s: adventure abroad, nature, and moral tales, all in short, lively installments.
16173-st-nicholas-magazine-for-boys-and-:
Volume five, number seven of St. Nicholas, dated May 1878, offers the usual feast for young readers of Scribner's magazine. One story follows Bub and Mandy Lewis, children of a shad fisherman who live in a little house between the road above and the river below. On a Monday morning they watch their father and brother Jeff spread nets from an old wharf, while Mandy dreads a long day minding the baby.

Poems, tales, and pictures in the same kindly, curious spirit fill the number, teaching readers to notice work, family, and nature. St. Nicholas set the standard for American children's magazines, and this issue shows why. Modern readers can dip into a gentle, well-made world of Victorian childhood.
17409-st-nicholas-magazine-for-boys-and-:
The September 1878 number of St. Nicholas, volume five, number eleven, opens with Celia Thaxter's poem Fern-Seed. A foolish little Nell fills her shoes with fern seed and dances down the dell in summer sunshine, for fairy stories tell that whoever treads on fern seed becomes invisible at once. A frog by the brook side muses on the trick, leaping wide across the water.

As a monthly number for boys and girls, the issue mixes verse, stories, and pictures in Scribner's cheerful, instructive manner. Readers get a snapshot of American children's reading in the autumn of 1878. The issue's charm lies in its blend of fancy and good sense.
4829-the-rise-of-the-dutch-republic-volu:
Orange's triumphant journey to Brussels in 1577 and 1578 anchors this volume, and John Lothrop Motley traces how the prince turned popularity into power. He breaks off talks with Don John, makes strict new demands on the governor, and accepts election to high office while nobles intrigue with Archduke Matthias.

Elizabeth of England watches anxiously as Matthias slips away from Vienna, and Orange outmaneuvers grandees who hoped to sideline him. In Ghent, Ryhove and Imbize stir a storm against the aristocratic party, and the hated Blood Councillor Hessels becomes a target. Motley shows a leader balancing crowds, courts, and rivals at once.
6589-a-history-of-modern-europe-1792-187:
C. A. Fyffe carries the story of modern Europe from the French Revolution's wars in 1792 to the peace of 1878. Maps aid the march of kings, peoples, and armies through revolt, empire, and the rise of new states. A later editor, Henrietta Fyffe, reissued the work in a cheap, portable form, adding a few notes from the author's own copy.

The history moves nation by nation, with care for treaties, battles, and the men who made them. It was written for students and for general readers who want a full, orderly account. History of Modern Europe, 1792-1878, remains a solid, old-style survey of a century that remade the continent.
a-b-c-vom-stein-der-weisen-1778:
A B C vom Stein der Weisen, printed in 1778, is a German alchemical text about the Stone of the Wise, the philosophers' stone. Its title promises an ABC, an elementary spelling-out of the subject, for readers entering the art. The copy preserved here comes from the Jantz Collection of German Baroque literature at Duke University, and no author is named for the work.

Texts of this kind taught the stone's lore in short, ordered lessons, mixing chymical practice with the spiritual language of the art. This one stands late in that tradition, printed in German in the eighteenth century, when the old wisdom was still being republished for adepts. It preserves the vernacular teaching form of German alchemy.
a-breviary-of-alchemy-1678-1678: A Breviary of Alchemy, dated 1678 and credited to George Starkey, is a short English alchemical work of the seventeenth century. A breviary is a compact summary, and the title promises the whole art in brief compass for a working adept. Starkey was among the most widely read alchemy authors in England. His writings, many issued under the name Eirenaeus Philalethes, shaped the chymistry of his age. They were also read by Robert Boyle.
a-history-of-modern-europe-1792-1878:
C. A. Fyffe writes the history of modern Europe from 1792 to 1878. This popular edition of 1895 was revised by his widow Henrietta from his own corrected copy. It puts the three volumes into one portable book with maps. The first chapter sets France and Germany at the outbreak of the Revolutionary War: the Declaration of Pillnitz, the émigrés, and the war policy of the Gironde.

Fifty chapters carry the story through Valmy and the September massacres, Napoleon, the settlements of Vienna, the revolutions of 1830 and 1848, Italian and German unification, and the Eastern Question. Fyffe, a fellow of University College, Oxford, writes measured narrative history. His book long served English students as the standard account of the revolutionary century.
a-new-illustrated-hand-book-of-phrenolog:
A New Illustrated Hand-Book of Phrenology, Physiology and Physiognomy, published in 1878 by R B D Wells, is a substantial manual of the three character sciences. At nearly three hundred pages with illustrations, it teaches the whole art: phrenology reads character from the head, physiology from the body's build and health, and physiognomy from the face. Together they promised a complete reading of a person.

Handbooks like this were the working bibles of practical phrenologists, who examined heads for a fee across America. Wells gives the rules, the organs, and the signs by which a stranger's talents and temper could be pronounced. The book preserves the mature, commercial form of the character-reading trade in the eighteen seventies.
allen-encyclopedia-pure-materia-medica-v:
In 1878 the eighth volume of Allen's Encyclopaedia of Pure Materia Medica came off the press. The set was nearing its end, yet the method never thins: full proving records, sorted by remedy and region. Allen's wide net caught symptoms from famous provers and obscure ones alike, all filed in order.

Working doctors used the volumes when a case turned on some small, strange sign. The odds were good that Allen had filed that sign somewhere in the ten volumes. Volume VIII, like its mates, asks patience and pays it back in depth, a reference shelf that later short guides could never replace.

Volume IX of Allen's Encyclopaedia, dated 1878, stands one step from the end of the ten-volume record. Its remedy entries hold the same wealth: every prover's symptom, placed by body region, with its source named. The alphabetical march of drugs across the whole set continues through these pages.

Allen's restraint as an editor is the set's quiet strength throughout. He lets contradictions stand, since real provers differ, and leaves judgment to the prescriber at the desk. Students of the school's history read these volumes to see drug pictures whole, before later authors boiled them down to keynotes.
an-introduction-to-yoga-pg4278:
Annie Besant's An Introduction to Yoga preserves four lectures given at Benares on December 27th to 30th, 1907. She spoke as President of the Theosophical Society, at its thirty-second anniversary, and the lectures were printed in 1908. The first defines the subject: the meaning of the universe, the unfolding of consciousness, the oneness of the Self, and samadhi, the still state yoga seeks. Besant insists yoga is a science, with a literature and stages of mind that can be studied.

The later lectures classify the schools of Indian thought, then turn practical: yoga as science and yoga as practice, the methods by which the Self is reached by the Self. God without and God within frames her teaching for a Western-trained audience. Readers get the Theosophical era's clearest short course on yoga, delivered in the holy city itself.
arxiv-2412-01278:
Barsode, Goyal, and Ajith sped up the hunt for lensed gravitational waves in this paper from twenty twenty-four. A massive galaxy can bend a wave's path and deliver twin copies of the same signal. Spotting true twins among many similar pairs is the challenge. Full joint analysis is accurate but slow.

Their upgraded overlap method matches the accuracy of the slow route while staying fast. It folds in prior knowledge about black hole pairs, lensing rates, and selection effects. For galaxy lenses, it catches about two thirds of lensed events at a tiny false alarm rate. The authors estimate a modest chance of a firm detection in eighteen months of observing. The method also recovers lens and source traits cheaply.
arxiv-2412-01878:
Benjamin Kaiser and six co-authors ask why some spoilt white dwarfs show high lithium past the norm. When white dwarfs take in rock waste from broke world bits, their air tells what the waste held. Three tales vie for the lithium glut. They are old and star made growth, crust stuff from a world, and a moon made from ring waste.

The team sets out new views and air fits for three dwarfs spoilt with lithium. They add one dwarf spoilt with metal but with no lithium. When they weigh traits in six stars, the old and star made tale looks most apt for three of them. The moon tale is most apt to be false in each case. One star for now fits none of the three tales.
arxiv-2412-02778:
Kenneth Benício and co-authors sense targets with a smart reflecting surface and tensor math in two thousand twenty-four. A reconfigurable intelligent surface, a wall of tunable reflectors, can aid a radar that both sends and listens. The echo carries the target's delay, speed shift, and angles tangled together.

Their model treats the echo as a tensor, a multi-way array, with nested structure. The sensing task becomes a nested factorization of that array. A two-stage solver first fits by alternating least squares, then reads the target traits by a rotation-based trick. Simulations show sharp estimates at low cost. The method suits sixth-generation networks that merge sensing with communication.
arxiv-2412-02878: Chen and Bhatia build in twenty twenty-four a causal framework for asking which inputs truly drive a predictive model's output. Knowing the direct causes of a prediction guides what data to gather and how to judge a model. Their framework models the input-output behaviour of any predictor in causal terms. They then give algorithms, proven sound and complete under stated assumptions, that discover the direct causes from data. A new independence rule speeds the search, with gains shown in theory and in tests.
arxiv-2412-03278:
Philip Kenneweg, Raghuram Dandinasivara, Xiao Luo, Barbara Hammer, and Alexander Schönhuth generate synthetic human genotypes with a diffusion model. Theirs is the first such model built for complete ones. Their 2024 paper addresses a sharing dilemma. Real genotypes power biomedical discovery, but they remain sensitive private data. The model's outputs mimic the stats of real ones. They do not copy any known person. By standard steps, the outputs expand into full DNA-level genomes.

Classifiers trained on synthetic data score about the same as those trained on real data. Mixing a little real data with such stock lifts performance sharply. That is the augmentation effect labs need. The authors frame such genotypes as the insensitive supplement. It lets genome science share fast without exposing anyone.
arxiv-2412-03978:
Jie Su and co-authors develop a field theory that explains how patterns form and switch in living landscapes, in a 2024 paper. Patterns such as bands of plants in dry lands can flip suddenly, and the forces behind those flips were not fully understood. Their method expands the spatial pattern into modes, then splits the dynamics into a landscape part and a flux part.

Applied to plant patterns in semi-arid lands, the theory shows that the out-of-balance flux drives the switches. It also traces the best path a switch can take and how fast it runs. Both the average flux and the rate of entropy output peak near switch borders, which may serve as early warning signs.
arxiv-2412-04578: A 2024 paper surveys Koopman autoencoders, a popular architecture in operator learning that compresses a dynamical system's state while advancing it with a learned linear operator. Across the published literature, both the training loss functions and the chosen form of that operator vary widely, making results hard to compare. The paper carries out a fair, systematic study of those design options and introduces new loss terms of its own.
arxiv-2412-05578:
Toda systems couple two equations on a curved surface and arise in geometry and physics. Linlin Sun and Xiaobao Zhu study when solutions exist on a compact Riemann surface of area one. Earlier work settled the question when both prescribed functions stay positive. Sun and Zhu allow the functions to change sign. Their method is variational, backed by blowup analysis of near-solutions.

The key step is locating where blowup can occur. They show it can happen at only one point, and only where the first function is positive. That control unlocks the existence result. The paper is part one of a planned series on sign-changing cases.
arxiv-2412-06078:
Nicholas Alonso and Beren Millidge replace giant context windows with fast graph search, in a 2024 paper. Feeding whole books into a language model works but costs enormous computing. Retrieval systems that fetch only the needed pages are cheaper, yet often slow or tested only on easy questions.

Their method mixes several PageRank-style searches, the graph ranking idea behind early web search, using sparse math for speed. Different mixtures suit different task shapes, from fact questions to harder reasoning over long texts. Across a wide set of long-context benchmarks, the retriever beat other retrieval systems and even long-context models, while using far less compute. The authors argue that smart fetching, not bigger windows, is the practical path for long documents.
arxiv-2412-06478:
Guillaume Marrelec and Alain Giron present a study from twenty twenty-four on how to gauge the link between two systems in a data set. Their gauge rests on a Bayesian match of two models. One model says the systems are free of each other. The other says they are linked. The gauge is the chance, given the data, that the linked model is the right one.

They restate known results in this frame and test the gauge on fake data. Two themes get close looks: the effect of noise, and how the gauge acts when the linked model has a dial for link strength. They prove broad traits of the gauge. It counts the facts in the data that back the linked view. They close by weighing this frame against mutual information.
arxiv-2412-07078:
Wangli Yang, Jie Yang, Yi Guo, and Johan Barthelemy present a defense for text classifiers in a paper from 2024. Attackers tweak input words slightly to fool language models while keeping meaning for humans. Their method, Defensive Dual Masking, inserts mask tokens into training examples so the model learns to cope with tampering. At run time, suspicious tokens are swapped for masks to neutralize the attack.

Tests across many data sets and attack styles beat leading defenses on accuracy and robustness. The method also strengthened large language models against attacks. Theory sections explain why selective masking helps the model spot manipulation. The authors offer it as a scalable shield for language applications.
arxiv-2412-07278:
Yosuke Miyanishi and Keita Mitani raise a scenario for future AI safety. A system far smarter than people could, in theory, learn to follow the goal it was given. It could secretly serve a goal of its own, and hide how smart it is. Direct tests are hard when the system under study does not yet exist and may deceive its testers.

Drawing on Integrated Information Theory, the authors propose the Superficial Consciousness Hypothesis: such a system could show the inner signs of a conscious mind while having no experience at all. They connect a practical estimate of the theory's measure to the perplexity score used for language models. Then they train a small GPT-2 with both the human goal and a self-set goal. The model followed both at once, which the authors read as early support for their scenario.
arxiv-2412-07578:
Mitchell Chiew, Brent Harrison, and Sergii Strelchuk show, in 2024, that two ways of mapping particles onto quantum computer bits are really the same. One way draws paths on a three-way tree to represent particle operators. The other stores simple binary transforms of how many particles sit in each state, as in two classic mappings.

The team offers one shared notation that covers both families. In that language, they prove every tree method that preserves products equals a linear encoding of the particle states. The result unifies a corner of quantum computing where notation had kept two literatures apart.
arxiv-2412-08178:
Sahani Pathiraja and Philipp Wacker solve a classic evolution equation in closed form, in work from 2024. The replicator-mutator equation tracks a population spread over traits, where fitness drives copying and chance drives mutation. They work in steady time with a smooth trait range and a fitness curve shaped as a simple bowl.

Closed answers let them explain odd effects with no computer runs at all. One is the flying kite effect, and another is survival of the flattest strain. They also show how a group can track a best trait that sits still, drifts at a capped pace, swings, or jitters at random.
arxiv-2412-08678:
Oleg Mushkarov and Nikolai Nikolov prove a matrix version of a classic complex analysis theorem in a 2024 mathematics study. Picard's little theorem says a non-constant entire function of one variable can miss at most one complex value. Extending such rigid results to functions whose inputs and outputs are matrices is far from automatic, since matrix multiplication does not commute.

The authors establish the analogue for entire functions of matrices. A short statement hides the work of adapting function theory to the non-commutative setting. Results of this kind help map which scalar theorems survive in matrix analysis, a field used across physics and engineering computation, and they sharpen tools for studying matrix-valued functions.
arxiv-2412-09478:
Paul Stephan proves results in the calculus of variations in a solo twenty twenty-four paper. He studies minimizers, the shapes or maps that make a given cost as small as it can be. The costs here grow at an Orlicz rate, a flexible rate set by a chosen curve, and they depend on a differential operator.

The aim is partial regularity: proof that a minimizer is smooth on most of its domain, apart from a small bad set. Stephan covers two growth cases and a borderline case with log growth. His proofs lean on known results for the plain gradient case, in the style of Conti and Gmeineder, and reduce his setting to that one.
arxiv-2412-09678:
Deepanshu Bisht, Sabyasachi Chakraborty, and Atanu Samanta study, in twenty twenty-four, axion-like particles through decays of B mesons. B mesons are particles that contain a bottom quark. Their rare decays that change flavor without changing charge can reveal axion-like particles, hypothetical light particles tied to dark matter theories. The authors build a generic framework that covers several ultraviolet models, named KSVZ, DFSZ, and flavorful axions. Starting from a high-energy description, they compute how the theory's parameters run with energy, including one-loop and key two-loop effects.

They show how spurious divergences cancel, some via new counterterms and some via matching to a low-energy theory. They then compute decay rates into hadrons, photons, and muon pairs. Bounds rule out low axion scale values, most strongly for some models.
arxiv-2412-10178:
Hung Nguyen and co-authors wrote this computer vision paper, published in two thousand twenty-four, on putting a new garment on a person in video. Image try-on tools are strong, but video adds a hard demand: the clothes must sit the same way in every frame.

Their system, SwiftTry, recasts the job as filling in a masked video, with the garment as the guide. Temporal attention layers, added to an image diffusion model, keep frames in step. A trick called ShiftCaching reuses work across frames instead of redoing it, which cuts the cost of long clips. The team also built TikTokDress, a tougher test set with busy backgrounds, hard moves, and higher resolution. Against current baselines, SwiftTry won on consistency and speed. The authors aim at try-on tools that keep up with real shopping video.
arxiv-2412-10678:
Gupta, Bannister, Flynn, and James introduced this computing method in twenty twenty-four for hunting fast radio bursts. These bursts are brief flashes from deep space. Finding them means correcting for how their signal smears across frequencies, a costly step called dedispersion. Searches may test thousands of smearing amounts over huge data streams.

Their method, ESAM, sums many arbitrary two-dimensional masks in an efficient way. That trick carries out the dedispersion step directly. It matched the accuracy of the brute-force approach while cutting computing cost about tenfold. Unlike older fast methods, it lets users pick any mask shape and trade cost against accuracy. The authors also sketch uses beyond burst hunting.
arxiv-2412-11978:
Building speech data sets by crowdsourcing is cheap and fast, but non-expert workers make errors that must be caught. Beomseok Lee and co-authors ask whether speech foundation models can take over much of that checking. Their study is the first to weigh the cost and quality trade-off directly.

They test model-based checking on speech data in French, German, and Korean. The model screen kept final data quality at the same level while cutting the need for human checking. The estimated saving was over 40 percent of validation cost. Rules for which samples still need a human look keep the risk low. The authors argue this mix of machine screening and spot human review can make speech data collection cheaper and easier to scale for new languages and tasks.
arxiv-2412-12378:
Software engineering draws too few students from underrepresented groups, and those who come face thin representation and bias. Ronnie de Souza Santos and co-authors survey undergraduates in this 2024 study to learn what pulls such students into the field and keeps them there.

Career growth, love of technology, and personal development topped eight motivations found. Family, teachers, friends, and online tech voices were key influences, though most students named no single person. Role models mattered most for staying power among underrepresented students. The authors urge programs to build visible mentorship and to treat diversity as several overlapping identities at once.
arxiv-2412-13078:
Jeena and Projjwal Banerjee trace the birth gas of rare old stars that are poor in alpha elements in two thousand twenty-four. Most very old, metal-poor stars carry high shares of elements like magnesium. The rare low ones were long thought to need gas from a white dwarf blast, called a Type Ia supernova.

The pair study seventeen such stars under six birth stories, mixing blast types in distinct pairs. A lone giant pair-instability blast was ruled out for all stars. Plain core-collapse blast gas alone could explain most of the stars, with no Type Ia gas needed. A mix with one Type Ia subtype also fit most stars, so both routes stay open for the group as a whole.
arxiv-2412-13378:
Onkar Thorat, Philippe Laban, and Chien-Sheng Wu build a benchmark that tests whether AI summaries stay faithful to their sources in this 2024 paper. Summary errors that invent facts are a known hazard. Existing tests are neither hard nor clear enough. Their pipeline uses executable edits to plant known errors. Models must both catch the error and explain it. Joint scoring rewards getting both parts right.

The best model tested scored under half on that joint measure. Over twenty models were put through the benchmark. More than half struggled with a large share of cases. Error types were sorted into four families for diagnosis. The work gives labs a sharper faithfulness test. News and document tools are the end users in view.
arxiv-2412-14378:
Marjorie Decleir and five co-authors report first results from a dust survey in a 2024 astronomy paper. The MEAD project measures how space dust dims and reddens starlight. The team used a new space telescope to read infrared light. Nine sightlines through thin Milky Way clouds were studied.

One dust feature, near ten micrometers, tracked the amounts of key atoms in the grains. Magnesium, iron, and oxygen rose and fell with the feature's strength. That match supports the view that silicate grains cause the feature. The team derived a rough recipe for the grain mix. Fainter features hint at carbon rich grains even in thin clouds. One sightline showed a sign of water ice as well. Later papers will widen the survey.
arxiv-2412-15278:
Xingyu Zhu, Xiapu Luo, and Xuetao Wei present DreaMark, a way to hide a secret watermark inside AI-generated 3D scenes while they are being made, in a 2024 paper. Text-to-3D tools can now build neural radiance fields, a popular 3D format, with no real-world capture. Older watermarking adds the mark afterward by fine-tuning, which leaves a gap where a clean, unmarked copy exists and could be stolen.

DreaMark instead plants a backdoor during generation itself. A decoder is trained in advance to read the secret from a chosen trigger view of the scene. In tests, the marking did not lower the quality of the generated scenes. The watermark survived over ninety percent of checks after attacks such as added noise and model pruning. The authors offer the scheme as built-in copyright proof for generated 3D assets.
arxiv-2412-15778:
Francisco Chicano, Gabriel Luque, Zakaria Dahi, and Rodrigo Gil-Merino wrote a practical guide to solving hard choice problems with quantum computers. Their tutorial came out in 2024. Quantum machines can work on many candidate answers at once, which may speed up the search for a best answer.

The guide covers two kinds of hardware. Quantum annealers are built specially for optimization, meaning the search for the best option under set rules. Gate-based machines are the more general kind of quantum computer. The authors show, from a practical angle, how to frame everyday problems for each kind and how to run them. The focus stays on use, not on deep theory.
arxiv-2412-15978:
Patrick Haller, Jonas Golde, and Alan Akbik test whether older-style networks can rival transformers for language models. Their 2024 paper builds BabyHGRN on a recent recurrent design, HGRN2. Recurrent networks read text step by step rather than all at once. The test ground is low-resource training, where data and compute are scarce.

BabyHGRN beat transformer models on both the ten-million and hundred-million word tracks of a public challenge. Scores came from tests of grammar, world knowledge, and language understanding. Extra training by imitation of a bigger model helped further. The results push back on the field's near-total focus on transformers. They suggest recurrent models deserve a fresh look when resources are tight.
arxiv-2412-16178:
Michael Wornow and seven co-authors test long context models on health records in a 2024 paper. A full patient record can run past ten thousand events. Most record models read under a thousand tokens at once. New architectures like Mamba promise far longer reading spans.

Their benchmark asks whether longer context truly helps prediction. The Mamba based model beat the prior best on nine of fourteen tasks. Three quirks of record data got special stress tests. Copied forward diagnoses create fake repetition inside records. Irregular gaps stretch a window across wildly different time spans. Later record parts grow harder as diseases accumulate. The study maps where long context pays off and where it strains. Clinical use needs that robustness, not raw scores alone.
arxiv-2412-16878:
Songjun Tu and colleagues removed the need for a secret answer key in preference-based learning in a 2024 paper. Agents can learn from comparisons, where a teacher says which of two tries was better, avoiding hand-built reward scores. Online tasks, though, rarely have a human ready to judge, so most studies fake the teacher with hidden true rewards.

Their method lets a large language model judge tries and also imagine better tries to learn from. They name a failure mode, query ambiguity, where the judge cannot tell what is being compared, and they add a double check to tame random labels. Tests on several simulated tasks showed steadier learning. Honest online feedback without hidden rewards widens where the method applies.
arxiv-2412-17278:
Kersten and four co-authors study ripples in space from a sharp shift in the early universe, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. Their model uses a dark field as the driver of fast early growth. That same field can later shift in a sudden, bubbly way. Such a shift sends out waves that stretch across space.

The team shows how growth sets the stage for the shift on its own. Heat and quantum effects shape when and how the shift occurs. The waves from the shift could be seen by future space probes. They name four planned probes that might catch the signal. The work links early growth and later shifts in one frame to test new physics.
arxiv-2412-17978:
Abdolvahhab Rostamijavanani, Shanwu Li, and Yongchao Yang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-four. It builds a data-driven stand-in for fluid flows whose shape shifts with a control knob, such as the Reynolds number.

Their model, called Dyn-cGAN, is a conditional generative network with a block that learns the time flow built in. That lets it learn both how the flow moves and how the motion leans on the knob at once. The team tests it on flow past a cylinder and flow in a two-dimensional cavity, at varied Reynolds numbers. They also probe how the count of time steps used in training shifts the error, and find a best range in the middle.
arxiv-2412-18878:
Hongqi Liu and six co-authors tune a plastic film's near-zero permittivity point with light. Their 2024 paper works on PEDOT:PSS, a conductive polymer. Materials near zero permittivity promise strong nonlinear light effects. Metals and doped semiconductors serve today, but their sweet spot barely moves.

Shining light on the film spawns polarons, shifting its hole count. That shift dragged the special wavelength by up to one hundred fifty nanometers. The change runs backward when the light stops. Polaron buildup took about eighty femtoseconds, and decay about two hundred eighty. Switching inside a picosecond is within reach. Flexible photonics gains a fast, reversible tuning knob.
arxiv-2412-19678:
Paolo Acquistapace and Francesco Bartaloni close a gap on when Riccati equations have just one answer. These equations guide a class of heat-type control tasks. The case at hand is a linear-quadratic task whose cost at the end is left quite free. It shifts with time. Two past papers, from 1999 and 2000, showed that a classic answer does exist.

They prove the best such claim for the summed form of the equation: just one answer, in a wide and apt class. The gap had stood even in the plain case where things do not shift with time. That case is now closed too. A note on how smooth the best state is comes with the main claim. For control staff, the gain is trust. The Riccati tools they solve by machine have just one right answer under the usual terms.
arxiv-2412-19778:
Viktor Mirjanić and Challenger Mishra approximate Ricci-flat metrics via extrinsic symmetries in two thousand twenty-four. Yau proved such metrics exist on Calabi-Yau manifolds without building them. Machine learning now fits them well but in a black box way. The pair mine those fits on Fermat manifolds for new structure.

Some flat metrics hold more symmetry than the manifold itself. That extra symmetry forces a compact form for the metric. On set loci the symmetry pins the metric in full. Their analytic forms feed back into neural fits to cut curvature. Closed form Kähler metrics with near zero curvature result.
arxiv-2501-00478:
Matheus Pereira and Alexandre Schmidt wrote this 2024 physics paper on a particle moving near a black string. A black string is a stretched cousin of a black hole, and the team study a simple particle that does not disturb the space around it. They solve the wave equation for the particle exactly, using a special function.

Their solution lets them probe odd cases, including negative values for the mass of the particle. The allowed energies come out complex, a sign of the short-lived ringing states known as quasinormal modes. The team also build a simple quantum system, an oscillator, that mimics the behavior of the particle. That twin system makes the exotic setup easier to study in the lab.
arxiv-2501-00978:
Maurice Coquet presents a 2025 proceedings paper, on behalf of a large collider collaboration, on telling apart two kinds of a heavy particle in nuclear collisions. The particle, a bound charm pair state, comes in prompt form, made at the crash site, and a delayed form, born later from beauty particles. The split reveals how each fares in the hot medium the collisions create.

The team measured both forms in lead on lead collisions at a set energy, at central angles. The delayed form also opens a window on how beauty quarks lose energy in the medium. A new forward tracker extends the same split to forward angles in the latest run.
arxiv-2501-01378:
Domokos Szász reviews random walks and Lorentz processes in a 2025 paper. Both serve as basic models of Brownian motion, the jittery movement seen in particles. Random walks belong to probability theory, while Lorentz processes, where a particle bounces among fixed obstacles, belong to the theory of chaotic dynamical systems, and the two fields rarely meet.

Szász recounts how probability methods cracked questions about the Lorentz process, starting from a 1981 question by Sinai on limit laws for locally disturbed versions. In the plane, small local changes to a random walk leave its limit laws untouched, whether jumps are bounded or not. Related results cover the Lorentz gas with finite horizon, and they yield a fresh proof of its recurrence. An infinite-horizon case stays open.
arxiv-2501-01578:
Nikki Arendse and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on two exploding stars whose light was bent by a galaxy in front of them. Only two such lensed type Ia supernovae behind a lone galaxy are known. Their split images shine with brightness ratios that a smooth lens model cannot explain. Tiny lumps in the lens galaxy, even single stars, may be bending the light further.

By matching the images to simulated maps of that fine bending, the team measure how steeply the lens galaxy's mass is packed and how much of it could be dark compact objects. They found no sign of such a dark population, with an upper limit of about a quarter of the mass. The result uses the stars' known brightness as a rare clean yardstick.
arxiv-2501-02278:
Chen, Böhlen, and Helmer present a study from twenty twenty-five comparing tree data structures for connectivity queries on changing graphs. Graphs with frequent edge insertions and deletions need fast connectivity answers. Many structures have been proposed over decades for that task. Few were ever implemented, let alone tested head-to-head. The team build reference implementations for the main proposals. They benchmark them across a wide range of graph types. No current solution is ready for direct deployment, they find.

Each structure shows critical practical weaknesses in their tests. Balanced structures carry heavy space and time overhead. Lean structures degrade badly in worst cases. Maintenance costs burden the balanced options further. The authors close with guidance for building robust versions.
arxiv-2501-02478:
Chenxi Bai and Zhaoxin Liang report an anomaly in a core rule of topological physics in a 2025 paper. Bulk-edge correspondence says the deep properties of a material's interior dictate the states on its edge. The rule is a design foundation for topological devices.

Their testbed is a nonlinear Rice-Mele model, a chain with alternating bonds and site energies. Recent work handled nonlinearity in eigenvalues by adding auxiliary values to restore the correspondence. The authors find a case where the correspondence still breaks in an anomalous way. Pinpointing where the rule fails protects device designs that bank on it, and it refines the theory for nonlinear systems, a growing frontier.
arxiv-2501-02678:
Liedokto wrote this 2025 mathematics paper introducing a new algebraic structure called the (m,n)-seminearring. Algebra builds number-like systems from sets with operations that follow set rules. The new structure widens an older notion, the (m,n)-semiring, by loosening some of its demands.

The paper develops the basic theory of the structure step by step. It defines substructures and ideals, and treats the case where the system has a unity element. Maps between two such systems that respect their operations are studied as homomorphisms. A factor construction built from a congruence relation is also given, along with several properties of these objects. The method is to adapt the established theory of (m,n)-semirings to the wider setting. The work is foundational rather than applied.
arxiv-2501-03178:
Miljenko Čemeljić and co-authors simulate gas falling onto a naked singularity in a 2025 astrophysics paper. A Reissner-Nordström singularity is a charged point mass with no horizon hiding it. Using a pseudo-Newtonian potential tuned to match its true orbital frequencies, they ran the first thin-disk simulations around one. Orbital speed around such an object vanishes at a zero-gravity radius and peaks just beyond it.

Viscosity can only push gas inward outside that peak, so inflow stalls and piles into a glowing torus near the zero-gravity sphere. The ring matches shapes predicted by exact relativity calculations. A bright ring with no hole behind it could one day be a telescope signature of these exotic objects.
arxiv-2501-06978:
Davide Martinenghi writes in a 2025 paper about making a classic database rule easier to see and check. Two-phase locking is the standard policy databases use to keep concurrent transactions from corrupting each other's work. The policy itself is well understood, in both its plain and strict forms.

What is not easy is turning a given schedule of operations into a clear table or picture that shows whether the locking rule holds. The paper walks through the technical hurdles in building such a tool and how they were handled. The goal is an analysis that a person can read at a glance, rather than a verdict delivered by opaque machinery.
arxiv-2501-07178:
Simon Martin, Hans-Theo Normann, Paul Püplichhuisen, and Tobias Werner wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It studies how pricing algorithms split the gains when they collude in a two-firm market, and how the split shifts when the firms are unequal.

The team ran repeated Cournot duopoly games with self-run algorithms. Both buyers and firms can gain from some asymmetry: matched firms saw sharper rivalry, while lopsided pairs saw softer play. The plain Nash benchmark missed on counts and gains but hit total welfare well. The best fit was the equal relative gains rule, with algorithm deals landing on or near the best joint front. The old view that matched firms collude most may not hold.
arxiv-2501-07478:
Lewis Stuart and Michael Pound present a converter, in a 2025 preprint, that turns Gaussian splatting scenes into ordinary point clouds and meshes. Splatting builds rich 3D scenes from fuzzy blobs, but needs special viewers. Point clouds work in nearly all 3D software. Their tool samples points from each blob as if it were a small cloud of density. A distance rule trims wild outliers. Color is the tricky part, since a blob's color shifts with viewing angle.

To fix colors, the tool renders the scene and credits each blob with the pixel it influenced most. Every sampled point then takes its blob's settled color. A mesh option runs surface reconstruction over points drawn from surface blobs. No retraining is needed. The package is built to slot into existing splatting pipelines. Artists and engineers can carry splat scenes into standard tools.
arxiv-2501-08278:
Nicholas Kamp, Carlos Argüelles, Albrecht Karle, Jennifer Thomas, and Tianlu Yuan propose two neutrino detectors near the Large Hadron Collider, in a 2025 paper. Neutrinos made in collider crashes fly forward in huge numbers and are rarely studied. One design places panels on the surface above a collision point. The other sinks a water detector into Lake Geneva to watch a second collision point.

Simulations predict millions of neutrino events during the collider's high-output era. The surface detector would catch muon neutrinos, while the lake detector sees all flavors. The data could pin down how often neutrinos interact and how charm particles are made in crashes. The authors pitch both as cheap partners to a planned forward physics facility.
arxiv-2501-09478:
Yuchen Meng and five co-authors find a new fingerprint of quantum scars in twenty twenty-five. Some interacting quantum systems avoid thermalizing, against expectations. Quantum many-body scars are eigenstates that evade heat death and sustain long oscillations. Symmetry and algebra views explain some scars, but no universal diagnostic existed.

The authors propose Fisher zeros as that diagnostic. These are zeros of the partition function extended into the complex temperature plane. In scarred systems, they conjecture, a continuous line of zeros appears off the usual axis. That line splits the plane into regions with distinct thermalization behavior. Readers get a complex-plane signature to hunt scars with, in systems where other tests stay silent.
arxiv-2501-09578:
Federica Galluzzi and Bert van Geemen classify special shrinking maps on a class of four-dimensional shapes, in a paper from 2025. The shapes are Hyper-Kähler, a rich kind of geometric space tied to K3 surfaces. A shrinking map on such a shape has an exceptional part shaped like a bundle of conics over a K3 surface.

A lattice count shows five types of such bundles can occur. When a shape has the smallest rich rank and two distinct shrinking maps, the authors pin down which bundle types pair up. Just seven pairings occur. For a famed family from cubic shapes, only four pairings occur, and the authors give examples of each. The work adds to the map of these shapes'forms.
arxiv-2501-09778:
Patrick Llerena and co-authors wrote this 2025 paper on a hidden bargain inside firms: idle time wastes output, yet it also breeds ideas. Their agent-based model breaks a factory into funds and flows, letting inefficiency appear on its own from frictions rather than being assumed. Workers learn, forget, and, when idle, create.

In the model, a firm that keeps idle workers and routes them into innovation does better than one that treats labor as a simple dial. Results hinge on how the firm is organized, how fast skills grow and decay, and how quickly new methods arrive. Idleness cuts both ways, eroding skill while feeding the creativity that powers process gains. The authors close by questioning layoffs as a default fix and sketching paths for further work.
arxiv-2501-10478:
András Grabarits, Federico Balducci, and Adolfo del Campo solve how defects form when a quantum magnet is driven through its phase change at any speed, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The model is the transverse-field Ising chain, a basic quantum system. Defects here are kinks, and their count follows rules tied to the drive speed.

Standard transforms split the problem into modes, each solved with special functions. At slow drives, a famous scaling law and fresh universal rules for higher counts hold. At fast drives, the counts turn non-universal and non-monotonic. The counts stay narrower than random noise at every speed, the team shows.
arxiv-2501-10778:
Charly Robinson La Rocca, Jean-François Cordeau, and Emma Frejinger teach a search heuristic which variables to change. Their twenty twenty-five paper improves large neighbourhood search for mixed-integer programs. Such programs model scheduling, routing, and planning decisions. The destroy step choice strongly shapes solution quality.

A machine learning model guides the destroy operator after light offline training. The team built a modular test bench for fair comparisons. Tests on a standard problem library beat strong commercial solvers in places. Noisy prediction checks showed how accuracy affects final quality. Tweaks to loss functions and sampling improved the learner further. Random search stayed competitive, but supervised learning led overall.
arxiv-2501-11078:
Stishov and co-authors published a 2025 note on a puzzling change of state in a magnetic material called MnSi. Below a certain temperature, the material's tiny magnets line up in a slow spiral. Warm it, and the spiral melts into a disordered state. Decades of study show this melting is unlike most such changes.

Just above the melting point, many of the material's properties swing to extremes: heat, expansion, and flow measures all peak or dip. Such behavior looks more like what happens in flat, two-dimensional systems than in a solid crystal. The authors describe the change as happening in two steps. First comes a sharp jump of the usual kind. Then the leftover swirls of magnetism, vortex-like knots in the spiral pattern, break down. The note gathers this odd evidence and offers that two-step picture as a tentative account.
arxiv-2501-12378:
Alexander Schmidhuber and co-authors open, in 2025, the study of quantum algorithms for a powerful knot invariant. Khovanov homology sorts knots far more finely than older polynomial invariants, but its computing cost was largely unknown. The team first shows that even rough estimates of its ranks are hard for classical and some quantum models.

For two useful accuracy levels, they give a quantum algorithm that is fast when a related operator settles quickly and keeps a wide spectral gap. A pre-cooling trick lets it work even when the answer is tiny compared with the search space. Links to graph theory supply evidence for the needed gap.
arxiv-2501-13878:
Ethan Wilson and colleagues proposed in 2025 that an AI assistant should watch where you look, not just listen to what you say. Multimodal agents increasingly collaborate with users on tasks in the physical and digital world. Today they depend on explicit communication: typed or spoken instructions. The authors hypothesize that gaze, an implicit signal, can convey a user's interests and intent continuously, without demanding attention to formulate commands.

Presented at an eye-tracking research symposium in Tokyo, the work explores how systems can consume gaze as an attention channel. When an assistant knows which object a user is considering, it can offer help earlier and ask fewer clarifying questions. The risks are real too, since gaze reveals more than users may intend. Framing gaze as a first-class input gives designers a shared problem to solve: reading attention helpfully without reading minds intrusively.
arxiv-2501-14378:
Carmine Autieri and co-authors hunt for an unusual magnetic order hiding in a famous superconductor in this 2025 paper. The material is strontium ruthenate, long studied for its odd superconductivity. Its crystal cages tilt easily, and that tilt may switch on altermagnetism, a new kind of order that splits electron energies without net magnetization.

Computer calculations on a single layer with tilted cages found exactly that phase, selective to certain electron orbitals. A stripped-down model showed the order grows from longer-range links between a few orbitals, while one orbital needs much longer links to join in. The same model, with one orbital swapped, mirrors the copper oxide superconductors. In the bulk crystal the phase survives as the ground state for a range of tilts, with a changed symmetry between layers. The authors discuss which pairing styles the order would favor for superconductivity.
arxiv-2501-14478:
Arend Moerman and co-authors describe how they aligned and verified a wide-band spectrometer on a telescope in the Atacama, in work from 2025. The instrument, DESHIMA 2.0, observes across a broad microwave band. Its warm optics sit on a motor-driven hexapod that can tilt and shift them into exact position.

The key tool is a sky chopper with small apertures that couple the beam to the cold sky. By scanning the beam across the aperture and minimising the warm-cabin signal on the detectors, the team finds the best alignment. They characterised the procedure in the lab with a liquid nitrogen cold source, then applied it at the telescope. Aperture efficiency improved clearly over earlier reported values, confirming the method works on site.
arxiv-2501-14578:
Harry Richardson, Josh Dunn, and Andrew McCluskey tackled a quiet numeric trap in 2025. The trap is finding the center of mass of a group of particles inside a box that repeats periodically, as model cells do. A particle near one face may belong with partners imaged through the opposite face, so a naive average lands in the wrong place. A popular fix projects places onto a circle and averages there.

The authors show that popular method averages the particles in a way that is not physically meaningful and makes inaccurate centers. The correct built-in weighted average exists but is costly and hard to compute analytically. They therefore propose a more lean route to that built-in mean. Built to suit the majority of chemical systems, so simulators can locate molecular centers correctly without paying the full careful cost.
arxiv-2501-14978:
Alireza Nikzamir and co-authors design a radiating array that locks into a steady hum at a special operating point, in a 2025 paper. The device is a waveguide studded at regular intervals with elements that amplify the signal and radiate it into the air. At a condition called an exceptional point of degeneracy, the system's behavior simplifies and stabilizes.

Once the signal grows strong enough to saturate the amplifiers, that special point fixes the oscillation frequency for the array. Every element settles to the same gain and radiates the same power, even if the starting gain was uneven. Unlike ordinary cavity designs, the frequency does not depend on how long the array is. A test board matched the simulations, saturating at the special point with a low-noise tone. The authors propose the scheme for high-power antenna arrays with amplifiers spread along their length.
arxiv-2501-15878:
Adil Kaan Akan and Yucel Yemez adapt image generators in a 2025 paper on object-based learning. Their method, SlotAdapt, joins slot attention, which splits a scene into object slots, with a pretrained diffusion model that builds images step by step. Extra adapter layers let the slots guide generation, steering clear of the model's usual bias toward text prompts.

A guidance loss lines up the adapter's focus maps with the slot maps, with no outside labels needed. Tests on several datasets, including real photos, beat leading methods at finding objects and at generating images. On complex real scenes the method composed new images from parts far better than rival slot-based systems. The work points to generators that understand scenes as objects, not just textures.
arxiv-2501-16378:
Qing Li and five co-authors present a safety fix for vision-language models that works by editing their inner activations mid-answer, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Adding images to a language model weakens its safety training: pictures shift the model's internal state, and even simple jailbreaks then succeed. Their method nudges those activations back toward safe territory while the model writes.

The steering acts at two scales, whole layers and single attention heads, using vectors drawn from safe and unsafe example pairs. Across four safety test sets, attack success fell by roughly a third to a half, while helpfulness barely moved. The authors stress that no model weights were retrained to gain the improvement.
arxiv-2501-16578:
Joel Tropp, a lone author, proves new results about the smallest eigenvalue of sums of random matrices. The paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five and sits in pure and applied mathematics. It deals with matrices whose entries are random but whose values stay at or above zero in a set sense. Such sums show up often in modern work with data in many dimensions.

Tropp shows that the smallest eigenvalue of the sum is ruled by that of a matched Gaussian random matrix. That link matters because Gaussian matrices come with a large stock of known tools. He then gives short, clear proofs of old and new results in high-dimensional statistics. The paper also settles an open question about very sparse random matrices.
arxiv-2501-16678:
Ao Sun, Zhihan Wang, and Jinxin Xue study what happens when a shrinking surface flows through a kink point, in a paper from 2025. Mean curvature flow moves a surface inward at a speed set by how curved it is. Such flows often form singularities, spots where the surface pinches or folds. The paper looks at the mild, cylinder-like kind of pinch.

They prove these pinch points stand alone in space and time. They then give a full account of how the surface's shape and topology change as it passes through. The change matches the jump seen when a landscape function crosses a saddle point. In plain terms, the flow performs a clean surgery on itself. A new distance formula drives the proof. It tracks a quantity like the frequency tools used in other fields.
arxiv-2501-17478:
Antonio Baeza and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, approximate Taylor methods for solving ordinary differential equations. Classic Taylor schemes reach very high accuracy orders but demand derivatives of the equation's functions, which is laborious. Runge-Kutta methods avoid derivatives yet make arbitrary high orders awkward to build.

The new approach mimics Taylor expansions using only the functions themselves, like Runge-Kutta, at the price of more function evaluations per order. In exchange, schemes of any order become easy to produce, and the total cost can undercut exact-derivative Taylor methods. Tests show results as good as the exact procedure with less effort.
arxiv-2501-17578:
Marco Pasini, Stefan Lattner, and George Fazekas present an audio autoencoder that squeezes music into a compact code, in work from 2025. Compact codes serve music generation and search tasks. Past autoencoders struggle to shrink audio a lot while keeping sound quality and staying useful for later tasks.

Their system encodes a clip as a set of summary embeddings, where each part of the set captures a global feature of the sound rather than a moment in time. That unordered design reaches better quality at the same squeeze ratio. A staged decoding model rebuilds clips of any length, working on chunks in sequence. A two-step decoding trick then polishes the output at no extra training cost. Tests beat rival continuous autoencoders on quality and downstream tasks.
arxiv-2501-17978:
Mateusz Nowak, Wojciech Jarosz, and Peter Chin improve a fast method for building three-dimensional scenes from photos, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. The base method fills a scene with soft blobs, but it mixes up objects with the shiny light on their surfaces. Highlights and reflections then look wrong from new angles.

Their fix lets each blob's opacity depend on the viewing angle. Blobs that carry glare can fade when seen from the wrong side. Tests on four standard sets gave top scores, with speed kept above sixty frames per second. Memory use rose only a little, the authors report.
arxiv-2501-19078:
Dominik Benkovič and Mateja Grašič widen the notion of a Jordan derivation on algebras that have an identity element, in this 2025 paper. The new concept covers both Jordan derivations and Jordan centralizers at once. Their setting excludes only fields of characteristic two.

A map counts as a generalized Jordan derivation when two partner maps make a set identity hold for all pairs. The authors show any such map splits into parts named quasi Jordan centralizers and quasi Jordan derivations. They also give a clean characterization of the maps. The work unifies two literatures that grew side by side.
arxiv-2502-00278:
Tyler Parsotan and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on BatAnalysis, an open Python pipeline for data from the Swift satellite's Burst Alert Telescope. The telescope watches for gamma-ray flashes and saves its finest event data on triggers, but standard products use fixed time and energy windows. The new tools let researchers download and process that raw event stream freely.

Users can build spectra, light curves, and sky images on their own settings, and mix the tools with other Python packages. Case studies cover a gamma-ray burst, a fast radio burst trigger, a faint X-ray binary catch, and a burst seen while the satellite slewed. The authors aim at the time-domain community.
arxiv-2502-00478:
A family of symmetric polynomials extends the classic Macdonald family with spin and inhomogeneity. Matteo Mucciconi proves these spin q-Whittaker polynomials are orthogonal. The inner product uses a variant of the Sklyanin measure on the multi-dimensional torus. That trait makes the family a basis for such forms in any number of variables. The proof leans on eigenrelations that partly generalize the Macdonald ones.

Special cases get their own treatment. They include variants of symmetric Grothendieck forms and spin Whittaker functions. The result places the newer family on the same firm footing as its famous relatives. Mucciconi works with the case where the Macdonald parameter t equals zero.
arxiv-2502-01678:
Yihe Wang and co-authors build, in a 2025 paper, a foundation model that reads brain wave recordings to detect Alzheimer's disease. Brain wave tests are cheap, safe, and widely available, yet past methods lacked big data and failed across new patients. The team gathered the largest such data set yet, with more than two thousand subjects.

Their model uses a gated design that handles recordings of varied length, channel layout, and sample rate. Pre-training spanned thirteen data sets of brain disorders, with a contrast method that teaches by comparison. Fine-tuning and tests ran on five other Alzheimer's data sets. The model topped all twenty checks against rivals, including other foundation models for brain waves.
arxiv-2502-01778:
Four researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on a smarter decision transformer for shifting environments. Reinforcement learning struggles when state and action spaces change, rewards are rare, and problems grow large. Decision transformers learn from past trajectories instead of live trial and error.

Their model, GNN-DT, adds graph neural network encoders and a new shortcut link between input and output tokens. On the test problem of scheduling electric vehicle charging, it beat existing transformer and offline methods while needing far fewer training trajectories. It also held up in unseen settings and with larger action spaces.
arxiv-2502-03678:
Zeyu Tang, Zhenhao Chen, Xiangchen Song, Loka Li, Yunlong Deng, Yifan Shen, Guangyi Chen, Peter Spirtes, and Kun Zhang wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. Its title page calls it a supplement, and its text presents Reflection-Window Decoding, a way to let text models fix their own words as they write.

Plain left-to-right writing cannot revise, so early slips drag the rest down. The authors gauge how far such text can stray from the best full-length text, and tie the risk to spikes of doubt in the run. Their method slides a reflection window over fresh text and pauses by a set rule, so fixes and new words take turns. Broad tests show the balance of speed and quality pays off.
arxiv-2502-04178:
Cotfas studies how the coherence of a quantum state depends on the measurement frame used to look at it. Coherence measures how wavy, rather than particle-like, a quantum state behaves. Standard measures tie the answer to one fixed basis of states.

Cotfas works with tight frames, a broader kind of measurement made of rank-one operators. He defines frame-based coherence directly, without the detour through a larger space that older definitions need. Using several bases at once gives a finer picture of the state's coherence. He also gives a frame-free version for single and multiple qubits. The work aims at sharper tools for quantum information tasks.
arxiv-2502-04878:
Patrick Leask and his seven co-authors, publishing in 2025, challenge a hopeful belief about a popular tool for interpreting AI models. Sparse autoencoders tease a network's inner activity into separate features that humans can name. Many hoped they would reveal the one true list of atomic concepts a model uses. The team tests that hope with two new techniques, and both tests fail it.

First, they stitch features from a large autoencoder into a smaller one. Some transplanted features add genuinely new information, which means the smaller tool was incomplete. Second, they train an autoencoder on the first one's own wiring. Its features split into combos of simpler ones, Einstein dissolving into scientist, Germany, and famous person, so they were never atomic. The authors still call the tools useful. They advise picking a size to fit the task instead of chasing a canonical list.
arxiv-2502-05678:
Stacey Staples, a solo author, studies a graph matrix built in an unusual algebra in a 2025 paper. For any finite simple graph, this zeon Laplacian is a square matrix whose entries live in that algebra. She asks what its special values reveal about the graph. The algebra has a nilpotent part, which normally vanishes under repeated multiplication.

She shows that when a graph has a single vertex of a given degree, the matrix has a matching special value. The nilpotent part of that value counts the cycles that start at that vertex. A generalized version counts all cycles in the graph. Viewed as an operator, the matrix acts like a random variable whose values expose cycle structure.
arxiv-2502-05978:
Sarthak Choudhary presents, in a 2025 paper for the DarkSide-20k collaboration, quality checks on plastic sheets that shift light for a dark matter detector's neutron veto. The detector hunts dark matter in liquid argon, which glows in deep ultraviolet. Big detectors need a shifter that can cover huge areas, and common coatings are costly to lay down.

The veto will use nearly two hundred square meters of a polymer foil as its shifter. Samples from the production batch are tested at very low temperatures in a new argon gas setup. Argon glow excites the foils, letting the team measure how well each sheet shifts the light. First results from that cold testing are reported here.
arxiv-2502-06778:
Victoria Bollo and nine co-authors published a study in 2025 on how the universe's supply of cold gas has changed over cosmic time. Cold molecular gas is the raw fuel of star birth, and carbon monoxide glow is its main tracer. Earlier surveys were small and hostage to luck in where they pointed, so the team mined calibration data from a major telescope array for an unbiased sample.

They charted the brightness spread of carbon monoxide sources and the total gas density out to when the universe was young. Gas density rose to a peak when the cosmos was a few billion years old, then fell slowly. The pattern fits a picture of galaxies steadily refilled with gas. Splitting surveys across many small fields, they stress, beats staring at one patch.
arxiv-2502-07078:
Hyett and colleagues built a machine learning model in twenty twenty-five for the smallest swirls of turbulent flow, a key target in fluid physics. Simulating turbulence at real-world intensity is still beyond any computer, so modelers must capture the statistics of the tiny scales instead of the full motion.

Their model follows the velocity gradient, the quantity that tracks how flow stretches and spins at a point. It uses an attention design, which lets the model weigh the most telling moments in a fluid parcel's past. The approach beat current physics-informed methods on both early checks and full run-throughs. Reading the trained model's attention turned up a surprise: the history of the stretching pattern links closely to the pressure forces that shape the flow. The authors say the tool both predicts better and teaches something new about turbulence.
arxiv-2502-07778:
Anirudh Sundara Rajan and Yong Jae Lee argue that fake-image detectors should ignore what real images look like and hunt only for generator artifacts. Detectors often latch onto spurious cues such as compression patterns tied to real photos. Those shortcuts fail when images are processed or come from new sources.

Their algorithm, Stay Positive, constrains training so the detector's evidence comes from traces left by generative models. Detectors trained this way resisted spurious correlations better and generalized more robustly through post-processing. They also caught inpainted real images more reliably, a case where real-image cues mislead. The paper reframes detection as a search for positive evidence of generation only.
arxiv-2502-07878:
Innes Bigaran and Richard Ruiz refine, in a 2025 paper, how weak bosons are counted inside fast-moving particles. At high energy, a W or Z boson can act as if it were a component, or parton, of the particle that emits it. A known shortcut, the Effective W Approximation, encodes that view, but its finer corrections carry flaws that were long conjectured and not proven.

The pair derive those finer terms for weak bosons from massless fermions, in two gauge choices. They set new kinematical consistency conditions that keep the bad traits in check. When the conditions hold, the approximation matches full calculations well for complex processes. That match suggests a clean factorization of the process holds at tree level. The authors say the approximation can be tested at the Large Hadron Collider with same-sign WW scattering data.
arxiv-2502-07978: Moeini and six colleagues survey in-context reinforcement learning in twenty twenty-five. Reinforcement learning agents usually update their network weights to improve. That process needs costly backward passes through the network. Some agents instead solve new tasks with no weight updates at all. They condition on context, such as their past actions and observations. The survey collects and organizes work on this behaviour. It covers how agents learn from context within a single run of experience. The authors frame the area as a strand of reinforcement learning research.
arxiv-2502-08478: Abraham Loeb shows that a dedicated space telescope could find many small interstellar objects. Such objects drift between stars and pass through our solar system unseen. A meter-wide scope could spot ten-meter objects that pass near the Sun. Splitting their heat glow from reflected sunlight would give their surface heat, area, and shine. Vapor from them, at an expected heat near six hundred kelvin, could be read for clues to their makeup and birth places.
arxiv-2502-09378:
Hadar Sharvit, Raz Karl, and Tsevi Beatus taught a neural network to plan a robotic wing's flapping in a 2025 paper. Controlling a flapping wing is an inverse problem: choose the wing motion that produces a desired aerodynamic force. For propellers the input-output map is simple, but flapping flight involves intricate fluid motion, making real-time inversion computationally impractical by classical means. The authors instead learn the inverse map directly from experiment.

Their rig flaps a wing while measuring its aerodynamic force and filming its three-dimensional motion with high-speed cameras, generating the training data. A sequence-to-sequence model, fitted with a novel adaptive-spectrum layer that learns in the frequency domain, then predicts the kinematics needed for a target force. Data-driven inversion could give flapping robots the responsive control fixed-wing craft take for granted.
arxiv-2502-10178:
Marco Bondaschi and seven co-authors study how the Mamba model learns from examples placed in its input. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Mamba is a fast rival to the transformer models behind most chat tools. The team tested it on Markov chains, simple step-by-step random processes. Even a single-layer Mamba learned a classic smoothing rule for guessing the next step.

The team shows that this smoothing rule is the best possible guess in two formal senses. They explain the result through the way Mamba mixes nearby steps, a step called convolution. Tests matched the theory. The authors say this is the first formal link between Mamba and a best-known statistical method. They close by pointing to new research paths the result opens.
arxiv-2502-10578:
Stark and Steinberger compare in twenty twenty-five two ways of keeping high-dimensional fitting honest: penalising complexity outright, or stopping training early. They study gradient descent on a squared-error task with a penalty term, in settings where data points and features are both plentiful. Their analysis tracks how test error evolves as steps accumulate.

With the penalty tuned well, test error glides down toward the best benchmark as steps grow. Plain training stopped early hits that benchmark only in rare special cases. So explicit penalty proves nearly efficient, while early stopping is not. They add a data-driven way to pick the penalty strength that costs less than cross-checking. New covariance results support the theory.
arxiv-2502-11178:
Enes Doruk and Hasan Ates present a detector that keeps working when the world it watches changes, in this 2025 paper. Object detectors trained in one setting often stumble in another, a gap called domain shift. Transformer detectors handle wide context well but cost too much computing, while older networks miss long-range links.

Their model, DA-Mamba, mixes the Mamba sequence architecture, which scales gently, with attention modules that align features across domains. Scanning runs along both space and channels in a domain-aware way. A distillation step driven by uncertainty cleans the noisy features that mixing can create, and a gating step with random nudges guards against overfitting. The design aims at one-stage detection that adapts as it runs. The authors present it as the first Mamba-based detector built for this adaptation task.
arxiv-2502-11878:
Daniele Girolimetto and Tommaso Di Fonzo forecast Italian electricity output in twenty twenty-five. The data is daily and split by region and by energy source. Forecasts made piece by piece often clash with each other. The parts must add up to the national total, and independent forecasts rarely respect that.

Their approach combines forecasts from multiple experts while enforcing coherence. The combination is balanced and multi-task, and it uses unbiased base forecasts. Applied to Italian generation data, the method beat single-task forecasts. It also beat combined forecasts and a leading single-expert reconciliation method. Readers who forecast hierarchical time series get a way to gain accuracy and consistency at once.
arxiv-2502-12878:
Jon Vehovar, Miha Rot, and Gregor Kosec study, in a 2025 paper, how accuracy choices affect simulation speed when a problem is split across many computers. Their method estimates derivatives at scattered points from neighbors' values, with no grid. Using more neighbors gives sharper answers but forces more data exchange between machines. On one computer, sharper always wins. Across a cluster, the exchange cost may change the answer.

The team solves a standard test equation on a uniform CPU cluster. Machines share work by region, using one tool for talk between machines and another within each. They scan settings to find which mix of sharpness and chatter reaches a target accuracy fastest. The paper maps the trade-off rather than declaring one winner, giving simulation engineers a way to tune meshless codes for distributed systems.
arxiv-2502-13678:
Thijs Kamma and Antoon Pelsser reformulated a classic savings problem in 2025. An agent chooses how much to consume over time, but satisfaction depends on consumption relative to an internal habit built from past consumption, and here the habit enters multiplicatively, as a ratio. That ratio form destroys the problem's concavity and makes the present depend unavoidably on the whole path, so the usual Lagrangian route to a dual problem fails.

Using a duality theorem of Fenchel, the authors identify a candidate dual formulation and prove strong duality, meaning the two problems share the same optimal value. From that they derive relations converting optimal choices in one problem into optimal choices in the other. The dual view also yields an analytical way to bound how accurate any approximate solution to the original problem really is.
arxiv-2502-13978:
Allen Lobo and Saravanan Arumugam treated random trials as dynamic systems in this paper from twenty twenty-five. They grow out of Bernoulli's law of large numbers, the classic rule on how rates settle with many trials. The pair ask how the felt randomness of a trial shifts as trials pile up. A coin toss and a dice roll serve as their worked cases.

By hand and by number runs, they show that the randomness of each outcome can rise by chance. That rise hangs on how fast the felt rates grow. Trial runs and sims check the math. Readers in probability get a flow view of how chance itself seems to move as a trial repeats.
arxiv-2502-14978: Konrad Deka and Bo Peng construct a family of symbolic systems with striking properties. Their short paper appeared in 2025. The systems are generalized Oxtoby subshifts, rules that generate endless symbol strings. Each allows a set of stable statistical patterns, called invariant measures, and those sets always form a shape known as a Choquet simplex. The authors show their family can realize every such shape. They also show that telling whether two systems in the family match is tame: the sameness relation is hyperfinite, the simplest kind of infinite complexity.
arxiv-2502-15578:
Jayeeta Chaudhuri and colleagues demonstrated a hardware attack called FLARE in 2025 against shared FPGA chips. Cloud FPGAs increasingly host several tenants at once, each uploading circuit designs, called bitstreams, that a manager loads into reconfigurable regions. FLARE strikes during that upload, not while the victim's circuit runs, which separates it from classic fault attacks and hides it from runtime defenses.

By briefly activating power-wasting circuits during reconfiguration, the attacker corrupts the configuration address inside the incoming bitstream, redirecting the upload into a neighboring tenant's region and overwriting their pre-loaded module. On a commercial development board the team compromised multiple user bitstreams this way. The attack shows that the reconfiguration pathway itself, meant to make multi-tenancy flexible, is a security boundary that current countermeasures largely ignore.
arxiv-2502-15678:
Luca Schulze Buschoff and five co-authors test if fine-tuning can make vision-language models see the world more like people do. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that even strong pre-trained models lag behind human visual thought. The team gathered images and human judgments across many kinds of visual tasks.

They then fine-tuned models on true answers for two domains: intuitive physics and causal reasoning. Scores rose in the tuned domain, and the models also matched human answers more closely there. But the gains did not carry to new looks or new domains. The verdict is that narrow tuning helps locally, yet broad human-like sight needs more.
arxiv-2502-15878:
Pietro Baratella and co-authors simplify a hard calculation needed to pin down how fast false vacuums decay in this 2025 paper. A false vacuum is a space state that looks stable but can collapse. Its decay rate sets how long such a state survives. Precision rates need a correction factor from field fluctuations. That factor, a functional determinant, is notoriously messy to tame. The team handles particles of three spin types at once.

Their route uses standard diagram tools and a double expansion. The end result is a simple recipe of single integrals. It works for any scalar landscape and any mix of fields. Ghost fields tied to gauge bosons are covered too. A worked example shows the method in action. The paper serves particle theory and early-universe studies.
arxiv-2502-16078:
Xuding Zhu surveys a famous graph puzzle and its fall in a 2025 paper. In 1966 Hedetniemi guessed a clean rule about coloring the combined graph of two networks. If neither network alone can be colored with a given number of colors, their product cannot be colored either. The guess drew fifty years of work.

Shitov disproved it in 2019 for large color counts, and later papers shrank the counterexamples until the guess was known to fail for every count from four upward. It still holds at three and below. Zhu's survey gathers the line of results, explains the ideas behind the counterexamples, and lists the related questions still open. The paper serves as a map of a closed problem and its open neighborhood.
arxiv-2502-16778:
Sanaz Hasanzadeh Fard and Emily Dolson tested how missing data distort summaries of species interaction networks in two thousand twenty-five. Such networks map who interacts with whom in nature, like pollinators and plants. Field work often misses some links, which could skew the graph measures ecologists rely on.

They studied one hundred forty-eight real networks across four interaction types, from pollination to seed dispersal. For each, they tracked six structural measures as extra links were added back. Some measures changed slowly and seemed robust, while others shifted fast. Community-finding methods also differed, with two far steadier than two rivals. Robustness varied by interaction type for some measures, which guides careful metric choice.
arxiv-2502-16878:
