Rezaie and Azizi study Z boson production in proton-lead collisions in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Such collisions, run at high energy, probe how quarks and gluons are spread inside heavy nuclei. The authors use a family of distribution functions that track partons' sideways motion. They test three versions of the approach: two orders of one model family and a parton branching scheme.

They set the predictions against data from the CMS experiment. Both model orders mostly match the data well. The lower order overshoots in some regions, while the higher order, with a stricter ordering rule, agrees better there. The paper shows how fine choices in parton modeling shape collider predictions. Nuclear physicists who model proton-nucleus runs are the readers.
arxiv-2502-16978:
Spin liquids are magnetic states that never settle, their moments rippling under strict local rules that mimic electric field laws. Naïmo Davier and co-authors design a family of such states in this 2025 paper where the telltale scattering signature stretches from a point into a line.

They build the states by stacking layers of two-dimensional algebraic spin liquids, and simulations confirm several worked examples. Along the line, the character of the emergent field can slide continuously, a feature tied to exotic fracton physics. The team also reads the line as the interference of two emergent electric fields and tests the idea on other lattices.
arxiv-2502-18778:
Qingpei Guo and co-authors present an open-source model that takes in and produces any mix of text, image, audio, and video, in a paper from 2025. Such omni models promise a single assistant that can watch, listen, read, and reply in kind. Training one is hard because data amounts and learning speeds differ wildly across the senses.

Their model, M2-omni, treats every input and output as one interleaved sequence. A step balance plan during early training evens out the data gaps between senses. During instruction tuning, an adaptive plan keeps the senses progressing together. Pure text skill is guarded throughout. The authors report performance rivaling a leading closed model, with real-time interactive use as the goal.
arxiv-2502-19478:
Sowmiya Balan and four co-authors link two big facts in one model: a hum of gravity waves caught by pulsar clocks, and a light form of dark matter. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Strong first-order shifts in a dark sector can make that low hum. The team asks if the same shift can give mass to a stable dark particle that fills the dark matter count. Their dark sector has a hidden force with a dark photon that talks to our world by a slight mix. The shift sits at a low heat, so the dark particle is light. It gains its count by wiping out into electrons and dark Higgs states. The plan can be tested in labs.
arxiv-2502-20178:
Zhaoxuan Wang and co-authors designed a stealthy attack on the satellite navigation that guides delivery and survey drones. Spoofing fake GPS signals is a known threat, but its success depends on how the drone is moving, a factor security studies often ignore. The team first showed that turning and other nonlinear motion makes position spoofing work better and makes speed-based detection less likely to fire.

Building on that, their attack, called SSD, waits for the right motion state before striking, acting as a state-triggered backdoor. In tests it greatly increased position errors and mission failure risk while staying invisible to three current detectors. The work warns that drone route planners must judge navigation security state by state, not on average.
arxiv-2502-20278:
Lior Gishboliner, Eoin Hurley, and Yuval Wigderson prove new results in a 2025 paper on graph homomorphisms, maps between graphs that keep linked nodes linked. Many classic results say, in rough terms, that a triangle-free graph with set traits can be mapped into a small triangle-free graph. Threshold results give this when the graph is dense enough, and an approximate version gives it for all graphs when the map is allowed some slack.

The authors study uneven versions, where the traits demanded of the source and the target need not match. For one case, a graph with no short odd cycles and a set density maps into a small triangle-free graph whose size rests only on that density. The cycle demand can be loosened when the graph has bounded complexity of a set kind. The work also sharpens a known proof.
arxiv-2502-20678:
Aaryan Garg, Akash Kumar, and Yogesh S Rawat tackle video grounding without box labels in a twenty twenty-five computer science paper. Their task locates a described subject in space and time inside a video. Only a text query is given for training. Recent vision-language models offer a starting point, but simple use of them falls short.

The team first links text queries to short video segments called tubelets. Then their STPro system learns in stages. One module builds up complex actions step by step. Another module raises scene difficulty in a guided way. Tests on three benchmark datasets show gains over earlier methods, including on crowded scenes.
arxiv-2502-20978:
Richard Gerlach, Antonio Naimoli, and Giuseppe Storti develop a method for forecasting financial tail risk several steps ahead. Their targets are Value-at-Risk and Expected Shortfall, the standard measures of extreme losses. The approach is quantile-based and semi-parametric: returns are scaled by an estimated quantile series, then resampled to build forecast distributions at multiple horizons.

The method works whenever the relation between the two risk measures is stable over time. It extends to models incorporating realized volatility measures, in the spirit of realized GARCH and CAViaR frameworks. Simulations check finite-sample behavior, and a forecasting study compares one-day and ten-day forecasts at the one and two-and-a-half percent levels against competitors.
arxiv-2502-21278:
Kulin Shah and co-authors ask whether image-making AI must memorize its training pictures to stay creative, in this 2025 paper. Top diffusion models often copy training images, above all when the training set is small. Past fixes for that copying tend to dull image quality. The team looks for a way to keep quality high and copying low at once.

Their theory shows copying is only forced at low noise levels, the stage that adds fine detail. So they train the model on noisy data at large noise scales instead. The change cuts memorization a lot without hurting image quality. It works for text-guided and unguided models, and across varied data supply. The paper offers a principled route to more original generative models.
arxiv-2503-00278:
Vedant Khandelwal and a team of co-authors built a search system for systematic reviews in medicine. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a slow step in such reviews: finding the right papers. Large language models help, but they lack niche terms and deep domain logic, and they can invent facts. Old tools lean on plain text methods and share the same gaps. The team mixed a domain tuned model with structured knowledge.

Their system, NeuroLit Navigator, draws on medical subject headings and a large medical language bank. That mix grounds search in set terms, not just raw text. Readers who run evidence reviews get a tool that aims for care and speed. Good search cuts the risk of missed or false claims in a review.
arxiv-2503-00378:
Rickard Brännvall proposes a privacy-friendly fix for uneven data in federated learning, in a 2025 paper. In federated learning, many clients train one model together without sharing their data. When each client's data looks different, the shared model can wobble and converge poorly.

His fix lets each client compute summary statistics of its own data, such as averages and spreads, and keep them private. During training, the model learns to adjust itself based on those local summaries. At use time, the same summaries steer each client's predictions. Experiments show the approach handles uneven data well and scales better than methods that hunt for similar peers. No extra information leaves the client, so privacy holds while accuracy improves.
arxiv-2503-02878:
Mendes and Ritter show language models can self-improve at state-value estimation for better search, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Ground-truth rewards for multi-step reasoning are costly, above all in web tasks. Their Self-Taught Lookahead framework needs no labeled rewards at all. The value model learns by simulating one lookahead step in language.

Training predicts next action, resulting state, and rationale for its value. That chain-of-thought value iteration refines estimates self-supervisedly. Sharper values let lightweight search expand fewer states at equal strength. Web agent success rises by thirty-nine percent with mid-size open models. Gains generalize to multi-hop questions and math puzzles.
arxiv-2503-03578:
Samuels sets out a design for fault tolerant quantum memory built in a doped crystal in twenty twenty-five. The memory stores units called qudits, which hold more than the two states of a qubit. Errors must be caught without wrecking the stored state. His plan for a europium doped crystal weaves three tools together.

Echo pulses draw out error clues without a direct read of the data. A Fourier method in a tweaked form names the error with fewer steps. A group based scheme then splits big fix steps into small ones, which keeps errors from spreading. The design skips the costly stacking used in qubit memory. It aims at long lived, large scale storage.
arxiv-2503-03778:
Wang and seven co-authors present a study from twenty twenty-five on making new brain scans by warping a learned template. Fake brain images must look plausible and match traits like age or disease. Direct image synthesis can miss fine shape details. Their method learns a template brain, then deforms it with a generated warp field. A diffusion model produces the warp rather than the image itself. An encoder blends image and template into a code that drives the warp. Alignment loss trains the whole system end to end.

Their method beats generative baselines on diversity and trait match. Shape measures on the fake brains also track real ones better. The code is posted in public for reuse. The authors aim at richer synthetic data for brain research.
arxiv-2503-04778: Jingxu Wu and Yuwen Yin read the unpublished thought notes of Lev Landau for the root of his shape-first physics. Landau held that laws fall out of symmetry breaks in bound state spaces, as sure things. His scorn for interpretation debates in quantum work and his lean-course fame grow, in this reading, from one root: a faith that truth must show through spare form. Economy of size is his test of a law. The 2025 note traces that faith through his notes and books.
arxiv-2503-04978:
Jake McNaughton, Abbas, and Ivan Maksymov present a 2025 paper on using a tunnel diode's physics as the activation function inside neural networks. The head title stresses full-precision and ternarised networks; the catalog title frames the same work as neuromorphic quantum networks. Activation functions shape how each unit in a network responds, and standard choices are pure math.

A tunnel diode has a bent current-voltage curve born of quantum tunneling. Used as the activation, that curve beat standard functions in deep networks, giving lower loss and higher accuracy in training and testing. The authors also argue the device suits future hardware for lean, energy-saving AI chips. The work links semiconductor electronics, quantum physics, and machine learning in one component.
arxiv-2503-05778:
Tapasvi Panchagnula published a paper in 2025 on a deep learning system that reads dream reports for themes and feelings. Dreams offer a direct record of the sleeping mind, yet they are usually studied by slow hand coding. The author's framework, DreamNet, scores the meaning and emotion in dream texts, with an option to add brain wave data from the dream stage of sleep.

On fifteen hundred anonymized dream reports the text-only version sorted emotions with about ninety-two percent accuracy. Adding the brain signals lifted accuracy to about ninety-nine percent. Some links were striking, such as falling dreams tracking anxiety closely. The author also releases the enriched data set, aiming DreamNet at mental health screening and sleep science.
arxiv-2503-05978:
Talking-head videos made from a photo, a script, and a voice usually stall at short clips and stiff faces. Hongwei Yi and co-authors present MagicInfinite, a diffusion transformer built to run without a length limit. It animates realistic people, full-body figures, and anime characters, even from back-facing poses, and can drive several characters at once, with masks naming who speaks.

Three ideas carry the design. Full three-dimensional attention with a sliding-window denoising scheme gives endless, coherent footage. A two-stage curriculum ties lip motion to audio, expression to text, and identity to a reference image. Region masks with adaptive losses balance global text control against local voice cues. Distillation speeds generation twentyfold, producing ten seconds of video in ten seconds at the smaller size. On the team's new benchmark, the system led in lip sync, identity keeping, and natural motion.
arxiv-2503-06178:
Usman Sanusi, Sona John, Johannes Mueller, and Aurélien Tellier study how parasite rest states affect the time until an epidemic dies out, in a research paper from 2025. Some parasites go inactive for a time, losing infectiousness, then wake again. Hosts with a resting parasite cannot recover, yet they also cannot spread it.

Their model splits hosts into susceptible, infected, resting, and again susceptible states. Resting does not change the basic reproduction number. For wide settings, the model acts like a simpler epidemic model on a slower clock. That clock is set by the share of time spent active. Resting thus works as a hedge against random die-out.
arxiv-2503-06378:
Zhou and colleagues proposed a new way in twenty twenty-five to evaluate artificial intelligence systems, built on general scales rather than fixed test scores. Benchmarks drive progress, but a score on one test says little about what a system can do on a fresh task.

Their method rates every test item by the demands it places on eighteen general ability scales, from knowledge to reasoning. Fifteen large language models were profiled across sixty-three tasks. The profiles explained what each benchmark truly measures and exposed how skills shift with model size and thinking style. Better still, demand ratings predicted a model's success on brand-new items, beating standard black-box predictors, above all on unfamiliar tasks. The authors call it a step toward evaluation that explains and forecasts, not just ranks.
arxiv-2503-06778:
Feng Gu and co-authors test large language models as annotators in a 2025 paper. Labeling events in news data matters for tracking markets and trends, but expert coding is slow and costly. Their test covers a full workflow: dropping irrelevant documents, merging reports of the same event, and labeling what remains.

Fully automated model labels beat older text methods but still fell short of human experts. The picture changed when models assisted the experts instead. Help with grouping events cut time and mental effort, and experts agreed more with model-extracted details than with fully automated labels. The authors favor models as assistants, not replacements, for careful annotation work.
arxiv-2503-08678:
Yuanhao Wang and co-authors present a tool for making three-dimensional clothes from one photo in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Non-expert users can design garments in flat images, but turning a single view into a full garment that can be edited is hard. Views made by older methods often fail to match each other.

Their system, called GarmentCrafter, builds new views step by step. It first predicts depth and warps the image to guess new angles. A diffusion model then fills in hidden areas, guided by the changing camera view. By inferring color and depth together, the method keeps views consistent. Tests showed better detail and coherence than leading rival methods.
arxiv-2503-09678:
Mitman and co-authors improve how the ringing tones of a merged black hole are pulled from simulations. After two black holes merge, the remnant rings with quasi-normal modes. Those tones can test Einstein's theory, if they are measured cleanly. Knowing when the tones truly describe the wave is part of the challenge. Their algorithm fits the wave over the whole sphere at once. It also searches backward in time with a sturdier fitting routine.

The fit yields a fuller model of the strain signal. Amplitudes of each tone come out with the timing. Cleaner extraction sharpens any test of gravity built on ringdown. The method extends earlier tools in three stated ways.
arxiv-2503-10978:
Ayoub Laayoun and Badr Missaoui prove an existence result in a 2025 probability paper. Their system is a stochastic equation with reflection, which keeps the solution inside a boundary, steered by a control the user picks. The question is whether a best control exists at all, in both strict and relaxed senses.

Using weak convergence methods in a strong topology, plus a representation theorem, the authors show that optimal controls of both kinds do exist. The paper is brief and technical, aimed at specialists in stochastic control. Its value is foundational: before anyone can compute a best control for such reflected systems, existence must be secured, and that is what the proof delivers.
arxiv-2503-11478:
Zubair Iftikhar and co-authors run an experiment testing a classic formula of physics in an extreme setting. The Kubo formula links the noise a conductor makes to how it responds to signals. It is usually checked near equilibrium, where systems sit at rest. The team drove a tiny tunnel junction far from rest with a steady voltage.

Their device joins two superconductors through a thin insulating layer. Following an old proposal, they measured the power the junction trades with a quiet detection circuit. From that power flow they extracted the noise the junction emits and the noise it absorbs. The gap between the two matched the junction's measured response, confirming the formula within experimental accuracy. The authors show the math still works when the detector pushes back strongly on the device. The result supports using noise as a probe of quantum electronics far from equilibrium.
arxiv-2503-11578:
Engl and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about unwanted effects in fresh ferroelectric hafnia devices and how to remove them. Ferroelectric hafnia stores charge states for memory devices. Fresh devices show imprint and split switching peaks, flaws that fade with cycling. The team inserted niobium oxide layers at varied positions in device stacks. Spectroscopy and electron microscopy probed how the added layer changes the hafnia. Charged vacancies from the niobium oxide likely create an internal bias field.

That field skews the starting polarization state of domains. Opposing bias fields in up and down domains likely cause the split peaks. One stack design placed the layer between ferroelectric and insulator. It produced a device free of both splitting and imprint from the start. Charge trapping near the new interfaces explains the fix, they argue. The result could simplify making reliable ferroelectric memory.
arxiv-2503-11778:
James Sunseri, Adrian Bayer, and Jia Liu study the information content of the cosmic web in a 2025 cosmology paper. The web splits into nodes, filaments, walls, and voids. Using large simulations and a modified structure finder, they ask whether treating each type separately sharpens estimates of cosmological parameters.

Splitting the density field by structure type and combining spectra gave much tighter constraints than a single spectrum. Gains were largest for neutrino mass, improving by large factors at some smoothing scales for the matter field. Gains were smaller for a field including baryons. A public software package accompanies the work.
arxiv-2503-12778:
Sorting breast cancer into subtypes from tissue images is hard: classes look alike, some are rare, and images vary by lab. Gul Sheeraz and co-authors build MultiRisk, a framework that first predicts where the classifier may go wrong. A risk model uses features from several neural networks to rank each case by its chance of misclassification.

That ranking steers a second stage, where the prediction model is fine-tuned with extra weight on risky cases and tuned to each dataset. On three collections, the risk analysis scored AUROCs of seventy-eight point one, seventy-five point six, and seventy-six point three percent. After adaptive training, subtype F1-scores rose to sixty-one point one five, sixty-five point nine eight, and eighty point five three percent. The authors say it holds across resolutions and domain shifts, and could make diagnosis steadier when labeled data are scarce.
arxiv-2503-13078:
Tobias Østmo Hermansen, Manuela Zucknick, and Zhi Zhao propose a Bayesian survival model that uses biological network knowledge to select cancer biomarkers. A central goal in cancer research is predicting a patient's survival from a small panel of genes or proteins. Purely data-driven models can produce results that are hard to interpret biologically.

Their penalized Bayesian Cox model uses graph-structured selection priors: a Markov random field prior built on a biologically meaningful graph of relationships between multi-omics features. Because the graph shapes prior probabilities rather than imposing hard constraints, the model can confirm known information and still flag novel biomarkers. Simulations show more trustworthy and stable variable selection than methods that treat covariates independently, with no loss in survival prediction. Performance also held up when the graph was only partially correct. That robustness matters, since real biological networks are never fully known.
arxiv-2503-13178:
Jin, Duan, and Hang built a lean game agent in twenty twenty-five for Gomoku, a five-in-a-row board game, that beats big net agents on small gear. Big net agents need vast compute to play at top strength. Their agent uses a small net with a book of board pat-terns drawn from big nets.

A step-by-step update trick cuts work when just a few stones change per move. That trick also speeds deep search by a large share. With tuned scores and search it beat the top open AlphaZero-like Gomoku agent sans fast chips. It ranked first in a large bot pool and won a known cup.
arxiv-2503-13678:
Roberto Biondo, Davide Castelnovo, and Fabio Gadducci published this study in 2025. It gives e-graphs a formal home in category theory. E-graphs are a data structure for program optimization: instead of rewriting code, they add equal versions and mark them the same. That equality saturation hunt finds cheaper programs efficiently. The authors describe e-graphs using adhesive categories, a setting where graph rewriting rules behave well.

The formal dress is not mere tidiness. It makes the structure's properties exact and provable. Adding an equal program piece becomes a standard graph transformation step. That opens the door to results about parallel updates and clashing edits, borrowed from the adhesive theory shelf. The paper serves formal-methods readers who want e-graph reasoning on solid ground.
arxiv-2503-15178:
Alireza Akbari and Peter Thalmeier show how a surface probe can photograph a spiral of trapped magnetic moments in this 2025 paper. A scanning tunneling microscope reads the wandering electrons at a surface, not the fixed ones. Yet experiments on a gadolinium compound showed the fixed moments' spiral order in the spectrum anyway, and the authors explain why.

The wandering electrons exchange energy with the fixed moments, which rebuilds their bands. That rebuilding stamps satellite peaks into the tunneling spectrum at the spiral's wave vector, even on a clean surface. The authors then work out how dirt on the surface scatters the rebuilt electrons, giving an interference pattern that carries more detail about the order. Bound states near impurities also shift under the coupling. The theory turns a surface tool into a camera for hidden magnetic textures.
arxiv-2503-15478:
Yifei Zhou and six co-authors presented SWEET-RL in twenty twenty-five, a method for training AI agents that work with a human partner over many turns. Such agents must judge which of their many steps helped or hurt, a hard credit problem. To study it, the team built ColBench, a test suite where an agent and a person solve real coding and design tasks together.

SWEET-RL trains a critic that sees extra facts available only during training. The critic scores each step, giving the agent fine-grained feedback. On ColBench it beat rival methods by six points in success and win rates. It let a modest open model match or beat a top commercial model on joint content creation. The work points to better training for partner-style AI tools.
arxiv-2503-16578:
Yang Chen and nine co-authors present SeniorTalk, a Chinese speech data set for very old adults in two thousand twenty-five. Voice tools serve more old users, but they lag for this group. Old voices have traits like weak tone and local speech forms that training sets miss. Data on those past age seventy-five is scarce.

SeniorTalk holds many hours of talk from over a hundred chats. Speakers are balanced by sex, region, and age. Rich tags span many traits of each clip. Tests cover speaker checks, speaker splits, speech to text, and speech edits. Results give a base for tools built for the oldest users.
arxiv-2503-17178:
Carlos Vargas studies the rare points where two eigenvalues of a matrix family collide, events called exceptional points. His families blend a fixed random matrix from the Ginibre ensemble with a rotating diagonal matrix whose entries travel along circles or other curves. By tracking the eigenvalues as the parameters loop, he can spot when they swap places, which betrays a collision inside the loop. Software to compute and visualize them accompanies the paper.

The counts show a regularity: for circular paths the number of collisions came out as the matrix dimension times itself minus one, under fairly general conditions. Elliptical and other curves produced even more. The pattern links random matrix theory to the topology of eigenvalue motion. Exceptional points matter in physics, where they mark sharp changes in a system's behavior. Vargas offers both a counting phenomenon to explain and tools to explore it.
arxiv-2503-17478:
Newman and a large team weigh a dormant black hole in a distant galaxy in twenty twenty-five. Black holes and their host galaxies grow together over cosmic time. Their masses follow linked patterns in nearby galaxies. To see if those patterns held long ago, astronomers need precise masses for distant black holes.

The target galaxy lies at redshift near two and is magnified by a foreground gravitational lens. The team used the James Webb Space Telescope to map how stars move near its centre. Fitting dynamical models gave a black hole mass of about six billion solar masses. That mass is high for the galaxy's bulge mass, by local patterns. It does match the local pattern that uses stellar velocity spread.
arxiv-2503-17578:
Sharon Lin and co-authors present a 2025 computing paper showing that a backdoored language model can recite long secret strings word for word. Backdoor research mostly studied image classifiers flipping labels. For language models, the dangerous trick is different: a trigger that makes the model print an exact planted sequence, such as a hard-coded encryption key.

The team poisoned fine-tuning data with trigger-response pairs buried in benign text. Triggered, the model reproduced random keys up to a hundred characters exactly, even under light low-rank tuning. The attack worked on models the size of a phone-class system. A round of clean fine-tuning afterward disabled the planted behavior in their tests. The paper flags supply-chain risk in borrowed fine-tunes.
arxiv-2503-18578:
Tianyu Chen and co-authors present Galaxy Walker in a 2025 paper, a geometry aware vision language model for astronomy at galaxy scale. Standard models embed images in flat Euclidean space. Astronomy needs spherical geometry for orbits and hyperbolic geometry for black holes, and backbones that handle such curved spaces.

Their geometry prompt creates geometry tokens from random walks across a multi scale physical graph spanning diverse spaces. A geometry adapter then compresses and reshapes the spatial anisotropy with a mixture of experts. The model set top scores on galaxy property estimation and morphology classification, beating both specialist and general models.
arxiv-2503-18978:
Tobias Timofeyev and Alice Patania link group synchronization in networks to graph spectra in a 2025 paper. Oscillators on a network often lock into clusters rather than one chorus. Fair partitions of the network, where each node sees the same mix of groups, were known to underlie such clustering. The authors build a general spectral framework around that link.

Eigenvectors tied to those partitions span a subspace of the graph's Laplacian spectrum that rules cluster behavior. Clustered states reduce to motion on a smaller quotient graph. The framework explains passing hierarchies and multi-frequency locking, tying them to symmetry and community shape. Real networks are imperfect, so the authors relax the partition idea with a tolerance level. The relaxed version keeps the useful traits under noise. They aim the results at systems from neural circuits to power grids.
arxiv-2503-19078:
Backhaus and co-authors present a new infrared survey of deep space with the James Webb telescope, in a 2025 paper. The MEGA survey images the Extended Groth Strip, a well-studied sky field, in four mid-infrared bands across twenty-five pointings. It overlaps most of an existing near-infrared survey of the same field. Mid-infrared light reveals the obscured universe: dust-hidden star formation and feeding black holes that shorter wavelengths miss.

The paper covers the survey's design, its data reduction beyond the standard pipeline, and the first public catalog. Warm pixel masking and custom background subtraction were added to clean the images. A shared, deep infrared map of a benchmark field becomes infrastructure for hundreds of later studies of how galaxies assembled their mass.
arxiv-2503-19678: Yuetong Fang, in a short mathematics paper from twenty twenty-five, proves a result about a special class of functions on compact Hermitian manifolds. These spaces are a broad form of the curved spaces used in complex geometry. Fang shows that all functions of this kind can be raised to a power and still have a finite total size on the space. The bound on the power depends on the size of the space and on a second number tied to the function class.
arxiv-2503-20578:
Alif Al Hasan, Subarna Saha, Mia Mohammad Imran, and Tarannum Shaila Zaman test whether large language models can extract failure-inducing inputs from bug reports, in a two thousand twenty-five software engineering paper. Developers need those inputs to reproduce and fix bugs, but reports are written in prose.

Their technique, LLPut, benchmarks three open-source generative models: LLaMA, Qwen, and Qwen-Coder. The evaluation runs over a dataset of two hundred six bug reports and measures the accuracy and effectiveness of the extracted inputs. Findings map where current generative models help automated bug diagnosis and where they still fall short, guiding both tool builders and practitioners.
arxiv-2503-20678:
Gabriel Palma, Mariusz Skoczen, and Phil Maguire test a recipe for predicting hourly price moves in a 2025 finance study. Their pipeline first splits price series into simpler waves with empirical mode decomposition. Features from a linear model and classic indicators are then computed inside a rolling window of recent hours, and a Gaussian mixture model sorts market conditions into clusters.

Trading tests cover a meme stock, an electric car maker, and a cryptocurrency, over samples of different lengths. The mix of decomposition, clustering, and machine learning aims to sharpen the decision to buy or sell. Cluster filtering is meant to skip hours when signals disagree.
arxiv-2503-21078:
Nedialko S Nedialkov and John D Pryce present a simpler way to build Taylor series solvers for differential equations, in this 2025 paper. Such solvers expand the solution as a power series at each step, which allows very accurate, large steps. The catch is that every function inside the equation normally needs its own hand derived recurrence, which makes the software heavy to build.

Their trick, the sub-ODE method, replaces each special function with the small differential equation that the function itself obeys. That turns a few lines of code per function into a place in a shared library. The change formally turns the system into a mixed form, so the authors prove the resulting recurrences stay sound no matter how many such swaps are made. Their Matlab solver compares well with standard tools.
arxiv-2503-21678:
Zsolt Páles and Tomasz Szostok examined a family of inequalities in a 2025 analysis paper. At the center is a blend of two points, weighted by a signed measure, fed into an unknown smooth function. They ask when the weighted average of the function over all blends stays at or above zero for every pair of points.

The answer turns on stronger forms of monotonicity, where not just the function but its higher rates of change keep one sign. From that they build rules for comparing random outcomes across whole classes of such functions at once. One necessary condition for a mixed ordering is also given. The results extend several classic facts about how risk and order compare.
arxiv-2503-22078:
Santiago Palumbo, Pablo Cornaglia, and Jorge Facio study in 2025 the band structure of a trigonal crystal known as a Weyl semimetal. The material shows a superconducting phase tied to its surface states. Knowing its normal phase is key to grasping that odd behavior.

Their calculations trace the semimetal state to a crystal distortion of a parent structure. The distortion breaks mirror symmetry of the lattice and also cuts its translation symmetry. That break, they find, is the dominant energy scale, larger than spin-orbit coupling. Even without spin effects, the distortion alone creates the Weyl nodes near the Fermi level.
arxiv-2503-22178:
Merging several fine-tuned models into one multitask model saves memory and compute, but the ingredients can clash. Chanhyuk Lee and co-authors study where the clashes live. Each task's update to a model can be split into directional components. The biggest components, they show, often cause the interference that drags other tasks down.

Their method, AdaRank, prunes those components adaptively instead of by a fixed rule. During a test-time tuning step it trims ranks by watching an entropy signal. Across many backbones and task counts, AdaRank topped earlier merging methods. It closed the gap to separately fine-tuned models to about one percent. The authors frame rank choice as the key decision in model merging.
arxiv-2503-22778: Francisc Bozgan, writing alone, studies a fifth-order wave equation known as the modified KP-I equation, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The equation is critical in the energy sense, which makes its long-term behavior delicate. Bozgan proves solutions exist for all time when the starting wave's mass stays below the ground state's. He also finds a region with short-time control, where sharply localized data can still blow up in finite time. On a half-periodic domain, small data give global solutions.
arxiv-2503-22878:
William Peria and colleagues build a capacitance probe that keeps working inside pulsed magnetic fields, where fields spike and vanish in milliseconds. Capacitance reveals how a material polarizes, but ordinary meters drown in cable artifacts when the field sweeps fast. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team uses an auto-balancing bridge with a high-bandwidth amplifier to cancel the parasitic signals from the coaxial leads. They test the rig on a magnetoelectric crystal whose magnetization they measured alongside.

The capacitance showed a clear hysteresis loop matching the magnetization, and the energy-loss peak sharpened at faster sweep rates, exactly the dynamics slower methods smear out. In steady fields the new readings agreed closely with a standard meter. The authors offer the technique for multiferroics and other correlated materials that only reveal themselves under extreme fields.
arxiv-2503-23478:
Ivan Anokhin and co-authors tackle delay in real-time reinforcement learning, where a learning agent must act on a fixed clock, in this 2025 arXiv paper. While the network computes, the world keeps moving, so each action rests on stale sight. Deeper networks see more but lag more, since every layer adds its own delay.

The team's fix joins two ideas: connections that skip forward in time, and observations enriched with recent history. Agents built this way stayed strong across neuron speeds, learning methods, and test worlds, from simulated robot bodies to classic arcade-style games. Running neurons in parallel also sped up decisions by six to three hundred fifty percent on ordinary hardware. The authors frame the work as groundwork for real-time agents.
arxiv-2503-23678:
Xiao-Ping Zheng and four colleagues use the Crab pulsar's largest glitch to test whether starquakes cause its long-term spin changes. After a glitch, the pulsar's spin-down rate stays elevated for years, which was taken as evidence of quake-driven changes in the external torque. The team analyzed seventeen hundred ten days of radio data after the 2017 glitch.

The persistent spin-down increase was extreme, letting them test the relation between glitch size and persistent shift predicted by starquake models. Their analysis does not support external torque variation from quakes. They suggest an internal mechanism instead, involving superfluidity inside the star. The absence of flux or profile changes around glitches fits that reading.
arxiv-2503-23878:
Schurmann and twelve co-authors forecast groups of evolved massive binary stars in the Small Magellanic Cloud from a rapid binary evolution code. Massive star paths hold large unknowns, and most such stars are born in close pairs that sway each other. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The code builds mock post contact pairs at a set mass transfer yield, with a merger rule that adjusts to that yield. One yield alone fails to match the seen groups. A high yield fits the Be star counts, while a low yield fits Wolf-Rayet counts better. A mixed picture follows.
arxiv-2504-00078:
Sebastian Harris, Yasuaki Hikida, Volker Schomerus, and Takashi Tsuda build a fresh family of interfaces in symmetric product orbifolds. Their paper from twenty twenty-five works in holography, where such two-dimensional theories mirror higher-dimensional gauge setups. Interfaces act like line operators and have drawn wide interest. Their family plays a dual role, akin to Wilson lines and to Karch-Randall walls at once.

The build starts from boundary choices in the seed theory. A folding trick turns those into boundary states for the interfaces. Overlaps of the states yield the spectrum of interface-changing operators through a modular swap. A worked case uses the supersymmetric four-torus as seed. There the interfaces match AdS2 branes in a tensionless string limit. The paper gives holographers a new set of walls to test duality with.
arxiv-2504-00178:
Craig Schmidt, Varshini Reddy, Chris Tanner, and Yuval Pinter present BoundlessBPE in two thousand twenty-five. Byte Pair Encoding is a core way to split text into tokens. A first step, pre-tokenization, cuts text on spaces and marks. That step skews token counts toward common full words.

Skew blunts the gain from larger vocabularies in the model. BoundlessBPE relaxes the boundary rule that causes the skew. It merges whole pretokens into units the team calls superwords. Counts across the corpus turn far more even as a result. Text also packs tighter, with more bytes per token.
arxiv-2504-01678:
Takumi Fujiyama and Yoshihiro Kanno design trusses under distribution doubt in two thousand twenty-five. Loads on a truss are unsure, and past data on them are scarce. Scarce data can spoil designs tuned to a guessed distribution. Past confidence based methods strain on cost and accuracy for hard constraints.

Their method pairs two goals for the worst case of compliance. One is the mean, the other a tail risk gauge. Kernel density estimates stand in for a fitted distribution. The problem cuts down to a second order cone program for two kernel types. Tests trace the Pareto front of the two goals.
arxiv-2504-02778:
Vincent Gbouna Zakka, Luis J. Manso, and Zhuangzhuang Dai present a radar-based activity recognition system in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Cameras raise privacy concerns and fail in darkness, so the authors use millimetre-wave radar, which yields privacy-preserving point clouds. Those clouds are sparse and noisy, and graph methods usually apply one fixed kernel everywhere. The team argues kernels should adapt to each local neighbourhood's geometry.

Their Multi-Head Adaptive Kernel module generates several dynamic kernels inside a graph convolution network, each capturing a different aspect of local structure. Features refine progressively while global spatial context is preserved. On benchmark datasets the method reached state-of-the-art accuracy for recognizing human activities. The target application is domestic service robots that monitor elderly or vulnerable residents safely.
arxiv-2504-02978:
Adrian van Kan, Alexandros Alexakis, and Edgar Knobloch simulate giant swirls in two-dimensional turbulence. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, removes bottom drag from the flow. In flat turbulence, energy can pile into a few huge vortices called condensates. Whether tidy theory predicts that state has been an open question.

Huge simulations of the flow equations map the steady state. Condensates appear once the flow strength passes a sharp threshold. Near that point, energy growth follows a clean power law. The big-scale spectrum matches a classic balance prediction there. At higher strength the spectrum steepens, and most energy loss happens inside the giant swirls themselves.
arxiv-2504-03778:
Stefano Cirillo and four co-authors test AI enrichment of anonymized data in twenty twenty-five. Data archives hold sensitive, identifying details about people. Anonymization techniques such as k-anonymity protect subjects, but they also thin the data. Thinner data weakens the predictive processes that use it.

The authors ask whether large language models can enrich anonymized sources. The enrichment must add value without breaking anonymity. They designed custom prompt templates for that delicate task. Feasibility and limits are both explored in the study. Readers in data governance get a careful look at a tempting idea: using generative AI to restore utility that privacy protection removed, without restoring the risk.
arxiv-2504-03978:
Francesco De Santis and co-authors tackle explainable AI in a 2025 paper on concept-based models. Such models first name human ideas found in the input, then decide from those ideas, so users can step in and fix a wrong idea. One model type is easy to fix but less exact; a second type is more exact but harder to fix once data shifts.

Their new model, V-CEM, uses a form of reasoning under uncertainty to make fixes work better. Tests on text and image data check plain accuracy, how well fixes help at home and on shifted data, and a new score for how clean the idea codes are. V-CEM kept the high accuracy of the second type while matching the first type on fixes for shifted data.
arxiv-2504-05278:
Zahra Atf and co-authors tackle how language models in medicine should state their uncertainty, in a 2025 paper. A model that sounds sure while wrong can harm patients. Honest odds help doctors weigh machine advice against their own judgment.

The authors blend math tools, from Bayesian methods to group voting and dropout tricks, with text based gauges of meaning spread. Extra parts handle closed model access, mixed data sources, and steady recalibration as models learn. Maps of doubt and clear scores aim to earn clinician trust. They argue for owning a degree of doubt rather than chasing false certainty, since medical knowledge itself shifts.
arxiv-2504-08178:
Zhang and three co-authors wrote a theory paper in twenty twenty-five about stochastic gradient descent, the step-by-step method that trains many learning systems. They study cases where the loss curve is steep near the best point but flattens out far away, a shape that shows up in robust fitting and in quantile regression.

The authors build a new piecewise tool, called a Lyapunov function, that tracks how the method settles down over time. With it they prove bounds on the error for shrinking and fixed step sizes, plus results on long-run behavior and bias. They then apply the theory to two tasks: fitting a line when some data are corrupted, and estimating quantiles from streaming data. The results match earlier rates reached under stricter assumptions, and they relax a common condition past work needed.
arxiv-2504-09378:
Kartik Ravisankar and co-authors published this paper in 2025. It asks how large language models manage to answer questions in many languages when most of their training text is English. The authors test whether the model first maps other languages onto English inside its own layers.

They built a score that measures this inner mapping for single examples, across twenty-four languages and three kinds of task. Wrong answers came with weak mapping, above all in the model's middle layers. The team then swapped in the matching English activations at those layers, and many wrong answers turned right. That swap test shows the mapping is not just linked to success; it helps cause it. The work gives builders a clearer target for improving weaker languages.
arxiv-2504-09878:
Yunpeng Tan, Junlin Hao, and colleagues speed up training for neural scene rendering in a 2025 study. Neural radiance fields render new views with high quality, yet even fast variants need minutes of training. Multimedia uses such as telemedicine want results in real time, and wasteful sampling is a major bottleneck.

Simple regions of a scene need less sampling than detailed ones, but older methods sample both at full fineness. Their method uses a tree search strategy to vary resolution by block, spending effort where texture is complex. Rays aimed at easy regions cost less. The payoff is faster training without giving up view quality where it counts.
arxiv-2504-10078:
Wanyun Zhou and co-authors mine social media for stock signals in a 2025 paper. Price and company data are the usual inputs for predicting stock moves. Posts on platforms like StockTwits add a live stream of opinion, but most posts are noise and public mood alone predicts little. The team's claim is that a few posters do know something, and they can be found.

Their algorithm traces posters over time and keeps those whose calls are consistently right, plus a surprising group whose calls are consistently wrong in a usable way, the inverse experts. Filtering out the rest sharpened trend prediction over older expert-finding methods. The authors also note a limit shared by the whole approach: turning expert calls into a precise return forecast stays hard. The work shows signal hides in social noise.
arxiv-2504-10278:
Jinyue Zhang and co-authors present, in 2025, a new method for spotting moving objects in satellite imagery. The targets are tiny, the images grainy, and older deep learning methods reason about probabilities in ways that limit how objects and frames inform each other. Their method works with points marking object centers instead.

Borrowing from diffusion models, the system denoises scattered points step by step until true centers emerge. Added modules let points exchange spatial and semantic information and carry memory across frames. A staged matching strategy sets the learning target at each denoising level, and an extra loss stops points from clumping onto only the brightest objects.
arxiv-2504-10378:
Qinyuan Zhang, Tian-Qi Huang, and Zhuo Li ask whether flashes of neutrinos born from cosmic ray collisions could appear as point sources in the sky. Their paper appeared in 2025. Ultra-high energy cosmic rays hitting background light make these cosmogenic neutrinos. If the cosmic ray sources are brief events like gamma-ray bursts, the neutrino glow should arrive as tight, time-limited spots. The team computed the spots' spectra and shapes over time.

Intergalactic magnetic fields steer the parent rays and so set the spot sizes, generally under a degree. Early on, a spot's flux can outshine the whole diffuse background within its patch. A recent record neutrino event fits a nearby transient source better than the diffuse glow. The authors say hunting such spots could finally reveal the cosmic ray sources.
arxiv-2504-10478:
Xingyu Dang and four co-authors report a simple fix for a training flaw in reasoning models in this two thousand twenty-five paper. As fine-tuning proceeds, a model's answers grow more alike. Its first guess keeps improving, but its chance of solving a problem in many tries falls. That loss hurts test-time strategies like majority voting. The authors blend the weights of the final model with an early checkpoint, a trick called WiSE-FT.

The blend nearly restores the lost diversity while keeping the first-guess gains. It also improves voting scores and later reinforcement learning results. Extra gains appear that decoding tricks alone cannot give. The team frames the effect as a bias-variance trade-off. The recipe is cheap and easy for model builders to adopt.
arxiv-2504-10778:
Christian Iliadis looks at why marks of spin and flip for core tiers so often muddle readers. These marks are key for work on core form and on how cores act. Yet rules for marks shift from source to source. Iliadis weighs the rules of a file of core data that has been judged next to work by Endt and his team.

He finds stock roots of muddle. One is vague use of strong and weak points. One more is new test finds merged with past bounds with no clear mark. His tips call for clear rules for marks. They call for clean splits of point strengths and for more teach in the group. They also call for new finds told on their own. The aim is core data that staff and judges can use with no wrong read.
arxiv-2504-11178:
The center of the Milky Way hides behind dust that blocks visible light, but radio waves pass through. William Cotton and co-authors surveyed the Galactic bulge with South Africa's MeerKAT telescope at 1.3 gigahertz. The maps cover about 173 square degrees around the center plus scattered fields farther out. They resolve details a few arcseconds wide.

Most sources are distant galaxies shining through our own. Polarization measurements pick out compact Galactic objects and reveal fine-scale magnetic twisting across the region. Hunting for giant radio galaxies, the team catalogued seventeen spanning more than 700 kiloparsecs. The survey releases full polarization images and source lists for other astronomers.
arxiv-2504-11278:
Tanja Auge and co-authors work toward a unified framework for workflow and data provenance in a 2025 paper. Provenance records where data and results came from, which is essential for tracing studies and trusting their findings. Two kinds matter: how the workflow ran, and how the data themselves evolved.

Their framework adds dimensions and granularity to both kinds, letting users answer a standard set of provenance questions. A biomedical use case demonstrates the approach, designed to transfer to other fields. Unifying the concepts, the authors argue, supports credibility and reproducibility of research findings.
arxiv-2504-11378:
Horndeski theory is the broadest healthy extension of Einstein's gravity with a scalar field. Hatice Özer and Özgür Delice ask what gravitational waves look like in a massive version of it that carries a general potential. Earlier work often ignored the potential's lowest point; here it takes center stage.

That lowest value acts like an effective cosmological constant, curving the background the waves cross. Solving the weak-field equations step by step, the authors get the background shape, then the wave solutions on top of it. The scalar-caused curvature shifts the frequency and spacing of the tensor waves in a way that sets them apart from the scalar wave. How the constant is introduced also changes the scalar wave's speed and polarization. The comparison clarifies what future detectors could test.
arxiv-2504-12378:
V Markov and co-authors present a 2025 astronomy paper on how dust dims and reddens the light of early galaxies seen by the James Webb Space Telescope. Dust curves vary a lot between young galaxies, and astronomers disagree on what drives the variety: the dust itself, how much there is, or how it is arranged around the stars. The team quantifies each curve by its ultraviolet slope and a bump feature.

They analysed 173 dusty galaxies from when the universe was young, spanning redshifts two to about eleven and a half. Correlating curve shape with galaxy traits aims to name the physical levers behind the variation, which matters because dust corrections shape every measurement of early galaxy growth.
arxiv-2504-12678:
Jerome, Klimchik, Maloletov, and Kulathunga planned vehicle paths over rough ground in this paper from twenty twenty-five. Car-like robots on uneven land face slopes that shift from patch to patch. The terrain is modeled as a mesh of triangles. Their planner, GAKD, searches with a genetic algorithm that breeds and mutates candidate routes.

The search works over a fixed look-ahead window and keeps controls within safe bounds. A heuristic mutation step steers the breeding toward workable routes. Against two sampling-based rivals, GAKD cut the cost of crossing terrain by up to twenty percent. Path length stayed about the same. The authors offer the method for robots that must cross broken, sloped ground.
arxiv-2504-14578:
Biao Dong and co-authors study, in 2025, a quantum phase that is at once a crystal, a superfluid, and a patterned spin texture. They create this chiral supersolid in a cloud of ultracold magnetic atoms with spin-orbit coupling. By tuning interactions, they map out how the system changes form.

Two kinds of transition appear: an abrupt jump to a triangular pattern and a smooth shift to a square one. The phases differ in lattice shape, spin texture, and how freely they rotate. Under a balanced gain-and-loss setup, current swings fade at rates tied to the superfluid share. The work points to cold atoms as a platform for designer quantum matter.
arxiv-2504-16978:
Yu Shi presents a 2025 paper on the scientific spirit of Chien-Shiung Wu, the great experimental physicist. In 1950 Wu and her student published a coincidence experiment on entangled photon pairs from electron-positron annihilation. It verified quantum electrodynamics precisely. It was also the first tightly controlled entangled state of separated particles, though Wu did not know that then. In 1956 she led the Wu experiment, which found that parity is not conserved. That result ranks among the century's greatest experiments.

The paper traces her career through the twin themes of precision and accuracy. It is the text of a speech for the 110th anniversary symposium of her birth. Physics readers get a career read as a lesson in experimental craft. Yang's remark that her experiments were famed for precision frames the talk. History of science gains a practitioner's view of how care in measurement changes what a field can know.
arxiv-2504-17278:
Raza and four co-authors set a cap in twenty twenty-five on how many look-alike graphs a directed graph can have. Two such graphs are mates if a set of score lists from their link tables match in full. Mates that are not the same graph can confuse work that tries to name a graph by its scores.

The team ties the cap to a count from a walk table built from the graph. As a side case, they give a test for when the sole mate is the graph flipped end to end. The tests link to how well a web of linked parts can be steered.
arxiv-2504-17778:
Paul Leask studies how a knotted light-like texture in a liquid crystal transforms in a paper from 2025. Hopfions and torons are three-dimensional topological solitons in chiral liquid crystals. Bending the molecular alignment creates strain, which generates electric polarization through the flexoelectric effect. That polarization makes its own field, which pushes back on the alignment. Computing this self-interaction is the hard part.

Leask adapts a method built for magnetic skyrmions to the liquid crystal case. Unlike their magnetic cousins, these textures feel the back-reaction strongly. As the flexoelectric strength rises, the hopfion converts into a toron. The transition is shown in confined three-dimensional systems. The results guide soft-matter soliton design.
arxiv-2504-18178:
Jiaqi Zheng and Tiow-Seng Tan unified two classic ball problems in a 2025 geometry paper. Given a set of compact convex objects, the smallest intersecting ball is the tiniest ball touching them all, while the smallest enclosing ball is the tiniest ball containing them all. Versions of these problems recur across computational geometry and machine learning, from facility placement to classifier margins.

Zheng and Tan show both problems can be written as zero-sum games, where two players' opposing goals encode the geometry. For the intersecting version they give an approximation algorithm, the first results of its kind in high dimensions for inputs like polytopes, balls, and ellipsoids. The game view may unlock algorithms for related covering problems.
arxiv-2504-18378:
David Holec and four co-authors model from first principles how alloying shifts phase change effects in beta titanium alloys, known by the short names TWIP and TRIP. These effects shape how the metal bends without breaking. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team used density based theory on pure titanium and on mixes with nine other elements. Some elements steadied the beta phase, yet the most stable phase sat between beta and alpha, a martensite form. Twin borders of one type face a positive energy wall that alloying raises. The other twin type shows no wall save for two elements, since its mid state looks like the alpha phase. Twin border energies round out design hints.
arxiv-2504-20078:
Kalyan Cherukuri and Aarav Lala present a smarter way to compress neural networks, in this 2025 paper. Big networks are heavy to store and slow to run. A classic trick replaces weight tables with low-rank versions, but picking one rank for every layer wastes capacity in some and starves others.

Their method reads the spread of each layer's singular values, a measure of how much real information it holds. Layers with rich content keep higher ranks, while redundant ones shrink hard. The result is layer-wise compression with better performance and lower space and time costs than fixed-rank cuts. The pair frame rank choice as an information budget problem.
arxiv-2504-20578:
Carpine and three co-authors test how the build and mix of space dust grains bend their light marks, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Dust models decode how grains cool gas, grow in disks, and seed planets. Most models are tuned to thin space gas and treat grown grains as plain balls.

The team grew one micron grains from a known small grain set and used a dipole sum to work out their light acts. They varied the grain's stuff, its holes, and its clump shape. In the heat and long wave bands where scopes read dust, all three choices moved the marks. Clumps could not be faked by smooth balls, and the long wave slope could shift at fixed grain size. The pilot warns model makers off easy cuts.
arxiv-2504-20778:
Arup Sarkar and Alessandro Lunghi compute the excited states of two molecular magnets eyed as quantum bits, in this 2025 paper. The molecules carry vanadyl or copper centers inside flat porphyrin rings. Excited states steer how the spins behave, yet they stayed poorly mapped.

Using heavy multiconfigurational methods with four active spaces of rising size, the pair sorted the low states by type. The biggest calculations show the lowest excitations come from the ring's own electrons jumping within quartet states. The picture matches lab observations. Knowing which states sit lowest should help explain spin motion and guide qubit design.
arxiv-2504-20978:
Shamil Asgarli, Sara Krehbiel, and Howard Levinson ask whether a graph's coloring web can name the graph itself, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Points of the web are legal colorings, and edges join colorings one vertex apart. Unlike graphs can share a web in the tight case.

With spare colors beyond the least needed, the web becomes a full fingerprint. Same web then forces same graph and same color count. No tight-case web can pose as a spare-case one. A build-it proof even tells which case a web came from, though slowly. Readers get a neat line where extra colors buy identity.
arxiv-2504-21478:
Zherui Zhang and six co-authors present CAE-DFKD in two thousand twenty-five. The method transfers knowledge from a teacher net to a student net with no real data. Past methods chase image scores on the source task. They neglect how well the learned codes travel to new tasks.

The new method works at the level of embeddings, not just images. Category aware codes shape what the student learns. A change in how the generator trains brings big speed gains. Tests show scores on par with the best data free methods. Codes learned this way moved to downstream tasks with rare strength.
arxiv-2504-21778:
Ayman Ameen, Thomas Richter, and André Kaup cut the computing cost of learned image compression. Their twenty twenty-five paper presents a design called LoC-LIC. Learned codecs can beat classic formats on file size. Their heavy maths blocks use on modest devices, though.

The design extracts features in a hierarchy across scales. Wide early maps use few channels to stay cheap. Narrow deep maps can then afford many channels. That split keeps compression strength while slashing operations. Computing per pixel fell to a fraction of the earlier level. Phones and small devices could plausibly run such codecs. The work points toward learned compression that fits everyday hardware.
arxiv-2505-01778:
Afan Ali, Abdelali Arous, and Hüseyin Arslan published a telecommunications paper in 2025 on signal design for future networks. Two chirp-based schemes are candidates for sixth-generation mobile systems. Both suffer from high peak-to-average power ratios. Large peaks waste energy and strain amplifiers.

The authors propose spreading the data before modulation to smooth peaks. They compare four spreading transforms under one shared approach. The method needs no extra side information for the receiver. It also adds little computing cost, unlike older peak-cutting schemes. Tuning the chirp settings improved resistance to difficult channels. Smoothing the spread signal also cut interference. The paper frames spreading as a cheap, general fix.
arxiv-2505-01878:
Misyura studies gravitational waves past the first, linear approximation in a twenty twenty-five paper. Real waves are weak, so most work treats space-time as flat plus a small ripple. At second order, the ripples themselves act as a source, and new effects can appear.

The author builds a general metric for this case and tracks bundles of paths for both massive and light travelers. For massive paths, the bundle spreads and shears but does not rotate. For light, all three effects vanish. A numeric run in a split space-time scheme finds one more trait: test particles drift slightly along the wave's own direction of travel, a second-order effect only.
arxiv-2505-02978:
Anushka Sharma, Anamitra Pal, Rajasekhar Anguluri, and Tamojit Chakraborty wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It gives power grid operators a practical way to estimate grid inertia, the stored spinning energy that keeps frequency steady when something fails, from ordinary sensor data.

As wind and solar replace spinning generators, inertia shrinks and must be watched live. The method uses ambient readings from phasor units scattered on the grid, plus a split form of the swing equation that governs machine motion. It allows for bounded errors in network data and in the readings themselves. A key trick is spotting stretches when mechanical power input truly stays constant, using knowledge of how plants run. Tests on two standard simulated grids, including versions with renewables, showed accurate estimates of inertia, damping, and power input.
arxiv-2505-03378:
Tasnim Ahmed and co-authors published this paper in 2025. It stress-tests hybrid quantum neural networks, which pair a small quantum circuit with a classical network. Today's quantum hardware is noisy, and the authors ask how two leading designs hold up as noise grows.

They fed five kinds of noise into the circuits, at levels from light to total, and watched image sorting accuracy. One design, QuanNN, stayed strong at low noise but buckled under two noise types at high levels. The other, QCNN, oddly improved under some noise at high levels, beating its own clean score. Other noise types wore it down step by step. The mixed picture shows noise is not simply bad. The authors say these maps should guide error-fixing work for near-term quantum machines.
arxiv-2505-04278:
Weiwei Ye, Zhuopeng Xu, and Ning Gui build NsDiff, a 2025 diffusion forecaster whose uncertainty can breathe over time. Standard diffusion forecasters assume a fixed noise level, but real series, driven by physics and outside shocks, get more or less predictable as conditions change.

Their framework swaps the fixed noise model for a location-scale one and pre-trains an estimator of the mean and spread at each step. An uncertainty-aware noise schedule then matches noise to the moment's true uncertainty. Across nine real and synthetic data sets, NsDiff beat existing probabilistic forecasters. Code is public.
arxiv-2505-05278:
David Johansson, Janne Nurminen, and Mikko Salo tackle an inverse task for a class of curved equations in two thousand twenty-five. The task is to learn the hidden rule inside the equation from tests made only at the edge of a region. The rule here can depend on both place and the unknown value itself.

They show the rule is fixed, apart from one known kind of freedom, by those edge tests near a known solution. The advance lies in how rough the rule and the solution may be. Past results needed smooth data, while real tests are often rough. Their proof gives the same claim under much weaker terms.
arxiv-2505-05578:
Lorenzo Malanga and six co-authors show a trap in how we read the life of discs of gas and dust around young stars, where planets form. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Two main views of how such discs fade have not yet been split by what we see. The team built fake groups of discs and let them age under one view, where drag and light from the star wear them down. Light discs vanish fast. The discs left then look, on the whole, heavier, even though each one lost mass. This seeming rise is a bias of who survives. The trap holds with or without links to the star's mass.
arxiv-2505-06078:
Yuta Murotani, Tomohiro Fujimoto, and Ryusuke Matsunaga unify theories of a light-driven Hall effect in a 2025 physics study. When light and a bias field act on a material, a sideways photocurrent can appear. Two mechanisms compete to explain it: Berry curvature created by the light itself, tied to topological change, and an asymmetry in how light-born carriers move, tied to the field.

Earlier work separated the two except in numerical studies. The authors build one theory covering both field-induced and light-induced curvature effects. A unified account helps experimentalists assign measured currents to the right cause when engineering optical responses.
arxiv-2505-07278:
Maksymilian Wojnar and co-authors published a 2025 paper on scheduling Wi-Fi transmissions when many access points share the air. As Wi-Fi grows denser, letting every device grab the channel at random no longer gives fast, steady service. A coming Wi-Fi standard lets access points coordinate. In the variant studied here, several devices send at once on the same channel, with power tuned to limit interference.

The hard part is choosing which devices send together, and at what settings. The authors first build an exact model that finds the best possible schedule, for speed or for fairness. That model is too slow for live use, so they add a learning method that probes the network and adapts. In simulations and on real hardware, the learning method raised total throughput by about eighty percent over legacy Wi-Fi. It did so without cutting any station's chances to send.
arxiv-2505-07978:
Anchal Gupta and nine co-authors demonstrate control of plasma detachment in the KSTAR fusion device after its upgrade to a tungsten divertor. The divertor takes the exhaust heat, and even tungsten can sputter and contaminate the core if heat flux runs too high. Detachment, lifting the hot plasma off the plates, is the standard remedy.

One method steered detachment using an attachment fraction estimated from Langmuir probe currents in the divertor. The second used DivControlNN, a neural surrogate of two-dimensional simulations, running live to estimate heat flux and adjust impurity gas. Both approaches worked in experiment. The paper also shares controller tuning lessons aimed at future burning plasma devices.
arxiv-2505-08278:
Álvaro Martín-Cortinas and co-authors present work from two thousand twenty-five on voice conversion using self-supervised features. Voice conversion changes who a recording seems to come from while keeping the words. Trained systems often need costly matched recordings, and separating content from speaker traits is hard, since pitch patterns can leak or be lost.

The team feeds combined features from self-supervised speech models, plus a speaker embedding, into a sound generator trained to rebuild the input. In zero-shot tests, where speakers are new, the method kept the source speaker's content and rhythm of speech. It matched the speaker likeness of a system based on phonetic features. The approach suits uses from anonymization to personal speech synthesis.
arxiv-2505-08678:
Precup and Stan pin down where critical points sit in Banach spaces, and show that more than one can exist, with the Nehari manifold, in work from twenty twenty-five. To find many answers inside ring-shaped parts of a cone once took heavy warping proofs. Their route pairs Nehari tools with the cone form of the Birkhoff-Kellogg invariant-direction theorem. The pair gives a much more plain path to both points.

The points are placed in plain terms, inside annular parts of a cone. A worked case on p-Laplacian boundary value problems shows the route in use. It does without Ekeland's rule and without squeeze-and-stretch gear at all. The one must-have part is a variational build, an energy-like score. Other classes of problems with that build should gain in the same way.
arxiv-2505-08778:
Guichard and four co-authors grew solutions to reasoning puzzles in this paper from twenty twenty-five. The ARC benchmark asks for the rule behind a few example grids, a task people find easy and AI finds hard. Their approach uses neural cellular automata, grids of cells that update by local rules. Growth-like dynamics echo how living systems develop.

One version adds hidden memory cells to the basic automaton. The developmental style is meant to build answers rather than recall them. Early results, the authors report, rival a leading chatbot on some tasks at a fraction of the cost. The paper frames the work as a proof of concept. It argues development is a promising path toward flexible reasoning.
arxiv-2505-08878:
Dor Tsur and colleagues analyzed text watermarking for large language models in 2025. Watermarks hide a detectable signal in machine-written text so the text can later be identified as machine-made, ideally without hurting its quality. The authors study the simplest one-shot setting, where a single piece of text must carry the signal.

Framing the problem as hypothesis testing with side information, they work out the basic trade-off between how reliably a watermark can be detected and how much the text must be distorted. A central choice is how the secret side information pairs with a random split of the model's vocabulary. They identify the best pairing strategy, give a formula for its detection rate, and compare the scheme with the theoretical best in numerical tests.
arxiv-2505-09778:
Mohammad Khalafi and Digvijay Boob present a first-order algorithm for two-level inequality problems with random data, in a 2025 methods paper. The problem class, called bilevel variational inequality, covers many tasks where one optimization sits inside another. Their method, R-OpEx, blends a smoothing trick with an extrapolation step borrowed from operator methods. It runs in a single loop and needs just one look at each operator per round.

The team proves cost bounds for the method across smooth and rough cases. Batching tricks cut the cost at the outer level when the inner level is smooth. Stronger assumptions cut the cost further. Computer tests back the theory. The authors claim the first study of the rough, random case with guarantees this strong.
arxiv-2505-10578:
Yunji Feng and co-authors build a drone system that maps rooms in 3D from plain photos in a 2025 computing paper. Lidar gear does this job well but costs and weighs too much for small drones. Their framework, ExploreGS, flies, photographs, and rebuilds the scene on board in real time. A word-bag model of image features keeps the processing light enough for the drone's own computer.

The scene is stored as a field of soft 3D blobs, a format that renders fast and trains quickly. Tests in simulation and in real rooms matched the quality of heavier rivals. Low overhead matters most where the drone must explore and map in one flight, such as disaster zones.
arxiv-2505-14478:
Geirnaert, Kappel, and Kidmose compare three ways to record brain waves for hearing aids that follow attention in twenty twenty-five. In a noisy room, a listener must pick one voice out of many. Future aids could read brain waves to learn which voice that is. Scalp sensors work best but are bulky and hard to wear all day.

The team recorded scalp, around ear, and in ear signals at the same time from the same people. A simple decoder named the right speaker most often from scalp data. Ear based sets scored lower, but still well above chance. Adding just a few scalp sensors lifted ear scores a lot. Comfort and accuracy trade off, they conclude.
arxiv-2505-14778:
Allison Lin, Maria Charisi, and Zoltán Haiman published this astronomy paper in 2025. Pairs of supermassive black holes should betray themselves by making their host quasars brighten and dim on a regular cycle. Searches usually rely on the Lomb-Scargle periodogram, a standard tool tuned to smooth sine-wave signals. Simulations, though, predict spikier, sawtooth-shaped pulses. The team tested how badly that mismatch hurts detection.

They built fake quasar light curves with realistic noise and injected both sine and sawtooth signals. They mimicked an older survey's data and the coming Rubin Observatory survey. Even sine signals were recovered less than half the time. Sawtooth recovery collapsed to about nine percent in survey-like data and near one percent in the cleaner sets. The authors conclude past searches missed most binaries, and future surveys need better tools than the standard periodogram.
arxiv-2505-15478:
Six researchers wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-five on spotting when a wireless link has a clear path. High-frequency links fail easily when buildings or objects block the line of sight. Knowing the state of the path in real time helps keep links reliable, but measuring it everywhere is costly.

The team trained AI models on data made by a network digital twin, a software copy of the network that can simulate radio waves. They compare training strategies for one general model. Their approach beat the best prior model, above all when the signal was weak. It also shrank the input the model needs while keeping its accuracy.
arxiv-2505-15978:
Zeynab Kaseb, Matthias Möller, Pedro P. Vergara, and Peter Palensky wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on running power grids with quantum-style machines. Power flow studies work out how electricity moves through a grid, and the optimal form also picks the cheapest safe settings. The authors recast both tasks as puzzle-like problems that annealers can solve.

The paper builds on their earlier quantum power flow method and adds a new one for the optimal case, written as binary problems with no extra constraints. They test both on grids from four buses up to 1,354 buses, using a D-Wave quantum machine, a hybrid solver, and two Fujitsu systems. The methods found valid answers and scaled in a hopeful way, though hard, ill-posed cases still need care.
arxiv-2505-16678:
Jimin Bai, Peter Keim, and Matteo Baggioli tracked shear waves freezing out of a two-dimensional colloid in a 2025 paper. Theory from Maxwell and Frenkel says liquids lose their shear waves at short wavelengths when they melt, opening a gap in the wave spectrum. Simulations agreed, but experiments across a gradual glass transition were missing.

The team measured the wave spectrum directly as their colloidal monolayer turned glassy. The gap opened continuously, right where the static stiffness vanished and the glass transition began. Shear relaxation times extracted from the data followed the classic super-Arrhenius law of glass formers. The authors present the result as direct experimental proof of the Maxwell-Frenkel picture.
arxiv-2505-16878:
Michael Levine presents a 2025 algorithm for mixture models whose parts lean on each other. A mixture reads a crowd as a blend of hidden groups. When the traits in each group move together, a copula, a link device, must join them. Past solvers either lacked a sure climb or worked by chance. The new MM method climbs a smoothed, penalized fit score at every step, never down.

Proof covers both the score's climb and the path of the guesses it makes. Runs on fake and real data match the best past solver. Monotone climbs make runs easier to trust and to stop. Such mixtures serve risk, gene, and market work where parts refuse to move alone.
arxiv-2505-17278:
Elisa G Vergamini and co-authors describe a test bench built to judge how robot joints handle physical contact, in a 2025 paper. A catalog record lists the work under a project code, but the head gives the plain title and author list used here. Robots that work beside people need to control not force or speed alone, but the relation between them, called impedance.
