The bench mixes straight and rotating motion, and accepts electric or hydraulic drives, with loads the user defines. It was built to be free of play and highly reliable, so teams can validate models of joint behavior and compare controllers fairly. The paper details the mechanical, electrical, and hydraulic choices behind it. Similar benches exist in many labs, but the authors stress this one's mix of versatility and trustworthiness.
arxiv-2505-17778:
Yu Xie, Jielei Zhang, and others generate realistic text inside scene images without any optical character recognition crutch in a 2025 computer vision study. Posters, signs, and packaging in synthetic images often carry garbled lettering, and current generators lean on extra conditioning modules fed by large annotated corpora, notably for multiple languages. Their diffusion transformer takes a leaner route.

Dropping the auxiliary modules while keeping glyph accuracy is the central claim under test. High-fidelity scene text matters for advertising mock-ups, film props, and training data for reading systems, where one wrong character ruins the illusion.
arxiv-2505-17878:
Matthias Grätsch studies families of functions with bounded generalized Schwarzian derivatives in this 2025 math paper. The Schwarzian derivative measures how far a function bends away from the simplest fractional maps. Bounding a generalized form of it turns out to control how wildly a whole family of functions can behave.

Grätsch shows such families are quasi-normal, meaning they stay close to the tidy behavior of normal families. Related families built from derivatives and their logarithms get similar results. A new formula for the generalized derivative yields extra findings for locally one-to-one functions and for entire functions. The classical case sits inside the framework as one special choice.
arxiv-2505-18578:
Celia González-Sánchez and co-authors present a 2025 physics paper on layered devices that mix superconductivity with a magnetic crystal. Such stacks are a hunting ground for new quantum phases, since the two orders usually fight each other. The team built junctions by sandwiching a magnetic layer between two superconducting flakes.

Single junctions behaved like interference devices, the kind normally made by looping two junctions together. The authors trace that surprise to the way the magnetic layer's spin texture plays against the superconductors on both sides. Their reading rests on how the current through the device responds, and it points to edge states inside the stack.
arxiv-2505-18878:
Kung-Hsiang Huang and co-authors published a benchmark paper in 2025 testing how well AI agents handle real business software work. Customer relationship platforms run sales and service for most companies, yet realistic public test data is rare, so earlier benchmarks felt artificial. The team expanded an existing CRM testbed into a broader, more faithful suite.

Their benchmark holds nineteen expert-checked tasks spanning sales, service, and price quoting, in both business-to-business and consumer settings. Conversations run over multiple turns with varied personas, and keeping secrets is graded too. Top agents passed only about fifty-eight percent of single-turn tasks and thirty-five percent of multi-turn ones. Workflow execution scored highest, while confidentiality awareness sat near zero without special prompting. Enterprise readiness, the authors conclude, is not here yet.
arxiv-2505-19178:
Akhila Yaragoppa and Siddharth published a research paper in 2025 on predicting how viewers will feel about a video from where their eyes are drawn. Emotion tech usually leans on self-reports, faces, or body sensors. Their approach instead measures the video's salient areas, the spots that grab attention, using a deep saliency model plus face-action software.

Two simple features did the work: how much of the frame is salient, and how many salient spots compete. Videos with many spots tended to spark pleasant, calm feelings. One dominant spot leaned toward unpleasant, charged feelings. Self-reports often clashed with face-based readings, a caution for the field.
arxiv-2505-19778:
A textbook zero turns out to be large, in a 2025 arXiv paper by Cañas, Yassine, and Ambacher on built in electric polarization in common semiconductors. The zincblende family was long assumed to carry no spontaneous polarization. Its wurtzite cousins are famous for it.

The authors first argue that the flat layered crystal, not zincblende, is the honest zero point for wurtzite measures. Turning the same logic on zincblende itself, they find a polarization about three times the wurtzite size. The result rests on how a ferroelectric flips. It also separates the bulk property from the charge that gathers at interfaces.
arxiv-2505-20478:
Jongmin Mun, Paromita Dubey, and Yingying Fan cluster high-dimensional data while picking the few traits that matter. Sparse clustering must assign groups and choose traits at once, a tightly linked pair. Their base is a semidefinite relaxation of K-means, which they show resists picking too many traits. On top sits a loop that swaps between clustering and trait choice.

Trait choice is cast as a bandit game solved by Thompson sampling. Rewards come from clustering runs and tough shuffle tests. Past picks feed a memory that steers which traits get explored next. The team proves exact group recovery for the adaptively picked trait sets. Fake and document data runs beat top sparse rivals.
arxiv-2505-22878:
Shams Tarek and co-authors fine-tune a language model to hunt security bugs in chip designs. Checking system-on-chip hardware for vulnerabilities is manual, slow, and hard to scale, and flaws at the design level are costly to catch late. Their framework, BugWhisperer, trains an open model on hardware security knowledge so it can read register-transfer-level code and flag weaknesses. The fine-tuning also aims at knowledge transfer, so lessons from one design help on others.

The team reports that the tailored model made verification faster and more flexible than standard practice. They also built a broad database of hardware vulnerabilities to support the training and share it with the community. The work treats hardware security as a language task: the same reading skill that models apply to software can, with the right training, be pointed at the blueprints of chips themselves.
arxiv-2505-23178:
Tonglin Liao and Youming Li solve a queueing model exactly in this 2025 mathematics paper. The model describes customers who arrive in patterned batches and are served by an endless pool of servers, so no one waits for a free one. Time runs in discrete steps rather than as a smooth flow.

The authors build a Markov-style description of the system that can be handled in closed form. From it they derive the exact distribution of the number of customers present at any time, along with its averages. Computer simulations matched the formulas. As a check, they worked out the classic case of random arrivals and random service times. They then compared that step-by-step result with the well-known smooth-time version of the same queue. Exact results like these give engineers a firm base for planning systems with ample service capacity.
arxiv-2505-23578:
When two fluids of unlike density meet and the boundary shakes, two kinds of instability compete to stir them. Tianyi Chu and co-authors study that contest in a 2025 paper on vibrated fluid layers.

One instability grows from the push of gravity on the heavier fluid; the other comes from the shaking itself, in short waves. The team found a new mixed pattern that appears when both act at once. Math analysis shows the shaking drives shifts between the two forms rather than simple boosting. Computer simulations confirm the analysis and follow the boundary as it breaks into fine, tangled flow. Even a fast-growing shaking pattern can be suppressed by the gravity-driven form.
arxiv-2505-23678:
Gabriel Sarch and co-authors published this study in 2025. It trains vision-language models to reason with their eyes on the evidence. Text-only reasoning chains have boosted math and coding skills. Visual tasks add a demand: the model must look at the right place at each step. Their system, ViGoRL, learns to tie each reasoning step to exact image coordinates. When fine detail matters, it zooms into the spot it named and reasons again.

Across spatial reasoning, visual search, and screen-grounding tests, the grounded model beat plain fine-tuning and standard reinforcement learning. It scored 86.4 percent on a hard visual search bench. Grounding also bred other good habits, like checking regions and setting visual subgoals. Human raters found the model's pointers accurate and helpful for following its logic.
arxiv-2505-24878:
Yaxin Luo and co-authors launch, in a 2025 paper, a public testing ground for how well AI agents handle CAPTCHA puzzles on the web. These puzzles block automated agents from finishing online tasks, yet the multi-step reasoning they demand had never been benchmarked properly.

Their platform covers twenty modern puzzle types and 225 challenges in total. A new score counts the thinking and clicking steps each puzzle needs. Humans scored near perfectly, while the best AI agent solved at most forty percent. The gap shows how far multimodal agents still lag on small, interactive visual tasks, and gives builders a clear target for improvement.
arxiv-2506-00178:
Anirudh Nair and four co-authors let prompts for language models compete in debates and evolve toward better wording. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Writing a good prompt takes skill, trial, and time. The pain is worst for tasks judged by taste, where no clean score exists to chase.

Their framework, DEEVO, pits prompts against each other in set debates. Winners and losers both feed lessons into the next round's wording. Ratings borrowed from chess rank the field and keep weak but diverse prompts alive. Smart crossbreeding mixes the strong parts of rivals rather than splicing at random. Tests beat both hand-written prompts and rival auto-tuners on open and closed tasks. No true answers were used as feedback. The method suits teams that need strong prompts but lack the hours to handcraft them.
arxiv-2506-02378:
Ukyo Honda and Tatsushi Oka lift in-context learning by probing explanations for each answer that could be picked, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. In-context learning lets a language model do tasks from a few shown examples. It often fails when the data at hand is not like those few.

A past variant adds notes on why the right label is right. The team takes it one step on: their frame writes out such notes for all candidate labels. To weigh rival notes side by side should make each call more full and more robust. Tests on a range of natural language understanding datasets back the idea. The work held up far better on data far from the norm than the old ways did, by a clear margin. To see why wrong picks tempt the model seems to help it hold firm.
arxiv-2506-02978:
Mohamed Djilani and a team of colleagues test how easily tabular foundation models can be attacked, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Models such as TabPFN and TabICL predict from examples in context, without retraining. Their strength raises a security question the field had largely left unexplored.

Across benchmarks in finance, cybersecurity, and healthcare, small structured changes to test inputs sharply cut accuracy. The training context stayed fixed during these attacks. The models could also be misused to craft evasions that transfer to random forests and XGBoost. As a defense, the authors propose adversarial training inside the context itself. Their strategy swaps in perturbed examples gradually to harden predictions.
arxiv-2506-03978:
Hieu Trung Nguyen, Bao Nguyen, and Viet Anh Nguyen report a surprise: cutting parts of a language model can make it reason better. Their two thousand twenty-five paper focuses on attention heads in transformer models. Pruning is usually done to save compute. Here, removing certain heads raised scores on hard problems. The team set out to find which heads to cut, and when.

Their method, SPRINT, learns to pick the best head and layer to prune during use. It matches question embeddings with head embeddings to guide the choice. Tests used best-of-N sampling, which draws many answers and keeps the best. SPRINT beat both plain best-of-N and random head choice. The gains showed on the MATH500 and GSM8K math datasets.
arxiv-2506-04278: Yumiko Nishiyama proposes a way to sort functions by the structures they build, in a 2025 paper. The idea, called Construction Defining Functionality, treats a function as a generator of structures through repetition, recursion, and logical steps. Nishiyama sets out the spaces that such generation creates and builds a framework to classify their traits. The framework aims to capture what functions do, by looking at the generated structures rather than at input-output pairs alone. It offers a fresh lens for sorting functions in logic.
arxiv-2506-04778:
Zhao Su, Zhiyuan Li, and Zongnan Li simulate the feeding of Andromeda's black hole in this 2025 paper. The galaxy's central black hole is huge yet strangely dim. It must feed at a trickle. The team tests whether winds from nearby old stars supply that trickle. A disk of aging stars circles the hole on tilted orbits.

Their three-dimensional simulation lets one hundred giant stars shed slow winds. Over millions of years a cool gas disk a few parsecs wide takes shape. It feeds the hole at a rate matching the dim glow seen by telescopes. The predicted X-ray brightness also fits observations. Sleepy giant black holes elsewhere may feed the same way.
arxiv-2506-04978:
Gabriele Digregorio, Elisabetta Cainazzo, Stefano Longari, Michele Carminati, and Stefano Zanero study security inside modern vehicles in a 2025 study. Cars exchange data over an internal network, and machine learning tools can spot intrusions on that network. Training such tools centrally, though, raises privacy and data movement concerns.

The authors build a federated version of a known intrusion detector based on recurrent autoencoders. In federated learning, models train locally and share updates rather than raw data. They compare detection quality and communication cost against the central version. Their evaluation presents the federated setup as a workable option for vehicle networks.
arxiv-2506-06178:
Policy gradient methods teach software agents by trial and error, but they usually throw away each run of experience after one use. Alessandro Montenegro, Federico Mansutti, Marco Mussi, Matteo Papini, and Alberto Maria Metelli ask whether reusing old runs can speed up learning. Their algorithm, RT-PG, mixes fresh runs with recent past ones and corrects for the mismatch with a special weighting.

The team proves that this reuse cuts the number of runs needed to reach a given accuracy. When all past runs are recycled, the rate they prove is the best known for this family of methods. Experiments back the theory, with RT-PG beating rivals that hold the previous best rates. The work gives a firm base for a trick practitioners already suspected was sound.
arxiv-2506-06278:
Lee and a large team of colleagues make model unlearn stick by pouring it into a fresh net in this twenty twenty-five paper. Unlearn drills strip a fact from a model, yet a short re-drill can bring it back. That flaw shows the fact's skill stays hid in the net's deep parts.

Inside, a fresh blank net is trained just on the unlearned model's words. The blank net picks up its acts yet leaves the hid skill behind in the move. Their full route adds noise to the copy step to widen that shed gap. At top strength it matched a from-scratch retrain for firm unlearn, at less cost. The route also held on a grave-harm test set that labs use for such checks.
arxiv-2506-06678:
Xin Li and Zhang-Qi Yin detect quantum phase changes from circuit settings in a 2025 paper. Phase transitions mark where matter reorganizes, and spotting them in quantum systems usually needs hard measurements. Circuit parameters themselves may secretly encode which phase a state belongs to.

Their framework feeds those parameters into an autoencoder with an attention mechanism borrowed from language models. Hidden correlations among the settings reveal phase structure without any labeled examples. The trained model doubles as a compact classical stand-in for the quantum states. It can also generate states belonging to chosen phases. Tests across several systems worked broadly, with the strongest results on topological transitions. The trick sidesteps measurement cost by reading the recipe instead of the dish.
arxiv-2506-07178:
Yong Zhang and Peng Ru study how a change in particle mass inside matter distorts a classic size measurement in a 2025 physics study. The Hanbury Brown and Twiss method infers the size of a particle-emitting source from correlations between identical particles. When a particle's mass shifts inside the medium, a squeezing effect reshapes those correlations.

The authors compute the effect on the three-dimensional radii for three particle pairs. Squeezing blunts the influence of outward flow on the sideways size while widening the source along the beam and in rapidity. Their result warns that naive size readings can mislead heavy-ion analyses.
arxiv-2506-08378:
The Euclid Collaboration reports the on-ground performance and calibration of the spectroscopy channel of NISP, the near-infrared instrument aboard the Euclid space telescope. Before launch, instruments of this scale must be tested and calibrated on the ground with great care. The paper documents that work for the channel that splits light into spectra, one of the mission's core tools for mapping the universe.

The huge author list reflects the scale of the Euclid project, with institutes across Europe and beyond contributing to the instrument. Ground campaigns of this kind verify that the hardware meets its design values and supply the calibration data that later science analysis depends on. The paper serves as the reference record for the channel's pre-flight state. Companion Euclid preparation papers cover the mission's other instruments and systems.
arxiv-2506-09678:
Zae Young Kim and Jae-Weon Lee wrote a 2025 paper that links black hole physics with quantum machine learning. The head of the text lists Kim first among the authors. The black hole information paradox asks how facts about what fell in can ever be read back from its glow.

Rebuilding operators from that glow can be cast as a linear inverse task on the joined black hole and glow system. In learning, a like shape shows up as double descent, where error dips twice as models grow. A key time in the black hole story, when both halves match in size, lines up with the learning threshold. A classic law for random matrix spectra lets them score the rebuild weights. Spread of those weights spikes near that point.
arxiv-2506-10478: Yihan Chen, Jialin He, and Tianying Xie present a 2025 arXiv paper on covering a graph's four-cliques. A classic 1966 result bounds how many cliques cover all edges of a graph. Later work did the same for triangles, ending in a guess: for larger clique sizes, the Turán graph is the worst case. The authors settle the guess for cliques of size four. Their proof mixes induction, a greedy partition method, local adjustments, and older clique-counting lemmas.
arxiv-2506-14578:
The SMARTHEP Network reviews machine learning in real-time analysis at the Large Hadron Collider in this 2025 whitepaper. The collider's four big experiments must judge each collision in a flash, keeping the interesting ones and dropping the rest. Learning algorithms now sit inside that split-second filter.

The paper samples real uses across the experiments, from spotting particle tracks to tagging jets. It stresses teamwork between physics labs and industry, where similar real-time problems arise. Examples from outside physics show shared tools and mutual gains. The authors frame the document as a high-level tour rather than a full catalog, meant to spark wider exchange.
arxiv-2506-14978:
Aayush Mishra and Anqi Liu improve how to guess a model's error rate on data from a new domain, in this 2025 paper. Safe systems need that guess before deployment, when no labels exist. A leading method pits classifiers against each other to bound the error. The authors spot a flaw: the fight wastes itself in the region where old and new data overlap, where disagreement should stay low.

Their fix, called ODD, only counts disagreement outside the overlap. Domain classifiers estimate how much the two data worlds share. The new bound then tracks true performance better than the older one while staying a valid bound. Tests across many benchmarks show smaller estimation error. Code and results are posted openly for reuse.
arxiv-2506-15278:
Reuben Binns and co-authors audited Uber's pay algorithm with drivers in a 2025 study of work on ride platforms. Uber markets driving as flexible, yet drivers must guess when and where the algorithm will offer work and at what pay. That guessing game sits at the heart of the paper.

Working with drivers and union organizers, the team analyzed one and a half million trips from a few hundred drivers in the United Kingdom. They compared pay before and after Uber rolled out dynamic pricing, which sets pay case by case. The long view shows how the change shifted driver earnings and risk. The study models a worker-led audit method that other platform workforces could copy.
arxiv-2506-15378:
Frank, Ripken, Lied, Müller, Unke, and Chmiela adapt in twenty twenty-five a powerful image generation method to sample the three-dimensional shapes of molecules. A molecule can fold into many shapes, and drug design needs realistic samples of them. The method, built on diffusion transformers, was not designed for molecules, which mix a fixed bond graph with smooth spatial geometry.

Their framework splits the work: one part handles spatial positions, another handles bond information. Two graph-based strategies feed bond data into the model, each paired with attention styles that either respect spatial symmetry or not. That choice trades accuracy against speed. On standard benchmarks their method reached top precision and physical soundness.
arxiv-2506-15778:
Supersymmetric cousins of quantum chromodynamics, called SQCD-like theories, can be rolled up on a circle to drop from four dimensions to three. Niall Macpherson and co-authors build the holographic duals of that roll-up: curved spacetime backgrounds that encode the same physics as the field theory. The circle shrinks smoothly while twisting with the theory's R-symmetry.

The construction only works when the flavor count is exactly twice the color count. That is the same condition the field theory needs to cancel its anomaly, a satisfying match. The authors compute several observables, including the central charge and Wilson loops. The rolled-up theory lands in a gapped three-dimensional phase described by a Chern-Simons theory. The work shows geometry enforcing a field theory's own consistency rules.
arxiv-2506-15878:
How tangled is the strong force's own quantum state? Twagirayezu tackles that question in a 2025 paper using a holographic model that maps the strong force onto a gravity-like picture. The twist is flavor: light and heavy quarks get their own fields, and the count of flavors is allowed to rival the count of colors.

Entanglement measures come out separately for space regions and flavor groups, tracked against heat and density. The sharpest flavor contrasts appear near the boundary where quarks break free of confinement. Checked against lattice simulations, the results link to patterns seen when heavy nuclei collide, offering testable signs of the tangling.
arxiv-2506-15978:
Toan Nguyen and three co-authors built a Vietnamese dataset for text segmentation and reading tests, in a paper published in 2025. The language ranks twentieth in the world, with more than a hundred million speakers, yet its tool data are thin. Their set pulls nearly 16,000 wiki texts for segmentation tasks. Machine-made multiple choice questions, checked by hand, add a similar count for reading tests.

A multilingual model beat monolingual models on both tasks. It hit high marks on the reading test and a mid-level score on segmentation. The team reads the gap as a hint that mixed training helps thin-resource languages most. The set is free on a known hub. They aim it at tools for similarly starved languages.
arxiv-2506-16178:
Alexander Sobolev bounded the eigenvalues of two matrices tied to an atom's quantum state in twenty twenty-five. For a bound state of an N-electron atom, the one-particle density matrix and its kinetic energy counterpart summarize what single electrons do. How fast their eigenvalues decay governs how well the state can be compressed or approximated.

He proves decay rates with constants that depend explicitly on the wave function, sharpening his own earlier results with more direct proofs. When the wave function vanishes where particles meet — as antisymmetric states do — extra smoothness speeds the decay further, and he proves the faster rates too. The arguments rest on derivative estimates that track distance to those meeting points. The results feed approximation theory for many-electron problems.
arxiv-2506-16678:
Ananth Agarwal and co-authors test whether probing a language model explains its grammar skill in a 2025 paper. Large models handle sentence structure well, which hints they store that structure inside. Probing is a method that reads such structure from a model's inner activity. The question was whether probe scores predict how a model does on targeted grammar tests.

The team checked thirty two open models across many English grammar cases. Probe scores for grammar features failed to predict test outcomes again and again. That gap suggests what a probe can find inside a model may not drive what the model actually does. Readers learn a caution for research that treats inner readings as proof of how a model works.
arxiv-2506-17978:
Salim Meddahi wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five as the sole author. It sets out a high-order numerical method for thermo-poroelastic systems, where heat, fluid, and solid strain act on each other in waves.

The laws are cast as a first-order system with solid and fluid speeds, heat flux, stress, pore pressure, and heat as the state. The author proves the base problem is well set with semigroup tools. The hybridizable discontinuous Galerkin scheme then keeps energy true for the joined system while staying local and cheap to condense. A joint accuracy proof in mesh size and order is given, and tests in mixed media match the forecast rates.
arxiv-2506-19778:
Alexis Ralli, Tim Weaving, and Peter Love set out firm properties of a special class of quantum Hamiltonians, in two thousand twenty-five. A Hamiltonian sums up the energy rules of a quantum system. This class, built from Pauli operators, avoids a deep quantum trait called contextuality, which makes it easier to simulate.

The team prove these Hamiltonians can hold more operators than simple diagonal ones. That means they can describe more physical interactions while staying tractable. They show the energy spaces have a neat classical description. For each energy, some state can be described with effort that grows only in step with the number of qubits. They also pin down where repeated energies can arise.
arxiv-2506-19978:
Gianni Dal Maso and Davide Donati build a new measure for rough deformation fields in this two thousand twenty-five math paper. Their setting is the space of functions of generalized bounded deformation, used to model materials that can crack or slip. For smoother fields, a symmetric gradient measure already exists. The authors extend that idea to the rougher space. They attach to each field a measure whose values are symmetric matrices.

They prove this measure splits into three parts: a smooth part, a diffuse Cantor part, and a jump part. The split mirrors the known case for simpler fields. Using it, they characterize a subspace that was defined only through slicing. The paper serves analysts who model fracture and plasticity.
arxiv-2506-20678:
Mira Welner, Andre Hazbun, and Thomas Beechem wrote this 2025 paper on a simpler way to detect gases with infrared light. Normal tools scan more than a thousand points of the spectrum, which makes the hardware costly and complex. The team asked how few points a sensor truly needs to name a gas.

Their method, called sparse infrared spectroscopy, picks a small set of filters based on a large gas database. Tests in a virtual setup found target gases at one to ten parts per million with just 20 to 50 samples. The method held up under noise and in gas mixtures. It points toward smaller, cheaper sensors that still do the job.
arxiv-2506-22678:
Nicolas Caytuiro and Ivan Sipiran survey deep learning methods that generate three-dimensional shapes in a 2025 review. Generative models can now synthesize objects that are complex, varied, and semantically sensible, from chairs to characters. The survey organizes the field around three components: how shapes are represented, how generation is modeled, and how results are evaluated.

Representations split into explicit forms like meshes, implicit forms like signed distance fields, and hybrids. Each choice trades detail, memory, and editability. For newcomers and tool builders alike, the map shows which representation suits which job and where evaluation still lags behind generation quality.
arxiv-2506-23778:
Smet presents a math paper from twenty twenty-five on special Lie superalgebras in characteristic three. A family is described using products of composition algebras. Named examples from earlier work sit inside this family. For one key algebra, the new view goes past its old construction route. More general forms of it become buildable as well. A semisimplification functor links these algebras to classic large symmetry types. The functor applies broadly across algebras from ternary structures in this setting.

The paper unifies scattered constructions under one method. Characteristic three quirks drive the whole story. It extends a line of work on exceptional symmetries.
arxiv-2506-23978:
Samuele Marro and Philip Torr argue that AI agents will break the walls around closed platforms, in work from 2025. The net's base was built open, but its app layer is ruled by closed services that hoard user data. Open links cost a lot to build, and leaders gain little by sharing. Agents change that math, the pair holds.

Agents can translate data forms and use human-facing screens on their own, which makes any two services able to swap data cheaply. That shift, called universal interoperability, cuts lock-in and frees data. The pair warns of fresh risks in security, upkeep, and law, and urges early guardrails.
arxiv-2507-00078:
Xie and co-authors tackle a puzzle about foundation models for time series: why should one model work across many unrelated streams of data? Time series come from distinct systems, so transfer looks unlikely, yet these models succeed widely. The authors study patch-based models, which read time series in short chunks.

They argue the models extend the language model idea, replacing fixed vectors with probability patterns. Their analysis shows chunks of a smooth series can be split into a discrete vocabulary whose statistics resemble those of natural language. That resemblance, they claim, explains the models' strong transfer. The work aims to ground the safety and design of large time series models.
arxiv-2507-00578:
Dizhan Du and co-authors study time delays between light and X ray emissions from black hole binaries in a 2025 paper. They used daily multi wavelength data for three well studied systems. A cross correlation method compared X ray emission from hot gas with optical and infrared light. The pattern flipped between the rising and decaying phases of outbursts.

During the rising hard state, X ray emission lagged the optical and infrared by several days. During decay, the optical and infrared lagged the X rays by roughly six to thirty five days. Viscous heating in the accretion disk explains the optical light, and a disk instability model fits both delay patterns, the authors argue. Readers see timing used as a probe of disk physics.
arxiv-2507-02178:
Stephan McCandliss and co-authors lay out a survey plan to count the universe's ionizing light sources, in a 2025 paper. Ionizing radiation keeps space mostly ionized, yet its makers across cosmic time are poorly tallied. The team wants counts binned by distance out to a set redshift.

The job needs a vast number of faint targets, far-ultraviolet sensitivity, and a spectrograph that reads many objects at once. Only a proposed instrument on the Habitable Worlds Observatory could carry it out, they argue. The counts would show how much newborn radiation is swallowed by gas and dust on its way out, and how much escapes to ionize space. The paper is a science case for building that capability into the next great observatory.
arxiv-2507-02778:
Ken Tsui shows, in a 2025 preprint, that language models often fail to fix their own mistakes even when they can. Telling apart cannot from does not is the hard part of studying self-correction. His benchmark, Self-Correction Bench, plants the same error in two frames. In one, the error is blamed on the user. In the other, the model supposedly wrote it. Fourteen open models were tested. They fixed the outside error far more often than the identical inside one.

The gap, about sixty-five percent, is named the self-correction blind spot. Training data explains much of it: fine-tuning sets rarely show anyone correcting a model. Adding a few thousand correction examples cut the gap by three quarters. Appending the word Wait helped even more, with no training. Tsui finds a direction inside the model tied to speaker role that switches correction on or off.
arxiv-2507-03378:
Seunguk Yu and three co-authors test language models on Korean endings in twenty twenty-five. Korean is an agglutinative language with complex sentence endings. Models strong in English may falter on such grammar. The authors built a data set, KoSEnd, to measure exactly that skill.

It holds three thousand sentences drawn from diverse sources. Each is annotated for the naturalness of fifteen sentence ending forms. Eleven language models were evaluated on the set. Analysis covered model size and how consistent each model's judgments were. Telling models that an ending might be missing improved their performance. That hints that explicit attention to a linguistic feature matters. Readers get a fine-grained probe of a low-resource language's hardest corner.
arxiv-2507-03578:
Yana Hasson and a team of co-authors present SciVid, a benchmark that tests video models across science domains. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that video foundation models are often built for one field and tested only there. Yet many science tasks can be cast as video problems, so a general model might serve them all.

SciVid holds five tasks from three areas: medical vision, animal behavior, and weather forecasting. The team adapts six top video models with small trainable readout parts. The general models matched or beat specialist baselines on several tasks, which shows real transfer. Gaps remain, and the team shares code to spur better general models.
arxiv-2507-04578:
Noam Horowicz and Tsvi Kopelowitz published this study in 2025. It settles costs for two linked data problems about closeness. One, the snippets problem, asks for the two closest occurrences of two patterns in a text. The other builds a color distance oracle: given two colors, find the nearest pair of points wearing them. Past work left gaps between the best algorithms and the proven limits.

Using fast matrix multiplication, the authors give near-optimal algorithms for approximate versions of both problems. Their tradeoffs between preparation time and query time match the lower bounds closely. For the exact oracle problem, they prove the older algorithm is essentially unbeatable, under a standard hardness assumption. So approximation is strictly easier here than exactness. The result draws a clean line that algorithm designers can plan around.
arxiv-2507-04778:
Artur Michalak and co-authors describe a hardware stand-in for the quantum behaviour of a single electron in a semiconductor nanowire. Instead of solving the wave function directly, they emulate it with classical analog electronics built on the Kron model, a circuit framework that mirrors the mathematics. Wires shaped as lines or closed rings can be mapped onto the model, matching the layouts used in position-based qubits.

The team compares measurements from the emulator with theory across several of these geometries, focusing on how signals are analysed spectrally. They also show how a two-dimensional wave function can be represented in the same framework. The authors present the method as a practical test bench for single-electron devices, and point to further experiments the setup makes possible.
arxiv-2507-06878:
Lucile Favero and co-authors wrote a position paper from 2025 asking whether AI tutors free learners or make them dependent. AI tools are spreading fast through schools and universities. The authors grant that such tools can support study. Their worry is the unchecked pattern: students leaning on AI for every step. That habit, they argue, can dull the very thinking skills school exists to build.

Drawing on cognitive science and teaching research, they trace several harms. Over-reliance can erode effortful learning and foster conformity. It can sap students' belief in their own skill, blur honesty lines, and put well-being at risk. Privacy practices of the tools raise further flags. The paper also centers what students themselves say about the tools. It closes with concrete strategies for teachers and schools: use AI on purpose, in the open, and with a critical eye.
arxiv-2507-07278:
Alvaro Gonzalez-Hernandez published a 2025 mathematics paper on the symmetries of genus-two curves. Every such curve has a Jacobian, a related geometric object whose internal type can be classified. The moduli space, the master map of all genus-two curves, is carved into strata: regions sharing an automorphism group, and regions whose Jacobians share a type, pulled back from another classification.

The author first lists which symmetry groups a genus-two curve can have in positive characteristic, and parametrizes each family. An algorithm then computes the curves of each Jacobian type. Finally he computes the intersections of the two stratifications: their dimensions and how many pieces each intersection has. Two curves can look alike by symmetry yet differ in Jacobian type, and this paper tallies exactly where the two classifications cross. Such explicit geography of moduli spaces feeds arithmetic geometry, where curves over finite fields are counted and used.
arxiv-2507-07378:
Shoji Yokura, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, constructs a co-working bivariant theory from cohomology operations in algebraic topology. Bivariant theories sort out how cohomology and homology interact across maps between spaces.

Fulton and MacPherson's working bivariant theory has a dual, co-working version. Starting from a contravariant functor, Yokura defines a generalized cohomology operation for maps that never break and have sections. The operation connects to Quillen's classic Steenrod power operations. From it he builds a certain co-working bivariant theory, shown to sit inside the general co-working theory tied to the functor. The paper is a basic building work for specialists rather than an application.
arxiv-2507-07778:
Wooseong Jeong, Jegyeong Cho, Youngho Yoon, and Kuk-Jin Yoon set out a test-time training way that keeps a model's many tasks in step as its world shifts. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Test-time training uses a side self-taught task to shrink the gap between the source world and the new one. But when a model must do many tasks at once, the steps that help one task can clash with the next. The team finds the tasks drift out of sync. Their way, S4T, rests on a claim: to keep tasks in step, the model must foretell how task links shift with the world. They show the way on known multi-task sets.
arxiv-2507-07878:
Jiayi Wu and a team of co-authors restore underwater photos in a single diffusion step instead of hundreds. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Murk steals color and contrast, yet marine science, farming, and archaeology all depend on clear images.

Their network, SLURPP, pairs a pretrained latent diffusion model with an explicit split of the scene. That split lets the model account for light fading and scattering with depth, the failure mode of earlier methods on complex scenes. Training data came from a physics-based pipeline that drowned ordinary photos realistically, with full annotations. On synthetic tests the method ran over two hundred times faster than diffusion rivals and scored about three decibels cleaner. Real-world images improved convincingly too.
arxiv-2507-08678:
Hossam Taha and two co-authors hunt for a dark particle at a future electron-positron collider. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The target is a dark gauge boson from a model rooted in Einstein-Cartan theory. Such a particle is a dark matter candidate. The International Linear Collider would smash electrons and positrons at high energy. Simulations stand in for the real machine.

The WHIZARD package generates both signal and background events. The study follows the boson's decay into muons. Several classifiers, from Fisher discriminants to boosted trees and neural nets, sort signal from noise. Most benchmark points prove reachable within current limits. The work maps discovery chances for this dark sector idea.
arxiv-2507-08878:
Xinyu Huang and co-authors present a 2025 paper on a smart home assistant that keeps household data in the house. Today's assistants ship voice commands, profiles, and home layouts to cloud servers, which worries users. Their system, HomeLLaMA, runs a small language model on local hardware, tutored by big cloud models before deployment.

Once installed, the local model keeps learning from the household and refreshing its user profiles. For hard questions, an optional shield decides which queries are safe to send out and which must stay home. The team built a benchmark to grade service quality across these modes. The design tries to keep personalization without the surveillance trade-off. Proactive help, they argue, should not require surrendering the front door's data.
arxiv-2507-09178:
Liang Ding, Simon Mak, and Jeff Wu wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives a Gaussian process model that can take in boundary facts on odd-shaped domains, for use as a cheap stand-in for costly simulators.

Gaussian processes learn from few runs, since each run of the true simulator costs much. Boundary facts from science can add free knowledge, but past models mostly fit box-shaped domains and gave no smoothness control or error bounds. The new BdryMatérn frame takes Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin bounds on a broad class of shapes. Its paths meet the bounds with set smoothness, and a finite element shortcut comes with a full error proof. Tests show the gains.
arxiv-2507-09478:
Cliff Sun and two co-authors design a superconducting diode that lets current flow freely one way and not at all the other, in this 2025 physics paper. Fast superconducting computers need such one way devices, the analogue of the semiconductor diode. Their design is a quantum interference device woven from several superconducting nanowires.

The model predicts a large critical current in the forward direction and exactly zero in reverse, a perfect efficiency of one hundred percent. The perfection survives small wobbles in the applied magnetic field, which matters for real hardware. Under broad conditions the same device becomes a range controller: supercurrent flows without voltage only inside a narrow, adjustable window that excludes zero. Both functions, the authors argue, suit the logic of future superconducting machines.
arxiv-2507-09678:
Balinsky, Krzemiński, and Balinsky tested in twenty twenty-five if fair odds tools still work on locked data, for private smart learning. They lock a known digit set with a fixed key so like pics lock to like codes. Odds tools give sets of calls with a stated trust rate.

Tools trained on locked pics still found real form, far past guess rates. One odds kind held true labels in its sets in most test cases, though its sets were wide. A second kind gave tight sets but missed more true labels. The trade twixt tight sets and trust is the key point.
arxiv-2507-10978:
Ayush Gupta and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on recognizing people by their walk when part of the body is blocked from view. Gait identification works at a distance, but fences, crowds, and furniture routinely hide limbs, and methods trained on paired blocked and full clips are impractical to gather. Their idea treats the blocked signature as a small deviation from the whole one.

A network learns that residual gap and blends it in adaptively, repairing blocked sequences without dulling accuracy on clean ones. On three demanding data sets the method improved blocked-gait recognition while keeping whole-body performance. The authors release the code, aiming at real surveillance and search scenarios.
arxiv-2507-11278:
Arnab Dhani, Jonathan Gair, and Alessandra Buonanno present a 2025 paper on catching model errors in cosmic distance measurements made with gravitational waves. Merging black holes act as standard sirens: their signals carry a distance, and matching them to galaxies yields the universe's expansion rate. The catch is that distances come from fitting waveform models, and a flawed model skews every answer.

Working inside a population analysis, the authors test whether the spread of single-event results is self-consistent, which exposes modelling error without knowing the true rate in advance. They use top-grade waveform models to size the effect for present and future detectors, and show where better waveforms matter most.
arxiv-2507-11878:
Jiachen Zhao, Jing Huang, and colleagues show that language models keep two safety concepts apart inside in a 2025 study. Models learn to refuse harmful requests, and earlier work found a single internal direction controlling refusal. The authors ask whether the model also represents how harmful a request is, separately from whether it will refuse.

A distinct harmfulness direction exists in the model's activations, apart from the refusal direction. Steering along it changes model behavior in causal tests, showing the representation does real work. Separating the two notions matters because a model might refuse by rote while misjudging harm, or the reverse.
arxiv-2507-12878:
Yaniv Shulman, in a solo paper from twenty twenty-five, framed a Bayesian way to model systems that change over time. The task is to read a linear time varying system from its in and out data. That task is ill posed: many systems fit the same reads. Shulman treats the system's impulse response as a chance process. It splits into a mean part and a random wobble part.

That split gives a clean read of doubt, both from the channel's own swings and from lack of knowledge. It also names a new class: systems that are time invariant in expectation. For the math, he uses Bayesian neural nets and Gaussian processes with scaled inference. Tests on worked cases show the frame in action.
arxiv-2507-13878:
Timothy Chan, Linfeng Jiang, and Dominik Krug build a predictive model for bubble-particle collisions in turbulent flow, a key step in froth flotation efficiency. Bubbles are typically much larger than particles, and no earlier model handled finite bubble size and particle inertia together consistently. Building on a frozen turbulence approach, they now predict collision rates a priori from bubble, particle, and turbulence properties.

Comparisons with simulations show good agreement for modest Froude numbers across a range of bubble and particle inertia values. The authors give a criterion for the model's validity beyond the tested range. At typical flotation parameters, particle inertia and settling usually matter, and smaller bubbles, larger particles, and stronger turbulence raise collision rates.
arxiv-2507-14378:
Shrunal Pothagoni and Benjamin Schweinhart add shape sense to tissue slide classification in a 2025 paper. Neural networks read tissue slides well but can lose the topology of what they see. In tissue, how cells are arranged often signals disease.

Earlier topology tools summed up a whole slide's shape, erasing where features sit. Their new convolution operator makes local shape summaries that move as the image moves. Persistent homology supplies the shape language behind them. Models trained with the new layer beat standard networks on slide tests. Several ways of showing slides to the model were matched head to head. Local shape gives the network what pathologists themselves rely on: not just texture, but arrangement.
arxiv-2507-14978:
Shabat, Sokolov, and Tsiganov study the Novikov equations for rings of differential operators that commute. The rings are built from ones of orders three, four, and five. Their 2025 paper sits in the theory of integrable systems. Such pairs are rare and rigid, and their equations encode that rigidity. The authors present them in explicit Hamiltonian form. That form turns them into a flow with conserved structure.

Compatible Poisson brackets then do the heavy lifting. With them, the authors separate the variables. The split takes place on a hyperelliptic curve of genus two. Separation turns a tangled system into independent motions in one dimension. That split is the classic mark of integrability. These forms serve specialists who classify commuting operators and their soliton equations.
arxiv-2507-15178:
Pei-Xi Liu and co-authors sketch a planet-wide quantum network held up by balloons in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Sharing quantum links across the globe is blocked by signal loss in air and fiber. Satellites help, but loss stays high.

Their backbone uses chains of balloon relays in the high air. Tuning beam shape and adding adaptive optics nearly wiped out air disturbance losses, beating satellite relays by a wide margin over ten thousand kilometers in their tests. Ground repeaters handle local links, and clients join by fiber for fast switching. Simulations with current quantum memories gave slow but real link rates across that distance. The authors call it a near-term path.
arxiv-2507-15678:
Amine Aboussalah and Abdessalam Ed-dib present a learning method that respects the geometry of physics in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Physical laws rest on symmetry and conservation. Standard neural networks often ignore that structure. Their forecasts can drift and break basic principles over long runs. The authors build networks around Hamiltonian mechanics, the frame that governs energy-based motion.

Their design hard-wires two geometric facts. It treats inertia with its natural curved geometry, and it keeps the phase space structure that Hamiltonian systems require. A constrained autoencoder enforces the second of these. The result is a model that learns motion while keeping physical law intact. Such models could stay stable on chaotic, high-dimensional problems where plain networks fail.
arxiv-2507-16378:
Roger Clay and Tadeusz Wibig ask if a near dwarf galaxy could be the source of the most energetic cosmic rays. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. A large observatory logged the top hundred events over many years, at extreme energies. The authors study the sky directions of those events.

The most energetic events bunch in one small patch of sky in a way that is not random. A long-suspected source, Centaurus A, lies near that patch. But the Large Magellanic Cloud, a dwarf galaxy that orbits our own, lies even closer in angle. They weigh the case that this cloud, not just the far galaxy, sends some of these rays our way.
arxiv-2507-17578:
Brian DeRenzi, Anna Dixon, Mohamed Aymane Farhi, and Christian Resch test whether fake voice data can teach speech tools for African tongues. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Most of the more than two thousand tongues in Africa have no speech tech at all. Real voice data is dear, so the team asks if made-up voice data can fill the gap.

Their flow makes text with a language model, speaks it with a voice tool, then tunes a speech model on it. They made vast hours of fake voice at a tiny share of real cost. For Hausa, a mix of real and fake data matched a much larger real-only run. Gains for two low-data tongues were mixed.
arxiv-2507-19078:
Digital tools carry an ecological cost that organizations rarely question. Valentin Girard, Antoine Martin, Maud Rio, and Romain Couillet propose a protocol for ecological redirection of digital practice. Rather than chasing efficiency, the approach asks which uses to give up. First, a survey maps how attached staff are to their tools. Next, training builds the knowledge needed for a real debate. A structured discussion then arbitrates which practices to close or transform.

The protocol will be tested in live organizations. The planned study measures how smoothly participants run it and whether it meets its redirection goal. Social and technical barriers are part of the scorecard.
arxiv-2507-19478:
Xuehui Wang and colleagues released a benchmark in 2025 that grades computer-using agents the way a patient examiner would, level by level. Their framework, MMBench-GUI, spans Windows, macOS, Linux, iOS, Android, and the web. It has four levels: understanding what is on screen, locating the right element, automating a task, and collaborating across tasks. Each level isolates a skill that real automation needs.

The team also proposes an efficiency-quality area metric, which scores how well an agent balances speed against success in live automation. Their evaluations identified accurate visual grounding, pinpointing the right screen element, as a critical bottleneck for current agents. As software agents move from demos to daily tools, hierarchical benchmarks like this show developers exactly which floor of the building is unfinished.
arxiv-2507-22178:
Martin Costabel and Monique Dauge studied how math solutions blow up near sharp corners. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with harmonic functions on domains with corners. At a true corner, the rates of change of a solution can grow without bound, even for smooth data. When the corner is rounded off, the solution stays tame but its norms can still surge as the rounding shrinks.

The pair checked two cases: a rounded corner in any dimension, and a flat corner split into smaller angles. They used an inner expansion from recent work on power series forms. From it they proved plain bounds for the norms and the singular parts. Readers in numeric math get clear rates for this blow up.
arxiv-2507-23178:
Siyuan Liu, Zhice Yang, and Huangxun Chen present AutoBridge, a tool that writes code to link smart devices to a central platform. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that each new device now needs hand-written code, a slow task that takes expert skill. AutoBridge aims to generate that code on its own.

The tool splits the job in two: first the device control logic, built by fetching device facts step by step, then platform-ready code. A debug stage tests the code on virtual devices, then on real ones with just yes or no feedback from the user. On thirty-four devices it hit high success and coverage rates with no human help.
arxiv-2507-23378:
Takaaki Ishii, Keiju Murata, and Keita Sugawara build new forms of a Kaluza-Klein monopole with scalar hair. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five. The base object is a known monopole in five-way gravity. Hair here means a scalar field that grows on it and changes its traits.

They write the field as a set of parts, using Wigner matrices to fit the shape of the base monopole. The plan works for a set of any size. They then solve the cases of a triplet and a quadruplet in full by computer. The range of mass and spin for these hairy forms grows as the set gets larger.
arxiv-2507-23578:
Min-Qi Li and co-authors wrote this 2025 particle physics paper on rare B meson decays. They predict how often the mesons decay into a charmonium plus a light scalar meson, and how lopsided those decays are between matter and antimatter. The light scalars are suspects in the hunt for glueballs, particles made of pure glue, possibly fragmented across several states. The calculations run in an improved perturbative QCD framework with next-to-leading corrections.

Mixing among the four scalar states is built into the flavor basis. One headline rate, for the strange B decaying through the 980 state into two pions, comes out near 2.87 times ten to the minus four, matching measurements within errors. The team also forecast large rates and large CP asymmetries for the 1500 state, squarely testable at LHCb and Belle II. Verdicts there could settle whether that scalar is a true glueball.
arxiv-2508-00278:
Gao and co-authors report a fifty-second pulsing rhythm in the fading X-ray glow of a gamma-ray burst, in this 2025 paper. Long bursts are thought to come from collapsing massive stars feeding black holes. Direct proof of the engine has stayed out of reach.

The slow pulse, near zero point zero two cycles per second, appeared in the early afterglow of burst GRB 220711B. The team read it as a wobbling jet from a greedily feeding black hole. Late X-ray energy input fit the wobble story, while the prompt flash showed no pulse. The split hints the star's core and envelope stored spin differently.
arxiv-2508-00778:
Jiankai Tang and seven colleagues wrote a 2025 paper on a smart ring built for research. Smart rings can track heart rate, motion, and skin heat all day without getting in the way. Most rings on sale are closed systems, which blocks scientists from checking or reusing the data freely.

Their platform, called τ-Ring, is open for research use. The ring packs light-based heart sensors, a motion chip, a heat sensor, tap-to-share tech, and on-board storage, all in sync. Its software lets users set sample rates and power modes fast. The team hopes an open ring speeds up wearable studies. The paper describes both the hardware and the tools that come with it.
arxiv-2508-01678:
Zhaochen Wang, Yiwei Wang, and Yujun Cai bake the task text into the picture itself and watch model hallucination swing both ways, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Three open vision-language models took the baked-in prompts. One channel must then carry all the facts.

One model gained four points on a truth test and lied less on photo sets. The other two crashed from near eighty-four percent to coin-flip levels. Their vision encoders stared too hard at the baked text and lost the scene. The winner's encoder stayed calm and its two channels drew closer. Readers get a cure for one model and poison for its kin, from one trick.
arxiv-2508-03678:
Yangtian Zi, Harshitha Menon, and Arjun Guha probe how prompt detail shapes code generation in two thousand twenty-five. Top language models score high on general code tests. They lag on niche suites like ParEval, though. The gap could stem from thin domain facts or thin prompts.

Their tool, PartialOrderEval, grows any code test with prompts from bare to full. They run it on HumanEval and on serial and parallel parts of ParEval. Two model families show varied prompt sensitivity by task. Close looks name input output specs, edge cases, and step splits as key drivers. Scores alone thus hide much of what prompts do.
arxiv-2508-03778:
Ai and Zhang give a sharp spectral condition for Hamilton cycles in tough balanced bipartite graphs, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. A Hamilton cycle visits every vertex exactly once and returns. Spectral radius, the largest adjacency eigenvalue, can certify such cycles. Bipartite toughness measures how hard a graph is to split apart.

For balanced bipartite graphs with toughness at least one, they find the exact spectral threshold. Above it, a Hamilton cycle is guaranteed to exist. At the threshold, the extremal structure is pinned down as well. The result settles an open problem posed in prior work. It links eigenvalue bounds and toughness in a tight, complete way.
arxiv-2508-03878:
Matias Cattaneo and Rocío Titiunik introduced the regression discontinuity design for medical researchers in twenty twenty-five. This design exploits cutoffs in treatment assignment. When a measurement crossing a threshold decides treatment, patients just above and just below are nearly alike. Comparing them then reveals the treatment's causal effect. The design is a workhorse in economics and is spreading in medicine.

Their article explains the design's logic with a running medical example. The focus is on causal interpretation — what the comparison does and does not prove — with brief coverage of estimation and inference. The piece is a primer, meant to help medical scientists read and use discontinuity studies soundly, recognizing both their unusual credibility and their local scope.
arxiv-2508-04478:
Bernardino D'Amico and three co-authors ask who actually saves from insulation in twenty twenty-five. Cutting home energy demand is central to climate and fuel poverty policy. Efficiency upgrades do not save equally for everyone, though. The team applies causal machine learning to nationally representative data on English housing.

They estimate average and subgroup effects of wall insulation on gas use. On average, demand falls by as much as nineteen percent. Households with low energy burdens capture substantial savings. Households with high burdens see little or no reduction. The explanation is behavioral, not wasteful: squeezed families spend the savings on warmth they previously could not afford. Readers in energy policy get a distributional warning: headline savings hide who was cold.
arxiv-2508-05878:
Martyna Majchrzak and Jacek Mańdziuk ask whether fake music can teach computers to hear chords. Recognizing chord sequences in recordings is a standard task in music technology, but training data is scarce because most recordings are copyrighted. Artificial multitrack music, generated rather than composed, offers a legal substitute.

The team trained two transformer-based models on mixes of three datasets: the artificial set, a dataset of Schubert songs, and a pop chart collection. They scored the models on how well they named chord roots, chord types, and full chord content. Artificial data alone could train a model that reads pop chords respectably when nothing else is available. Mixed with a small human-made set, it strengthened results further. The authors note that generated music is simpler than composed music, so it cannot replace real recordings outright.
arxiv-2508-07378:
Paul Mella studies a question in geometry and dynamics in a twenty twenty-five paper. He looks at the geodesic flow on curved surfaces and spaces known as Riemannian manifolds. The question is whether ergodic measures, a special kind of invariant measure, are generic there. Generic here means that almost all such measures have that property.

Mella gives a new condition under which the answer is no. If the metric splits as a product near a certain complete submanifold with a closed geodesic, the ergodic measures fail to fill the whole set. His result answers a question tied to a specific three-dimensional example from Gromov. Readers in dynamics get a clean test for when genericity breaks down.
arxiv-2508-07978:
Hamidreza Mazandarani and co-authors present, in a 2025 paper, a joint plan for placing image-generating AI services on edge servers and sharing access to them. Diffusion models make rich images but need many costly steps, which strains real-time mobile use. Their framework splits the cleaning steps of generation across mixed edge machines.

A learning algorithm moves service pieces as demand shifts, while cutting steps when quality allows. A greedy access rule joins a deep learning placement method that weighs reward now and later. Sending the hidden image state between servers adds cost, which the model counts. Simulations beat fixed, single-server plans on scale and delay, the authors report.
arxiv-2508-09478:
Moinak Bhattacharya, Gagandeep Singh, Shubham Jain, and Prateek Prasanna present GazeLT, a method that uses radiologist eye gaze to sort chest X-ray diseases, with stress on rare classes. A reader's gaze holds both fine and broad disease clues, and it shifts over the read. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Experts also glance at minor finds, which make up many rare classes. GazeLT folds gaze in and out over time to mimic that search. Tests on two large public sets for rare class sorting beat the best rare class loss by a clear margin. It also beat a gaze based baseline by a far larger margin, the authors report.
arxiv-2508-09578:
Ai-Jun Ma and Wen-Fei Wang calculate a subtle effect in the decays of B mesons, heavy particles whose breakup patterns test the Standard Model, in this 2025 physics paper. Inside some three body decays, a short lived resonance can act while off its natural mass, and such virtual steps can sway the outcome more than expected. The authors study that effect for one resonance in two decay families.

Working inside a standard calculation framework, they first derive the needed coupling strengths from a known cousin coupling, using flavor symmetry. The predicted rates for the virtual channels come out extremely small, in a range experiments cannot yet reach. One family lands at about half the rate of the other, mostly from space for the products. Data from two running experiments are expected soon.
arxiv-2508-10278:
Dark matter may collide with itself, and simulating that process inside dense halos is slow with standard methods. Sarah Schon and co-authors present a hybrid scheme that switches to fluid equations where the gas of particles is dense. A local measure of particle crowding sets where each method runs. The switch targets the deep collapse stage of halo centers, where density climbs steeply.

The hybrid runs reached center densities about a hundred times higher in much less time. Results looked much like those from older methods, though details of the halo shape differed. The authors call this a first step and plan to add non-ideal fluid effects. The method could open collapse studies in varied, changing settings.
arxiv-2508-11078:
Yacine Mokhtari tackles network design problems with tree-shaped backbones in this 2025 paper. Many flow networks must ride on a spanning tree, a choice that explodes combinatorially. The test case limits how many hops each delivery may take across shared goods.

The method relaxes the yes-no choices into smooth values and glues them to a tree answer through a penalty scheme. Each round solves a smooth subproblem, then snaps the result to the cheapest valid tree, a fast classical step. A distributed twin lets agents cooperate by local messages alone. Experiments found near-best designs in many cases. The author frames the approach as a practical heuristic for large, hard design problems.
arxiv-2508-13278:
Fabio La Monaca and co-authors measure the polarization of X-rays from a neutron star system called GX 340+0, a bright member of the Z-source class. Three space telescopes took part, one built to read polarization and two that read spectra. The team studied the source in its normal branch state and compared it with an earlier horizontal branch reading.

The light was clearly polarized in both states. The share fell from about 3.7 percent in the horizontal branch to about 1.4 percent in the normal branch. The angle stayed on the same trend. The glowing gas component blamed for much of the signal was more polarized than plain theory predicts for a boundary layer. The authors suggest a wind or an extended corona above the disk adds to the signal, and they argue polarization data sharpen our picture of how such stars feed.
arxiv-2508-13378:
Yiting Wang and co-authors set out a deployment plan for small language models in medical imaging in a 2025 paper. The head title frames the work as governance-ready models, covering prompting, abstention, and hospital system integration. Small models suit narrow imaging chores where privacy, speed, and cost rule. Their test task is tagging chest X-rays by view direction, a small but real workflow job.

Four compact vision-language models were tried on a public chest X-ray set. Prompts that made the model reflect helped the lighter models most. Stronger models cared less about prompt style. The authors stress measures beyond accuracy: how often the model abstains, how well its confidence matches its hit rate, and how much human oversight it needs. Outputs are mapped to hospital data standards so results slot into record systems. The plan is offered as a playbook, not as clinical proof.
arxiv-2508-13678:
Xiao-Wen Yang and a large team survey neuro-symbolic methods for fixing the reasoning of large language models. Fluent models still stumble on logic, planning, and multi-step deduction. Marrying neural learning with symbolic machinery is a leading remedy. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the survey first formalizes what reasoning tasks demand, then introduces the neuro-symbolic paradigm. Methods are sorted by the direction of the marriage. Some feed symbolic structure into the model. Others extract symbolic artifacts from it. A third family runs the two in tight partnership.

The review closes with open challenges and promising directions. A public repository collects the papers and resources. The intended reader is a researcher choosing where symbolic scaffolding can still move the needle on machine reasoning, a milestone on the road the authors link to general intelligence.
arxiv-2508-14178:
Flavio Benevenuto da Silva Junior and Anderson Caproni wrote a study from 2025 on a bright, jetting galaxy core named AO 0235+164. Such cores, called blazars, fire a thin jet of fast matter close to our line of sight. The jet of this one seems to swing slowly, like a wobbling top. The pair studied public radio maps made at two bands.

They tracked thirty-six parts of the jet and measured how each part moved across the sky. A model in which the jet swings in a steady circle fit the motion well. One swing took about eight years, close to a cycle long seen in the light of the core. The pair suggest that two giant black holes at the core may drive the swing, though they note other causes could fit too.
arxiv-2508-15678:
Ronald Richman, Salvatore Scognamiglio, and Mario V. Wüthrich propose a new neural network design in this 2025 paper. Their model, called a Tree-like Pairwise Interaction Network, is built for tabular data where pairs of features matter together. Insurance pricing is their main example, since rates there depend on how risk factors combine.

The network copies the shape of decision trees while learning only pairwise effects between features. Because of that design, a user can inspect the interaction effects directly instead of treating the model as a black box. Scores that explain each prediction are also cheap to compute. On a well-known French motor insurance dataset, the model beat both older methods and modern neural networks in accuracy, while still showing how each feature pair shaped the price.
arxiv-2508-17478:
Xuhao Shan and nine co-authors, including Changmiao Wang, predict patient outcomes by fusing several kinds of medical data inside a graph neural network. Prognosis improves when imaging, clinical, and molecular data speak to each other, but their structures differ wildly. Modeling those cross-modal relationships, near and far, is the core difficulty.

GraphMMP builds feature graphs using mutual information to decide which features connect. A global fusion module based on the Mamba architecture then mixes information across the whole graph. The two-stage design targets both local interactions and global dependencies. On liver prognosis data and the METABRIC breast cancer study, the model surpassed existing methods, supporting the fusion strategy.
arxiv-2508-17578:
Job Feldbrugge and Ue-Li Pen examine the hidden paths that shape how a quantum particle crosses or bounces off a step in potential energy. In the Feynman path integral picture, allowed motion follows real classical paths, while forbidden motion is carried by complex paths called instantons. The authors study these complex paths in a smooth step and in a sharp one, following their role in the particle's propagator.

The complex paths turn out to have a rich structure: they connect to caustics and can vanish as plain solutions when they strike a singularity of the potential. By widening the definition into equivalence classes, the authors track the paths past such crossings and identify the instanton behind quantum reflection. Most complex contributions are tiny, but some survive at full strength into the classical limit. The authors also give ways to detect these paths from propagation amplitudes.
arxiv-2508-19778:
The ATLAS Collaboration hunts for physics past the Standard Model with anomaly spotting in busy lepton events. The paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. The search takes proton clash data from the full Run 2 at the LHC. It asks for ends with at least four light leptons.

Event kinds are split by shape, and untrained machine learning flags the odd ones out, with no model in mind. No clear excess past the known background shows. Bounds are set in a model-free way for each shape, and on set test models, from kin of known leptons to smuons. One flavour-rich model gets its first bound here.
arxiv-2508-19878:
Brains made of light could compute with far less energy, and disorder may be a feature, not a bug. Matthew Wilson and three co-authors built a tiny learning chip in a 2025 paper whose core is a stadium-shaped cavity where light bounces chaotically. The input is written into the color of laser light entering the cavity, and the scattered speckle pattern at a surrounding wall serves as the readout layer.

Because the cavity's response shifts wildly with tiny color changes, the speckles carry rich information. On four different classification tests the device performed well, and widening the readout area let the team tune it per task. The work shows wave chaos as a practical computing resource.
arxiv-2508-19978:
Fabrizio Sgobba and co-authors demonstrate momentum-resolved two-photon interference with weak coherent states, in a research paper from 2025. Hong-Ou-Mandel interference is a classic quantum optics effect used for precise position sensing. Its range is limited by how alike the two photons are, since distinct photons stop interfering in the usual setup.

Their scheme resolves the transverse momentum of photon pairs with single-photon detector arrays. Fourth-order correlations then recover interference even for independent, partly distinct photons. Results are checked against the best precision bounds from quantum estimation theory. The method extends sensing range and suits high-resolution imaging. It also eases demands in quantum information tasks.
arxiv-2508-20378:
William Detmold, Rohan Kanchana, and Cagin Yunus study the spread of paired reads from grid runs of the strong force, for systems with one to four heavy parts. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

Such paired reads are the raw stuff from which masses and traits are drawn. Their true spread is not known for this theory. Past work found tail forms for the spread in simpler theories. The team tests if those forms fit the real data. With many stats tests, they find the simple model's forms fit well at zero momentum, across a wide span of gaps in time. The fit holds most of all at large gaps.
arxiv-2508-21578:
Mosquera and Sanz-Vicario analyze how electrons and nuclei entangle in molecules in a 2025 paper. A molecule can be seen as two linked parts, one electronic and one nuclear. The authors compare several standard ways of writing the joint wave function, using simple models that include the hydrogen molecular ion. A math split method lets them measure entanglement with an entropy score.

Ground state molecules under the classic split look almost separable, with little entanglement, they find. Exciting the nuclear motion raises entanglement step by step. Sharp changes in the electronic wave shape across nuclear positions raise it further. Crossings between energy curves boost it strongly in one picture but far less in another. Readers learn what drives a hidden link inside molecules.
arxiv-2509-00278:
Maria Chudnovsky, David Eppstein, and David Fischer study string graph obstacles in 2025 among graphs of restricted girth and degree. A string graph records which curves in a plane cross each other. An obstacle is a graph that is not a string graph, but becomes one after any single edge contraction or vertex deletion.

Kratochvíl's known obstacles hold huge cliques, so their girth is three and degree is unbounded. The team builds an infinite family of obstacles with girth four that also avoid a set pattern and sit near planar. They prove a subcubic obstacle of girth three exists, and none exist at high girth. Subcubic string graphs are characterized, with a fast recognition method to match.
arxiv-2509-00578:
Abdellah Zakaria Sellam leads six authors in total, with Ilyes Benaissa, Salah Eddine Bekhouche, Abdenour Hadid, Vito Reno, and Cosimo Distante, in improving car damage detection from images. Fine damage is hard to spot reliably, even for human experts, and context can decide whether a mark counts as damage.

Sellam and his co-authors build C-DiffDet+, which extends a diffusion-based detector that refines guesses by denoising, removing noise step by step. Their Context-Aware Fusion uses cross-attention, a way for each object proposal to weigh scene information, to blend global scene context from a separate encoder with local features. Results on the CarDD benchmark beat leading models and set new marks for context-aware detection.
arxiv-2509-00678:
Qintong Xie, with three co-authors, Edward Koh, Xavier Cadet, and Peter Chin, presents a Nash Q-Network for cybersecurity simulation. Defense pits defenders against hackers, so multi-agent reinforcement learning, where several learners adapt at once, fits well, but simultaneous training in complex settings is unstable and non-stationary.

Xie and his co-authors design a policy-based Nash Q-learning method meant to converge directly onto a steady equilibrium, a strategy pair neither side wants to leave. Their network blends ideas from proximal policy optimization, deep Q-networks, and the Nash-Q algorithm. In a two-player zero-sum Markov game, a contest where one side's gain is the other's loss, distributed data collection and tailored architectures yield robust defenses.
arxiv-2509-00778:
