Pair ranks fit how staff sort a queue by eye. For health teams, the set gives a fair way to test tools that may one day help sort notes by risk.
arxiv-2601-13278:
Don MacMillen gives a clear tour of a neat quantum case, an electron held between two grounded planes. The case joins two famed toy systems. One is the bit in a box, a free bit in a closed space. The other is the Coulomb pull, the force from a lone charge. The third famed toy, he notes, is the harmonic spring.

Here an electron sits in the gap of an endless capacitor, two flat plates held at zero volts. MacMillen works out the allowed energies and wave forms for that bind. Such toy cases teach how bind shape sets the ladder of states. For physics students, the piece is a bridge from first toys to a more rich real set up.
arxiv-2601-13378:
Lucas Pasquevich, Gustavo E. Romero, and Matias M. Reynoso ask if hid ultra bright X-ray sources in our galaxy beam neutrinos at Earth. Such sources shine in X-rays past the cap for a star mass hole fed at a calm rate. The lead view is that they are binaries fed too fast.

At that feed rate, trap of light puffs the disk thick. A thick disk can hide the core from most views, hence a hid source. The team models if such hid cores can still beam neutrinos, bits that pass through the puff with ease. A find would give a new way to see cores that light cannot leave.
arxiv-2601-13578:
Qian Feng, JiaHang Tu, and co-authors study a hard task for trained AI models in 2026. When users ask for their data to be deleted, the model must forget it step by step. Old methods often block some weights or scramble what the model knows. The team notes that such forgetting can stay shallow, with traces of the data still left to find.

Their method, called FG-OrIU, adds rules at two levels at once. It guides both the learned features and the gradients, the signals used in training. The aim is deeper forgetting that still keeps the rest of the model's skill intact. Weak forgetting, they warn, can risk leaks and harm trust in the model.
arxiv-2601-13878:
Hossein Safi and co-authors show a gigabit Ethernet link sent through open air with light in 2026. The link runs both ways at one gigabit per second over a one-meter free-space path. It uses a VCSEL-PIN pair, a laser source and a light sensor. All parts are commercially available, with no amplification.

The transparent system ran error-free in their tests. Latency stayed under twenty-five nanoseconds, a very short delay. Alignment tolerance reached the centimetre scale, so aim need not be perfect. Simple optical links like this could join boards or racks without cables.
arxiv-2601-14078:
Mathieu Lehaut, Anca Muscholl, and Nir Piterman revisit how to split asynchronous automata across machines in 2026. Zielonka's asynchronous automata model systems whose parts run at their own pace. Distribution splits one automaton into local parts that communicate. The team works in restricted settings with tree-like process architectures.

An architecture is tree-like if a spanning tree underlies it and communications stay local on the tree. They show a simple, quadratic distribution construction for this case. They also revisit synthesis for such automata. Tree-like layouts fit sensor nets and modular robots well. Quad cost is low for a build of this kind. That makes the method fit for large nets with many small parts.
arxiv-2601-14278:
Marc Walden, Jason Liu, Ryan Liu, and Hamza Khan model campus access in this 2026 paper. Their concern is students who use wheelchairs. Stairs and steep slopes make many campus paths hard or barred. The team wants a map of routes that work for all.

They build the campus as a network on a graph whose edges carry time weights. Data come from Strava and other APIs, merged into one model. A depth-first search then walks the graph to find paths. The aim is clear insight into which routes are wheelchair-accessible. Such a map can guide both daily trips and campus planning.
arxiv-2601-14378:
Erin Motherway and seven co-authors describe an odd binary star in this 2026 paper. The system is 2M07515777+1807352, a post-common envelope eclipsing binary. Its orbit takes 10.3 days and is nearly, but not quite, circular. The pair holds a massive white dwarf of 1.08 solar masses. Its partner is a main-sequence star of 0.66 solar masses at 4,400 kelvin.

A white dwarf that heavy should be compact. This one is oversize for its mass, which is why the title calls it a not-so-compact companion. The team gives a detailed characterization of the system. Readers get measured facts on a pair that tests how such binaries evolve.
arxiv-2601-14478:
Sasha Ronaghi and a team of health researchers study AI help for qualitative research in this 2026 paper. Large language models show promise for improving the efficiency of qualitative analysis in large, multi-site health-services research. Yet guidance on how to integrate them into that work is limited. Evidence of their impact on real research methods and outcomes is also scarce.

The team developed a model- and task-agnostic framework for human-LLM qualitative analysis. It is designed to support diverse analytic aims. Their title stresses scale and rigor together. Readers get a method for using language models on interview and field data without giving up the care qualitative work demands.
arxiv-2601-14578:
Naoki Seto studies gravitational waves from double white dwarfs in this 2026 paper. He investigates the detectability of post-Newtonian higher harmonics from Galactic double white dwarfs in the centihertz band, near 0.01 hertz. The quadrupole mode is the main signal such pairs emit. Higher harmonics are weaker overtones that carry extra detail about the orbit.

Using a synthetic population of these systems, Seto reaches a clear verdict. Unlike the quadrupole mode, higher harmonics remain undetectable with LISA, except for rare nearby systems. His title frames the upside: those harmonics could link LISA and DECIGO, two planned detectors in distinct bands. Readers get a sober forecast for a hoped-for signal.
arxiv-2601-14678:
Justin Cheung, Samuel Savine, Calvin Nguyen, Lin Lu, and Alhassan S. Yasin study cancer classifiers in this 2026 paper. Supervised deep learning models often perform excellently within their training distribution. They struggle to generalize beyond it. In cancer histopathology, a convolutional neural network may classify cancer severity accurately for cancer types in its training data. It may fail on related but unseen types.

The team applies transfer learning from one cancer to another via deep learning domain adaptation. Domain adaptation retunes a model so skill gained on one data source carries to a distinct one. Readers get a test of whether a severity classifier for one cancer can be adapted to serve another.
arxiv-2601-14978:
Nilanjana Chatterjee, Sidharatha Garg, A. V. Subramanyam, and Brejesh Lall work on finding a person from a written description. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with text-based person search. Vision-language models drive the field, but the training data stays small.

These models also were not pre-trained for spotting pedestrians. So each dataset gets its own fine-tuned model, shaped to that dataset alone. The authors train one model across many datasets at once. One single unified model then serves all of them well, instead of a whole shelf of separate, narrow, single-use models.
arxiv-2601-15078:
Juan J. Segura turns the study of myth into math. His 2026 arXiv paper deals with structural approaches to story, in the line of Lévi-Strauss. Such readings are strong up close but hard to compare across cultures, media, and scale.

Segura builds a formal frame that keeps the reading clear. Myth variants become typed rewrite programs. Each runs on a two-register state. One register holds the everyday social channel. The other holds the symbolic channel that grants legitimacy. Superhero continuities and long franchise arcs both fit the same formal frame well.
arxiv-2601-15278:
Mingyue Zha and Ho-Chun Herbert Chang read TikTok videos as full messages, not as separate tracks. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with short-form video and mental health discourse. A post mixes text, visuals, and audio into one communicative act.

Past work tends to study those parts in isolation. The authors build a pipeline that joins them. Automated tools extract features from all three modes. Shapley value methods then show how each mode drives engagement. The study scales that joint reading to a large set of real, public TikTok videos on health.
arxiv-2601-15378:
S. Sartori, S. Contarini, and co-authors find cosmic voids by running the universe backwards. Their 2026 arXiv paper deals with voids, the vast underdense regions between galaxies. Voids are a powerful probe of cosmology, but they are hard to pin down.

Their size and emptiness make them sensitive to shot noise and redshift distortions. Observational systematics add more trouble, above all for density-based definitions. The Back-in-time Void Finder uses optimal transport reconstruction. It rebuilds the past density field, then identifies the voids in that cleaner, rebuilt early-time picture of the cosmos.
arxiv-2601-15778:
Jiaxin Zhang, Caiming Xiong, and Chien-Sheng Wu study confidence in AI agents in a 2026 arXiv paper. Agents are moving from passive models to autonomous systems. They execute complex, multi-step tasks on their own. Overconfidence in failure remains a fundamental barrier to high-stakes use. An agent that does not know it is failing will not stop or ask for help. Existing calibration methods were built for static, single-turn outputs.

Agent runs break those methods' assumptions. Errors compound along trajectories. External tools inject their own uncertainty. Failure modes stay opaque across long runs. The title names the goal: agentic confidence calibration. Calibrated agents could slow down, verify, or escalate when doubt grows. That behavior is a precondition for trusting agents with real work.
arxiv-2601-15878:
Antonis Kalogirou studies a scalar field's heat effects in de Sitter space in a 2026 arXiv paper. It is Part II of a series. The setting is the Poincaré patch of de Sitter spacetime. He uses the thermo-field dynamics approach to compute semiclassical backreaction. Backreaction means the field's energy reshapes the spacetime it lives in. The resulting bulk equation takes Whittaker form, a known special-function shape.

Two applications follow. At leading order, curvature perturbations match a constant-roll model in its frozen attractor regime. That match gives an ultraviolet enhancement of the spectrum. The spectral index there runs near two. The second application concerns holography, per the title. Early-universe physics uses such models to explain the seeds of cosmic structure.
arxiv-2601-16178:
Luca Di Persio, Matteo Garbelli and Adrian Zălinescu link late growth tasks to back and forth chance maths. Their 2026 preprint deals with growth tasks that rest on the whole past path. Edge terms are of the Neumann type, which set flow at the rim. The chance maths pair a forth path with a back path. The forth path holds a bounce part writ as a Stieltjes sum.

The team shows the pair solves the growth task in the mild sense. Mild means the task holds in sum form, not point by point. Such links let chance tools solve hard path tasks. They also give ways to price path based claims. The work joins two fields that oft sit apart.
arxiv-2601-16278:
Branislav Pecher and five coauthors use large models as makers, not judges, for low stock tongues. Their 2026 preprint deals with text sorts in tongues with scant tagged data. Large models show strong skill in many tongues. Small sort models need tagged data that such tongues oft lack. The team has the large model make fake tagged texts.

Small models then train on the fake set for the sort task. The test checks if fake train beats use of the large model as judge. Fake data may give strong small tools at low cost. That path serves tongues left out of big data sets. The work weighs maker use as the best role.
arxiv-2601-16378:
Bridget Leonard and Scott Murray use mind based tokens to fix self view bias in joint models. Their 2026 preprint deals with models that join pics and words. Such models do well on sense tasks that join the two. They fail on space tasks that need the view of an other. That fail is a self view bias that will not fade with scale.

Tokens drawn from mind study aim to break that bias. The tokens push the model to hold an other view in mind. Gains would show that form cues can fix space thought. Space thought counts for robots and aid tools in real rooms. The work tests a low cost fix path.
arxiv-2601-16678:
Avraham Gal pays tribute to three late leaders in a niche field of nuclear physics. Tullio Bressani, Bogdan Povh, and Toshimitsu Yamazaki all died in the past two years. Each helped shape the study of strange nuclei. These are nuclei that hold a strange quark for a brief span. Gal's 2026 talk text honors their lives and work.

The piece traces the field from its start in the 1970s. Groups at CERN used beams to make the strange nuclei in flight. Later work moved to labs in the United States. Gal also notes the record of Yoshinori Akaishi, who died in 2025. The text serves as a brief past of the field.
arxiv-2601-16778:
Simon Lämmer, Mark Colley, and Patrick Ebel build fake crowds to test travel plans. How folks pick buses, cars, or bikes is hard to gauge. Taste, norms, and faith in new tech all play a part. Old ways use fixed rules and dear field polls. Their 2026 preprint swaps those rules for AI agents that act like folks.

Each agent weighs trips with its own tastes and traits. Crowds of them then show how a town may move. Planners can test new tech or rules in this fake town. That test costs far less than a real trial. It may steer green travel plans with more care.
arxiv-2601-16878:
Tim Johnston and Pierre Monmarché build a safe step rule for chance flows with sharp traits. Such flows drive grain packs in physics and trade. Their drift traits can spike to huge size in spots. Plain Euler steps fail to track such flows. Proof of sound steps was thin on the ground. Their 2026 preprint gives a tamed Euler rule with proofs.

A Lyapunov gauge, a kind of energy cap, tames the steps. The drift's slope must sit below such a cap. That need still lets drift blow up in a fin zone. Tamed steps let sims run where plain steps die. Physics and risk teams gain a tool they can trust.
arxiv-2601-17078:
Aras Bacho, Svetlana Selivanova, and Martin Ziegler ask what fast-compute means for a class of functions. Their class holds functions whose square sums stay fin. Two plain takes on fast compute arise for them. Their 2026 preprint shows the two takes do not match. That split holds short of a famed count-class merge.

One take builds from digit reads of the function. The next builds from mean-square fits by fast nets. If the two takes split, terms in proofs must be picked with care. Such care shapes how real-number compute is taught. It also guards claims in numeric code work.
arxiv-2601-17278:
Wei-Shan Su and four co-authors model what a passing star does to dust in a young planet-forming disc. Stars are born in clusters, so flybys are common. A close pass can warp the gas disc. Its effect on dust is less clear, mostly when dust and gas are weakly linked. The team runs three-dimensional fluid simulations of such passes.

They test flat passes and tilted passes side by side. They track how dust moves and clumps after each pass. Clumping feeds the streaming instability, a step toward planet birth. The results help link disc shapes seen today to past flybys. They also guide hunts for young systems shaped by a near miss.
arxiv-2601-17378:
Mohammad Zare and Pirooz Shamsinejadbabaki test privacy in federated learning. In that setup, data stays on user devices and only model updates move. It sounds private by design. Membership inference attacks test that claim. An attacker asks if one sample was in the training set. The authors present Res-MIA, an attack that needs no training of its own.

Their attack rests on resolution, a trait of how models treat data. If the attack works, private facts can leak from shared models. Health and finance models face the most risk. The work gives defenders a new test to run. It shows where federated claims need proof, not trust.
arxiv-2601-17678:
Zhiyu An and Wan Du study inverse mechanism learning. The task is to recover a hidden incentive mechanism from observed play. Self-interested agents learn and act under that mechanism. Their traces are the data. Past inverse work infers rewards inside a known structure. Here the target can be unstructured, even a neural map.

A differentiable method, DIML, learns the mechanism from trajectories. It works across multi-agent learning paths. Knowing the true incentives helps audit markets and platforms. Designers can check if rules drive the play they see. The work widens inverse game theory to black-box rules. That matches modern platforms, whose rules are learned, not written.
arxiv-2601-18278:
Indrė Žliobaitė asks what a learned model really measures when it is used as an instrument. Her 2026 preprint addresses a shift in how models are used. In science and data work, models now often serve as measurement tools, not just predictors of set labels. When the measurement rule is learned from data, the map from observations to quantities is set by the training mix and the model's biases. Several unlike maps can fit the same data. Žliobaitė examines what that freedom means for trust in the readings.

A measure whose meaning shifts with its training set is a shaky instrument. Naming the problem is the first step to standards for learned measurement. The work speaks to any field that reads nature through a model.
arxiv-2601-18378:
Takahiro Yamamoto studies a space task that aims to hear a faint hum from the young cosmos. The craft, called DECIGO, will listen for waves in space in a band where pairs of dense dead stars make a loud front noise. Those pairs spiral in and merge, and their waves crowd the band.

To hear the faint hum, staff must first strip that front noise away. Yamamoto checks how well that strip can work. He bases the check on what a past run of ground based sensors has taught us about such pairs. The count of pairs and their traits set how much noise is left. If too much noise stays, the old hum stays hid. If the strip works well, the craft could open a new view on the first age of the cosmos.
arxiv-2601-18678:
Eslam Zaher and three colleagues hone a way to tell a user what small change would flip a model's call. Such a tale, called a counterfactual, should be small, close to real cases, and in line with how the facts hang as one. Past ways pick the change by a flat gap count. A flat count can pick changes that look near on the page but could never occur in life.

The team pick the change by a path that rides the true shape of the data. That shape is built from how real cases spread in the model's hid space. A path on that shape keeps the tale in the world of real cases. Such tales could help a user act: to gain a loan, say, by a change they can truly make. Fair tales count for trust in smart calls.
arxiv-2601-18878:
Eugenio Carretta mines an old sky hunt's data to pull fresh counts of four kinds of stuff in a huge set of stars. The hunt was famed for a find that split old star groups in two by their light stuff: each group holds more than one crowd of stars, with un-like mixes. That find set the field's view of such groups for a score of years. Its shots still hold more than was pulled at the time.

Carretta pulls the counts of four mid-weight kinds of stuff for a vast set of red big stars in a score of groups. All counts are made in one way, so group can be set next to group with trust. The four kinds split by how they were made: some in calm burn, some in blasts. A clean, wide set is a gift to that work.
arxiv-2601-18978:
José Ignacio Burgos Gil and three co-authors close in on a stubborn number in number theory. For height functions, which grade how complex a point is, the essential minimum is a key floor value. For many common heights, no one has pinned that floor down in exact terms.

The team pairs two old routes. One is a lower bound method that goes back to Smyth. The other is an upper bound method based on how whole points spread out in the limit. Joining the two with linear programming narrows the gap. Each closed gap sharpens what number theorists can say about the smallest, simplest points of a given kind.
arxiv-2601-19178:
Jingyu Li and seven co-authors share cached memory across steps in sequential recommendation. Models that suggest the next item from a user's history lean on transformer attention. That math grows costly as histories lengthen, which hurts response time for long sequences.

Key-value caching, borrowed from language models, stores past work for reuse. Their method, CollectiveKV, decouples and shares that cached data across the team of computations. Shared caches could let recommenders read long histories at a price that products with strict speed limits can pay. The gain comes from not recomputing the same past steps again and again for each new pick the system must make.
arxiv-2601-19378:
Ziyang Xu and seven co-authors build an open encyclopedia of skin pathology images with an AI run workflow. Clinicians and trainees in dermatopathology often struggle to find high quality open image sets for learning and cross checking. Good sets are scattered, small, or locked away.

Their resource, DermpathNet, aims to be comprehensive and open for teaching, reference, and machine learning alike. An AI based workflow helps gather and organize the images at scale. Open, well ordered image sets lift both training of doctors and training of the models that may one day assist them.
arxiv-2601-19778:
Ahmad Farooq and Kamran Iqbal argue that peer review in software engineering research is in crisis. Submissions keep growing, incentives are misaligned, and reviewers are exhausted. Surveys report that researchers see the process as broken. The authors frame these failures as mechanism design problems, the study of how rules shape behaviour.

If the rules are the problem, better rules can be computed. Their position paper proposes a multi-agent mechanism design approach to reimagining review. Agents could match papers to reviewers and balance loads under clear incentives. The argument is programmatic: it sets out a direction rather than a finished system. It speaks to a debate every research community is having about its own gatekeeping.
arxiv-2601-20078:
R. N. Robert Bush, J. T. John Stefan, and A. G. Alexander Kosovichev investigate shock waves in the Sun's corona that appear without an eruption. A leading theory ties sunquakes to flare-accelerated particles dumping energy into the visible surface. Simulations suggest such events also excite wavefronts travelling through the corona and chromosphere. These resemble the classic Moreton-Ramsey waves and the large-scale fronts seen sweeping the corona.

The puzzle is extreme ultraviolet shockwaves with no coronal mass ejection behind them. If no eruption launched them, something else must. The authors investigate observations to test the flare-driven account. Coronal waves are diagnostics of the Sun's magnetic atmosphere. Explaining the orphan waves would complete a corner of flare physics.
arxiv-2601-20578:
Dimitris Michailidis, Sennay Ghebreab, and Fernando P. Santos ask who benefits when transport networks expand, using congestion games with learning agents. Bigger networks are meant to improve mobility, yet they can also create inequality. The authors show that disparities arise not only from the shape of the network but also from how commuters adapt to it.

Different travelers learn and adjust at different rates and in different ways. Those differences can leave some groups with worse trips after an upgrade. The finding warns planners that a fair network on paper can still play out unfairly in daily use.
arxiv-2601-20778:
Lisa Marquand and Sasha Viktorova construct new families of a classic object in algebraic geometry. Their 2026 paper studies cubic fourfolds, shapes cut out by a cubic equation. The authors focus on smooth cubic fourfolds that contain highly singular hyperplane sections. A hyperplane section is the shape left when a flat cut passes through.

The pair construct five irreducible divisors in the moduli space of such fourfolds. Each divisor parametrizes fourfolds with one of these singular sections. They then prove that none of the five is a Noether-Lefschetz or Hassett divisor. The proof uses a computational method due to Addington and Auel. The result adds new landmarks to the map of how cubic fourfolds can vary.
arxiv-2601-20978:
Omid Khosravi and Mehdi Tatari solve a wave equation with neural networks that respect physics. Their 2026 paper studies the one-dimensional advection equation. Advection describes a quantity carried along by a flow. The hard cases here have discontinuous initial and boundary conditions. Sharp jumps are where physics-informed neural networks, or PINNs, often struggle. Spectral bias makes them favor smooth answers over sharp ones.

The authors stack three techniques against that bias. A Fourier feature mapping layer feeds the network richer inputs. A two-stage training strategy tunes the features first, then the weights. Adaptive loss weighting balances the terms during training. Together the steps help the network honor sudden jumps. The work serves engineers who simulate transport with learned solvers.
arxiv-2601-21178:
Antonio Smecca examines whether a broken symmetry of QCD heals as matter heats up. The 2026 paper studies the axial U(1) symmetry at finite temperature. In the massless QCD Lagrangian, this symmetry is explicit. Quantization breaks it through the anomaly. At some finite temperature, it may be effectively restored. That restoration would carry important consequences. It would bear on the order of the chiral transition and the QCD phase diagram.

Mesonic correlators are the probe. These functions track how quark-antiquark pairs behave in hot matter. Their patterns differ depending on whether the symmetry is restored. Heavy-ion collisions create such heat for an instant. Lattice simulations can compute the correlators directly. Smecca's study helps read those signals. The result feeds the map of matter at extreme temperature.
arxiv-2601-21278:
Mohit Talreja and nine co-authors test whether vision models can explain how they guess where a photo was taken. The best models now rival top human players at naming the place. Yet many give poor reasons for their guess, even when the guess itself is right.

Their benchmark, GeoRC, grades the chain of evidence behind each answer. A model must point to the clues in the image that support its call. Right answers with wrong reasons reveal luck rather than skill. The benchmark pushes models toward answers that people can check, trust, and learn from.
arxiv-2601-21478:
Kang You builds a new way to model causal links in the brain from scalp recordings. Modeling how brain regions drive each other, from tiny circuits to the whole brain, is hard. Group comparisons make it harder, since wiring thousands of neurons cannot be modeled directly at that scale.

The author constructs differential causal networks straight from EEG data. The networks highlight where causal patterns differ between groups. That focus suits studies of illness, where the change from healthy wiring is the signal of interest. A direct route from raw traces to causal maps could speed clinical research.
arxiv-2601-21778:
Zijie Xu and co-authors examine a shortcut that often fails. Spiking neural networks can be made by converting an already trained ordinary network, which avoids costly retraining. That is attractive for reinforcement learning, where training through live interaction is expensive and can be unsafe.

In practice, though, converted networks perform poorly on continuous control, tasks where actions vary smoothly, like steering or balancing. The 2026 preprint studies how errors grow during conversion and what limits the method in these settings. Knowing where the shortcut breaks helps engineers decide when conversion is safe to use. And it points to what a better conversion method would need to fix first.
arxiv-2601-21978:
Shiqi Fan and co-authors work on reasoning over temporal knowledge graphs, networks of facts that change over time. The task is to predict future events by inferring missing entities as the graph evolves. Language model methods for this job tend to favor context over structure.

As a result, they struggle to pull the right subgraphs out of a dynamic graph, lose structural information, and produce unstructured, sometimes hallucinated reasoning. The team's 2026 preprint bridges graph structure with knowledge-guided editing to keep reasoning interpretable. Better temporal reasoning would help forecasting in finance, politics, and logistics. Where events build on chains of earlier facts that a model must respect, not invent.
arxiv-2601-22478:
Khiem Le and six co-authors lift a training method by showing it the same task in fresh dress. Their 2026 preprint notes that models learn by next-word prediction, which makes them pattern matchers at heart. A reworded task can trip them, though the core ask is the same.

Their tweak, Transform-Augmented GRPO, trains on such reworded forms. The aim is to lift Pass@k, the chance that one of a few tries is right. Robustness to wording is key for real use, where no two users ask alike. The work makes training match that fact.
arxiv-2601-22878:
Rajini Makam and four co-authors present DIVER, a method for cleaning up underwater photos. Underwater images fade and blur because water absorbs colors unevenly, scatters light, and lights scenes poorly. These problems shift with water type and depth, so one fixed fix rarely works.

DIVER blends hands-on corrections with a physics-guided model, and it learns without labeled examples. The design aims to work across many waters, not just the ones it trained on. Clearer images help divers, biologists, and robots inspect reefs, wrecks, and pipelines. The method is unsupervised, so it needs no hand-cleaned example images, which are almost impossible to gather underwater.
arxiv-2601-22978:
Jonathan Baumann and co-authors build a verified defense against speculative control-flow attacks. These attacks, of the Spectre family, trick a processor into leaking data while it guesses ahead. Their defense, SpecIBT, joins hardware control-flow checks with compiler-added hardening for risky loads.

The key insight is that hardware checks can flag exactly when a guess went wrong, so hardening applies only then. The whole defense is formally verified, meaning its safety is proved, not just tested. Proved defenses matter for chips that guard secrets. Compiler-inserted hardening is applied with precision, guided by exactly where the hardware protection says speculation went wrong.
arxiv-2601-23078:
Timo Feistl, Severin Schraven, and Simone Warzel prove symmetry-protection theorems for quantum lattice systems. The classic Mermin-Wagner result limits which symmetries can break in low dimensions. Their version covers systems with multipole symmetries, symmetries tied to higher moments of charge.

They show that higher-order symmetries protect lower-order ones from breaking. In particular, charge symmetry needs more dimensions to break when multipole symmetries are present. Such theorems set firm rules for what phases of quantum matter can exist. Higher multipole symmetries raise the critical dimension for breaking the charge symmetry, a concrete, checkable consequence.
arxiv-2601-23178:
Chenxi Kong, Michael Gurnis, and Zachary E. Ross run mantle convection both forward and backward with neural operators. Reconstructing the mantle's past thermal state means reversing convection, which is an important but very costly computation. Those reconstructions link seismic images with what we see at the surface.

Neural operators learn the convection mapping itself, making repeated runs far cheaper. Fast forward and inverse runs let geophysicists test many Earth histories against data. That speed could clarify how plates, plumes, and the deep Earth evolved. Seismic tomographic images supply the observations the reconstructions must respect, tying deep structure to present-day measurements.
arxiv-2602-00078: Piercosma Bisconti and Marcello Galisai examine the technical basis for trusted AI standards in the European Union under the AI Act. They explain how harmonized standards create a presumption of conformity, and they describe the CEN and CENELEC process. AI resists neat standards through random behavior, data dependence, weak test practice, and changing life cycles. Since AI tools sit inside larger social and technical systems, they urge layered standards with horizontal rules for process and sector profiles for thresholds.
arxiv-2602-00578: Matthew Bolan and Ben Williams prove the least degree among irreducible factors of a binomial t^n − α divides every other such degree. As a consequence, for relatively prime natural numbers m and n, any polynomial has the mn-Hartley condition exactly when it has both. These are the m-Hartley and n-Hartley conditions.
arxiv-2602-00878: Beatrice Franzolini and colleagues bound the work cost of Dirichlet process slice samplers with high probability. Slice sampling is a standard Monte Carlo tool for Dirichlet process models, but its per-iteration cost is random and maybe endless. Their main result shows slice-variable overhead, versus posterior cluster count, is log n across all cluster-growth regimes. Even in worst cases, superlinear blow-ups in per-iteration cost occur with tiny chance. The analysis covers Dirichlet process models broadly, with no likelihood assumptions, for sampling on any datasets.
arxiv-2602-01078: Tong Xia and co-authors build AutoHealth, a team of agents modeling health data alone and rating model surety. Past auto-model teams fit one data kind poorly, lean on fixed plans, and skip doubt scores, vital in care. Five agents loop through data looks, model builds, training, and tuning, chasing hit rate and doubt scores at once. The team also writes full reports for safe reads and risk-wise calls. On a hard real-world set of 17 jobs, it finished all and beat the best baselines.
arxiv-2602-01178: Elena Caviglia and co-authors stretch ideal-based normality from semirings to broad algebras with two new set kinds. Inductive and deductive sets match the two sides of Mal'tsev's test for a congruence class, giving ideal-hood and subtractivity back in semiring cases. Build rules via polynomials or semi-congruences yield two rank counts for steps needed across a family. Save for dull cases, any pair of counts or infinity shows up as a rank pair, with semirings at one pole and Mal'tsev families at the other.
arxiv-2602-01278: Zhengbo Zhang and co-authors build DSFC-Net, a twin-encoder net picking rural roads from sharp satellite pictures. Rural roads foil city-tuned plans with varied surfaces, leaf cover breaking road lines, and thin widths hiding roads. A convolutional branch catches fine road edges and short links, while a hybrid transformer tracks broad road webs through leaf gaps. A cross-frequency focus trick splits high and low frequency cues via a Laplacian pyramid, keeping thin links whole. Tests on three sets back its lead over top plans.
arxiv-2602-01378: Poushali Sengupta and co-authors build RISE, a redundancy-proof score for explaining language-model outputs. Big models draw on rich context full of repeats from prompts, retrieved passages, and chat history, yet standard explanation scores wobble when context parts overlap. Tiny input tweaks can swing credit wildly. RISE gauges each input's unique pull relative to the rest, damping repeat effects for clearer, steadier credit. Tests show RISE beating classic explanation plans on robustness, proving conditional info matters for trustworthy explanation and watch.
arxiv-2602-01478: Silvan Horvath and Tan Özalp introduce Laver ultrafilters, defined by Laver forcing having the Laver property. Simple characterizations place them among known classes, including P-points, rapid ultrafilters, and Baumgartner I-ultrafilters. The Laver class properly contains rapid P-points, yet sits inside both hereditarily rapid ultrafilters and measure zero ultrafilters. Finally, they study generic existence, bounding that number, and show it is consistent that P-points fail to exist while Laver ultrafilters exist generically.
arxiv-2602-01978: Roel Koopman and colleagues train spiking neural networks online with SpikingGamma, using smoothed delays and no surrogates. Neuromorphic hardware promises efficient low latency AI through sparse event computation, but fine temporal training remains hard, blocking hardware mapping. Current methods model spiking neurons as self recurrent units, training with BPTT or RTRL on surrogate gradients, scaling poorly with resolution. SpikingGamma combines neurons with recursive memory and sigma delta spike coding, with direct backpropagation. It learns fine temporal patterns with minimal spiking, scales feedforward networks to complex tasks at any resolution.
arxiv-2602-02078: Jean-Philippe Bouchaud retells econophysics origins through Benoît Mandelbrot, not as fractal father, but as spark of a posture. The guiding thread: accept stubborn data traits and use models for instinct rather than proofs. Scaling, bursts and peaks are no side flaws; they are economic swings' texture. Focus shifts to inside moves from outside tales: links, feedback, and boosting make systems deeply fragile. Taking concepts from physics, tipping, mess, arising, and growing chains, should be read not as fake transfer but as a candid search for generic gears.
arxiv-2602-02178: Liang Lin and others propose AR-MAP, a transfer method letting preference-aligned autoregressive language models teach diffusion language models. Aligning diffusion models straight is costly because likelihood figures from the evidence lower bound vary wildly. The team transfers match knowledge through simple weight scaling, exploiting the shared architecture between the two output paradigms. The method sidesteps both the variance and the compute burden of direct diffusion match. Across diverse preference match tasks, it matches or beats current diffusion-given methods with a strong average score.
arxiv-2602-02378: Raunak Jain argues reliable human-AI partnership in deep-uncertainty decisions requires moving from answer output to collaborative premise governance. It bakes in assumptions and pushes checking costs onto experts, but outcomes arrive too late to act as reward signals. Challenge allocated by value rations probing under contact cost, so trust attaches to auditable premises and evidence standards.
arxiv-2602-02578:
Baktiar Wasir Farooq and 3 co-authors release a small, open code for three-flavor neutrino oscillation studies, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Neutrinos switch among three flavors as they travel, and the pattern depends on a phase tied to CP violation, the matter-antimatter asymmetry in particle physics. Large toolkits simulate experiments, but their bulk hides the equations.

NeutrinoOsc3Flavor solves the Schrödinger evolution equation directly in the flavor basis. It builds and diagonalizes the effective Hamiltonian in plain view, in both vacuum and constant-density matter, using only NumPy. A separate analytic check computes the matter-modified eigenvalues by the Cardano method and agrees closely with the numerical route. The phase dependence itself serves as a sharp check on numerical stability. The authors aim the tool at checking, teaching, and benchmarking rather than full experiment simulation.
arxiv-2602-02778:
Hao Meng and 2 co-authors weigh the dark matter halos hosting the universe's earliest quasars by measuring how strongly those quasars cluster, in a 2026 paper. The sample combines over twelve hundred spectroscopically confirmed quasars with over eight hundred machine-learning-selected candidates, all near the end of cosmic reionization.

Projected clustering gives large bias values in two redshift slices, translating into characteristic halo masses around ten to the twelfth point six solar masses. Quasar duty cycles come out near one percent in both slices. Only a small fraction of suitable halos host a luminous quasar at any moment. That scarcity suggests much supermassive black hole growth happens during obscured accretion phases, hidden from optical view. The measurements agree with earlier studies and the known duty-cycle relation, tightening constraints on how black holes and large-scale structure grew up together.
arxiv-2602-02878:
Junyi Jessy Li and 4 co-authors describe a new university course in a 2026 paper. The course joins discourse, the study of how language holds together across sentences, with natural language generation. Large language models have changed both fields, yet textbooks rarely connect discourse theory to long-form generation.

The team taught the course first in fall 2025 to advanced undergraduates. It was cross-listed between linguistics and computer science. Lessons mix theory with hands-on exploration, in class and in assignments. The paper details the design and reports survey feedback from an independent survey. It closes with lessons learned and plans for future versions of the course.
arxiv-2602-03078:
Four magnetars are tracked over seven years by Han-Long Peng and 11 co-authors in a 2026 paper. Magnetars are neutron stars with extreme magnetic fields, appearing as anomalous X-ray pulsars or soft gamma-ray repeaters. The team monitored four anomalous pulsars with the NICER telescope from twenty seventeen to twenty twenty-four, watching their rotation timing for sudden changes in spin behavior.

Ten timing events were identified in total. They include glitches, sudden spin-ups, anti-glitches, sudden spin-downs, and one unusual state transition. One source showed both anti-glitches, with hints of regular pulse profile evolution. Another continued to show frequent timing anomalies and underwent the state transition. Pulse profiles of two sources evolved over time, consistent with profile change being a generic magnetar feature.
arxiv-2602-03478:
Routing a question to a small cheap model or a large expensive one is supposed to save money. Guannan Lai and Han-Jia Ye document a failure of that idea in a 2026 paper. As budgets grow, routers default to the priciest model even when a cheaper one would do. They name this failure routing collapse, and it quietly wastes computation.

The authors trace the problem to a mismatch between training and decisions. Routers learn to predict scalar scores, but routing is a discrete comparison, so small scoring errors flip the ranking. Their EquiRouter learns model rankings directly instead. On RouterBench it reaches GPT-4-level quality at roughly 17 percent lower cost than the strongest earlier router.
arxiv-2602-03778:
Safety-critical control cares about the worst tail of outcomes, not the average, and that preference breaks the usual Bellman machinery. Aneri Muni and 4 co-authors repair it for conditional value-at-risk objectives in a 2026 paper. Static CVaR depends on whole trajectories, so naive state augmentation produces sparse rewards and degenerate fixed points.

Their reformulated augmentation yields a Bellman operator with dense per-step rewards. The operator contracts on the full space of bounded value functions, a cleaner foundation than earlier restricted versions. On top of it they build risk-averse value iteration and model-free Q-learning over discretized augmented states, with convergence guarantees and discretization error bounds. Experiments show the algorithms learn genuinely CVaR-sensitive policies.
arxiv-2602-03978:
Transparent reasoning may come free during training, or not. Zidi Xiong and 2 co-authors test when chain-of-thought traces truly reveal a model's internal work. Their 2026 study follows reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards across model families and training domains.

Monitorability improved in some settings but not everywhere. Data diversity and instruction-following data proved key. Clearer traces also did not track stronger performance; openness and skill moved independently. Mechanistic analysis credits sharper response distributions and closer attention to the prompt, not deeper reliance on the trace itself. The warning for safety checkers: do not assume readable traces mean honest ones.
arxiv-2602-04078:
Róisín Luo's 2026 doctoral thesis asks why neural networks resist small attacks and generalize to new data. The central tool is Lipschitz continuity, a bound on how much a network's output can change when its input changes slightly. That worst-case sensitivity governs both robustness and generalization in theory.

Earlier work mostly used Lipschitz ideas through empirical regularization tricks. Luo instead pursues the underlying principles directly, asking what the bound means for how networks should be designed and trained. The thesis aims to turn a widely used constraint into understood science, so robustness can be engineered rather than stumbled upon.
arxiv-2602-04178:
Coordinated gene programs across cell types drive development and immunity. Qi Xu and 2 co-authors estimate those multi-cellular programs with Sparse Group PCA in a 2026 paper. Existing methods are heavy to run and weak in power on huge expression datasets.

Their double-thresholding algorithm alternates between picking gene groups and picking active cell types within them, inside a power iteration. Cost grows only linearly with data size. Theory backs the estimator with guarantees on the components recovered. Group sparsity mirrors biology: whole pathways switch on, but only in the cell types where the program runs.
arxiv-2602-04278:
Training recommenders with reinforcement learning burns data most of which teaches little. Lin Wang and 6 co-authors present MiniRec, a data selection framework tailored to that setting, in a 2026 paper. Generic selection criteria based on loss or coverage misalign with how reinforcement learning actually improves.

MiniRec prunes samples that are too easy or hopelessly hard, judging learnability from reward signals. It keeps samples whose gradients align with the ideal global update direction, and enforces diversity. The goal is a small training set that drives real updates. Data-efficient training matters because language-model recommenders are expensive to tune at full scale.
arxiv-2602-04378:
The Frank-Wolfe algorithm cannot beat a certain speed on strongly convex problems, and Jannis Halbey and 5 co-authors prove it. Their 2026 paper constructs a lower bound matching the known guarantee when both objective and constraint set are smooth and strongly convex.

Extra assumptions about the optimizer's position allow faster linear convergence, but uniform improvement was in doubt. The authors study a strongly convex quadratic over the Euclidean ball with the optimizer on the boundary. A computational approach constructs worst-case trajectories, guiding an analytic proof. The matching bounds close the question: in this regime, Frank-Wolfe's classical rate is exactly right.
arxiv-2602-04678:
Forecasters need not only a best guess but also an honest range of uncertainty. Zhen Zhou and 5 co-authors build a multi-expert forecasting framework in a 2026 paper that predicts full probability distributions for time series instead of single values.

One variant uses several experts with different learned parameters to capture diverse temporal patterns. Another splits a series into interpretable parts: trend, seasonality, sudden changes, and volatility, each handled by specialized sub-experts. A distance measure between distributions drives the learning. On sales data from a major forecasting dataset, the continuous multi-expert version performed best overall. The pattern-aware version added interpretability through component-by-component analysis.
arxiv-2602-04978:
Siyan Daniel Li-Huerta wrote this 2026 mathematics paper, in English with an appendix by Peter Dillery, on a global version of p-adic Hodge theory. The setting is the Fargues-Fontaine curve, a geometric object that has reshaped number theory. Li-Huerta studies its analogue over function fields, where the curve parametrizes bundles tied to the global Langlands program.

The paper proves basic results about the space of G-bundles on this curve, which encodes a set of arithmetic data known as the global Kottwitz set. Using that space, the author restates the global Langlands conjecture in terms of a local categorical form, sharpening earlier conjectures by several groups. The new statement is then verified when the group is commutative. Along the way, the paper proves a GAGA comparison theorem for schemes over sousperfectoid spaces, of interest in its own right.
arxiv-2602-05078:
Estimating how much food is on a plate from a photo is harder than it looks, because a flat image hides depth. Gautham Vinod and Fengqing Zhu survey the field of food portion estimation in this 2026 computer vision paper. Reliable portion estimates would make image-based diet tracking practical, supporting care for chronic disease and obesity.

The review organizes the strategies researchers use to recover three-dimensional size from two-dimensional input. Some add auxiliary information, such as depth maps or multiple views. Others lean on models, matching the food against templates, or train deep networks on images alone or images plus the extra inputs. The paper walks through these families and how they perform, giving readers a structured map of a problem where the central difficulty is geometry, not recognition.
arxiv-2602-05478:
Heavy ion collisions create a hot bath of particles, and physicists track how heavy particles move through it to learn about the matter formed. Aditya Kumar Singh and Swatantra Kumar Tiwari study the D0 meson, a particle that contains a charm quark, as it travels through hadronic matter. Their tool is the Fokker-Planck equation, paired with Tsallis statistics, which handle systems that are not in perfect thermal balance.

A parameter in the statistics tracks how far the bath sits from equilibrium, and mass cutoffs control which particle species count as part of the bath. The authors find that drag and momentum diffusion grow with temperature, with the non-equilibrium parameter, and with the mass cutoff. Spatial diffusion moves the other way, falling as those quantities rise. At high values, spatial diffusion drops below a bound linked to AdS/CFT theory, read as a cap on that parameter.
arxiv-2602-05578:
Segmenting an image into labeled regions for any category a user names in text is called open-vocabulary semantic segmentation. Junyang Chen, Xiangbo Lv, and 4 co-authors propose LoGoSeg, a single-stage framework that joins local detail with global context for this task. Vision-language models like CLIP give the text-image link, but their image-level training often yields sloppy spatial alignment and invented or missed objects.

LoGoSeg adds three pieces: a prior that weights likely categories by global image-text similarity, and a region-aware module that ties regions to text precisely. A dual-stream fusion mixes local structure with global meaning. It needs no outside mask proposals, extra backbones, or added data sets. Across six standard benchmarks, it showed competitive scores and strong generalization to unseen categories. The paper targets computer vision researchers who need segmentation beyond a fixed label list.
arxiv-2602-05778:
Wind and current data pair a heading with a strength, a mix experts call cylindrical data, and such data often vary smoothly across space. Francesca Labanca, Anna Gottard, and Nadja Klein propose a layered added conditional copula fit model for spatially linked cylindrical data. Earlier copula models for this data type usually held copula settings fixed and limited the side fits to simple linear rules.

In the new model, the round part follows a wrapped Gaussian process and the straight part a spread-out fit, both allowing input effects. The copula itself can vary with inputs, tying heading to strength in a richer way. A known match between Gaussian random fields and their Markov twins keeps math work doable. The authors aim the method at fields such as weather study, ocean study, and medicine, where heading plus speed must be modeled jointly.
arxiv-2602-06078:
Big machine learning conferences get far more papers than reviewers can handle well. Elliot L Epstein and 3 co-authors argue that spare reviews should go to papers near the accept-or-reject line. Papers far above or below that line gain little from one more review.

Their plan uses a language model to rank papers by paired comparisons before human review starts. A classic ranking model turns those comparisons into a borderline band. Extra reviewers then go to that band at assignment time. The language model never decides acceptance itself. The authors give a simple formula for the expected gain, plus ways to estimate it from past conferences.
arxiv-2602-06178:
Diseases carried by insects, such as those spread by mosquitoes, can be fought by the predators that eat the carrier. Rocio Balderrama and 2 co-authors build a math model joining disease spread with predator-prey ecology. Hosts move between susceptible, infected, and recovered states, while the insect carrier has its own infection cycle.

They define an ecological reproduction number linking predator-prey cycle swings to whether the disease persists. Natural control hinges on the ratio between peak carrier numbers and lowest predator numbers. When nature falls short, they solve for the best predator release plan, balancing infections against costs. Simulations show releases can blunt the epidemic peak and steady the system.
arxiv-2602-06278:
Self-driving cars need to signal their intentions to people outside the car, and a decade of research has proposed many such interfaces. Tram Thi Minh Tran and 2 co-authors ask whether the field is settling on shared answers. They analyzed hundreds of publications, plus industry deployments and regulatory documents.

Three patterns emerged. Research agrees on a safety-first core of simple visual cues that clarify intent. It still diverges on whether such signals are needed and how to build them. And a filtering funnel appears: wide exploration in papers narrows in real deployments, then narrows again into the few signals regulators allow. The authors urge a shift from new prototypes toward consolidating evidence.
arxiv-2602-06678:
Shayla Sharmin and Sadia Afrin Ratna ask how mothers use large language models when they want support without being judged. Earlier work covered medical advice and plain information, but not this emotional use. The authors ran a ten-day mixed-methods survey of 107 mothers about their chatbot habits around childcare and their own feelings.

The mothers said they ask chatbots about childcare decisions, guilt, and late-night caregiving, valuing that no social consequences follow from the questions. More than half still valued human warmth above the chatbot, but a notable minority, especially mothers in joint families, preferred the model precisely because it does not judge. The authors frame such tools as low-risk support alongside human care, shaped strongly by each family's social setting.
arxiv-2602-06878:
D. Serrano and six co-authors test coils that could watch the magnetic surroundings of the LISA space mission. LISA will be the first space observatory for gravitational waves in the millihertz band, and magnetic forces bite into its sensitivity at low frequencies. Each craft must therefore track its own magnetic environment closely.

The coils in question flew on LISA Pathfinder, and here they serve as sensors in the audio band, where they can catch high-frequency magnetic noise from onboard electronics. At the low end of that band they beat mission needs by a factor of ten. They read noise of 1.45 picotesla per root hertz at 50 hertz, 0.17 at 500 hertz, and reach a floor of 0.1 above 1 kilohertz.
arxiv-2602-06978:
Rômulo Damasclin Chaves dos Santos builds a rigorous frame for fractional systems with spread memory and time delays. In such systems, present change depends on the whole past. That trait shows up in material and neuron models, yet general theory was lacking. The paper builds new fractional integral bounds of Grönwall-Wendroff type. They fit multi-input functions with singular kernels and implicit links.

Those bounds yield the key estimates for the analysis. From them, the author proves solutions exist and are unique, using fixed-point theory in weighted Banach spaces. He also proves Ulam-Hyers stability. Small tweaks to the equations yield proportionally small shifts in solutions. For a fractional FitzHugh-Nagumo neuron model with delay, the work gives strict rules for limit cycles tied to action potentials. It shows how fractional order and delay jointly tune excitability and regime shifts.
arxiv-2602-07278:
Deep graph convolutional networks suffer oversmoothing: node states collapse into sameness as layers pile up. Sai Vamsi Alisetti proposes Laplacian-LoRA, a low-rank spectral tweak to the fixed Laplacian step that spreads signals, rather than a redesign of message passing.

It weakens contraction in a targeted way while keeping stability and the low-pass bias of the network, delaying oversmoothing and roughly doubling usable depth across benchmarks. Spread checks confirm the gains come from delayed collapse, not a side effect. Graph learning teams get a simple, clear fix that lets deep graph networks stay deep.
arxiv-2602-07378:
Neural networks can lose features they once learned over long training, a phenomenon called feature unlearning whose mechanism was unclear.  Shota Imai and two co-authors analyze the infinite-width limit of a two-layer network under large-batch stochastic gradient descent, deriving equations on two time scales.

First-layer match develops fast while second-layer weights move slowly, and the direction of flow on a critical manifold, set by the slow dynamics, decides whether unlearning occurs.  Numerical tests validate the theory.  Theorists get a mechanism, not just an observation, for when training erases its own earlier progress.
arxiv-2602-07778:
Personalized language models should remember a user's history, but stuffing long profiles into the prompt wastes tokens and money. Shenglai Zeng and twelve co-authors ask whether the model's own attention patterns can reveal which profile pieces actually matter, then use that signal to compress context intelligently.

Their Attn-GS framework uses attention feedback from a marking model to flag important personalization signals and drop the rest, replacing crude heuristics like keeping only recent interactions. Fine-tuning further sharpens the model's ability to separate relevant from irrelevant details. The paper gives builders of personalized assistants a principled way to cut costs and latency without losing what makes the response personal.
arxiv-2602-08078:
Forecast from odds often needs stable numeric derivatives, especially when models are black boxes that auto sloping cannot touch. Nikolina Šarčević and two co-authors present DerivKit, a Python package for slope-based stats judgment.

The package gives stable sloping and build tools for Fisher-matrix forecast, bias gauges, and non-Gaussian odds spreads built on the derivative approximation for odds, handling scalar- and vector-valued models including tabled functions. By extending judgment beyond the Gaussian approximation, it bridges fast Fisher forecast and costly Markov-chain Monte Carlo sampling. Cosmologists and statisticians gain a usable middle path for uncertainty quantification.
arxiv-2602-08278:
Dexterous robot hands differ in kinematics and dynamics, forcing most methods to train separate policies per hand. Ke Zhang and six co-authors offer DexFormer, a policy that works across robot bodies, stays aware of dynamics, and runs on a transformer that conditions on historical data.

Temporal context lets the policy infer morphology and dynamics on the fly and produce embodiment-appropriate actions. Trained on procedurally generated hand assets, DexFormer generalizes zero-shot to the Leap Hand, Allegro Hand, and Rapid Hand. Roboticists gain evidence that one policy can span heterogeneous dexterous hands, a step toward general manipulation skills that transfer across hardware instead of being rebuilt for each new hand.
arxiv-2602-08478:
Modeling unsteady flows and chaotic dynamics usually forces a choice between interpretable linear methods and powerful deep models. Albert Alcalde and two co-authors propose a time-delayed transformer that bridges the two. Their arXiv paper shows a one-layer transformer with a single attention head can be read as a nonlinear version of time-delayed dynamic-mode analysis.

The design stays deliberately minimal, with one attention layer, one query per prediction, and one feedforward layer, giving linear cost in sequence length. Tests on synthetic signals, unsteady aerodynamics, the Lorenz system, and a reaction-diffusion model show it matches linear baselines where systems are near-linear and beats them clearly in nonlinear and chaotic regimes. Readers get an efficient, interpretable model for complex dynamics.
arxiv-2602-08578:
Telling two faint, incoherent light sources apart in time faces an analogue of the Rayleigh limit in space. Salvatore Muratore and Vincenzo Tamma show that quantum beat patterns in frequency space can beat that analogue. Their arXiv paper studies interference at a beam splitter between a reference photon and photons from two weak signals.

By counting bunching or antibunching events across measured frequencies, the method reaches half the quantum limit in precision, regardless of wavepacket shape or the delay being measured. Relatively few measurements suffice. Readers get a feasible technique with uses in astronomy, microscopy, remote clock synchronization, and radar ranging.
arxiv-2602-08778:
Largeness notions from logic measure how rich a set of numbers is, and partition theorems say rich sets contain homogeneous subsets. Quentin Le Houérou and Ludovic Patey develop the framework of alpha-largeness introduced by Ketonen and Solovay. Their arXiv paper proves a partition theorem for alpha-large sets below epsilon-zero, generalizing earlier theorems.

A concrete consequence follows: for every omega-to-the-nk-plus-three-large set whose smallest element is at least eighteen, every coloring of pairs with k colors admits an omega-to-the-n-large homogeneous subset. That bound cannot be improved except by a constant shift. Readers get a sharp partition result in the Ketonen-Solovay tradition, with the tightness result showing the bound is nearly best possible.
arxiv-2602-09278:
Trait-credit ways often praise traits that carry no real facts, such as masker traits born from trait links. Benedict Clark and three co-authors ask whether whitening, a standard un-linking pre-step, can fix that flaw. Using the XAI-TRIS test set with fake ground truth, they try 16 popular credit ways paired with five distinct whitening twists.

A tiny two-way straight-line sorting puzzle adds theory work on whether whitening can drop masker effects from Bayes-best models. Results are mixed: some whitening tricks lift credit scores, but gains shift a lot across ways and builds. The findings stress a tangled dance among data curves, pre-step quality, and credit faithfulness that no single whitening recipe fixes.
arxiv-2602-09478:
Raffaella Morganti and three co-authors present deep MeerKAT views hunting neutral hydrogen absorption in powerful radio galaxies at mid-range redshifts. Seventeen sources were targeted, with fifteen spectra clean enough for sensitive limits, yielding three new detections. Two are linked absorbers, a detection rate near one in eight, and both sit in young radio sources, confirming that young sources show hydrogen absorption more often than evolved ones.

One linked case, in quasar PKS 1151-34, surprises: its radio lobes still appear embedded in the circumnuclear disc. The other, PKS 1306-09, shows strongly blueshifted gas likely driven out by a jet. A third detection is an intervening galaxy in front of another source's southern lobe. Together the results echo low-redshift patterns: source age, gas conditions, and gas geometry jointly set whether absorption appears.
arxiv-2602-09878:
World models that imagine before acting promise better robot manipulation, yet most support only image forecasting or partial 3D geometry. Jiaxu Wang and nine co-authors present MVISTA-4D, an embodied 4D world model for robotic manipulation, in their 2026 paper. From a single-view RGBD observation, the model imagines the remaining viewpoints and fuses them into a fuller 3D structure across time.

Cross-view and cross-modality fusion keeps RGB and depth consistent and aligns views geometrically. Instead of inverse dynamics, which is ill-posed since many actions explain one transition, the team optimizes actions at test time by backpropagating through the generative model. A residual inverse dynamics model then turns the trajectory prior into executable actions. Tests on three datasets show strong 4D generation and downstream manipulation, with ablations clarifying the key design choices.
arxiv-2602-10078:
Long-lived dark sector particles could slowly leak energy into the gas between galaxies, warming it over cosmic time. A 2026 paper by Laura Lopez-Honorez and Sonali Verma uses Lyman-alpha forest measurements of intergalactic gas temperature to limit such models. Decays into ordinary particles would alter the late-time thermal history, making the forest a keen test of hidden sectors with cosmic-scale lifetimes.

Late-time heating limits complement cosmic microwave background limits on the same parameter space. The authors also revisit Planck limits from the optical depth to reionization and update them for very long lifetimes. Their model-independent limits reinterpret broadly, including evaporating primordial black holes and dark photons coupled to ordinary matter.
arxiv-2602-10278:
Making 3D content from one image is ill-posed, since hidden regions hide shape and texture facts. A 2026 paper led by Zehua Ma, with six co-authors, offers ERGO, an adaptive tuning setup steered by excess risk splitting for sharp one-image 3D Gaussian splatting. Top generative models can make extra views, but those views carry shape mismatches and texture misalignments that amplify flaws during rebuilding.

ERGO splits tuning losses into excess risk, the gap between present and best parameters, and Bayes error, the built-in noise in made views. Estimating per-view excess risk on the fly lets the method adjust loss weights as it goes, while shape-aware and texture-aware goals add a global-local tuning plan. The result resists supervision noise while improving shape sharpness and texture quality of rebuilt content.
arxiv-2602-10378:
Score-debiased kernel density estimation beats classical density estimation on asymptotic convergence, but its empirical score has made it far slower in practice. A 2026 paper led by Elliot L. Epstein, with two co-authors, reorders the computation to expose matrix-multiplication structure, letting tensor cores accelerate the graphics-processor implementation. On a thirty-two-thousand-sample, sixteen-dimensional problem, their Flash-SD-KDE runs up to forty-seven times faster than a strong graphics-processor baseline and three thousand three hundred times faster than the scikit-learn implementation.

On a larger task of one million samples in sixteen dimensions, evaluated on one hundred thirty-one thousand queries, the method finishes in about two seconds on a single graphics processor. The paper thus turns a theoretically attractive estimator into a practical tool at scales where it was previously infeasible, opening score-debiased density estimation to much larger problems.
arxiv-2602-10778:
Maximilian Thang and six co-authors improve the security of AI-generated code at the neuron level in a 2026 paper. In fast, informal vibe coding workflows, speed wins and security requirements stay implicit, so models produce functionally correct but insecure code. Current fixes rely on costly full fine-tuning or coarse adaptations with limited control.

Their system, GoodVibe, rests on the insight that security-relevant thinking localizes to a small subset of neurons. Slope-based attribution identifies those neurons, enabling targeted intervention that improves security by default without retraining everything. The neuron-level approach offers clarity and control that coarse methods lack. It aims at code assistants that write safe code as readily as they write working code.
arxiv-2602-10878:
Alexander Demin and Gleb Pogudin present a recipe for simplifying generators of rational function fields in a 2026 paper. Given a set of generators for a subfield of rational functions in several factors, the recipe finds a simple generating set. A build improves upon the state of the art in both speed and result quality.

The main novelties are partial Grobner basis runs via sparse interpolation and fast search for many-term math of fixed degree inside the subfield. Case studies from domains like structural parameter identifiability show the utility of simplified generators. Cleaner generators make downstream analysis, from identifiability to symbolic runs, much easier. The paper pairs recipe innovation with working code.
arxiv-2602-11078:
Point patterns in the plane can jump between sparse and dense phases. David Dereudre and Christopher Renaud-Chan study Gibbs point processes whose local energy in crowded regions depends only on point count. Building on Pirogov-Sinai-Zahradnik ideas adapted to the continuum, they craft a general proof method.

The method yields two distinct infinite-volume Gibbs measures with other intensities, which is the mark of a first-order phase transition. It extends earlier results for the Quermass model and covers a new class of diluted pairwise contacts offered here. The work widens the set of continuum models known to support sharp phase change.
arxiv-2602-11178:
Normal spaces can be described by separating closed sets with a continuous function. Robert Maxton, writing alone, translates Urysohn's description into the language of lifting properties in the category of topological spaces. His translation corrects a frequently cited earlier version that was erroneous.

He also translates hereditary normality, where every open subspace is normal, by mapping the normal-space translation at once. The paper is short and technical, but it repairs a standard reference point. Future work that cites the lifting-property view of normality can now build on a correct statement rather than a flawed one.
arxiv-2602-11378:
Reduced-order models usually freeze once trained, then drift when systems leave their training range. Amirpasha Hedayat and two co-authors formalize adaptive non-intrusive reduced-order models that update latent subspace and reduced motion online. Three formulations are proposed: sequential refits, joint Riemannian tuning, and a hybrid that starts from a refit update.

On a transiently perturbed cavity flow, static models drift or destabilize beyond training, while adaptive variants hold up. Sequential refits suppress amplitude drift cheaply, joint tuning tracks energy nearly exactly under frequent updates but needs careful initialization, and the hybrid proves most reliable under regime change and minimal offline data. The paper also demands cost-aware, transparent reporting of online budgets and model queries.
arxiv-2602-11778:
Belyi maps are a bridge between geometry and group theory, and their full space has lacked a natural geometric organization. Noémie Combe shows that space admits a parametrization by an infinite-dimensional sphere drawn from Voiculescu theory of noncommutative probability spaces. The sphere splits into sectors, each matching a class of Belyi maps distinguished up to isomorphism by monodromy, encoded by a finite-index subgroup.

For Galois Belyi maps the correspondence sharpens into a genuine bijection between spectral sectors of the sphere and algebraic quotients. Distinct sectors thus capture the algebraic constraints that monodromy imposes, organizing Belyi maps by their group-theoretic data. Geometry, in this account, does not merely picture the maps but sorts them according to the algebra that governs them.
arxiv-2602-11878:
Quantum corrections to the effective potential in scalar field theories were summed before in the leading logarithmic approximation. Iakhibbaev and three co-authors extend that approach to the next-to-leading order. Using a standard renormalization procedure and its central theorem, they construct step rules and renormalization group equations that sum leading and subleading logs to all orders of perturbation theory.

The method applies to any scalar potential, renormalizable or not, giving it unusual breadth. To verify the results, the authors compare them with a model treated with standard group methods. The extension matters because next-order terms can shift predictions where leading terms alone prove too crude, and a method that handles arbitrary potentials widens the class of theories under quantitative control.
arxiv-2602-12178:
Tomographic volumetric printing builds whole shapes at once by curing liquid resin only where light dose passes a threshold. Nicole Pellizzon led this work with three co-authors, studying how the choice of penalty in the light-plan maths shapes print quality. The plan must cure target zones while leaving the rest liquid, and small choices ripple through the result.

The team tests several penalties and maps each one to dose ranges inside and outside the target shape. They also vary the threshold settings that mark minimum dose for printing and maximum dose for staying liquid, on old and new methods alike. All of it sits in TVAM AID, a reusable frame built on the open Core Imaging Library.
arxiv-2602-12278:
Retrieval-augmented generation helps language models handle long documents, but most retrievers were not built for long texts. David Jiahao Fu led this work with three co-authors, presenting AttentionRetriever, a model that treats attention layers themselves as long-document retrievers. It tackles three long-text problems at once: context awareness, causal dependence, and choosing how much to retrieve.

The method joins attention signals to entity-based retrieval, building context-aware embeddings for long documents and fixing the scope of retrieval. In tests, it beats existing retrieval models on long-document sets by a large margin, while staying as efficient as dense retrieval. The result suggests that a model can find its own evidence in long texts, without a separate heavy retriever.
arxiv-2602-12378:
Sodium-ion cells need cathode parts that are cheap, stable, and good at carrying charge, and a sodium iron manganese oxide is a hopeful choice. Veenavee Nipunika Kothalawala led a large team here, probing Na_xFe_1/2Mn_1/2O_2 with X-ray Compton scattering, SQUID tests, and theory models. The goal is to track how electrons and spins evolve as sodium enters and leaves the material.

Comparing patterns with sodium in and with sodium out, the team finds oxygen 2p states drive the redox process. Metal 3d electrons grow more spread out, which explains the metal-like phase at x equal to two thirds. Pattern gaps define a numeric marker for the sodium uptake range tied to better charge flow. Oxygen holes, seen in the oxygen magnetic signal, confirm oxygen's central role in cathode work.
arxiv-2602-12478:
Medical time series such as ECGs and PPGs are often corrupted by artefacts from ambulances or daily activity, and automated tools that use them can mislead clinical decisions. Jad Haidamous led this work with one co-author, Christoph Hoog Antink, formalising signal quality as task- and metric-specific, rather than generic. Most existing signal quality indices ignore which algorithm and metric will use the signal downstream.

Their perturbation-based index, pSQI, is defined as the worst-case metric value under additive, coloured Gaussian noise with a lower-bounded signal-to-noise ratio. Formal requirements include monotonicity of the metric in expectation and maximal separation under thresholding. Tests on R-peak detection and atrial fibrillation classification show pSQI beating feature-based and deep-learning indices at flagging unreliable inputs, without any training.
arxiv-2602-12878:
Language models trained in different countries may absorb different cultural values, but measuring that gap needs natural, debatable material. Vlad-Andrei Negru and three co-authors build Sociocultural Statements, an open dataset drawn from real debate statements and labelled synthetically along Hofstede's cultural dimensions. Human checks on a sample verify the synthetic labels.

Comparing models developed in the United States and China against human measurement patterns, the authors find that culturally distinct models mirror the values of their home countries. That mirroring also reveals a limit: the models do not readily adapt to the cultural backgrounds of their users. For builders of global systems, the finding argues for explicit attention to whose values a model carries into conversation.
arxiv-2602-12978:
Robot arms that act in chunks can stutter at chunk boundaries, breaking smooth motion. Yufeng Liu and eleven co-authors propose Legato, a method that teaches continuation during training for action-chunked flow policies in vision-language-action models. Real-time chunking patches the problem from outside the policy, but can cause spurious mode switching and paths that lack intrinsic smoothness.

Legato instead starts denoising from a schedule-shaped mix of known actions and noise, letting the model see partial action information during training. It reshapes flow dynamics so denoising stays aligned in training and in use, under per-step guidance, with randomised schedule conditioning for varying delays and controllable smoothness. Real-world tests across five manipulation tasks show Legato beating real-time chunking, with about 10% gains in both smoothness and completion time.
arxiv-2602-13178:
Koszul Artin-Schelter regular algebras in dimension four are a testing ground for noncommutative shape, and their fixed traits can distinguish groups. Vishal Bhatoy and Colin Ingalls compute superpotentials for known groups using Magma, then apply Schur-Weyl duality to find relevant fixed traits. Through the Borel-Weil theorem, those fixed traits become bundle sections over partial flag varieties, yielding shape fixed traits that sometimes correspond to K3 surfaces.

Discrete fixed traits of those shape objects are then worked out and used to tell algebras apart. The pipeline, from computer algebra to picture theory to shape, shows how abstract fixed traits become concrete distinguishing tools. For algebraists, the paper supplies worked out fixed traits and a method for separating groups that might else look alike.
arxiv-2602-13778:
Most dance generation trains in the skeletal domain and ignores mesh-level physics limits.
