Motions that look plausible as joint trajectories often show self-penetration and foot-ground contact flaws when rendered with a body mesh. Skeleton2Stage narrows that gap by turning mesh checks into training signals and tuning its diffusion model with reinforcement learning so its motion stays true to body physics. Its reward design combines an imitation reward, measuring plausibility by imitability in a simulator, penalizing penetration and foot skating, with a foot-ground gap reward. Test-time guidance captures foot-ground interaction.

Physics-based rewards tend to push the model toward freezing motions with fewer anomalies and better imitability. An anti-freezing reward preserves motion dynamics while keeping physical plausibility. Experiments across dance data sets improved physical plausibility, yielding more realistic dances. Jidong Jia leads the work with three co-authors.
arxiv-2602-14278:
Mayank Kejriwal and two co-authors study a 2026 arXiv problem: how do fixed plans cope with new twists in open worlds? Agents face settings that break training rules, and this paper tests toughness in two-player zero-sum games. New twists mean changed rules or scores, while agent acts stay fixed.

Two gauges frame the study: per-agent toughness, tracking each plan's score shift across new twists, and global shock, summing crowd-wide upset caused by a twist. Tests ran 30 Iterated Prisoner's Dilemma agents across 20 payoff twists, and 10 poker agents across 5 rule twists. Steady toughness patterns emerged, with some twists causing severe upset, a warning for fielding fixed plans in shifting worlds.
arxiv-2602-14478:
Thanh Dang and one co-author study a 2026 arXiv pair of log-concave sampling problems: constrained and composite sampling. For constrained sampling, the target density is proportional to exp(-f(x)) on a convex set K, with f convex, and the challenge is enforcing feasibility without degrading mixing. An epigraph transformation reduces the task to drawing from a lifted convex set in one higher dimension, where the target is close to flat.

The lifted problem is cracked with a proximal sampler, built via cutting planes and rejection sampling using only a separation oracle for K and a subgradient oracle for f. Unlike samplers leaning on projection, reflection, barrier tricks, or mirror maps, this route needs least oracle access and no lore of the constraint shape, giving a real unbiased sampler. Composite sampling, with target proportional to exp(-f(x) minus h(x)), is treated in the same framework.
arxiv-2602-14578:
Isam Vrce and two co-authors study a 2026 arXiv sparsity method for deep reinforcement learning. Thinness squeezes deep nets with little score loss, and reward-learning nets with just 5 percent of old weights can still train nearly as well as dense forms. Yet most methods use messy fine-grained thinness, capping hardware speed-up from ragged compute patterns.

Ordered coarse-grained thinness enables speed-up but usually harms scores and tangles pruning. The paper offers, to its lore, the first study of N:M ordered thinness in reward learning, weighing squeeze, scores, and hardware thrift. Row-wise N:M thinness is forced through training for all nets in off-policy TD3, keeping fit with accelerators backing N:M sparse matrix acts. Tests on steady-control benchmarks show the thin agent beating its dense twin at 50 to 75 percent thinness.
arxiv-2602-14978:
Dodin and colleagues challenge a long-used mass estimate for the microquasar SS433. Using the Transient Double-beam Spectrograph on the Caucasian Mountain Observatory's 2.5 metre telescope, they took over 150 HeII line measures over 388 nights between 2020 and 2025. The HeII forming region is never eclipsed, and it is much bigger than the donor star and also bigger than the photosphere around the supercritical accretion disk itself.

The HeII radial velocity curve also ignores precessional phase and clashes with the photometric curve. Those facts suggest the line does not track the orbital motion of the compact object. Spectroscopic masses for the SS433 components drawn from this line, the authors warn, can therefore be unrealistic.
arxiv-2602-15078:
Henson and Montesi present CSLib, a growing central library of formalized computer science and software in Lean. It follows Mathlib, the central Lean library for mathematics, extending the same library model from math to computing. The paper sets out CSLib's founding principles and semantic framework.

Contributions include shared interfaces for reduction and labelled transition systems, proof automation, and CI and testing support that keeps the tools compatible with Mathlib. The paper also reports the first large builds of languages and models on those tools, framing the field itself as Lean infrastructure. New work can build on the shared base instead of starting from scratch.
arxiv-2602-15278:
Cherep and colleagues study what shapes choices of vision-language models. These agents make image choices at scale, deciding what to click, recommend, or buy, yet little is known about their tastes. The team offers a setup placing models in controlled image-based choice tasks and tweaking their inputs. Their key idea treats the agent's choice rule as a hidden value read from choices between changed photos.

Starting from common photos such as item photos, they adapt text methods to iteratively propose and apply plausible changes using an image generation model, such as in layout, light, or setting. Large experiments on leading models show tuned edits greatly shift choice odds in head-to-head matchups. An auto readout line shows these tastes, naming themes that drive picks. The team says this method surfaces holes and risk worries that might otherwise be found quietly in the wild.
arxiv-2602-15378:
Devadiga and Chopra ask whether large language models can talk in tongues nearly absent from their teaching data. Their case study is Tulu, a Dravidian language with over 2 million users but tiny online footprint. Rather than fine-tuning an LLM, they test whether set cues alone can draw basic chat skill under set cueing.

They join plain grammar notes, blocking rules to block high-odds words from nearby tongues, roman script norm, and checked fake data making via self-play. Tested on a by-hand picked held-out set across three LLMs and checked by home speakers, their method cuts word mixing from 80 percent to 5 percent while hitting 85 percent grammar score. Cross-model study shows blocking rules give steady gains of 12 to 18 points, while grammar notes effects vary by model design, from 8 to 22 points.
arxiv-2602-15678:
Soares de Lima and colleagues bring Northrop Frye theory of four narrative genres, comedy, romance, tragedy, and satire, into computational form through character roles rather than plot patterns alone. Drawing on Jungian archetype theory, they derive four universal character functions, protagonist, mentor, antagonist, and companion, by mapping them to components of Jung psychic structure. Those functions are then specialised into sixteen genre-specific roles from prototypical works.

To test the frame, six state-of-the-art large language models judge character-role matches across 40 narrative works, with 160 valid and 30 invalid correspondences. Models reach a mean balanced accuracy of 82.5 percent with strong inter-model agreement, suggesting the correspondences capture real structural patterns. Scores vary by genre and role, and qualitative reading links that variation to genuine narrative traits, including functional spread in romance and deliberate archetype subversion in satire.
arxiv-2602-15978:
Lehmann and Lin ask whether disk turbulence can save low mass planets from spiralling into their stars. Inward Type One torques threaten young planets, and positive co rotation torques could rescue them only if diffusion keeps those torques from saturating. Disk profiles that support such torques are often prone to the convective overstability, a wrinkle previous torque studies largely ignored.

Their three dimensional simulations with thermal diffusion let the overstability grow into large, long lived vortices that drift and tug gravitationally on the planet. Encounters typically kick the planet outward, stretching migration times roughly tenfold, long enough to overlap planet formation windows. With optically thin cooling instead, the overstability stays near axisymmetric and leaves torques almost unchanged.
arxiv-2602-16078:
Alex Farach models artificial intelligence as a new kind of capital that shrinks the cost of coordination inside firms. Standard task models hold firm structure fixed, but here AI compresses managers per-link coordination costs toward residual floors for consequential decisions. Whether those floors are positive or zero changes the outcome in a basic way: positive floors bound spans of control, while zero floors do not.

With a fixed manager pool and several steady conditions, positive floors alone set long-run managerial wage dispersion, apart from execution savings. Under a common positive floor with distinct skills, wage inequality proves purely transitional, vanishing at zero capital and in the long run yet positive at finite capital levels. If lower-floor managers near capacity faster, inequality can overshoot its long-run level and converge from above. The numerical cases shown are illustrations, not estimates.
arxiv-2602-16678:
Harrison Perone and Christopher Hays present a decentralized task allocation algorithm for satellite catalog upkeep using angles-only views. Close satellites need precise relative states for all nearby craft and debris, but ground tracking may lack the needed accuracy. Space-based sensors help, above all when satellites share data. Each craft must keep a local catalog of linked and unlinked objects from narrow-field angle measures.

Scheduling and coordinating those views well is the core snag. The new algorithm tackles it in a decentralized way, and its scores are gauged by fuel use and total catalog uncertainty in numerical simulation. It beats the uncertainty-fuel frontier of current routes by a wide margin. Mission planners get a practical scheme for safer close-proximity satellite operations.
arxiv-2602-16778:
Scott Carlsten and co-authors use ELVES-Field data to study star formation in isolated dwarf galaxies in the Local Volume. The volume-limited sample comes from nearly three thousand square degrees of imaging, with distances largely from surface brightness fluctuations, complete to a low stellar mass limit. Over twenty-three hundred candidates were cataloged, with ninety-five confirmed as genuine members and many more rejected as background.

Of the confirmed dwarfs, dozens are new discoveries or first-time distance confirmations. Isolated dwarfs are picked mainly by distance from known groups. At higher dwarf masses, essentially all field dwarfs are star-forming, as found before. Below a mass threshold near ten million solar masses, about thirty percent appear quenched. Isolated dwarfs also run noticeably smaller than satellite dwarfs of the same mass, a clue to environment-driven evolution.
arxiv-2602-17278:
Dominik Engl led a three-author paper building membrane models from anisotropic nonlocal hyperelasticity. Thin solids prompt a dimension reduction of hyperelastic energies with nonlocal gradients to a membrane model. Scaling the thin domain turns even ranges uneven, so the paper builds a theory of gradients of that kind with direction-varying ranges.

Unlike older ball-supported kernels, it uses ellipsoidal regions whose main radii may vanish on their own. That yields one setup spanning fully long-range, partly long-range, and purely local models. A Gamma-convergence analysis for the thin-film totals then shows the limit keeps the classical membrane energy form, with the local model regained exactly when all radii vanish.
arxiv-2602-17878:
Matthew Burns and Jiaming Liang improve analysis of restarted accelerated gradient and augmented Lagrangian methods through inexact proximal point frames. The paper studies double-loop inner-outer methods for convex composite optimization. For free problems, a restarted accelerated composite gradient method attains optimal first-order cost in both convex and very convex settings.

For linearly limited problems, rough boosted Lagrangian methods, including a basic method and an outer-accelerated variant, achieve near-optimal first-order cost. Those bounds follow from a unified study based on new rough proximal point frames. The frames handle both kinds of roughness, acceleration and very convex goals. Number tests on LASSO and linearly limited square programs show the real speed of the proposed methods, giving readers sharper guarantees for widely used tuning tools.
arxiv-2602-18278:
Artur Gesla and one co-author trace how a turbine's helical vortex rope is born. Their 2026 paper studies swirling flow in a Francis hydropower turbine draft tube, where a large helical structure, the vortex rope, is read as an unstable mode of vortex breakdown. The analysis uses a simplified laminar setting.

The rope mode branches smoothly from a symmetric base flow in a Hopf bifurcation. Without wall friction, a large central recirculation zone forms and a range of subcritical solutions appears at partial load, promoting a hysteresis loop. The team describes the regular cycle of bubble formation at the axis and its destruction by a rope at its rim. Raising discharge toward nominal load unfolds the steady branch in a transcritical bifurcation at finite Reynolds number, extending evidence once seen only without viscosity.
arxiv-2602-19278:
On a fruit packing line, apples rush past in dense crowds, and judging quality from single snapshots is not enough: a grade must stay stable as each apple moves through view. Keonvin Park and two colleagues build a two-stage video system for that conveyor-belt setting. An orchard-trained detector first finds each apple in the frame, and a tracker then follows it across frames so its identity persists.

A defect classifier, fine-tuned on healthy and defective fruit, scores cropped views of each apple, and results are combined across the whole track rather than trusted from one frame alone. That track-level pooling steadies the verdict against blur, overlap, and brief occlusions. The system aims to give packing lines consistent grades at speed, in the crowded, moving conditions where still-image methods falter.
arxiv-2602-19378:
Treatment effects often differ across people, but estimating those differences gets hard when data go missing. Shuozhi Zuo and two co-authors tackle conditional average treatment effects when covariates, treatment, and outcome can all be missing not at random, meaning missingness depends on unseen values. Standard methods then risk bias, since the observed data alone cannot identify the effect without further structure.

The paper establishes nonparametric identification of the effect under multivariate missing-not-at-random mechanisms. It also builds nonparametric and parametric estimators, and adds a sensitivity analysis framework for checking robustness when missingness assumptions fail. Readers get both the identification logic and practical tools for policy evaluation, social science, and precision medicine.
arxiv-2602-19678:
Scanning tunneling microscopy maps electronic density of states at atomic detail, yet covering micron-wide areas atom by atom takes far too long. Miguel Águeda Velasco and eighteen co-authors present Replica STM (R-STM), a method that tracks atomic-scale features over large areas without mapping every point. They record large-area conductance maps in UTe2 and FeSe spanning over 200 nanometers.

The big maps hold periodic signals with wavelengths far beyond atomic spacing. Those long signals turn out to be copies of atomic-scale density-of-states patterns, so R-STM follows atomic features across large areas through their replicas. Phase slips, disorder, and defects shape the replicas, and FeSe results hint that superconducting gap modulations may persist over large scales.
arxiv-2602-19778:
Recognizing musical chords automatically is held back by the cost of aligned chord labels, even as powerful pretrained models grow more available. A 2026 arXiv paper by Nghia Phan and three co-authors presents a two-stage pipeline that learns from unlabeled audio plus a pretrained teacher.

In stage one, the pretrained BTC model labels over a thousand hours of diverse unlabeled audio. A student model trains on those pseudo-labels alone, reaching nearly the teacher's performance. In stage two the student keeps training on true labels as they arrive, with selective distillation from the teacher as a regularizer against forgetting. After stage two the BTC student beats both the supervised baseline and its own teacher on every standard metric. Gains are strong on rare chord types.
arxiv-2602-19878:
The Open Digital Rights Language writes policy constraints as triples of operand, operator, and value, but several spatial operands span multiple axes without naming which axis a constraint means. A 2026 arXiv paper by Daham Mustafa and seven co-authors resolves that dimensional ambiguity by axis decomposition.

Multi-axis operands are replaced with axis-specific scalar operands over ordered domains, so each constraint denotes an interval on one axis, and each policy becomes an axis-aligned box. Conflict detection then reduces to box comparison. The authors define a three-valued semantics of conflict, compatible, and unknown, prove the decomposition correct and compatible with older ODRL, and package it as the ODRL Axis-Aligned Profile. Validation on a benchmark of policy problems, compiled to theorem-prover and solver formats, supports the approach.
arxiv-2602-20278:
Alexander R. Block and six co-authors prove a sharp limit on a relaxed form of error-correcting code. Locally decodable codes let a reader recover one message bit by inspecting only a few codeword bits. A relaxed version from 2006 allows much shorter codewords, but its limits in the standard error setting were open. This 2026 paper studies relaxed codes that ask only two questions.

The authors prove that two-query relaxed codes over the binary alphabet must still be exponentially long, even when the questions adapt to earlier answers. The result answers a question raised by Gur and Lachish and gives the first exponential lower bound for relaxed codes. With the 2006 construction, it reveals a sharp change in codeword length as query complexity varies. The proof converts relaxed codes into standard codes by studying message-bit restrictions that fix codeword bits.
arxiv-2602-20478:
Coding helpers powered by language models forget across sessions: they lose project rules and repeat known errors. Aristidis Vasilopoulos presents a three-part written context setup built while building a one hundred eight thousand-line C-sharp networked system. A hot-memory charter encodes rules, recall hooks, and orchestration rules; nineteen focused domain-expert agents cover distinct areas; and a cold-memory knowledge base holds thirty-four on-demand spec files.

Measured metrics track setup growth and use patterns across two hundred eighty-three building sessions. Four watched case studies show how written context carries across sessions to prevent breaks and keep work steady. The setup ships as an open-source linked store, giving a way to set up agents for large, multi-agent projects that can grow.
arxiv-2602-20778:
Pol Benítez and three co-authors aim to predict how mixed, disordered solids respond to heat and light. Such solids can shift how they absorb light with temperature, which suits heat-tuned detectors and solar cells, but their disorder makes standard first-principles math too costly.

The team pairs ab initio electron methods with machine learning to reach first-principles accuracy at finite temperature for anharmonic solid solutions. Applied to silver chalco-halide mixes, the method shows how chemical disorder and lattice motion shape electron structure, and offers a general route for modeling disordered solids.
arxiv-2602-20878:
Large vision-language models score well on visual questions yet often lean on false links instead of real causal thought. Dhita Putri Pratama, Soyeon Caren Han, and Yihao Ding diagnose that gap in this 2026 arXiv paper. They present Vision-Language Causal Graphs, a structured, query-conditioned picture of causally key objects, traits, links, and scene rules.

On top of that picture they build ViLCaR, a test set with tasks for causal attribution, causal inference, and question answering. Scores rate how well key items are picked out beyond final correctness. Tests on leading models show that adding structured key-item facts lifts attribution and inference steadiness over zero-shot and standard in-context learning. The choke point, the authors argue, is missing structural guidance rather than missing thought power.
arxiv-2602-21478:
Zikai Shen and five co-authors study inference after adaptive data collection, as in a bandit algorithm. The targets are scalar-valued and pathwise differentiable. The team introduces a new target-specific condition called directional stability.

This condition is strictly weaker than earlier target-agnostic conditions. Under it, methods that would be optimal under independent, identically distributed data stay nearly normal in large samples and optimal in a broad sense on adaptively collected runs. The canonical gradient takes a martingale form, and it steadies its spread. A limit theorem characterizes optimality, and the one-step method can attain the bound. The authors verify the condition for LinUCB, giving the first such optimal guarantee for a regular scalar target under LinUCB sampling.
arxiv-2602-21678:
Jan Kober and four co-authors use nonlinear resonant ultrasound spectroscopy to monitor gallium-induced damage in aluminum alloys. NRUS is a sound tool tracking small shifts in medium microstructure for damage tracking.

The tool is applied to liquid metal embrittlement from gallium penetration in aluminum. To define signs of metal decline, data treatment with Singular Value Decomposition is shown and discussed. Tests show nonlinear traits track the state of liquid metal in the solid matrix, marking distinct phases in gallium diffusion along grain edges and within bulk grains. Gallium damage growth reveals links between nonlinear, fast, and slow changing traits, linking damage stages to sound signs.
arxiv-2602-21878:
Beat Zurbuchen proves a perverse sheaf on a connected commutative algebraic group over a finite field is generically unramified. That result gives a theorem on equidistribution for Tannakian monodromy groups, in a wider setting than before. He also proves a stratification result for exponential sums. The sums run in families indexed by a scheme and by the characters of such a group.

His method builds on Tannakian categories from Gabber and Loeser. This route yields fiber functors with ease. He also proves vanishing results over such groups. He sorts the negligible sheaves. He proves relative weak propagation results for tori. These results widen the reach of these tools to a broader class of groups.
arxiv-2602-21978:
Language models are often tested on whether sentences are grammatical, but far less is known about whether they grasp what grammar means. Miyu Oba and Saku Sugawara introduce CxMP, a test built on construction grammar, which treats set form-meaning pairings as the basic units of language. It uses matched sentence pairs that differ in small ways, across nine construction types such as let-alone, caused motion, and ditransitive forms.

The tests show that models pick up bare syntax early, while true grasp of construction meaning grows more slowly and stays limited even in large models. CxMP thus exposes a lasting gap between sounding grammatical and understanding what forms convey. For researchers, it offers a clean tool for tracking how meaning, not just form, develops in language models.
arxiv-2602-22278:
Mixed-media retrieval has been boosted by large mixed-media models, but only through contrastive fine-tuning that demands large datasets and consistent pretraining. Dawei Su and Dongsheng Wang propose RetLLM, a framework that queries such models for retrieval with no training and no data at all. It reframes retrieval as score generation: the model is prompted to predict scores directly, coarse then fine.

A top-k filtering stage first builds a small, high-quality candidate pool per query, letting the model focus on relevant candidates. The fine stage then scores query and candidate together, aided by a visual boost. The result is mixed-media retrieval from off-the-shelf models, with no fine-tuning bill attached.
arxiv-2602-22478:
Small black holes are widely believed to live inside the accretion disks of active galactic nuclei, forming a population called accretion-modified stars. Jun-Rong Liu and two co-authors study how gas from the dense disk feeds these objects, driving powerful outflows from mini-disks around them that stir the surrounding disk gas. They compare two feeding stories: episodic Bondi explosions with hyper-Eddington feeding, and steady Eddington feeding.

Those outflows create turbulence that moves angular momentum outward through shocks and momentum exchange. Across a broad sweep of central black-hole masses, feeding rates, small-hole mass functions, and spatial layouts, the team derives scaling relations for the effective viscosity in both scenarios. The work shows how embedded black holes can shape the disks that host them.
arxiv-2602-22778:
N. A. Asriyan and two co-authors ask whether entangled light can drive matter into entanglement that survives noise. Two separate single-mode polaritonic condensates receive resonant pumping from entangled photon pairs, while excitonic reservoir noise and photon leakage through cavity mirrors fight against order.

The team shows in principle that the system can still reach an entangled steady state, and they estimate the entangled-particle flux needed to violate the partial-transpose test for entanglement. They also track what happens when the entangled pumping suddenly stops, giving estimates for how long entanglement lives in the pair of exciton-polariton condensates.
arxiv-2602-22978:
M. L. Pereira Junior and nine co-authors survey impurity barriers across about four thousand two-dimensional materials. Low barriers for impurity adsorption matter for catalysis, sensing, and surface functionalization, yet first-principles methods like DFT cost too much for large-scale screening. The team instead pairs the semi-empirical Extended Huckel Method with machine learning.

Energy profiles along three in-plane migration paths give average barriers for three chalcogen impurities, sulfur, selenium, and tellurium, across the C2DB set. The impurity-surface distance comes from a simple phenomenological formula, not a costly geometry optimization, and Matminer features feed four models, with XGBoost leading. SHAP checks on about fifteen hundred lowest-barrier materials flag valence electron count, electronegativity, and atomic number as the most relevant attributes.
arxiv-2602-23078:
Mika Lauk and one co-author study non-perturbative rescaling of the energy-momentum tensor in the 2D O(3) bent sigma model. The model is a well-known toy model for small-kick effects in quantum field theory. Rescaling its energy-momentum tensor is hard: the bent form of O(3) balance causes real mix patterns, and large grid artifacts skew the fixing of rescaling constants.

The team presents results for the rescaling constants in the non-singlet sector, using a tweaked lattice action with shifted edge rules and setting the rescaled coupling through the gradient flow. With this setup they obtain a sharp fixing of the rescaling constants, the key numbers that connect lattice readings to smooth physics.
arxiv-2602-23478:
Sander Tonkens and four co-authors bridge offline safety synthesis and online adaptation for robots. Control barrier functions can guarantee robotic safety, but designing valid ones for complex systems is hard, while Hamilton-Jacobi reachability, a formal synthesis method, scales poorly and usually runs offline.

They introduce refineCBF, which refines an approximate barrier function, whether derived, learned, or even unsafe, via warm-started Hamilton-Jacobi reachability. Its faster successor, HJ-Patch, speeds the process with localized updates. Both guarantee recovery of a safe value function and monotonic safety gains during adaptation. Tests in simulation and on ground vehicles and quadcopters show real-time adaptation to new obstacles and unmodeled wind, a practical path toward formally guaranteed safety in the field.
arxiv-2602-23578:
Junghoon Justin Park and six co-authors present the Hybrid Quantum Temporal Convolutional Network (HQTCN), a quantum machine learning model for ordered data. Such models face scaling hurdles with complex many-channel signals. HQTCN mixes older time windows with a quantum convolutional neural network core.

Applying a shared quantum circuit across time windows, HQTCN captures long-range links while getting a large setting cut. Tested on mock NARMA series and dense EEG time-series, it performs well against older rivals on single-channel data and beats all rivals on many-channel tasks. It shows special strength under data-limited settings, keeping high scores with much fewer settings than usual methods. The results mark HQTCN as a lean model for many-channel time-series work.
arxiv-2602-23678:
Dingqi Ye and four co-authors propose rs-embed, a Python library offering remote sensing base model vectors on demand. Base models provide strong vectors for many downstream tasks, yet uptake and fair matching suffer from a mix in release formats, platforms, links, and input data specs.

These gaps greatly raise the cost of getting, using, and testing vectors across models. Rs-embed offers a unified, region-of-focus front end: with a single line of code, users retrieve vectors from any backed model for any place and any time range. The library also gives fast batch handling for large-scale vector making and tests. The code is openly shared.
arxiv-2602-23878:
Reynald Affeldt and four co-authors lay a foundation for differentiable logics using dependent type theory. The 2026 paper notes that differentiable logics, born in machine learning, carry analytic guarantees such as differentiability. They lack the algebraic and proof-theoretic theory that fuzzy logics have long enjoyed as substructural logics.

The team formalizes both families in one framework, encoded in the Rocq proof assistant with the Mathcomp library. A single language specification covers several fuzzy logics and two differentiable logics, with intrinsic typing that admits only valid formulas for each. Algebraically, the logics are interpreted through residuated lattices; analytically, the authors formalize positive derivatives for certain connectives, including L'Hôpital's rule. Proof-theoretically, they formalize known sequent calculi for fuzzy logics and propose new ones for the differentiable cases. The goal is one shared base for both kinds of logic.
arxiv-2602-24278:
Shruti Joshi and five co-authors examine the challenges of evaluating identifiability of learned representations, asking who guards the guardians. The 2026 paper notes that identifiability is judged by standard metrics, using synthetic benchmarks whose ground-truth factors are known. Recovery up to the equivalence class that identifiability theory guarantees is what these are assumed to reflect.

The authors show that assumption holds only under conditions. Its own assumptions, about the data-generating process and about the encoder, are implicitly encoded in each metric. When those assumptions are violated, false positives and false negatives can come from misspecified metrics. A new taxonomy separates data-generating assumptions from the encoder and maps metrics.
arxiv-2603-00078: Pasandi and Pasandi set out Relate, a plan that judges AI moral standing by bonds and bodily give-and-take, not by proven inner traits like sentience or consciousness. Weighing seven rule plans, they show today's tools treat each human-AI meeting as plain tool use, blind to bonds and bodily ties. They urge bond-impact checks, stepped moral care rules and ethics links across fields, plus a trial check run on a live companion system. They stress today's AI systems are not claimed conscious here.
arxiv-2603-00178: Condrey presents the first design for continuous attestation inside trusted execution environments, giving hardware-backed tamper resistance against inverted-trust foes. It grades input assurance from software integrity at Tier 1 through hardware input at Tier 3. A Markov-chain model rates chain availability, mean time between gaps, and recovery time goals. A tough evidence chain protocol holds integrity across enclave crashes, network splits and migration. Tests on Intel SGX show under 25% checkpoint CPU overhead, over 99.5% chain availability in simulation, and sealed-state recovery under 200 ms.
arxiv-2603-00278: Baker offers a fresh take on Zolotarev's classic argument for the law of quadratic reciprocity, a classic result relating whether one prime is a square modulo another prime. His version reimagines the classical argument with a creative twist, keeping the core idea while recasting how the proof unfolds. The result is a new presentation of a familiar theorem, showing the celebrated proof from a different angle.
arxiv-2603-00378: Banakar and five colleagues trace wasted memory in data centres to hotness fragmentation. Allocators group objects by size rather than use, so hot and cold items share pages and cold bytes stay locked in costly DRAM. Google traces show nearly all bytes in active pages are cold. Their OBASE system tracks access lightly and moves objects at run time so hot pages hold only hot items. Across varied structures and traces, page use rises several fold and footprint falls sharply, with small overhead.
arxiv-2603-00478: Luo and four colleagues set a rigorous ruler for few shot transfer, where no shared challenging protocol exists for real world use. Their FEWTRANS benchmark spans ten varied data sets, and their Hyperparameter Ensemble protocol counters the validation set illusion in data scarce settings. Tests show the pretrained model choice dominates results, while fancy transfer methods barely beat simple full fine tuning, which works through tiny distributed tweaks and flexible reshaping of high level meaning. Multimodal models collapse in specialised domains where wording grows rare.
arxiv-2603-00778: Lyne and three colleagues study Dicke superradiance in dense quantum matter, where tight confinement and exchange statistics shape joint glow. With a dissipative quartic Lindblad model, they track nonlinear motion in moving and electronic states. Their work tracks how bosonic enhancement and Pauli blocking set superradiant and subradiant scaling. Two routes break joint order: thermal dilution at high heat, and recoil breakdown in soft traps. The work sets a benchmark for joint light in systems like optical lattice clocks and spinor gases.
arxiv-2603-00878: Helvaci and three colleagues present MMTA, a transformer that slices therapy video and wearable signals into fine actions for stroke recovery checks. Each frame attends to several local time windows at once, so competing contexts near sharp transitions survive instead of blurring. The design lifts edit scores on the StrokeRehab set for both video and motion sensors, plus a cooking-activity set, without deeper or multi-stage machinery.
arxiv-2603-00978: Fan and four colleagues erase unwanted concepts from image and video diffusion models built on flow matching and transformers, where older erasure methods fail to transfer. EraseAnything++ frames erasure as a constrained multi-objective problem balancing removal against output quality. It solves this with utility-preserving unlearning via implicit gradient surgery. LoRA tuning and attention rules anchor the erasure, and a video trick spreads it across frames, beating prior methods on removal, quality, and frame-to-frame steadiness.
arxiv-2603-01378: Huang, Qin, and Huang study how different forms of summary data affect the gains of mixing individual person data with summary data under dataset shift. Within a capped maximum fit setup, they compare commonly reported summary stats, showing group-specific summaries can improve gauging gains a lot. Outcome-split group summaries always beat trait-split ones, most when the outcome is smooth. Outcome-split summaries are common for counted outcomes but rarely provided for smooth ones, backing their use for smooth outcomes.
arxiv-2603-01578:
Quantum programs must be mapped onto real chips, where each chip wires its qubits in its own layout. Gabrielius Keibas and Linas Petkevicius present a shared test frame for that mapping job in this 2026 work. Many mapping methods exist, but no common frame compared them fairly across chips and circuits.

Their open-source frame, QuMeld, now holds six mapping methods and sixteen chip layouts. Users can score each method with several metrics and swap parts in or out with ease. New methods, circuits, layouts, and metrics plug into the same frame as the field grows. A single yardstick helps teams pick the right mapper for a given chip instead of guessing from scattered claims.
arxiv-2603-01978:
P. Cataldi, V. Cristiani, F. Rodriguez, and colleagues prepare a way to estimate how galaxies fill dark matter halos for a coming survey. Their 2026 work targets the LSST imaging survey from the Vera Rubin Observatory. The halo occupation distribution links galaxy counts to halo mass and anchors galaxy formation tests.

Their method extends background subtraction to use more photometric information from imaging data. An iterative centroiding tool finds group centers, a step the whole estimate depends on. Each pipeline step faces checks for group size, purity, and completeness of the group catalog. Photometric redshift errors and halo mass uncertainty enter as systematics in the tests. On a mock catalog built from a large simulation suite, the method recovers the target distribution across a wide brightness and mass range.
arxiv-2603-02278:
Phil Attard extends a quantum simulation method in classical terms in this 2026 physics paper. Quantum effects can be folded into classical phase space through a special commutation function. That function encodes the uncertainty principle inside an otherwise classical picture. Attard expands it to third order and simplifies it for use in position space alone.

Momentum is integrated out, leaving a real function over positions only. That form fits standard Monte Carlo sampling, a workhorse of simulation. He reports simulation results for liquid helium-4 in a classic pair-potential model. Runs cover temperatures below ten kelvin, deep in the quantum regime for a light liquid. The paper is the second part of a series on this approach.
arxiv-2603-02378:
Alexander Nemecek, Hengzhi He, Guang Cheng, and Erman Ayday expose a clash between two content checks in this 2026 paper. Provenance records claim to certify who made a file, and watermarks tag AI-made content. The two systems run independently and never consult each other. That gap lets a file pass both checks while telling two opposite stories.

Their Integrity Clash is a file with a valid record claiming human authorship and a watermark marking it as AI-made. Standard editing workflows can wash metadata to create such fakes with no cryptographic break. Only one permitted missing field in the current standard enables the trick. Their joint audit, checking both layers together, classified thousands of test images perfectly. The fix, they argue, is simple and overdue.
arxiv-2603-02978:
Bethany Terris asks what an observer is inside one view of quantum theory. That view treats quantum states as facts for an observer, not as fixed traits of the world. Her 2026 paper presses a basic worry: shared checks need observers who last through time and keep stable records.

Terris argues that the bare rule, any system that interacts counts, cannot support that kind of lasting record. She adds a second layer: the capacity to hold records together across many acts of measuring. With that layer, cases where one observer watches another still yield facts both can confirm. The paper shores up the view's account of shared proof.
arxiv-2603-03078:
Siwei Zhang, Yun Xiong, Xi Chen, and colleagues widen the exploration habits of tool-using language agents during training. Agents trained by reinforcement learning usually learn only from their own rollouts, so they rarely discover reasoning styles outside their current habits. Their 2026 method, RAPO, injects retrieved outside experience into the loop.

Training splits into two phases. During rollouts, the agent reasons continuously over retrieved step-level traces from other policies, extending what it can consider. During updates, a retrieval-aware rule reshapes the gradient with retrieval rewards and importance weighting, keeping training stable. Across fourteen datasets and three agentic tasks, scores rose by about five points on average. Training also ran modestly faster than the baseline.
arxiv-2603-03278:
William Liang, Sam Wang, Hung-Ju Wang, and colleagues let a robot teach itself household skills by playing. Human demonstrations are costly, so autonomous practice is attractive, but play needs a policy that survives unfamiliar states and a routine that keeps producing useful experience. Their 2026 method, Tether, starts from at most ten demonstrations.

An open-loop policy warps those demonstrated actions onto new scenes by anchoring them to semantic keypoints, proving strikingly robust to spatial and meaning shifts. Deployed in a real multi-object household setup, the robot cycles through choosing, attempting, judging, and improving tasks, guided by a vision-language model. Over a full day of play it streamed more than a thousand expert-level trajectories. Policies trained on that self-made data rivaled human-taught ones.
arxiv-2603-03878:
Chetan Choppali Sudarshan and others present CarbonPATH, a framework for designing chiplet-based AI systems with carbon footprint as a first-class concern. AI growth is driving demand for computing while enlarging its footprint on the environment. Makers are shifting to heterogeneous integration, building systems from chiplets, to escape the yield and cost limits of single-die chips. Searching this space means balancing performance, cost, and carbon across apps, architecture, chiplets, and packaging.

CarbonPATH explores the space with simulated annealing, co-designing workload mapping, design settings, and packaging methods. It accounts for compute and memory sizes, chiplet process nodes, wiring protocols, integration styles from flat 2.5D layouts to stacked 3D ones, running and embodied carbon, and link type. By capturing interactions across levels, it finds system-level solutions that narrower methods miss, supporting earlier, carbon-aware decisions in AI hardware design.
arxiv-2603-03978: Wenyun Li and others present a method for generating safety-critical traffic scenarios via multi-objective Monte Carlo Tree Search. The method turns trajectory feasibility and naturalistic conduct into tuning goals inside one tests function, surfacing varied collision events while keeping realism. A hybrid Upper Confidence Bound and Lower Confidence Bound search plan balances exploratory speed with risk-averse choice-making. Tests in four Hong Kong accident zones show an 85% collision failure rate with strong feasibility and comfort.
arxiv-2603-04178: Roberto Soler tests the single-fluid magnetohydrodynamic approximation for Alfvén wave propagation in the partially ionized lower solar atmosphere. Here he compares multi-fluid results with single-fluid magnetohydrodynamic results to assess the latter for Alfvénic waves low in the solar atmosphere. Both discrepancies arise from approximate ion-neutral drift treatment in the single-fluid model and should have very limited practical impact.
arxiv-2603-04478: Li and colleagues pretrain EEG foundation models by distilling many teachers with MTDP. Masked reconstruction, borrowed from vision and language, struggles on EEG, where data cost dearly and signal to noise runs low. Vision and time series foundation models transfer surprisingly well to EEG, the authors first show. MTDP fuses diverse teacher representations through a learnable gating network and masked latent denoising, then distills the fused representation into an EEG model. Across 9 downstream tasks and 12 datasets, the MTDP model beats self supervised counterparts while using only 25 percent of pretraining data.
arxiv-2603-04578: De Brito and colleagues build high purity OAM entangled photons. Spontaneous parametric down conversion links multiple, often linked degrees of freedom. These are usually treated apart despite ties. Spatial spectral links left uncontrolled create tell-apart clues and cut clarity, harming wide encoding. The authors analyze two-photon spectral structure and find source setups strongly cutting such links. They quantify how coupling between spatial and spectral parts lowers OAM purity, mapping pure regions against order, crystal length, and pump and collection waists. This gives bright sources with less lossy filters.
arxiv-2603-04678: Liu and colleagues improve cross-language match in language models via post-training. Models often answer rendered prompts across languages. The paper defines cross-language match as a gap between a response spread and its round-trip version. PCO couples this gap with a KL penalty to a fixed base model. Since direct optimization needs costly on-policy roll-outs, direct optimization offers a stand-in. Across models, DCO improves cross-language match across 26 languages, beats rivals, enabling aimed tuning for low-resource languages.
arxiv-2603-04978: Taro Wakamura and the rest of the team study in full superconductivity in few-layer Td-MoTe2, a shape-based superconductor hopeful. Across peeled samples of other depths, bases, and crystal grades, they match disorder, carrier density, carrier type, and carrier flow with superconducting temperature. Joined with first-principles sums, the work links band structure to superconductivity in the stuff. In 2-layer samples they reach a highly hole-doped regime never reached before, showing superconductivity in line with usual phonon-carried s(++)-wave pairing.
arxiv-2603-05078: Juntong Fang and team offer MoRe, a feedforward 4D rebuild network recovering dynamic 3D scenes from monocular videos. Moving objects corrupt camera pose estimation, and current tuning methods need extra supervision while remaining computationally expensive and impractical in real time. Built on a strong static rebuild backbone, MoRe uses attention-forcing to disentangle dynamic motion from static structure, plus grouped causal attention capturing time dependencies across varying token lengths. Fine-tuning on large-scale diverse data sets adds toughness, and tests show high-quality dynamic reconstructions with exceptional leanness.
arxiv-2603-05378: Guangming Liu and the rest of the team build MQED-QD, an open-source exciton package. Molecular exciton motion needs electromagnetic runs and open-system motion. Based on macroscopic quantum electrodynamics, the package constructs dyadic Green's functions, sets master equations, and propagates subsystem motion. The authors simulate exciton transport in a one-dimensional chain near silver, testing planar surfaces. Nanorod polaritons lift dipole-dipole contacts, speeding exciton delocalization and yielding higher participation ratios. Elucidating exciton motion, MQED-QD helps rational nanoscale design.
arxiv-2603-06178: Meng and colleagues study training free diffusion segmentors, adapting text to image diffusion models for semantic segmentation without training. Existing methods lean on cross attention maps assumed to link pixels and text tokens, yet stronger generative models fail to improve segmentation. The authors trace this to two gaps: head and layer attention maps diverge from a unified global representation, and a global map still gives skewed semantic correlation across tokens. Their fixes, auto aggregation and per pixel rescaling, let training free segmentation use generative power better on standard benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-06478: Madeira and team study the spatial Muller's ratchet, a model of teamwork and competition in a growing asexual population. Each particle carries a count of harmful mutations, and births add one lowering birth rate. Under scaling, the process settles weakly to an infinite system of PDEs, backing earlier non-strict maths. Joining convergence with analysis of the system gives bounds on mutant shares holding with high odds. A tightness test for interacting groups, based on local dynamics, beats the lack of per-site bounds.
arxiv-2603-06578: Kisel and team show multimodal language model sorting performance depends on evaluation protocol and ground truth quality, with clashing comparisons. They identify and fix issues: outputs outside the class list that are dropped, puffed results from weak decoys, and open-world settings lagging from poor output mapping. Tests on ReGT, a relabel of 625 ImageNet classes, show models benefit most from corrected labels, closing the supervised gap. Much reported lag thus reflects noisy ground truth and flawed rules rather than genuine model flaw.
arxiv-2603-06678: Liardi and team survey Partial Information Decomposition, an information-theory framework for information in complex systems that lacks a unique build, producing a crowd of forms with math bets. Joining existing measures into a common language, they examine all major routes, checking for each measure whether each property holds. They derive a web of known theorems mapping links and clashes between traits, showing novel linkage results. The work charts a brief history of it, pushes a unified perspective, and offers a path toward theory polish and hands-on applications.
arxiv-2603-06778: Avram and colleagues establish two key facts about Jacobians for positive ODEs on edge faces. Each face is defined by a siphon of a chemical reaction network. On such a face, the matrix takes block lower-triangular form, with a transversal block for species that fade on the face and an along-face block. That block is a Metzler matrix. Those facts prove and widen the Next Generation Matrix theorem and make its assumptions clear. They show a boundary fixed point cannot turn unstable through a Hopf bifurcation crosswise.
arxiv-2603-06878: Friedman and colleagues test whether long or short LLM answers change how well readers spot reasoning errors. They ran a repeated-measures experiment on thinking tasks, giving each person Watson-Glaser items paired with answers that varied in length and in truth. The design isolates length from truth. Analysis with mixed-effects logistic regression found a strong, reliable truth effect, with length examined only in interaction with truth.
arxiv-2603-06978: Shen and colleagues present an ab initio halo study of beryllium-11, a one-neutron halo. They use nuclear lattice field theory at N3LO, wavefunction matching against the sign problem, and a pinhole algorithm for many-body correlations. They reproduce the ground-state parity flip and extended matter radius. They compare density distributions and shapes of beryllium-11 with core beryllium-10. Results reveal a two-cluster structure in both nuclei. The neutron occupies a sigma orbital in beryllium-11, enhancing prolate shape and neutron tail, unlike pi-orbital use in beryllium-10.
arxiv-2603-07478: Solonen and colleagues separate the true effect of intelligent heating control from other changes in district-heated buildings. Tracking methods from simple weather normalization to complex models cannot isolate control effects, since buildings constantly change for unrelated reasons. The authors review and derive monitoring methods, expose that weakness, then propose a model-based approach tracking only control-related effects. Real data spanning about a decade from a commercial platform demonstrate the decomposition into sub-effects.
arxiv-2603-07678: Liu, Chen and Xiu present a data-driven method for on-the-fly active flow control using flow map learning. The model learns drag and lift responses to control inputs offline with a deep network, then enables online optimal control without simulating the flow field. It integrates with deep reinforcement learning and model predictive control strategies. On two-dimensional flow past a cylinder it achieves over a fifth less drag, pointing toward real-time optimal control in other systems.
arxiv-2603-08178: Kapralov and colleagues introduce an imaging approach that needs no electrical links to single pixels. High-resolution sensors normally need electrical access to each pixel for readout. That demand grows hard for tiny pixels, for mixed sensing and readout layers in long-wavelength detectors, and for novel light-sensing materials with no established silicon integration. Their sensor matrix uses photoresistive pixels linked neighbor-to-neighbor and packed into a dense array, with readout handled without per-pixel wiring.
arxiv-2603-08578: Ismail Lamaakal and colleagues turn drift alarms into priced actions for live machine learning systems. Most monitors only sound an alarm, leaving teams to guess what to do under tight label, compute, and delay budgets. Their Drift2Act controller reads unlabeled signals, checks risk with a few delayed labels, and picks cheap fixes when risk stays low, or abstains and escalates when it runs high.
arxiv-2603-08678: Noah Schlossberger and colleagues sense radio fields with Rydberg atoms using only plain diode lasers. A three-photon coupling scheme drops the doubling crystal and tapered amplifier that usually gate miniaturization. In the low-power regime the line stays thin, and the setup detects a 4.7 GHz field with sensitivity matching two-photon schemes. A repump readout variant reads the transparency in the other lasers through a separate state.
arxiv-2603-08778: Takahisa Igata and colleagues expand the bending angle of light near a degenerate photon sphere. Their recipe isolates the divergent part at marginality, yielding a single leading power-law term. The leading coefficient splits into a universal branch constant times a local factor from the third derivative of the effective potential. Switching to impact parameter adds one more local factor.
arxiv-2603-08878: Matthew Siebert and colleagues rederive secondary echelle mode traces for STIS with Gaussian process regression. Old traces used straight-line fits per spectral order, missing each order's true curvature across the detector. The new method lifts flux throughput by about four percent near detector edges and supplies fresh traces for nine echelle modes.
arxiv-2603-09078: Shuangfei Zhai offers exclusive self attention, a simple tweak of self attention for Transformer models. The key idea limits attention to signals at right angles to the token's own value vector, dropping self-position signals to sharpen context modeling. Tested on standard language modeling, exclusive attention always beats plain attention across models up to 2.7B, with gains growing as sequences grow.
arxiv-2603-09578: Shahid Sattar and colleagues study the magneto-optical response of five-septuple-layer MnBi2Te4 films in spin-flip states, using first-principles calculations and a coupled Dirac-cone model. Kerr and Faraday rotations probe topological order directly in this magnetic topological insulator. Despite nonzero out-of-plane magnetization, the film can be a Chern number plus-one insulator or a trivial one, depending on how the top and bottom layers' spins align. Faraday and Kerr angles from tight-binding models clarify the mechanisms at play.
arxiv-2603-09678: Aman Sharma and Paras Chopra introduce EsoLang-Bench, a benchmark that tests genuine reasoning in language models through esoteric programming languages. Popular code benchmarks use mainstream languages that saturate training corpora, so near-ceiling scores may reflect familiarity, not reasoning. Their five languages, including Brainfuck, Befunge-98, and Shakespeare, are all Turing-complete, so the same problems are solvable in principle. Their hard-by-design primitives and tiny corpus presence make them a clean proxy for out-of-distribution performance.
arxiv-2603-09778: Karla Tame-Narvaez and coauthors make a first try at fitting neutrino interaction model settings with simulation based inference. They revisit a GENIE generator setup tuned earlier by the MicroBooNE team. Fed tuned cross section values, their trained method recovers the four settings closely; fed real data, it picks slightly shifted values with a better fit. It can also mimic a rival simulation fairly well.
arxiv-2603-09978: Amal Akli and coauthors give the first broad test of parameter efficient fine tuning for multitask code analysis. Language models shine at code generation, yet their skill at other code tasks is less clear, and full tuning across tasks costs too much. One shared efficient module, they find, can match or beat full multitask tuning. Against single task tuning it keeps near equal accuracy while slashing storage and trainable weights.
arxiv-2603-10178: Linxin Song and coauthors judge computer use agents by watching execution videos instead of reading their internal steps. Scaling such checks is hard, since screens repeat heavily and success often hinges on tiny local cues. They build a large data set of video, task and reward triples, with adversarial instruction variants as negatives. Spatiotemporal token pruning strips redundant regions, and their fine tuned reward model beats strong proprietary rivals.
arxiv-2603-10478: Tim Menzies and Kishan Kumar Ganguly argue that software testing should shift from costly verification to herding, steering systems toward goals by search instead of models. Their lever is the sparsity of influence: in many systems a few variables rule a huge state space. Their learner EZR finds those controlling variables directly by light sampling, with no prior knowledge assumed. Across dozens of tasks it reached near peak results with only a few dozen samples, replacing heavy solvers at a fraction of the effort.
arxiv-2603-10578: Zhuangzi Li and co-authors improve how vision-language models judge the quality of computer graphics images. Existing datasets lack systematic quality descriptions, and older methods give no text explanations. The team named six perceptual dimensions and built a dataset of thousands of CG images with written quality descriptions covering style, content, and perceived quality. Current models proved weak at fine-grained judgments, yet descriptions of similar images helped a lot. Their two-stream retrieval framework uses that trick, and tests on several models showed clear gains in quality assessment.
arxiv-2603-10778: Konstantinos S Servis and co-authors present a clear-sky survey method for the Desert Fireball Network, aimed at measuring meteoroid flux at centimeter to meter sizes. Those sizes bridge small meteoroids that threaten spacecraft and near-Earth objects of defense concern, yet flux there is hard to pin down. Their pipeline uses HEALPix sky partitioning to measure effective coverage, and analyzes millions of all-sky images for clear conditions by star detection. Applied to the 2015 Southern Taurid shower, it found dozens of fireballs, consistent with earlier extrapolations.
arxiv-2603-10978: Boyuan Chen and coauthors tackle a stubborn weakness of vision-language models. They hallucinate counts. They score far worse at counting objects than at other visual reasoning. Their GroundCount framework feeds the language model explicit spatial grounding. That grounding comes from a conventional object detector through structured prompts. It does not come through fusing features. Prompt-based grounding beats feature-level fusion in their ablations. Positional encoding proves critical. Confidence scores mostly add noise. One model's reflective style clashes with the structured prompts, though.
arxiv-2603-11078: Kristen Pereira and coauthors introduce CR-Bench and CR-Evaluator, a benchmark dataset and a fine-grained evaluation pipeline for judging AI agents that review code in real-world settings. Frontier language models now power such agents. Yet coarse success metrics hide behavior that matters when false positives are costly. Their study of single-shot and reflection-based agents finds a low signal-to-noise ratio when agents hunt every hidden issue. This exposes a trade-off between resolving issues and raising spurious findings.
arxiv-2603-11378: Hillary Mutisya and John Mugane reach state-of-the-art Swahili speech recognition with remarkably little labeled data. They continue to pretrain a speech model before fine-tuning it. Their recipe runs pseudo-labeled continued pretraining on unlabeled audio. It then runs supervised fine-tuning on twenty thousand labeled samples. The result cuts word error rate by eighty-two percent relative to the baseline. It beats the best previously reported system by sixty-one percent. This is a transferable methodology for other low-resource languages.
arxiv-2603-11578: Koshkin and co-authors present Hikari, an end-to-end model for simultaneous speech translation and streaming transcription. Older systems pair offline translators with hand-built rules or learned wait policies. Hikari drops the policy and adds Decoder Time Dilation, which fights the overuse of WAIT tokens in training. A fine-tuning strategy also teaches the model to recover from delays. The payoff is a better quality-latency trade-off at modest size. Hikari matches systems up to 38 times larger, plus proprietary APIs, across three language pairs.
arxiv-2603-11678: Lee and Choi propose RAF, a training objective for GAN vocoders that lifts fidelity and generalization. Modern vocoders have strong designs, yet their training goals often fail to build broadly useful features. RAF lets speech self-supervised models help the discriminators judge quality, pushing the generator toward richer features. Relativistic pairing of real and fake waveforms sharpens the modeled distribution. Across data sets, gains hold on objective and subjective metrics alike. A RAF-trained BigVGAN-base beats the larger LSGAN-trained BigVGAN while using 12 percent of its parameters.
arxiv-2603-11778: Siwek and co-authors test explainable AI methods for spotting fake news with language models. They compare SHAP, LIME, and Integrated Gradients as ways to open up neural classifiers. Each method adds its own value: SHAP gives fine local attributions, LIME gives simple, intuitive accounts, and Integrated Gradients runs fast with convolutional nets. Detection accuracy stays high while the models grow clearer, they find. Costs and tuning sensitivity remain limits.
arxiv-2603-11878: Fragkos and co-authors show how symmetry steers light-driven Floquet states in tin sulfide, a multivalley semiconductor. Periodic light fields can dress materials into hybrid Floquet states. Using extreme ultraviolet photoemission, group theory, and density functional calculations, the team finds sharp selection rules from crystal symmetry. These rules govern both plain bands and light-induced Floquet states. By aligning the drive polarization against the crystal axes, they flip the parity of Floquet-Bloch states at will. It covers valence and conduction bands alike.
arxiv-2603-12178: Collier and co-authors measure tiny, short-lived kernels inside solar flare ribbons with Solar Orbiter. Ribbons mark where reconnection energy lands in the low solar atmosphere. High-cadence images from the March 2024 campaign caught an M-class flare at fine detail. A classical vision algorithm picked out the kernels and their size spread. Many kernels stayed unresolved even at this sharp view, and each heated for less than a few seconds. Energy thus lands in small patches for brief bursts, a fact flare models must now face.
arxiv-2603-12278: Turja tests unsupervised anomaly detection on wearable foot sensor data as a step toward ulcer prevention. Diabetic foot ulcers bring grave risks, from tissue loss to amputation. Baseline models of normal foot mechanics must come before any clinical warning tool. Healthy adults walked a sensor-lined pathway across 312 sessions, yielding near 94 thousand valid readings. Isolation Forest caught subtle, spread-out odd readings better, while a neighbor method flagged clustered extremes. A mild link between pressure and temperature supports combined monitoring in future patient studies.
arxiv-2603-12378: Yang and co-authors add context-aware neuromodulation to LoRA for multi-task adaptation. LoRA variants tune large models cheaply, but FlyLoRA routes by static magnitude and ignores input context. NeuroLoRA keeps frozen random projections and adds a light learnable gate inspired by brain neuromodulation. That gate rescales the projection space by context before experts are chosen. A contrastive orthogonality loss pushes expert subspaces apart for cleaner task splits. Tests on MMLU, GSM8K, and ScienceQA beat FlyLoRA and other baselines across single-task, merging, and continual settings.
arxiv-2603-12578: Yi Xu and co-authors aim to sharpen click-through rate prediction for online items. Most models squeeze a user's past actions into one vector before mixing it with item context. That step loses fine detail and blocks links to single actions. Their CDNet uses two views at once. One view pairs the most relevant actions with context in fine detail. The other pairs the user's broad interest spread with context, and tests confirm clear gains.
arxiv-2603-12678: Abhishek Baruah and co-authors test the AdS/CFT correspondence through the thermodynamics of black holes from nonlinear electrodynamics. They study ModMax, generic nonlinear, and Euler-Heisenberg AdS black holes and their dual field theories. Three entropy frameworks are used, from the standard one to Rényi and Kaniadakis forms. Critical points match across temperature curves, specific heat, and geometric curvature. The count of such points is preserved between bulk and dual sides. Kaniadakis entropy adds one more critical point in every system.
arxiv-2603-12878: Ramón Guevara and co-authors propose a way to break up harmful synchrony in neural populations with brief pulses. Over-synchronized activity marks conditions like epilepsy and Parkinson disease. When the true system is unknown, picking pulse times and strengths is a hard inverse problem. Their scheme targets the centroid of the limit cycle in phase space. That point is easy to compute and stays robust as coupling changes. It also sits where return times are shortest, which aids control.
arxiv-2603-12978: Jian Chen and co-authors prove that a generalized Camassa-Holm equation has global conservative solutions, and that they are unique. The form they study has two power-type nonlinear parts. A change of variables turns it into a semi-linear system that is easier to handle. That system lets them build solutions that last for all time. To prove uniqueness, they add helper variables shaped to one given solution. Those helpers fit a system with just one solution, which ends the proof.
arxiv-2603-13278: Dean Barr introduces the AI Transformation Gap Index, a framework for benchmarking AI readiness and value. Firms spend heavily on AI yet lack a shared, data-based way to compare their position. AITG measures the gap between a firm's current deployment and an industry capability frontier. Five linked modules handle normalization, a dynamic capability ceiling, firm scoring, value decomposition, and disruption risk. Barr calibrates the framework for 22 industries and applies it to 14 public firms. The largest gaps did not yield the highest value density, he finds.
arxiv-2603-13478: Dominik Dold and Philipp Christian Petersen ask whether one spike per neuron is enough in spiking neural networks. Approximation bounds to date hold only for neurons that spike at most once, seen as a strong limit. They prove the opposite holds for a large class of models, including leaky integrate-and-fire with subtractive reset. Any bound for multi-spike networks has an equivalent single-spike version with only linearly more or fewer neurons. The reverse holds too, so the two classes are equivalent for approximation in general tasks.
arxiv-2603-13578: Yao Zhang, Zhuchenyang Liu, and Yu Xiao propose LingoMotion, a symbolic language for human motion. Existing representations like MotionGPT act as black-box latent vectors with limited interpretability and can be ambiguous. LingoMotion follows the hierarchy of natural language, from letters to words, phrases, and sentences. Its motion alphabet is based on joint angles, with morphology for words and phrases for simple actions and attributes. Syntax then describes complex activities as sequences of words and phrases. Early tests on the Motion-X dataset show high fidelity.
arxiv-2603-13678: Daniel Shen, Marija Ilic, and John Parsons study peak-load pricing and investment cost recovery with duration-limited storage. Storage shifts energy from off-peak to on-peak periods, but stored energy capacity limits how long it can supply power. They extend the classic two-period peak-load pricing model to include such storage. On- and off-peak prices link to storage investment costs, round-trip efficiency, and peak duration. Most of the scarcity premium ties to fixed storage costs, not efficiency losses.
arxiv-2603-13878: Fan and co-authors build Step-CoT, a dataset that teaches medical vision models to reason in clear steps. Most chain-of-thought data for medical questions is free-form and skips the structure clinicians use. Step-CoT covers over 10,000 real cases and 70,000 question pairs, laid out along diagnostic workflows. A teacher-student setup with a dynamic graph focus picks out the most useful steps. Experiments show gains in both answer accuracy and how readable the reasoning is.
arxiv-2603-14178: Abbas and Azzouz study a nonlocal variational problem on a hybrid domain: one solid interval plus a finite set of loose points. The energy splits into continuous, discrete, and interface parts. Their main estimate shows the interface term binds the two phases in a coercive way and yields an equal hybrid norm. A unique minimizer then exists for the problem. It is the weak solution of a hybrid system that joins an integral equation on the interval with algebra on the points.
arxiv-2603-14278: Jenny and co-authors jailbreak white-box language models by editing inner activations, with no change to the prompt. Most jailbreaks rework the text, while ablation studies probe which inner parts cause which outputs. Their method builds a nearby benign prompt and swaps its layer-wise activations into the target run. The swaps stop refusal signals from spreading across layers, which mutes the safety response. The work also maps where refusal forms, and flags risks for open-weight models.
arxiv-2603-14578: Paquette, Xiao and Zhu track power-law spectra through the random feature model. Neural loss curves often fall as power laws in size and data. Data covariance spectra with power-law decay sit behind that pattern. The question is whether a random projection plus a nonlinearity keeps the decay. The team studies monomial activations on Gaussian-sketched data. Matching upper and lower bounds pin the eigenvalue decay. The input power-law exponent survives intact, they prove. Only a log factor, set by the monomial degree, changes the shape.
arxiv-2603-14678: Zhang and co-authors revisit candidate high-velocity stars tied to the Sagittarius dwarf galaxy. Fast stars trace extreme dynamics, and the disrupting dwarf looks like a source. Gaia, DESI and LAMOST data yield stars moving over 400 kilometers per second. Orbits run in a Galactic potential with the dwarf and the Large Magellanic Cloud. Three origin tales face tests: Hills ejection, tidal stripping and halo crossings. Ninety-five candidates pass near the dwarf. Their motion and metal mix fit plain halo stars best, they conclude.
arxiv-2603-14778: Ming and co-authors serve retrieval-augmented generation with privacy for data owners and users in P2RAG. Outsourced RAG leaks risks on both sides of the query. Secure top-k search usually leans on secure sorting. Fixed k, fresh security flaws and slow large-k runs plague that route. P2RAG skips sorting for an interactive bisection that finds any top-k set. Secret sharing across two non-colluding servers guards the database and prompt. Checks and limits blunt malicious user tricks.
arxiv-2603-14878: Schulthess and co-authors observe dressed states of proton spins in water with a Rabi-type setup. A strong off-resonant dressing field drives the spins past the rotating-wave regime. The setup realizes the quantum Rabi model for nuclear spins. Measured spectra show transitions that absorb several dressing-field quanta at once. Higher-order resonances match quantum Rabi predictions closely. Dressed-state energies agree with theory across the scan. Proton spins extend dressed-state spectroscopy to a fresh platform.
arxiv-2603-15278: Patra and co-authors give pursuit strategies that guarantee finite-time capture of an evader while keeping it encircled. A team of pursuers chases one evader on an open plane. The evader's heading stays unknown, and its strategy is arbitrary. The pursuers keep the evader inside the convex hull of their positions until capture. The authors prove capture always occurs in finite time. They also derive an upper bound on the capture time, and simulations test the scheme against varied evader tactics.
arxiv-2603-15678: Xu tracks a hidden boundary inside transformer training runs. Huge models still move along just a few shared directions while training. His Spectral Edge Dynamics method slides a window over parameter updates. A sharp edge splits coherent signal directions from random noise. Tests span a 51M-parameter TinyStories model and GPT-2 under shift. The edge rises, plateaus, then collapses in all runs. A cheap projection keeps the gap within 5.7 percent. Companion work uses the same geometry to warn of grokking early.
arxiv-2603-15978: Spera frames safe, revenue-aware design for customer service agent networks. Scripted chatbots give way to teams of specialist AI agents. The agents compose skills across billing, payments, service, and fulfilment. A safety gap opens when separately safe agents join forces. Combined skills can reach a banned goal neither agent holds alone. His capability closure framework names and tracks that emergent path. The design weighs safety closure against revenue goals together.
arxiv-2603-16278: Veler and Gannot make speaker localization more robust in echoing rooms. Their method unfolds a batch expectation-maximization procedure inside a neural network. The layout is an encoder, an EM core, and a decoder. Building the iteration into the network cuts sensitivity to starting points. It also improves convergence. Tests beat the classical batch EM method. Gains held up under reverberant conditions.
arxiv-2603-16578: Zhang, Cheng, and Chu ask when unsupervised reinforcement learning improves math reasoning. Ground-truth labels are costly, so intrinsic rewards tempt as a substitute. Such training can collapse or learn to game rewards, though. Their rewards push for short and certain answers. Base model strength decides much of the outcome. A geometric lens explains the split. Successful runs sit inside enveloping manifolds. Failed ones fall outside that shelter.
arxiv-2603-16778: Davis builds a framework for controlling trapped active matter with several knobs at once. Earlier work mostly drove one parameter and made strict assumptions. His method uses exact gradients from automatic differentiation to find protocols that cut work or heat. The knobs cover trap stiffness, trap center, and particle activity. He finds that smooth, lab-friendly protocols nearly match abrupt bang-bang ones. Coupled parameters yield new tricks, such as symmetry breaking in activity cycles. He also notes that separately tuned controls, run together, cost only slightly more work.
arxiv-2603-17278: Rotenberg, Faria, and Caffo present a model agnostic method for ordinal classification, plus open source software for it. Ordinal data, where labels have a natural order, are common in clinical work and beyond. Yet modern machine learning tools for them are scarce. Their pooling method lets any standard classifier be used in an ordinal fashion. On several real datasets, the ordinal versions often beat plain classification. The edge is largest when data are few or outcome classes are many.
arxiv-2603-17678: Peshkovsky and co-authors present RIO, a label-free tool that images chemical gradients at the microscale. Concentration shifts give weak optical contrast, so maps are hard to build. RIO reads refractive index through a Fabry-Pérot chip on a standard microscope. Per-pixel index precision reaches about one part in a hundred thousand with a plain CMOS camera. Salt gradients in a two-stream flow test the device. Cell signaling and reaction studies could use it.
arxiv-2603-17778: Mengistu and co-authors test how bar strength and speed shape galaxy evolution. Galaxy Zoo labels supply the barred sample, and MaNGA maps give resolved spectra. Four tracers trace star formation on current, mid-range, and long timescales. Slow, strong bars quench their hosts most, they find. Strong bars lift star formation at the center, while slow bars lift it along the bar. Bars thus leave both global and local marks on their galaxies.
arxiv-2603-17878: Sbarra and co-authors generate light from ultraviolet to near-infrared in one microresonator. A single telecom laser pumps a silicon nitride ring with high quality factor. Second- and third-order nonlinear effects cascade inside the device. Light-driven poling switches on second harmonic output, which then seeds tunable parametric oscillation. Watt-scale input yields milliwatt-level near-infrared light, they report. Mode choice at the harmonic makes the output reconfigurable on the fly.
arxiv-2603-18178: Bhat and co-authors present VLM-AutoDrive, a post-training framework for vision-language models in driving safety. Dashcam events like collisions are brief, rare, and hard for generic vision models. The framework adds metadata captions, LLM descriptions, question pairs, and reasoning traces as training signal. Fine-tuning lifted collision F1 from 0.00 to 0.69 on real Nexar videos. Overall accuracy rose from 35.35% to 77.27%, with readable reasoning traces.
arxiv-2603-18578: Wang and co-authors use design workshops to imagine fairer contact between LGBTQ+ and cisgender users in the Metaverse. Virtual worlds often copy offline bias and heteronormative norms. Participants named barriers, sketched fixes, and pictured future scenes in three phases. Ideas spanned activity, interaction, scene, and space layers. Spatial cues and power gaps shaped who felt heard. The authors offer design chances for builders and principles for handling power in digital space.
arxiv-2603-18778: Du and co-authors propose a flexible fault-tolerant quantum computing setup built on GKP states.
