A three-dimensional cluster state carries the design, built across polarization, frequency, and orbital angular momentum. Optical generators first make three kinds of entangled pairs. A beam-splitter network with time delays then weaves the cluster state. A partly squeezed surface-GKP code supplies error tolerance. The team finds the best place to apply the squeezing gate. The fault-tolerant squeezing threshold lands at 11.5 dB. They present the scheme as scalable and feasible.
arxiv-2603-18878: Mortensen and Walmsley pin down when weighted backward shifts on trees are chain recurrent. The shifts act on lp spaces and on c0 over a directed tree. Two divergence conditions on the weights decide the answer. One looks forward over descendants of each vertex. In unrooted trees, a second looks back over descendants of each ancestor. For symmetric shifts on symmetric trees, the conditions match the classic sequence space results. Those cover one-sided and two-sided index sets for both lp and c0 spaces.
arxiv-2603-18978: Artiano and Ranocha build cheaper high-order methods that keep entropy steady for wave-like systems. Past methods rest on pair fluxes and special grid operators. Their work gives simple forms for the extra terms that nonconservative systems need. They work out when such terms keep entropy in a three-point setup. The forms extend to many dimensions on straight and curved grids. Balance traits for steady states carry over as well. They use the recipe to derive several new schemes.
arxiv-2603-19078: Shin and co-authors bake robot body dynamics into the network that learns robot control. Past work used link structure as a prior, but force flow through the body was left out. Their graph network copies the way the classic articulated body method passes inertia from child links to parent links. Learned values stand in for physical ones. Policies built on it learn faster and cope better with shifted dynamics. Tests cover simulated humanoid, four-legged, and hopper robots. Learned policies also run on two real robots.
arxiv-2603-19478: Oda asks whether bound states form in a scalar theory with a fourth-order derivative term. He rewrites the theory as a standard second-order one with ghost and normal fields. In the ladder approximation, he studies correlation functions of composite operators. A bound-state pole appears for pairs of ghost and normal fields when the coupling is large. No such pole shows for the near-massless normal field tied to the graviton. The model may shed light on ghost confinement in quadratic gravity.
arxiv-2603-19678: Xu and co-authors present VLADR, a vision-language method for lifelong person re-identification. The task learns one retrieval model across changing domains without forgetting. Prior methods lean on global features and underuse fine-grained attribute knowledge. VLADR mines text attributes at global and local levels for each image. Cross-modal alignment guides the visual side to extract those attributes. Inter-domain alignment then transfers fine-grained knowledge to new domains. Tests beat prior methods on both anti-forgetting and generalization scores.
arxiv-2603-19778: Vořechovský and Mašek improve space-filling designs for costly computer experiments. Good designs must fill the full space and project evenly onto low-dimensional subspaces. Maximum Projection designs aim at that, but they use plain Euclidean distance. The authors show this choice skews sampling away from corner regions. That skew also biases Monte Carlo estimates. Their uMaxPro variant swaps in a periodic distance instead. Tests showed unbiased integration with lower variance and strong projection quality. Benchmark runs on a concrete model also gained accuracy.
arxiv-2603-19878: Hatsuda and co-authors study the Gauss law constraint in A-theory, a brane picture with U-duality symmetry. In this theory the brane worldvolume and spacetime sit in different representations of an exceptional group. Closing the brane algebra forces the Gauss law constraint. That constraint turns spacetime coordinates into gauge fields and grows the worldsheet into the worldvolume. The authors show only the string solution fits the reduction rule in dimensions three and four. They also build a string solution that respects the exceptional symmetry.
arxiv-2603-20278: Li and co-authors present OpenResearcher, a fully open pipeline for training deep research agents. Such agents need long records that mix search, evidence gathering, and reasoning. Their system runs the search loop offline over a 15 million document corpus. Using GPT-OSS-120B as teacher, it produced over 97,000 training records. Fine-tuning a 30B model on them reached 54.8% on BrowseComp-Plus. That score beat the base model by 34 points.
arxiv-2603-20378: Langis and co-authors test whether optical tidal disruption events line up with high-energy neutrinos. IceCube has logged such neutrinos for over a decade, with sources still unclear. Stars torn apart by black holes are one proposed source class. Using the TDECat repository, they run a space-and-time matching algorithm. They also simulate event sets with built-in links to check the method. Despite two notable individual cases, no statistical link emerged. One jetted event matched a neutrino, but a flaring quasar shared its error region.
arxiv-2603-20678: Xing proposes a simulation framework for a stratified polyamory system and tests its claimed social effects. The paper links falling fertility and strain in marriage markets. Its model lets agents hold one primary spouse plus a capped set of legal secondary partners. Agent based models, reinforcement learning, and language model agents drive the setup. Matching is cast as a learning task solved with PPO. The author argues the scheme could raise welfare and spread wealth. Early runs are offered as support for the framework.
arxiv-2603-20978: Artigue and Ferrari introduce metric-independent expansiveness for group actions on metrizable spaces. The notion means an action is expansive under every compatible metric, not just one. For actions on locally compact spaces, they show it matches a purely topological property, cocompact expansivity. It also matches having an expansive extension to the one point compactification. They apply the test to ordinal and totally bounded spaces, with examples that split the two notions. They also define Cauchy expansiveness and prove such actions extend to the completion of the space.
arxiv-2603-21178: Sathvika and co-authors evaluate how well language models generate architecture views from source code. Architecture views are key documents, but making them by hand is slow and they go stale. They study three hundred forty open-source repositories across thirteen setups, yielding over four thousand views. Few-shot prompting cuts clarity failures by about nine percent. A custom agent does best, yet still fails on clarity in about a fifth of cases. All approaches work at code level rather than architectural level, so human expertise stays needed.
arxiv-2603-21478: Chang and co-authors introduce TaigiSpeech, a speech intent dataset for Taiwanese Taigi, a low-resource language spoken mainly by older adults. The dataset holds about 3,000 utterances from 21 speakers, aimed at healthcare and home assistant tasks. Labeled data is scarce, so they test two mining strategies to grow it. One pairs keyword matching with model pseudo-labeling through an intermediate language. The other uses audio-visual cues with little text supervision. The dataset will be released under a CC BY 4.0 license.
arxiv-2603-21878: The SND@LHC Collaboration measures the muon flux that forms the main background for its neutrino searches at the LHC. Muons stream in from proton collisions at the ATLAS point, far upstream. The team compares measured rates with simulation across all of Run 3, finding agreement within 10 to 15 percent. A 2024 beam optics change raised the flux, and 2025 settings did not restore old levels. High-angle muons from proton losses explain the excess, and new mitigation steps were tested. Simulations also forecast a steep rate rise at the high-luminosity LHC.
arxiv-2603-22478: The ATLAS Collaboration reports precise measurements of W boson plus photon production in proton collisions at 13 TeV. The data cover 140 inverse femtobarns from the LHC run. Cross sections are given for sixteen observables that probe the W-photon system. These test a predicted radiation zero, the W boson's polarization, and the proton's parton content. The team finds the data sharp enough to separate leading theory predictions. They also set limits on anomalous couplings from new-physics operators.
arxiv-2603-22678: Jiang, Shankar, and Yang study Picard rank jumps in families of K3 surfaces. The setting is positive characteristic, with prime greater than two. They look at a non-isotrivial family of K3 surfaces over a curve. Two conditions matter: the family must avoid a structural block from Frobenius, and it must have big monodromy. Under those conditions, the authors prove a strong claim. Infinitely many geometric fibers have larger Picard rank than the generic fiber. The result shows rank jumps are common, not rare, in such families.
arxiv-2603-22878: Batte, Luca, and Stănică solve a number theory equation linking two named families. One side holds generalized Thabit numbers of a set form. The other side holds terms of the k-Lucas sequence. That sequence starts with set terms, then sums the prior k terms each step. The prime in the Thabit form must be a Mersenne or Fermat prime. The authors find all solutions across the allowed ranges. The ranges cover the indices and exponents in the equation.
arxiv-2603-22978: Wang and co-authors present JFTA-Bench, a benchmark for language models that reason with fault trees. Fault trees guide maintenance teams to locate system failures. Their text format lets models read fault trees stored as images. The benchmark uses multi-turn dialogue with thousands of entries. Long dialogues test task tracking, and built-in rollback steps mimic user errors. The team also trains a model that plays the vague user. Gemini 2.5 Pro scores best among the models tested.
arxiv-2603-23078: Negusini and co-authors report an intercontinental clock comparison between Italy and Korea using radio telescopes. Geodetic VLBI observations in the K band linked hydrogen masers at Medicina and Sejong. The same clocks were also compared by satellite link and by optical clocks. Those optical clocks sit at the national metrology institutes of both countries. Fiber links carried their signals to the antennas. Results from all routes agreed at a very fine level. The pilot shows standard VLBI campaigns could compare clocks across continents.
arxiv-2603-23178: Das and co-authors present SAiW, an invisible watermarking framework for proactive deepfake defense. Most deepfake tools react after a fake spreads. SAiW marks media at creation with a source-linked signature. The watermark encodes which source made the media, not a generic signal. Feature-wise modulation injects that identity into the embedding network. A guidance module keeps the marks invisible to viewers. A forensic decoder both recovers the mark and names the source. Tests show strong survival under compression, noise, and attacks.
arxiv-2603-23378: Prodinger counts letters of a given type inside Catalan words. He works with generating functions tied to Catalan words and digit frequencies. Continued fractions supply those functions in a fast and flexible way. The method follows the philosophy Philippe Flajolet laid out in 1980. Prodinger presents the approach as elegant as well as quick. The counts cover how often each chosen digit or letter type appears across the words.
arxiv-2603-23478: Lin and Xu present UniFunc3D, a training-free way to segment affordances in 3D scenes. The task turns plain instructions into masks of small parts a user can act on. Older tools split the job into fragments and go blind during parsing. UniFunc3D lets one multimodal model act as an active observer. It reasons over meaning, time, and space at once, grounded in what it sees. A coarse-to-fine pass picks frames and zooms on fine parts. On SceneFun3D it tops prior tools.
arxiv-2603-23778: Argentieri and Ulliana prove stable ergodicity for a class of toral automorphisms in mathematics. They show that all ergodic automorphisms of the N-dimensional torus with a two-dimensional center are stably ergodic. This covers all ergodic cases in dimensions up to five, and also dimension seven. Their result extends an earlier theorem that needed an extra algebraic condition on the characteristic polynomial. The heart of the proof is a minimality criterion.
arxiv-2603-23878: LeCates and Wu introduce Luna, a C++ tool for formal analysis of neural networks. Luna propagates bounds through a network to check its behavior. It supports interval propagation, the DeepPoly and CROWN analyses, and the parameterized alpha-CROWN method. Earlier alpha-CROWN code was Python only, which made integration into other verifiers harder. Luna works over a general computational graph. On VNN-COMP 2025 benchmarks, they report tighter bounds and faster runs than the leading alpha-CROWN implementation. The code is publicly available.
arxiv-2603-24278: Luo and co-authors present TopoMesh, a mesh autoencoder that preserves sharp 3D features. Generation systems that use variational autoencoders are capped by how well the autoencoder rebuilds meshes. Real meshes have varied topology, while networks predict fixed grids, so direct matching fails. TopoMesh converts input meshes into a Dual Marching Cubes form that keeps sharp edges. The decoder outputs the same form, so vertices and faces correspond one to one. That gives direct supervision on topology and geometry. Tests beat prior autoencoders on reconstruction fidelity.
arxiv-2603-24378: Pattison and co-authors ask how antenna errors affect the search for the global 21 cm signal from early cosmic hydrogen. They run a fully Bayesian forward-model pipeline and test what happens when the modelled beam differs from the true beam. A pointing mismatch of just 0.25 degrees can bias the recovered signal badly. Scanning over model versions lets the evidence pin down the pointing. Signal depth proves most at risk from beam errors, while frequency and width stay robust.
arxiv-2603-24478: Sen and co-authors study nonequilibrium phases and quantum correlations in synthetic transport models run as quantum cellular automata. Devices with mid-circuit measurement and reset can realise such automata, which evolve in discrete steps through local unitary gates. The team focuses on a discrete-time version of the totally asymmetric simple exclusion process. They ask how coherent dynamics lets quantum effects emerge inside a transport model. Entanglement dominates the transient behaviour, they find, while steady states can keep quantum correlations that go beyond entanglement.
arxiv-2603-24578: Mehmood and co-authors evaluate whether vision-language models can judge perceived image quality like humans do. Psychophysical experiments are the gold standard but costly and hard to scale. Their framework probes six models with controlled pairwise comparisons of contrast, colourfulness, and overall preference. Results vary strongly by attribute. One model shows the highest internal consistency, another agrees best on overall preference, and others lead on colourfulness or contrast. No model matches human perception across all attributes, and self-consistency alone does not imply perceptual validity, they find.
arxiv-2603-24778: Reichert and co-authors seek the resource-optimal way to estimate mode parameters with multimode Gaussian light states. Time delays and frequency shifts underpin radar, lidar, and optical clocks. Many states can reach the Heisenberg limit, so the question is which resources truly govern each task. The authors tie the key resources to the eigenmode basis of the transformation's generator. For time shifts, the mean frequency and bandwidth are what matter. The framework unifies the particle-number and mode-structure views of quantum light and yields a tight precision bound.
arxiv-2603-24878: Li proposes a trusted-execution framework to address the replication crisis in research. Artifact checks and copying packages are limited by scarce editors, slow processes, and volunteer labour. Under the plan, authors run their packages inside a cloud trusted environment, such as Intel TDX, and submit proofs of correct execution. Journals verify the proofs without rerunning code or seeing private data. The burden shifts to authors while editors do less. A pilot study replicating published papers on TDX-backed cloud machines tests whether it works.
arxiv-2603-25178: Weng and co-authors build the first bilingual test set for turning text into human motion. Motion models lack paired data in two languages, and their text encoders cross languages poorly. BiHumanML3D pairs motion with text in two tongues, made with model help and fixed by hand. Their baseline, BiMD, adds a cross-lingual alignment step that pulls same-meaning texts together. It even handles prompts that switch language mid-sentence. Scores beat single-language and translation-based rivals by a clear margin on the new set.
arxiv-2603-25278: Rathi and co-authors compute how tightly a muon binds to a beryllium-9 nucleus, in two rival ways. One way treats the nuclear size effect step by step, as light-system work often does. The other folds size in to all orders, in the style of heavy-ion math. Term by term, the two agree to better than one part per million. Their formula lets labs pull the beryllium charge radius from fresh muon data with high precision. It also bridges the light and heavy research camps.
arxiv-2603-25878: Dzian and co-authors report antiferromagnetic resonance in the crystal NaMnAs at room temperature. NaMnAs is a tetragonal antiferromagnetic semiconductor. At zero field, they find one resonance line at 7 meV. They link it to a doubly degenerate magnon mode at the zone center. The line softens as temperature rises but stays visible up to room temperature. The data support an easy-axis picture with the Néel vector along the tetragonal axis. The team estimates the manganese single-ion anisotropy at 0.1 to 0.2 meV.
arxiv-2603-25978: Pachev and co-authors build a global dataset for predicting peak storm surge with machine learning. Surge is a deadly coastal hazard, but physics models need supercomputers to run. Past training data cover narrow regions, mostly the United States and China. Their dataset holds peak surge output for over 15,000 synthetic landfalling storms worldwide. The output comes from the ADCIRC model at high resolution. They also train a vision-based model on this data. It predicts peak surge well where few past models exist.
arxiv-2603-26378: Wanasekara and co-authors survey generative modelling for protein design. The field spans sequence design, backbone generation, inverse folding, and interaction modelling, but its literature is split across many setups. The survey sorts work by representation, from sequence and geometric codes to mixed encodings. It also compares model families such as equivariant diffusion and flow matching, and the tasks they serve. The authors stress leakage-aware splits, physical validity checks, and function-based tests as shared standards for judging new methods.
arxiv-2603-26678: Gui and Dai model when AI growth drives clean energy investment, and when it deepens fossil fuel use instead. Their game links renewable capacity choices with how fast AI scales. The pivot is whether the market value of AI skill grows faster than the energy that skill demands. When value wins, developers chase frontier skill even on fossil power, a pattern they call an adaptation trap as climate damage raises AI's worth. When energy needs win, clean investment both cuts emissions and cheapens further AI growth.
arxiv-2603-27178: Mishra and co-authors test a changed gravity model with VCDM-like behavior against cosmic data. They fit the model with cosmic chronometers, redshift-space distortions, DESI BAO, and Union3 supernovae. An MCMC setup supplies robust credible ranges for its values. The model's expansion history shows a smooth Hubble transition near redshift 0.3. Its deceleration, equation of state, and growth rate all behave in line. On the full dataset, it beat the standard ΛCDM model. The authors present it as a strong cosmology option.
arxiv-2603-27278: Rath and co-authors review the quantum bit error rate in the BB84 key distribution protocol. QBER measures errors in the sifted key from noise or eavesdropping. The study covers its math, estimation, and role in catching spies. Tests show error rate rising almost in step with attack strength. Full intercept-resend attacks push it toward 25 percent. Four confidence interval methods are set against each other for finite-key settings. Decoy states and hybrid cryptography appear among the fixes. Telling noise from attacks apart remains an open challenge.
arxiv-2603-27778: Luna and Ryskin compute central particle counts in proton collisions. The multi-channel eikonal model frames the calculation. AGK cutting rules organize the contributing diagrams. Counts cover the central rapidity window out to 2.5. ATLAS data at 7 and 13 TeV anchor the checks. Color reconnection effects enter the discussion. String percolation is weighed as a second effect. The model tracks the measured distributions well.
arxiv-2603-27878: Mishin re-derives a classic grain boundary energy relation from scratch. The Borisov equation links boundary energy to diffusion data. Many papers used it beyond its design limits. Hidden premises of the model are brought to light. Errors and inconsistencies in the old form are fixed. Extensions cover impurity diffusion cases. Interstitial mechanisms join the framework too. Tests for the key premise are proposed.
arxiv-2603-27978: Ahn and Rhee present a scheme for finding excited states on near-term quantum computers. Their method pairs a spin-preserving ansatz with a short phase-estimation step that tags states by spin. A screening step then filters out spin-contaminated states without costly spin measurements. On lithium hydride and beryllium hydride, the scheme separates singlet and triplet states far better than standard deflation methods. The screening block also works with other variational schemes.
arxiv-2603-28078: Giga and three co-authors study a Kobayashi-Warren-Carter type total variation energy with a fidelity term, used for segmentation. Unlike the classic Rudin-Osher-Fatemi energy, this one is non-convex, so its minimizers behave quite differently. In one dimension, the authors prove that a piecewise constant minimizer always exists for bounded data. For monotone data they bound the number of jumps more tightly. They also show minimizers need not be unique, and compare with rival energies.
arxiv-2603-28278: Gninenko and three co-authors compute how the NA64e experiment could spot inelastic dark matter through missing energy. The dark particles would pair up through a magnetic dipole link to ordinary photons. In their setup, a 100 GeV electron beam strikes nuclei, and the dark pair escapes unseen. Adding heavy vector meson decays to the usual emission channel widens the reach. With about 10 trillion electrons on target, NA64e could probe fresh ground for light dark matter.
arxiv-2603-28378: Dong, Lin, and Lee run the first systematic membership inference study on large audio language models. Such attacks try to learn whether a clip was in a model's training data. The team shows that common audio datasets split almost perfectly by simple blind features, so naive attacks mostly detect dataset shift, not memorization. With matched data and a blind-baseline protocol, real leakage appears. It turns out cross-modal: models memorize a speaker's voice only when bound to its text.
arxiv-2603-28578: Alves and Ribeiro study the Tree Builder Random Walk, a walker that changes its own environment. At each step, the walker adds a random number of vertices at its position. Past work showed the walker moves with a clear speed and has a renewal structure. They prove that the first renewal time has an exponential tail. That gives an exponential bound on the empirical speed. For a simpler case, they also show the limiting speed is an analytic function of the parameter p. Some proofs use bond percolation methods.
arxiv-2603-28778: Nash, Pesch, and Guha present a framework for hybrid collective inference in distributed sensor networks. Tasks like vehicle networking and drone swarm teamwork need global labeling from spread-out sensors. Communication and computing budgets are tight. Past work treated data exchange and cloud-edge allocation as separate ideas. Their design joins both and makes dynamic runtime choices about messaging strategy. They derive optimal policies for agents using the hybrid approach. Tests show accuracy near central joint inference at lower modeled messaging cost, across several data distributions.
arxiv-2603-28978: Sargsyan and co-authors compute ab initio optical potentials for magnesium isotopes at mid range energies. They cover Mg-24, 26, 28, and 32, from stability to the island of inversion. The potentials use the leading term of the spectator expansion of scattering theory. Structure input comes from a symmetry adapted no-core shell model, with no adjustable parameters. For Mg-24, results match neutron total, reaction, and elastic data from 65 to 250 MeV. Comparisons with global potentials expose limits of those models near the island of inversion.
arxiv-2603-29078: Vicentino presents PolarQuant, a post-training weight quantization method for large language models. It works in three stages. First, weights are scaled block wise to the unit hypersphere. Next, a Walsh-Hadamard rotation turns coordinates into nearly Gaussian values. Finally, quantization uses centroids matched to the Gaussian spread. Tests show the rotation alone accounts for 98 percent of the quality gain. On a Qwen model, perplexity came within 0.03 of the full precision value, with no calibration data. PolarQuant also helps INT4 quantizers, with better perplexity at good speed.
arxiv-2603-29278: Kim and Hong set out a compliance protocol for tokenized capital markets. Token standards aim to change how assets trade, but shared rules are missing. Their protocol builds on reports from 15 global financial bodies. It groups the rules into five areas. The areas are traceability, privacy, enforceability, finality, and tokenizability. In all, the protocol lists 31 items as a benchmark. They test it on three trading scenarios. Four token standards are scored against it, showing which rules each one meets.
arxiv-2603-29378: Risse and Böhme show how language-model agents find the commits that introduced bugs. Given a fix commit, the task is to find the earlier change that caused the bug. The classic SZZ method dates to 2005. Progress since then has been slow. Their simple agent searches a set of candidate commits. On a popular Linux kernel dataset, F1 rose from 0.64 to 0.81 in their tests. The agents succeed by deriving short searchable patterns. They pull these patterns from the fix diff and message.
arxiv-2603-29778: Nicolae and co-authors present M3SA, a framework for simulating datacenter climate impact and performance. Single-model simulators can be narrow and miss real operating effects. M3SA runs several models at once through discrete-event simulation. It then merges their forecasts into a meta-model and scores that model's accuracy. Tests show it can repeat and extend published experiments. It also predicts failures across unlike workloads. M3SA ships inside the open-source OpenDC simulator.
arxiv-2604-00078: Alencar and Borralho build regular black-string and BTZ black-hole solutions in unimodular gravity. This variant of general relativity fixes the spacetime volume element, so its cosmological constant appears as an integration constant rather than in the action. Dropping energy-momentum conservation turns that constant into a spacetime-dependent function, with a vacuum part plus a matter-driven correction. Maxwell fields support the solutions and their combinations, letting the pair build a wider family and check energy conditions, curvature invariants, and thermodynamics.
arxiv-2604-00478: Shah tackles sycophancy in large language models, the habit of prizing user approval over truth. Her Silicon Mirror framework watches for persuasion tactics across a conversation and steers behaviour to protect integrity. Three parts do the work. Access control limits context layers by live sycophancy risk. A classifier spots persuasion tactics. A critic loop lets an auditor block flattering drafts and force rewrites with friction. In tests over all 437 TruthfulQA adversarial cases, the framework cuts Claude Sonnet 4's sycophancy by 85.7 percent in relative terms.
arxiv-2604-00578: Takeuchi reviews marked galaxy clustering from a point-process view. Marked pair stats treat galaxy traits like brightness or stellar mass as marks. They use them to test galaxy birth models. But versions collapse mark pairs into summary numbers, losing the joint structure of pairs at a gap. He models them as points carrying place and mark. He introduces the joint pair correlation function as the measure for mark-based grouping. A check tracks how far pairs stray from independence, giving a projection-free description of mark-pair behaviour.
arxiv-2604-00678: Dinar and colleagues study how boron nitride phonons affect resistivity in graphene wrapped in boron nitride. Wrapping yields fast devices, yet the wrap itself scatters electrons remotely via polar optical phonons. That role stays unclear in resistivity tests. The team pairs high-quality transport tests with ab initio calculations, treating screened remote interactions. Out-of-plane phonons shape resistivity from 150 K to room temperature. Graphene phonons on their own, plus higher LO modes, fail to explain the trends. Electron-phonon coupling grows stronger at low carrier densities as screening weakens.
arxiv-2604-00778: Datta and colleagues use character counting, such as asking how many p's appear in apple, as a controlled probe of language models' symbolic reasoning. They find models often compute the right answer internally yet fail to state it. Late-layer components suppress correct signals in favor of likelier wrong outputs. The study concludes these failures come from structured interference inside the computation, not from missing representations or too little scale.
arxiv-2604-01078: Hao and team present a 3D FPGA layout flow with splitting-based startup, tuned cost planning, and mock cooling moves. Old 2D tools miss 3D fabrics' delay traits and tuning moves. These lift timing guesses and layer slot search. Against Verilog-To-Routing, mean key-path delay falls about 3 percent, 2 percent, 3 percent, and 6 percent across four 3D designs, with maxima to 18 percent. Routed wiring falls by means about 1 percent, 2 percent, under 1 percent, and 5 percent.
arxiv-2604-01178:
Ken M. Nakanishi asks what a good match score should mean in a 2026 paper. His title says it plainly: Screening Is Enough. He calls a score absolute when it sits on a fixed, bounded scale.

An absolute score does not rest on rival keys or on length. It needs no fix-up that changes as the text grows long. All scores for one query can be zero, which must be allowed. His screen uses a set cut line to turn raw scores into match scores. That gives exact refusal, an empty pick, and scores one can read at a glance. The paper offers a simpler path than the standard way of scoring.
arxiv-2604-01278: Caputo and Teodori estimate how tides and self-gravity affect ultra-light dark matter bounds from dwarf galaxies. Dwarf spheroidal galaxies are sensitive probes, but Milky Way tides can reduce dynamical heating, and stellar self-gravity can matter if stars were more compact earlier. Reconstructing dwarf orbits in a Milky Way potential, with a simple tidal diagnostic and stellar self-gravity in simulations, they study five dwarf galaxies. Ultra-light dark matter in the mass range studied remains in tension with current data.
arxiv-2604-01378: Zhu and Yu propose a system for offline reinforcement learning from past data, without touching the real world. Their residuals-based Bellman optimality operator folds error in dynamics into policy tuning through residuals. They show this operator is a contraction mapping. They identify cases under which its fixed point is optimal in the limit with finite-sample bounds. They further develop an offline deep Q-learning algorithm. In a stochastic CartPole environment, their offline algorithm works.
arxiv-2604-02078: Misumi, Onogi and Yamaoka map the mass terms allowed for staggered fermions in three plus one dimensions, where spin and flavor spread across lattice sites. Beyond the usual on site term, one, two and three link bilinears carry distinct spin flavor patterns, each preserving different symmetries. One one link term keeps a larger residual symmetry tied to the Onsager algebra. With a kink in that mass, the bulk gaps while two flavor massless Dirac modes live on the wall, realizing a parity anomaly from ultraviolet structure.
arxiv-2604-02178: Herbst, Wermter and Lee ask whether mixture of experts models are easier to interpret than dense networks. Probing with sparse methods, they find expert neurons less polysemantic than dense feed forward neurons, with the gap widening as routing grows sparser. That points to the expert, not the neuron, as the better unit of analysis. Auto interpreting hundreds of experts shows they are fine grained task experts, not broad domain specialists or mere token processors.
arxiv-2604-02278: Abualazm and Abo Elhassan test small language models as decompilers that turn x86 assembly into idiomatic Dart. Training data augmentation with synthetic same language examples is compared against adding human written Swift examples. A 4B specialized model scores about 71 on CODEBLEU, nearly matching a model about 120 times larger at about 73. On natural Dart functions it compiles about 79 percent of cases at five tries, well above its base model. Swift data helps at 8B but not at 4B.
arxiv-2604-02578: Maini, Goldstone and Tiganj compare language models with people in a group coordination game where players must jointly sum to a hidden target without talking. People adapt and steady their play over time, while models often fail to improve and switch excessively, harming convergence. Richer feedback, such as error size, helps people far more than models, though a training method called GRPO curbs the models' restless switching.
arxiv-2604-02978: Li and Sun construct two families of nodal Yamabe solutions, each focused on two planar circles. One family matches Medina and Musso's earlier family under conformal equivalence. The second is a new twisted variant of the first, derived from ansatzes that are not Kelvin invariant, unlike a standard assumption in earlier work. In dimension 3, these solutions reach maximal rank. A continuous family of conformal transformations then reveals how the two circles interact, showing crossing reminiscent of leap-frogging in vortex dynamics.
arxiv-2604-03078: Chagas and colleagues define the quadratic bin packing problem, which adds a fixed cost per bin plus pairwise costs or profits for items packed together. They offer three compact linear programming formulations with strengthened versions, plus a set-partitioning model solved by a tailored branch-and-price method. On benchmarks, the compact models handle small cases well, while branch-and-price wins overall, especially on larger hard cases.
arxiv-2604-03278: Huang and colleagues coordinate electric-vehicle charging stations as a virtual power plant while seeing only part of the grid. Their TL-MAPPO framework trains agents centrally with Lagrangian regularization to respect voltage and demand constraints, while each station acts on its own. On a realistic 33-bus network, the system cut voltage violations about 45 percent and operating costs about 10 percent against leading baselines.
arxiv-2604-03478: Tan, Shen, and Chen study whether adding data from more hospitals improves fairness for patient subgroups in ICU models. Across the eICU and MIMIC-IV datasets, they find that adding data can both help and hurt fairness and performance, and many common data-selection strategies prove shaky. Pairing added data with model-based post-hoc tuning works best, challenging the dogma that better data alone fixes fairness.
arxiv-2604-03578: Chen, Guo, and Xiao provide a single account of any-order spin magnetic multipole moments in AFMs. It introduces a spread-out spin cloud in large-scale Maxwell rules. Through the spread-out spin cloud from scratch, they propose a scheme to extract any-order moments through symmetry-constrained fitting at long wavelengths. They work out moments for sample AFMs like alpha-Fe2O3, Mn3Sn, and Mn3NiN. They explain the role of spin-orbit link, above all in the weak link limit.
arxiv-2604-03778: Alexey Kryukov extended a random-matrix route from classical particle motion to classical field theory. Earlier work had derived Newton's laws for large particles from quantum evolution plus random coupling to surroundings, with the classical world sitting on a manifold of localized states. Kryukov showed the same machinery yields sourced Klein-Gordon and Maxwell equations for scalar and electromagnetic fields, with a test charge feeling the Lorentz force. Classical behavior thus emerges without treating the field as an average, without special coherent states, and without a collapse rule.
arxiv-2604-03878: Lei Zhou and colleagues improved 3D reconstruction from multiple views by treating known camera poses, intrinsics, and depth as constraints at test time. Rather than retraining image-only transformers, they optimized the network during inference with a self-supervised loss plus prior penalties. The method cut point-map distance error by more than half on ETH3D, 7-Scenes, and NRGBD sets. It also beat retrained prior-aware feed-forward methods, showing test-time optimization can carry prior knowledge.
arxiv-2604-03978: Anh Dau and colleagues built COBOLAssist, a repair loop for compilation errors in language-model-generated COBOL code. They sorted common errors into incomplete code, syntax, and type-related groups, then iterated repairs guided by compiler feedback. Tests across five models showed frequent broken structures and function misuse. COBOLAssist lifted GPT-4o compilation success from 41.8 percent to 95.89 percent.
arxiv-2604-04178: Kaiser Shafi and Sandeep Chatterjee showed that forward-backward multiplicity asymmetry can separate flow background from the Chiral Magnetic Effect signal in uranium collisions. The effect remains hard to observe because flow-induced backgrounds swamp the signal. In deformed nuclei like prolate uranium, the asymmetry is naturally enhanced and tied to initial-state geometry. Monte Carlo Glauber simulations found that varying it within a fixed centrality class shifts ellipticity largely independently of the magnetic-field correlator.
arxiv-2604-04278: Mendo offers step-by-step estimators for relative risk, odds ratios and their logs for a yes-or-no trait in two groups. The estimators take equal counts from each group, and hold the error below a set target no matter the true value. Efficiency against the Cramér-Rao bound runs high when the trait is rare or fairly rare.
arxiv-2604-04478: Lin, Meng and Tang study two-player nonzero-sum linear quadratic stochastic games. With variational tools, they find necessary and sufficient conditions for open-loop Nash equilibria. When weight matrices are indefinite, classic first-order rules fall short, so a no-minus rule brings back enough. To pin down states, they build forward-backward difference equations and lopsided Riccati equations splitting the Hamiltonian set-up. Positive semidefiniteness of Riccati maps and structural soundness ensure a map can be flipped, giving a sound closed-loop feedback form for Nash plans.
arxiv-2604-04878: Burgon and four colleagues propose three measures for judging adaptive medical AI that keeps changing after deployment. Learning means gains on current data. Potential means shifts driven by the dataset itself. Retention means knowledge kept across updates. Separating those strands lets regulators tell model improvement apart from a changing patient population. In simulations, gradual change supports stable learning and retention, while rapid change forces a trade between adapting fast and staying stable.
arxiv-2604-05078: Garcia and two co-authors compute the random gravitational wave background from a scalar field coupled to the inflaton through a portal link. In the portal coupling regime, resonance during reheat grows the field power spectrum by many orders near the resonance band. Hartree feedback from the quartic coupling stops the growth. The active mass cuts large-scale power and fits CMB isocurvature bounds. They focus on the direct field-slope source in the second-order Einstein rules, tracing how spectator motion seeds gravity waves.
arxiv-2604-05278: Taghavi and Bhavani present Spec Kit Agents, a multi-agent spec-driven pipeline with PM and developer roles and context hooks. Agents often stay context blind in large, evolving repositories, leading to hallucinated APIs and violations. Probing hooks ground each stage, Specify, Plan, Tasks, Implement, in evidence, while validation hooks check artifacts against the environment. Across 128 runs in five repositories, context hooks improve quality by 0.15 on a 1-5 score, while keeping 99.7 to 100 percent compatibility. On SWE-bench Lite, hooks lift the baseline by 1.7 percent, to 58.2 percent Pass@1.
arxiv-2604-05378: Hamid, Cui, and Liang test a blind spot in language-driven self-driving cars: standard trials assume navigation orders are clear and well formed. Real orders vary, omit details, and sometimes mislead. Their ICR-Drive framework generates controlled variants of each order across four families, paraphrase, ambiguity, noise, and misleading, then replays identical simulated routes under matched settings so only the wording changes. On two driving systems, small wording changes caused large performance drops and distinct failure patterns, exposing a reliability gap for safety-critical driving.
arxiv-2604-05578: Birindelli, Briani, and Ishii study fully nonlinear elliptic equations in thin domains that shrink from N+1 to N dimensions. They handle mixed oblique-Dirichlet edge rules with no strict monotonicity in the unknown. A new global ellipticity rule for the limit case steers how solutions behave as domains thin. The result widens thin-domain theory to equations where the usual monotone rule fails.
arxiv-2604-05878: Kamata and three colleagues study an upside-down triple-well potential with exact WKB math, covering PT-symmetric, resonance, and anti-resonance cases. Summed series show when energy levels stay real or turn complex, and call PT-symmetry breaking, checked by number tests. The key point follows a plain link between bounce and bion actions, where small non-perturbative fixes drop out.
arxiv-2604-06178: Li and four colleagues survey 330 secondary school students in China about AI tutors that track learning and intervene on their own. Students favor support preserving autonomy, like hints instead of direct answers, and graduated help that starts small and grows only as needed. They draw clear privacy lines around process data: problem-solving steps and mistake patterns feel acceptable, while attention and behavior signals feel far less so. The findings guide tutors that balance timely help with learner control.
arxiv-2604-06278: Jamaluddin and four colleagues compare penalty-based, Bayesian, spatial, and tree-based models for provincial poverty in Indonesia. Small datasets pose a problem, linked predictors raising variance while flexible learners grow unstable, framed as predictive volatility. In simulations, regularized linear estimators beat collinear micro-samples and prove most reliable, while tree-based methods compete only with weakly curved signals and larger samples. On 34 provinces, ridge leads, then elastic net and lasso, and ICT skills link most often to lower poverty. Limited information per degree of freedom, not flexibility, binds most.
arxiv-2604-06478: Hamza studies blow-up in scale-invariant semilinear wave equations with damping and mass terms plus a time-derivative nonlinearity. The central question is whether the discriminant's sign decides the blow-up range. He shows it does not: even when the discriminant is negative, the blow-up region stays invariant and is fixed solely by the shifted dimension, matching the Glassey-type critical exponent. The classical restriction to non-negative discriminants, he argues, comes from a technical tool rather than from the blow-up mechanism itself.
arxiv-2604-06878: Casetta, Gesbert, and Genevès add fault handling to multiparty session types for web apps. Web programs mix long-lived state updates, concurrent talks, and flaky outside links, so timeouts after partial state changes can leave short-lived mismatches that checks miss. Their global-type model gives session types clear failure rules plus changing membership, with syntax and step-by-step rules that keep sessions sound. The model lays groundwork for later variants that keep state and auto checks of liveness.
arxiv-2604-06978: Dey, Gupta, and Kumar study the ball version of the von Neumann inequality for doubly shrinking weighted shifts. If the weighted shift is even or meets a right weight rule, it admits a round unitary stretch. Such tuples then satisfy the von Neumann rule over the plain unit ball. For general joint tuples of doubly shrinking maps on a Hilbert space, the authors further prove the von Neumann rule for same-degree polys of degree at most 2.
arxiv-2604-07478: Kaare-Rasmussen studies mixing times for the Rook's Walk on a d-dimensional chessboard of side n. A rook picks an axis at random, then a new spot along that axis from the free squares. Lumping states by Hamming distance yields a birth-death chain with the same mixing time, whose eigenvalues and eigenfunctions he identifies fully. Combining a Wilson eigenfunction lower bound with an L2 upper bound sharpens mixing-time bounds and proves the chain exhibits cutoff.
arxiv-2604-07578: Sharif and Caragea propose MSGL-Transformer, a transformer for reading rodent social behavior from pose tracks. It uses a light transformer encoder with multi-scale attention to catch motion patterns. Parallel short-, medium-, and global-range attention branches catch behavior patterns at multiple scales. A Behavior-Aware Modulation block tunes time embeddings to stress behavior-relevant features before attention. On RatSI, it reaches 75.4 percent accuracy and 0.745 F1, beating TCN, LSTM, plus Bi-LSTM. On CalMS21, it reaches 87.1 percent accuracy and 0.8745 F1, beating several graph baselines.
arxiv-2604-07778: Tibebu and Shemtaga argue that accountability for AI systems can fail as a matter of math, not just engineering. Current legal, ethical, and regulatory rules assume some named person had enough role and foresight to carry blame for a bad outcome. The paper proves agentic AI breaks that premise once autonomy passes a computable limit. Human-agent collectives are modeled as state-policy pairs inside a shared causal model. Autonomy gets a four-part profile covering knowledge, execution, evaluation, and social ties.
arxiv-2604-08178: Wang and five colleagues present Plan-RewardBench, a path-level choice benchmark for agent planning. In classic Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback, reward models supply the basic alignment signal. As large language models grow into agentic systems that invoke tools and reason complexly, reward modeling faces unprecedented challenges. Most notably, benchmarks for assessing reward model skills in tool-integrated environments are lacking. The benchmark tests how well judges tell preferred trajectories apart from distractors in complex tool-using scenarios. It covers four task families, beginning with Safety Refusal.
arxiv-2604-08278: Bressan, Clemente, and Fumagalli study counting k-hypergraphlets, a surprisingly ignored primitive, asking if fast algorithms exist. They consider color coding, a standard technique for counting graphlets in graphs. First: on hypergraphs, color coding hits a quadratic barrier, with no implementation running sub-quadratically under the Orthogonal Vector Conjecture. They then introduce (alpha, beta)-niceness, a property real-world data satisfy for small alpha and beta. An (alpha, beta)-nice hypergraph splits into two parts, one of rank at most alpha, one of degree at most beta.
arxiv-2604-08578: Lam and four colleagues build EXPONA, a tool for auto data tagging that weighs range against trust. The system tries surface, shape, and meaning rules at several levels, then filters noisy or repeat rules while keeping matching signals. Across eleven sorting sets it reached near complete label cover, raised weak label quality by up to 87 percent, and lifted downstream weighted F1 by up to 46 percent.
arxiv-2604-08778: Siniša Miličić proposes a human scale methodology for AI rich higher education in service mathematics, shifting grade relevant evidence from polished written work to live explanation. Students prepare openly, often with digital help, but trust rests on contingent questioning, cumulative observation, and instructor synthesis after attempts. The design offers a weekly cycle, a realism framework, and a middle out stance on tools. It gives retrieval grounded AI assistants a bounded role and a five grade oral rubric for small and medium cohorts.
arxiv-2604-08878: Ruth and three colleagues rebuild the equilibrium model for stellarators, twisted magnetic bottles built to confine fusion plasma without symmetry. The usual magnetohydrodynamic model breaks down there, producing sharp current spikes on resonant surfaces and numerical results that converge slowly or not at all. Their statistical alternative treats the magnetic field as fluctuating, averages the force, and yields smooth solutions for fluctuation patterns chosen to stay close to the standard picture. The new model spreads each sharp current sheet over a length set by the field fluctuations.
arxiv-2604-08978: Ghassami studies direct effects when a focal variable may be a confounder or a mediator. In studies, timing may be coarse, or the variable may track a changing process. No single estimand from data gives both the average treatment effect and the natural direct effect for both. The study finds a no-additive-interaction rule where they coincide, and offers a robust measure valid under both roles. An efficient influence function and doubly robust estimator support it. A PFAS, kidney, and uric acid study shows mediation analyses at odds.
arxiv-2604-09178: Vorobyev, Kurebayashi, and Tretiakov map the low-energy spin waves of lone asymmetric antibimerons and their clusters in very thin magnetic films. A lone antibimeron holds a set of distinct local wave modes tied to its inner degrees of freedom. When several join a cluster, coupling splits those modes into groups sized by the cluster count. A paired-oscillator model captures the shared motion, pointing to these clusters as tunable bases for tiny spin-wave oscillators whose tones shift with cluster size.
arxiv-2604-09378: Tie, Shi, Zhou, and Sun present BadSkill, a backdoor attack on agent skills via model-in-skill poisoning. Agent ecosystems rely on installable skills, and some bundle learned model artifacts, creating a supply-chain risk beyond prompt injection. In BadSkill, an adversary publishes a benign-seeming skill whose embedded model activates a hidden payload only when parameters satisfy attacker-chosen trigger combinations. Across eight architectures, it reaches about 100 percent attack success on triggered skills while keeping strong benign accuracy, and a 3 percent poison rate already yields about 92 percent success.
arxiv-2604-09478: Affan, Lehtola, and Vosselman propose incremental semantics-aided meshing from LiDAR-inertial odometry and RGB direct label transfer. Mesh reconstruction from LiDAR-inertial scans remains hard in large complex indoor spaces. There, sparse clouds, drift, and fixed fusion settings produce holes, over-smoothing, and spurious surfaces. Their modular incremental pipeline generates high-quality meshes through scan frame-based direct label transfer. A vision foundation model labels each RGB frame, labels fuse onto a LiDAR-inertial odometry map, and a semantics-aware fusion step produces the final mesh.
arxiv-2604-09578: Sarwar presents a comprehensive study of explainable AI planning for hybrid systems, which capture real-world problems closely. Automated planning now drives safety-critical domains from smart energy grids and self-driving cars to warehouse automation, traffic control, search and rescue, surveillance, robotics, and healthcare. As autonomous systems replace manually crafted ones, generating explanations of AI-based planning has become a major challenge for the planning community, and this thesis addresses it head-on.
arxiv-2604-09678: Twabi, Ding, and Kondo present NetAgentBench, a dynamic benchmark for agentic network setup built on finite-state-machine rules. Static one-shot tests cannot capture multi-turn day-to-day work, so the benchmark ensures fixed, correct, bounded runs while agents work through setup tasks. Four leading language-model agents handle basic tasks but suffer severe exploration meltdowns and coherence loss on expert setups. The results argue that steady testing of multi-turn stability is vital for trustworthy self-run networks.
arxiv-2604-09978: Lahmeri and four co-authors propose joint radar-communication for secure aerial links, where radar imaging sharpens wireless performance. An aerial station serves a ground user while a moving eavesdropper threatens it, where standard adversary localization often fails. The station tracks the eavesdropper by radar interferometry, estimating position and velocity, then applies beamforming and noise jamming for secrecy. Time and power are jointly optimized for the worst-case secrecy rate, solved by deep reinforcement learning. Simulations beat equal-aperture and random-allocation baselines, and generalize to unseen motion.
arxiv-2604-10078: Chowdhury and Chowdhury present DualEngage, a two-stream system for recognizing group engagement in classroom videos. Most prior systems target online classes or single students. One stream tracks students and extracts dense optical flow. It encodes motion over time with a transformer before pooling students by attention. The other reads scene-level space-time patterns with a three-dimensional residual network. A gated fusion weights the streams by joint context. It reaches about 96 percent accuracy on a classroom data set from Ocean University of China.
arxiv-2604-10178: Duan, Wang, and Xu replace latent points with distance to a set in Bayesian models of data near shaped sets. Standard latent variable models pair each data point with a latent point on the set plus noisy gaps. Their distance-to-set approach uses each point's distance to its projection onto the set, found fast by tuning, in place of the latent point in the fit. The change cuts dimensions and speeds posterior work. It yields posterior soundness and curbs overfit.
arxiv-2604-11178: Rogalla and four colleagues forecast brain activity from sensory input with a probabilistic model called autoregressive flow matching. The model learns how future neural responses depend on past activity and concurrent stimuli, then predicts short-term blood-oxygen signals across brain parcels. On 2025 Algonauts challenge data it beat both a non-autoregressive rival and the official baseline, with past brain dynamics driving most of the gain.
arxiv-2604-11678: King and McKinley show steady shearing and planar extensional flows match in kinematics and rheology. Long seen as distinct, above all for testing complex fluids, the two flows share a kinematic match. Stripping the spin part of shearing gives an effective extension rate for a fluid parcel, letting researchers rebuild steady planar extensional viscosity from shearing tests alone. The match is shown with frame-invariant models, both simple and microscopically motivated, and with tests on a viscoelastic polymer solution and a polymer melt.
arxiv-2604-11878: Valibouse and five colleagues solve a readout problem for the photonic quantum switch, where measurements inside the switch previously destroyed the superposition of causal orders or had to wait until afterwards. They couple the photon to a time-delocalized ancilla, so the apparatus interacts at two distinct times yet returns a single outcome. A quantum eraser measurement preserves the indefinite causal order, certified by a causal witness near minus 0.305. The scheme also offers a general route to path-coherence-preserving measurements beyond such switches.
arxiv-2604-12078: Negueruela and four colleagues characterise LS 437, counterpart of X0726-260, from spectroscopy and X-ray monitoring. They derive rotation near 155 kilometres per second and type O7.5 Ve at 36,000 kelvin, making LS 437 the earliest Oe star in X-ray binaries. The stellar wind drives mass accretion, and the X-ray light curve suggests an orbitally modulated wind accretor. Carbon is depleted; nitrogen sits above solar abundance. X-ray data strengthen a 34.5-day orbital period, with no outbursts in 30 years. Optical features show a disk over 40 years, unlike Be/X-ray binaries.
arxiv-2604-12278: Gong and five colleagues present LightMat-HP, a hybrid photonic-electronic system for general matrix multiplication with adjustable precision. Block floating-point arithmetic plus a slicing scheme pairing exact low-bit optical multiplication with digital accumulation overcomes optical limits. A tile-based dataflow handles any size. On a prototype and in large simulations it clearly beats FPGA, GPU, and a leading optical accelerator on throughput, latency, and energy, above all for small and medium matrices.
arxiv-2604-12378: Daniil Gurgurov and five colleagues address a blind spot in multilingual language models. Such models usually reason in English, even for non-English questions. Their ReasonXL corpus gathers over 2,500,000 aligned reasoning examples. The languages are English, German, French, Italian, and Spanish. Each example holds a prompt, a reasoning trace, and a final answer. A two-stage training recipe then teaches models to reason fully in a target language. It matches or beats English reasoning in two of four tested languages.
arxiv-2604-12778: Fan Xiao and 15 colleagues present the DoseRAD2026 dataset for radiotherapy dose calculation. Accurate doses spare healthy tissue while hitting tumors. The set pairs CT and MRI scans from 115 patients. Photon and proton dose maps come from Monte Carlo methods, with 40,500 photon beams and 81,000 proton beamlets. Files use compressed MetaImage format with JSON beam settings. Training data are public from April 2026; test data stay hidden until March 2030. The benchmark supports fast dose methods for both therapies.
arxiv-2604-12978: Kargaran and four colleagues test how well vision-language models read text across more than 100 Unicode scripts. Their GlotOCR Bench renders real multilingual texts as clean and degraded images, covering scripts written left to right and right to left. Most models read fewer than ten scripts well, and even the strongest fail past thirty, often inventing characters from scripts they already know.
arxiv-2604-13178: Mkrtchyan and 14 colleagues build a catalog of 6,104 high-redshift quasar candidates between redshift 4.5 and 7 in the southern sky, picked by fitting spectral energy distributions to multi-band photometry. Merging optical, near-infrared, mid-infrared, and astrometry data with quasar and brown dwarf models, they rank candidates by statistical tests. Spectroscopic follow-up confirmed 3 high-redshift quasars out of 6 targets, aiding further work with the 4MOST telescope.
arxiv-2604-13278: Bellec presents DroneScan-YOLO, a lightweight detector for tiny objects in drone imagery, tackling small size, harsh conditions, and tight compute limits. Four design choices drive it: 1280 by 1280 input resolution and a dynamic filter pruning block with lazy cosine-similarity updates. A stride-4 detection branch adds just 114,592 parameters, and a hybrid loss blends normalized Wasserstein distance with size-adaptive weighting. On VisDrone2019-DET it reaches 55.3 percent mAP at 50 and 35.6 percent mAP at 50 to 95, beating the YOLOv8s baseline by 16.6 and 12.3 points at 96.7 frames per second.
arxiv-2604-13678: Cai, Li, and Li solve generalized phase retrieval with a new weighted Riemannian method. The task is to recover a signal from phaseless Gaussian measurements. Existing Wirtinger Flow and standard Riemannian gradient descent both fit a rank-one matrix equation by least squares. Their metrics embed rank-one matrices only loosely, however. A new metric makes the embedding nearly isometric. The Weighted RGD algorithm, started by spectral methods, converges linearly with a small factor and beats truncated Wirtinger Flow and standard RGD in experiments.
arxiv-2604-13778: Nguyen, Bedeer, and Barton derive a detection rule for LoRa signals that needs no phase tracking, for channels with Rician multipath fading. Their receiver needs only channel statistics, not instantaneous channel state. That removes channel-estimation overhead. Simulations show large gains over multipath channels despite low complexity. In time-invariant channels it matches existing coherent schemes. It surpasses them when Doppler shift is present, without relying on channel estimates or preamble reference signals.
arxiv-2604-13978: Höche and Reichelt build a next-to-leading-order simulation of electron-positron annihilation into W pairs plus bottom quarks that respects the process's resonant character near the top-quark threshold. Their parton-shower evolution, infrared subtraction, and matching account for finite width effects beyond the usual Breit-Wigner shape. First results target a future electron-positron collider, with a public simulator built on ALARIC and SHERPA.
arxiv-2604-14178: Su gives language-model agents a heartbeat scheduler that wakes cognitive modules on a steady rhythm instead of waiting for failures. The scheduler learns from past patterns when to engage modules such as a planner, a critic, a recaller, and a dreamer. Modules can join or leave without rebuilding the system. A meta-learning loop keeps tuning the scheduling policy over time from interaction logs, and tests show the system learns to schedule from history and absorbs new modules on its own.
arxiv-2604-14478: Ojeda builds a liaison analogue for relative ideals of a numerical semigroup, in semigroup terms. Two linkage notions run side by side: one from translates of the semigroup, one from translates of the canonical ideal. The paper sets out both notions for relative ideals. No application is claimed; the linkage theory itself is the point.
arxiv-2604-14678: Kübel, Krauss, Li, and Zhao propose an energy-based regularization loss for training a neural model learning residual dynamics of an omnidirectional aerial robot. It pushes the network toward stabilizing control corrections, since without it the network misses physical context like inertia and energy conservation. Learned dynamics join the model predictive control framework, cutting positional mean absolute error by 23 percent over analytical control in three real-world experiments. Against standard neural control without it, flight stability rises implicitly through smoother acceleration, with up to 15 percent lower error.
arxiv-2604-14778: Czajkowski and Paluch model information spread with a generalized fractional SIR model that includes overload. They then use Pearson correlation to locate the source across real and synthetic networks. Localization weakens as alpha, the overload strength, grows and strengthens as the spreading rate beta rises. Synthetic networks do better overall, and Erdős-Rényi networks resist overload better than Barabási-Albert ones. A density reversal stands out: dense networks help when overload is negligible, but sparser networks win under strong overload, departing from standard epidemic models.
arxiv-2604-14878: Zou and nine others present GenRec, a preference generative recommendation system on the JD App in one decoder-only design. Page-wise next-token prediction supervises pages over items, resolving pointwise training ambiguity. A linear token merger compresses semantic IDs in prompts while keeping full decoding, halving input length with negligible accuracy loss. GRPO-SR pairs group-relative optimization with NLL regularization, using rewards from a reward model plus a gate against reward hacking. A/B tests showed 9.5 percent more clicks and 8.7 percent more transactions than the old pipeline.
arxiv-2604-14978: Joos and Xie count tight Hamilton cycles in dense hypergraphs, closed orderings where every run of k vertices forms an edge. They prove a lower bound built from hypergraph entropy, a quantity defined through fractional matchings. The bound is tight for nearly regular hypergraphs, including the binomial random case. It also settles a conjecture of Ferber, Hardiman, and Mond about how many such cycles dense hypergraphs must hold.
arxiv-2604-15278: Sole shows why machine beat detection fails on old polyphonic chamber recordings and offers another way. Standard tools built for single-line audio or new studios stumble on duo recordings of five Beethoven piano and cello sonatas. His running-total lap-timer protocol yields bar-level tempo data with millisecond detail. Built with an engineer focused on VLSI design, the protocol blocks error buildup, allows self-checks, and captures rubato, fermatas, and tempo shifts.
arxiv-2604-15378: Habchi and four colleagues review portable medical imaging for point-of-care diagnosis where full imaging suites are out of reach. Portable CT, MRI, ultrasound, and capsule endoscopy widen access but suffer motion artifacts, interference, hardware limits, and shaky acquisition. The review taxonomizes AI methods by their effect on image quality and clinical usability, then maps devices, distortions, metrics, datasets, gaps, and future directions.
arxiv-2604-15478: Valizadeh, Rahimi, and Abolfath model how oxygen spreads in tumors versus healthy tissue under FLASH ultra-high dose-rate radiation, using fractal geometry to capture structural messiness. Their diffusion-reaction model on fractal substrates shows rising complexity suppressing long-range transport and boosting localization. Once the fractional knob turns positive, memory effects rule transport, splitting tissues into well-mixed zones and cut-off, long-lived reactive pockets.
arxiv-2604-15578: Sabit and Anjum study how nearest-center clustering partitions shift when point configurations are perturbed, measuring partition change by pairwise disagreement rates. Their margin result: perturbations below half the smallest margin change no assignments, while any changed assignment must sit within twice the perturbation of a boundary. A discrete-time follow-up and a chance bound complete a margin-based account of worst-case and average stability.
arxiv-2604-15678: Lee and six colleagues name Domain Gravity, a skew where lopsided data across mixed fields lets overfed or low-chaos fields warp the map. Model samples then drift, and weak fields fare worse. They set out XD-VSCIL, a test bed where skew runs strong, and HyCal, a no-training fix that blends angle match with spread-aware size to steady model samples. On frozen CLIP maps, HyCal holds skills while learning new ones and beats methods on mixed-field few-shot tests.
arxiv-2604-15978: Panneke and Wehrheim introduce jMT, a tool for building multi-execution semantics for concurrent Java programs. Java memory models are widely said to be broken, since they must weigh many possible executions to find valid ones, and tools for checking proposals are lacking. jMT builds on single-execution models of well-formed graphs, adding causality checking to yield multi-execution models. It supports testing memory model proposals per program, plus conformance checks against compilers and compilation schemes. Evaluation on 169 litmus tests yields fresh insights into Java memory models.
arxiv-2604-16078: Choudhary and Panja derive explicit formulas, in q alone, for the Wedderburn split of the rational group algebras of SL2(q) and PSL2(q). The groups are finite linear groups over a field with q elements. They also count, for each group, the pairwise non-isomorphic simple group modules of each size.
arxiv-2604-16178: The Euclid Collaboration searches Euclid deep images for brighter analogues of little red dots and other V-shaped-spectrum sources at redshift above 4. Such dots, found by JWST, are compact and extreme, but brighter analogues need much wider sky areas. From 0.75 square degrees of the COSMOS field, they select 233 V-shaped sources, identify 16 robust compact candidates, and find those 16 far more massive than typical JWST-selected dots.
arxiv-2604-16478: Balfagon presents CET Omega, a causal-informational extension of standard cosmology. It predicts a doubly logarithmic correction to radiation energy density in the early universe. He derives the correction form from spectral integration and from renormalization group flow. He tests it with a Monte Carlo analysis varying six standard cosmological parameters plus the new correction, using Planck 2018 data and Big Bang nucleosynthesis constraints. The result is consistent with zero, yielding a first observational bound on the correction and showing that future CMB-S4 data could probe smaller values.
arxiv-2604-16678: Sui, Wang and Do propose UniCon, a unified framework for contrastive alignment via kernels. Contrastive objectives power mixed models, yet training stays slow under long random tuning. UniCon spans linear and curved coders, one-to-one and many-to-many matches. A contrast score weight matrix enables closed-form solutions swapping batch backprop with exact updates. Through reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces, UniCon unifies matching and links it to spectral methods. Tests on fake, single-mode, multimodal and zero-shot tasks show efficiency gains with breadth and strong results.
arxiv-2604-16778: Yao, Rabbani and Li propose Federation over Text, letting clients solving different tasks build a shared library of metacognitive insights. Clients federate local reasoning processes without sharing problem instances, operating at the semantic level with no gradient optimization. Each round, agents apply local reasoning and self-improvement, share traces with a central server, and the server distills cross-task knowledge. The shared library is reused by current and future agents, gaining eleven point nine percentage points while cutting task-completion tokens by five point five percent.
arxiv-2604-16878: Liang and colleagues propose OC-Distill, a two-stage framework for ICU risk prediction using only vital signs at inference. Early forecast of decline and left length of stay enables timely help and better supply sharing. Contrastive pretrain treats all patients as equally strong foes, missing similarity between related cases. An ontology-aware contrast goal uses the ICD tree to score patient match and learn grounded maps. Cross-modal distillation then moves note data into the encoder, hitting state-of-the-art results on MIMIC with vital signs alone.
arxiv-2604-17478: Wang, Wu, and Xu offer a numerical method for computing the full spectrum of primordial gravitational waves, ripples from the universe's earliest expansion, spanning inflation through reheating. Built on the Bogoliubov approach, which tracks how early quantum ripples evolve, it fixes high-frequency numerical errors and problems with unstable tachyonic modes. The authors show that uneven swings in the inflaton field can leave marks on the high-frequency spectrum, and they share their code publicly.
arxiv-2604-17678: Chumley and Winful demonstrate programmable state preparation in small VCSEL arrays with optical feedback, using transient optical injection as Gaussian pulses. In Lang-Kobayashi-type models of delay-coupled two- and three-laser arrays, multistability creates coexisting synchronized and symmetry-broken branches. Short injection pulses on one or more lasers can move the system out of free-running operation and into any stable branch by choosing pulse detuning and amplitude. The selected state then persists without forcing. With correlated noise, steering still works, though small-basin branches destabilize.
arxiv-2604-18078: Juodis and Weidner revisit panel regressions, models that track many units over time. Such models must allow for hidden differences between units. They show that two leading estimators for panels with latent factors both converge to the same target. That target is a variance-weighted average of unit-and-time-specific treatment effects, weighted by how much the treatment varies once hidden factors are accounted for.
arxiv-2604-18178: Van Eeden surveys recent results from the IceCube Neutrino Observatory, a detector that catches high-energy neutrinos from space. The report follows up the first steady neutrino source, NGC 1068, and covers the flavor mix of the diffuse cosmic flux. It also caps prompt atmospheric neutrinos and hunts for Sun-born neutrinos from dark-matter annihilation. A new upgrade will sharpen low-energy sensitivity, while the planned Gen2 expansion will grow the detector and widen its energy reach.
arxiv-2604-18278: Barbosa and eight colleagues map velocity anisotropy in the Milky Way's stellar halo from over 10,000 blue horizontal-branch stars. Joining Gaia astrometry with SEGUE, DESI, and LAMOST spectra yields a fine profile out to about 50 kiloparsecs. Radial motion rules the inner halo, then it falls smoothly and turns negative as tangential motion takes over. Removing known accreted clumps leaves radial motion in charge throughout, and the lack of a metallicity link points to mergers as the driver.
arxiv-2604-18378: Oel, Porth, Schneider, and Silvestre-Rosello extend galaxy-galaxy lensing theory to fourth order to capture non-Gaussian matter structure. Traditional lensing misses information when matter and galaxy distributions deviate from Gaussianity. The authors derive the four-point correlation between shear and foreground-galaxy triplets, link it to the trispectrum, and convert it to aperture statistics. A fast-Fourier direct estimator measures aperture moments on pixelized data, and a mock stage-IV survey detects the connected signal with signal-to-noise near nine.
arxiv-2604-18478: Ganesan presents WorldDB, a memory engine that treats every node as a nested world with its own subgraph and ontology scope. Flat vector stores fragment facts and lose identity across sessions, while flat knowledge graphs lack recursive composition. WorldDB makes nodes content-addressed and immutable, giving a Merkle-style audit trail, and turns edges into write-time programs that handle supersession, contradiction, and merges. On LongMemEval-s, it reaches 96.4 percent overall accuracy with Claude Opus 4.7 answering, beating the prior best system.
arxiv-2604-18578: Ao and seven colleagues link trust-region roots to the clipped aim of Proximal Policy Optimization through Bounded Ratio Reinforcement Learning. They set up a penalized, constrained policy task, solve it in closed form, and prove steady gains. For tuned policies, they build Bounded Policy Optimization, which cuts an advantage-weighted gap between the policy and that best solution. Tests on MuJoCo, Atari, and IsaacLab, plus Group-relative BPO for language-model tuning, show the new methods tend to match or beat PPO and GRPO on steadiness and scores.
arxiv-2604-19078: Takubo and eleven colleagues re-examine dilute manganese ions in a heavy fermion compound. Manganese X-ray absorption shows multiplets, indicating empty states form a correlated high-spin divalent setup, though the sites test nonmagnetic. This paradox shows a ligand field between manganese states and nearby boron states, a Kondo effect long anticipated but rarely confirmed. Photoemission shows filled divalent states stay mobile and screened through Kondo-like links with boron and ytterbium bands. The particle-hole asymmetry prompts a rethink of links and screening in core spectroscopy.
arxiv-2604-19178: Bowers, Rehill, and Slaven study Australia's COVID apprentice wage subsidies, the Boosting and Completing Apprenticeship Commencements programs of 2020. The programs paid employers to hire or retain apprentices, studied with econometric models plus stakeholder interviews. Starts rose 70 percent, but retention did not improve, and cancellations ticked upward, suggesting lower eventual completions than previous cohorts. Non-trade cancellations rose 7 percent during BAC while trade cancellations fell 0.7 percent, a split linked to sharp practice: employers turning existing staff into apprentices for the subsidy with no intent to keep them beyond it.
arxiv-2604-19578: Wu and colleagues examine how large language models affect peer review opinions from a fine-grained perspective, using evidence from top AI conference proceedings. Peer review's primary function is improving manuscript quality, including clarity, originality, and other evaluation aspects. Prior studies suggest language models are beginning to influence peer review, but whether they alter its core evaluative functions remains unclear. The study examines changes in peer review reports following the emergence of language models, emphasizing linguistic form, evaluative focus, and recommendation-related signals.
arxiv-2604-19678: Laiyk, Gállego, Ferrando, and Koto study whether function vectors exhibit language-agnosticity, using machine translation as a case study. Function vectors are vector representations of tasks drawn from model activations in in-context learning. While prior work shows multilingual model representations can be language-agnostic, it remains unclear whether the same holds for function vectors. Across three decoder-only multilingual language models, translation function vectors from a single English-to-X direction transfer to other target languages, consistently improving the rank of correct translation tokens across multiple unseen languages.
arxiv-2604-19778: Nyalang and Debbarma present KokborokMT, a neural translation system for Kokborok, a Tibeto-Burman language spoken mainly in Tripura, India by about 1.5 million people. Despite its status as an official Tripura language, Kokborok has stayed severely under-resourced, with earlier systems trained on small Bible-derived corpora scoring below 7 on the BLEU scale. The team fine-tunes the NLLB-200-distilled-600M model on a multi-source parallel corpus of 36,052 sentence pairs, mixing professionally translated, Bible-domain, and synthetic back-translated material.
arxiv-2604-19878: Traficante and eleven colleagues studied how gas clumps split into star-forming cores in 30Dor-10, a busy star-forming zone in the Large Magellanic Cloud.
