These are crossed with five thinking levels adapted from Bloom's taxonomy, a standard ladder of learning depth. Twenty-five models were judged by automated scoring plus an expert panel.

The surprise is an inverted pattern: models do better on higher-order analysis than on seemingly basic factual recall and integrative judgment. Planning's basic knowledge, it turns out, is soaked in local rules, jurisdictions and timing, which resists pattern matching. The authors name four failure modes, including regulatory hallucination, inventing rules, and phronetic deficit, a lack of practical wisdom. Their advice is differential delegation: let AI help with synthesis, literature review and scenario drafts, but keep institution-specific judgment human.
arxiv-2606-11878:
Igor Santos-Grueiro names a new GPU attack family in this 2026 arXiv paper. CUDA programs run threads in lockstep groups called warps, and collective operations let the group vote, pool values, pick a representative lane, or synchronise. Security checks built on these collectives assume the membership data, masks, predicates, source lanes and group labels, is honest.

His attack family, Collective Semantic Corruption, corrupts exactly that data. The kernel reaches the intended collective and runs the expected primitive, but over the wrong membership, so a decision is approved by the wrong lanes. In a conformance suite spanning four authority aspects, corrupted data caused a mismatch with the trusted reference in all one hundred two instances. Hardened variants preserved the reference in all one hundred two. The defence, Collective Integrity Contracts, is a wrapper discipline: derive, recompute, check or freeze the membership data before any guarded collective consumes it.
arxiv-2606-12178:
Lobatskii and Shubin solve an extremal puzzle about sign patterns, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Consider vectors whose entries are only zero, one, or minus one, each with exactly four nonzero entries. The inner product of two vectors, their entrywise product summed, measures how much they overlap and agree. The puzzle bans most overlap values: pairs may only meet at a short allowed list, never at one, two, or four. How many such vectors can coexist in high dimensions?

The authors determine the exact maximum for all sufficiently large dimensions. The answer is eight times the dimension minus forty-eight, and they give a construction reaching it. The proof blends graph methods with careful counting over the shapes a family can take. Results of this kind belong to extremal set theory, the study of how large a family can be under forbidden patterns.
arxiv-2606-12278:
Romana Qureshi and co-authors slim neural networks during a single training run instead of many, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pruning deletes unimportant weights to shrink models for phones and edge devices. The lottery ticket hypothesis says sparse subnetworks can match full accuracy, but finding them takes repeated train-prune-reset cycles. The proposed method raises sparsity gradually on a linear schedule while training proceeds, updating masks each epoch from the sizes of still-active weights. One cycle is all it needs.

On CIFAR-10 tests, a ResNet-18 kept 95.12 percent accuracy at 72.9 percent sparsity, beating the lottery ticket result of 90.5 percent. At extreme sparsity near 97 percent, VGG-style networks held about 93 percent accuracy, ahead of the SNIP and GraSP baselines. Across 70 to 85 percent sparsity, accuracy stayed within a tenth of a point of the dense model. Tests span MNIST and three architectures, supporting progressive pruning as a practical single-cycle route.
arxiv-2606-12378:
Xu and Nordling let robots read a person's pulse from a camera, even as room lighting shifts, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Remote photoplethysmography extracts heart rate from tiny skin-color changes in facial video, no contact needed. But illumination changes swamp the faint pulse signal and wreck accuracy. The authors build an end-to-end spatial-temporal transformer designed to resist lighting variation.

The pipeline aligns faces in 3D, augments training clips with artificial lighting changes, and standardizes each clip's timing statistics. A hybrid loss supervises both the waveform's shape and its frequency content, with a tuned weight balancing the two. On their new multi-illumination dataset, the best setting reaches a heart-rate error of 0.79 beats per minute. Correlation with true heart rate hits 0.982. Against the PhysFormer baseline, error falls by 93.6 percent, and correlation leaps from 0.088, essentially useless, to that strong value. Physiological sensing becomes deployable on ordinary robots.
arxiv-2606-12478:
Kim and Park let the spots in an attention map influence each other, like magnets in a grid, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Standard attention scores each position pair independently, then normalizes; positions compete, but attention decisions never interact. Boltzmann attention governs the pattern with an Ising model, physics' model of coupled magnets. Learnable pairwise couplings let attention choices cooperate or conflict, beyond what the local scores express.

Inside an ordinary Transformer, the method beats softmax attention on character-level language modeling and synthetic bracket matching. The advantage grows with sequence length, exactly where long-range structure matters. Gains reach about a point of perplexity on Shakespeare text and nearly three points of accuracy on brackets at the longest settings tried. A four-way ablation confirms the couplings themselves cause the improvement. Training can use diabatic quantum annealing, sampling the Ising patterns on quantum hardware, at performance competitive with exact computation.
arxiv-2606-12578:
Riyazat and co-authors make drug-interaction AI name the mechanism, not just flag a clash, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Two drugs can interact through an enzyme or axis, in a direction. Yes-no predictions give clinicians nothing actionable and feed alert fatigue. The team builds a mechanism-level protocol: a taxonomy of seven families and one hundred forty-seven subtypes, and leakage-safe test splits.

Their MARD model is a 7B reasoner trained with three innovations. A single-token loss ties predictions to a direction tag. Preference training weighted by a process-reward model, with step labels checked against DrugBank records, uses built hard negatives. A retrieval channel adds evidence without leaking test drugs. On the DrugBank release, among thirty-two systems, MARD keeps its accuracy on novel drug pairs. It beats the best baseline by fourteen points and GPT-4o by seven, at one percent of API cost.
arxiv-2606-12978:
Puthumanaillam and colleagues identify a trajectory-level redirection vulnerability in vision-language-action robot policies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such policies take a natural-language instruction at every replanning step, so the prompt persistently shapes closed-loop behaviour. Existing attacks elicit low-level actions, but the authors formalise a stronger failure mode called command-preserving trajectory redirection. In this mode the prompt still appears to specify the intended task, yet the rollout's outcome is redirected to an attacker-chosen target.

The threat model is prompt-only: the attacker chooses 1 prompt before the episode, and everything else remains fixed. To find such prompts, the authors introduce an on-policy search that uses rollouts to discover perturbations whose closed-loop behaviour tracks a target task while satisfying the command-preserving constraints. Tests in simulation and on hardware show near-benign prompt perturbations can redirect vision-language-action rollouts to attacker-specified targets.
arxiv-2606-13078:
Pollock and colleagues report chemical signatures of the first stars embedded in metal-poor gas in galaxies at cosmic dawn, from JWST spectroscopy, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The first stars, Population III, formed from pristine gas and burst as supernovae, seeding the first heavy elements. Abundance studies have relied on emission lines, which are brightness-weighted and biased toward recently formed stars, hiding the oldest chemical record.

The team studies near-infrared spectroscopy from the JWST-SPURS program for 3 ultraviolet-bright galaxies at redshifts 7.8, 8.6, and 9.3, seen within the first 650 to 520 million years after the Big Bang. Metal lines detected in absorption show metal-poor gas, more metal-poor than the emission lines tracing the central star-forming regions suggest. The authors read these signatures as the chemical fingerprints of the first Population III supernovae, preserved in gas that later star formation has not overwritten.
arxiv-2606-13178:
Sevetlidis studies a neglected way that transfer learning can fail in this 2026 arXiv paper. Transfer learning means reusing a model trained for one task on a new task. Most research blames failure on data changing between settings. Sevetlidis instead holds the data fixed and changes only the loss, the rule that scores how wrong a prediction is. He calls this loss shift. Different losses need different information from the input, so a compact summary built for one loss may discard what another loss requires.

The paper formalises this with Bayes quotients, groupings of inputs that a loss treats as equivalent. When the target loss is strictly finer than the source loss, a minimal source summary cannot support the best target predictions. For log loss the shortfall is exact: the useful information the summary threw away. Tests on controlled, synthetic, and real image data confirm the predicted effect.
arxiv-2606-13878:
James and colleagues present AnyGoal, a robot-team navigation system needing no training for new homes or goals. Robots must find objects named by word, photo, or description, remembering what they learned across tasks. Earlier zero-shot systems were capped by closed-set detectors or heavy memories. Their 2026 arXiv paper centers exploration on a vision-language model. Robots share one Bayesian value map scoring each pixel for goal relevance, and it keeps learning between subtasks.

On GOAT-Bench unseen scenes, with three hundred sixty episodes and two thousand six hundred sixty-nine subtasks, the two-robot system succeeded on fifty-two point four percent of subtasks. That beats the Modular GOAT baseline by twenty-seven point five points. One robot alone reached forty-one point nine percent, so gains come from design, not headcount. Strong detectors shifted failures: most errors became false stops at wrong objects.
arxiv-2606-14078:
Zhu's team removes implanted backdoors from neural networks by weaponizing the forgetting that plagues continual learning. A backdoored model behaves normally until a trigger appears, then obeys the attacker. Existing safety tuning often suppresses the backdoor only in part. Their 2026 arXiv paper recasts backdoor learning and unlearning as a three-stage process, defines complete unlearning, and derives necessary conditions from catastrophic forgetting, where new training erases old associations.

Their method, BI-BAU, generates attack examples meeting them by blind inversion, solved through bi-level adversarial training inside an expectation-maximization framework. It extends to untargeted attacks and to multimodal contrastive learning. Experiments spanned ten typical backdoor attacks and benchmarks including CIFAR-10 with fifty thousand training images. A backdoored CLIP model was cleansed using fifty thousand image-text pairs, about zero point six percent of its fine-tuning source. The method fully removed backdoor effects.
arxiv-2606-14278:
Yin asks whether AI judges grade the answer or its language, re-presenting the same comparisons in English, Chinese, and a code-switched mix. LLM-as-a-Judge pipelines now rank model outputs at scale, but a judge swayed by presentation language corrupts every ranking. His 2026 arXiv paper proposes Judge-LS, a training-free protocol transforming the 419-item LLMBar benchmark into language variants and testing four API judges: 13,408 successful pairwise judgments in total.

The instability is real: Chinese and switched presentations flipped ten point seven to fourteen point four percent of preferences relative to English. Every judge scored highest in English. Yet translation-equivalent tie probes, where both answers say the same thing, showed no systematic English preference: most were ties, and non-tie verdicts more often favored Chinese. The central risk is thus sensitivity, not crude favoritism: presentation changes correctness and interacts with position bias.
arxiv-2606-14578:
Paul Koch and co-authors review generative AI methods for building training data in a 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is industrial computer vision. Factory inspection systems need large labeled image sets to behave in predictable ways. Such data build user trust. Yet collecting the data is slow. Active learning grows the set during deployment. But early mistakes can destroy trust that is hard to win back.

The review looks at recent generative methods. These create or augment images to jump-start the first data ramp-up. The authors test how well the methods adapt to an industrial classification case. They see real potential for automatic ramp-up. But they also find a domain mismatch. It sits between the training setting and the factory target. It shows up in the language used to describe objects. It shows up in the objects' traits. Closing that gap remains the central challenge.
arxiv-2606-14878:
Võ and coauthors study electron transport across valley domain walls in rhombohedral graphene in a 2026 study. Rhombohedral graphene stacks layers in an ABC pattern, and a moderate electric field polarizes them into an unusual metallic phase. That phase may also condense into a chiral superconductor, which conducts without resistance in a handed fashion. Recent imaging and transport experiments suggest domain walls separate regions polarized into opposite valleys.

The authors show that valley domain walls are impenetrable barriers in the metallic regime, so current cannot cross them directly. Transmission must instead come from intervalley interactions, and the team derives which such terms symmetry allows. Microscopic simulations confirm those terms do let electrons pass through the wall. In the superconducting phase, intervalley mixing proves essential for an appreciable supercurrent across a junction joining opposite-chirality regions. The results clarify how these walls govern transport in an experimentally active material.
arxiv-2606-15178:
Belbachir and Zeggada build a probability distribution from a dice problem in a 2026 mathematics paper. In 1711, Abraham de Moivre asked how likely each total is when rolling dice with many faces. The coin-toss case leads to the Bernoulli and binomial distributions, but many-faced dice were never modeled this way. The authors define an s-Bernoulli law for one die and a bisnomial law for many dice. These laws count bounded compositions, tied to the bisnomial coefficients de Moivre introduced.

The paper derives the new laws' expectation, variance, skewness, and kurtosis. It also gives their moments and generating functions in closed form. The formulas connect to Eulerian and Bernoulli numbers and to partial Bell polynomials. The main limit result mirrors the classical binomial theory. As the number of dice grows, the bisnomial law approaches Poisson and normal limits. The work completes a three-century-old gap in probability.
arxiv-2606-15278:
Liu and Shoaran present RECTOR, a self-supervised framework for learning from brain signals in a 2026 neuroengineering paper. EEG and stereo-EEG recordings could give markers of mood and cognitive disorders. But the signals spread across brain regions, channels, and time in ways. Most models hard-code brain regions from anatomy, though functional regions shift during tasks. RECTOR instead learns adaptive functional regions from the data itself. Masked modeling objectives teach it to predict signal parts and respect brain topology.

The framework set state-of-the-art results on EEG emotion recognition benchmarks. It led on stereo-EEG task-engagement classification tasks. It stayed robust when channels went missing from the recordings. It generalized across electrode montages without retraining. Attention maps at region and channel level stayed neurophysiologically plausible. The authors pitch RECTOR as a foundation for pretraining on EEG datasets. Such pretraining could yield diagnosis of affective disorders.
arxiv-2606-15678:
Leonhart studies whether a pretrained transformer can carry memory between forward passes in 2026, without retraining it. Transformers are stateless: nothing inside evolves between calls except position within the context window. Her Reservoir Attention Network injects a fixed, random reservoir, in the echo-state tradition, into a middle layer and carries its state across passes.

The injection route proves decisive. Writing the reservoir state additively into the residual stream fails: the model learns to ignore it, and cross-context recall sits at chance. Re-injecting the same state as content-addressable prefix tokens that upper layers can attend to yields perfect recall, against a near-chance reset baseline. The edge-of-chaos regime near unit spectral radius also survives real transformer activations. Experiments span GPT-2 up to a 1.5-billion-parameter Qwen model, all on one consumer GPU. Untrained recurrence alone can supply usable cross-pass state when addressed properly.
arxiv-2606-16178:
Shah and colleagues give robot policies a usable short-term memory in 2026, so past views can guide present actions. Many tasks need memory: fetching an object no longer visible, or switching off an appliance after a delay. Imitation-learned visuomotor policies are usually myopic, reacting only to current input. Their PRISM architecture adds memory in two stages.

First, local interactions are compressed into compact tokens, which keeps the compute and memory footprint small. Gated attention then retrieves from those tokens selectively, filtering out irrelevant details. This filtering reduces spurious correlations between history and action prediction, a failure mode of naive memory. Together the pieces scale short-term memory to spans of up to two minutes. To measure such memory, the team introduces ReMemBench, eight household manipulation tasks. Success rates there cluster near 30 percent, which the authors read as headroom for the whole field.
arxiv-2606-16378:
Fabris and Kamenshchik revisit generalized unimodular gravity in 2026, a variant of Einstein's theory where matter-like effects emerge from geometry alone. Unimodular gravity, proposed by Einstein in 1919, fixes the metric's determinant. The generalized version lets the lapse function depend on the determinant of the spatial metric. In a cosmological setting, that freedom produces the usual matter components of the universe in a purely geometric way.

The effective dark fluid that appears has an equation of state restricted to a linear relation between its density and pressure. Background expansion histories match those of general relativity, but with a different reading: what looks like dark matter and dark energy content is geometry in disguise. The authors also carry out a perturbation analysis and recover the standard relativistic results. The reframing gives the dark sector a new perspective, suggesting part of it may be a bookkeeping artifact of the gravitational variables chosen.
arxiv-2606-16578:
Bao and co-authors solve heat problems in 2026 by walking paths on 'heat stars,' extending mesh-free Monte Carlo solvers from steady problems to transient ones. Monte Carlo methods like Walk on Spheres and Walk on Stars evaluate PDE solutions pointwise, with no volumetric mesh and no global linear solve. Parabolic equations resisted this treatment because space and time couple through anisotropic scaling: a sampler must draw spatial and backward time steps jointly, with no exact distribution available.

Walk on Heat Stars extends the boundary integral framework of Walk on Stars to the parabolic setting. Its non-cylindrical boundary integral handles the time-varying domains heat-ball sampling induces. Writing the heat ball in a logarithmic time coordinate makes the double-layer kernel factorize, enabling exact importance sampling. The method also yields a gradient estimator for source-free problems, though Neumann flux terms and variance remain open issues.
arxiv-2606-16678:
Jahani, Boguslawski and Tecmer present a cheap way to compute ionization potentials in a 2026 quantum chemistry paper. An ionization potential is the energy needed to remove an electron from an atom or molecule, a basic quantity for judging chemical behavior. Accurate methods exist, but their cost grows fast with system size.

Their method joins the extended Koopmans' theorem with a pair coupled cluster doubles wavefunction whose orbitals are optimized. Once that wavefunction is computed, the extra cost of the ionization values is tiny, scaling mildly with system size. Benchmarks cover atoms, small molecules and a set of organic acceptor molecules, checked against experiment and high-level theory. The new model clearly beats an earlier modified Koopmans' approach and nearly matches far costlier methods. Its mean error against a trusted reference is very small, and results barely change with basis set size, so small cheap bases already give reliable values.
arxiv-2606-16778:
Gröner and Chiou compare human and simulated research participants in a 2026 human-computer interaction study. Language models write text that can look human, so some researchers hope to replace costly human subjects with prompted model stand-ins. Whether study findings survive that swap is an open question.

Their testbed is a writing style task, where preference inference algorithms adapt to a participant over repeated interactions. Thirty human participants provide the reference results, and a model prompted as a synthetic participant runs the same protocol. The simulation shows hints of bias and a lack of depth in both its writing and its judgments, so it fails to mirror human behavior well. Human data also reveal biases of their own, which matter for judging human-automation systems. The authors present the work as a case study of method and design pitfalls, not as a final verdict on simulated participants in general.
arxiv-2606-17178:
Rahvar computes particles created by an orbiting black hole pair in a 2026 theoretical astrophysics paper. Quantum fields in curved spacetime produce particles, the effect behind Hawking radiation. A binary black hole's spacetime churns in time, and that motion should excite the vacuum too.

Treating a massless scalar field on the binary's weak-field inspiral background, Rahvar computes the particle flux and radiated energy two independent ways. The Bogoliubov method and the S-matrix approach give matching amplitudes, a consistency check on the mechanism. The emission is non-thermal: a steep power law in orbital frequency, not a Hawking-like spectrum. A resonance condition ties the created particles to the gravity-wave frequency. The calculation stays in the large-separation regime where quadrupole formulas hold; the merger itself, needing numerical relativity, is future work. Such bursts would add a particle channel to the binary's multi-messenger signals.
arxiv-2606-17378:
Huang and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on serving text-to-image diffusion models jointly from edge servers and user devices, instead of picking one side. Big edge models give high fidelity but slow replies, while small on-device models are fast but lose semantic coherence in their images. Their system, RISE, splits the denoising work itself: the big model runs the early steps that set the scene's structure, then hands the half-finished latent image to the small model.

The handoff works because latent values barely shift when models from one family swap mid-generation, and it needs no extra training. A contextual bandit scheduler picks the relay setup per request using prompt difficulty, user preferences, network quality, and live node loads. Benchmarks show speedups of up to about twofold at full-model quality. The scheduler also balanced quality against delay well under mixed workloads.
arxiv-2606-18078:
Lee and colleagues run a head-to-head contest among ways to teach random forests about geography, in a 2026 statistics paper. Environmental prediction is classically done by kriging, a Gaussian process method that respects spatial correlation, while machine learning wins on non-spatial tasks. Many hybrids have been proposed to give forests spatial awareness, from Gaussian process add-ons to local fitting, but nobody had compared their predictive performance side by side.

The authors benchmark the main families on environmental data, tracking both accuracy and prediction interval quality. Random forests are the test bed because they are simple to run and easy to grasp. Across their experiments, the Gaussian-process-flavored hybrids posted the slimmest interval widths while holding coverage near the nominal level, with basis-function and local approaches close behind. The comparison gives environmental scientists direct guidance on which spatial trick to reach for.
arxiv-2606-18478:
Chen and colleagues present Data-Forcing Distillation, a fix for two persistent flaws in fast video generation models, in a 2026 machine learning paper. Distilling a many-step video diffusion model into a few-step student through distribution matching tends to shrink the variety of videos produced and to push colors into an over-saturated look unlike real footage.

Their remedy changes a single line of the earlier DMD2 method. Instead of scoring only the student's own generations, the teacher scores real videos. That creates a discrepancy signal that pulls the student toward modes it had dropped and away from modes real data never shows. A short fine-tuning run on two video models restored diversity and fidelity and removed the saturation artifacts. Theoretical analysis accompanies the method, though the authors note that tight budgets of two steps or fewer still blur fast motion and fine detail.
arxiv-2606-18878:
Amarilli and colleagues study gap-constraint languages for complex event recognition in 2026. Event systems search long data streams for a pattern as a subsequence, with rules on what may fall in the gaps between matched parts. Each gap rule names a regular language for the skipped factor. In general this matching task is NP-complete. Past tractable cases had to limit how the gap intervals could nest or overlap in structure.

The authors show matching can be solved well even with arbitrary interval structure. Their method runs in time that is optimal under a standard hardness assumption. That result widens the set of event patterns that can be checked fast in practice. It also sharpens the border between hard and easy cases for subsequence search. For event recognition, richer gap rules no longer force a choice between expressiveness and tractable run time, at least for the language class studied here.
arxiv-2606-19078:
Kokkeler and colleagues show in 2026 how supercurrents can move magnetic domain walls, a step toward cryogenic magnetic memory. Cold computing lacks a fast, low-power memory, since room-temperature options fail or waste power when cooled. Superconducting spintronics aims to fill that gap with equal-spin triplet supercurrents. Short spin relaxation lengths and strong anisotropy in ferromagnets have blocked that path for years.

The team uses a superconductor and magnetic insulator bilayer instead. A supercurrent creates spin accumulation in the superconductor, and Gilbert damping of the magnetization then drives the domain wall to move. That motion shows up as a local voltage across the wall, so its position can be read electrically. Power needed to keep the wall moving is orders of magnitude lower than in the normal state. Most input power there is wasted just to sustain the current, a contrast that makes the superconducting route attractive.
arxiv-2606-19378:
Moon and colleagues propose a hybrid graph neural network and finite element framework for phase-field fracture simulation in 2026. Phase-field methods robustly simulate complex crack growth. Their cost is high, since each load increment solves a coupled, nonlinear, history-dependent system. Pure learned surrogates are fast but can drift away from physics on history-dependent problems, where the whole loading path shapes the current crack state.

The hybrid design replaces only the phase-field update at each increment with a graph network surrogate. The finite element solver still handles displacement, enforcing mechanical equilibrium and boundary conditions. Keeping the staged solution structure preserves the true fracture history. The surrogate never has to approximate the full solution trajectory at once. The structured learning target is the key design move. The framework aims for surrogate speed with finite element trustworthiness. That balance is what engineering simulation needs.
arxiv-2606-19778:
Yuki Yasuda and Tsubasa Kohyama bound the seasonal rhythm of El Niño through thermodynamics in 2026. El Niño events peak in boreal winter, a pattern called seasonal phase locking. Their model is a linear stochastic recharge oscillator with noise and a seasonally varying growth rate.

Phase locking shows up as seasonal swings in sea surface temperature anomaly variance. Energy drives change, but entropy decides whether change may occur. A thermodynamic uncertainty relation turns that entropy side into a hard inequality. The relation ties variance trends to a partial entropy production rate. That rate tracks the irreversibility of temperature transitions, set by the growth rate. Irreversibility peaks in autumn and late winter, loosening the bound at both times. Variance can then peak in winter, matching observations. Too little irreversibility would freeze El Niño growth and decay alike.
arxiv-2606-20378:
Goutham Vinjamuri, Ashutosh Dubey, and Ankur Das test whether a Weyl semimetal can be realized in a driven lattice with synthetic dimensions. Their 2026 paper uses two incommensurate drives whose phases act as synthetic momenta, adding two artificial dimensions to a one-dimensional lattice. Weyl points appear in the mixed Floquet band structure. In a static Weyl semimetal, power transfer between drives should measure the Chern number, the topological charge tied to the separation of Weyl nodes.

The mixed lattice captures that topology only in a momentum-resolved sense. For fixed real momentum, the power transfer does track the resolved Chern number and detects node separation. The full real-space response is qualitatively different: total power transfer follows an effective Rice-Mele pumping structure instead of the static phase diagram. Gapless semimetal phases, unlike gapped insulators, do not translate straightforwardly into Floquet synthetic dimensions.
arxiv-2606-20678:
Yifeng Guo, Jin-Hong Du, and Xiang Chen introduce a method in 2026 to separate two roles that transformer parts can play. A component may matter because it carries task content. Or it may matter because removing it damages the whole computation. Single importance scores merge those roles. Their paired method, Interchange-Group Sobol Decomposition, compares activation replacement with zero ablation on the same component.

Two variance indices are estimated, and their signed difference separates content transport from general damage. A diagnostic checks whether interventions stay valid. In factual recall, the method finds an early-layer content channel in GPT-2 small and Qwen2.5 models. Standard methods underrate that channel. Donor tests show early parts carry relation-frame content. Late attention carries subject retrieval content. Separating those roles gives a sharper map of how transformers store and move facts.
arxiv-2606-20878:
Bahrul Nasution presents an empirical study in a solo 2026 paper of latent flow models for synthetic tabular data. Synthetic tables let regulated data be shared with less risk. Continuous-time generative models are flexible. Yet choices that look equivalent in theory can behave differently in practice. Finite sampling steps and fixed compute budgets expose those differences. Seven datasets are used for tests.

Four learning targets are compared: velocity, score, noise, and posterior matching. Two probability paths are also compared, plus two sampling methods and varied budgets. The learning target largely sets the utility and risk regime. Velocity and posterior matching tend to give higher utility. Score and noise matching tend to give lower disclosure risk. Sampling choices shift fidelity further. Clear guidance on those tradeoffs helps data holders pick a generator that fits their legal and analytic needs.
arxiv-2606-21178:
Bilal Khalid and five colleagues apply Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks in 2026 to digital predistortion for 5G analog radio-over-fiber links at low complexity. Radio-over-fiber carries wireless signals over fiber in dense 5G and future 6G networks. Analog links based on VCSEL lasers distort signals. Digital predistortion pre-warps the signal to cancel that distortion. The predistorter must stay cheap and fast.

Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks replace fixed activation functions with learnable ones on edges. That structure can fit strong nonlinear response with fewer parameters. Their work, called DPD-KAN, targets the system model of a VCSEL-based analog link shown in the paper. Low-complexity predistortion matters at scale: fronthaul links are deployed in huge numbers, so a predistorter that needs a large neural network per link would never be economical in real base station hardware.
arxiv-2606-21678:
Vatsal Ananthula and Adarsh Kumarappan probe a subtle honesty problem in language models in 2026: an explanation can be readable, checkable, and still not the real reason. A model can emit plausible rationales that do not reflect its internal process. Their verifier-coupled reasoning inserts inline claims into reasoning traces and trains a helper head to predict a program's verdict from the hidden states of the rationale text.

The headline result is a gap between decodability and faithfulness. Training reliably makes verifier information decodable from the rationale, yet generated explanations can stay unfaithful: fluent prose with correct structured claims describing entirely unrelated algorithms. Tests span Lean theorem proving, KataGo commentary, code, and FEVER fact-checking. Activation patching confirms the traces do exert causal influence. The lesson: consistency losses are sharp diagnostics, but decodable is not the same as true.
arxiv-2606-21978:
Li and Wang prove, in 2026, a weighted sum formula for finite multiple mixed values. These are special numbers built from multiple zeta values, infinite sums that recur across number theory and physics. Sum formulas package many values into one identity, revealing structure in the space they span. The finite and mixed variants studied here are newer, level-two relatives of the classical objects.

The proof works through iterated integral expressions for multiple polylogarithms, the functions whose values at special points produce these numbers. Establishing the weighted sum formula for finite multiple mixed values is the paper's central result. As applications, they derive relations among level-two variants of finite multiple zeta values. Such identities enlarge the known web of relations and give other researchers concrete formulas to test conjectures against. The line of work stretches back to classical weighted sum formulas for double zeta values.
arxiv-2606-22078:
Dobozy and Poppitz study, in 2026, how fractional instantons change shape in Yang-Mills theory placed on a twisted four-dimensional torus with a double-trace deformation. Instantons are lump-like field configurations carrying fractional topological charge. The authors vary the twists and the torus period ratios to move between geometries with different numbers of flat directions.

By numerically minimizing the lattice action, they track the lowest-action configurations across those geometries. Monopole-instantons, center vortices, and fractional instantons morph continuously into one another as the shape changes. The authors argue that a recent analytic picture of monopole chains merging into vortex sheets holds in pure Yang-Mills theory too, for torus shapes where two alignment effects coincide. With the deformation switched on, some transitions instead jump discontinuously, with level crossing.
arxiv-2606-22778:
Yuichi Tateno built a lightweight way to compare search systems in this 2026 paper. Retrieval-augmented generation, which grounds chatbot answers in searched text, depends on picking the right embedding model and settings. Full benchmarks are too heavy to rerun during development, and production choices like compression are rarely compared on equal terms.

His HAKARI-Bench rebuilds existing retrieval benchmarks into small nano-sets sharing one format of corpus, queries, and relevance labels. It covers 35 benchmarks and 551 tasks across 43 languages. Five retrieval families can be tested, from keyword search to rerankers, along with efficiency variants such as dimensionality reduction and quantization, which shrink stored vectors. Evaluating 55 models, Tateno found its rankings closely matched the official large benchmarks, with rank correlations above 0.97 in each comparison made.
arxiv-2606-22978:
Alexander Beiser and colleagues tackle air traffic flow and airspace capacity as one joint problem in a 2026 paper. The task is to balance flight demand against sector capacity so flights stay safe and on time. Past work treats flight paths and sector layouts apart, leaving open whether joint treatment helps. The team builds a joint model and encodes it in Answer Set Programming, a logic method where rules define what counts as a solution. They test it against a top mixed integer programming model and a stepwise heuristic, on cases drawn from a generator fitted to past OpenSky flight data.

Beiser and colleagues find the logic model beats the integer programming model. It stays close to the heuristic on small cases. Changing sector layouts gave the largest boost to solving speed, ahead of rerouting and delaying flights. Letting either lever run free caused the search to thrash, which hurt performance.
arxiv-2606-23278:
Bernat Espigule builds explicit bridges between three famous fractals in a 2026 mathematics paper. The Sierpiński gasket, the Rauzy gasket, and the Apollonian gasket are all triangular fractals built by endless repetition of simple rules. Espigule defines two one-parameter families of shapes around the Sierpiński gasket. The first family interpolates toward the Rauzy gasket through affine and projective maps, keeping the first-level hole fixed throughout.

Espigule's second family deforms the Sierpiński gasket into the equilateral Apollonian gasket through Möbius maps. For each parameter value the maps form, on a shared disk, a conformal iterated function system, with an exact formula for the Hausdorff dimension. At the endpoint, an explicit Apollonian model shares its distinguished side with the Rauzy side. That match yields a canonical homeomorphism between the two gaskets.
arxiv-2606-23478:
Jay Kueny and colleagues present a freeform modeling pipeline for planet-forming disks in a 2026 astronomy paper. These disks are the dusty rings around young stars where planets form. Traditional modeling assumes the dust follows a fixed parametric shape. Common starlight subtraction methods also distort the faint disk's true shape, especially close to the star. Their pipeline, ffortissimo, instead models the disk pixel by pixel with no fixed shape. It forward-models reduced high-contrast images directly, inside the Jax machine learning framework. Automatic differentiation makes the huge pixel-wise optimization fast.

Kueny and colleagues designed the pipeline to characterize extended objects in images processed with the KLIP subtraction method. By avoiding both rigid shapes and subtraction artifacts, it can measure the full range of the dust's scattering behavior. The tool targets the fine disk features at small distances from the star that parametric fits tend to mangle.
arxiv-2606-23578:
Yamanaka revisits a long-standing puzzle about two mesons and the symmetry breaking behind their masses, in a 2026 particle physics contribution. Quantum chromodynamics, the theory of the strong force, breaks chiral symmetry on its own, and the light mesons that result are usually read as Nambu-Goldstone bosons, particles born from such breaking. The eta and eta-prime mesons never quite fit that story. Textbooks credit an anomalous breaking of axial symmetry for their extra mass, a puzzle called the U(1) problem.

Recent work argues that this anomaly is not actually physical, and Yamanaka reviews that claim first. A mechanism then follows in which both mesons really are Nambu-Goldstone bosons after all. Their masses arise in a way that stays consistent with the U(1) problem instead of leaning on the anomaly. The proposal reopens a basic question about how hadron masses are generated in the strong interaction.
arxiv-2606-23678:
Han, Lan, Qiu, and Zhong teach multimodal models to write and run code in the middle of their own reasoning, in a 2026 paper on multimodal AI. Interleaved reasoning lets a model pause its chain of thought to use tools, as frontier systems do with image operations. Work so far centers on visual tricks chosen by fixed heuristics, leaving numerical computation untouched, where models stumble most.

The team builds training data in two stages, filters it for reinforcement learning, and adds an adaptive tool strategy driven by a group constrained reward. Benchmark performance then rises by about six points on average. Accuracy on samples that actually interleave code climbs by about ten points, and tool use succeeds more than ninety five percent of the time. The model learns to trigger Python when calculations grow complex.
arxiv-2606-23778:
Sok and colleagues use the narrow emission lines of Little Red Dots to test a popular picture of what surrounds these early universe objects, in a 2026 paper on observational astrophysics. One leading model wraps an accreting black hole in a spherical, optically thick gas envelope. Hard radiation would be reprocessed into a star like glow, and the narrow lines would come from the host galaxy's stars. If so, line ratios should look like star formation.

Analyzing high quality spectra for about twenty Little Red Dots, the team finds at least forty percent show line ratios demanding high ionization and hot electrons, signs of hard radiation. Stellar photoionization alone cannot explain them. The envelope must have lower density channels letting energetic photons escape and excite the surrounding gas. Yet most sources lack the strongest high ionization lines, implying a softer spectrum than a standard active nucleus.
arxiv-2606-23878:
Luu defines an operator that singles out the vacuum state of a classic integrable system, then extends it across the whole Riemann sphere, in a 2026 paper on mathematical physics. The Drinfeld Sokolov KdV hierarchy is a family of integrable equations attached to any simple Lie algebra, and its vacuum is a distinguished point. Luu builds a connection on the formal disc from the algebra's cyclic element. He proves this vacuum operator stabilizes no deformation of the vacuum except the vacuum itself.

As a connection, the operator extends canonically, in Katz's sense, from the disc to the sphere. Luu expresses that extension using Kac coordinates attached to a suitable conjugacy class of the Weyl group. The payoff is conceptual: the Katz extension describes an additional symmetry of the integrable hierarchy itself.
arxiv-2606-24178:
Lindner and colleagues fix tilted, stretched inputs for pretrained vision models without retraining anything. Classifiers often fail on rotated, scaled, or sheared images even though the object's class is unchanged. Test-time canonicalization instead straightens each input back toward the training distribution before classification, leaving the classifier untouched. Previous canonicalizers leaned on a narrow family of logit-based energy scores and handcrafted searches.

Reframing canonicalization as out-of-distribution detection lets any such score serve as the energy to minimise over transformations. Lindner's team systematically evaluates around twenty scores and nine search algorithms across handwritten characters, sketches, natural images, and 3D point clouds. Distance-based scores paired with random search plus local refinement perform best overall. Because straightening an already-aligned input can hurt, a gate transforms inputs only when needed. The 2026 sweep maps a design space earlier work left unexplored, and names a dependable default recipe.
arxiv-2606-24278:
Guo and colleagues test Einstein's gravity on extragalactic scales, using galaxies that bend and delay light. Strong gravitational lenses split a distant source into multiple images. The images' light arrives at different times. That time delay depends on a post-Newtonian parameter: how much space curvature a given mass produces. General relativity fixes that parameter at exactly one. 

Model independence is the priority. Gaussian process regression reconstructs angular diameter distances directly from the newest DESI baryon acoustic oscillation data. Combined with four time-delay lenses from the H0LiCOW programme, the distances yield a parameter estimate close to one. It is consistent with Einstein within the stated uncertainties. Guo's team notes the pairing is the first of its kind, obtained without assuming a cosmological model or a theory of gravity.
arxiv-2606-24378:
Moulai computes a central extension of surface mapping class groups from skein algebra representations, using only two-dimensional tools. Mapping class groups collect the symmetries of a surface up to deformation. Stated skein algebras, built from tangles drawn on the surface with states at marked points, furnish projective representations of them. Every such representation hides a central extension, a slightly enlarged group on which the representation becomes honest. Identifying it is a classic quantum topology problem.

For surfaces of any genus with zero or one boundary component and marked points, and any finite-dimensional factorizable ribbon Hopf algebra feeding the construction, Moulai identifies the extension explicitly. The proof is purely two dimensional, avoiding topological quantum field theory arguments, the usual heavy machinery for such results. Writing alone from Montpellier in 2026, Moulai shows the extension can be read off the surface itself, inside the skein world where it was born.
arxiv-2606-24678:
Víctor Velasco-Pardo, Nathan Constantine-Cooke, Charlie Lees, and Catalina Vallejos build a prediction method for time to event medical data. Health records now track huge patient groups for years. Repeated biomarker readings can update a patient's risk as new results arrive. Most dynamic prediction methods assume everyone follows similar biomarker trajectories. Real patients do not. Hidden subgroups bend those trajectories in different ways, and joint latent class models that capture this are too slow for record scale data.

The proposed fix is landmarking combined with latent class mixed models. Landmarking restarts prediction at chosen time points using data gathered so far. Latent classes absorb the hidden differences between patients. The method ships as a modular R package called landmaRk, available on CRAN. In simulation studies, the approach improves prediction accuracy when latent heterogeneity is present. It does so compared with traditional landmarking that ignores subgroup structure.
arxiv-2606-24878:
Varun Sivashankar improves a lower bound in a combinatorics problem Erdős himself counted among his favourites. The setting is intersecting hypergraphs, where every two edges share a vertex. For a given uniformity and the largest possible cover number, one asks the fewest edges such a hypergraph can have. Erdős and Lovász bounded that minimum below by roughly eight thirds of the parameter, minus a constant. That bound stood for about fifty years. Sivashankar's attack stays elementary at first.

A first argument gives a clean bound of three times the parameter minus four. Building on the same approach, he then applies Kahn's edge colouring theorem for hypergraphs of small codegree. The result lifts the lower bound to about sixty one twentieths of the parameter, for large cases. To his knowledge this is the first improvement on the Erdős Lovász bound in half a century.
arxiv-2606-25078:
Lei Wang develops a framework for measuring neutron skins at the Electron Ion Collider, using gluons rather than electrons. A neutron skin, the excess of neutrons at a nucleus's surface, connects to how nuclear forces treat neutrons and protons, and to neutron star physics. Coherent quarkonium production at the collider can image the small x gluon radius of a nucleus, a mechanism complementary to parity violating electron scattering. Wang's radius sum rule framework links that gluonic radius to the neutron skin, with the limitations quantified.

Coherent J psi production carries information for a neutron skin programme. The precision, though, is not limited by luminosity. It is controlled by how well the gluon density at small x is calibrated. The upsilon channel stays limited at collider luminosities. Wang identifies what the measurement adds to symmetry energy studies, and which controls must be in place before the numbers count as structure.
arxiv-2606-25178:
Training a reasoning model across maths, programming, and science at once raises a scheduling question: how often should each domain be sampled? Yongjin Yang and five colleagues note that skills transfer unevenly between domains, while existing curricula adapt only to where the model is currently improving.

Their Transfer Aware Curriculum is a bandit style scheduler that favours domains whose updates help the rest of the suite. It reuses signals the training run already produces. Per domain advantages capture local learnability. Projected gradients from the current step estimate cross domain transfer by gradient alignment. The extra cost stays under one percent. Across a six domain suite, the method posts the best average accuracy on both Qwen3-1.7B and Llama3.2-3B. It beats random sampling, a hand tuned schedule, and a learnability only bandit, the last by ten percent in relative terms.
arxiv-2606-25378:
Tiny defects in diamond, called nitrogen vacancy centres, can image magnetic fields with fine spatial detail, but squeezing and heating a sample at once strains the technique. Masahiro Ohkuma and colleagues show in 2026 that wide field magnetic resonance imaging with these centres survives truly combined extremes. Their pressure cell reached five gigapascals at five hundred kelvin while the optical readout still worked cleanly. A second run pushed an iron sample to seven gigapascals at the same temperature.

Through the cell, the stray field of the iron spread across the image field exactly where the sample sat. No scanning probe was needed, since the whole field of view reports at once. The authors present the result as a platform for watching magnetic behaviour inside materials under conditions that mimic planetary interiors and industrial synthesis.
arxiv-2606-25478:
Adapting an image trained model like CLIP to recognise actions in video risks trading away its gift for naming things it has never seen. Minghao Zhu and colleagues propose TACO in 2026 to keep both sides of that bargain. Fine tuning usually warps the representation space in ways that only show up on unseen data. Their fix distils the relative geometry of the original space, penalising harmful shifts in how concepts sit relative to each other during training.

A light projection layer then holds the task specific changes, so the space used at test time stays closer to the pretrained one. Across cross dataset and base to novel benchmarks, the method set new state of the art results for open vocabulary video recognition. The authors frame the lesson broadly: match the training objective to how the model will actually be judged.
arxiv-2606-25878:
Song He, Jiajie Mei, and Yuyu Mo study Yang-Mills wavefunctions in de Sitter space, the expanding spacetime of cosmology, for gluons at tree level. Their tool is the cosmological cut, a discontinuity that splits a wavefunction into smaller ones joined by cut propagators. Understanding these building blocks matters for computing what inflation-era physics leaves behind in the sky.

For ray-like trees and one-loop polygons, the largest cuts take a strikingly simple form. A scalar discontinuity appears, dressed by a Yang-Mills numerator that is ordered and built from local gluing maps. Using cuts as reconstruction data, He and colleagues rebuild the wavefunctions for four, five, and six gluons in momentum space. Each splits into a part the cuts reveal and a completion that current conservation and the flat-space limit fix, and the rebuilt forms match direct Feynman-rule calculations.
arxiv-2606-26578:
Qingcan Kang and five colleagues present EvoOptiGraph, a framework that trains language models to build optimisation models. Turning a word problem into a mixed-integer linear program is a valuable automation target. Such programs encode scheduling and allocation decisions. Training data for the skill lacks structural variety, and data pipelines usually ignore what the model gets wrong.

EvoOptiGraph represents each program as a graph with two kinds of nodes. Validity-preserving changes then evolve new, structurally diverse instances. Graphs become solver code and natural language by fixed compilation steps, with back-translation as a check. Training first fine-tunes the model on an initial set. Reinforcement learning follows, guided by weakness signals from the graphs. New instances target the model's current failures, closing the loop. On six public data sets, the system beat larger general models and specialist baselines.
arxiv-2606-26678:
Martin Berglund, Brink van der Merwe, and Iain le Roux speed up backtracking regular expression matching. Regular expressions search text for patterns. Most practical engines backtrack, exploring choices one by one. Hostile inputs can force exponential running time, a known denial-of-service risk. Remembering past work, called memoization, restores linear time. Full memoization, though, uses impractical amounts of memory.

Their scheme memoizes selectively. It computes a minimum feedback vertex set of the matching automaton, a smallest set of states whose removal breaks all loops. Only visits to those states are recorded. The authors relate the scheme to existing memoization methods. They analyse it under two standard automaton constructions, Thompson's and Glushkov's. The result aims at linear-time matching with a memory bill programs can actually pay.
arxiv-2606-27178:
Mezzanotte and colleagues solve Fredholm integral equations of the second kind with a special polynomial approximation. Such equations mix an unknown function with its own weighted integral against a known kernel. De la Vallée Poussin type approximations at Jacobi zeros replace plain interpolation here. They keep error constants uniformly bounded in weighted spaces and nearly match the best possible uniform fit. In 2026, the Gibbs phenomenon, ringing near jumps, also shrinks compared with standard Lagrange interpolation.

Endpoint singularities of algebraic type are handled naturally by the weighted setup. Kernels with weak singularities or rapid oscillation also fit the framework. Stability and convergence are proved in weighted uniform spaces under stated assumptions. Implementation reduces to solving one well-conditioned linear system. Numerical tests confirm the predicted error rates. Local accuracy beats the matching Lagrange-based projection method in those tests.
arxiv-2606-27278:
Bianchi surveys how chemistry can reveal the birthplaces of planets while they are still forming. Young disks, still embedded in their natal envelopes, hide their mass and composition from easy measurement. Without those numbers, comparing young disks with mature planet populations stays shaky. Upcoming European missions will inventory planet makeup fully, raising the stakes. In her 2026 astrochemistry overview, she introduces the iSEEDs project, built to mine high-resolution observations of those environments.

Machine learning and data mining join classical chemistry craft in the project. Together they extract conditions and molecule counts buried in large datasets. Early disks are the focus, since evidence suggests planet formation starts younger than once thought. Systematic extraction replaces case-by-case handwork. It aims to make disk makeup comparable across many objects. Planet formation theory gains the observational footing it has lacked.
arxiv-2606-27378:
Seddik and Fard grade the hidden thought vectors of large language models against four axioms, instead of trusting benchmark scores. Latent reasoning replaces written chain-of-thought with continuous vectors, promising speed. But accuracy alone cannot tell whether the representation itself is sound or the model is compensating. Their axioms, Causality, Minimality, Separability, and Stability, each get a quantitative measure computed directly on the representation. In the 2026 language model paper, open-weight models are audited across twenty-three reasoning tasks.

No candidate satisfies all four axioms at once. The representations do separate task types reliably, a partial pass. They cannot, however, distinguish two different questions within the same task. Worse, they encode little information beyond what the input embedding already held. The failure repeats across dense, distilled, and reinforcement-trained model families, marking it as structural rather than a matter of scale.
arxiv-2606-27578:
Reward models guide chatbot training by scoring answers. Most are calibrated with ratings pooled from thousands of annotators. Arnav Raj notes a flaw in that pooling. Raters use scales in different ways. Some are strict, and some are generous. A single pooled fit therefore matches no actual person. His 2026 method, PEBS, calibrates each rater separately.

PEBS fits a linear calibration for each annotator. The fit uses a held-out slice of that person's ratings. The method then shrinks each fit toward the population average using empirical-Bayes shrinkage. It borrows strength from the group where personal data is thin. The adjustment has a closed-form solution. It needs no retraining of the reward model. On the PRISM dataset, PEBS cut held-out error for individual users by about eight and a half percent against the pooled baseline. On separate harm ratings, the error fell by nearly ten percent.
arxiv-2606-27678:
Cervical cell images look different at different institutions. Scanners, stains, and habits shift the images, and disease stages differ only subtly. Models trained at one site then fail at another. Jincheng Li and eight colleagues propose a two-stage fix in 2026. Stage one builds a synthetic middle domain to soften the shift. Stage two aligns features between the source and target models.

The bridge in stage one is called SC-UNSB. It models image translation as an entropy-regularised optimal transport process. Spatial continuity is preserved along the way. Stage two uses knowledge distillation with dual-level alignment. Shallow structural features align first. Deep semantic features align after them. Domain-invariant knowledge thus moves from the source model to the target model step by step. Experiments show the method reduces domain shift and category confusion. Cross-domain detection performance improves as a result.
arxiv-2606-27978:
Pixel-space autoregressive models generate images patch by patch from raw pixels, avoiding tokenizers entirely. Two problems hold them back. High-dimensional patches cause large single-step errors. Teacher-forced training then lets those errors accumulate at inference. Jiayi Xu and Guolin Ke propose Parallel Rollout Approximation in 2026. The model generates low-dimensional intermediate states instead of pixel patches. A pixel decoder maps them back to pixel tokens.

Inference-like inputs are built through the same decode path used at generation time. Training stays parallel, avoiding slow sequential rollouts. On class-conditional ImageNet generation, the small model reaches an FID of two point five eight with 135 million parameters. The previous billion-scale pixel-space result was three point six zero. The large model, at 511 million parameters, reaches one point nine four. That sets a new record among pixel-space autoregressive models.
arxiv-2606-28278:
Saeed Masiha, Negar Kiyavash, and Patrick Thiran pin down the best possible speed of first-order optimization under a relaxed curvature condition. The alpha-Polyak-Lojasiewicz condition bounds how far a point is from optimal by a power of the gradient's size. Its strongest form is classical, but weaker powers arise near degenerate critical points of analytic functions.

Masiha and colleagues first prove an impossibility: demanding smoothness and the weak condition everywhere forces the function to be constant. Restricting the condition to the starting sublevel set, the region descent methods never leave, restores a rich problem class. There they prove sharp lower bounds on the queries any first-order method needs, in both exact and noisy settings. Plain gradient descent matches those bounds exactly, settling its optimality.
arxiv-2606-28478:
Mark Glass and Meir Feder revisit maximum cut, the problem of splitting a graph's vertices into two groups so the total weight of edges crossing between them is as large as possible. For flat, planar graphs an efficient exact algorithm has existed since 1975, but only for nonnegative weights.

Glass and Feder map the general planar problem to a minimum T-join problem in the absolute dual graph, a reformulation that unlocks shortest-path machinery. Hadlock's classic algorithm then extends straightforwardly to arbitrary weights. For doughnut-shaped toroidal graphs, which are not planar, they prove that ignoring the topology and running the planar algorithm yields a valid upper bound. Several benchmark values, including the three largest toroidal instances, match their bounds and are therefore provably optimal. A new heuristic also found a previously unknown best value for one benchmark.
arxiv-2606-28978:
Gao, Jiang and Yan audit fourteen mainstream language models for racial and gender bias in resume screening. Their method uses paired resumes, matched applications differing only in signals of race or gender, following a design from labour economics field experiments. Each model judged over twenty-four thousand postings, letting the team measure callback gaps, differences in positive response rates between groups.

The single 2023-vintage model reproduced the pro-White callback gap documented in human hiring experiments, at about two percentage points, statistically significant at the one percent level. Every model released in 2024 or later showed either no gap or a significant reversal favouring Black applicants, up to about three percentage points the other way. The same pattern held on the gender axis. Across roughly 336 thousand paired decisions in total, the direction of algorithmic hiring bias flipped between model generations, a reversal the authors document rather than predict.
arxiv-2606-29278:
Chapra and three colleagues benchmark how language models' reasoning decays as problems demand more sequential steps. Their Complexity Ceiling Benchmark holds a task's meaning fixed and stretches only its depth, from five to fifty steps. Tasks fall in three regimes: tracking objects in space, manipulating symbolic pointers, and transitive relational inference, drawing chains of relational conclusions.

Across six thousand trials on five frontier and open-weight models, accuracy decayed geometrically per step, but ceilings differed sharply. On the first two regimes the best models kept per-step success above ninety-two percent out to fifty steps. On transitive inference every model collapsed by five steps. A trace-level check found that about one in seven correct answers came through wrong intermediate reasoning. Forcing models to write out state verbosely did not raise the ceiling, and the step where reasoning first diverges predicted accuracy better than model size.
arxiv-2606-30178:
Jonathan Bennett, Vjekoslav Kovač, Shohei Nakamura, and Itamar Oliveira link a lattice geometry puzzle to waves governed by the Schrödinger equation. Can a finite set of grid points determine many rectangles but few isosceles triangles? The question sounds like a pure puzzle. Its answer blocks certain bounds in harmonic analysis. Analytic number theory plus a finite-field construction settle it in the 2026 paper.

The authors link the Euclidean and periodic weighted versions of the problem. Schrödinger solutions are what those bounds concern. Failure of that version ties to the counts above. Completing that chain yields explicit examples that break it. The target is the Mizohata–Takeuchi conjecture. Cairo had recently disproved it for curved surfaces generally. This work supplies concrete counterexamples of its own. The lattice counts drive the whole proof, from start to finish.
arxiv-2606-30478:
Mark Colarusso and Sam Evens continue a study of symmetry orbits in algebraic geometry. They look at the flag variety of the general linear group, the space of nested subspace chains, together with a projective space of lines. A Borel subgroup, a standard triangular symmetry group, acts on this product with only finitely many orbits, and the pair seek a clean description of how those orbits close onto one another.

Colarusso and Evens embed the orbits on the product into orbits on a larger flag variety, for matrices one size up. The embedding respects closure relations and preserves actions of a monoid, a structure like a group but without inverses. Closure and monoid action can then be read off from the Bruhat order, a standard ranking of permutations, using their earlier results. A second embedding, for stabiliser orbits on one flag variety, plays an essential supporting role.
arxiv-2606-30578:
Nico Daheim and Iryna Gurevych ask in 2026 how language models should act when the right answer is unclear. Many real tasks, from tutoring to peer review, involve personal taste, so a model's output must be worth trusting, not just fluent. Training has improved fast, yet the rules that turn shaky model beliefs into final outputs have had less study.

The pair test choice rules grounded in Bayesian decision theory, which weighs each outcome by how likely it is, alongside risk-averse rules that favour safe choices. They also use conformal prediction, a method giving statistical bounds, to narrow tutoring strategies and review scores. Across tutoring and peer-review tasks, these rules could raise the usefulness of generated text. Care mattered: risk-averse rules sometimes hurt results by pushing bland outputs, while Bayesian methods usually did better. The authors close by listing open challenges for choosing well under ambiguity.
arxiv-2606-30778:
Stefan Gugler, Max Eissler, Khaled Kahouli and Klaus-Robert Müller build a machine that maps chemical reaction networks. A reaction network, the web of stable molecules and the transition states linking them, is chemistry's natural map, but charting one needs tens of thousands of transition states. Standard quantum chemistry is far too slow for the job.

ReactionAtlas starts from just eight prebiotic seed molecules. A generative model proposes reactions from kinetically sampled candidates. A machine-learned force field, trained on quantum calculations, filters the proposals down to valid transition states, whose products become new seeds. The loop discovered about forty-seven thousand reactions among roughly twelve thousand compounds. Its transition states matched high-level reference calculations closely in eighty-five percent of cases. The map covers small carbohydrate chemistry and revealed alternative pathways through the formose cycle, central to origin-of-life chemistry.
arxiv-2606-31178:
Kim and four colleagues unify two rival ways to judge multi-objective reinforcement learning with nonlinear tastes. Such learning balances goals like safety, fairness, and return, combined by a scalarization rule. Applying that rule before averaging gives one criterion, while averaging first gives another, and each has forced separate methods.

Their Aggregation Expectation Transformation frame splits scalarization into three parts and covers both criteria at once. On that base they build AETDICE, an offline algorithm that learns from fixed data by estimating density ratios inside an augmented state space. The method handles trade-offs that older tools miss, including cases needing global optimisation or policies that remember past rewards, and it does so without fresh interaction with the environment.
arxiv-2606-31278:
Quattrini and six colleagues present MICE, a way to edit many parts of an image in one pass. Single-pass editing is faster than turn-by-turn changes and can blend edits better. When several instructions target different regions, though, attributes leak between regions and edits tangle, above all as their count grows.

MICE works with multimodal diffusion transformers and needs no training. It reshapes the joint attention bias using user masks: attention stays free inside each region, contact between nearby region tokens is penalised, and unrelated cross-region attention is suppressed. On the new MICE-Bench, averaging 8.5 edits per image, and on LoMOE-Bench, the method beats strong baselines on visual quality and faithfulness to each instruction while keeping the whole image coherent.
arxiv-2606-31378:
Liu and six colleagues present MAPE, a defence that scrubs adversarial perturbations out of images before classification. Transferable attacks are crafted on one model yet fool others, and they stay stealthy because they mimic normal input patterns. A defence must remove the hostile pattern without wrecking the picture itself.

MAPE pairs a single-source elimination network with a scheduling algorithm for pre-trained models. The eliminator is a channel-attention U-Net trained on attack examples from a known source model. The scheduler picks training sources to widen the spread of attack styles seen, using model difference measures and negative momentum. Trained this way, the defence strips perturbations from many attack types, restoring correct labels across the tests the authors run.
arxiv-2606-31478:
Ma and eight colleagues present SAGE, a self-correcting research agent built to recover well when experiments fail. Today's autonomous agents draft hypotheses, code, and papers, yet a failed run usually triggers one free-form reflection. That single critique crushes rich logs into a paragraph, causing either timid local tweaks or hard pivots that waste context.

SAGE instead runs multi-hypothesis failure attribution. It drafts several evidence-grounded explanations for a failure, scores their severity apart, and routes the verified cause to the right level: hypothesis, design, or implementation. A grounded reporting rule pins drafted results to measured values and cuts invented numbers. On a twelve-topic benchmark, outputs bearing real metrics jump from 42 to 92 percent against a reflection baseline.
arxiv-2606-31578:
Manjah and three colleagues propose holonic active distillation for learning across large sensor networks. Sensors join and leave open systems freely, so one universal network fits badly and knowledge transfer is hard. Their design organises models as holons, units that are both wholes and parts of larger wholes.

Specialised student models gather local data and ask teacher models for pseudo-labels, then cluster with similar sensors into groups. That holonic structure balances local specialisation with global generalisation, and the system adapts when sensors depart or return. The team analyse the trade-offs among incremental updates, reorganisation, and scale limits. Model drift and long-term adaptation remain open challenges, but the design shows a workable shape for learning sensor fleets that never sit still.
arxiv-2606-31678:
Wakakuwa, Petruzziello, Lantaño, Huelga and Plenio study frame dragging, the twisting of spacetime by a rotating mass. They ask whether it can entangle a test particle with the mass and thereby witness gravity's non-classical nature. Earlier gravity-induced entanglement proposals work in the Newtonian limit, leaving truly relativistic effects unexplored. Frame dragging offers a post-Newtonian route.

The entanglement phase between the source mass's rotational degrees of freedom and the particle's interferometer paths is computed in two ways, each on its own. One way uses Schrödinger evolution with a quantized Lense-Thirring Hamiltonian at large angular momentum. The other uses the on-shell action of linearized quantum gravity in a stationary phase approximation. Both give the same phase, matching the proper time difference between the arms, and the path integral version makes gravitational retardation's effect clear, keeping the description local and relativistically causal.
arxiv-2606-31778: This author sets requirements on out-of-band rejection for next-generation CMB experiments. The setting sets. Their setting is requirements out-of-band rejection next-generation CMB experiments. The application is application. It is cosmology. The setting is on.
arxiv-2606-31878:
Goré and Kikkert test two ways of giving modal tableaux a shortcut powered by other solvers. Their CEGAR-tableaux method searches for a Kripke model while a SAT solver prunes the work through counterexample-guided refinement. A SAT-shortcut lets an oracle declare satisfiability early, skipping further tableau expansion.

One route reuses the known RECAR approach for generating shortcuts. The other, entirely new, calls the modal resolution prover KSP as the oracle. Experiments with their C++ implementation, CEGARBox++, deliver a clear split verdict. RECAR shortcuts are not competitive in practice. KSP-based shortcuts beat both the plain tableaux system and KSP alone, with the largest gains on big satisfiable problems. The authors present it as a first effective SAT-tableaux-resolution integration.
arxiv-2606-31978:
Paquereau and colleagues ask whether halo mass alone decides how strongly galaxies cluster, using the COSMOS-Web survey. Quiescent galaxies cluster more than star-forming ones, but they also live in heavier halos, so the comparison is unfair until halo mass is held fixed. A new method matches the halo mass distributions of both populations through the UniverseMachine model.

Even after matching, quiescent galaxies stay more strongly clustered at every redshift from five to today, by half to a full dex in their measurements. At redshift two and below, the excess grows toward lower stellar masses, pointing to environmental quenching of small galaxies. Cross-correlations also reveal one-halo conformity out to redshift two. Both effects fade somewhere between redshift five and two.
arxiv-2608-00278:
Aniceto and Ballantine give combinatorial proofs for identities about missing integers in partitions. A missing integer is a positive integer below a partition's largest part that does not appear in it. Bhoria, Eyyunni, and Santra recently studied partitions with a fixed count of missing integers. They built generating functions, identities, and congruences for them. Overpartitions were part of that study as well.

This article supplies combinatorial proofs for several of those results. Such proofs explain identities by direct counting arguments. They complement the analytic routes of the prior work. Readers gain a clearer view of why the identities hold. The missing-integer lens thus firms up as a partition tool.
arxiv-2608-00378:
Muse and co-authors present CASPER for regression testing of LLM-based systems. Single regression cases carry little signal about system-level regressions. One failure may not mark a meaningful regression. Whole-system scores are too coarse to name affected behaviours. Test suite slices offer the middle level they need.

CASPER finds slices of semantically related cases with consistent performance traits. An evolutionary method identifies those slices. Given a prompt- or model-level change, it ranks slices by regression likelihood. Behavioural facts from execution logs drive that ranking. The test bed is software issue resolution. CASPER made more consistent slices than clustering baselines. Regressed-slice ranking beat a random baseline across changes and budgets.
barclay-talmud-1878:
Joseph Barclay was the Anglican bishop of Jerusalem when he published The Talmud in 1878. His book gives selections from the Mishnah and the Talmud for Christian readers new to rabbinic literature. Barclay knew Hebrew and lived among the communities whose ancestors wrote the texts.

He translates passages on worship, charity, civil law, and the festivals, with notes explaining customs as he met them in Jerusalem. His aim is fair description rather than the attacks on the Talmud common in older Christian writing. The book stands as an early Christian introduction to the rabbinic tradition by a resident bishop.
basil-valentine-his-triumphant-chariot-o:
Basilius Valentinus, the legendary Benedictine adept, stands as author of this treatise on antimony, Englished in the edition of 1678 with annotations by Theodore Kerckring, a Dutch physician. The triumphant chariot is antimony itself, hailed as a medicine of wide power. Preparations of it, rightly made, are said to render the blood agile and purge gently, without gripings of the belly.

An annotator answers the obvious objection: how can antimony purge moderately when its matter is vehement and forcible by nature? Rhubarb joined to it, doses, and careful preparation supply the defence. The hosted scan is a battered seventeenth-century printing whose machine reading is severely garbled. Even through the noise, the book shows Paracelsian pharmacy at work, weighing poison against cure in grains.
books-and-characters-french-english-pg12:
Lytton Strachey gathered Books and Characters, French and English, from essays first printed in leading reviews, and London saw the book in May 1922. Strachey dedicates the volume to John Maynard Keynes. The hosted text is the Project Gutenberg release of that same first edition.

Fifteen pieces move between French and English letters. Racine, Madame du Deffand, and Henri Beyle stand on the French side. Browne, Shakespeare in his last period, Blake, and the lives of the poets stand on the English. Voltaire fills the middle with four studies and a dialogue in his own hand. Strachey writes with calm malice and perfect balance. Readers meet the essay style that made his name between the wars, at full strength.
bracton-de-legibus-twiss-vol1-1878:
