Judah ben Simon Tiktin Ashkenazi was a Polish commentator on the Shulhan Aruk. He served as dayyan, assistant rabbi, at Tikotzin in Poland in the first half of the eighteenth century. His work, whose title means Explaining Well, comments briefly on the first three parts of the Shulhan Aruk.

A matching commentary on the fourth part, the Hoshen Mishpat, was written by Moses Frankfurter, dayyan of Amsterdam. Ashkenazi's work was appended to the Shulhan Aruk in the Amsterdam editions of 1753 and 1760 and went through many editions after that. The entry rests on Benjacob, Furst, and Steinschneider. It gives his town, his office, and his book's printing history, and no dates for the man himself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-athach-2078: Athach was a town in Judah. David sent part of the spoil taken from the Amalekites to its people, as I Samuel xxx. 30 reports. The entry says the town has not been firmly placed on the map. Several scholars take Athach to be the same town as Ether, named in Joshua xv. 42. If that is right, no one can tell which spelling is the true one. The Greek copies of both passages give still more spellings, which deepens the doubt.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baba-mezi-a-the:
Baba Meẓi'a, the Middle Gate, is the second of three Talmudic treatises on damages and property. It treats a man's duty toward his fellow's property that has come into his hands by lawful means. For the time, he holds it as a trustee. The treatise rests on a passage in Exodus that names four kinds of trustee.

The four are the unpaid keeper, the paid keeper, the borrower, and the hirer. The unpaid keeper is treated first, at the greatest length. A finder of lost property counts as such a keeper until the owner is found. The entry spells out the finder's duties: what counts as finding, how to guard against false claims, and when the duty binds. The borrower stands under the hardest rule. He pays for nearly every loss, even by accident, unless the lender was at work beside him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bak-2378:
Bak is the name of a family of Hebrew printers in Italy and Prague who worked at their craft for two centuries. The entry doubts the claim that the name shortens "Bene Ḳedoshim" (Children of the Holy). It then walks through eleven men of the family in numbered order, from Gerson Bak, the founder, who flourished in the first quarter of the sixteenth century in Italy.

Jacob ben Gerson Bak printed a Midrash at Verona in 1595 and worked at Prague after 1605. His sons Joseph and Judah ran the press as "The late Jacob Bak's Sons" from 1620 to 1660. Later men carried the firm on under names such as Judah Bak's Sons and Judah Bak's Grandsons. The last printer named worked from 1757 to 1789, and the firm still stood in 1784.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-jacob-ko: Jacob Baruch [Kohen-Ẓedeḳ] ben Moses Ḥayyim was an editor at Leghorn in the latter part of the eighteenth century. He compiled "Shibḥe Yerushalayim" (Praises of Jerusalem), a volume on Jerusalem and the Jewish centers in Palestine, above all the graves of old Jewish worthies. Its author drew largely on the "Zikkaron Birushalayim" of 1743. Attached is a journey account from Venice to Palestine, begun on 17th Elul, 1521. The work first appeared at Leghorn in 1785 and was often reprinted.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baynus-bayne-ru: Rudolphus Baynus was a Christian Hebraist of Cambridge who taught Hebrew in Paris near the middle of the sixteenth century. His known work is a Latin summary of the first part of Kimhi's Hebrew grammar. It treats letters, reading, nouns, regular and irregular verbs, and prefixes and suffixes in methodical order. The book came out at Paris in 1554, with a Hebrew title beside the Latin one. No life dates are given.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-behrends-leffma:
Leffmann Behrends, also called Liepmann Cohen, was a money agent to the dukes and princes of Hanover. Born about 1630, he died at Hanover on Jan. 1, 1714. Mannasseh ben Israel praised his high standing in a famed book of hope for Israel.

Behrends used his place to help fellow Jews and to guard Hanover's cemetery and rights. He set up a study house in his own home and aided scholars. The great library of his son-in-law, Rabbi David Oppenheimer, was moved to Hanover under his care. A new synagogue rose there in 1703. Two of his sons later faced a charge of false bankruptcy and were forced to leave Hanover in time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ben-kalba-sabbu:
Ben Kalba Sabbua was a rich and prominent man of Jerusalem who flourished about the year 70. Talmudic tradition says his name came from his open house. Any guest who arrived hungry as a dog, Kalba in the wordplay, left satisfied, or Sabbua.

He ranks with two other rich men whose stores could have fed the besieged city for ten years. The entry says Zealots burned those stores, causing famine. A later Talmudic tale makes Akiba his son-in-law, but the entry doubts that account and notes a respected grave north of Jerusalem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-ben-mo: Benjamin ben Moses, an Italian scholar, lived at Rome at the start of the fifteenth century. He took an active part in running the Jewish community of Rome. In 1426 he went as a delegate to a meeting of the Jewish communities of Italy at Forli. He also wrote a work of argument against Christianity, built on biblical and logical grounds. That work still survives in manuscript form, and the entry gives the shelf marks for the copies it names.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berkowicz-josef: Josef Berkowicz was an officer in the Polish army and a son of Colonel Berek. He fought in the battle of Kock in 1809, where his father was killed. After leaving the service in 1815 he became a government forester, rising to chief forester of a district by 1826. In the Polish rising of 1830 he served as a squadron chief. He ended his days in England, where his novel of a Polish lancer in Napoleon's suite came out in 1846, after his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-besalu-latin-bi: Besalu, called Bisuldum in Latin, is a city in Catalonia, Spain. Its small Jewish community shared the privileges of nearby Gerona. The two towns were also taxed together. The entry notes that tax documents survive. They rest in the archives of Aragon at Barcelona. Besalu was the birthplace of the Caslar family. Abraham b. David Caslar came from that family. So did Joseph ibn Zabara and others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bevis-marks-syn:
Bevis Marks Synagogue is London's oldest Jewish house of worship. Sephardic Jews established it in 1698. Rabbi David Nieto then led the congregation. Growth soon forced a move from Cree Church lane. A building contract was signed in February 1699. The cost was £2,750. The land lay at Plough Yard in Bevis Marks.

The synagogue was dedicated in 1702. Queen Anne gave a beam from a royal ship. For over a century it centered Anglo-Jewish life. Distant communities sent their troubles there. A demolition plan arose in 1886. A defense league stopped it. The bicentenary was celebrated in 1901.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bidkar-3278: Bidkar was a captain who served under Jehu. The whole entry is one sentence long. It rests on a single verse of Second Kings. Jehu ordered Bidkar to throw a body down. The body was King Jehoram's. It was cast into the field of Naboth. The entry gives no other facts about him. No family, place, or later fate is recorded.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-blitz-jekuthiel: Jekuthiel ben Isaac Blitz was a press corrector at Amsterdam. He worked in Uri Phoebus's Hebrew printing-office. He lived in the late seventeenth century. In 1679 he published a Bible translation. It rendered the whole Old Testament into Judæo-German. It was the first of its kind. The book carries three introductions. One is his own in Hebrew, one in German. He also translated Gersonides' work on Joshua, Judges, and Samuel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bokhara-3478:
Bokhara, capital of the khanate of the same name in Central Asia, is treated as an old seat of Islam. Jews likely lived there from early Muslim rule. Their tongue points to Persian origin.

Local Jews held themselves heirs of the Ten Tribes. They linked the name Bokhara with the Biblical Habor. The entry follows them under Mongol rule and in later verse. A Hebrew-Persian word book of 1338 shows learning near the Oxus. Under Russia, the entry says, Jews gained full civic standing and backed Russian rule. A later poet there, Yusuf Yehudi, won notice beyond Jewish circles. His verse belongs to a Jewish-Persian school that the entry traces in detail.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bornstein-arthu: Arthur Bornstein was a German author born at Breslau on March 23, 1867. He studied at Breslau, Berlin, and Bern. He passed the state examination in Berlin in 1888. He took up dental surgery as his trade. At the same time he gave himself to literature. His short stories came out as Klippen in 1894. A drama, Der Theaterarzt, followed in 1895. He also wrote humorous sketches, learned articles, and poems for the press.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-breithaupt-john: John Frederick Breithaupt was a Christian Hebraist and rabbinical scholar of the early eighteenth century. He served as aulic councilor to the emperor and to the duke of Gotha. In 1707 he issued an edition of Yosippon with a Latin version at Gotha. Its subject index still gives it reference value, the entry says. His larger feat was a Latin version of Rashi on the whole Bible. That work filled three thick volumes, printed from 1710 to 1713.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-brutzkus-judah-: Judah Loeb Brutzkus, son of David, was a Russian writer born in 1870 at Polangen, in the government of Courland. He studied at the gymnasium and the University of Moscow. His family was expelled from that city in 1892. He took his diploma as a physician in 1894. Brutzkus helped with a Russo-Jewish bibliographical work on literature about the Jews. From 1895 he wrote for the periodical Voskhod. In 1899 he became its assistant editor. The entry is brief, giving his training and posts without discussing any single work by him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cantarini-hayyi: Hayyim Moses Angelo Cantarini was an Italian physician, rabbi, poet, and writer at Padua. He lived in the later seventeenth century and the first half of the eighteenth. He also taught in the yeshivah there. In Italian he published a practical surgery book at Padua in 1677. His Hebrew works stayed in manuscript at his death. They included glosses on later legal writers and responsa. One manuscript described a persecution of the Jews at Padua. He also traded letters with the Christian scholar Unger on Italian Jewish history.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chariot-4078:
Chariot and wagon are covered by two chief Hebrew words. One word names the wagon used for heavy loads and general work. The other names the chariot of war or of state, with two further words derived from it. Wagons for burdens or persons appear among many ancient peoples. They replaced the sledge at an early time.

Wheels first were solid disks. A finer type then grew up, with hub, spokes, and rim. Assyrian pictures show wheels of eight spokes, and Egyptian wagons four or six. The pole carried a yoke for two animals only. Extra animals were hitched at the side. Oxen were the chief draft animals for Israelites at first. Horses came into general use only in Solomon's time. Poor roads in Palestine made wagon travel hard, so people rode asses for long journeys.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chumaceiro-aron:
Aron Mendes Chumaceiro, hakam of Curacao in the Dutch West Indies, was born at Amsterdam on Jan. 28, 1810, and died there on Sept. 18, 1882. Trained at the bet ha-midrash Ets Haim, he won the royal gold medal in 1848 for the best sermon in Dutch. He then fought, and beat, resistance to preaching in Dutch instead of Ladino.

In 1852 he edited the first Dutch Jewish weekly and took charge of Ets Haim. Three years later King William III named him chief rabbi of Curacao, a post he took after clashes with the ultra-Orthodox party. The entry goes on to list his four sons and their careers, then his sermons and books, including a Spanish catechism.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-henry-ema:
Henry Emanuel Cohen, judge of the supreme court of New South Wales, was born at Port Macquarie in December, 1840. He clerked in 1856, tried business at Bathurst, then went to London in 1868 to study law. Called to the bar in 1871, he went home and built a strong practice, serving at times as crown prosecutor.

Voters sent him to Parliament for West Maitland in 1874 and again in 1877. He held office as colonial treasurer, then as minister of justice. Out of politics after 1885, he practiced law until his court appointment in 1896. The entry calls him the first Jew in New South Wales to hold that seat in any lasting way, and the only Jewish judge of his rank across the British dominions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-compiegne-de-we: Ludwig Compiegne de Weil, a convert to Christianity, lived at Paris and later at Metz. He worked in the later seventeenth century. He descended from Rabbi Jacob Weil of Nuremberg. Baptized while still a youth, he studied theology at the Sorbonne. His labor centered on one book. He rendered parts of Maimonides' Yad ha-Hazakah into Latin. The Temple service volume came out at Paris in 1678. He also translated Abraham Yagel's catechism into Latin, at London in 1679.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-corriere-israel: Corriere Israelitico was an Italian monthly magazine devoted to Jewish history and literature. Abrama Vito Morpurgo founded it at Triest in 1863 and edited it for six years. After his death his son-in-law, A. di S. Curiel, took over. Early issues mixed reports of Jewish events with scholarly articles. S. D. Luzzatto and Lelio della Torre wrote for it. Poems, stories, and translations also appeared. In later years the magazine turned fully to cabalistic theories current in Italy. Elia Benamozegh and his pupils became its chief contributors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crown-4778:
Crown renders five distinct Hebrew words in the Bible, and the entry sorts them. One word names the golden molding on the Ark and the altar of incense. A second carries the sense of consecration. It marks the circlet of a Hebrew king or of the high priest. A third word is the general term, used for wreaths at banquets and prizes at games. A Persian loan-word serves in Esther for the crown royal.

The article then follows the word into the New Testament and rabbinic writing. Two Greek words are both rendered crown there. Paul dwells on the incorruptible crown won in a race. James promises a crown of life to those who love God. Sayings about crowns of glory that do not fade close the survey of verses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-david-samuel-be: Samuel ben Judah Löb David was a Polish rabbi who died at Dzialshitz, Poland, in 1751. He first followed his father as rabbi of Shidlow. About 1731 he was called to Cracow to fill the post left empty by his father's death. Opponents resisted him there, and while he was away another rabbi was installed. David returned and resumed the office anyway, but he finally retired to Dzialshitz. His signature appears on the ban published against Moses Ḥayyim Luzzatto.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-demetrius-5078: Demetrius was the son-in-law of King Agrippa I of Judea. Mariamne, Agrippa's daughter, left her first husband and married Demetrius, who stood among the foremost Jews of Alexandria by birth and wealth. He held the office of alabarch, the head of the Jewish community there, about the year 49. The couple had a son, Agrippinus. The entry warns against one common guess: Demetrius was probably not a son of Alexander, nor brother of the apostate Tiberius Alexander. It suggests he belonged to the priestly family of Onias.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dickens-charles:
Charles Dickens, the English novelist, was born on February 7, 1812, at Portsea and died on June 9, 1870, at Gadshill. This entry treats him only for his place in Jewish interest, through two novels. "Oliver Twist," printed from 1837 to 1839, gave the world Fagin. "Our Mutual Friend," from 1864 to 1865, gave the world Riah.

Fagin, a thief and fence, became the accepted picture of the Jew, though Dickens took the name from a Christian friend and the character from a Christian fence. The entry argues that Dickens came to see the harm. Riah, his next Jewish character, stands at the other extreme, almost impossibly good. Both portraits, it concludes, show how little Dickens knew real Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-donmeh-5278:
The Dönmeh were a sect of hidden Jews, followers of Shabbethai Zebi, living mostly at Salonica. Their Turkish name means apostates. They called themselves Ma'aminim, Believers, among other names. Outwardly they lived as Muslims, as Shabbethai had done. In secret they kept certain Jewish rites.

Their prayers, part Hebrew and part Ladino, were read in hidden meeting rooms called kals. Their houses stood linked together, lit by green-shaded lamps. Men kept two names, one secret and one for trade. They visited mosques and fasted in Ramadhan, yet did not marry Turks. The entry describes their dress, trades, and the sixteen or eighteen rules that governed them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eichthal-gustav:
Gustave d'Eichthal was a French publicist and Hellenist. He was born at Nancy on March 22, 1804. He died at Paris on April 9, 1882. At thirteen he turned Roman Catholic. Leaving school in 1822, he became Auguste Comte's disciple. He gave part of his fortune to Saint-Simon's cause.

D'Eichthal traveled to Greece in 1832 and printed his reflections in 1836. He then pushed Greek as a universal language. His books treat the Mediterranean peoples, Buddhism's supposed American roots, and the first chapter of Genesis. In 1881 he helped found a society for Greek studies. His son issued his work on the Greek tongue after his death, in 1887.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliakim-5578: Eliakim was a Palestinian scholar of the third century. No rulings on law carry his name. In it he reads a verse from the first psalm. God hides the path of the wicked, he taught, to guard the righteous. The entry thinks he is the man called Jakim in other sources. The first part of the name was dropped to save repeating the name of God. One more teaching is given. To covet a neighbor's wife, Eliakim held, breaks all ten commandments at once.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elimelech-my-go: Elimelech was a man of the tribe of Judah. He lived at Bethlehem in the days of the Judges. A famine drove him out of his home town. He took his family to live in the land of Moab. There he died far from his own soil. One of his sons wed Ruth in that land. He was kin to Boaz through the Hezron line. A rabbinic view makes him a chief of Israel. In that view his early death paid for leaving the Holy Land.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-enoch-s-5778: S. Enoch was a German rabbi and school founder. He was born in Hamburg on Oct. 8, 1814. He died in Fulda on Dec. 31, 1876. He heard Talmud talks from Hakam Isaac Bernays in youth. He took his doctor's degree at Erlangen in time. At Altona he set up a Jewish secondary school. He ran that school till 1855, when Fulda called him as rabbi. For years he edited an Orthodox weekly paper. Its name was the Faithful Watchman of Zion. He also helped edit a Berlin Jewish press paper.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-estrumba-estrun:
Estrumba, also spelled Estrunza, Strumza, or Estrosa, was an Eastern Jewish family named for Strumnitza in Macedonia. The entry says the family produced several rabbinic authors. It gives fuller space to two of them, Daniel Estrumsa and Hayyim Abraham Estrumsa, father of a line of Salonica rabbis.

Daniel died at Salonica, perhaps, in 1654, after heading the Portuguese school there. His responsa, Magen Gibborim, were printed by his grandson in 1753. David Conforte studied under him. Hayyim Abraham, called Rab ha-Zaken, was chief rabbi of Serres and died about 1824. His two books of responsa and casuistic writing appeared at Salonica in 1820 and 1826.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-faenza-5978: Faenza was a city in the province of Ravenna, and family seat of the Finzi by family tradition. Mazliah Finzi lived there as early as 1450. The entry names the doctor Lazarus Hebraeus, famed in the fifteenth century for wealth, learning, and free care of the poor. The liturgical poet Raphael ben Isaac da Faenza also lived there. Some of his poems stand in the Roman prayer book. Raphael sold a prayer book to Uzziel da Camerino at Florence in 1458. Nothing later is reported.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-flax-hebr-pisht:
Flax, in Hebrew pishtah, was grown in Palestine before the Hebrew conquest. The entry describes how it was made ready for cloth. Stalks were pulled and spread on flat roofs to dry in the sun. They were then peeled, and the fibers were split and sorted. Last, the fibers were combed and made ready for weaving. Each of these steps is hinted at in the Bible, the entry says.

One fine kind of linen thread served for priestly dress and rich clothing. Angels too are described as clothed in linen. Coarser linen served for cords and lamp wicks. Linen for dress could not lawfully be mixed with wool. The flax trade stood high among the Hebrews. Proverbs praises the good woman who seeks wool and flax and works with willing hands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frank-jacob-and:
The Frankists were a semi-Christian body that arose among the Jews of Poland about the middle of the eighteenth century. Two causes lay behind it. One was the Messianic movement that followed Shabbethai Ẓebi, the false Messiah from Smyrna. The other was the social and economic breakdown of Polish Jewry. Secret Shabbethaian circles formed in Podolia and Galicia. Their members cast off strict dogma and many religious laws.

Jacob Frank came out of those circles as the sect's founder. He posed as a direct successor of Shabbethai Ẓebi. He claimed revelations from Heaven calling him and his followers to Christianity. In 1759 the Frankists debated the rabbis at Lemberg and lost ground. Frank then urged his followers to be baptized, and the rite was held. Frank's own saying sums up his aim. He came, he said, to free the world from the laws that had existed until then.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedlander-max:
Max Friedländer was a journalist born on June 18, 1829, at Pless in Prussian Silesia. He died on April 20, 1872, at Nice. After law study at Berlin, Breslau, and Heidelberg, he became an officer of the Breslau city court. In that post he printed a book on the rights of authors in 1857. He began in the press in 1856, writing for a Vienna paper.

He soon moved to Vienna and joined its staff. His pieces on trade and money caught the eye of leading statesmen and bankers. After the Italian war he fought a minister's policy in print and pled for a free frame of government. In September 1864 he founded a great Vienna daily. He stayed its chief editor until his death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-galipapa-hayyim:
Hayyim Galipapa, a Spanish rabbi born at Monzon about 1310, died about 1380. He was a son of Abraham Galipapa. He served as rabbi at Huesca and later at Pamplona, where he ran a Talmud school. Galipapa leaned to the liberal school. He set aside strict rulings and followed laxer views even in old age.

He let hair be combed on the Sabbath. He let children take cheese from Christians. He also changed some rites at Pamplona. Those steps drew a complaint to Isaac ben Sheshet, who rebuked him in a mild tone. Galipapa wrote a tract on the 1348 killings of Jews in Catalonia. He also glossed a tractate on idolatry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-generation-6578: Generation renders two Hebrew words, dor and toledot. Dor first means a period of time. By a second sense it means the people who live in that span. Proverbs speaks of a generation that curses its father, treating the class as one unit. Toledot stresses birth and descent. In Genesis x it means family lines in order. In Genesis v it can mean a history told as a birth list. The word sits mostly in the Priestly Code.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gimel-6678: Gimel is the third letter of the Hebrew alphabet. Its name may come from its old shape, said to look like the neck of a camel. In speech it matches the Greek gamma or the English g in go. Grammarians class it among the four palatals. It swaps at times with the harder letters bet and kaf. As a numeral it stands for 3.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-golgotha-litera:
Golgotha, literally "the skull," is the place named in the New Testament for Jesus' execution. The name is Aramaic and matches a Hebrew word for skull. The site lay outside the city wall. It stood near a tomb, a gate, and a road.

Two spots fit that account, the entry says. One is the Church of the Holy Sepulcher site, held by tradition. A temple of Venus once stood there. The other is a skull-shaped rock above Jeremiah's grotto. Jewish tradition ties that rock to a place of stoning. The name never occurs in Talmudic writings.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-grenoble-6878:
Grenoble, capital of the Isère department in France, had Jews from the late thirteenth century. Jacob ben Solomon died there as a martyr in 1296. When France expelled its Jews in 1306, some fled to Grenoble. The dauphin Humbert I welcomed them and let them open banks. Two bankers won wide privileges for a yearly tax.

Trouble came in waves. In 1388 the province's Jews faced charges and a fine of 10,000 francs. Rules of 1413 set Jews apart in worship, ovens, wells, and markets. Men had to wear a cloth badge on the chest. Under Charles VII a charge of aiding his enemies cost them 1,500 gold crowns. The Jews then left Grenoble for good. Only a few families lived there in 1903.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-habaziniah-6978: Habaziniah receives only two lines in this entry. He was head of a family of Rechabites. His grandson Jaazaniah was a chief of the Rechabites in the time of Jeremiah. The entry supports that much with Jeremiah xxxv. 3 and gives nothing else: no dates, no place, and no deeds are recorded for Habaziniah himself. Readers get a name, a family role, and one named descendant, and no more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halakot-7078: Halakot is the older name for the body of religious law that forms one of the three main divisions of Jewish oral tradition. In time the singular form halakah came into general use even for a whole set, just as haggadah replaced haggadot. R. Judah ha-Nasi codified the Halakot, and they formed the legal body of his Mishnah. After that, the term Mishnah pushed out Halakot in most places. In Palestine the old usage held on, and the Mishnah itself was known there as Halakot.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hananeel-ben-hu:
Hananeel b. Ḥushiel, born at Kairwan about 990, was a rabbi of Kairwan and a commentator on Bible and Talmud who died in 1050. His father was his only master, though he learned much by letter from Hai Gaon. After his father's death he and Nissim b. Jacob led the Kairwan school together. He was rich in business too, leaving ten thousand gold pieces to his nine daughters.

He ranks among the first rabbis after the geonic schools fell, and he spread Talmud study far. His Talmud commentary fixed the true text from the oldest copies and fed the work of Isaac Fasi and the 'Aruk. He wrote on the Pentateuch against the Karaites, kept to plain reading without mysticism, and wrote all in good Hebrew. A prayer-book and responsa also carry his name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hart-aaron-know: Aaron Hart, also known as Uri Phoebus, was the first chief rabbi of the Ashkenazic Jews in England. Born at Breslau in 1670, he studied in Poland and married into a learned family. His brother Moses founded London's Great Synagogue. Aaron became rabbi of the first Ashkenazic synagogue in London, opened in 1692. In 1707 he published "Urim we-Tummim." The entry notes that this small book was the first Hebrew book printed in London. He died in 1756.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hawkers-and-ped:
Hawkers and pedlers traces traveling traders from Bible times through rabbinic law. In early Palestine, trade sat mostly with foreigners, often Canaanites. Farmers viewed the wandering seller with doubt. Hosea speaks of the trafficker with false balances. The Hebrew word for slanderer grew from the word for a traveling merchant.

The long article follows Jewish pedlers after the dispersion. Their boxes held many goods, with spices a staple item. Ezra is said to have protected their right to sell in towns, so that cosmetics could reach Jewish women. Local merchants could not shut them out. The piece also notes the talkative image that clung to the trade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-jacob-be: Hayyim Jacob ben Judah Lob Slutzki was a Russian rabbinic scholar of the early nineteenth century. His printed work takes up the Midrash Konen, a text on creation. He gave it two commentaries, one explaining the sense and one adding glosses. That book came out at Wilna in 1836. Four further works of his stayed in manuscript. They include commentaries on other Midrashim and a word list for hard terms in Talmud and Midrash. The entry lists them but gives no life dates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hazzanut-lit-th:
Hazzanut names the traditional chanting of the synagogue service. At first, in Saadia's prayer book, the term covered the hymns a hazzan recited. As that official came to chant the whole service, the word shifted to the manner of chanting itself. Fine singing as a force on feeling dates, the entry says, from later Talmudic times.

This chant is not a set of fixed tunes. It is a free unfolding, on old lines, of themes tied to each occasion. One service differs from another chiefly in tone. Much is left to the moment and to the singer's voice and sense of the room. Under it all, devotion and reverence should show.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hegesippus-7478:
Hegesippus names two figures tied to early Christian and Jewish history. The first was one of the earliest writers of the Christian Church. He lived at Rome from about 150 and died about 189. By birth he was likely a Jew. His five-book work defended Christian teaching and listed bishop lines.

Only scraps of that work survive, quoted by Eusebius and Photius. He names seven Jewish sects, among them Essenes, Sadducees, and Pharisees. The second Hegesippus is a supposed author. The name is a garbled form of Josephus, stuck to a free Latin version of the Jewish War. That version was used by the writer of the Hebrew Yosippon.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hep-hep-7578:
Hep! Hep! was a cry used during attacks on Jews, the entry explains. It is linked in some accounts to the Crusaders. Clearer use came in the riots of 1819 at Frankfort-on-the-Main and along the Rhine. Students at Würzburg used it against a professor who had written for the Jews.

The entry weighs several claims about the word's origin. One links it to a Latin phrase about Jerusalem lost. Others derive it from a word for Hebrews or from a Franconian animal call. The phrase later stood for any outbreak against Jews. George Eliot used it in an essay title. Jewish replies in 1819 are also noted.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hezron-7678:
Hezron is treated under three headings in this entry. The first Hezron was a son of Reuben. He founded the family of the Hezronites. The second was a son of Pharez and grandson of Judah.

That second Hezron was a direct ancestor of David. His sons included Jerahmeel, Ram, and Caleb. Later marriages in his line brought Segub and, after his death, Ashur. The third Hezron was a place marking Judah's southern limit, between Kadesh-barnea and Adar. A parallel list seems to join it with Addar as one place, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hiyya-bar-abba-:
Ḥiyya bar Abba was a Palestinian amora of priestly descent, active at the end of the third century. Babylonian by birth, he moved to Palestine young. He studied under Ḥanina and Joshua, son of Levi, and grew close to Simeon, son of Laḳish. He was a pupil of Johanan.

After Johanan died, Ḥiyya with Ammi and Assi led on law in Palestine. His care in noting his masters' exact words made his versions favored in disputes. Poor, he lectured town to town for a living. Judah II sent him to raise funds and to renew Law study in towns. His praise, in one letter, was that he would say he did not know when he did not.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-horowitz-leopol:
Leopold Horowitz was a Hungarian painter born in 1837 at Rozgony, near Kaschau. He trained at home, then studied at the Vienna Academy for seven years and won first prize at graduation. From 1860 he traveled to Berlin, Dresden, and Munich. He then lived eight years in Paris.

In Paris, Horowitz built a name for portraits and scenes of child life. In 1868 he went to Warsaw to study the life of Polish Jews. Paintings of prayer in a Polish synagogue and of a Polish tutor came from that turn. He painted many nobles and writers. In 1891 he won a gold medal at the Berlin International Exhibition.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-jacob:
Isaac ben Jacob the Levite was a rabbi and cantor at Venice, born in 1621. He was the son of a cabalist and a grandson of Judah de Modena. At only fourteen he set de Modena's "Bet Yehudah" in type. The entry says he had persistent personal enemies in Venice, and that he described their persecutions in an autobiography known in manuscript to Ghirondi.

Among his writings were a short summary of Moses Cordovero's "Pardes Rimmonim" and several poems, some printed in 1661. His "Ma'ase Hakamim," printed at Venice in 1647, retold events from the lives of the Talmud's teachers. The stories came from Jacob ibn Habib and from the "Bet Yehudah," each closed with a moral sentence, and Isaac was both the book's author and its printer. He also added notes to works by other authors.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-jacob-82:
Jacob Israel was a Russian rabbi and author of the seventeenth century. He is said to have been born in Temesvar and to have served as rabbi in Belzyce and Lublin. Fürst adds Slutsk as well. He was a contemporary of Samuel Keidanover. The entry says he perished in the Chmielnicki persecutions. A Bodleian manuscript holds his homilies on the Pentateuch, called "Tif'eret Yisrael."

His larger work was the "Yalkut Hadash," first printed at Lublin in 1648. It came out without his name on it. The book gathers midrashim in alphabetical order, drawn from early midrashic works and from cabalistic books such as the Zohar. Later editions appeared at Prague, Amsterdam, and Wilmersdorf, and the work is sometimes called "Yalkut Yisraeli" after its maker.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacobsohn-paul-:
Paul Jacobsohn, a German physician and hygienist, was born in Berlin on Sept. 30, 1868. He took his medical degree in 1891 after study at Berlin and Freiburg. From 1892 to 1894 he worked as assistant physician at the Jewish hospital in Berlin, then at a dispensary until 1897.

His special work was better nursing care and nurse training. In 1899 he founded a society of German nurses, and he coedited a nursing journal he had founded. He also invented a stretcher for moving patients and a scale for weighing, and co-wrote a handbook on care of the sick.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jekuthiel-ben-l:
Jekuthiel ben Löb Gordon was a Russian physician and cabalist born at the start of the eighteenth century. Even young, he had a name as a strong Talmud student. At Padua, where he went to study medicine, he met Moses Hayyim Luzzatto and took up Cabala under his lead. His warm letters home praising Luzzatto as a seer helped bring on Luzzatto's persecution by strict rabbis.

After Luzzatto was forced out of Padua, Gordon stayed two more years and kept up secret Cabala study with friends. Back in Lithuania he won many converts to the Cabala. From 1742 his path is unknown. He left many works in manuscript, most of them cabalistic.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jhiratkar-solom: Solomon Ballajce Jhiratkar was a Beni-Israel soldier. He joined the Fourteenth Regiment of Bombay Native Light Infantry in 1818. He rose by steps: jemidar in 1839, subahdar in 1843, and subahdar-major in 1856. He also served five years as a native adjutant and in time became sirdar bahadur. His field service named in the entry covers the siege of Mahadewghur in 1832, work at Kolhapur in 1836, and action against the Waghers in 1859-60. He received both stars of the Order of British India.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jones-alfred-t-:
Alfred T. Jones was an American editor and community worker born in Boston on July 4, 1822. He moved to Philadelphia in 1842 and worked first in wholesale clothing and then in printing. In 1875 he started the Jewish Record, a newspaper that lasted until 1886. He died at Philadelphia on Oct. 3, 1888.

His entry is a roll of offices held for Jewish causes in that city. He served as secretary of the first Jewish Publication Society, head of the Jewish Hospital body, and first head of a society aiding Jewish newcomers. He led societies for the poor, the sick, and fuel aid, sat on charity boards, and held top posts in his congregation and in a Masonic lodge for over thirty years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-b-petros: Joseph b. Petros was a Palestinian amora of the first generation, in the third century. He was the father of the first wife of Joshua b. Levi. He stood on friendly terms with Bar Kappara, and the two debated how to explain a certain Bible verse. The entry also notes a dispute between him and Zabdai b. Levi on a point of Bible reading. No rulings, writings, or life events beyond these exchanges are recorded in this short notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-de-blanis: Judah de Blanis was an Italian doctor who lived at Perugia in the middle of the sixteenth century. David de Pomis counts him among the leading doctors of Italy. He was a keen student of the Cabala and spent much time with Emanuel of Benevento, editor of the Tikkune Zohar. In 1553 he had a copy made for himself of the cabalistic book Sefer ha-Kaneh. He may be the same man as a Judah ben Solomon of Pesaro whose rulings Lampronti later cites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-julian-the-apos:
Julian the Apostate, Flavius Claudius Julianus, was a Roman emperor born on November 17, 331. He reigned from November 361 to June 363. Where Constantine's turn to Christianity had brought fresh pressure on the Jews, Julian at once granted freedom and equal rights to all faiths. A fierce pagan, he fought Christianity hard but showed Jews steady regard.

His writings show wide knowledge of Jewish practice, from the Sabbath to the food laws. In his polemic he ranks Judaism below Greek religion but far above Christianity. The entry gives his famed letter promising to rebuild the Temple at Jerusalem at his own cost. Julian died on campaign against Persia, and the hope died with him.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kiev-6078:
Kiev, called "the mother of Russian cities," stands on the right bank of the Dnieper. In 1902 it held 249,830 people, about 20,000 of them Jews. The entry traces Jewish settlement to the Chazar period, not later than the eighth century. Jews likely came with the Chazars from Byzantium, the Crimea, Persia, and the Caucasus. A large community existed under Grand Duke Vladimir. Jews there lived undisturbed under several early rulers.

Chmielnicki's uprising destroyed the community in the seventeenth century. Jews were readmitted in 1794, on condition of paying double taxes. Nicholas I expelled them again, by ukase in 1827 and finally in 1835. Readmission under Alexander II brought renewed growth and a leading role in trade. The riots of May 8, 1881 destroyed property worth about 2,000,000 rubles. Thousands were left homeless, and many Jews emigrated.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-klein-julius-le:
Julius Leopold Klein was a Hungarian poet and writer. He was born at Miskolcz in 1810. He died at Berlin on Aug. 2, 1876. The entry notes that he was a convert to Christianity. He studied at Budapest, Vienna, and Berlin. After travel in Italy and Greece he settled in Berlin. He graduated there as a doctor of medicine. He practised only briefly, then gave himself wholly to literary work.

His dramas had little success on the stage. His influence as a critic was more pronounced. His greatest work was a history of the drama in thirteen volumes. It appeared at Leipsic from 1865 to 1876 and was never finished. His collected dramatic works filled seven volumes. The entry lists his tragedies and comedies by name and date.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kos-cos-or-coos:
Kos, an island in the Sporades group in the Aegean Sea near the Carian coast, was also called Meropis and Nymphæa. Its harbor and spot on Aegean trade routes gave it weight. The entry places Jews on the island early. Under Alexander and the Ptolemies, from 336 B.C., the town grew into a large Jewish center.

Banking, banishment, and return shape the later story. Jewish bankers are thought to have held temple funds and the 800 talents tied to Queen Cleopatra. The Knights of Rhodes banished the Jews in 1502. A synagogue built in 1747 still anchors the account, while family counts fell from 40 in 1850 to only 10 in 1901. A false ritual murder charge in 1850 also gets a full telling.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lawrence-john-z: John Zachariah Lawrence, an English surgeon born in 1828, died in London on July 18, 1870. He studied at University College, London, taking his degree in 1857. Fellowship of the Royal College of Surgeons came in 1855. He served at the hospital for epilepsy and paralysis, then as eye surgeon at St. Bartholomew's. He edited the Ophthalmic Review from 1864 to 1867. His books treat surgical cancer in 1855 and 1856, eye surgery in 1863, and eye defects in 1865.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lerner-joseph-j:
Joseph Judah Lerner, a Russian journalist, was born on Jan. 1, 1849, at Berdychev. In 1866 he went to Odessa and studied law for a year. Then he turned to journalism. He spent ten years on the "Odeski Vyestnik" and served as its war correspondent in the Russo-Turkish war of 1877-78.

In 1880 Lerner founded a Jewish theater at Odessa. He wrote many plays for it in Judaeo-German. He also wrote Hebrew tales and studies, and many Russian articles on the Jewish question. His 1902 sketch of Jewish life in South Russia reads, the entry says, more like a memoir than a history. By 1904 he lived at Odessa as a convert to Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levi-ben-japhet:
Levi ben Japheth ha-Levi, called Abu Sa'id, was a Karaite scholar. He flourished, most likely at Jerusalem, in the first half of the eleventh century. Karaites ranked him with his father as a top authority and called him Al-Shaikh, the master. Yet Karaite sources give no details of his life, and some confuse him with kin.

Levi wrote in Arabic a large work on the precepts. Parts of its Hebrew version still survive in manuscript. Nearly all later Karaite law writers used it. The book holds rich notes on how Karaites and Rabbinites differed, and on fights among Karaites themselves. Its calendar section names the year 1007.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-benjamin-9: Benjamin Levy was a colonial resident of Philadelphia. On Nov. 7, 1765, he signed the noted agreement with other citizens of that city. By it they pledged not to import goods from England until the Stamp Act was repealed. On Dec. 27, 1776, the treasurer of the United States named him an authorized signer of the bills of credit. The short entry gives these two acts and nothing more of his life.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lodeve-10078: Lodève was a small town in the department of Hérault, France, with a Jewish community founded as early as the fifth century. The community stood under the bishop and paid him a yearly tax. In 1095 the bishop banned marriages between Jews and Christians. In 1188 the king upheld the bishop's rights over the Jews. Jews from Lodève appear later at Montpellier, Perpignan, and Nimes. A local bishop in the 1600s traded Hebrew poems with a rabbi from Carpentras.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lucuas-10178:
Lucuas, leader of a Jewish revolt under the emperor Trajan, is treated in a short Jewish Encyclopedia entry of 1906. Toward the end of Trajan's reign, in 116, the Jews of Cyrene rose in rebellion. Eusebius names their leader Lucuas, while Dio Cassius calls him Andreias. The article weighs whether the two names point to one man.

The entry argues the names cannot easily be merged, since neither ancient author explains them as symbols. It suggests the two writers describe different phases of the revolt. A later source says Lucuas fled to Palestine and was beaten there by Marcius Turbo. Eusebius adds that he was proclaimed king. For readers, the piece shows how the encyclopedia handled clashing ancient sources, weighing them openly instead of hiding the conflict.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-magnus-sir-phil:
Sir Philip Magnus, an English educationist, is profiled in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born in London on October 7, 1842, he studied at University College and the University of London. Destined for the Jewish ministry, he studied further at Berlin. On returning he became a minister of the Berkeley Street Synagogue.

The article follows his move from pulpit to national education. His textbook on elementary mechanics long stood as the standard work. In 1880 he became secretary of the City and Guilds Institute for technical education. In that post he grew into the leading British authority on the subject. He served on a royal commission and toured Europe's chief centers of instruction. He was knighted in 1886 for services to education. He also led Finsbury Technical College and sat on the London School Board. The entry notes his Jewish communal posts, kept alongside his public career.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mansur-marzuk-1:
Mansur Marzuk, an Egyptian rabbi and author, gets a short entry in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He settled at Salonica toward the close of the eighteenth century. The article names no dates for his birth or death. His reputation rests on three works printed at Salonica.

The first, Zur Todah, appeared in 1783 and comments on Maimonides' Yad ha-Hazakah. The second, Ben Pedahzur of 1786, is a volume of sermons. The third, Korban Elizur, is a commentary on the Talmud. The entry's sources are Azulai's Shem ha-Gedolim and Franco's history of Ottoman Jewry. Brief as it is, the notice preserves an Egyptian scholar who carried his learning to Salonica and left his mark in its printing houses.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mathematics-104:
Mathematics among the Jews, from the Talmud to the Arabic-speaking Middle Ages, is surveyed in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. Joseph Jacobs, Isaac Broydé, and S. Gundelfinger wrote it. The need to fix the calendar by astronomy, the authors explain, pushed the ancient Hebrews into arithmetic and geometry. The Mishnah and Talmud are full of both. They work out the four rules of arithmetic, fractions, and measures across whole tractates.

Particular details anchor the survey. The Talmud knows figures called bigon, trigon, tetragon, and pentagon. R. Nathan's forty-nine rules give the circle's circumference as three and one-seventh times its diameter. The first Hebrew mathematics book, the “Mishnat Middot,” belongs to the Judaeo-Arabic age. After it, the article turns to the Jewish algebraists and geometers who worked inside the Greco-Arabic scientific world.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-meir-ha-kohen-1:
Meir ha-Kohen was a French scholar of the thirteenth century. Richard Gottheil and M. Seligsohn profile him in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Narbonne and emigrated in 1263 to Toledo, where he died. His specialty was the Masorah, the apparatus guarding the exact text of Scripture. Menahem Me'iri counts him among five rabbis who collated many manuscripts to establish a correctly revised Pentateuch for France and Germany.

Most of the entry is spent untangling him from other men: Bartolocci confused him with the German author of the “Haggahot Maimuniyyot.” Zunz mixed him with Moses ha-Kohen of Lunel and gave him strictures on Maimonides he never wrote. Carmoly made him a poet against the “Guide.” A fourth attribution, of the “Sefer ha-Me'orot,” in fact goes to Meir ben Simeon. The notice is a warning label for a crowded name.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mene-mene-tekel:
"Mene, mene, tekel, upharsin" are the words the hand wrote on Belshazzar's wall. Isidore Singer and M. Seligsohn examine them in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The article first retells the scene from Daniel: the feast, the Temple vessels, the astrologers baffled, and Daniel's reading. God has numbered the kingdom and finished it. The king is weighed and found wanting. The realm is divided to the Medes and Persians.

Then the article asks why only Daniel could read. Talmudic answers multiply. The script had changed since Ezra's day. Or the letters were substituted in cipher pairs. Or the words ran vertically, backward, or with their letters transposed. Modern scholars, the entry continues, find their own difficulties in the doubled "mene" and the grammar of the interpretation. Few short entries hold so much: a Bible story, a rabbinic puzzle, and an open critical problem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-micha-10778:
Micha is one of the briefest entries in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906, just two numbered lines by Emil G. Hirsch and M. Seligsohn. It exists to sort out a minor biblical name. Readers who land on it are pointed to the fuller article on Micah for the family line it belongs to.

The first figure is a son of Mephibosheth, listed here with a cross-reference to the third Micah of the main entry rather than a story of his own. The second is one of the Levites who sealed the covenant with Nehemiah, cited to chapter ten of Nehemiah, verse eleven. Nothing more is claimed for either man, and the entry's honesty about that is its whole value.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-morais-sabato-1:
Sabato Morais, an American rabbi born at Leghorn on April 13, 1823, is given a full early life by Cyrus Adler and Cyrus L. Sulzberger in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The family had fled Portugal's Inquisition generations before. His father Samuel was an ardent republican, at one time imprisoned for his political views, in an Italy struggling for freedom.

Responsibility came early: as a child Sabato earned money teaching Hebrew hymns and prayers to other children, while studying under Rabbi Piperno and winning honorable mention in belles-lettres. He commanded Aramaic, French, and Spanish beside Hebrew and Italian. In 1845 he went to London to apply for the vacant post of assistant ḥazzan of the Spanish and Portuguese congregation — the first step toward Philadelphia, where he died in 1897.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-moses-ben-enoch:
Moses ben Enoch is remembered as the founder of Talmud study in Spain. Solomon Schechter and Meyer Kayserling tell his story in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was one of four scholars sent from Sura to collect funds for its declining academy. On the voyage from Bari, a Moorish-Spanish admiral captured their ship.

The story tells that the admiral desired Moses' wife, who drowned herself rather than be taken. Moses was ransomed at Cordova and sat quietly in a corner of the schoolhouse there. His answers soon showed a learning far beyond the local rabbi Nathan, who resigned in his favor that day. Moses built a school independent of the gaonate, and Cordova became a seat of Jewish learning.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mosul-arabic-ma:
Mosul, on the Tigris in Asiatic Turkey, stands near the site of ancient Nineveh. Gotthard Deutsch and M. Franco wrote the Jewish Encyclopedia article on its Jews. Tradition settles Jews there from the days when Assyria conquered Samaria. Benjamin of Tudela in 1165 found seven thousand Jews in the town.

The article follows the community through its Davidic exilarchs to its decline after 1289. By 1903 only eleven hundred Jews remained, driven by persecution from trade into peddling. It describes the two synagogues, the shown tombs of Obadiah, Nahum, and Jonah, and the Jewish villages of the province. A table counts over three thousand eight hundred Jews in the district in 1884.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahman-ben-hayy: Nahman ben Hayyim ha-Kohen was a French tosafist of the late twelfth century. The Jewish Encyclopedia gives him a short notice by its editorial committee and A. Peiginsky. Gross makes him a son of Hayyim ben Hananeel ha-Kohen. His Sefer Nahmani survives through quotations in Joseph Colon's responsa. Gross also identifies him with a tosafist Nahman cited in the Shittah Mekubbezet.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nathanson-josep:
Joseph Saul Nathanson was a Polish rabbi and author. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Berzan in 1808. His father was a rabbi and author there. He studied Talmud at Lemberg with his brother-in-law Ettinger.

The two men published several joint works on Talmud. Their first appeared at Lemberg in 1828. In 1857 Nathanson became rabbi of Lemberg itself. He served there for eighteen years, until his death in 1875. Rabbis far and wide treated him as an authority. His responsa fill the work Sho'el u-Meshib. He also left notes on the Talmud and Alfasi.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-neurath-wilhelm:
Wilhelm Neurath was an Austrian writer on economics. Isidore Singer and Max Cohen wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at St. Georgen on May 31, 1840. He won his doctor's degree in due course. Vienna's Technische Hochschule took him as privat-docent.

He rose to associate professor at the Hochschule für Bodenkultur. His essays on economics and social philosophy appeared in 1880. His Elements of economics teaching followed in 1882. A third edition of that work came in 1896. He wrote on the right to work in 1886. He probed the true causes of overproduction crises. Falling interest rates drew a lecture from him in 1893. His last lecture named modern economics' chief problem.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-orpah-11778:
Orpah was a woman of Moab in the book of Ruth. The board and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote her entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. She was the daughter-in-law of Naomi, a widow. She was the wife of Mahlon, Naomi's son. When Mahlon died, she was left with no husband.

Orpah and Ruth both wished to go with Naomi to Judah. Naomi talked Orpah into turning back to her folk. She went back to her own gods and land. Rabbis of later days told more of her fate. They made her the mother of four Philistine giants. They said her name came from her turned back. That is, she turned her back on Naomi at the parting. They said four tears at that parting won her four sons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-paltiya-pelatya: Pelatya of Naweh was a teller of tales from the Bible. The board and S. Mendelsohn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He lived in Palestine in the third century of our era. He is cited just once, as the source of one talk. That talk deals with a phrase in the book of Ecclesiastes. It says the earth stays for ever, in that text. Pelatya taught that the word earth there means Israel itself.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-piotrkow-12178:
Piotrkow is a town of Russian Poland, near Warsaw. Herman Rosenthal and A. S. Waldstein wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The Polish diet often met in the town. Its sessions made hard law for Jews. A famed Hebrew press worked there for years.

In 1538 the diet barred Jews from farming taxes. It forced them to wear a marked dress. More harsh laws followed in the 1560s. In 1648 the Cossacks fell on the town. Of fifty Jewish families, nearly all were killed. By 1897 the town held thirty-six Hebrew schools.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-popper-william-:
William Popper was an American scholar of the East, born at St. Louis in 1874. Cyrus Adler and Frederick T. Haneman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He took three degrees at Columbia, the last in 1899. He then studied at Berlin, Strasburg, and Paris. In 1901 he set out on a long trip east.

Popper traveled through Egypt, Syria, and Palestine for a year. He crossed the north Syrian desert and Mesopotamia as well. Back in New York in 1902, he joined the Jewish Encyclopedia staff. He served as a revising editor and ran its translation bureau. Columbia named him a lecturer in Semitic tongues in 1903. His book on the censorship of Hebrew books came out in 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rabbah-b-hanan-:
Rabbah bar Hanan was a Babylonian teacher of the fourth set of amoraim. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was a pupil of Rabbah bar Nahmani. He was a fellow student of Abaye, a man of his own age. Both had learned at the feet of the same master.

Their master said a kind word of both pupils. Both would speak praise of him after his death, he said. Rabbah bar Hanan often talked with Abaye in study. He put hard questions to him again and again. The tractate Erubin holds one such talk in its first lines. The entry traces their bond through the Talmud's pages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rappoldi-edouar:
Edouard Rappoldi was an Austrian violinist born on February 21, 1839. Isidore Singer and Joseph Sohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Vienna. He studied at the Vienna Conservatorium under several masters.

The article traces posts at Vienna, Rotterdam, Lübeck, and Prague. He taught violin in Berlin from 1871 to 1877. He then led violin teaching at the Dresden Conservatorium. He also led the Dresden opera orchestra until 1898. The writers praise his playing for art over show. He was known as a fine quartet player too. His own works include symphonies, quartets, sonatas, and songs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-renan-joseph-er:
Ernest Renan was a French Semitic scholar born on February 23, 1823. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He was born at Tréguier. He died at Paris on October 2, 1892.

The article says he was meant for the priesthood at first. Study of German thought and Semitic tongues changed his path. His 1855 history of Semitic languages made his name. A trip to Syria prepared his Life of Jesus in 1863. That book treated Jesus in a purely historical way. It cost him his Hebrew chair at the Collège de France. The republic restored him to that chair in 1870. He later wrote a five volume history of Israel. The entry traces a scholar who reshaped Bible study.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-riva-di-trento-:
Riva di Trento is a small town on Lake Garda. Joseph Jacobs wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. It lay under the Bishop of Trent's rule. Its place in Jewish history is Hebrew printing.

The article says Cardinal Madruz granted a printing privilege in 1558. It went to Joseph Ottolengo, a German rabbi at Cremona. Jacob Marcaria, a local physician, did the actual printing. After his death in 1562 the press stopped. Thirty four works appeared in those four years. Most bore the cardinal's coat of arms. The first was Alfasi's Halakot in three folio volumes. Two Mishnah editions and two Pentateuchs also appeared. The type was exceptionally clear, they note. A cardinal's patronage made the press remarkable.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-rosenthal-solom:
Solomon Rosenthal was a Hungarian scholar born at Moór on June 13, 1764. Isidore Singer and Alexander Büchler wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. His father had been a youthful friend of Moses Mendelssohn in Berlin.

Rosenthal traded in his home town and studied Jewish letters in his spare hours. He wrote for Ha-Meassef and other early Hebrew journals of the time. His Bet Awen, printed in 1839, attacked three reform-minded scholars by name. He also issued Leo da Modena's Ari Nohem, with his own preface and notes. A Hebrew version of Mendelssohn's Phädon survives from his hand in manuscript.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-sachs-michael-j:
Michael Jehiel Sachs was a German rabbi born at Glogau on September 3, 1808. Isidore Singer and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. He took his doctorate at Berlin in 1836 and preached at Prague.

In 1844 Sachs was called to Berlin, where he served until his death. Reform disputes there broke the harmony between him and his congregation. He accepted dropping feast-day hymns, but he flatly refused the organ in services. At last he withdrew into private life and gave himself to study. His works include a German Psalms and a history of Spain's Jewish religious poetry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-samuda-13078:
Samuda is an old Spanish and Portuguese family tied to London's Jewish community. Joseph Jacobs, Goodman Lipkind, and Isidore Harris wrote the entry for the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Its first English member was the physician Isaac de Sequeyra Samuda.

Isaac preached a funeral oration over Haham David Nieto in 1728. Later, David Samuda founded a Leman Street firm and sat on the Board of Deputies. His descendant Jacob was a rich broker and president of Bevis Marks' Mahamad. Another Jacob Samuda, an engineer, died young in 1844. His tombstone calls him the first Jewish engineer in England.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-schlesinger-lud:
Frederick T. Haneman and Isidore Singer wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia entry, published in 1906, on Ludwig Schlesinger. He was a Hungarian scholar of mathematics. Schlesinger was born at Tyrnau on November 1, 1864. He studied at the Realschule in Presburg. He then went to Heidelberg and Berlin for his studies. He took his doctorate in 1887.

In 1889 Schlesinger became a privat-docent at Berlin. In 1897 he moved up to assistant professor at Bonn. Since 1902 he has taught mathematics at Klausenburg as a full professor. He writes essays for the learned journals. His chief book is a handbook on linear differential equations. It appeared at Leipsic from 1895 to 1898. In 1900 he added a short guide to the theory of such equations.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-seder-olam-zuta:
M. Seligsohn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, issued with the Executive Committee of the Editorial Board in 1906. It treats the Seder 'Olam Zuṭa, an anonymous chronicle. Zuṭa means smaller, marking it against the older Rabbah. The work builds on that older chronicle. It continues and completes its record. Its aim is to prove one line of descent.

The first part covers fifty generations, from Adam to Jehoiakim. The second part lists thirty-nine generations of exilarchs. It begins with Jehoiachin, the captive king. The point is that Babylon's exilarchs descend directly from David. The book also fills gaps in the older chronicle. It gives the lengths of the generations before Abraham. It names each king's high priests and prophets too. Solomon, crowned at age three, had Zadok and three prophets.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shabbethai-raph:
Shabbethai Raphael was a seventeenth-century agitator for the false messiah Shabbethai Zebi. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and M. Seligsohn wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. A native of the Morea, he preached the new teaching across Italy around 1667. News traveled slowly, which helped him keep working.

When the false messiah turned Muslim, Raphael moved on to Germany. There he posed as a prophet and broke basic Jewish rules. At Amsterdam he won followers, even among Portuguese Jews. Once he claimed direct contact with Elijah, they drove him out. At Hamburg, Jacob Sasportas fought him hard. The entry follows a preacher who fed on delay and distance.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-shiloah-13578:
Shiloah names the waters and pool of Siloah at Jerusalem in the Old Testament. Emil G. Hirsch and Schulim Ochser wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on the place. Isaiah speaks of the waters of Shiloah flowing softly. Nehemiah names the pool of Siloah in his wall account.

Royal gardens surrounded the pool on the city's south side. Part of it belonged to Jerusalem's fortress defenses. Its spring stood at the mouth of the Tyropoeon valley. From Solomon's time, water may have fed a tank in Kidron. That tank watered the royal gardens below the city. A conduit bearing the famed Siloam inscription served it. The entry ties a Bible phrase to real stone, spring, and tunnel.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-simeon-13678: Simeon was a tanna, or early rabbinic teacher, of the first generation. Wilhelm Bacher and Jacob Zallel Lauterbach wrote the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia entry on him. He was brother of Azariah and uncle of Eleazar ben Azariah. The Mishnah mentions him only once, in tractate Zebahim. One saying of his is preserved in that single place. He took his name from his brother Azariah, a merchant. Azariah paid Simeon's living costs so he could study the Law undisturbed.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-singer-simeon-1:
Simeon Singer was an English rabbi born in London in 1848. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He studied at Jews' College in London. He received his rabbinical diploma in 1890. He served as head master of Jews' College School. He then ministered at two London synagogues in turn.

Singer led the Borough New Synagogue and the New West End Synagogue. He was seen as the lead voice of progressive Orthodoxy. He edited and translated the Authorized Daily Prayer-Book. With S Schechter he edited Talmudical Fragments in the Bodleian Library. That joint work appeared in 1896. He also published sermons and read papers before learned bodies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-solomon-michael:
Michael Solomon was a British merchant and politician born in England in 1818. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He emigrated to Jamaica at the age of twelve. He eventually became head of the firm of Bravo Brothers. He spent more than sixty years of his life in Jamaica.

For most of that time he served in the island's government. He sat on the Legislative Council with distinction for years. He also served as custos of St Anne's parish. He helped organize an exposition in the island as well. In 1887 Queen Victoria honored his many services. She made him a companion of the Order of St Michael and St George.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-spitzer-sigmund:
Sigmund Spitzer was an Austrian physician born at Nikolsburg in 1813. Isidore Singer and Frederick T Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. He took his medical degree at the University of Vienna. Two years later he became professor of anatomy at Constantinople. There he founded an anatomical museum with his own specimens.

His influence helped overcome local opposition to dissections in Turkey. In 1845 he cured Sultan Abd al-Majid of a dangerous illness. He then became chief private physician to the sultan himself. Envy at court led even to an attempt on his life. He resigned and later served the Porte at Naples. He died at Vienna in 1894.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-strauss-paul-14:
Paul Strauss was a French senator born at Rongchamp on September 23, 1852. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied in Paris and graduated in medicine. In 1876 he entered political journalism instead. He wrote for several radical Paris newspapers.

In 1883 Strauss won election to the Paris town council. He served the city and the Seine assembly until 1897. That year voters sent him to the French Senate. His chief work reshaped French public charity care. He won new departments for deserted children and pregnant women. He helped found asylums for mothers after childbirth. In 1897 he founded a journal on philanthropy. The entry shows medicine turned into social reform.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-szilasi-moriz-1:
Moriz Szilasi was a Hungarian philologist born in 1854. Isidore Singer and Frederick T. Haneman wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about him in 1906. He studied philology at Budapest and Leipsic. He taught at a Budapest gymnasium and at Eötvös College. He died at Klausenburg on May 15, 1905.

In 1902 Szilasi took the chair of Hungarian language at Klausenburg. The post also covered Finnish philology. He translated Plutarch and Thucydides into Hungarian. Greek and Roman histories reached Hungarian readers through him. He built a dictionary of the Vogul language. A second vocabulary covers the Cheremiss tongue. Both serve the study of Finno-Ugric languages. The entry honors a scholar of kindred tongues east and north.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-tebet-14278:
Tebet is the tenth month of the Hebrew religious year. Emil G. Hirsch wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article about it in 1906. It ranks fourth in the civil year count. It always holds twenty-nine days. Its name comes from Assyro-Babylonian speech.

The Babylonians called their tenth month Tebetu. They described it as the month of violent rains. It fell near the close of Palestine's rainy season. A Talmud gloss says a rainy Tebet means fertility. A dry Tebet can also promise a good year. That reading assumes enough rain fell before it. The month's first days close the Hanukkah festival. Its eighth day marks the Septuagint translation's end. Tradition says darkness covered earth for three days then. The entry ties a winter month to rain and memory.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-transliteration:
Transliteration of Greek and Latin words into Hebrew letters is mapped here. Isidore Singer and Isaac Broydé wrote this Jewish Encyclopedia article, published in 1906. Talmud, Midrash, and Targum transcribed foreign words by sound alone. Etymology played no part in the process. Hebrew lacks many Greek and Latin sounds, though.

One Hebrew letter must serve several foreign sounds. Bet can stand for b, p, or f. Ayin has no Greek or Latin match at all. Vowels shift even more freely between the alphabets. Letters drop out by apocope and syncope in many words. Breathing marks, though, are kept with great care. The article then turns to Jews writing under Arabic rule.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-verein-fur-cult:
The Verein für Cultur und Wissenschaft der Juden was a Berlin study society. Gotthard Deutsch and Ernst Cohn wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Leopold Zunz, Eduard Gans, and Moses Moser founded it. The founding date was November 27, 1819. About fifty Berlin intellectuals joined at the start.

The society aimed to lift the social standing of Jews. It also hoped to slow a wave of conversions to Christianity. Its tools were general culture and Jewish learning. It planned schools from primary grades to advanced study. It even opened a school for young Polish scholars. Heinrich Heine joined the society in 1822. Older friends of Mendelssohn joined later as well.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-warburg-14778:
Warburg is a family spread across Europe and America. Joseph Jacobs, Isidore Singer, and Louis Roth wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Family tradition traces the line to Bologna, Italy. From there it moved to Warburg, in Westphalia. It later settled at Altona, near Hamburg.

The earliest known bearer is Levi Joseph Warburg. His grandson Jacob Samuel died at Altona in 1667. Two main branches descend from Jacob's sons. One line founded a Hamburg banking house in the family name. Another branch settled at Göteborg, in Sweden. Its head helped found that city's synagogue. The entry maps bankers and merchants across five lands.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-west-virginia-1:
West Virginia is an east central American state. Cyrus Adler and Harry Levi wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It was part of Virginia until June 19, 1863. Single Jews traveled west there from 1825. No communities formed before 1840. In 1849 Wheeling gained a Jewish cemetery association.

That same year Wheeling organized Congregation Leshem Shomayim. It later became B'nai B'rith, the city's Reform body. Rabbi Harry Levi has led it since 1897. Charleston formed Congregation Bene Yeshurun in 1873. It counts forty four members today. Parkersburg has aid societies but no congregation. The entry surveys schools, clubs, and charities statewide.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-wolf-johann-chr:
Johann Christoph Wolf (1683-1739) was a Christian scholar of Hebrew books and many fields. Crawford Howell Toy and Joseph Jacobs wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Born at Wernigerode, he studied at Wittenberg. He then toured Holland and England to meet top minds.

In 1712 he won a chair in eastern tongues at Hamburg. There a great Jewish book hoard lay close at hand. Wolf chose to map all of Jewish letters from that hoard. The fruit was his Bibliotheca Hebraea in four books. It lists Jewish authors and sorts works by theme. For near one hundred fifty years the West learned of the Talmud from him. His work still underlies the great Bodleian list of Hebrew books.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-yerushalmi-solo: Solomon ben Menahem Yerushalmi was a scholar of the early 1500s. The Executive Committee of the Editorial Board and Schulim Ochser wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was also called Solomon Isaac Ashkenazi. He wrote a work on the Book of Ruth. Its name is Perush al Rut in Hebrew. It came out at Salonica in 1551. A second form came out at Sabbionetta in 1554. That form bound his work with a second book as one.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zarzal-abraham-:
Abraham ibn Zarzal was a Spanish doctor and star man of the 1300s. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He worked at the court of the Nasrid kings at Granada. He died at some date past the year 1369.

Fear of a court crime drove him to flee that court. He went north to Castile to seek a safe post there. His fame in cures and stars went ahead of him. A word from the king of Granada helped him as well. The king of Castile took him as star man and doctor. That king was Pedro, called the Cruel by men since. Zarzal stood near that king at all times of day. He used that place to smooth strife twixt the two realms. Star men told Pedro he would take Jerusalem in time.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-zohar-called-al:
The Zohar is the central book of the Cabala, cast as a commentary on the Pentateuch. Joseph Jacobs and Isaac Broydé wrote this entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It claims to record teachings of Simeon ben Yohai, an ancient sage, given to his chosen pupils. In fact it first appeared in thirteenth-century Spain, spread by Moses de Leon.

Written partly in Aramaic and partly in Hebrew, the Zohar sets out a full mystical account of God. It treats the making of the world, the soul, sin, redemption, good, and evil. Doubts about its age arose at once, fed by a tale that de Leon's widow called it his own work. Even so, most cabalists and many Talmudists accepted it, and it opened new paths in Jewish mysticism.
john-cross-ascent-mount-carmel-1578:
John of the Cross wrote the Ascent of Mount Carmel in Spain in the late 1500s. David Lewis turned the work into English. John was a Carmelite monk and a close friend of Teresa of Avila. His book is a strict guide to prayer and the dark night.

A poem of the soul's climb frames the whole text. John glosses each line to teach how to drop all ties to sense and self. The dark night, he says, strips the soul bare for union with God. The book stands with his Dark Night as a peak of Spain's soul lore.
jonston-description-four-footed-beasts-1:
John Jonston, a Polish-born scholar who worked in the Dutch world of learning, wrote vast Latin surveys of nature. This English Description of the Nature of Four-footed Beasts appeared in 1678. It brought the great Central European natural history to English readers in their own tongue.

Jonston gathers beasts both real and rumored, from the lion to the manticore. Each entry packs in names, habits, and reports drawn from many authors. His learning is deep and his pages are crowded. English readers could set this book beside Topsell's earlier beast book and compare them. Together the two show how Europe pictured animals before modern science.
lessing-dramatic-works-bell-1878:
Ernest Bell's Dramatic Works of Lessing, published in 1878, holds four plays that remade German drama. Miss Sara Sampson brought everyday middle-class sorrow to the stage in place of kings. Philotas gives a captured young prince one fierce choice about honor and death.

Emilia Galotti, the darkest of the four, shows a prince's lust destroying a virtuous girl and her family. Nathan the Wise closes the volume with its plea for tolerance among faiths. Bell's Nathan differs from Taylor's older version, and the two are kept as distinct translations. Together the four plays show why Lessing is counted the founder of modern German drama. No other single volume shows his range so well.
mackey-encyclopedia-freemasonry-1878:
Albert G. Mackey was the great voice of Masonic lore in the States. His Encyclopedia of Freemasonry came out in 1878. Its full title adds the kindred sciences to the craft. The book aims to hold all a Mason might need to know in one tome.

Heads run from rites and signs to lives of famed Masons of the past. Long tales give the craft's past, its laws, and the sense of its marks. Mackey writes with care and with love for the lore. The book stayed the stock desk guide for the craft for scores of years.
maxwell-ether-1878:
James Clerk Maxwell wrote this piece on the ether for the Encyclopaedia Britannica in 1878. The ether was the unseen stuff men thought filled all space. Light waves, they held, must wave in something, and the ether was that something.

Maxwell sums up what the ether must be like to bear light at such speed. He tells how stiff and yet how free of drag it must be, from the proof at hand. Short and calm, the piece is the great man's own word on what the ether was meant to be.
musaeum-hermeticum-reformatum-et-amplifi: Matthaeus Merian's Musaeum Hermeticum, reformed and enlarged, was printed at Frankfurt in 1678. Its long Latin title promises teaching on the philosopher's stone and its healing medicine. Catalog notes say it gathers twenty-one chemical tracts, first issued by Luca Jennis in 1625. The hosted sample preserves only a garbled scan of the title page, with no readable body text, so the work's contents cannot be described from the sample itself.
openalex-w1990847378:
A. Roth and co-authors reported this Pacific outbreak wave. The sample cites Eurosurveillance, published in October 2014. The catalog record lists the year 2012, which the sample corrects. Since January 2012, the Pacific saw many new outbreaks. Dengue, chikungunya, and Zika spread at the same time.

Twenty-eight outbreaks and circulations were documented by 2014. More than one hundred twenty thousand people were reported affected. True numbers were likely far higher, they warn. Island health systems bore an already heavy burden. Better surveillance and response were urgently needed, they argue. The wave was called unprecedented in forty years of data.
openalex-w2019284478:
Eva Ramirez-Llodra, Paul Tyler, Maria Baker and colleagues reviewed human impact on the deep sea. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2011. The deep sea is Earth's largest ecosystem. It is also one of the least studied. New technology now lets people exploit its resources.

The review covers fishing, oil and gas, and other deep sea uses. It traces how knowledge of deep life grew through exploration. Early surveys found animals at all ocean depths. The authors weigh the wealth of resources against rich biodiversity. They stress how little is known about deep ecosystems. That gap makes careful management hard. The paper frames the deep sea as a last great wilderness under pressure.
openalex-w2052410578:
