Just over half of the four hundred seventy-five recently delivered mothers they surveyed, in mid 2023, had given birth by caesarean, a strikingly high share. The study linked how a woman delivered to her out of pocket spending and her physical and mental quality of life in the weeks after birth.

High risk pregnancies and private facilities were the strongest predictors of a caesarean. Mothers who delivered surgically faced roughly double the odds of heavy out of pocket costs, and markedly worse physical quality of life scores, while the mental side differed less. The authors say the pattern, surgical birth concentrated in private care and paid for by families, deserves policy attention in a state where one in two births now arrives by operation.
plos-pone-0359278: Kinsman and two co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on psychiatric prescribing in Botswana. At the country's only referral institute for mental illness, they counted how many adult patients receive many psychiatric drugs at once, a practice called polypharmacy. The snapshot design covered patients at one point in time. Many drugs at once can help, yet raise risks, so a clear count guides safer care.
plos-pone-0359778:
Yi-Chao Zhou, Yi-Chang Chou, Yin-Ling Hung, and Yen-Jung Chang wrote this 2026 PLOS ONE research article on ageing in Taiwan. It is a longitudinal cohort study running from 2005 to 2016. The authors link marital status to incident screen-positive cognitive impairment, new cases flagged by screening tests for thinking decline.

The title itself warns that the links vary with the cognitive screening instrument chosen, meaning the answer depends on which test defines impairment. That caution matters for every study that sorts people by a single screen. Researchers of marriage, widowhood, and dementia risk are the readers, and they gain a lesson in measurement as well as a result.
plos-pone-0359878:
Jingmei Liang, Yuyun Hu, and Bing Liao traced in 2026 a chain of signals that injures kidney filter cells in acute kidney injury. The cells are podocytes, which wrap the kidney's tiny blood vessels and keep protein out of the urine. The authors show that signaling between cells through a pair of proteins, GAS6 and its receptor AXL, can trigger a form of cell death called cuproptosis in these podocytes.

Above that pair sits a regulator named CEBPD, which the team places upstream of the signal. Acute kidney injury strikes suddenly, often during severe illness, and has few targeted treatments. Mapping a death pathway step by step gives drug researchers named points where the chain might be cut.
plos-pone-0360478:
Wen Li and colleagues piloted in 2026 a blend of music therapy and artificial intelligence for university students. Their exploratory randomized study added verbal suggestions, generated by a large language model and adapted to the students' culture, into music therapy sessions. The spoken guidance was designed to deepen the therapy's calming and focusing effects.

As a pilot, the study's job is to test whether the approach is workable and promising enough to justify a larger trial, rather than to settle its value. Culturally adapted wording matters because therapeutic language lands differently across backgrounds. The work sits at a new crossing point, where universities search for scalable mental health support and AI tools are eager to supply it, with evidence still catching up.
pmc-10671078:
Jessica A Clark and co-authors published a study in 2023 on two inherited dog eye diseases and how breeding choices moved their gene frequencies worldwide. One disease slowly blinds by killing the retina's light sensors; the other deforms the eye from birth in collies and relatives. Commercial DNA tests for both have existed for years.

The team analyzed test results for over eighty-six thousand dogs for the blinding disease and nearly thirty-four thousand for the eye anomaly, spanning fifteen years, eighty-two countries, and sixty-seven breeds. Frequencies differed sharply by breed and shifted over time, mostly downward as breeders used the tests. Yet dogs carrying two copies of the blinding variant still appeared fourteen years after testing began. Testing works, the authors conclude, but only where breeders keep using it.
pmc-10673478:
Yang Liu and co-authors work out the mechanical, electronic, and optical traits of a set of caesium lead halide materials. Their 2023 study uses first-principles density functional theory. It runs across four types, split by which halogen they hold.

All four materials showed good stability in the sums, and good elastic modulus, hardness, and wear resistance. Each acted as a semiconductor with a direct band gap. The gap shrank as the halogen atom grew in size. The sums for light found peaks in the dielectric values at low energy. They found the most strong absorption in ultraviolet light. Absorption moved toward the red end of the scale, and grew in strength, across the set. The team puts the results forth as a guide, based on theory, for devices in microelectronics and in optoelectronics.
pmc-10688678:
Drew Duckett, Kailee Calder, Jack Sullivan, David Tank, and Bryan Carstens test if reduced data approaches match whole genome sequencing for common place based heredity studies, using the North American water vole. Study design forces a choice among many marker types. The study came out in twenty twenty three.

The team gathered five data kinds, from single genes up to low depth whole genomes, for the same voles. Genetic gaps, population structure, and past population swings were each estimated per data kind and compared. Results differed by marker, above all in fine detail. A cost check found genotype by sequencing markers the most cost effective route.
pmc-10689478:
A color change test that needs no DNA extraction can spot mpox and its relatives, report Zhiru Li and co-authors in a 2023 study. Their method uses loop mediated amplification, a technique that copies DNA at one steady temperature, paired with a probe that tells mpox apart from other Old World poxviruses.

Swab fluid goes straight into the test, which skips the lab step that low resource settings struggle with. The team also mapped 200 poxvirus genomes to place the assay on firm ground. They offer the test as a fast, scalable tool for diagnosis and outbreak watching where it is needed most.
pmc-10692078:
Ahmed Abdel Gawad and four co-authors measured natural radioactivity in Nubian sandstone from Egypt, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Builders use this stone widely, so its safety matters. The team checked levels of uranium, thorium, and potassium isotopes in samples of the rock.

All three came in below world average limits for building materials. The dose people would absorb from the stone, and the added lifetime cancer risk, also sat below world means. Statistical tools showed the three elements drive what little risk exists. The authors conclude the sandstone is safe to use. Its radioactivity is too low to pose a health risk under normal use.
pmc-10693078:
Soha Mohammadi and co-authors describe a surgical workaround for the riskiest plumbing in free-flap reconstruction. Rebuilding a lip after cancer surgery with tissue moved from the forearm depends on stitching tiny veins together; a size mismatch or a doubtful join can starve the flap. Their patient, a 77-year-old man, had a lower lip tumour removed with a safety margin, neck glands cleared, and the lip rebuilt with a forearm flap.

Faced with a venous join they did not fully trust, the surgeons did not redo it. Instead they added a second vein connection in a Y configuration, so the flap's outflow had two supports. The authors argue the Y anastomosis eases the operation and cuts the complications that size mismatches cause. A literature review accompanies the case, which they offer as an option when a single venous join looks doubtful.
pmc-10693878:
Samrachana Adhikari and co-authors describe a new research cohort in a 2023 paper. The cohort was built to study whether heart failure patients take their medicines as directed. Missed chances to help are common because doctors cannot easily spot who is at risk of skipping doses.

The team linked electronic health records with pharmacy refill data and neighborhood social data. Patients came from a large New York City health system and had heart failure or weak heart pumping. All had active prescriptions for at least one of the four main drug types. The linked data aim to improve models that flag patients likely to miss doses.
pmc-10694578:
Erin Jay Feliciano and a large team of co-authors call for action on cancer disparities in Southeast Asia in a two thousand twenty-three commentary. The region holds over six hundred eighty million people, and cancer incidence and mortality are projected to climb.

The authors argue disparities run deeper than country-level statistics. Within each nation, minoritized groups face unequal risk, screening, treatment access, and survivorship along lines of ethnicity, gender, wealth, religion, and geography. Their lens is intersectionality: overlapping identities compound disadvantage in ways single categories miss. Pandemic-driven poverty has widened the gaps. The piece urges researchers and policymakers to study and serve these overlooked populations directly.
pmc-10694878:
Five researchers led by Koichiro Hirayama asked how arm skill scores relate to real arm use in people soon after a stroke. They studied two hundred three patients with a first stroke. One test scores how well the weak arm moves, and the other logs how much the patient uses it in daily life.

A split-point method found the link changed at a score near forty-five. Below that point, more skill did not mean much more use. Above it, use rose more steeply. The authors say rehab plans should push arm use with longer practice once patients pass that score. The finding helps match training to each stage of recovery.
pmc-10694978:
Giving the right amount of fluid during big abdominal surgery can speed recovery. Yanxia Sun and co-authors ran a randomized trial of goal-directed fluid therapy in one hundred patients having major cancer surgery on the abdomen. One group got fluids guided by two heart measures, with set targets. The other got standard care based on blood pressure and vein pressure. Neither patients nor assessors knew the groups.

The guided group left hospital in about nine days, against twelve for standard care. Gut problems after surgery struck two guided patients but sixteen in the other group. The guided group also passed gas sooner and ate sooner. The trial supports measure-guided fluids for major abdominal operations.
pmc-10695378:
Jin-Sung Yuk and Ji Young Park linked menopause hormone therapy to gallstones in a 2023 Korean cohort study. Hormone care eases menopause symptoms, but its effect on the gallbladder was worth a hard look at national scale. The team also asked whether it shifts gallbladder cancer risk.

They drew on national health insurance records from 2002 to 2019. Women on hormone care were set against those never on it, and the care group was split by drug form, from combined pills to skin-applied estrogen. Gallstone rates ran higher in the care group. Such data help women and doctors weigh symptom relief against gall risk.
pmc-10698478:
Hansraj Gautam and Vidya study conflict among female Asian elephants in a 2023 paper. A long-standing model links animal conflict to how food is spread out and how many rivals live nearby. Clumped, rich food should spark fights between groups, while scattered food should not.

The pair watched elephant clans in the Kabini grassland of southern India. Fights between clans were stronger there than in nearby forests, and females fought outsiders more than clan mates. The grassland is a rich food patch, which fits the model's forecast. Fights within clans were also common, though they did not track the expected factors as neatly. The study refines how food maps onto social tension in a species that splits and rejoins often.
pmc-10706478:
Xiaofeng Lu and nine co-authors seek a way to make oolong tea that keeps its healthy catechins high while still tasting good. Catechins give tea much of its flavor and health value, but high levels and good taste are hard to get at once. The study came out in twenty twenty-three.

The team varied one step at a time through the full tea making run, then used chem-ical sorting methods to weigh the results. Their best route uses red light wilting, leaf turning with long rests, drum roasting, cold rolling, and microwave drying, each for set times. This route kept far more catechins and gave a smooth, brisk taste, the authors report.
pmc-10708378:
Huang, Wang, and Tang catalog the ZF-HD gene family in moso bamboo. These zinc finger proteins guide plant growth, development, and stress responses. Knowledge of their history in bamboo was limited before this work. The team found 24 family genes spread unevenly on 12 chromosomes. Two subfamilies emerged from the family tree: ZHD and MIF types. ZHD genes split further into seven groups by kinship with rice and Arabidopsis.

Whole-genome and segmental duplications grew the family over time. Ratio tests showed purifying selection on all duplicate pairs. Promoter scans found stress and hormone response elements in most genes. Many genes switched on under abiotic stress in expression tests. The authors map structure, motifs, and control elements per gene.
pmc-10708678:
Felici-Castell and five colleagues build a low cost air pollution sensor network in twenty twenty-three. Cheap sensors can densify air quality monitoring in cities, where breathing problems are rising. Their raw data are error prone and need correction and processing. The team pairs such sensors with 5G links and neural networks.

The goal is to forecast pollutant readings twenty-four hours ahead for early warnings. Four network designs were trained and compared on a large prepared data set. A long short term memory design performed best overall. Average estimation error was about seven percent across pollutants. Carbon dioxide forecasts were especially accurate, and fine particles also scored well. The authors target support for citizens with respiratory problems.
pmc-10709878:
Kang Huang and nine co-authors test whether small gene variants in a fat-processing gene shift heart disease risk in Han Chinese. Their case-control study was published in twenty twenty-three.

The study matched four hundred and eighty-seven heart patients with the same number of healthy people. Five variants in the gene CYP4V2 were typed. One variant's T form raised risk by about a third overall. The link was sharper in people over sixty, men, smokers, and drinkers. A second variant raised risk in drinkers, while a third lowered risk when diabetes joined the picture. The gene handles fatty acids, which fits a heart role. The findings add population-specific markers to heart risk research.
pmc-10710578:
Toshihide Tanaka and co-authors report a trial of drug treatment given before surgery for a harsh brain tumor, in a paper from 2023. The tumor type is malignant glioma, most often glioblastoma. One drug, bevacizumab, is standard before surgery in bowel cancer but not in brain tumors. The multi-center trial tested safety first, then looked for signs of gain.

Fifteen patients got the drug plus a chemo pill before their operations. Surgery followed about three weeks later. Two patients had severe side effects tied to the drugs, such as wound infection and low blood counts. Tumors shrank in nearly all cases, and patient function scores improved before surgery. Average time before the disease grew again was about nine and a half months. The authors call the plan safe and worth study for some patients.
pmc-10714478:
Reda and seven co-authors sequenced malaria parasites across Ethiopia in this study from twenty twenty-three. Parasite genetics can reveal how intensely malaria spreads and whether control works. The team collected dried blood spots from trial patients at three endemic sites. Five highly variable gene markers were read deeply in one hundred eighty-one infections.

Diversity ran high across all markers. About seventeen percent of infections carried multiple parasite strains. Two sites' parasite populations looked nearly identical in twenty fifteen, while others stood apart. The pattern suggests frequent parasite flow between sites with moderate local structure. The authors offer the data as a baseline for tracking future control efforts.
pmc-10716178:
Ritsch and Armanios put forth a way in twenty twenty-three to use built works as a social sense tool to spot groups at risk in a crisis. Past work reads bias in built works after the fact, as a kind of post-mortem. Their way reads gaps live to guide aid to the right spots fast.

They test if county web reach rates can guess job loss rates in the Covid wave in the United States. A two-by-two map shows where the sense is sharp or blunt and where it errs each way. Adding bridge, build, and library web facts makes an array that reads more sharp. The plan aims at fast, fit aid.
pmc-10716378:
Daniele Antermite and co-authors found a late-stage way to build drug-like chimera molecules in a 2023 chemistry paper. PROTACs are two-headed molecules that drag a target protein to the cell's trash system. Making them is slow, since each head and the link must be built and joined with care.

Their method uses a ruthenium catalyst to add the second head at a late step, by direct work on a carbon-hydrogen bond. It starts from parts that are easy to buy or make. A modular route like this lets chemists spin out many variants fast. That speed helps map which shapes degrade targets best.
pmc-10719078:
Yu and co-authors train machine learning to predict delirium after child surgery. Emergence delirium is a distressed wake-up state in children. Records came from one large children's hospital, 2015 to 2019. The data held 54,776 visits across 43,830 patients. Four common learning models were built and compared. The set held a shrinkage model, a ridge model, a random forest, and a boosted tree model.

All four models scored near 0.74 to 0.75 on curve tests. Adenoid and tonsil surgery raised predicted risk. Younger age raised risk as well. Midazolam before surgery and ondansetron added risk too. IV induction and ketorolac linked to lower risk in the data.
pmc-10719278:
Bereneice Sephton and colleagues demonstrate a way to send rich information with quantum light, in a 2023 study. Quantum networks aim to share information between distant parties without moving the particles that carry it. Packing more dimensions into each particle raises capacity and resists noise, but doing so has been hard.

The team's method uses a nonlinear crystal process, boosted by a strong laser field, to read the shape of a single photon's light pattern. One photon of an entangled pair was converted to a new color, which carried its spatial pattern across. The channel handled fifteen distinct states. They faithfully sent patterns shaped as twists, grids, and blended forms, without knowing in advance what was sent. The work joins two young fields: shaping light and quantum processing.
pmc-10719378:
Jeppesen and André combine two tools to predict the shapes of large, symmetric protein assemblies. AlphaFold predicts protein shapes well, but it has limits on chain and residue counts. Symmetric docking can place copies of a known subunit into ordered shells. The team joined the two: AlphaFold first folds the single unit, then docking builds the full shell. The method targets assemblies with cubic symmetry types.

On 27 test systems, the built assemblies matched the true shapes closely. The median match score was 0.99, and most models rated acceptable to high quality. The finished models are energy-tuned for study of contacts between subunits. The work extends accurate shape prediction to very large protein shells.
pmc-10719578:
JongCheol Pyo and co-authors review a deep learning method used to forecast water quality in lakes and rivers, in a paper from 2023. The method, called long short-term memory, reads sequences and holds onto long past patterns. Water quality shifts with weather, land use, and seasons, so long memory helps. The network is the most used of its kind for this task.

The review first weighs the plain network against physics-based models and other learning tools. It then covers add-ons that clean the data before training. Later sections pair the network with image-style layers, attention steps, and transfer from other sites. Those pairings beat the plain form in most tests. The authors also flag the role of fixed traits like land shape. They close with open problems for the field.
pmc-10720078:
Measuring the pulmonary artery on scans usually means widths or areas, but a full 3D volume might say more about pulmonary hypertension. The six authors studied 59 patients who had both right heart catheterization and CT pulmonary angiography. They split patients into 18 without and 41 with pulmonary hypertension, measured artery diameters by hand, and used 3D software to get cross-sectional areas and volumes of the central pulmonary arteries.

Every scan measure ran higher in the hypertension group and tracked the catheter pressures. For the main and right pulmonary arteries, 3D measures correlated more strongly than widths or areas. The right artery volume beat its width and area clearly in curve analysis, and decision curve analysis favored the 3D measures. The team also built simple equations that estimate catheter pressures from the main artery volume and width.
pmc-10722978:
Dandan Tian and co-authors present a 2023 study of banana resistance to Fusarium wilt. The fungus behind it, race 4 of Fusarium oxysporum, is the most lethal banana disease in Asia. Roots of a resistant variety and a susceptible one are compared after infection. Gene activity and metabolite profiles are both measured. The susceptible variety changes only 172 genes, while the resistant one changes 1,856. Between the two varieties, 800 genes differ directly.

Those genes cluster in oxidation control, cell wall building, and protective chemistry paths. Plant breeders get named candidate genes for resistance work. The contrast is the lesson: resistance looks like a broad, fast mobilization, not a single gene. Banana farming feeds millions and the crop is genetically narrow, so wilt resistance is a food security topic. Dual profiling ties gene switches to the chemicals that actually fight the fungus.
pmc-10725178:
Ricardo Martín-Moya and co-authors compare movement quality and fitness in male and female semi-professional soccer players in this 2023 study. Twenty-eight players, evenly split by sex, took a seven-part movement screen plus sprint, agility, and endurance tests. The goal was to see whether screen scores predict field performance.

Men changed direction faster, but movement screen totals did not differ between the sexes. Screen-related factors predicted a fair share of endurance and sprint variation in combined models, though relationships varied by person. The authors conclude that no single test tells the story: coaches should combine several field tests and weigh training history and individual traits when reading results.
pmc-10729078:
James McGowan and co-authors (2023) asked what makes quality improvement collaboratives work, using the Michigan programme as the case. Such teams, where hospitals join to raise care quality, show mixed results elsewhere. The Michigan programme has lifted care across many fields for years. The team spoke with 38 clinicians, managers, and programme staff from ten sites. They watched meetings and read programme papers.

Five traits marked the programme's success. It learns from positive deviants, the sites that quietly excel. Coordination is strong, checks are strict, and sites share honest score feedback. These levers are used with care, not to punish. Senior professionals are drawn in as leaders, building community. Winning buy-in, duties, and sparing sites needless forms all helped. The authors offer the findings as a design guide for leaders building such teams. Michigan's lesson, in short, is that structure and culture must be built as one.
pmc-10735378:
Jane Lowers and co-authors interview adults who live alone with early dementia in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. About one in three people with dementia lives solo, though care needs grow over time. The team asked what helps and what hinders these adults as they plan ahead.

Fifteen solo adults named their assets: speaking up for themselves, friend networks, money, and care institutions. A self-reliant streak, fear of being a burden, and worry about being exploited held them back from asking for help. Asking felt easier when help seemed rewarding for the giver, when favors could be returned, or when framed as self-advocacy. The authors stress the strengths these adults bring.
pmc-10736178:
Jenny van der Steen and Ida Korfage report a study, published in two thousand twenty-three, that asked experts in thirty-three countries how to plan care ahead with people who have dementia. The work came from the European Association for Palliative Care.

Over four rounds, a panel of one hundred seven experts agreed on a shared framework for advance care planning in dementia. It rests on three themes: a person's capacity, the role of family, and steady contact and talk. The authors also share advice given directly by people living with dementia, which the panel found eye-opening. The framework treats planning as an ongoing talk, not a one-time form, and adjusts as capacity changes.
pmc-10736478:
Michael Vale wrote this research paper, published in 2023, on loneliness among sexual minority adults and how it ties to minority stress, the strain of living with stigma. The study spans ages eighteen to ninety.

Vale first examined baseline data from 333 people, weighing seven kinds of minority stress against loneliness. Older participants reported less loneliness and less stress than younger ones. But age changed how some stressors bit: hidden shame, expected rejection, and family stigma tracked loneliness more strongly at some ages than others. A second part followed 112 people over twenty-one days. On days when people hid their identity or felt more inner shame, loneliness rose. On days they disclosed it, loneliness fell. The paper shows loneliness in this group shifts with both age and daily experience.
pmc-10736978:
Darina Petrovsky and Anne Mitchell introduce a symposium in two thousand twenty-three on age-friendly care built around the 4Ms framework. The framework names four evidence-based elements of good care for older adults: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, and Mobility. Following it makes high-quality, needs-based care more likely.

The session gathers four nurse scientists, one for each element cutting across the others. Talks include disparities in advance care planning across social groups, drawn from a national retirement study. Another reports a pilot trial of primary palliative care for nursing home residents with serious illness, testing whether the approach is workable and welcome.
pmc-10737078:
Donnette Narine and Takashi Yamashita studied breast cancer screening in an often-overlooked group in a 2023 paper. Black women die of breast cancer at far higher rates than white women, yet research often treats them as one block. Caribbean Black women differ in background and culture, with many immigrants among them.

Using seven years of a national health survey, the authors analyzed 552 non-Hispanic Caribbean Black women aged 40 to 75 in the United States. The longer a woman had lived in the country, the more likely she had been screened in the past year. Age itself showed no link. The authors urge prevention work aimed at this subgroup, above all at newcomers.
pmc-10737878:
Björn Slaug and seven co-authors catalogued life changes around retirement age in Sweden and Germany, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Lives alternate between stable spans and events that force adjustment. How changes cluster, and in what order they arrive, may matter as much as each change alone.

Interviews with fifty people covered about ten years around retirement. Each person faced close to four changes on average, and a quarter faced more than five. Retirement and moving home often came together. Illness often followed a chain of earlier events, while a new partner often started one. Gaps between events varied widely. The study maps how change piles up in this stage of life.
pmc-10737978:
Vera Gorbunova wrote this conference paper, published in 2023, introducing a session on what gene activity patterns can reveal about aging and long life. The session compared these patterns across species with very different lifespans.

Gene activity in cells shifts fast and in steady ways when the body faces stress or change, so it offers a close-up view of aging. The talks covered shared gene patterns tied to long life across species. They also covered ways to merge gene data with protein data. Other speakers presented clocks that estimate biological age from gene activity. Still others covered single-cell studies of immune aging in humans. One talk dealt with how joining the blood flow of young and old animals can renew old tissue.
pmc-10738078:
David Russell, Christina Miyawaki, and Erin Bouldin interview dementia caregivers in rural Appalachia about services they cannot get, in a 2023 study. Dementia risk runs higher in rural areas while help runs thinner. The team wanted the local picture in western North Carolina.

They spoke with twenty-two caregivers and people with dementia between 2021 and 2022, recruited through local agencies. Families described fragile support networks, confusion about what services exist, and feeling behind in planning for the future. Whether they used a service turned on the illness's stage and family context as much as on supply. The study gives rural planners ground-level detail: names of the gaps, in the words of the people who live with them.
pmc-10738178:
Kexin Yu and colleagues described in 2023 how an online dementia research registry kept its Asian American volunteers engaged. Recruiting minority older adults is one of the hardest problems in Alzheimer's research, and weak recruitment slows treatment development. The registry, based in Oregon and Washington, lets adults enroll themselves online for future studies. By early 2023 it held just under five hundred participants.

The paper reports response and retention patterns and the adaptations the team made to recruit Asian Americans. Registry members averaged about sixty-four years old, and twenty research projects had already drawn participants from it. Most studies that tried the registry used it again. The lessons are practical: which outreach adjustments moved enrollment, and how an online-first design can still build trust with communities that research has historically underserved.
pmc-10740178:
YangHao Fu, TianDuo Wang, and John Ronald built a blood test that reports what immune cells are doing inside a tumor, in a study from twenty twenty-three. Cell therapies work well against blood cancers, but doctors lack cheap ways to watch the cells at work inside solid tumors. Blood signals rarely mirror tumor activity.

Their trick uses a synthetic receptor that switches on a custom gene when the immune cell touches its target. Engineered T cells carrying the receptor released a marker enzyme only when they met target-positive cancer cells. In mice, blood levels of the marker rose for target-positive tumors and stayed flat otherwise. The authors say the system could help explain why responses differ across patients.
pmc-10740578:
Liquan Cai and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-three, a cell pump and its control of heart cell power plants. The pump, Na/K-ATPase, moves sodium and potassium across the cell wall. It also talks to a kinase called Src, a switch protein. That talk has emerged as a way to tune mitochondria, the cell's power plants. The team used gene editing in human stem cells to make a pump variant that cannot signal through Src. Total pump activity stayed the same, but Src and related signals fell sharply.

Both normal and mutant stem cells grew into heart muscle cells, with markers and beating to prove it. Yet the mutant heart cells breathed much less at rest and at max. The axis thus shapes heart energy use.
pmc-10741078:
A team of researchers links common pain relievers to gut inflammation through mitochondrial stress in a paper from 2023. Crohn's disease mixes genetic risk with environmental triggers. Certain gene variants weaken a recycling process in gut cells, and pain drugs called NSAIDs are known triggers. The team showed these drugs stress mitochondria, the cell's energy units, in intestinal cells. In tissue models from Crohn's patients, the drugs switched on a mitochondrial stress response.

Stressed cells released mitochondrial parts that act as danger signals. Gut biopsies from patients in remission or with mild disease showed the same stress pathway active. Severe cases did not. The authors argue mitochondrial stress helps explain flare-ups after NSAID use.
pmc-10741178:
Menconi and co-authors sweep worm risks from fresh fish in Italy and kin lands. Fish fare has surged in Europe as a health food of late. Fresh fish holds weight for lake folk and guests who seek old dishes. That surge lit risks from worms borne in fish to men. Such worms now rank as world food germs in the text. Clans span round worms, fluke worms, and tape worms in the set.

Past 50 worm kinds can strike men from raw fish fare. Half-cooked fare with live worms drives those strikes in hosts. Yet such worms get less note than peer food germs in print. Slow ill pace and dim finds drive that gap in care. The sweep homes on six fresh-fish worms in the zone. Their rates in fish and hosts form the core facts.
pmc-10741778:
Paul Holvoet presents a 2023 review on why stem cells from fat tissue disappoint in heart disease trials. In animal studies these cells shielded arteries and hearts from stress and inflammation. In patients, the same cells have shown little benefit, and the author searched the literature for the reason.

Aging and metabolic change are the likely culprits. Older stem cells divide less, tire faster, and lose mitochondrial power. They also stir more inflammation and lay down more fat, weakening their ability to grow blood vessels and save heart muscle. The review names small regulatory RNAs whose rise or fall tracks these failures. Fixing that RNA pattern might restore the cells' healing power.
pmc-10742878:
Fairuz Bestari and co-authors pool studies on ultra-processed food and chronic disease in a 2023 analysis. Such foods, classed by the NOVA system, are engineered for taste and shelf life. They tend to pack energy, salt, sugar, and fat, while shorting fiber. The team gathered eighteen studies to measure dose-response links with major diseases.

Eating more of these foods raised intakes of sugar, salt, saturated fat, and energy by wide margins. Fiber intake fell far below the advised level. Each ten percent rise in their share of the diet tracked with higher hazard for diabetes most strongly. Heart disease, obesity, and cancer followed with smaller but clear links. The authors say capping daily intake of ultra-processed foods could help prevent obesity and its companion diseases. They frame dose, not mere presence, as the measure that matters.
pmc-10742978:
A research team published a research paper in 2023 on how well teeth can reveal a young person's age, tested in a large multiethnic sample. Age checks matter when migrants arrive without documents, and courts need to know if someone is a minor. The team compared three dental methods on jaw X-rays from 324 patients aged four to twenty.

All three methods overestimated age on average. After age eighteen, accuracy within one year fell below half for every method. Two methods missed by roughly 1.2 to 1.3 years on average, while the third missed by about two years. The authors conclude dental estimates alone cannot reliably decide minority.
pmc-10744078:
Muftah Mahmud, Swati Vasireddy, Krisstina Gowin, and Akshay Amaraneni review a family of blood diseases in which the marrow makes too many blood cells, in a 2023 paper. These diseases, and the overlap forms that share traits with a second group, can look very unlike from patient to patient. That range makes them hard to name and sort.

The review covers gene faults, chemical marks on genes, and chromosome changes, plus how they interact with immune cells. It then walks through signs, sorting rules, and treatments. New gene reading tools have widened what doctors know, the authors note. For advanced disease, a stem cell transplant remains the main path, even as drug care improves.
pmc-10744178:
Margo Hammond and co-authors published this transplant study in 2023. It asks whether traits of a heart donor predict whether the person who receives the heart later dies of heart-related causes. The authors reasoned that some causes of donor death stir the immune system strongly, and that this early immune activity could harm the recipient over time. They linked records for local adult donors to the outcomes of their recipients.

Donor age was known for 706 donors and donor sex for 730. Three donor traits went with more heart-related deaths among recipients: donor age over 40, female donor sex, and donor death from bleeding inside the skull. The authors suggest that watching for and calming donor immune activation might protect recipients. They note the study covers a single center, so wider checks are needed.
pmc-10744878:
A 32-year-old woman with an underactive thyroid from Hashimoto's disease arrived at hospital with worsening muscle pain, weakness, and frequent falls. Ergeta Ktona, Blerta Budani, Ioannis Kostas-Agnantis, and Alma Idrizi report her case because the trigger turned out to be unusual. Two weeks earlier she had been treated for what looked like ordinary flu.

Blood tests showed normal thyroid function but high levels of muscle damage markers. Antibody and DNA tests pointed to a heavy cytomegalovirus infection. Scans showed fierce inflammation across the muscles of her pelvis, thighs, and calves. A muscle biopsy on day seven confirmed polymyositis, an autoimmune attack on muscle. With medicine and physical therapy she improved markedly within two weeks. The authors discuss how virus and autoimmunity may intertwine.
pmc-10746078:
Children with inflammatory bowel disease face risks to growth and bone health. Their skeletons are still developing, which raises the stakes. Moon Bae Ahn and In Hyuk Yoo studied 51 Korean children and adolescents with newly diagnosed disease. The patients were aged 10 to 18. All had Crohn's disease or ulcerative colitis. The team measured bone mineral density in the spine and thigh bone at diagnosis. They compared the scores with body measurements and blood markers.

More than half the children had scores in the low-normal range. About one in five had thigh bone scores below minus 2. The authors report how common low density is at diagnosis. They also name the risk factors clinicians should watch.
pmc-10746978:
Claudio Cubillos and co-authors review, in 2023, digital tests that measure thinking skills in older adults. Spotting decline early matters, and software could make testing cheaper and wider. The team searched three databases and, after screening, kept twenty studies of apps and platforms for this purpose.

Most tools were computerized versions of paper tests, or test batteries run on computers, tablets, or the web. A few used simulators, virtual settings, or games built around daily tasks. The review maps which thinking skills were tested and how the tools were validated, and it flags gaps, such as thin evidence on some accuracy measures, for future developers.
pmc-10747478:
Anton Poroykov and four colleagues published a 2023 paper on measuring error in close-range photogrammetry. This method builds 3D shapes from flat photos, giving touch-free measures of a surface. It is used in fields from engineering to medicine.

Because the method chains many steps, its true error is hard to pin down. Math estimates and computer models miss real-world factors like lighting and lens flaws. The team built a system that gauges error from real test setups instead. A known test object lets them compare measured shape with truth. Direct checks give users a firmer sense of how much to trust each measure.
pmc-10747678:
A team of surgeons studies CT scans to plan nose-based pituitary surgery in a paper from 2023. The operation reaches the pituitary gland through the nose and a thin wall called the septum. Cutting away less septum is gentler, but the surgeon still needs room to work. The team simulated tool insertion on scans from twenty patients and compared the results with cadaver dissections.

The average predicted cut was about thirteen millimeters. In cadavers, a one-centimeter cut let a straight tool reach the key artery edge. A two-centimeter cut gave wider reach and a better view. Nasal width measures did not predict the needed cut. The authors say one centimeter suffices for standard tumors.
pmc-10747878:
Jiahong Yang and five co-authors build a machine learning system to detect autism spectrum disorder from brain scans and personal data, in a two thousand twenty-three neuroimaging paper. Autism's causes remain elusive, but its fingerprints appear in functional brain activity.

Their framework first prunes the imaging features with recursive feature elimination, then feeds survivors into a graph neural network over brain connectivity. A separate extractor handles phenotypic information such as age and test scores, and the two streams are fused. On the ABIDE benchmark the combined system reached about seventy-nine to eighty-one percent accuracy, competitive with leading methods. The authors present it as a step toward objective diagnostic support.
pmc-10747978:
Jiajun Ran and co-authors build a reliable gene-transfer system for watercress. Their 2023 paper improves how the salad plant takes up new genes. Watercress germplasm holds promise, but gene studies lacked a working pipeline. A strong regeneration method in their lab gave them the base.

Pretreatment, co-culture, and differentiation steps were each tuned. A marker gene for the hormone auxin was inserted as proof. Glow checks and DNA tests confirmed the transformed plants. The inserted reporter maps where auxin gathers during growth. The system now supports gene function studies in this crop. Breeders gain a tool for a small but valued plant.
pmc-10751078:
Akshay Athavale and Bridin Murnion review a drug family used for seizures and nerve pain. The drugs are gabapentinoids, sold for a short list of cleared uses. In Australia they are cleared for stubborn focal epilepsy and nerve pain. Use for vague back or leg pain is common, yet proof for it is thin.

The drugs can cause a mild high, sleepiness, and loose control, which invites misuse. Harm from misuse, both by chance and on purpose, has climbed. Long use can breed dependence, and a sudden stop can bring withdrawal. If the reason for use is murky, the authors urge a slow taper off. Kidney trouble raises the risk of harm. Each new script, they say, needs a clear weighing of help against harm.
pmc-10758678:
Sumit Acharya, Suraj Lama, and Durga Anil Kanigicherla published a review in twenty twenty-three on anti-thymocyte globulin, a frontline rescue drug when a transplanted kidney faces T-cell attack. The antibody preparation, made in rabbits or horses, depletes the T cells driving rejection, including cases that resist steroids. It is powerful but not benign.

The review walks through how the drug works beyond simple cell depletion and compares the commercial products. Trials disagree on the best dose and course length, leaving no firm standard. Early side effects like fever and rash contrast with long-term infection and cancer risks from deep immune suppression. The authors synthesize the efficacy evidence for reversing rejection episodes.
pmc-10772578:
Savary and a large team of co-authors grow mini-tumors in the lab to test drug pairs against a childhood muscle cancer. Rhabdomyosarcoma cure rates after relapse have stalled for two decades, partly for lack of good lab models. Their organoids come from relapsed tumors of the fusion-negative type.

The mini-tumors kept the molecular marks of the original cancers and grew for months. That stability suits them to drug screening with long follow-up. As a proof of concept, the team retested drugs that trigger cell death, guided by gene activity data. The authors present the model as a sharper way to pick drug combinations worth trying in patients.
pmc-10773678:
Martin Dufwenberg and four co-authors propose flushing the fluid that bathes the brain and cord with clean fluid as a way to guard nerves after harm. Brain and cord ills are hard to treat since the system is sealed by bone and a tight barrier. The article came out in twenty twenty-three.

That seal traps swelling agents, germs, and toxic waste near a wound, which can feed a harmful loop. Neck level access points can reach the fluid, though back taps are the norm. With tiny tubes and fluid filters now at hand, the authors ask if two tubes, one in and one out, could wash the fluid and break the loop. They lay out the case for trials of this flush idea.
pmc-10774478:
Hoang Kieu Chi Ngo, Hoang Le, and Young-Joon Surh wrote a perspective article in 2023 on a protein that controls how cells handle chemical stress. In healthy cells, turning the protein on helps block the start of cancer. In cells that are already cancerous, the same protein can help tumors grow, spread, and resist chemotherapy and radiation. Changes in its gene can lock it in an active state, and patients with that pattern tend to fare worse.

The authors review what is known about those gene changes and what they mean for judging a patient's outlook. They also weigh treatment ideas aimed at the protein, including small drug molecules, gene-silencing tools, and gene editing. For readers, the piece frames why a single target can be both protective and dangerous, and why treatment may need to match each tumor's exact state.
pmc-10792178:
Amirhossein Mirzaei and co-authors offer a 2023 systematic review of two citrus flavonoids, hesperidin and hesperetin, against diabetes and its complications. Plant compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory actions are much studied as add-on therapies. Proof from cells and molecules needed to sit in one place.

Three databases were searched through mid 2023. Hesperetin calmed inflammatory signalling through a major immune pathway. Hesperidin kept nerves safe in diabetes by switching on an antioxidant defence switch. Effects ran from cell level to whole-body metabolism across the studies covered. The pair emerge as credible options for human testing under tight control.
pmc-10800478:
Miwako Nishio and co-authors read antibody patterns in a rare, fatal disease where the Epstein-Barr virus infects the body's own killer cells. Their study appeared in 2023, though the catalog lists 2024. Using a Japanese nationwide survey, they analyzed 84 patients across childhood to old age. Antibodies against the virus's hidden nuclear protein appeared in most patients, but at lower levels than in healthy people. Antibodies against the virus's outer shell ran higher.

Patients with strong shell and early-protein antibody levels survived better at three years than those with weak ones. The authors read the pattern as a dulled immune aim at infected cells, partly compensated by anti-particle responses. They suggest antibody profiles could help predict the disease's course.
pmc-10808478:
Fangxiang Mu and co-authors survey what women with repeated pregnancy loss know and do about their condition in a 2023 study from Lanzhou, China. Self-management matters greatly in this condition, so 497 patients answered a questionnaire on knowledge, attitude, and daily practice.

Knowledge scored poor at about 58 percent of the maximum, attitudes were middling, and practice was surprisingly proactive at about 81 percent. Education and income fed knowledge, which in turn shaped attitudes and habits. Age mattered in a curved way, helping only under thirty-two. The authors pinpoint weak knowledge items for targeted teaching and groups needing extra support, so self-care guidance can close the knowing-doing gap they documented.
pmc-10863778:
When brain arteries narrow, doctors need to know how badly blood flow reserve has failed in each brain territory. Martina Sebök and co-authors tested whether an MRI-based measure can stage that failure as well as the standard PET method. Patients with one-sided narrowing had both scans. Experts staged each territory by eye on the PET images. The MRI measure, based on blood oxygen changes with carbon dioxide, was then matched against those stages.

The team derived cutoff values that split territories into failure stages. Training and test splits checked that the cutoffs held up. A working MRI cutoff would spare patients a scarce, costly PET scan. The study moves the MRI method toward routine stroke-risk care.
pmc-10962678:
Halil Koyu, Serdar Demir, and Mehmet Haznedaroglu study microwave extraction of red cabbage. Their study from twenty twenty-three seeks brain active compounds in the plant. Good extraction should cut solvent, time, and energy use.

Red cabbage is a mass grown food plant with health promise. Microwave settings were tuned for two enzyme block targets. Phenol, flavone, and pigment content were measured in extracts. Best settings split by which target was in focus. Microwave extracts beat standard solvent extracts on both counts. A key pigment fraction was isolated for more checks.
pmc-11018978:
Silage, the fermented feed that carries livestock through winter, depends on the microbes that arrive on the plants themselves. Xiaolong Tang and co-authors asked how much the source of those microbes matters. They took the natural microbe communities from alfalfa, from corn, and from the two mixed, and seeded each into alfalfa and corn mixed silage. The alfalfa born community performed best: it kept ammonia and acidity low while building more lactic acid, the preservative that good silage needs.

Silage seeded with the alfalfa community also kept more sugar and protein and less tough fiber than the other batches. Its bacterial community stayed richer and more diverse late into storage. The authors conclude that where the starter microbes come from shapes the whole fermentation, through competition during airless storage. The paper, published in 2023, suggests farmers could improve feed quality by managing the microbes riding on their forage.
pmc-11182278:
Tais Estrela and Linda Dagi review optic nerve damage in children born with fused skull seams in a paper published in 2023. The catalog lists 2024, but the journal record in the text gives 2023. Fused seams can raise pressure inside the skull. That pressure swells and then wastes the optic nerve. Sleep apnea, odd vein growth, and a brain malformation can add to the harm.

The review walks through causes, checks, and care for the nerve damage. Eye doctors also manage crossed eyes, uneven focus, and exposure damage in these children. Their reports help decide when skull surgery must be done or redone. Early spotting of nerve swelling is the main defense against permanent sight loss.
pmc-11225478:
Tumwine wrote an editorial in twenty twenty-three welcoming readers to a December issue of African Health Sciences. He surveys the papers chosen for that issue. The issue appeared while the COP28 climate talks met in the Middle East amid major conflict.

The papers cover infections such as tuberculosis and COVID-19, plus other bacterial, fungal, and viral illness. Others deal with breast cancer, high blood pressure, and diabetes, along with goiter, kidney disease, and trauma. Further sets cover sexual and reproductive health, nutrition, and mental health. Tumwine closes by hoping the goodwill at the climate talks spreads, and he wishes readers a peaceful festive season.
pmc-11446378:
Ziman Chen and co-authors published a report in 2023 on China's first national student competition for carbon dioxide capture, conversion, and use. The contest, called the Bloomag Cup, was launched by professors at Beijing University of Chemical Technology and held in Beijing in July 2023. Universities will take turns hosting it each year.

Students and researchers from across the country presented ideas for trapping carbon and turning it into useful products. Organizers say the point is to surface breakthroughs early, train new talent, and push the young field forward. The hope is that the yearly contest keeps seeding technology that helps curb climate change while supporting greener growth.
pmc-11532478:
Shuhui Hou, Hui Xu, Shating Lei, and Dong Zhao studied an enzyme that runs high in tissue from women with endometriosis, in a paper from twenty twenty-four. In this condition, tissue like the womb lining grows where it should not, causing pain. The enzyme helps control cell chemistry, and its role in the disease was unclear.

The enzyme was higher in patient tissue and in lab-grown cells from patients. Blocking it slowed cell growth, movement, and spread, and shrank lesions in mice. The hormone estrogen and signals from immune cells both raised the enzyme. Cutting it lowered activity in a growth pathway inside the cells. The authors name this pathway as a possible drug target.
pmc-11539678:
Rui Li and eleven co-authors published this study in 2024. It compares the milk-producing cells of two sheep breeds at the gene level. East Friesian sheep are champion milkers; Sewa sheep, a hardy breed of the Qinghai-Tibet Plateau, give far less milk, and the difference's genetic roots are sought here.

The team grew mammary cell lines from both breeds and confirmed their identity with marker stains. Sequencing the cells' active genes found 1,813 differences, over eleven hundred turned up in Sewa cells and the rest turned down. The differing genes clustered in signaling, metabolism, and cell-process categories, with signal transduction the largest single group. Two genes, ATF3 and MPP7, emerged as candidate regulators of lactation. The authors offer the comparison as a starting map for breeding and gene studies aimed at milk yield. They note the work is in cultured cells, so whole-animal confirmation must follow.
pmc-11569378:
Jinxing Wei and four co-authors review how small RNAs steer cell self-eating and drug proof in cancer. Their review appeared in twenty twenty-four. Small RNAs tune gene use post-birth and can switch self-eat paths on or off. Self-eat keeps cells in line but can help tumors live and shrug off chemo.

Some small RNAs act as tumor drivers and some as brakes, by which self-eat path they hit. That split makes the RNA and self-eat pair a rich cure field. The review maps the links by gene and path in each cancer kind. It then weighs cures that tune the pair and calls for deep work on the webs.
pmc-11571878:
Liqin Lu and co-authors present a 2024 journal article building a questionnaire on what university students know, feel, and do about novel psychoactive substances. These lab-made drugs spread fast on campuses, and educators need a sound measuring tool. The team drafted items from the literature and expert advice, then tested the survey on 587 students in Fujian.

Weak items were cut through statistical screens, and factor analysis settled on five subdimensions. The final model fit well, with reliability scores above 0.9 overall. One weakness remained in separating the dimensions cleanly. The authors offer the tool for gauging drug education needs and effects.
pmc-11575778:
Islam and co-authors warn that landfill leachate quietly harms soils in the temperate Himalayas. Landfills are the cheapest, most common waste option in much of the world. In developing nations such as India, poorly managed dumps let hazardous liquid seep into the ground around them.

That liquid, called leachate, is a strong point source of pollution for soil, water, and other media. The study examines how it lowers soil quality near Himalayan dump sites. Mountain soils recover slowly, so damage can last for decades. The authors press for better dump control in fragile highland regions.
pmc-11585978:
Yongping Cao, Mengyun Zhou, and Tianhong Xu report a 2024 study on whether three joint diseases cause a scaly skin disease. The three diseases attack joints in adults and in children, and the skin disease often shows up near their diagnosis. Shared genes may drive both, which a gene-based method can test without a trial.

The team drew gene data from a large open bank for all four diseases. Single-disease checks found causal links from each of the three joint diseases to the skin disease. Checks for bias and noise backed those finds. A joint check that weighed all three at once kept two as risk factors, while the adult joint disease lost its effect. The work adds to grasp of how the skin disease starts.
pmc-11586978:
Som Singh and colleagues wrote an opinion article in 2024 arguing that medicine's favorite yardstick for patient handouts measures less than its users think. Pamphlets and digital handouts increasingly carry the work of explaining care, and readability formulas grade how hard their text is to comprehend. Study after study finds medical materials missing the recommended sixth to eighth grade reading level, and the field has responded by demanding simpler text.

Reviewing the literature across pediatrics, internal medicine, prevention, and surgery, the authors caution that readability is not health literacy, and neither is the same as a patient actually understanding and acting. A formula counting syllables cannot see layout, prior knowledge, fear, or trust. Their nominated frontier is generative artificial intelligence, which might rewrite and personalize materials on demand, though they note few current tools match that promise, so the innovation gap remains open.
pmc-11587678:
Immune cells can be rebuilt by design to do jobs they never evolved for, and Naoki Hosen, a solo author, introduces a series of reviews on these designer immune cells. The model case is CAR T-cell therapy, where a patient's T cells are fitted with a synthetic receptor that hunts cancer. Versions aimed at blood cancers have shown striking power in the clinic.

Other cell types are joining in, including natural killer cells, macrophages, and cells grown from stem cells, armed with a growing range of synthetic receptors. The reviews he gathers cover stem-cell-grown killer T cells, fresh cancer targets, T-cell wear-out and how to beat it, and gene editing tools. Hosen frames the field as a new kind of medicine built from living cells.
pmc-11588678:
Niels Brevé and co-authors published this habitat study in 2024 on the European sturgeon, a critically endangered fish. Bringing it back to the Rhine needs proof the river still offers spawning and nursery ground. The team reviewed the fish's needs, then modeled depth and flow over more than 350 kilometers of the delta and lower Rhine, in two lands.

Prime spawning ground came to just 0.75 square kilometers, enough for about 2,500 females. That is ample, since at most 750 adults of the fish are thought to live. Most spawning ground sits in Germany's North Rhine-Westphalia, and most nursery ground in the Netherlands. Dams and shipping lanes cut the true supply. The authors say the map can guide where to guard or restore habitat, and the method can travel to other rivers.
pmc-11590278:
Qiaoqiao Zhang and colleagues report a rare success against a brain lymphoma tied to HIV, in this report from twenty twenty-four. The cancer, a diffuse large B-cell lymphoma growing in the brain, is one of the most common tumors in people with AIDS. Its outlook is usually grim. Whether surgery helps was long debated.

Their patient was a man of thirty with AIDS. He arrived with dizziness and headache, after a first hospital read his scans as a different tumor. New scans and tissue tests showed the lymphoma in the left cerebellar hemisphere. Surgeons removed it. He then had two weeks of radiotherapy and seven rounds of a drug mix, DA-EPOCH. His symptoms eased, the cancer vanished on follow-up, and four years on it had not returned. The authors argue that surgery fits lone, reachable tumors, best when paired with radiation and drugs.
pmc-11590478:
Yuki Suzuki and colleagues tested a local antibiotic method in 2024 for infected knee replacements. Infections around artificial knees are among the hardest problems in bone care. The method washes the joint nonstop with strong antibiotic fluid. The team reviewed fourteen patients with such infections. Acute cases got cleaning surgery plus the wash, keeping the implant. Chronic cases got a two-stage implant swap with the wash. Gentamicin flowed into the joint daily for two weeks. Vein antibiotics ran alongside in all cases.

All acute patients kept their implants after one-stage care. Most chronic patients cleared infection with the two-stage plan. Two chronic patients failed the first attempt at keeping implants. A later two-stage redo succeeded for both. No side effects from the local drug were reported. Follow-up ran well over a year on average. The authors judge the wash safe and likely helpful.
pmc-11591578:
Yu and co-authors test whether chatbots can diagnose a mouth disease from photos in this 2024 study. Oral lichen planus is a chronic inflammatory condition that is hard to spot early. Diagnosis usually rests on a clinician's experience and judgment.

The team gathered lesion images from 128 confirmed patients. Three AI platforms judged the images, first cold and then after feature training. Training lifted recognition sharply: one model rose from 59 to 77 percent, another from 68 to 80, and a third from 15 to 50. Cheek lesions were easiest, reaching the mid-90s for two models. Gum lesions stayed hard, near 60 percent at best. The authors see promise with clear site limits.
pmc-11595178:
Gabriela Fonseca-Camarillo and colleagues measure guidance proteins in inflamed bowel tissue. Their study from twenty twenty-four covers semaphorins and their plexin receptors. These proteins steer cells and regulate immune activity. Their pattern in inflammatory bowel disease was unknown before.

Fifty-four patients and twenty controls supplied intestinal tissue. Gene and protein levels were measured for the family. One guidance gene fell in ulcerative colitis tissue. Its receptor fell too, while another receptor rose. Stains located the proteins near immune cell types. Expression levels tracked clinical disease features in patients. Immune steering molecules may shape bowel inflammation course.
pmc-11595578:
Scherer and five co-authors mine a German trauma registry for how often badly injured patients lose a limb. Their data covered 32,572 severely injured patients with limb fractures treated between 2009 and 2019. Car crashes caused most injuries, and over half the patients also had severe chest trauma.

Amputation stayed rare: 242 upper-limb and 422 lower-limb cases. The share rose steeply when overall injury severity passed the highest band. Patients with severe chest injuries were amputated more often in both limb groups. The authors offer the numbers as a planning base for trauma centers. They note the salvage-versus-amputation call still hinges on the limb's state and the patient's stability.
pmc-11597378:
Yushuo Wu and co-authors test a fungicide, thifluzamide, against a rot that attacks stored Huangguan pears. The fungus Rhizoctonia solani breaks into fruit by releasing enzymes that chew through cell walls. The team measured how the treatment changed those enzymes in lab culture, and how it changed the pear's own defense chemistry.

After three days, the treatment clearly slowed all six wall-breaking enzymes the fungus makes. In the fruit, it raised the work of three defense-linked enzymes and lifted levels of flavonoids and total phenols, compounds that help plants resist attack. Gene activity in the same defense pathway rose as well. The authors conclude the fungicide fights the rot two ways at once: it weakens the fungus's tools and primes the fruit to defend itself.
pmc-11599278:
Yan-li Zhang, Chao Ran, and Wei Li present a 2024 study of scan traits in lung infection by a fungus called cryptococcus. Patients answer care at unlike speeds, and scans may show who will lag. The team compared records and images from 70 patients: 37 full responders and 33 partial ones. They hunted scan and clinical traits that split the groups and weighed each trait's call power.

Partial responders more often had weak immunity, mid-course spread, and disease on both sides. Fluid near the lung and swollen chest nodes also clustered in that group. Three traits stood as lone risk marks: weak immunity, mid progress, and two-sided spread. Joined, the three called the outcome well. Scan reads could warn teams early about slow cases.
pmc-11600878:
Collin Sakal, Wenxing Zhao, Wenxin Xu, and Xinyue Li present a 2024 study of caffeine, sleep, and activity in older adults living their normal lives. Good sleep and daily movement both support a long life after sixty-five. Caffeine might lift activity, but it could also cost sleep, and that trade off was untested in daily life.

The team used data from a national health survey of adults aged sixty-five and older, from 2011 to 2014. Wrist sensors gave sleep and activity measures, worked out with a learning method. Caffeine intake was sorted by dose, both by body weight and by total amount. The study then looked for links across the dose groups.
pmc-11600978:
Duan and co-authors test if depression raises the risk of acid reflux disease, using genetics as a tool. Reports link depression with gastroesophageal reflux, but cause and effect were unclear. Mendelian randomization uses gene variants tied to depression to probe that direction of influence.

The method is less prone to the lifestyle mix-ups that cloud watch-based studies. The team also asked which risk factors carry part of any effect, acting as middle steps. Traits like body weight or smoking may sit on the path. Results help explain how mood and reflux connect and where prevention may work.
pmc-11602778:
Sana Barakat, Mohamed Abdel-Fadeel, Ola Sharaki, Mohamed El Shafei, Basant Elbanna, and Aml Mahfouz wrote a 2024 paper on a stomach bacterium and fatty liver in children. The bacterium, Helicobacter pylori, lives in many stomachs and can cause ulcers. Fatty liver not caused by alcohol is also rising in children. The team asked whether the infection raises the odds of the liver disease.

They compared one hundred children with fatty liver, found by ultrasound, with one hundred without it. Stool tests found the bacterium in sixty-four percent of the liver group and twenty-five percent of the others. Blood tests then checked which strains the infected children carried. A link this strong in children argues for more study of whether treating the infection helps the liver.
pmc-11602878:
Fatemeh Estaji and co-authors present a 2024 review of Epstein-Barr virus in stomach cancer. Stomach cancer stays a top cause of cancer death worldwide. Its causes join lifestyle, family history, gene faults, and infections. Epstein-Barr virus infects over ninety-five percent of people, usually silently for life. It was the first virus found in a human tumor. Its role in stomach cancer is now a settled research topic, though key mechanisms stay disputed.

The review centers on epigenetic mechanisms: chemical marks that switch genes without changing DNA. Immune shifts and gene mutations get coverage as well. Contradictions on whether the virus worsens outlook are weighed openly. Oncologists get a map of how a near-universal virus can drive one cancer in a small minority. That minority question is the puzzle: the marks the virus leaves may explain why only some carriers develop tumors.
pmc-11603178:
Li and seven colleagues publish the full gene map of the Suminoe oyster from south China in twenty twenty-four. The oyster is a key species for both sea ecology and fishery trade around the world. Their map spans the full set of ten chromosomes, built from three kinds of gene reading tools. It is sharper and more complete than past maps of the species.

The map holds close to thirty thousand protein coding genes, most with known roles. More than half of the genome is made of repeated stretches. The team also logged over a thousand non coding RNA genes. The map can guide breeding, stock care, and study of oyster diversity and evolution.
pmc-11606178:
Caitlin Caspi and eight co-authors ask how low-wage parents fared with COVID-19 relief aid. Aid ranged from cash payments and food support to a larger child tax credit and a pause on evictions. The team held long interviews in 2022 with forty parents in two United States cities. Parents named red tape, office errors, and poor information as blocks, even when they clearly qualified.

Aid that arrived on its own, with no forms to file, reached families best. Most parents spoke well of the help once it came. The paper draws lessons for how relief can reach working families with less strain.
pmc-11607278:
Fei Teng and co-authors published this study in 2024. It hunts for shared roots between preeclampsia, a dangerous pregnancy condition, and endometrial cancer of the womb lining. Both involve immune imbalance, vessel trouble, and new blood vessel growth. The team mined gene and immune data for overlaps. From that search they built a five-gene risk model for the cancer.

The model split patients into high- and low-risk groups with clearly different survival. Low-risk patients lived longer and showed richer immune activity in their tumors. The five genes also play roles in preeclampsia, backing the shared-roots idea. The authors suggest the genes could serve as outlook markers for the cancer. They also see a path toward treatment plans tuned to each patient's risk profile.
pmc-11607978:
Ching-Hua Yeh and co-authors study a gene that is switched off in liver cancer and helps tumors spread, in this 2024 paper. The gene, PAX6, guides early body development and is often silenced by chemical tags in cancer. Its role in liver cancer was unclear.

The team confirmed that heavy tagging silences the gene in tumor cells. Restoring it slowed cell growth and invasion in dishes and shrank tumors in mice. Blocking it had the opposite effect, speeding growth. Gene-reading work then traced which target genes carry out its protective effect. The findings name a possible new lever against liver cancer spread.
pmc-11608878:
Luana Maroja and co-authors re-examined a famous hybrid zone where two field cricket species meet and interbreed. Earlier genome scans found patches of strong difference between Gryllus firmus and Gryllus pennsylvanicus, mostly on the X chromosome. Those patches were read as islands where genes cannot cross between species, set in a sea of free exchange. The team sequenced a reference genome and sampled eight populations far from the hybrid zone to test that reading.

Away from the zone, the high-difference patches did not show the high absolute divergence the islands model predicts. Nuclear DNA also put the species split near eight hundred thousand years ago, four times older than mitochondrial estimates. The authors argue the island story needs rethinking, and that some patches may reflect other forces.
pmc-11612378:
Bive Bive Zono and a team including Marie-Pierre Hayette screen people with advanced HIV in Kinshasa for a hidden fungal infection. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. The fungus, Cryptococcus neoformans, can invade the brain and kill, yet it can sit silent in the blood first.

The team tested two hundred and sixty-two outpatients whose immune counts were very low. Forty-seven, about eighteen in each hundred, tested positive for the fungal marker in blood. Half of those who agreed to a spinal tap turned out to have the fungus in their spinal fluid, though they had no symptoms. The team typed the fungi and compared them with strains from sick patients in the same clinics. The results back routine screening so treatment can start before the brain is hit.
pmc-11612578:
Huitong Ding, Katherine Gifford, Ludy Shih, and a large team ask older adults what they think of brain health technology in this two thousand twenty-four cohort study. Digital platforms promise earlier Alzheimer's risk prediction and monitoring, but older users' perspectives had not been studied. Twenty-eight participants from a Boston University Alzheimer's research center used a digital brain health platform. The initial assessment period lasted fourteen days. Semistructured interviews about their experiences were transcribed and analyzed with natural language processing.

Word counts leaned positive: like, well, and good were the most frequent positive terms. Words like problem and hard flagged real friction points in using the platform. Sentiment analysis showed a slightly positive overall emotional tone toward the tool. The authors present the study as early evidence on acceptability. A monitoring platform only works if intended users actually engage with it; this study probes that human side.
pmc-11613378:
Xiao Zheng and Jinjuan Xu test a liver-protecting drug during tuberculosis treatment in a study from two thousand twenty-four. TB drugs strain the liver, and a licorice-derived compound may shield it. Records of one hundred thirteen patients at one hospital were reviewed.

Fifty-eight patients got the compound alongside standard TB therapy; fifty-five got therapy alone. The protected group fared better overall and suffered less liver injury. Liver blood markers rose in both groups during treatment, but stayed lower with the compound. Side effect rates did not differ between groups. The authors conclude the add-on improves the treatment's overall effect while easing liver harm. They frame it as a practical companion to standard regimens.
pmc-11614878:
Finding the slip face a slope will fail on is a search with many false floors. Wei Qin and Jiancheng Zhao breed computer guesses at the face in 2024 with a tuned gene-style search. Their cross-breeding step mixes two codings at once, a tweak they first set right on six toy puzzles with known bests. The slope's safety score comes from a classic slice method.

On five slopes from past studies, the search found the true worst face and its score, matching the known answers. Knob tests showed the count of face-shaping points is the make-or-break set. Head to head, the search beat two rival hunters on the same slopes. The team pitch it for dam and road cuts where a missed face costs lives.
pmc-11615378:
Yang Chen and co-authors reviewed chromatin accessibility in a 2024 paper. A cell's DNA is packed into chromatin, and only the open stretches can be read, copied, or repaired. Closed zones sit in dense heterochromatin, while open ones hold fewer packing spools and far more control switches.

The review maps what open chromatin does, how the cell tunes it, and how genes, marks, and surroundings all play in. It then turns to therapy: drugs that pry chromatin open or seal it shut. Reading the open map has become a standard lens on disease, from cancer to rare syndromes.
pmc-11616378:
Bo Xiong, Yuxiao Chen, and Ning Chen ask, in twenty twenty-four, whether living longer means living healthier, across two hundred four countries from nineteen ninety to twenty nineteen. Life expectancy and healthy life expectancy both rose globally, but at different rates. The gap between them is years lived in poor health. Using Global Burden of Disease data, the team tracked both measures at birth and at age sixty-five. Countries were sorted into three types: optimization, low deterioration, and high deterioration, by how the gap moved.

Statistical models then weighed which risks drive each type: environmental, behavioral, and metabolic. For men at birth, drug use mattered most in optimization countries. Low physical activity led in low deterioration ones. Childhood abuse and bullying led in high deterioration ones.
pmc-11619178:
Andrea Mudd and co-authors present a 2024 analysis of how health research uses a complex systems lens. The lens treats health inequality as the product of many linked parts, with feedback loops and delays. It has grown popular in studies of income gaps in health and behavior, but its use may lag behind its fame.

Building on a prior scoping review, the authors graded studies with a traffic-light tool. They checked how fully eight key ideas, such as feedback loops, were applied and reported. Studies that used more of the ideas also reported the direction of links more often. The deepest level of the paradigm was rarely reached. The authors call for reporting guidelines so future work states its methods plainly.
pmc-11620678:
Xinmei Li and co-authors compare two ways to track where a drug spreads in the body, in a study from 2024. The drug is mefuparib, a cancer drug, tagged so its spread can be measured. The team worked with two common types of lab rat and asked if the method or the rat type changed the results.

One method takes images of thin slices of the whole body, and the other burns tissue samples and counts the tag. Both methods found the drug in the same set of tissues, and most results matched well. Blood and brain results were alike in both rat types. Liver and kidney levels, though, were much higher in one rat type. The work helps labs choose methods and animals for such tests.
pmc-11622478:
Jinghui Chi, Shuping Li, and eight co-authors studied loneliness in people with schizophrenia in China, in work from twenty twenty-four. Loneliness is the felt sense of being cut off; social isolation is the plain fact of few ties. Both run high in this group. The team asked if the two differ by sex, and how each ties to symptoms and thinking skills.

They assessed three hundred twenty-three long-term patients, more women than men. Set scales scored mood symptoms, brain skills, loneliness, and isolation side by side. The team then weighed the pull of each factor, alone and paired, for men and women apart. The aim is care that fits the distinct needs each sex shows.
pmc-11623478:
Jinhuan Tang and co-authors present a study from two thousand twenty-four on rivalry between car makers under a green policy. China's dual credit policy pushes makers of new energy vehicles and gasoline vehicles to balance output and emissions. The authors model the two sides as a long-term game played with production delays.

Using complex system theory, they track stable zones, sudden splits in behavior, and chaos in the joint decisions. Fast adjustment by either side can tip the system into disorder. In stable zones, gasoline makers' emission changes did not move output for either side. Delayed production choices, they find, can help steady the market.
pmc-11623978:
Six clinicians report a rare immune side effect of a cancer drug in a case report from 2024. The drug, durvalumab, boosts the immune system against tumors but can turn it against healthy tissue. A seventy-two-year-old man treated for lung cancer developed muscle weakness and skin hardening. He was admitted with breathing failure from weak muscles and raised lung pressure.
