pmc-11685278:
Jin-Hong Yoo introduces the contents of a journal issue dated 30 December 2024 in this editorial summary. The issue holds one review and four original research articles. Rather than a study of its own, the piece walks through each article in turn, giving the main question, the data, and the headline result. It serves as a guided table of contents for readers of the journal.

The first summary covers a study of a tumour protein in 229 surgically removed small intestine cancers, where high levels meant better survival. The second looks at genetic testing in 1,554 Korean patients with suspected heart muscle disease, which found disease-causing variants in over forty percent. Later summaries take up caesarean delivery on request and other topics. The piece lets busy clinicians scan the issue's worth in a few minutes.
pmc-11688178:
Nizar Mourad and Pierre Gianello review, in a 2024 paper, a new line of pigs bred so their insulin-making cells release far more insulin. Pig islet transplants could treat diabetes, but pig cells respond weakly to sugar, so huge cell numbers are now needed. Most gene edits in donor pigs aim to calm the immune attack on the graft.

Recent work found signal pathways that amplify insulin release in pig cells, as they do in mice and humans. Pigs were bred with those pathways switched on only in insulin cells. Their islets released more insulin in the body, in the dish, and after transplant into diabetic mice. Stronger cells could cut the dose each patient needs.
pmc-11688778:
Korijna Valenti and Sara Bybee present a set of studies on the health care needs of older adults who are gay, trans, or in kin groups summed up as LGBTQIA+. The set is from two thousand twenty-four.

The studies look at bias, being made welcome, and clear talk in care. One drew on twenty trained doctors who treat the very ill, and asked how they speak with such patients and their chosen care partners. One asked care home heads in a midwest state how they find and treat such residents, and what blocks full welcome. The set argues that these older adults have needs of their own, in voice, in policy, and in daily support.
pmc-11688978:
Ryan McGrath, Kelly Parker, and Jeremy Hamm test whether finer grip measures detect cognitive impairment in older adults better than raw strength, in work published in 2024. An electronic grip device can record more than peak force. It can also capture how steadily a person holds a set force and how fast force rises.

The study covered 125 adults aged 65 and over. Thinking status was graded with a standard mental status exam. People with impairment held a grip at a quarter of their peak far less steadily than intact peers. Men with impairment also raised force more slowly. Peak strength itself did not differ between groups. The authors suggest the finer measures, which respond to behaviour change, may flag early decline that strength misses.
pmc-11689378:
Alexander Garbin presents a 2024 conference presentation summary on screening older veterans' fall risk through video visits. Primary care often lacks time for full fall assessments. The study used the veterans' health system's video platform to measure risk remotely in patients already flagged as high risk. Tests adapted for the home included a sit-to-stand measure, fear-of-falling and home-hazard surveys, and a medication review tool.

Interviews with veterans and their primary care providers explored how fall risk is currently handled and how telehealth fits. The presentation reports the prevalence of falls and risk factors found, plus the perceived barriers and facilitators of virtual assessment. Garbin argues virtual platforms can carry much of this work outside crowded clinics. The piece aims to reassure clinicians worried about safety and measurement quality at a distance.
pmc-11689578:
Emma Nichols and five co-authors ask, in twenty twenty-four, if the time taken on brain tests adds useful facts in surveys. Fast tests have long hinted that speed holds a signal. Surveys often record time per item but rarely use it. The team used a large India aging study with more than four thousand people. It held thirty-five test items, from simple facts to hard recall tasks.

Taking longer than the middle group linked to worse brain scores on many items. Answering fast linked to better scores on simple items. But fast answers linked to worse scores on hard items. The authors say time is worth using, but its meaning flips by task type.
pmc-11689778:
Amy Kelley presented this session description in 2024. It introduces the National Institute on Aging, part of the United States National Institutes of Health. The session was aimed at researchers who are early in their careers and want to know what the institute funds.

The institute supports research on aging across the lifespan, from basic biology to the care of older adults. It gives special weight to Alzheimer's disease and related dementias. The session outlines the kinds of grants on offer and gives advice on applying, with tips for students, junior faculty, and new scholars. It ends with small group talks led by institute staff, where attendees could ask about paths that fit their own stage.
pmc-11690378:
Kristen Beavers and five co-authors report a trial on weight loss and bone health in older adults. Their twenty twenty-four paper covers the INVEST trial. Weight loss can thin bone and raise fracture risk. The trial asked if wearing a weighted vest, to replace lost weight, could guard bone. A third group did strength training instead of vest use.

One hundred fifty adults joined, and most finished the year-long trial. All groups lost about nine to eleven percent of body weight. Vest users wore the vest about seven hours a day. They replaced most lost weight in the vest. Strength group members came to most of their sessions.
pmc-11690778:
DeGroot develops in 2024 a digital palliative care tool that includes the patient's social convoy, the partners, family, and friends who give care. Digital health often leaves that circle out. The Convoy-Pal program was built with user centered design input from clinicians, older adults with serious illness, and their convoys, 81 people in all.

The twelve week program gives a tablet, a smartwatch, and phone access options, shared between patient and convoy. It tracks symptoms and offers care resources based on answers. Early users rated its information highly. A small waitlist trial with 46 people then tested feasibility, with retention at 67.4 percent and caregiver recruitment the main strain.
pmc-11691278:
Alex Laffer and co-authors published this 2024 quality improvement report on training nurse practitioners for hospice and palliative care inside the Veterans Administration. Palliative services are scarce because the workforce is thin, and clinicians who grow interested mid-career face steep routes back to school. The project builds the training into the job instead.

The twelve-month program asks at least 500 clinical hours from nurse practitioners working in a VA Community Living Center. Its curriculum is mostly practical: interprofessional teamwork, hard conversations, and medical, psychosocial, cultural, spiritual, and ethical content woven longitudinally. Two protected hours a day pair hospice experiences with team learning, while participants keep their regular duties. The authors offer the model as a workforce lever other centers can copy.
pmc-11691678:
Hui-Ching Weng and three co-authors published a study in 2024 comparing preferences and attitudes toward advance directives in Taiwan and Thailand. An advance directive is a written document that states what medical treatment a person wants if they later become unable to speak for themselves.

The researchers matched 259 pairs of people from the two countries by sex, age, education, and background in medical work. Both groups felt much the same about the need for advance directives at their current stage of life, and both supported family decision-making during hospitalization. Differences appeared in how comfortable people felt discussing death and end-of-life care, with comfort higher in Taiwan. People in Taiwan also had more confidence that peers their own age would consider advance directives. All eight qualities sought in a health care proxy were rated higher in Taiwan.
pmc-11691778:
Erik Knight and co-authors published a 2024 study on a mundane question with real consequences: does eating before a blood draw change hormone readings in older adults? Biomarker studies usually demand fasting samples, yet the same volunteers often do thinking tests fed. If a meal shifts hormone levels, mixing the two states corrupts the science.

Thirty older adults, averaging sixty-seven years, attended two morning lab sessions after fasting overnight. Blood was drawn hourly, four times per session. A meal arrived after the second draw in one session and after the fourth in the other, so each person served as their own control. Eight hormones were measured with precise chemistry. The team modeled the meal's effect with Bayesian methods. The study is the kind of methodological housekeeping that quietly decides whether flashier findings can be trusted. Aging research leans on these markers; knowing their meal sensitivity protects every study downstream.
pmc-11691878:
Emma Quach, Lauren Moo, Emily Franzosa, Pengsheng Ni, Shibei Zhao, and Christine Hartmann wrote a 2024 paper on home services for veterans with dementia in the United States. Home care and adult day programs help such veterans stay in the community. The team asked which veterans use them, and whether the kind of care team they belong to matters.

They used 2019 records for more than one hundred forty-three thousand veterans with dementia. Patients were grouped by their other illnesses and by team type, such as home-based primary care or a dementia clinic. Use of both services together was linked with every team type at every illness level. The results show care teams act as gateways to support at home.
pmc-11692078:
Victoria Cirone and six co-authors published a pilot study in 2024 on high-intensity interval training for women in perimenopause, the transition period before menopause. Hormonal changes during this stage can harm memory and brain health. Interval training alternates short bursts of intense exercise with periods of active recovery, and it may help while fitting into busy lives.

Six women took part over twelve weeks, recruited across seventeen months. Most adhered to the program, with a high attendance rate. One woman withdrew, slightly above the team's target rate. Cardiovascular fitness barely changed. Delayed recall of word lists, however, improved by a large and statistically clear margin. Brain scans also tracked the volume of a key memory region and the state of myelin, the insulation around nerve fibers. The team describes the program as feasible and worth testing in a larger trial.
pmc-11692878:
Jessica Bibbo and five co-authors evaluate an online training that teaches prison staff about dementia. Their study came out in 2024. People aging in prison develop dementia at higher rates than the general population, and the share of older inmates is rising fast, yet staff training is rare.

The course, built with Ohio's corrections department, was offered to all staff; several hundred took optional surveys around it. Knowledge improved on a key item about environment and dementia. Attitudes improved on five measures, including confidence in interacting with people who have dementia. About nine in ten respondents called the material useful and said they would recommend it to co-workers. The authors see e-learning as a scalable way to fill a neglected training gap.
pmc-11692978:
Duy Nguyen and three co-authors ask, in a 2024 study, whether early childhood experiences shape cognitive function in late life. They study older adults in China, a group often overlooked in past work on childhood adversity. Their data come from the China Health and Retirement Longitudinal Study, a national survey that tracks health and life history, with waves from 2011 to 2020.

The sample held 9,941 people aged 50 and over at the start, all free of cognitive impairment then and still living at the last wave. Weak neighborhood quality and social cohesion in childhood, poor social relationships, and poor childhood health all tracked with worse cognitive scores in late life. Self-rated memory told the same story. The authors argue that steps to improve child health and social bonds could protect minds decades later, in China and beyond its borders.
pmc-11693178:
Esther Shin, BoRin Kim, and Sojung Park sort the long care paths of older adults who live at home and tie them to well being, in a 2024 journal article. Care can come from kin for free or from paid hands, and the mix shifts with health, wealth, and place. Past work often read one source alone.

Using a national aging study from 2011 to 2022, the team kept 1,200 adults over seventy who had care all through. A joint path model found four patterns: thin care all along, one kin carer for most, many kin carers, and a dual mix of kin and paid help. Most sat in the one kin group. The thin care group was more often unwed, schooled, and living alone with movement ills. The authors map who lands where.
pmc-11695878:
Eman Abdellatif and Emad Hamouda test whether a simple ratio of two blood markers can forecast survival in sepsis, in this 2024 study. One hundred seventy intensive care patients in Alexandria were followed, with the ratio of C-reactive protein to procalcitonin taken on admission and again on day three. Standard severity scores were recorded beside it.

Patients who died carried a markedly lower ratio at both time points, and the ratio also ran lower in septic shock. A low ratio tracked with worse severity scores across the board. As a day-one predictor of death, the ratio scored close to the best standard score and beat either marker alone. The authors propose it as a cheap early warning.
pmc-11709378:
Cory Funk, Tom Paterson, Jennifer Rohrs, and Timothy Hohman published this Alzheimer's study in 2025. It explores a tipping-point idea about microglia, the brain's cleanup cells. These cells swallow debris and store its fats in droplets. The authors propose that disease accelerates when the droplets saturate and the buffering fails. They tested the idea on data from the ADNI cohort, grouping 608 people by a cognitive score and comparing blood fats with spinal fluid proteins across the groups.

One score band stood out sharply, the range where people slip from normal thinking toward mild impairment. Within it sat two groups progressing at different speeds. The faster group's proteins pointed to droplet signaling in microglia and to fat-processing changes. Certain gene variants tied to Alzheimer's risk also split between the groups. The authors say the signature might one day help predict, at diagnosis, whose disease will move fast.
pmc-11709578:
Cristian Bernabe and nine co-authors test an Alzheimer risk gene variant in mice in a 2025 paper. Genome wide studies tied the ABCA7 gene to late onset Alzheimer's disease. One variant, A1527G, was flagged as a likely risk factor. What it does in a living brain was unknown.

Gene editing inserted the variant into mouse lines already carrying other risk genes. Brains were profiled for gene activity at several ages. The variant shifted expression patterns resembling known disease changes. A second, fuller model line received the variant as well. Those mice faced behavior, imaging, fluid marker, and tissue checks up to two years old. The consortium's pipeline aims to judge whether this variant deserves drug targeting. Results build the case step by step.
pmc-11710078:
Wenjie Luo and Hao Chen share a 2025 conference abstract on a microglia adapter protein in tau disease. The protein, DAP12, passes signals for receptors such as TREM2, a known risk gene. Mice without it resist tau harm despite more tau buildup, and the team set out to learn why, using gene readouts from cortex and hippocampus.

Without DAP12, tau inclusions rose, yet inflammation and synapse loss were blocked. Microglia stayed in their calm state instead of shifting to a disease state. Tau also pushed insulation-making cells into a weak middle state, and removing DAP12 blocked that shift and raised myelination. The work maps cross-talk among three cell types.
pmc-11710278:
Mark S Overby and co-authors compared two versions of a common thinking test used in Alzheimer's trials, in a study published in 2025. The standard test, called ADAS-Cog, can miss mild memory problems because some scores bunch at the top. Their longer version adds tasks for speed, language, learning, and space skills.

The team grouped scores from healthy older adults, people with mild memory loss, and people with likely Alzheimer's into a few broad factors. For the standard test, a general factor split all three groups apart, while a hands-on skills factor did not split the mild group from controls. Both factors from the longer test split the groups well. The results suggest the added tasks make the test sharper for early stages.
pmc-11710578:
Yoav Piura and co-authors describe a rare form of dementia that strikes within a single week, in a 2025 paper. Doctors know the broader class of rapidly progressive dementia, where thinking collapses within a year or two. A small share of patients fall faster still, reaching full incapacity within seven days of the first symptom. What causes that abrupt form, and how those patients look, was not known.

The team drew on 187 patients with rapidly progressive dementia enrolled at Mayo Clinic and Washington University between 2016 and 2023. Those whose collapse took a week or less were classed as abrupt onset. The authors charted their features, test results, and final causes. They also searched published reports to sharpen the list of possible causes. The work gives doctors a clearer approach for these rare, urgent cases.
pmc-11710778:
Nattayaporn Apaijai and co-authors test a diabetes drug in rats with heart failure in a 2025 study. The drug, dapagliflozin, blocks a sugar transporter and is now standard care in heart failure. It had also helped thinking in older adults with diabetes. The team asked whether it protects the brain when heart failure follows a heart attack.

Rats with surgery-induced heart failure showed weak hearts, poor thinking, and damaged brain mitochondria, the cells' power units. Eight weeks of the drug improved heart pumping and thinking about as well as a standard heart drug, enalapril. Both drugs cut swelling and voltage loss in the power units, though not oxidative stress. The authors say the drug guards the brain through its power units.
pmc-11710878:
Callie Moran and a large team of co-authors survey disinfectant use in health sites, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. The study asks whether use of quaternary ammonium compounds rose during the COVID-19 pandemic. These chemicals fill most sprays approved against the virus, yet animal and human studies link them to harm.

The team phoned hospitals, private offices, and dental sites in six states picked to mirror national health data. Staff answered open and closed questions on how their cleaning habits changed. The paper pairs that survey with known risks: fertility harm in animals and weaker cell energy in humans. It flags a cleaning gain that may carry quiet costs.
pmc-11712078:
Natalia Palacios and co-authors trace care paths for United States veterans with Alzheimer's disease in a 2025 records study. Veterans face distinct risks and can face hurdles in reaching new treatments through the VA health system. The team used health records from late 2015 to early 2024.

They found more than 110,000 veterans with an Alzheimer's code in their records. Over forty percent were first coded by a primary care doctor, far more than by any specialist type. Within a year, about a quarter saw a neurologist or a dementia clinic. Black veterans moved to specialist care more often than white or Hispanic veterans. The authors see room to strengthen follow-up care after a first diagnosis.
pmc-11712178:
Louisa I Thompson and co-authors report early data on digital screening for memory problems in primary care in a 2025 Rhode Island study. New Alzheimer's drugs have raised the need for fast, timely diagnosis, and digital tests could speed referrals. The team tried three routes: an online test taken at home, the same test self-run in the waiting room, and a tablet test given by the doctor.

Thirty-four older adults were screened and twenty-three joined the study. Most finished the home test by smartphone, and all who tried it completed it before their visit. Most said they preferred screening at home. The doctor-run tablet test succeeded in nine of eleven visits, with time pressure and tech faults causing misses. The waiting room option was dropped for lack of space and staff.
pmc-11712478:
Yejin Kang and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on signs of cell rust in people with mild memory loss tied to blood vessel damage. The work sat inside a trial that tested a supplement meant to mop up that rust. The team asked whether rust markers set these patients apart from healthy peers and hinted at who would gain from the treatment.

Patients came from a heart rehab program and were split by test scores into a mild loss group and a healthy group. One rust marker ran lower in the loss group while a second ran higher, a mixed picture. The loss group then took the supplement or a dummy pill for half a year. The study shows rust signs in vessel-based loss are not simple.
pmc-11712578:
Bery Mohammediyan and co-authors published a research paper in 2025 on sleep and the pace of Alzheimer's changes in older adults who still think clearly. Poor sleep has been tied to the disease, but which comes first was murky. The team followed 220 adults from a cohort of people with a parent who had dementia.

Sleep was tracked by surveys and wrist devices, while scans measured amyloid and tau over about four years. About a hundred people had repeat scans, and thirty-two went on to mild impairment. Higher amyloid went with more broken sleep from night to night. The study helps sort out how sleep and brain changes feed each other before symptoms start.
pmc-11712678:
Most dementia cases go unnoticed for years, and the pen-and-paper screening tests are slow and can misjudge people with little schooling. Laili Soleimani and co-authors build an alternative in a 2025 study: software that reads doctors' notes for warning signs. The cohort drew on more than four thousand older patients at one New York health system, using their last five notes before a memory test.

The software pulled out hundreds of clinical features, and a forest of decision trees learned to flag risk. On held-back patients the flag caught most true cases with few false alarms, though a stricter test set scored lower. A live screening rollout at the hospital comes next.
pmc-11712778:
Aygun Badalova published a research paper in 2025 on an app that helps people with dementia relearn the names of family and friends. Forgetting the names of loved ones is a common and painful part of the illness. The app, called Gotcha!, trains one face a day with photos and gentle, error-free practice.

Before the six-week training block, patients took weekly naming tests to set a baseline. A speech checker in the app gives feedback at once when a name is spoken. Among the first twenty users, four in five named faces better during training, and eight gains passed strict checks. Group tests backed the trend. The team also asked why patients join such projects.
pmc-11712878:
Jean-Paul Soucy and co-authors present a 2025 research paper on how to group brain scan data when modeling the spread of tau in Alzheimer's disease. The team worked with data from the TRIAD cohort at McGill University. The study asks how much fine detail a model needs before its forecasts stop getting better.

Inside, the authors compare four ways of grouping the data, from one pool for the whole brain to groups split by both brain region and brain network. They used scans from 113 people who each had tau PET and MRI at least twice, a year or more apart. The work helps researchers pick a model size that stays accurate without needless cost.
pmc-11713378:
John Alam and co-authors report blood test results from a drug trial in dementia with Lewy bodies, in this 2025 paper. The drug, neflamapimod, had earlier improved thinking and movement scores in a sixteen-week trial with ninety-one patients. The team now asked what the drug did to two proteins in the blood.

Stored blood samples were tested for GFAP and a second marker linked to nerve harm. Levels were checked in all patients and in those with pure Lewy body disease, without Alzheimer's changes. The title reports that the drug lowered GFAP levels in the pure group, a sign worth tracking in later trials.
pmc-11713678:
Apoorva Safai and co-authors link poor neighborhoods to changes in brain layout in a 2025 study. People in poor areas tend to have worse health and weaker thinking skills in old age. The team uses a new scan method that maps how alike the shapes of brain regions are. They ask whether this map can show how neighborhood strain gets into the brain.

The study covers 526 adults with no thinking problems from two Wisconsin research programs. Each person's home area got a hardship score based on income, schooling, jobs, and housing. The team compared the brain maps of people from the hardest-hit areas with those from the best-off areas. Shape patterns differed between the groups. Such maps may help explain how place shapes later memory loss.
pmc-11713778:
Lucia Crivelli and co-authors describe a lifestyle trial for dementia prevention across Latin America in a 2025 paper. The trial, called LatAm FINGERS, is the first of its kind to span the region. It covers twelve countries, from Mexico to Argentina and Uruguay. The team writes about how to recruit fairly in places that drug research often leaves out.

The trial randomly assigns older adults to a lifestyle program shaped for local food, habits, and culture. Staff used outreach methods that respect local customs and languages. The paper shares what worked and what proved hard. Broad trials like this one matter because results from one rich country may not fit the rest of the world.
pmc-11714278:
A landmark 2020 report listed twelve changeable risk factors for dementia across the life span. Matěj Kučera tests how many of those factors truly predict dementia in the Czech Republic in a solo 2025 study.

The analysis used a European aging survey and followed more than thirty-five hundred adults aged 65 and over who began dementia-free. Of ten factors with usable data, five tied to later dementia after adjustment. Physical inactivity carried the strongest risk, ahead of low education, diabetes, and depression. Living alone also ranked among the five. Sex seemed to modify a few links, including alcohol use and living alone. Local evidence can help national prevention plans aim at the factors that matter most at home.
pmc-11714878:
Joseph Geraci and co-authors report a 2025 project that uses phone and wearable data to spot early loss of thinking skills. Such devices can gather health data all day without a clinic visit. The team built data sets that mix many kinds of measure for each person. They also set up ways to share the data while guarding privacy. A first study drew on sixty-four people from a Boston research center.

A new machine learning tool sorted the people with loss of skills into clear sub-groups. One small group stood out for sleep measures, such as drops in blood oxygen at night. A second group stood out for high heart rate readings. Most members of both groups did have loss of skills. The team calls the results early, but they show how daily data might sort patients in useful ways.
pmc-11714978:
Prevention clinics for Alzheimer's disease tailor diet, exercise, and other steps to each patient's risks. Kellyann Niotis and a large team of co-authors ask whether blood markers can show if that tailored care works. They describe a study enrolling adults with a family history of the disease, plus some already diagnosed. Staff collect gene type, thinking scores, and blood markers such as amyloid ratio and tau forms. Some blood tests use a finger-prick card done at home.

Repeated marker readings could track whether risk care slows disease change. The study also gathers markers tied to Lewy body disease, which shares risks with Alzheimer's disease. If blood markers prove steady, clinics could judge care plans without costly brain scans. The paper sets out the study design and its goals.
pmc-11715078:
Robyn A Honea and co-authors weighed how genes tied to cell power plants shape brain fuel use. The power plants, called mitochondria, carry their own small set of genes. Brain fuel use drops early in Alzheimer's disease, which hints that these genes may play a part. Two genes near the cell core were in the frame as well.

The team used data from a Kansas aging cohort with three groups of adults. One group had the disease, one had mild thought loss, and one had neither. All had scans that map how much sugar each brain zone burns. Carriers of a known risk gene burned less sugar in zones at the front and midline of the brain. Two other gene marks showed no such link in the healthy group. The split points to the risk gene, not the power-plant genes, as the driver here.
pmc-11715478:
Yi Ling Clare Low and co-authors present a 2025 study of immune cells in the blood of people with Alzheimer's disease. The team also studied people with mild memory loss and people with normal thinking. A key gap, they note, is how immune cells in the blood link to swelling and harm in the brain. Blood samples came from a large Australian health study.

Flow tests sorted B cells and T cells in samples from 142 people in the three groups. The Alzheimer's group had fewer of one type of calming T cell and more of a rare T cell type. The mild loss group stood out in another cell group. Readers see which blood cell patterns differ by stage of memory loss.
pmc-11715678:
Kseniya Nevzorova and co-authors ask how often the logopenic variant of primary progressive aphasia rests on Alzheimer's disease as its underlying pathology. The variant centers on language impairment, with word and speech faults. Spinal fluid tests can show whether the hallmark Alzheimer's proteins sit behind the signs. Their 2025 study examined 20 such patients at one clinic. Each patient had a lumbar puncture so the fluid could be analyzed.

Fluid results split the group into four established cases, eight probable cases, and eight patients with no sign of Alzheimer's. In all, three in five patients had the disease at the root. Onset ran a little younger in that group, but the gap was not significant. Test scores hinted that worse memory with less speech loss may flag the disease before laboratory work. The team urges fluid testing for all such patients, since the root guides the choice of care.
pmc-11715978:
Gyujin Heo and five co-authors scan nearly seven thousand blood proteins to find a strong signature of Alzheimer's disease, in this 2025 study. Single blood markers exist, but each is weaker than spinal fluid tests. A wide sweep across the protein set might find a panel that closes the gap.

The sweep covered more than 3,300 people across three study groups. Two hundred fifty-seven proteins differed between patients and controls in both discovery and check samples. A machine learning model built on eighty-nine of them sorted patients well and did not fire for Parkinson's disease, which supports its specificity. The signature also flagged faster decline and marked some healthy people at very high later risk. Pathways pointed to fat transport in the blood.
pmc-11716178:
Jordan Teague and co-authors model when tau buildup starts in each person's brain and how fast it grows, in a 2025 paper. Tau is one of the two proteins that mark Alzheimer's disease, and its timing differs from person to person. A method first built for amyloid scans estimates the age at which buildup begins. The team checked whether the same method works for tau scans across several cohorts.

The main sample held 273 people from two Wisconsin studies, with repeat tau scans over time. Their average starting age was about seventy-one. The model produced a personal estimate of tau onset age for each participant. The authors then tested how well it forecast later scans and how well past scans fit the curve. Work like this helps trials pick the right moment to treat and judge whether a drug slows the clock.
pmc-11716378:
Ismail and four colleagues review the evidence linking cigarette smoking to Alzheimer's disease, in a study published in two thousand twenty-five. They also ask what happens neurologically when smokers switch to e-cigarettes. Nicotine's effects on the brain, they note, have been studied far less than smoking's effects on heart and lungs.

The authors searched MEDLINE, PsycINFO, and the Cochrane trial register through October two thousand twenty-three. They also checked several clinical trial registries for ongoing work. The findings conflict. Some studies report nicotine improving cognition and easing deficits. Others link active smoking to higher Alzheimer's risk. The review lays out this unsettled picture and the need for clearer evidence.
pmc-11716478:
Jinghang Li and ten co-authors published a study in 2025 on a brain-age score built only from white matter in midlife women. Brain-age models guess a brain's age from scans, and a gap from real age signals poorer health. The team wanted a version focused on white matter, where vessel damage tied to Alzheimer's risk shows up.

Their deep learning model was trained on healthy adults and then tested in 239 women in a midlife brain study. They compared the white matter age gap with blood markers of amyloid, tau, and nerve damage. A focused score like this could help track vessel-related brain risk in women before symptoms start.
pmc-11721078:
Timo Risch and co-authors trace how Escherichia coli escapes a new antibiotic family in a 2024 study. Cystobactamids attack the bacterial machinery that untangles DNA, and they break through many existing resistances. Knowing how resistance to them arises guides development, so the team bred highly resistant mutants and read their genomes.

Every mutant carried a single-letter change in the control region of one gene, ygiV, which turned up production of its protein. The protein latches onto the drug tightly and keeps it from its targets, and exposure to the drug pushed production higher still. Unlike a related drug class, resistance here came from a control tweak, not gene copying. A side benefit appeared too: the mutants dialed down several virulence factors.
pmc-11724678:
Daniel Rabin, Max Spiro, Connor Rachford, Timothy Fahey, and John Farrell report a rare chain of complications from a common antibiotic in a case report from 2024. A twenty-six-year-old woman with a congenital heart condition was treated with ceftriaxone for a heart valve infection. On day twenty-one she returned with a septic, clot-infected spleen. The trigger was acute pancreatitis caused by the drug itself, only the third such case in a decade.

Stopping the antibiotic brought steady improvement and falling inflammation markers. No surgery was needed in the end. The authors credit close teamwork across specialties. The case warns that a routine drug can set off an unusual cascade.
pmc-11726878:
Zhihe Yang and co-authors wrote this 2024 review of lab models used to study biofilms, the slime bound communities microbes form on surfaces. Inside a biofilm, microbes resist drugs far better than when floating free. Sound models are needed to study their traits and defenses.

The review sorts the designs in use, from classic flow cells and plates to newer printed and chip based setups. Each design's strengths and limits are laid out in turn. The authors note where lab models drift from real life conditions. They close with ways that three dimensional printing and other new tools could close that gap.
pmc-11727278:
Laura Acquaticci and six co-authors measure the active compounds in acorn flour extracts. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-four. Acorns from an oak tree hold many plant compounds that may aid health. The team asks how the heat of extraction changes what comes out, and how strong the extracts act.

They scan extracts made at four heat levels with a fine mass tool. The mid-heat extract holds the most of two key acids and shows the strongest anti-oxidant action. It also blocks two enzymes tied to diabetes and to nerve decay. That extract stands out as a hopeful base for health, drug, and skin products.
pmc-11727878:
Angeliki-Erato Sterpi and a large team of co-authors report, in 2024, a case of brain lesions that look like multiple sclerosis but arose after radiation treatment. Radiation can harm nerve support cells and their precursors, which may yield a pattern much like that disease on scans. The authors pair their case with a systematic search of past reports.

Their patient was a thirty-seven-year-old woman whose scan showed white matter lesions after her radiation sessions. The search found seven prior cases that met strict scan criteria, with a mean age near thirty-nine. The paper maps how these lesions present and how they differ from true disease, which helps clinicians avoid a wrong diagnosis and needless treatment.
pmc-11728178:
Mengjie Zhao and co-authors find a gene that links bud timing to cold hardiness in mulberry trees, in a 2024 study. Winter dormancy protects woody plants from cold. When buds wake, frost risk rises. The team scanned two hundred one natural mulberry populations. A gene called MaFAD2 showed the strongest tie to bud break timing. The gene was already known for cold resistance. Its activity peaked in dormant buds and faded as dormancy ended.

Trees from cold regions carried selected versions of the gene. Forcing the gene on in early-budding lines delayed bud break. That confirmed a causal role. The findings tie the two traits at one locus. Breeders can use bud timing as a visible proxy. Selecting later buds may buy cold tolerance. The work serves silk regions where mulberry is a crop. Climate swings make such markers more valuable.
pmc-11728278:
Park and Park sequence the full chloroplast genome of Sium serra, a plant found in Korea, China, and Japan. Some Sium species serve as herbal medicine and get confused with a look-alike plant. The species was first placed in another genus, then moved to Sium. Chinese sources still file it under the old name, so its genome had been skipped. The team took DNA from fresh leaves and read it on a high-throughput machine.

Software assembled and labeled the genome, and related species were compared. The analysis places the plant within the Sium group. The work gives a firm genetic reference for telling this herb from its look-alikes. It also adds to knowledge of diversity in the genus.
pmc-11728578:
Schuerger and co-authors gauge wet loss in mass gravel bike races in the field. Gravel race is a new bike form, with first worlds in 2022. It blends road, cross, and mount traits in long, hard runs. Stops for food and drink are rare in such race spans. Three race spans gave the facts at an April 2023 meet. In sum, 121 racers filled pre-race forms for the work.

Of those, 53 gave pre-race weight and spit salt marks. Just 38 racers came back for post-race tests in the set. Past one fifth, 22.6 percent, were wet-full pre race. Most were mild-dry at 56.6 percent in the pre counts. Post race, just 15 percent stayed wet-full in the set. Mid-dry rose to 47.5 percent and grave-dry to 17.5 percent. Weight fell and spit salt rose from pre to post reads.
pmc-11738078:
Saif Azzam and seven co-authors shared a review in twenty twenty-four on borderline personality disorder. People with this condition have emotions that shift a lot. Their ties to others shift too, and so does their sense of self. The review looks at how it is found and how it is treated. It looks at where experts still do not agree.

The authors weigh the set and proposed criteria used to find the disorder. They note the limits of the tools in use. They note how common it is and what else often comes with it. They weigh four psychotherapies. Two of them are dialectical behavior therapy and mentalization-based treatment. They set those next to the small role of drugs. They take up misdiagnosis, the role of trauma, and stigma. They ask if recovery is possible. The aim is to ground research and day-to-day clinical choices.
pmc-11758278:
Haiqin Zhu, Qintuo Pan, Zhaoliang Zhang, and co-authors compare two operations for a torn retina in this study, published in 2024. The condition is a retinal detachment that splits the center of vision in eyes that still hold their natural lens. Surgeons can fix it from outside the eye with a buckle, or from inside by removing the gel inside the eye.

The team reviewed 101 patients under fifty-five, with fifty-one eyes treated by buckling and fifty by the inside operation. Both methods reattached the retina in every case by the end. Clear vision at six months was reached by about six in ten buckle cases and about four in ten of the others, a gap that was not firm. Side effects differed: the inside operation brought more growth of scar-like tissue on the retina. The authors advise care in picking the method for each patient.
pmc-11772178:
Yajie Zhang, Cong Lu, Lili Li, and Hongyu Li study a cholesterol ratio and infertility in United States women, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The ratio compares non-HDL cholesterol to HDL cholesterol in the blood. Its link to infertility had not been well explored.

They used national survey data from two thousand thirteen to two thousand eighteen, covering two thousand nine hundred forty-seven women aged twenty to forty-five. About eleven percent reported infertility. Higher values of the ratio were tied to higher odds of infertility, and the top third showed the strongest link. Subgroup checks gave near-consistent results. The authors say more work is needed on the link and its causes.
pmc-11782278:
Luis Felipe Oliveira Ribeiro and ten co-authors published a forestry study in twenty twenty-five on spraying eucalyptus sprouts from a remotely piloted aircraft. Drone spraying is spreading in agriculture, but its quality in forestry was poorly documented. The team also measured how much spray reaches the workers doing the job.

They flew a DJI AGRAS T40 at three swath widths and three droplet sizes, comparing it with a manual backpack sprayer. Sensor cards placed in the sprout canopy measured droplet spread at upper, middle, and lower layers. Protective clothing captured exposure on the applicators. Narrower ranges with finer droplets distributed spray best through the canopy.
pmc-11807978:
Fereshteh Asgharzadeh and co-authors test a fruit extract for womb scarring in this study. The head of the text dates the work to 2024. Scar bands inside the uterus can block fertility, and gentle oral treatments are scarce.

Rats with induced uterine adhesions received the jujube extract by mouth. The team measured scar bands, womb shortening, and regrowth of the inner lining. Gland counts and lining thickness showed how well the tissue healed. Inflammation signals and antioxidant enzyme activity were tracked in the tissue. Treated animals showed far less fibrosis on staining and marker tests. Pregnancy outcomes in the model improved alongside the tissue repair.
pmc-11827678:
Dana Rocio Chavez-Yacolca and co-authors study how internet addiction feeds study delay among university students in Peru, in a paper whose journal record is dated 2024. Putting off schoolwork is common, and heavy internet use is a suspect cause. The team asked whether belief in one's own study skills sits in the middle of that link. They surveyed 334 students with three standard scales covering addiction, delay, and academic self-belief.

Stronger internet addiction came with weaker self-belief, and weaker self-belief came with more delay. Addiction also raised delay directly. Put together, self-belief carried part, but not all, of the addiction effect, which makes it a partial bridge between the two. The authors suggest universities build students' confidence in their study skills as one lever against procrastination, alongside tackling the internet habits themselves.
pmc-11970178:
Ping Zou, Ke Li, Yiting Qian, Tingting Wu, and Yue Qian present a 2024 study on predicting outcomes in breast cancer from blood tests. Doctors already track several tumor markers in the blood. The team asked whether adding immune and inflammation counts sharpens the forecast of a patient's three-year course.

They followed 112 patients who had surgery for breast cancer. Patients with poor outcomes had higher levels of the three tumor markers and of several cell counts and inflammation scores. Regression analysis kept five measures as real predictors. A combined model using the three markers with two cell counts reached a strong accuracy score. Such a cheap blood panel could help flag patients who need closer follow-up.
pmc-11976078:
Bader Alzaben and seven co-authors measured a jaw hollow that can complicate implant work in the east of Saudi Arabia, in a study published in 2024. The hollow sits on the tongue side of the lower jaw, near the first molar. A drill that breaks into it can cause bleeding or numbness. Their set held 256 cone-beam scans of that spot, sorted by ridge shape: round, flat, or cut in.

The cut-in shape led, at more than half the scans. Its depth and slant ran nearly even for men and women. One height reading split by sex; the rest did not. The authors warn that most jaws in their group hold the hollow. They urge a scan check of the spot before each implant in the zone.
pmc-12091078:
Seyed Abdosaleh Jafari and co-authors ask whether a person can be stripped of human dignity in a 2024 philosophy paper. Schools of thought disagree on what grants dignity in the first place. The authors take free choice of good and virtue as the mark. They then ask how anyone can tell that mark is present in a real person.

The paper draws on Islamic sources, above all the Qur'an, to find signs of dignity in action. It compares how people differ in showing those signs. Hard cases that strain each school's rules are worked through one by one. The authors argue that ideas like right and good are matters of judgment, so dignity shows itself in more than one way.
pmc-12480278:
Lee, Kwon, and Lee report shot rates for young youth in South Korea for the year twenty twenty-two, in a report from twenty twenty-three. Shots are the cheapest way to stop spread of many germs. The state gives shots free and aims for rates above ninety-five percent. This report checks if that aim held for each age group.

The team used records for about one point two million youth. Rates were high at age one and fell with age. By age six, the rate was below eighty-nine percent. Rates also varied by place and by shot type. The authors say more work is needed for groups that miss shots and for those who doubt or refuse them.
pmc-12660978:
Quanming Pu and co-authors hunted the genes that turn radish leaves purple, in a 2025 study. The purple comes from anthocyanins, pigments with health appeal and defense roles in plants. Root color genetics in radish were known, but leaf color was not. The team crossed a purple-leaf line with a green-leaf line and bred several generations from them.

Leaf color proved to be set by nuclear genes, with purple partly dominant. Mixing DNA from extreme offspring of the second generation pointed to one stretch of chromosome seven. That stretch holds thirty-nine genes, and activity tests sorted them by leaf type. One gene, akin to a known color switch called MYB114, was active only in the purple line. The authors name it the likely master switch for radish leaf color.
pmc-12669978:
Mai Sri Lena and colleagues built and validated a questionnaire about how parents support young children learning English in Indonesian primary schools. Parental help shapes motivation and effort, but no trusted local tool measured the roles parents play. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team drafted items from the literature and expert feedback, then surveyed parents of fifth graders at public and private schools in Padang. Statistical factor methods were used to test whether the items grouped sensibly and measured steadily.

Five dimensions emerged: general involvement, expectations, access to resources, enrichment, and out-of-school activities. A confirmatory analysis fit the five-part model well, and reliability scores passed standard cutoffs. The authors offer the questionnaire as a diagnostic tool for schools and researchers who want to understand and strengthen home support for language learning.
pmc-12679078:
Hemorrhoids after childbirth are common and painful, and Chinese herbal care offers two topical treatments for them. Xiao-Hui Wang and co-authors compared a combined routine against a standard one in two hundred sixty-eight patients at a Hebei hospital. One group used a herbal lotion sitz bath plus an ointment. The other used a magnesium compress plus the same ointment. Each group held one hundred thirty-four patients treated between twenty twenty-three and twenty twenty-five.

Before care, the groups matched in swelling and hemorrhoid size. After care, the herbal bath group showed smaller hemorrhoids and less swelling. Pain, comfort, mood, and cooperation with care were also compared. The authors report an edge for the combined herbal routine, with few side effects.
pmc-12690778:
Xuqian Wei and co-authors describe two families with severe clotting from inherited antithrombin deficiency in this 2025 study. Antithrombin is one of the blood's main natural brakes. Lacking it is among the worst inherited clotting risks. The condition is rare and often missed by standard checks. One patient, a man of thirty-nine, had extensive leg vein clots. The other, a woman of twenty-one, had a risky lung clot.

Both had antithrombin activity near half of normal. Lab tests measured the protein directly as well. Gene faults that cut the protein short were found in the gene. Family studies like this guide screening of relatives. Early knowledge can prevent a first fatal clot. The paper is a genetic case series.
pmc-12690978:
George John and a large team at a cancer center in India report on multiple myeloma in adults aged forty or younger, in a study published in twenty twenty-five. This blood cancer mostly strikes older people, so facts about young patients are scarce.

The team looked back at new cases treated from twenty thirteen to twenty twenty-one. Of one thousand nine hundred and eighty people screened, one hundred and ten were forty or younger, with a middle age of thirty-six. Bone harm was very common, seen in more than nine in ten, while high calcium and kidney harm were less so. More than a third had the most advanced stage at diagnosis. Common drug mixes paired bortezomib with other drugs, and about a quarter got a stem cell transplant.
pmc-12695878:
Stem cells grown in the lab can form beta cells, the insulin producing cells destroyed in type 1 diabetes, yet the lab grown versions stay immature and work poorly. Anne Lietzke and co-authors compared these cells with real human islets and found weak output from their energy centers. Genes driven by a regulator called PPAR alpha, which sets up fat burning inside those centers, were largely switched off, even though the cells' mass and structure looked normal.

Treating the growing cells with a drug that activates that regulator switched the missing genes back on. The treated cells secreted insulin better and formed many more beta cells, both in dishes and after transplant. The authors argue that fixing this energy program early in growth could make lab grown replacements stronger and more useful for people with type 1 diabetes.
pmc-12699378:
Wei Cong, Jingfu Sun, Zhanyu Hao, and Maosong Gong tested a plant compound, called IDET, as a booster for a standard cancer drug in thyroid cancer. The drug, paclitaxel, often loses force as tumors resist. The team paired the two in cancer cells and in tumor-bearing mice.

Together, the pair curbed cell growth, movement, and invasion more than the drug alone, while sparing normal thyroid cells. They jammed a defense switch that tumors use to clear cell stress, so harmful oxygen byproducts piled up and drove cell death. Tumors in mice shrank more with the pair, and organs and blood stayed sound. The compound looks like a safe sensitizer.
pmc-12701878:
Nine authors present a study in two thousand twenty-five on treating fully blocked hip arteries through the wrist. Catheter treatment of aortoiliac disease increasingly uses the radial artery in the wrist, thanks to purpose-built tools. Whether the wrist route can handle total blockages was unclear.

One center reviewed forty-six wrist-route procedures drawn from one hundred five blockage cases treated over five years. Patients averaged about seventy-four years, with long lesions, mostly severe. Stents were placed successfully in every patient, most often bare metal ones, guided by ultrasound imaging inside the vessel.
pmc-12704978:
Teja and five co-authors report a rare tumor found behind common belly pain in a young man. Their twenty twenty-five case report comes from a family medicine clinic. Abdominal pain is an everyday complaint, but this case had red flags: three months of right loin pain, ten kilograms of weight loss, and a month of cough.

Scans showed a large, mixed mass above the right kidney, with spread to nearby nodes and the chest lining. The picture fit a malignant pheochromocytoma, a rare adrenal tumor. The patient was sent to endocrinology for care. The authors stress the family doctor's role in spotting red flags early and pushing fast referral, which can change outcomes in serious disease.
pmc-12706078:
Hiroshi Ageta and co-authors find that common cholesterol drugs may quietly help cancer immunotherapy. Tumors shed tiny vesicles carrying PD-L1, a protein that switches off immune attack, and patients with many such vesicles answer checkpoint drugs poorly. The team shows PD-L1 gets tagged by a small modifier called UBL3, and that tag is what routes it into the vesicles.

Statins block that tagging. In patients with heavily PD-L1-positive tumors, those already taking statins had clearly fewer PD-L1 vesicles in their blood. Gene data also tied UBL3 and PD-L1 levels to lung cancer survival. The authors propose adding statins to existing combination therapies as a cheap way to cut the vesicle traffic and sharpen immunotherapy, a hypothesis ready for clinical testing.
pmc-12711078:
Stachowicz and co-authors compare in 2025 the physiques of elite Polish swimmers with non training peers, split by sex and by sprint or distance training. Body measures guide weight targets and training plans, and may also mark health risk. Thirty women and thirty men at top level were measured.

Swimmers had lower body mass index and waist to hip ratios than peers in the reported groups. Body fat was lower in the female sprint group. Long distance groups were very small, with six per sex. The authors ask how far elite swimming physiques match health promoting profiles, given the low fat and lean build found.
pmc-12712678:
Yasmin Begum and co-authors make gold particles with a plant extract and test them on dye and germs, in work from 2025. The particles broke down a common orange dye fast under visible light, clearing over ninety percent in ten minutes with a helper compound. They kept most of that strength after four reuse rounds. Tests also showed germ killing against two species.

Computer models probed the particles' energy gaps and stability to back the lab work. Three learning models then forecast those gaps, with one tree model landing closest to the computer values. The authors pitch the particles for cleanup work.
pmc-12712778:
Yusuke Hoshino, Sachiko Horie, Masayuki Maki, and Ikumi Dohzono report a 2025 study on how a wild plant copes with pollen from a new kin species. Pollen from the wrong species can cut seed yield, yet plants that live near kin may have grown some guard over time. Proof from species with a known contact past is rare, so the team used two sorrel kin in Japan.

One sorrel is native and the other is a new arrival, and each grows both near and far from the other. Crosses with the wrong pollen cut seed yield in the native plant, most of all in groups that live near the kin. A second test, with right pollen first and wrong pollen next, also cut seed yield. The pattern defies the plain hope that near groups guard best.
pmc-12714078:
El-Sayed, Alsenany, Asal, and Alasqah build and test a scale for AI addiction among researchers in twenty twenty-five. Heavy use of AI tools boosts output but raises fears of over reliance. No validated measure existed for addictive use in research settings. The team drafted items from literature and interviews.

Data came from seven hundred eighteen nursing researchers. The final scale has twenty-two items across five dimensions. Those dimensions cover compulsive use, over dependency, harm to function, withdrawal, and tolerance. Factor analyses confirmed the five part structure, explaining most variance. Reliability scores were excellent across several measures. The authors say the tool can flag unhealthy dependence on AI in academia.
pmc-12716478:
Kofi Aduo-Adjei, James Akazili, Øystein Ariansen Haaland, and Lumbwe Chola measure how often blood pressure care crushes household budgets in Ghana's Greater Accra Region, in a 2025 study. Ghana's national insurance aims to keep care from pushing families into poverty, yet out-of-pocket costs stay high. The team surveyed 382 patients at two district clinics about direct and indirect costs of managing hypertension.

By the lower threshold, 65 percent of patients faced catastrophic spending; by the stricter one, 58 percent did. Most respondents were women, and nearly all were Christian. Widowhood and joblessness linked to lower odds in the team's model, while larger households raised them. The authors conclude that hypertension care still imposes a heavy financial burden despite insurance, and they call for stronger protection for these patients.
pmc-12720278:
A European Food Safety Authority plant health panel weighs the pest risk of sweet chestnut plants shipped from the United Kingdom, in work from twenty twenty-five. The trees move as graftwood, whips, bare root stock, and potted plants. Import rules list the commodity as high risk.

All pests tied to the commodity were screened against set criteria. Three regulated pests found in the United Kingdom counted as relevant. One unregulated fungus like organism, Phytophthora kernoviae, passed every test for deeper review. Experts judged the stated safeguards and rated pest freedom per product type. Bare root and potted plants carried the pest most often in expectation. High confidence bounds were given for clean units.
pmc-12722778:
Pneumonia caught outside hospitals still sends many older adults into wards each year in Korea. Kyeo Rae Ju and co-authors chart who those patients are and what infects them in a 2025 study at one large hospital.

From more than seven thousand people with pneumonia signs between 2005 and 2019, the team confirmed about four thousand cases. The average age was seventy, and two thirds were men. Chronic lung disease was the most common background condition, ahead of cancer and weakened immunity. Sputum cultures most often grew a Klebsiella species, with staph and other bacteria behind it. Regional maps of this kind help doctors choose first antibiotics before lab results return.
pmc-12722878: DeBroff reviews the history of double optic capture, a method for seating artificial lenses during cataract surgery. The lens optic is held through openings in both the front and back walls of the lens capsule. The grip keeps the lens centered and can cut later membrane growth behind it. The review traces how the method was done and how it has changed. Newer variants serve both child and adult cataract cases. DeBroff also weighs wider use in routine adult surgery to prevent haze behind the lens.
pmc-12723178:
Haiping Zhang and co-authors trace, in 2025, a chain of RNA signals that drives inflammation in artery disease. Immune cells called macrophages fuel the disease when fat metabolism goes wrong. A long noncoding RNA was found at high levels in such cells after exposure to oxidized cholesterol, a key trigger.

Silencing that RNA calmed the inflammatory response. It works by soaking up a small RNA, which frees a third factor that switches inflammation on. Raising the long RNA raised that factor, confirming the chain. The authors propose blocking the long RNA as a treatment strategy for atherosclerotic heart disease, to be tested beyond the dish.
pmc-12724478:
Leon Gerardo Kreis and co-authors weigh the costs and gains of auto feedback after online depression screening in a 2025 study. Adults who screened positive but had no diagnosis joined a trial with three arms. One group got no feedback, one got plain feedback, and one got feedback shaped to their symptoms, wishes, and local care. All feedback shared the result and urged pro advice.

Over six months, with just over one thousand people in the study, cost and health gaps between groups were not firm in statistical terms. Yet plain feedback looked worse than both no feedback and shaped feedback on value for money. Curves and extra checks probed how sure that ranking was. Readers learn that more contact after screening is not always better value.
pmc-12729078:
Semahat Incikabi and Oktay Erbay test if math fit tween math and science class plans steers kids' science marks. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-five. Six hundred twenty fifth and sixth grade kids in eleven Turkish state schools took science tests. Each test item was classed as math-linked or math-split by its fit to the grade math plan.

Kids scored far low on split items, though talks showed they oft held the science but tripped on math forms past their class scope. The pair hold that plan gaps put kids at a loss and split their grasp. They urge plan teams, teachers, and law heads to bind the two plans tight.
pmc-12729278:
Ruben Nurmohamed and a large team published a 2025 study on a new attack against infections on medical implants. Germs on implants form biofilms, slimy shields where dormant bacteria hide. Inside a biofilm, standard antibiotics lose much of their power, which feeds the wider crisis of drug resistance.

The team's plan is radioimmunotherapy. Antibodies that home to one germ type are linked to radioactive atoms, actinium-225 or lutetium-177. The antibodies carry the radiation straight to the biofilm, where it can kill the sheltered bacteria. Tests in living animals give the first proof that the idea can work. Success could open a path for infections that drugs alone cannot clear.
pmc-12730278:
Ugo Testa and co-authors published a 2025 review on gene therapy for two inherited blood diseases. Sickle cell disease and beta-thalassemia both stem from faults in the gene for a hemoglobin part. In severe cases they demand lifelong intensive care, and the only cure, a donor stem cell transplant, is open to few patients. Gene therapy offers a way to use the patient's own cells instead.

The review draws on a systematic search of the literature. In this approach, the patient's blood stem cells are collected and fixed outside the body, then returned. One route adds or silences genes using a lentivirus shuttle. Another edits the faulty code directly, with CRISPR tools or base editing. Several products have now been tested in patients. Many achieved freedom from transfusions and lasting correction of blood measures. Some products have won approval, offering a possible cure without a donor.
pmc-12731378:
Mehmet Siddik Cadirci develops new goodness-of-fit tests in a statistics paper from two thousand twenty-five, written alone. Such tests check whether data match a claimed distribution. The tests rest on Tsallis entropy, a generalized measure of uncertainty, with emphasis on two flexible distribution families.

The test statistic compares a closed-form entropy under the assumed model with a neighbor-based estimate from the data. Cadirci proves the estimator settles on the true value under mild conditions. Cutoff values come from resampling methods. Wide simulations report the tests' false alarm rates, power, and running time across settings. An applied example shows how to calibrate the tests in practice.
pmc-12731678:
Feifer and six co-authors link social conditions with what palliative care visits cover for children with cancer, in work from twenty twenty-five. Pediatric palliative care improves symptom control and end of life outcomes. Access to it is unequal by social determinants of health.

Less was known about how visit content itself varies by race, income, or language. The retrospective cohort included patients up to twenty-seven years old with cancer. Domains addressed in each visit were charted against family social factors. Content gaps matter as much as access gaps: a visit that skips financial or spiritual needs serves a family less fully.
pmc-12732278:
Busra Bulbul and thirteen co-authors hunt for real world marks of survival in spread breast cancer treated with CDK4/6 blockers, a standard first line care for hormone driven cases. High estrogen receptor levels may mark who lives longer. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

Records came from many centers for hundreds of patients treated across four years with one of two drugs of this class. Single factor checks tied longer survival to no prior hormone care, no liver spread, bone only spread, and a second hormone mark. Very high estrogen receptor levels showed a strong trend the same way. In joined models, no prior hormone care kept its link to better survival.
pmc-12732878:
Sonja Zrilić and co-authors study a weak kind of bond that turns out strong in metal complexes holding phenanthroline, in a paper published in twenty twenty-five. The bond links a carbon-hydrogen group to oxygen. In the setting studied, the oxygen comes from water sitting just outside the metal's inner shell.

The team mined a crystal database and found thousands of these contacts in stored structures. They then computed bond strengths for the free molecule and for complexes with cobalt and palladium. Binding the molecule to a metal made the bonds much stronger. The strongest matched the bond between two water molecules. Strength tracked the electric charge felt at the hydrogen atom almost perfectly.
pmc-12733578:
A research team compared blood markers of one cell process across four joint and immune diseases in this 2025 study. The process is called NETosis, a way white blood cells release web-like strands that can fuel inflammation. The diseases studied were lupus, rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, and ankylosing spondylitis.

The team measured free DNA in blood plus two markers tied to the webs, and compared patients with healthy subjects. Free DNA was higher in all four diseases, but the two web markers stood out most in lupus, where they also linked to heart and vessel disease. A signal protein that can trigger the process was raised in all four groups. The pattern suggests the process is strongest in lupus, present in arthritis, and weaker in the other two diseases.
pmc-12733878:
Hashimoto and co-authors evaluate a new bone cement mix for joint and spine repair. Standard PMMA cement is the clinical mainstay, but it is far stiffer than spongy bone, never resorbs, and can heat tissue as it sets. Those flaws can loosen implants and harm nearby bone over time.

Their composite blends cyanoacrylate glue with round, porous particles of beta-tricalcium phosphate that were sintered for strength. The phosphate ceramic can conduct new bone growth and slowly resorb. Tests weighed handling, strength, and setting traits of the mix. The aim is a cement that works more like living bone.
pmc-12734278:
Nuria Andrea Tort and colleagues tested in two thousand twenty-five whether hydrogen-rich water boosts standard painkillers for nerve pain in mice. Nerve pain often needs long, high-dose treatment with heavy side effects. Male mice with a tied sciatic nerve received a cannabis-like drug, a gabapentin-like drug, the water, or combinations.

Each treatment eased pain behaviors in a dose-related way, and combinations worked better than single drugs. Brain-related tissue checks showed less oxidation, inflammation, and overactive pain signaling with combined care. The results suggest an add-on that might let patients use lower drug doses, though human testing remains far away.
pmc-12734578:
Mamta Dhyani and co-authors show that a workhorse power transistor ages by rules its standard theory does not predict in a 2025 study. The devices are 1700-volt silicon carbide MOSFETs, prized in electric vehicles and grid gear. Under heat and voltage stress, their turn-on threshold drifts, a wear-out called bias temperature instability.

Switching the devices at realistic speed under combined gate and drain stress, the team found the exponent itself changes. Lifetime forecasts built on the fixed rule would then mislead. Power electronics designers need the corrected picture before these parts anchor fast chargers and drives at scale.
pmc-12735278:
Diana Tatarciuc and her co-authors offer a 2025 narrative review on how the mouth's microbes may affect stomach health. Most attention goes to Helicobacter pylori, a stomach germ tied to gastritis. Yet the mouth hosts a vast microbial community, and its imbalance may feed stomach disease. The authors gathered studies from 2000 to 2025, favoring reviews and strong human research.
