pmc-13271978:
Mónica Conesa Giménez and coauthors test in 2026 a phone app called Kalmer for young people who injure themselves without suicidal intent. Self-injury is rising among adolescents and young adults, and clinic care is hard to reach. The app blends therapy exercises with moment-by-moment mood checks on the phone.

Twenty-six volunteers aged sixteen to twenty-five, drawn from a non-clinical group, rated the app's function and appeal. Usability scores were high, and users judged objective quality as good while personal appeal needed work. The authors report gains in self-awareness and willingness to seek help, marking the app as ready for clinical testing.
pmc-13272278:
Nicholas Pischke and Thomas Powell present a 2026 mathematics paper on how fast a noisy step-by-step method settles down. Their method mixes two older schemes for finding fixed points, which are points that a map leaves unchanged. Noise is treated in a fully general way, with no fixed sampling rule assumed.

The authors prove rates at which the method becomes steady, called rates of asymptotic regularity. For special cases the rates are linear, matching or beating the best known results. In inner product spaces, which are spaces with a way to measure angles, the general rate is quadratic. They also discuss minibatch sampling, cost bounds, and use in Q-learning.
pmc-13272478:
Ting Xu and coauthors pool in 2026 studies of medication literacy among people with cardiovascular disease, the skill of understanding and using medicines safely. Heart patients often juggle many drugs for life, so weak medication literacy invites errors and harm. Overall levels and their drivers had not been summarized across studies.

Searches of seven databases in English and Chinese ran to the end of 2025 under standard review rules. Scores were pooled with random-effects models given the wide variation among studies. Influencing factors were organized through a health ecology model spanning personal, family, and system levels, giving educators a map of where interventions can bite.
pmc-13272578:
Kaitlyn Coppetti and colleagues studied patients with many recorded allergies after gynecologic cancer surgery in a 2026 cohort report. Having four or more allergies listed in the medical record is called polyallergy. The team asked whether these patients use more extra services after surgery.

They reviewed 398 patients treated at one center, of whom 77 had polyallergy. Those patients had higher rates of anxiety, depression, and panic disorder. They also had more visits to emergency, urgent care, primary care, and mental health services in the year after surgery, with a typical count twice that of other patients. The link held after adjusting for other factors. The authors suggest earlier primary care and case support for this group.
pmc-13272878:
Jessica Foley leads a 2026 study of how long life evolved in Heliconius, a genus of tropical butterflies. Lifespans in animals range from days to centuries, and these butterflies are known for living unusually long for insects. The team gathered data from butterfly houses, field mark-and-recapture work, and captive colonies.

They found a three-fold lifespan extension in Heliconius over close relatives, with some species living nearly a year at most. Captive tests showed the longer life came with slower ageing in both survival and body function. The authors present Heliconius as a strong new model for studying how long life evolves and what drives healthy ageing.
pmc-13272978:
Hiroyuki Kodama leads a 2026 case report of a 61-year-old man with esophageal cancer who responded again to an immune therapy he had received before. His cancer, a squamous cell type of the food pipe, had returned in neck lymph nodes after surgery, chemotherapy, radiation, and maintenance immune therapy. Later chemotherapy lines failed.

Gene profiling showed extra copies of the PD-L1 gene, with a copy gain of 8, and tissue tests showed high PD-L1 levels. Doctors restarted nivolumab 8.8 months after the first immune therapy ended. The tumor shrank partly after 3.1 months, though it grew again after 5 months. The authors suggest PD-L1 gene gain may help predict rechallenge benefit.
pmc-13273278: Correction notice for a 2025 paper on upper mantle temperatures, the Iceland hotspot track, and ice-Earth interactions in Greenland. One methods sentence is corrected: the wave curves came from a global shear wave model, not a North Atlantic one. The acknowledgments add thanks to Pascal Audet for input on the joint inversion work. Two scientists, Chiara Civiero and Sergei Lebedev, are added as co-authors in eighth and ninth place. The author list and contributions have been updated.
pmc-13273478:
Yuki Okazaki and co-authors tested combined surgery for a torn meniscus root plus a cartilage lesion in a 2026 study. The medial meniscus anchors at its posterior root, and tears there threaten knee function. Some patients also carry a small patch of damaged cartilage, and outcomes for the combined problem were unreported.

Ten patients received pullout repair of the root plus microfracture, a bone marrow stimulation step for the cartilage patch. Thirty-seven others received repair alone for tears without cartilage damage. In the combined group, all knee scores and pain measures improved clearly at one and three years after surgery. The authors conclude the added cartilage step can succeed, with results in line with repair alone in their comparison.
pmc-13273778:
Monica Luciana, Kelly A. Duffy, and Wesley K. Thompson examined the structure of thinking skills over time in a 2026 analysis of the ABCD study. This large United States study follows children's brain and cognitive development. Its test battery shrank across waves, which threatened the comparability of scores.

Using a Bayesian statistical method, they extracted three components from baseline, year two, and year four data: general ability, executive function, and learning and memory. Even as the battery fell from nine tests to five, the same three part structure fit well, with similar task loadings. Scores across versions correlated strongly. The shrunken battery still showed age and practice gains, and component scores linked in distinct ways to mental health measures and brain scan activity during a working memory task.
pmc-13273878:
Wu and colleagues test diet education for older adults in China in a 2026 cluster-randomized trial. The intervention taught a dietary pattern designed to cut cardiometabolic risk. Participants were community residents aged 61 to 80 in Tianjin.

The trial enrolled 694 older adults in four clusters. The intervention group had 349 people and the control group 345. Education ran for twelve months. The main outcome was a clustered cardiometabolic risk score. That score fell more in the intervention group. The beta value was minus 0.25. Artery wall thickness also fell, by a beta of minus 0.05. Cholesterol, blood sugar, blood pressure, and body weight all improved. The authors conclude the education lowered disease risk.
pmc-13274678:
Jin Zhang and co-authors report a 2026 journal article uncovering an extra way the chemotherapy drug gemcitabine fights ovarian cancer. Beyond its known DNA damage, the drug's full mechanism was unclear. The team traced a chain involving HIF1A, a low-oxygen sensor, and UBR5, a protein that tags other proteins for disposal.

In ovarian cancer, HIF1A switches UBR5 on, and UBR5 destroys LATS2, a brake protein in the Hippo growth-control pathway. Gemcitabine lowered HIF1A and UBR5, sparing LATS2 and switching the Hippo brake back on, which quieted two growth signals, YAP1 and FGFR1. Treated cancer cells grew, moved, and invaded less, and tumors shrank in an orthotopic mouse model.
pmc-13275478:
Kun Liu, Xuanying Lv, and Wen Wen review how daily body clocks shape natural killer cells in a 2026 article. These immune cells vary in number and killing power across the day and night. The review gathers human, animal, and cell evidence on what drives those rhythms.

Core clock genes, stress hormones, melatonin, and nerve signals all feed into the daily pattern. Short sleep loss may briefly raise activity, while repeated disruption or shift work tends to lower it. Disease states often shift the timing or flatten the rhythm rather than erase it. The authors call for frequent repeated sampling in future studies to pin down timing clearly.
pmc-13275578:
Yael Dann and Noa Gueron-Sela present a 2026 daily diary study of how war news exposure affects Israeli families with young children during active regional conflict. For seven days, 193 Jewish-Israeli parents of children averaging four and a half years old reported each day on media use, direct war exposure, mood, and friction with their child.

On days when children saw more war media, they showed more negative mood and more parent-child strain, and the same held between families. Parents' own news engagement reached children indirectly: heavier parental viewing raised the parent's negative mood and relationship strain, which in turn predicted the child's worse mood. Direct exposure and media exposure also combined to shape well-being. The authors highlight media habits as a lever for protecting family emotional climate.
pmc-13276278:
Ying Lu and co-authors wrote a 2026 review on the horse genome and what it reveals about horse history and traits. Horses have served humans for thousands of years in transport, farming, war, and sport. Their DNA also records how domestication reshaped an animal.

The review tracks better reference genomes, capped by a complete Y chromosome sequence, the male sex chromosome. DNA from ancient and modern horses points to a domestication heartland in the Volga-Don region. Later Bronze Age herds replaced earlier lines almost entirely. Maternal lines stayed diverse while paternal lines narrowed sharply under human breeding. The authors link specific genes to racing performance, high-altitude living, coat color, and inherited muscle diseases. They look ahead to complete genome assemblies and population-wide references for breeding and conservation.
pmc-13276578:
Yifei Sun and colleagues study how the redness of a drink changes its perceived sweetness, in a 2026 experiment. Cutting sugar without losing sweetness is a central problem for drink makers. Colour is the first signal a drinker gets, and it may quietly steer taste.

Forty participants rated sugar solutions across a range of strengths and graded redness levels. Medium redness lifted sweetness most, with the biggest relative gain at low sugar levels. The boost shrank as the drink grew sweeter, forming an inverted U pattern. Brain recordings lined up with the ratings, and the authors propose a target redness range for sugar-reduced drinks.
pmc-13276778:
Xinji Yang, Herong Zhu, Xiaofei Hou, and Ke Liu report a 2026 case of catastrophic kidney injury with a misleadingly calm presentation. A 42-year-old woman suffered a blunt crush injury that tore the kidney's main blood vessels completely. Such a Grade V injury would normally cause rapid, life-threatening bleeding and shock.

Her vital signs stayed stable on arrival, which defied textbook expectations. The first CT scan also suggested a congenital misplaced kidney rather than trauma displacement. Surgeons confirmed the full vessel tear and removed the kidney in an emergency operation, with a good outcome. The authors explain how the body can mask this injury and warn against trusting a stable appearance.
pmc-13277078:
Augustus Osborne and Morie Vandi wrote a 2026 viewpoint arguing that women's leadership in health systems needs direct support. Women form most of the health workforce yet hold few top posts in ministries, hospitals, universities, and aid bodies. The gap is sharpest in fragile and conflict-hit settings, where schooling and civic life are disrupted.

Looking through gender plus class, disability, place, and other factors, the authors trace how authority and chances are shared out. They propose four steps: online mentoring and training, local leadership incubators, reform fellowships, and shared research and advocacy networks. Without changes to workplace culture and promotion, they warn, training alone will change little.
pmc-13277278:
Citing Guo leads a 2026 review of a cancer protein called PD-L1 when it appears inside the cell nucleus. PD-L1 is best known on the cell surface, where it helps tumors hide from the immune system. Inside the nucleus, it seems to act on the cancer cell itself, without that immune route.

Nuclear PD-L1 has been linked to aggressive disease, resistance to treatment, and poor outcomes in several cancers. It may aid DNA repair, shift cell fuel use, and reshape nearby tissue. Measuring it well is still hard, and firm proof in patients is limited. The authors outline drugs that could block its move into the nucleus or its actions there, as a future treatment path.
pmc-13278778:
Xin Wang and co-authors identify what drives soil carbon build-up on the northeastern Qinghai-Tibet Plateau in a 2026 study. The high plateau stores vast carbon, yet the controls on its fragile soils are poorly known. Ninety-eight sites were surveyed and modelled with Bayesian statistics.

Topsoil carbon thinned from east to west and fell by about a quarter with depth. Plant cover and yearly rainfall emerged as the dominant positive drivers in both soil layers. Together with plant diversity and litter quality, they explained over two thirds of the variation. Cover mattered most near the surface, while rainfall's influence grew with depth. Forecasts for the plateau must track both factors together, the authors conclude.
pmc-13278878:
Jie Chen and Tao Tao survey social media, body image, and self-compassion in teenage athletes, in a 2026 study. Young athletes face appearance pressure on top of performance pressure, and image-heavy platforms intensify both. Four hundred forty-nine adolescent athletes in China completed standard questionnaires.

Heavier social media exposure matched stronger body dissatisfaction and lower self-compassion. Self-compassion carried part of the effect, meaning kinder self-talk buffered the harm of exposure. Fear of negative judgement sharpened the damage, making exposure bite harder on self-compassion for worried teens. The model confirmed both paths. The authors recommend courses that build self-kindness and ease fear of being judged in youth sport.
pmc-13279178:
Lei Chen and colleagues published a 2026 laboratory study of why esophageal adenocarcinoma often stops responding to oxaliplatin. Reflux of acidic bile salts is the main risk factor for this cancer. The team modeled reflux by exposing cancer cells to those salts in flat cultures, three-dimensional tissue models, patient-derived organoids, and mouse grafts. They focused on PRDX2, an antioxidant protein that shields cancer cells from damaging oxygen radicals.

Bile salt exposure switched PRDX2 on through APE1 and NF-κB signaling. PRDX2 then protected a second protein, GPX4, from destruction. GPX4 normally blocks ferroptosis, an iron-driven form of cell death. Silencing PRDX2 restored oxaliplatin sensitivity by letting ferroptosis proceed. A drug blocking APE1's redox function achieved the same effect. Combining it with oxaliplatin shrank grafts in mice more than either agent alone. The work nominates this redox pathway as a target for resistant disease.
pmc-13279378:
Alena Vollmannova and colleagues report a 2026 study of quince fruit peels as a food resource. Quince is a hard yellow fruit, and its peels are a main waste from food plants. Turning waste in new foods cuts strain on land and water. The team checked nine quince types from an organic farm in the Czech Republic over three years.

Peels proved rich in potassium, calcium, magnesium and phosphorus, with low salt metal sodium. Trace metals like iron and zinc sat in safe, useful ranges, while lead and cadmium stayed below test limits in most lots. Peel extracts held strong plant phenols, health linked plant compounds, and good defence against cell harm in lab tests. A key phenol was chlorogenic acid. Waste peels could add worth to new foods.
pmc-13279478:
Sonia M. McCallum and colleagues report a 2026 study that builds a web resource for parents of youth with mental health strain. Parents often act as gatekeepers who spot trouble and seek help, yet few digital tools serve them. The team used a three phase design that put parent views at the centre. Work ran with Australian parents.

A survey of six hundred thirty one parents proved strong demand for such a web tool. Top topics were anxiety, low mood, self harm and suicide in children and teens. Fourteen parent interviews then shaped the draft content. A test version went back to parents for feedback and polish. Step by step parent input aims to make a tool families will trust and use when worry first strikes.
pmc-13280878:
Gabriela Chamorro Gil and colleagues published a 2026 study upgrading banana peel, a food waste, into a water-cleaning adsorbent using a deep eutectic solvent. Here choline chloride with methanesulfonic acid treated the peel and enriched its lignin content. The team benchmarked the product against peel treated with the acid alone and challenged both with three drugs, propranolol, metformin, and tinidazole.

The solvent-treated peel selectively grabbed propranolol, removing almost 90 percent of it from a solution without acidity adjustment. Its capacity reached 284.6 milligrams per gram, beating the acid-only version's 238.1, and uptake followed the kinetic and isotherm models expected for a varied surface. Energy calculations described an entropy-driven process. The peel kept more than three quarters of its performance after three reuse cycles. The authors present the treatment as an eco-friendly way to give farm waste a second job in water cleanup.
pmc-13280978:
Jake Sypniewski and colleagues reported a new chemistry route to imaging tracers in a 2026 study. Doctors scan the body with tracers that carry a short-lived form of fluorine. The tracers must be made fast and pure, since the fluorine fades in about two hours. The team made a family of salts based on selenium, a chemical cousin of sulfur. They tested how well each salt handed its fluorine slot to the tracer form.

Many salts gave high yields of the wanted tracers, above seven in ten tries. Some weaker salts still gave useful yields. Helper groups on the salt pushed some yields close to full. In direct tests the selenium salts matched or beat the sulfur salts used now. The team also built two known tracers this way. They say the route widens the menu of scans doctors can order.
pmc-13281478:
Yingying Huang and colleagues built a smart grading tool for knee arthritis in a 2026 study. Doctors grade knee wear on X-rays with a five-step scale, but grades vary by reader. The team gathered more than two thousand seven hundred knee X-rays from three hospitals, spanning 2018 to 2024. Their tool reads the image and also uses facts like age and weight. A new fusion step blends the two streams and weighs how sure it is.

On a fresh hospital's images, set aside for testing, the tool matched expert grades at a very high level. It beat eight rival designs, including image-only and facts-only tools. It caught most severe cases while rarely flagging healthy knees. A chart version of its logic also sorted risk cleanly. The authors say such tools could make knee grading faster and more even across clinics.
pmc-13281578:
Zhihang Zhang and colleagues hunted gut fungi for signs of colon cancer in a 2026 study. Most gut work in this cancer has centered on bacteria and viruses. Fungi are scarce in the gut and their gene records are patchy, so they were skipped. The team pooled gene data from nine public groups, with more than fourteen hundred stool samples. They charted how fungal mixes shift in cancer and how fungi pair with bacteria.

Fifteen fungal species changed again and again across the groups. Two were richer in healthy people, and two others in cancer patients. Fungal signs alone sorted patients weakly. But added to bacterial signs, they sorted cancer a bit better in fresh test groups. Sorting rose in five of six outside groups. The authors call fungi a helpful extra signal, not a test on its own. They urge better fungal gene records to sharpen the signal.
pmc-13281878:
Shiyang Li and colleagues linked a copper gene to sun damage in skin in a 2026 study. Strong sun rays scar skin over time, a process called photodamage. A cell death path tied to copper has been floated as part of the story. The team mined public gene data from sun-exposed human skin. They crossed changed genes with copper-death genes and a network module tied to damage. One gene survived all three cuts. It moves copper across cell membranes.

Single-cell data showed the gene fell sharply in skin cells after sun exposure. Cells rich in the gene linked tightly with support tissue through glue-like signals. Cells poor in it answered weakly to their surroundings. Lab tests in cells and mice confirmed the gene's drop after damage. The authors say the gene may guard skin's ties to its base. They propose it as a care lead.
pmc-13282378:
Wenqian Wang and colleagues published a 2026 study hunting new bacteriophages against Dorea longicatena, a gut bacterium linked to obesity and metabolic disease. Phages, the viruses that infect bacteria, could trim such targets precisely, but almost none are known for this gut resident, and bacteria evolve resistance quickly. The team turned that into a tool: they bred bacterial mutants resistant to a known phage set, then used those strains as bait to fish phages from the environment.

The strategy landed two new lytic phages that between them infected 27 of 30 strains, including the original and resistant strains. Genome checks confirmed the phages kill rather than integrate and carry no virulence or dormancy genes. Resistance mapped to mutations in a tail protein gene, and fully resistant bacteria shared the same seven changes in it. The authors say the expanded phage library and the resistance map sharpen prospects for phage-based microbiome editing.
pmc-13282478:
Alexander O Everhart and co-authors present a 2026 study tracking two decades of digital components in medical devices authorised in the United States. Regulators at the Food and Drug Administration lack a systematic way to flag which authorised devices contain software. That gap limits safety monitoring and understanding of digitisation by specialty. The team pioneered text analysis of tens of thousands of regulatory documents for newly authorised devices.

Their method reads device records to detect digital features, building the first broad map of the trend. Devices with digital components grew substantially over the two decades. Growth varied meaningfully across clinical specialties and product categories, digitising some fields far faster than others. The authors argue such tracking is a prerequisite for software-aware oversight after devices reach the market.
pmc-13282778:
Tsering Yangzom and co-authors tested in 2026 whether nicotinamide riboside, a building block for the cell fuel helper NAD+, calms inflamed brain support cells. Their model used human stem-cell-derived astrocytes and brain organoids carrying POLG faults, which cause mitochondrial disease. In that setting, support cells turned harmful to neurons.

Single-cell profiling showed more toxic-type astrocytes and fewer protective ones, plus fewer neurons in the faulty organoids. Neurons grown with the faulty astrocytes looked stunted and lost synaptic markers. Treatment with the compound lowered two inflammatory signals, raised mitochondrial DNA counts and energy output, and improved neuron shape. The results support NAD+ boosting as a candidate strategy for these diseases.
pmc-13282978:
Allergy shots against dust mites can trigger whole-body reactions in children, the risk profiled in Qin Wang's 2026 hospital study. The treatment can ease asthma and hay fever but may trigger reactions. The team looked for child traits that raise that risk.

Records covered 250 children treated from July 2022 to July 2025 at one hospital. Just under half had a body-wide reaction across more than nine thousand shots. Most reactions were mild and fast, with only two severe cases and no deaths. Risk rose when asthma and hay fever occurred together. Risk also rose with high total and mite-specific antibody levels in blood tests.
pmc-13283178:
Deer fed mixed plant toxins barely change intake, while a urine marker tracks dose faithfully, in Katie L Anderson's 2026 feeding trials. Wild deer eat plants rich in defense chemicals that need detox work. A key idea is that mixing toxin types spreads the load across body pathways.

Two captive deer species ate five mixes of four pure plant chemicals. Intake, urine markers of detox work, and gut bacteria in dung were tracked. Mix type had little effect on how much deer chose to eat. A urine acid marker rose steadily with toxin intake in all mixes. Plant phenols shaped gut microbes more than scent oils did. Results only partly fit the mixing idea for large ruminants.
pmc-13283378:
Difficult preschool behavior erodes mothers' flexibility through stress, unless partner teamwork is strong, Tianqi Qiao's waves of surveys show in 2026. Most past work asked how parents shape children, not the reverse. Parenting stress and partner teamwork are the focus paths here.

Families with preschool children were surveyed three times, six months apart. More than one thousand mothers and children stayed in the final sample. Early child problems predicted lower maternal flexibility later through higher parenting stress. Good perceived teamwork between parents softened that harm in the second path. When teamwork felt weak, stress cut flexibility more sharply. Support for parents may protect maternal mental health.
pmc-13283678:
Yusuke Hashimoto and co-authors asked in 2026 how much meniscus width surgeons should leave when reshaping a discoid lateral meniscus. In this condition the knee cartilage pad is disc-shaped rather than crescent-shaped, and trimming it to shape is called saucerization. The best leftover rim width was unknown. The team reviewed 77 knees, average age about thirteen, and grouped them by rim width right after surgery.

Widths were classed as large, middle, or small. By two years, the small group kept the least width, while large and middle groups ended much alike. Function scores did not differ across groups. The large group, though, had the highest rate of problems such as retears and repeat surgery. Modelling flagged wider starting width as a risk for fast shrinkage, and the title points to about ten millimetres as the preferred target.
pmc-13283978:
Matjaž Klemenc and co-authors tried three computing approaches in 2026 to forecast fainting during a tilt table test. In the test, patients lie on a table that tilts upright while heart tracings and blood pressure are recorded, provoking vasovagal syncope in susceptible people. Predicting a faint early is hard because body control systems interact in complex ways. Data came from 105 patients with a fainting history.

One approach used boosted decision models on heart rhythm variation features. A second used nearest-neighbour regression on transformed signals. A third used a growing neural network. The neighbour method forecast faint probability most steadily, keeping errors low up to five minutes ahead. Boosted models classified outcomes fairly well. The authors see early-warning tools for personal faint management in these signals.
pmc-13284478:
Eifumi Hashimoto and colleagues showed in 2026 that a tumour needs an iron-sulfur building factor to start, but not to keep growing. Iron-sulfur clusters are small mineral units that many proteins require, and the factor FDX2 helps assemble them. Lab work had hinted these clusters matter for cancer growth, yet their role inside living animals was unclear. The team used switchable gene loss in transplanted human ovarian cancer cells in mice.

Turning FDX2 off blocked tumour initiation and spread, while established tumours kept growing without it. Under low oxygen, cells raised their iron-sulfur protein levels broadly, which softened the damage from losing FDX2 and let cells grow regardless. The authors draw a stage split: cluster building matters most at seeding and spread, less once a tumour is settled.
pmc-13284878:
Jiangjiao Qin and co-authors build a prediction tool, published in 2026, for airway over-response in toddlers with suspected asthma. The standard methacholine challenge is risky and hard in children aged zero to three years. The team used records of children who had breathing tests, nitric oxide breath measures, and the challenge on the same day.

Seven factors predicted the challenge result, led by family asthma history, wheeze, and breath nitric oxide levels in the model checks. The tool sorted cases well in training data and fairly in a held-out group. The authors offer the chart as a non-invasive aid for early asthma judgment, while noting it still needs outside testing before wide use.
pmc-13284978:
Zhiqiang He and fellow researchers built computer models that flag poor nutrition around the time of hip fracture surgery in older adults. Their 2026 study responds to a common problem: many older patients arrive undernourished, yet older screening tools are slow and hard to apply in an even way across hospitals.

Data came from 526 patients at four large hospitals in Xi'an during 2024. Five learning methods were trained and checked against standard nutrition criteria. Age, body mass, appetite loss, lung disease, and blood albumin ranked among the strongest signals. Logistic regression and gradient boosting performed best, and an online calculator was released so staff can score new patients quickly.
pmc-13285278:
Sumra Irum and co-authors present a 2026 case report of bowel telescoping backward after weight-loss bypass surgery. Backward jejunal intussusception is a rare late problem after Roux-en-Y gastric bypass and its vague signs overlap with other post-surgery ills. Contrast CT plays the central role in spotting its shape, level, and threat to bowel health.

The patient developed a high-grade small bowel blockage several years after bypass. Imaging showed the backward slide at the bowel join, a known weak point where gut motion changes after surgery. Scan findings shaped the surgical plan. The authors urge early CT when bypass patients show blockage signs, since delays risk bowel damage.
pmc-13285378:
Tiny lab-grown liver tissues help untangle how two signal paths steer early liver cell fate in a 2026 study by Brock Grenci and co-authors. Liver growth needs tight timing of chemical and physical cues, yet few models let researchers vary the setting cleanly. The team built flat microarrays and 3D microwells to test Wnt and YAP signals in liver precursor cells.

Cutting a Wnt brake gene boosted bile duct markers and switched on Notch targets, but scrambled the spatial layout. Blocking YAP mainly shifted liver cell fate on flat arrays, yet blocked bile fate hard in 3D tissues. Paired tweaks showed Wnt and Notch team up on bile fate, while YAP acts through shape-linked routes.
pmc-13285678:
Jean-Pierre Chaboureau built a giant fake sky to train a coming storm-watching satellite, detailed in a 2026 dataset paper. The C2OMODO mission will read up-and-down air speeds inside storm cores from microwave glints taken moments apart, yet real core speeds are almost never measured. A twenty-five day run of a storm-resolving model at fixed warm sea heat fills the gap.

The set holds nine hundred twenty million air columns across thousands of half-hour steps, each with paired snaps one and two minutes apart. Layers include full 3D air fields, surface facts, radar echoes, and fake satellite views in heat and microwave bands. Teams can now test how well space signals betray hidden storm motion.
pmc-13286078:
Darian Lawrence-Sidebottom and colleagues review family digital care for children's oppositional behavior in a 2026 retrospective analysis. Angry, defiant moods in youth strain the whole household, wearing down parents' sleep and calm along the way. A family-centered online program paired coaching and therapy for children with support for their caregivers, and the team checked both sides of that bargain.

Records held 3,781 child-caregiver pairs for children aged 6 to 17 in real-world care. About one in five children began with clinical-level symptoms, and those children carried more co-occurring problems and more strained caregivers. By the end of care, most children with marked symptoms had improved, with the fastest gains in the first months. Caregiver stress, burnout, and sleep also eased fastest where the child improved fastest, which shows the family-wide reach of the program.
pmc-13286778:
Shuyun Jiang and co-authors uncover a chain of events by which a protein called RSPO2 slows breast cancer, reported in 2026. RSPO2 levels run low in malignant breast tissue. The team restored it in cancer cells and watched growth, movement, and invasion, then traced which molecules carried its effect.

Restored RSPO2 curbed cell growth in dishes and shrank tumors in mice. It recruited a partner that tags another protein, PTBP1, for destruction. Without PTBP1, a message that normally blocks iron-driven cell death decayed faster, so cancer cells underwent that death process, called ferroptosis. Forcing the blocked pathway back on reversed the benefit. The three-step axis, the authors say, is a new drug target candidate.
pmc-13286878:
Frantisek Nehaj and colleagues probe a hidden flow problem behind a young man's cardiac arrest in a 2026 clinical case report. The 31-year-old collapsed in his sleep with ventricular fibrillation and was revived by a single shock. Angiography revealed his right coronary artery was completely absent, leaving a single coronary system to feed the whole heart. Heart scans looked normal in structure, and he received a defibrillator implant.

Stress testing and nuclear imaging both came back clean, which might have closed the case as unexplained. A CT flow scan told another story: a sharp flow drop through the middle and far reaches of his remaining arteries. The authors argue this flow-based scan can unmask dangerous flow limits in coronary anomalies that ordinary tests bless as safe, sharpening risk judgments for survivors.
pmc-13286978:
Hongwei Yi and colleagues report implanting a resynchronization defibrillator in a 73-year-old man whose heart sits as a mirror image on the right side of his chest. The 2026 case tackles a rare anatomy that reverses every landmark operators rely on. The patient had advanced heart failure and a complete electrical block in the left bundle branch.

Before surgery, the team mirrored their tracing and imaging setups to match his anatomy. During the operation they heat-shaped the delivery sheath in reverse to steer leads along his flipped vessels. The device, using pacing of the heart's own conduction bundle, went in successfully. Experience with this pacing style in mirror-image hearts is extremely limited, so the case offers a practical template.
pmc-13287178:
Gargi Yonatan and colleagues looked for repeatable patterns in 2026 in how the blood pressure drug noradrenaline is dosed over ten days during septic shock. Records covered 1,111 adults treated in Israel and 9,343 adults in a large United States database, used to test whether patterns held elsewhere.

Clustering hourly doses found five pattern groups in one cohort and six in the other, yet the same broad families appeared in both. Death rates by ninety days rose steeply across groups. Total dose and timing during days two to four mattered most. Using only the first day of data, models could already predict the final group with good accuracy.
pmc-13287878:
Yin Fang and co-authors present an AI system that matches bile duct cancer patients to clinical trials, in a 2026 report. Matching by hand is slow, since eligibility rules are complex and patient records come in mixed formats. The system accepts both structured electronic health record data and free-text clinical summaries. It ranks candidate trials and explains each rank with reasons for and against eligibility.

Clinicians checked the system on 19 patient cases, nine structured and ten written as narratives. Agreement with clinician judgment on eligibility reached about 73 percent for structured cases and 78 percent for narratives. Reviewers judged many of the truly eligible trials worth recommending, with narrative cases scoring higher. The system proved good at finding biomarker-specific trials hidden inside broad solid tumor studies. Clinicians also valued its clear notes on missing information, and each trial took only a minute or two to review.
pmc-13287978:
Omar Fitian Rashid and co-authors build a malware detector for network traffic in a 2026 study. Signature-based tools spot known attacks well but miss new or reshaped ones. Anomaly-based tools can catch fresh attacks but cry wolf too often. The team aims to join the strengths of both styles in one framework.

Their method first encodes each network flow in an RNA-like form, a letter string that a neural network can read. Three classifiers then work on those strings: one tuned to known threats, one tuned to odd traffic, and a hybrid that runs both stages in a row. On ten thousand samples, the hybrid did best, catching ninety-five percent of malware with a strong balance of precision and recall. The authors offer the design as a scalable shield for networks.
pmc-13288478:
Rana Hameed Jabr and Omar Husham Ali compared spit stress markers in 2026 among 400 adults classed as gum-healthy, having gum inflammation, or having deep gum disease. Saliva from ninety of them was lab-tested for cortisol, chromogranin A, and an enzyme tied to stress response, beside a standard stress questionnaire.

All three markers ran higher in both disease groups than in healthy controls. One marker climbed in a clean staircase from health to deep disease. Self-rated stress also scored higher in patients. Exact group means are reported in the study. The authors suggest spit markers could support gum assessment, while stress itself may feed the disease.
pmc-13288578:
Ahmed Alkhafaji reports a case of mad honey poisoning in the United Kingdom in a 2026 article. Mad honey carries grayanotoxin, a nerve toxin from rhododendron nectar that bees pass into honey. A 75-year-old man ate roughly 20 to 30 milliliters of wild honey brought as a gift from abroad. Within an hour he felt faint, dizzy, tired, and sick, with one bout of diarrhea.

At the emergency department his blood pressure had fallen to 65 over 41, and his pulse was only 45 beats per minute. A heart tracing showed a slow sinus rhythm, with no other abnormal findings. Fluids and a small intravenous dose of atropine restored his pressure and pulse within seconds. He stayed under observation for 36 hours and went home with no lasting effects. The author warns that honey-linked slow pulse and low pressure should trigger suspicion.
pmc-13288678:
Rebecca M Smith and colleagues report mixed-methods results from a 2026 UK feasibility trial on treating positional vertigo after head injury. Hospital patients with post-traumatic benign paroxysmal positional vertigo at three major trauma centers were assigned by chance to repositioning maneuvers, Brandt-Daroff exercises, or advice alone, while interviews explored how the trial ran.

Recruitment pace and screening success differed between sites for local reasons. Being assigned to advice alone landed differently with staff and patients, hinting that a later full trial should rethink that arm, while assessment and hands-on treatment were acceptable to participants. Blending counts with interview material exposed strengths and flaws that will shape the design of a definitive effectiveness trial.
pmc-13288778:
Nanami Seshimo and colleagues trace a chromosome error in HPV-infected cervical cells to a destroyed motor protein in 2026. Before cells divide, chromosomes must line up at the cell center. In early cervical lesions, some chromosomes linger near the poles instead, a defect the team calls ECAC. The viral E6 protein was suspected, since it already targets cell guardians for destruction. Experiments tested whether E6 also destroys the motor CENP-E.

E6 did send CENP-E to the cell's disposal system, alongside its known target p53. A version of CENP-E built to resist destruction restored normal chromosome lining up. That rescue showed the motor's loss is the main cause of the defect. The same effect appeared with E6 proteins from several high-risk virus types. Cells kept under E6 for long periods gathered abnormal chromosome numbers. The authors link this early defect to the instability seen in cervical cancers.
pmc-13288978:
David Dasa and Philip Davies test a camera-based blood pressure app in Nigeria. Their 2026 field study ran at three hospitals. All adults had dark skin types V or VI. The app reads blood flow from face video. Cuff readings served as the true standard.

Of 306 adults, 249 gave usable readings. Errors ran large for top and bottom numbers. The app missed most true high readings. It flagged few false highs, though. Slow internet links tied to failed readings. Most patients and staff liked the tool. Darker skin raised the odds of failure. The authors warn of unfair care without fixes.
pmc-13289078:
Cecilia Bolling and colleagues present a 2026 trial plan on sleep and cannabis in the US. The trial deals with adults who use cannabis often. Poor sleep and heavy use feed each other. Sleep therapy may cut both at once. The host is the University of Michigan.

The trial will enroll 200 adults aged 21 and up. All will have chronic insomnia and frequent use. Half will get six online sleep therapy sessions. Half will get sleep hygiene lessons. Checks run before, after, and months later. Brain wave sleep tests will run twice. Sleep depth is the key body measure. Data will be shared in a national archive.
pmc-13289178:
Muhammad Homayoon Manochehr and colleagues map sex health access for teens with HIV in 2026. Their scoping review covers sub-Saharan Africa. Such teens face blocks to sex and birth care. Stigma and fear of disclosure loom large. Three databases plus grey sources were searched.

The search screened 6,835 records in all. Just 14 studies met the entry rules. Programs ranged from broad to narrow fixes. Schools, clinics, and phones hosted them. Most stressed that services feel welcoming. Peer support helped teens engage. Outreach and digital tools also helped. Fit to local culture stood out most. Cost and distance got less focus.
pmc-13289378:
Zhineng Xu and three co-authors chart candidemia, a yeast infection of the blood, at a hospital in Yunnan over twelve years, in a study published in two thousand twenty-six. They matched sixty-seven patients with the infection to sixty-seven without it and compared risks, survival, and drug response. Five Candida species were found in the blood samples.

Patients with candidemia waited longer for blood tests to turn positive, stayed longer in hospital, and died more often. All yeast strains were killed by four key antifungal drugs in lab tests. Chronic kidney disease, some infections, and two antibiotics stood out as possible risks. A prediction model built from the data flagged slow test growth, many infections at once, and blood transfusion as the strongest risk signs.
pmc-13289978:
Omar Asdrúbal Vilca Mejia and colleagues argue a 2026 editorial case for recognizing coronary bypass surgery as a formal superspecialty in Brazil. Bypass grafting remains the gold standard for complex coronary disease, yet state death rates for isolated bypass ranged from 2.6 percent to 13.1 percent between 2008 and 2017 in national data. Such spread signals a policy crisis, not just surgical variation, the authors contend.

Focused training can raise graft use, speed operations, cut harm, and improve survival and patient experience, they argue. The plea is framed as democratizing excellence, not excluding generalists from practice. Small-cut methods and enhanced recovery plans should anchor the new specialty, backed by multi-site registry proof from Brazil. State gaps make that case hard to ignore.
pmc-13290078: A short 2026 correction in Gut Microbes adds a conflict of interest addendum to an article on a bile acid network and probiotics in colitis by Biagioli and coauthors. Three senior authors clarify co-founder roles in a university spin-off, Precision BioTherapeutics, founded in 2019. The notice states neither that company nor a partner firm played any role in the study at any stage. Disclosure was omitted at submission because the authors saw no competing interest. The journal confirms handling was unaffected. No research content changes.
pmc-13290378:
Luke Thompson and co-authors report a case where imaging pointed to cancer but pathology found inflammation, in 2026. A 78-year-old woman arrived with breathlessness, fatigue, and weight loss. A CT scan showed thickening of her caecum, the pouch where the small bowel meets the colon, in a pattern suggesting malignancy. Colonoscopy was skipped because doctors feared tearing the inflamed wall. She went ahead with removal of the right side of her colon.

Lab study of the removed tissue told a different story. It showed xanthogranulomatous inflammation, a rare benign process packed with foamy immune cells, and no cancer or precancer. The authors note that scan-only judgment struggles to separate this inflammation from true tumors. They urge clinicians, radiologists, and pathologists to keep the condition on the list when a biopsy is missing. Colonoscopy with biopsy remains the surest route where it can be done safely.
pmc-13290678:
Posting ultrasound pictures online is remaking what it means to become a parent, Ilenia Picardi and Maria Carmela Agodi argue in a 2026 article. Three- and four-dimensional scans have moved from clinics into commercial studios and social platforms, and the authors ask what that does to expectant parents.

Using multimodal critical discourse analysis on two UK parenting forums, they studied how parents describe and emotionally handle their scan encounters. The images cut both ways: they promise reassurance and bonding, yet spark anxiety when the pictures fall short of idealized images of the foetus and of good parenthood. Forums act as emotional infrastructure where members trade stories, humor, and support. The authors name the result a digital foetus, socially recognized before birth, and call the process digital birth.
pmc-13290778:
Combining every weapon at once lengthens survival when glioblastoma returns, Jean-Baptiste Barbe-Richaud and colleagues report from the FROST study in 2026. Three of four patients see this brain tumor recur within a year, and no standard playbook exists for that moment.

The multicenter real-world study followed 271 patients treated at first recurrence. Most (70%) received systemic therapy alone, 21% got a multimodal mix of drugs, radiation, and surgery, and 9% had local treatment only. Median survival from recurrence was 9.9 months overall, but the multimodal group reached 16.2 months against 9.3 for local therapy alone and 7.9 for systemic therapy. Adjusted analyses kept the ordering. The authors argue for planning recurrence care as a package rather than a sequence of single moves.
pmc-13290978:
Austrian guidance for opening the chest to restart the heart after severe injury is set out in a 2026 consensus study led by Martin W Dünser. Resuscitative thoracotomy is advised only for selected cases of traumatic cardiac arrest, and most prior evidence comes from busy centers with many penetrating injuries, unlike the setting studied here.

Twenty-four specialists from 10 Austrian medical societies and two emergency services worked through a modified Delphi process over four rounds. A literature review fed 22 open questions, which became 28 agreed statements: a single strong recommendation, fifteen weaker ones, and a dozen best-practice statements. The guidance gives lower-volume settings a shared, structured way to prepare for a rare and urgent procedure.
pmc-13291078:
Blocking tiny abnormal blood vessels through an artery to ease long-lasting shoulder pain is reviewed in a 2026 narrative article led by Nicolò Ubaldi. Conditions from frozen shoulder to tendon pain and muscle pain share inflammation and new vessel growth that can feed pain signals, and many patients stay sore after standard care.

Transarterial embolization aims to shut those vessels down while sparing the joint itself, using materials that range from antibiotic particles to calibrated microspheres. Reports in frozen shoulder describe strong pain relief and better movement with few side effects, and tendon and muscle cases show similar gains in the papers surveyed. Safety looks favorable overall, though the authors flag antibiotic resistance worries and call for firmer trial evidence before wide use.
pmc-13291878:
Subhrajyoti Ghosh and colleagues build a porous crystal that turns visible light into ultraviolet light in 2026. The trick, triplet-triplet annihilation upconversion, merges two low-energy excitations into one high-energy glow. Doing it in solids has failed often because the active molecules clump and fade. The team locked a light-harvesting iridium compound and a glowing partner inside a zirconium metal-organic framework. The framework's rigid pores keep the partners close yet orderly.

Under blue light at 445 nanometers, the material emitted ultraviolet light in suspension. Its upconversion efficiency reached 0.60 percent, respectable for this class. The structure also resisted the photodamage that plagues loose mixtures. As a working demo, the crystal released glutamate from a caged precursor on command, acting as a lamp-free ultraviolet source. No mercury lamp or direct ultraviolet bulb was needed. The authors pitch the platform for greener photochemistry and light-driven materials.
pmc-13292578:
Jay Prakash and co-authors write a 2026 letter building on a review of tracheal intubation in critically ill patients, which framed the procedure as a hemodynamic event, not just an airway task. Induction, apnea, and positive-pressure ventilation each batter circulation in sequence, and the review named the physiologically difficult airway. The letter writers propose sharpening that framework at the bedside.

They suggest classifying patients by their dominant physiological vulnerability rather than by anatomy alone. Vasoplegia calls for pre-emptive pressor support, preload dependence warns that ventilation will slash venous return, and a failing right ventricle can collapse under rising airway pressures. Severe metabolic acidosis needs its own handling. Because several problems often coexist, the point is spotting the main actionable derangement first. Individualized preparation, they argue, beats one-size intubation routines.
pmc-13292678:
Bende Zou, Xinmin Xie, and Ludmila Gerashchenko present a 2026 methods shortcut for recording brain waves in mice without drilling the skull. Standard EEG implants demand stereotaxic drilling and screws, eating time and stressing animals. Their approach presses thin needle electrodes into set skull positions, hooks extra needles along the skull's sides for grip, and cements a connector in place with dental composite.

The whole surgery finishes in under fifteen minutes, with no drilling or screw placement at all. Recordings from the needle setup proved no worse than those from conventional screw electrodes in the team's comparisons, across the sleep and brain-activity measures they examined. The authors pitch the method as faster, gentler, and accurate enough for epilepsy, sleep, and drug-response studies. Animal welfare and lab throughput both gain, they argue.
pmc-13292778:
Moran Drucker Iarovich and colleagues study a heart imaging measure called the blood pool T2 ratio in a 2026 paper. The analysis covered 718 people, most of them patients with cardiomyopathy scanned between 2018 and 2020, plus healthy controls. Ratios ran clearly higher on 1.5 tesla scanners than on 3 tesla machines, so each field strength needs its own cutoff. Lower ratios predicted major cardiac events and matched worse exercise test results. The measure looks promising for risk sorting, provided thresholds stay tied to the scanner used.
pmc-13293278:
Daniel J. Ahn and colleagues assess, in a 2026 study, a new transplant policy meant to help stable heart patients on long-term pump support. A 2018 rule change had lowered their priority, so a time-based status rise was approved.

Using national transplant data, the team tracked 4967 listed adults who got a durable left ventricular assist device after the 2018 change. By six years, most had a device problem, a status upgrade, or had left the list, and only 47 of those fully followed remained waiting, a count the authors give. Applying the new rule at once would shift status for just 4.7% of the waitlist.
pmc-13293378:
Richard Kronick and co-authors weigh, in a 2026 study, the money effects when sicker members leave Medicare Advantage plans for traditional Medicare. Prior work shows high-need members leave more often, but the cost to plans had not been counted.

Leaving was rare, though, at 1.7% of members that year and lower later. Spread across all members, the added cost to plans was only about 0.6% overall. A measured policy reply still seems apt.
pmc-13293478:
Mirijana Irnich and colleagues build, in a 2026 study, a classification system for video-based artificial intelligence that watches for epileptic seizures. Tools vary widely in cameras, methods, and aims, and no shared scheme existed to compare them.

Five rounds of work blended a literature review, a market scan, and checks with ready products, drawing on studies from 2013 onward found in three databases. A total of 40 original studies shaped 16 starting dimensions, and nine experts added more through a Delphi process. The final scheme holds 23 dimensions with 102 traits. Gaps in the evidence base were also mapped for future work.
pmc-13293978:
Sachith Gallolu Kankanamalage and colleagues detail a 2026 protocol for finding transgene RNA and protein in the same mouse spleen cells. The PrimeFlow method mixes flow cytometry with branched DNA probes, so single cells reveal both messages and products. Steps cover spleen breakup, fixing, staining for luciferase protein inside cells, and marking T cells, B cells, monocytes, and other groups with CD antibodies. Probes target luciferase and a control gene. Reading both signals by cell type shows which cells took up the drug and how RNA timing compares with protein timing.
pmc-13294178:
Michal Trnka and colleagues observe polarized light therapy added to standard care for chronic skin wounds in a 2026 single-arm study. Fifty patients, mostly women with mean age 69.4 years, got light at 626 nm for 10–20 minutes per field several times daily alongside normal conservative and surgical care. No sham group was used, a limit the authors state plainly.

Healing moved in a good direction for 92% of patients, and 52% closed fully. In the chronic pain subgroup of 17 people, pain eased for 12 and vanished for 5. Only two mild short-lived skin reactions appeared. Gains tied to wound type and treatment length, but proof needs a controlled trial.
pmc-13294378:
Klaudia Sztolsztener, Brintha Croos, and Adrian Chabowski test a common antioxidant supplement against fatty liver change in rats, in a 2026 experiment. The authors suggest the compound could limit early fatty change by correcting how the liver handles lipids.
pmc-13294678:
Muyoung Lee and colleagues hunt for a hidden class of gene switches that begin life fixed in cell membranes, in a 2026 study. A few known proteins work this way, held in place until a signal frees them to enter the nucleus and turn genes on. The team reasoned that odd pairings of protein parts, a membrane anchor joined to a gene-control part, could point to more of them.

Their screen looked for such pairings that are rare yet kept across species. It found the known cases and raised fresh ones, among them membrane-bound enzymes that alter histones. pmc-13294878:
Kun Liu and co-authors report saturating a designer plastic with hydrogen using cheap nickel catalysts, in a 2026 polymer chemistry study. pmc-13294978:
Jennifer McEachron, Susan C. Modesitt, and Jamie N. Bakkum-Gamez offer a master class on writing case reports, in a 2026 editorial for Gynecologic Oncology Reports. The journal began as a home for case reports in women's cancer care. Its editors ran a webinar to open the genre to new authors, and here they walk through one report from the same issue as a model.

The chosen case involves a rare gynecologic cancer treated with tumor-infiltrating lymphocyte therapy, a cell treatment newly applied to metastatic vulvar melanoma, with a good outcome. The authors draw lessons on picking a case that teaches something new and on setting findings against past work. Their tips include drafting the case story first and leaning on mentors. A recording of the webinar sits with the piece.
pmc-13295378:
Maksuel Gatto de Vitt and a large team add a protein-cutting enzyme to Jersey cow diets in a 2026 study. Better protein use could cut feed costs, the biggest expense in dairy diets. Free enzyme and a coated, rumen-protected form were compared in milking cows.

Milk from enzyme-fed cows, especially the free form, carried more fat and protein and held production longer into lactation. Protein digestion and rumen fermentation markers improved, and blood signs pointed to better protein handling. The coated form sat between the free form and no enzyme on most measures.
pmc-13295778:
Karlijn de Joode and colleagues test blood enzyme patterns as immunotherapy predictors in lung cancer in a 2026 study. Altogether 210 patients with advanced disease gave blood before treatment across several centres. A model mixing enzyme patterns with the tissue score sorted patients by later progression in a validation group. Predicted-benefit patients stayed progression-free longer, and the combined model beat the tissue score alone. The blood test may sharpen selection for costly immune treatment.
pmc-13295978:
Attila Nemes and colleagues chart how the right atrium of the heart behaves in healthy mid pregnancy, in a 2026 imaging study. Pregnancy raises blood volume and heart output, so the heart's chambers adapt in shape and work. Using three-dimensional speckle-tracking ultrasound, the team gauged the right atrium's volumes and strain in twenty women in their second trimester and thirty matched women who were not pregnant.

Early and late filling volumes of the atrium ran lower in pregnancy, while the end-squeeze volume held the same. Active emptying fell and passive emptying rose, with most other gauges alike between groups. Strain checks varied by region, lower at the base and higher at the top of the chamber in pregnant women. The authors read the pattern as healthy adaptation worth knowing before judging scans in pregnancy.
pmc-13297278:
Marios Sagris and a large team contrast vessel imaging with pressure-based physiology for borderline coronary narrowings in a 2026 review. A standard angiogram shows only a flat silhouette, leaving severity genuinely uncertain in many cases. Two tool families answer different questions about the same lesion.

Ultrasound and light-based imaging from inside the vessel reveal lumen size and plaque makeup, guiding stent work. Pressure measures instead ask whether the narrowing actually starves heart muscle of blood. Trials link both approaches to better outcomes than angiography alone. The review sorts which tool suits which lesion type, helping interventionists choose rather than treating the families as rivals.
pmc-13297778:
Carmen Steffani Perez-Parrella and colleagues review clinic records for a mouth-applied form of amitriptyline in burning mouth syndrome, in a 2026 study from Murcia, Spain. The syndrome brings lasting mouth burning with no visible cause, and standard care often disappoints. Twenty-seven patients used a one percent preparation on the mouth for four weeks.

Burning scores fell clearly over the month, with the typical rating dropping from seven and a half to five. Anxiety and depression scores eased as well. Felt dryness and measured saliva flow, by contrast, barely moved. Side effects were few. The authors present the gel as a promising option, while asking for proper controlled trials to confirm it.
pmc-13297878:
Cutting one gene weakens the seals in lymph vessel walls, Nada S Ahmed and her team report in a 2026 cell study. The gene, ZEB1, is known for guiding cell change in other tissues. Its role in the lymph system was not mapped.

The team read both protein and gene data from lymph vessel cells. Cells that lost ZEB1 showed less of a key mark on VE-cadherin, the glue protein at cell seams. The cell sheet leaked more, and white blood cells crossed it more freely. Loss of ZEB1 also cut the kinase YES and shifted YAP1, and muting YAP1 alone copied much of the leak. The work ties ZEB1 to the upkeep of lymph vessel walls.
pmc-13298978:
Aging eyes lose teamwork at reading distance more than at arm's length, shows a 2026 vision study by Bingqing Sun and co-authors. Using a rotating ring test viewed through red-blue glasses, they measured dynamic vision at four distances in 54 presbyopic and 77 non-presbyopic participants.

Sharpness discrimination and dynamic depth perception showed no group differences. Binocular integration, how well the two eyes' images merge, told another story: presbyopic participants passed less often at 0.4, 0.7, and 1 metre, though not at 3 metres. Those needing stronger reading additions, at least 1.5 diopters, lagged at every distance. The authors say the test exposes addition-dependent deficits that static charts miss.
pmc-13299878:
Y Yamazaki and colleagues compare heart injury markers across three pulsed field ablation systems for atrial fibrillation, in a 2026 single-hospital study. Eighty-one patients received vein isolation with one device only, and blood markers of muscle injury were measured before and one day after the procedure. Application counts differed notably between systems.

Changes in four injury markers differed significantly across the groups. One system showed the smallest rises, while another tended toward the largest increases, a pattern the authors note may partly reflect red blood cell breakdown. Device choice and application number may matter when selecting treatment for patients with kidney problems, they suggest.
pmc-13299978:
Khaldoun Tabbah and a large student-era team compare lung function between smokers and non-smokers at a university in the United Arab Emirates, in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Smoking included cigarettes, vaping devices, shisha, and a regional pipe. Spirometry followed international guidelines for 630 students whose tests met quality criteria.

Smoking prevalence ran far higher in men than women. Smokers showed a significantly lower ratio of forced air measures than non-smokers, an early obstruction signal, despite slightly higher volume percentages. Body mass also shaped results, with higher weight tied to lower ratios. Male smokers fared worst in layered analysis. Early screening and cessation programmes for young men are urged.
pmc-13300178:
A Keresteci and co-authors present a 2026 retrospective study of catheter ablation for sustained ventricular tachycardia in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a genetic heart muscle disease tied to sudden death. Defibrillators prevent many deaths, yet some patients still receive repeated shocks from fast rhythms. The authors reviewed sixteen patients treated at a university electrophysiology unit between January 2017 and December 2024.

The group averaged about fifty-one years of age, and three quarters were men. Most had an implanted defibrillator, and low-voltage scar was found in half, mainly near the apex and septum. Over a mean follow-up near fifty months, seven patients had a recurrence, and no major procedural complications occurred. The authors judge ablation feasible and reasonably safe for selected patients with recurrent tachycardia.
pmc-13300278:
Miruna Popovici and co-authors report a 2026 exploratory study of low-cost digital support for people with heart failure and reduced pumping strength. Many such patients stay undertreated because dose increases stall and follow-up fragments. The pathway combined smartphone messaging, home blood pressure and heart rate reports, daily weight checks, and scheduled video visits, and it was compared with matched historical usual care.

After matching, one hundred patients sat in each group. Six-month adherence reached 82 percent with digital support against 64 percent under usual care. The supported group also gained more drug classes, more dose increases, and larger gains on an optimization score covering the four foundational drug groups. Hospitalization and death outcomes favored the pathway but were exploratory only. The authors recommend a prospective multicenter trial to confirm the effect.
pmc-13300978:
F Notaristefano and co-authors test whether focal pulsed field ablation can be tolerated under local anesthesia alone, in a 2026 study. Single shot devices usually demand general anesthesia because their pulses trigger muscle contraction, while the newer dual energy focal catheter was expected to recruit less muscle. Twenty-four patients with persistent fibrillation received pulsed field energy at the back of the left atrium for vein isolation and a floor line, with every symptom logged by site.

No muscle contractions appeared. Cough struck about two thirds of patients, most often at the left upper vein, and patients who coughed there had shorter distances between that vein and the nearest airway branch. Pain also affected about two thirds, without any link to esophagus position on scans. Switching a few applications to radiofrequency solved symptoms, and isolation succeeded in everyone with no acute complications. The authors call the approach feasible and safe.
pmc-13301078:
F Klein and co-authors investigate why women respond better to resynchronization therapy than men, using ultra-high-frequency electrocardiography, in a 2026 two-center study. The cohort held 345 patients with wide QRS patterns, seventy percent men, whose specialized tracings measured the true electrical spread between the first and last activated ventricular regions.

Women arrived with more left bundle branch block and far more non-ischemic disease than men. Overall QRS duration matched between the sexes, yet inside the bundle branch block subgroup women ran shorter QRS values even after accounting for body size and cause. The surprise sat in the middle ranges: at matched QRS widths between 140 and 179 milliseconds, women showed greater electrical dyssynchrony than men. More hidden dyssynchrony at the same headline number, the authors argue, means more for the therapy to fix, which could explain women's superior response.
pmc-13301578:
A Delaet and co-authors test whether smartwatch monitoring survives three months of real life in a 2026 analysis from the STAROSA study. Forty-four patients with atrial fibrillation and sleep apnea wore watches that sampled pulse pattern for one minute every nine minutes, while doing twice daily spot checks. Recordings were color coded by quality and rhythm, and patients rated the experience.

The watch installed in ninety-five percent and ran a median eighty-eight days. Nearly fifty-nine percent of data rated high quality, with a median sixty-eight measurements a day. Compliance sat above ninety percent for both methods, though motivation ran higher for the watch. Detection was the rout: fibrillation found in eighty percent of patients by watch against forty-three percent by spot checks, with nine and a half times as many episodes logged. Satisfaction scored fifty-four of sixty, supporting wearables in structured care.
pmc-13301778:
Stefania Chiappinotto and colleagues reflect, in a 2026 paper, on running cross-border research with people in fragile life situations. Their experience comes from Protecting You & Others, an Erasmus+ project spanning five countries. Ethics rules protect such people, yet applying broad principles inside varied local settings proved hard for the team.

Working from reflexive notes and group discussion, the authors describe recurring problems and the fixes they adopted. Defining who counts as at risk, in a way both inclusive and workable, caused repeated debate, and labels themselves risked stigma. Some people rejected the at-risk label that outsiders assigned to them. The authors argue for flexible procedures centred on the person, adjusted during a study rather than fixed rules set at the start.
pmc-13302278:
Zhiyu Duan and co-authors publish, in a 2026 protocol, a three-stage plan to predict the early kidney-function dip that follows starting an SGLT2 inhibitor drug. These medicines protect kidneys long term, yet filtration commonly drops within the first weeks. Routine clinical clues predict that dip inconsistently, so urine proteins may add signal.

The study will recruit roughly six to seven hundred patients with stage three or four kidney disease across discovery, internal validation, and external validation groups. Mass spectrometry will screen urine proteins tied to a filtration fall of at least ten percent at one month. Top candidates face confirmatory testing, then join seven routine variables in a statistical prediction model. Stopping rules and performance measures are fixed in advance.
pmc-13302778:
Sebastião Freitas de Medeiros and Gustavo Arantes Rosa Maciel review, in a 2026 narrative review, the two-way chemical conversation between fat tissue and the liver in women with polycystic ovary syndrome. The syndrome commonly travels with belly fat, insulin resistance, and metabolic syndrome. Signals released by fat and liver cells may drive much of that overlap.

Excess belly fat floods the liver with fatty acids, fuelling toxicity, oxidative stress, and inflammation there. Liver-made signals such as fetuin-A run abnormally high and track with insulin resistance and fatty liver progression. Fat-made signals including resistin and chemerin add inflammation and hormone disturbance, while a falling adiponectin-to-leptin balance worsens matters. The authors frame this crosstalk as a target for earlier risk detection.
pmc-13303278:
Fikriye Kalkan and co-authors profile, in a 2026 clinic study, why older adults come to an allergy service and what they actually have. Ageing reshapes immunity, and many complaints blamed on allergy in later life turn out to be something else. Records covered every patient aged sixty-five or more seen at a large Ankara hospital clinic during 2024 and 2025.

The group held 1,302 patients with an average age near seventy-one, and almost two thirds carried another illness, most often high blood pressure. Runny nose and sneezing led the complaints, followed by itching and drug reactions. Most rhinitis proved non-allergic, pollen was the commonest true sensitivity, and antibiotics topped the drug culprits. The authors urge thorough, individual work-ups in this age group.
pmc-13303878: Wenqi Chen and colleagues issue a 2026 author correction to a study on epigenetic control of thymus homing and T cell development in embryos. Control graphs, source data entries, and images in several main and supplementary figures were copied or swapped by mistake. Two supplementary figure titles were mislabeled, and an extra data file was included. All listed items have been corrected in the article and its source data file. The notice gives a figure-by-figure account of each fix so readers can check the updated record for themselves.
pmc-13305278:
James Alex Sumawe reports a 2026 radiology case of parotid gland cancer spreading widely through the body. Cancers of this saliva gland are rare, and spread to lung, brain, and liver at once is rarer still.

A 60-year-old man first had face nerve weakness and bulky local disease treated with surgery plus chemo and radiation. Scans later showed many lung nodules with a large mass near the airway, ring-shaped brain deposits with heavy swelling, chest lining spread, and liver spots. A thyroid lump proved harmless on needle testing. Gentle chemo and support care followed.
pmc-13305578:
Huisen Yu, Bin Gao, and Yuanyuan Li review monitors that gauge anesthesia depth during surgery in a 2026 narrative synthesis. Brain-wave tools such as the bispectral index promise steadier dosing than clinical signs alone.

Keeping depth in the right band lowers chances of waking mid-surgery, blood pressure drops from overly deep dosing, and confusion or thinking problems afterward. Brain-guided care looks most helpful for older patients and those with heart disease. Tool limits remain, including varied algorithms and uneven drug sensitivity. Mixing several signals plus smart computing may sharpen personal dosing next.
pmc-13305778:
Bharat Chandra Das and colleagues test the newer antibiotic tedizolid against resistant staphylococci and enterococci in a 2026 study from a level-one trauma centre in India. They compare it with linezolid, an older drug of the same family that some strains now resist. The collection held 103 isolates gathered between 2023 and 2025.

Seven linezolid-resistant enterococcal isolates still showed low tedizolid levels needed for inhibition, which supports tedizolid as a backup option. Agreement between the two drugs was strong for enterococci and complete for staphylococci when gradient strips were used. Disc testing for staphylococci missed some susceptible results, so the authors urge care in choosing the test method. They note the work is the first such report from India.
pmc-13306378:
Wentao Cheng mapped where glacier-fed debris flows are likely in China's Gaizi River Basin in a 2026 hazard study. The alpine basin, crossed by the Karakoram Highway, faces complex terrain, active faults and shifting ice that make forecasting hard.

Hybrid models joined statistics with one-class anomaly detection trained on past disaster records, since labelled safe and unsafe sites are scarce. Land shape factors such as slope, roughness and wetness carried most signal, while distance to ice and rainfall added little in this dataset. One generative model gave the most balanced maps, avoiding the over-warning seen in rivals.
pmc-13307578:
Balcha Girma Masresha and co-authors review in 2026 a quarter century of measles and measles rubella campaigns across the WHO African Region, from 2001 to 2025. They drew on campaign reports and post campaign surveys sent to the regional office, as the region aims to end both diseases in most countries by 2030.

In all, 326 campaigns in 44 countries gave more than 1.5 billion doses to children in the years covered here. Most campaigns hit the national cover goal on paper, yet district goals were rarely met in full. Survey based cover lagged the paper figures, which hints at weak counts. Better tools to find unvaccinated children are now urgent.
pmc-13308478:
Bird flu can sweep through a chicken flock even when the birds have been dosed against it. Ahmed Salaheldin and co-authors report a 2026 study of an outbreak of the H5N1 strain in vaccinated laying hens in Egypt.

The flock held 15,000 brown hens, each dosed four times with flu vaccines. About seven weeks after the last dose, infection was confirmed by lab tests and full gene reads. Egg output fell and about a third of the flock died over 52 days. Gene checks showed the virus closely matched strains then spreading in Egypt, with changes near the spots that immune defenses target. The case shows how a shifted virus can slip past current vaccines.
pmc-13308578:
Ivana Bureš Valentić and Krešimir Reiner report in 2026 anaesthetic care for a first time mother with Klippel-Feil syndrome who needed a planned caesarean birth. The syndrome fuses neck bones from birth and often brings spine curve and other body quirks that make airway and spinal care hard.

The woman, aged 32 years, had fusion from the third neck bone to the first chest bone, plus raised shoulder blades and right side deafness. Spinal anaesthesia worked for the birth, yet the team stood ready to switch to general anaesthesia if the block failed. No single method suits all such patients, so each plan must fit the body at hand and put safety first.
pmc-13308778:
Jiadong Yu and co-authors probe in 2026 why people follow health guidance when rival claims flood formal and informal channels, using survey data from 742 adults in the United States. They modelled how trust in each channel shaped risk views, plot beliefs, and plans to mask and vaccinate during COVID-19.

Trust in formal sources tracked with graver risk views, weaker plot beliefs, and stronger plans to act for safety. Trust in informal sources pulled each of those the other way in the model runs. Felt severity sat at the hub, lifting mask use at once and vaccine plans through lower plot belief. Crisis teams must work both channels, not just the formal one.
pmc-13309478:
Oskar W. Persson and co-authors track swelling signals in blood and spinal fluid after severe head injury in a 2026 study. Swelling drives much of the damage after such injury, yet its first-week pattern in both fluids was poorly mapped. Two lab platforms for measuring these signals had also rarely been compared head to head.

Twenty-one adults with severe injury gave samples in the first days and again later in the first week, with orthopedic patients as a comparison group. Many signals rose in both fluids, and three key signals rose in both places. Agreement between the two lab platforms varied by signal. The authors offer the paired fluid data as a guide for timing future anti-swelling care.
pmc-13309578:
Mhamed Benaissa models heat and mass flow of a special nanofluid over a stretching round cylinder in a 2026 study. Such flows appear in heat exchangers, pipelines, and vehicle bodies. The fluid here is a second-grade nanofluid, meaning it carries tiny particles and resists flow in a memory-like way, under a magnetic field.

Governing equations were reshaped into simpler forms and solved on a computer with a finite-difference method. The study varies magnet strength, fluid grade, chemical reaction rate, and slip at the surface to see how heat and particle spread respond. Density that shifts with heat is also included. The author reports trends meant to guide design of cooling and coating systems.
pmc-13310378:
Maryam Hekmat and co-authors present a face rash that mimicked a common pigment disorder in a 2026 case report. The true disease was lichen planopilaris, a rare immune condition that scars hair follicles and causes permanent hair loss. On the face rather than the scalp, it is exceedingly rare and easy to misread.

A 38-year-old man showed a flat dark patch across cheek and forehead that looked like melasma, the common pigment condition. Tissue study proved the scarring follicle disease instead. Standard melasma care would have missed it, costing time while damage advanced. The authors urge tissue checks when facial pigment patches resist usual treatment, and call for more published skin-scope images of this presentation.
pmc-13310778:
