The review traces CAR architecture from first-generation constructs to armored and fifth-generation designs, compares viral and non-viral gene delivery, and surveys in vivo engineering, off-the-shelf allogeneic products, logic-gated receptors, and safety switches. Readers gain a full tour of how CAR-T works, where it succeeds, and what must improve next.
pmc-13394878:
Yuvraj Pathak, David Muhlestein, and Matthew Balcarras show, in 2026, that one doctor can charge many prices for the same office service. New United States rules force insurers to post the rates they strike with providers. The team pulled files from the biggest national payers for late 2025. They studied the twenty most used office services.

For a single provider, the gap between the lowest and highest rate averaged a large share of the public Medicare rate. The same visit or test can thus cost plans very different sums. The authors say employers and rule makers can use the data to pick leaner networks. Sunlight on rates, they argue, is a first step to lower spending.
pmc-13395478:
Mitchell Manware and co-authors measure, in 2026, how far public views of deadly weather stray from science in the United States. Death rates from wildfire smoke, heat, cold, floods, and drought have now been mapped by county. Yale survey maps give what adults in each county think about climate harm. The team set views beside the death maps to size the gap.

Perception gaps followed the same map pattern as real death rates. Counties where more people accept that warming is happening showed smaller gaps for every weather type. Fewer than half of adults think warming will harm them in person. The authors say lifting basic climate grasp is key to cutting health risk.
pmc-13395878:
An Wang and colleagues report a two thousand twenty-six materials study aimed at spinal cord injury repair. Spinal cord damage usually leaves lasting loss of movement. Natural gel materials may help rebuild the injured area.

The team modified peach gum sugar chains and loaded them with nerve growth factor. Tests confirmed the chemical change and measured strength, heat behaviour, and self-healing. The loaded gel showed strong performance on those checks. In cell experiments it encouraged nerve fibre outgrowth and eased the hostile injury environment. The work offers a plant-based candidate scaffold for nerve repair research.
pmc-13395978:
Marcus Vinicius Almeida Marques and co-authors hunted for new chemistry in a fungus living inside a plant, and report a new compound in 2026. The fungus, Talaromyces pinophilus strain J6, came from the plant Euphorbia umbellata and was part of a wider search for useful natural products.

Rather than test every extract blindly, the group first scanned the fungus with high-resolution mass spectrometry and matched signals against a home-built library of known Talaromyces compounds. Seven known products were named that way, which pointed them toward one unknown. Purifying the extract yielded a new polyketide, named (-)-R-talaropinophiloic acid, plus a known relative, and lab methods fixed both structures.
pmc-13396178:
Guo and co-authors optimize, in 2026, a bacterial gene-insertion system for use in human cells, for therapies that need whole genes delivered to exact addresses. The IS621 recombinase uses a bridge RNA with two programmable loops, one gripping the target site and one the donor DNA. The team engineered the protein and its RNA partner, producing a system they call enIS621-tebRNA, and tested it across five cell types including kidney, colon, retinal, immune, and liver lines.

The engineered system inserted kilobase-scale DNA cargos at rates up to 27.75 percent of treated cells, without leaving scar sequences. As a demonstration, they installed the gene for a CD19 chimeric antigen receptor, the targeting unit of CAR T-cell cancer therapy, at chosen loci. They also integrated the gene encoding Factor IX, the clotting protein missing in hemophilia B. The authors present the platform as a versatile route to gene insertion.
pmc-13396378:
Zhang and colleagues identify, in 2026, a biomechanical driver of radioresistance in glioblastoma, the brain tumor that accounts for 50.1 percent of primary intrinsic malignant brain tumors and still carries a median survival under two years. Stiffening of the tumor's surrounding matrix helped cancer stem cells survive radiation. Gene analysis showed stiff matrices switch on the protein IQGAP3 through the YAP1 and TEAD transcription factors in these stem cells.

IQGAP3 binds and stabilizes SOX2, a core stem-cell transcription factor, sustaining self-renewal and survival after irradiation. Blocking IQGAP3 lowered SOX2 levels in cells and animals, resensitizing tumors to radiation and slowing growth in their models. Screening approved drugs for ones that disrupt the IQGAP3-SOX2 grip identified trimetrexate, an existing drug that reaches the brain, as a pharmacologic disruptor. The authors propose pairing such a drug with radiotherapy to attack the stem-cell niche that stiffness creates.
pmc-13396578:
Hannah Demleitner and co-authors evaluated what it was like to build a patient guide with patients, rather than for them, in palliative care. Their 2026 qualitative study follows the making of a German patient guide linked to a best-practice recommendation on intentional sedation at the end of life.

Between April and September 2024, participants answered open-ended questionnaires and then sat for interviews about the joint work. The authors sorted what helped the partnership, such as clear roles and time to build trust, from what hindered it. Patient involvement is praised worldwide in guideline work, but reports on how it plays out for patient-facing material in palliative care remain rare.
pmc-13396778:
Itsuma Nagao writes a 2026 perspective on gut-on-a-chip systems that grow human intestinal microbes alongside gut tissue, and what they could do for drug testing. Many swallowed drugs are changed by the gut before reaching the blood. This first-pass effect varies by person, which helps explain why the same dose acts differently across patients.

Chips that pair a living gut lining with a cultured microbial community let researchers measure host, microbe, and drug acting on each other directly. Nagao argues such platforms could feed predictive models of a person's gut ecosystem, guiding dose choices and flagging drug-microbe clashes that current rules-based testing barely covers.
pmc-13397578:
N A Vernice and co-authors review what to do when a silicone breast implant breaks silently in an older patient. Their 2026 scoping review searches medical databases through January 2025. Regulators advise scans starting five to six years after placement, yet no guidance covers symptom-free ruptures in elderly patients, whose surgical risk and life horizon differ.

More than 3.5 million people in the United States carry implants, and break risk grows as devices age, though modern gel implants last better. The review weighs watchful scanning against removal or exchange, balancing operation risk, comfort and quality of life. From the gathered evidence the authors draft practical advice meant for shared decisions with older patients.
pmc-13397778:
In a 2026 study from Shanxi Province, Jilin Ren and coauthors examined how ready endocrine nurses are for digital diabetes care. The focus is nurse-led telehealth and remote glucose monitoring in China, where digital tools are spreading but staff readiness remains uneven. The authors also asked which personal and workplace factors shape nurses' willingness to use those tools in daily care.

They surveyed 230 nurses in five public hospitals between October 2024 and January 2025, pairing questionnaires with interviews. Readiness was moderate to high overall, with strong openness and drive but weaker perceived support and resources. Phone follow-up and WeChat contact were common, while video visits and structured remote monitoring were rarer. Recently trained nurses reported wider tool use and more favorable views. The findings guide training and support for nurses moving diabetes care online.
pmc-13398178:
Longbiao Yao and colleagues traced how fat cells turn into wound-healing fibroblasts and what controls that switch. Their 2026 paper uses lineage tracing in skin wounds to follow cells that began as adiponectin-expressing fat cells. Fat cells are known to be plastic, but it was unclear whether their fibroblast-like turn was a lasting change or a brief loss of fat traits.

Cells derived from fat cells appeared beside wounds, joined the wound fibroblast pool, and gained collagen, smooth muscle actin, and cell division while losing fat traits. Active PDGFR alpha signaling boosted their growth and improved blood vessel growth and skin closure, while deleting its receptor did the opposite. Wound-derived cells stayed fibroblast-like after healing ended. The work reframes fat cells as durable repair contributors, with implications for scarring and regeneration research.
pmc-13399078:
The Journal of Diabetes Investigation issued this Expression of Concern in 2026 about a 2017 article by M. Xue and colleagues. That article studied fatty change in donor livers as a risk factor for new diabetes arising soon after liver transplantation. The journal, its editor-in-chief, and the publisher Wiley agreed to alert readers.

A third-party organization raised doubts about where the transplanted organs came from. The study covered transplants done between 2001 and 2014, when most cases in China predated the voluntary donation program. Reporting suggests organs were widely taken from executed prisoners before 2015. The authors did not answer the publisher's questions, so consent records and ethics approvals could not be checked. Readers are warned that the organ sourcing may not have met the ethics standards of its time.
pmc-13399178:
Samantha L. Beeston and team used CT scans to test whether air-filled tail vertebrae evolved once or several times in sauropod dinosaurs. Their 2026 work focuses on postcranial skeletal pneumaticity, air spaces inside bone, which is common before the hips but rare in tail vertebrae. Outer pits alone cannot prove air spaces, so inner imaging is needed to confirm them.

New scans of six Middle to Late Jurassic sauropods found several tail vertebrae without air spaces, including specimens of Cetiosaurus and Wamweracaudia. By contrast, Tornieria africana showed deep outer pits that joined inner chambers across its tail vertebrae. Joined with a critical review of earlier claims, the work supports multiple independent origins of extreme tail pneumaticity. It also warns that older outer-only identifications need rechecking.
pmc-13399478:
Jie Gao and colleagues propose a combined scheduling and routing system for fleets of automated guided vehicles in warehouses with movable containers, in a 2026 engineering study. The team's design attacks all three problems at once and tests the result in a simulated multi-zone warehouse.

First, each job is split into two sub-tasks: a long-distance haul and a precision in-racking placement, each handed to the vehicle type built for it. Second, a pre-allocation algorithm lines up a vehicle's next assignment before it finishes the current one, cutting the empty running that plagues conventional dispatch. Simulation comparisons showed a lower system no-load rate, less path congestion, and better overall throughput than the baseline methods. The authors present the package as a step toward warehouses that replan themselves continuously.
pmc-13400478:
Zirui Luo leads a randomized trial, published in 2026, of combined magnetic stimulation for swallowing problems after stroke. The method pairs stimulation over the brain with stimulation of peripheral nerves. How it changes brain networks was unclear, so brain activity was measured alongside swallowing tests.

Forty-four patients were split into four groups mixing real and sham versions of each stimulation type. The fully active group gained most on eating ability and on a scale grading how safely food passes the airway. Video X-ray measures of throat movement also improved most there. Light-based brain scans showed stronger links within the front and movement-sensing network on the stroke side, tied to better throat closure.
pmc-13400578:
Francisco José Navarro-Triviño and colleagues review, in 2026, a signaling pair called OX40 and OX40L that helps T cells persist in inflamed skin and airways. The pathway was long tied to type 2 inflammation, the kind behind allergy. New work widens its role across both tissues.

Acting late in T cell activation, OX40 keeps effector cells alive, builds tissue-resident memory and tunes regulatory cells. Alarm signals from surface tissue switch on its partner on presenting cells, reinforcing allergic-type responses. The axis feeds chronic disease in eczema, asthma, rhinitis and nasal polyps, and also appears in other immune patterns and disorders. Antibody drugs targeting the pathway are discussed as a shared treatment angle.
pmc-13400678:
Iulian D Toader argues, in 2026, that the nineteenth-century mathematician Hermann Hankel held to his guiding principle for extending number systems for a subtle reason. The principle says formal laws should stay permanent when mathematics grows. Hankel used it both to extend numbers and to justify formal theories detached from intuition about size.

Yet he admitted limits: some extensions clashed with the principle, and a formal account of irrational numbers looked inconsistent to him. Toader reads his loyalty as a conservative strategy that still allows revising basic arithmetic laws when reasons to revise outweigh reasons to keep them. Later critics, by contrast, hardened the principle into an anti-revision stance that cost them parts of modern mathematics.
pmc-13400878:
Alicia-Sophie Schebesta and colleagues test, in 2026, whether the chemistry and length of separation columns still matter for proteome depth on the fastest mass spectrometers. Protein detection once depended heavily on good separation. Modern instruments sample so quickly that the balance may have shifted.

The team ran five column chemistries across eight lengths on a high-speed instrument. Despite differing materials and sizes, results converged. The standard chemistries all found over 150,000 precursors and roughly nine thousand protein groups. Retention patterns still differed by chemistry. Yet those differences did not turn into real coverage gains. Column choice, within modern ranges, appears far less critical than before.
pmc-13401278:
Amirali Alizadeh wrote a 2026 letter to the editor about a study by Kalantari and colleagues that counted workflow interruptions during 251 operations in five academic teaching hospitals. That study logged over fifty thousand minutes of operating room activity and attributed 45 of 319 identified causes, about 14 percent, to teaching and trainees.

Alizadeh argues the harder question is what those trainee-related pauses actually do. The 14.1 percent figure is a share of identified causes, not of the 281 interruption events, since one event could have several causes. A pause might mean poor preparation, slower supervised learning, or a senior surgeon stopping a trainee to prevent harm. Lumping them together, the letter warns, hides whether teaching moments protect patients or simply disrupt work.
pmc-13401378:
Corneille Kabagale Ansima and a large team of co-authors describe a 2026 study of past records on drug-resistant bacteria. The records come from Bukavu Provincial General Referral Hospital in the eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo. Data on resistance in the region are scarce, even though resistant germs hit low- and middle-income countries hardest.

The team analysed 1,801 distinct bacterial strains from routine samples collected during 2024. Standard lab methods named the germs, and drug response was read against EUCAST 2024 rules. Enterobacterales dominated the set, at just over 80 percent of strains, followed by Gram-positive cocci at about 11 percent and non-fermenting Gram-negative bacilli at about 8 percent. Results are broken down by bacterial group, antibiotic class, and major resistance patterns, giving a local picture of how much multidrug resistance the hospital faces.
pmc-13401578:
Kaoru Niimi and colleagues tracked a rare, severe late complication of chemotherapy for high-risk gestational trophoblastic neoplasia, a pregnancy-related tumor. Their 2026 series examines therapy-related myeloid neoplasms, including therapy-related leukemia, after multi-drug chemotherapy. These second blood cancers are uncommon but often fatal, and their frequency in this patient group had been unclear.

Reviewing 47 patients treated from 1990 to 2023, the team found four, or 8.5 percent, who developed therapy-related myeloid neoplasms three to five years after starting treatment. All four had received etoposide-containing regimens at cumulative doses of at least 6,000 milligrams per square meter, with KMT2A rearrangements or IDH mutations. Despite stem cell transplantation, all four died. The paper urges long-term blood monitoring after high-dose etoposide, even as curative chemotherapy remains essential.
pmc-13401678:
Addae Boateng Adu-Gyamfi analysed anaemia among women of reproductive age in Lesotho using the country's 2023 to 2024 Demographic and Health Survey, in a 2026 study. Globally, more than 600 million women aged 15 to 49 live with anaemia, with the heaviest burdens in South Asia and sub-Saharan Africa.

The analysis covered 3,105 women with complete haemoglobin measurements, surveyed between late November 2023 and the end of February 2024. Overall prevalence came out at just under 54 percent of women, a level classed as a severe public health problem. Descriptive statistics set the scale, and a binary logistic regression model identified associated factors, reported as crude and adjusted odds ratios with confidence intervals. The findings give Lesotho's health planners a current national estimate and a set of risk markers to target.
pmc-13401778:
Inès Lakbar and Daniele Poole wrote a 2026 essay on why meta-analyses of the same question can disagree, using melatonin drugs for preventing delirium in critically ill patients as their worked example. Meta-analysis is widely treated as the top of the evidence ladder, but the authors argue the pooled number is built, not simply found.

Investigators must decide which studies are similar enough to combine and how much to trust each one, and those judgement calls construct the estimate. Chaves and colleagues included both melatonin and ramelteon and found support for prevention. The authors' own group restricted the pool to melatonin alone and concluded the evidence was too weak to recommend routine use. Quantitative pooling, they warn, can hide the contribution of the most credible studies rather than clarify it.
pmc-13402878:
Motahare Baghestani and co-authors set out reference values for healthy bone density around tooth roots, measured from digital dental images. Bone density reflects the balance of bone building and breakdown, shifts with age, hormones, and diseases from osteoporosis to thyroid trouble, and guides dental decisions from implants to treatment planning. The bone holding teeth differs between jaws, with upper jaw bone typically thinner and more porous.

Their descriptive analysis reads normal periapical density, the tissue at root tips, on digital radiographs to define what healthy looks like before disease enters the picture. Such baselines matter because dentists judge loss against an expected norm, and alveolar bone thins naturally with age even without illness. The authors frame the values as groundwork for spotting abnormal change and for planning care around teeth and implants.
pmc-13403278:
Tanemura and co-authors report, in 2026, a severe complication of leadless pacemaker implantation. During retrieval of the device in an 86-year-old man treated for heart block and syncope, the heart's papillary muscle was caught between the delivery sheath and the pacemaker. It tore away, causing massive leakage through the tricuspid valve. Leadless devices avoid many lead-related problems, but effects on the tricuspid valve were known; this rupture route was new.

Resistance during removal was the warning sign of the entrapment, a lesson the authors stress for operators. The patient then developed worsening heart failure needing non-invasive ventilation and intravenous furosemide at 20 milligrams twice daily, and imaging showed sharply reduced left ventricular function with an ejection fraction of 26.7 percent in follow-up studies. He received a transvenous pacemaker, recovered on medication without valve surgery, and transferred to rehabilitation, a benign ending the authors document.
pmc-13403478:
Madeleine Nicolas led a 2026 map study of child leukemia deaths across Mexico over two decades. Death records for ages 0 to 19 covered every local district from 2003 to 2023. The team hunted for clusters and then matched them against land, water, and industry data.

Ten strong clusters appeared, five with high death rates and five with low rates. High-rate areas hugged the Gulf coast and the southeast. All five high clusters overlapped oil and gas sites, on wet land where rain can soak pollutants into ground water. Low clusters sat mostly in the dry west. The pattern points to preventable local causes worth urgent checks.
pmc-13403578:
Abhishek Ghosh and team weighed remote buprenorphine start-up for opioid use disorder in India through a rollout lens. Their 2026 qualitative work looks at TABI, a hybrid model joining in-person start with remote follow-up, which trials had shown no worse than standard care. Process proof on reach, uptake, and staying power had been missing.

Talks with 14 patients and four providers, guided by the RE-AIM frame, found that remote care cut travel and time blocks and improved function while curbing opioid use. Tech literacy gaps, shaky networks, stigma, and provider bias about fit held use back, while family backing and provider trust aided uptake. Fidelity held despite connectivity workarounds. The work ties staying power to structured follow-up and hybrid backup.
pmc-13403678:
Monika Stompor-Gorący and colleagues gave a first review in 2026 of pedalitin, a plant compound in the flavonoid family. Plants make such compounds as pigments and as part of their chemical defenses. Lab reports credit pedalitin with fighting cancer cells, easing swelling, and guarding inner organs.

It may also sharpen insulin response and shield nerve cells, based on early studies. The review gathers how the compound is obtained and how its actions have been tested. Small chemical changes to its shape could yield new drug leads. The authors frame it as a hopeful base for work on diseases tied to modern lifestyles.
pmc-13403778:
Ji-Seok Yoon and co-authors tested in 2026 a long-acting form of human C-peptide as a shield for the mouse retina. Excess glutamate signaling kills the nerve cells that carry sight, a process tied to glaucoma. Their version links the peptide to a carrier polymer for slow release in the eye.

A toxin that mimics glutamate harm raised cell stress, swelling signals, and nerve cell death in untreated eyes. The treated eyes kept more nerve cells, a thicker retina, and working signal flow along the optic nerve. Protection lasted at least three weeks from delivery. Calmer cell stress, not calcium change, seemed to drive the gain.
pmc-13404178:
Phung Van Nguyen laid out in 2026 a simple rule for picking how to rebuild a missing eyebrow with hair-bearing tissue from the temple. Eyebrows frame the face and shield the eye, so rebuilds must restore cover plus hair grain and density. The choice turns mainly on whether the temple on the same side can spare tissue.

Two cases show the rule at work. When the same-side temple was intact, a flap swung over on its own stalk did the job. When past surgery had spoiled that side, a free flap crossed from the other temple. Both flaps lived fully, and both patients liked the lasting match.
pmc-13404378:
Arianna L Williams-Katek and a ten-author team showed in 2026 that two probe sets can fish for gene messages on one tissue slide at once. Tissue gene mapping tools force a trade: small probe sets read each gene keenly, while large sets cover far more genes. Their test used 17 human lung samples on one shared slide platform.

The hybrid run paired a keen set of up to 480 genes with a broad set covering 5,000 genes. Early prep steps for the two chemistries already matched, which made the pairing workable. Readout steps differ sharply, so the blend needed care. Success gives labs both depth and breadth in a single pass.
pmc-13405178:
Sajid and colleagues chart an American trend: deaths where heart failure and psychoactive substance abuse appear together, using a quarter century of death records before and after COVID-19. Either condition strains the heart and health system; together they mark a growing overlap. Their 2026 study mines the CDC WONDER database for 1999 to 2023, computing age adjusted death rates and trend breaks by sex, age, race, and region.

Deaths reached 771,739. The rate climbed from under two per hundred thousand people in 1999 to over twenty by 2023. The steepest surge came in the first six years, with steady growth after. Men died at more than double the women's rate, and the burden sat heaviest on adults over sixty five, non-Hispanic White Americans, and rural counties. Most deaths occurred in facilities or at home. The authors argue the overlap needs integrated cardiac and addiction care, not two doors.
pmc-13407578:
Regine Lohss and team tested whether virtual height exposure can gauge postural balance in children with and without cerebral palsy. Their 2026 prospective case-control work places 22 children with cerebral palsy and 24 typically developing children on force plates wearing headsets. Each child stood on a virtual plank at ground level versus 10 meters above virtual ground. Children with cerebral palsy often have gait and balance deficits, yet virtual height tools for balance testing were novel.

Children with cerebral palsy tended toward larger sway ellipse area, greater front-to-back amplitude, and faster sway velocity at virtual height. They also tended to sway more than typically developing peers, though gaps were not statistically clear-cut. Self-reported instability and fear of falling rose at virtual height in both groups. The work suggests virtual height plus force plates may become a useful balance test tool, pending larger studies.
pmc-13407678:
Oluwatoba T. Balogun and co-authors audit, in 2026, misleading reporting, known as spin, in the summaries of systematic reviews published by leading upper-extremity surgery journals. Such reviews steer practice guidelines, so spin in an abstract can distort what surgeons take away, and the team scored ten years of abstracts against nine recognised spin types.

Spin appeared in 28 of 54 reviews, just over half, and 21 reviews carried more than one type. The commonest trick, found in exactly half, was claiming benefit while glossing over a high risk of bias in the underlying studies. Other spin types included selective framing of results. The authors call for stronger reporting frameworks so that evidence summaries in hand and arm surgery can be read at face value.
pmc-13407878:
Adeel Shehzad and team built a machine-learning frame to predict friction stir welding outcomes for naval brass. Their 2026 work targets weld temperature, strength, and hardness, key quality traits in a process where trial-and-error runs are costly. Thin trial data had curbed model exactness, so the team grew data with a variational autoencoder checked for physical-statistical fidelity.

Among support vector regression, AdaBoost, XGBoost, and decision tree models, support vector regression did best, with mean absolute percentage errors of 1.0 percent for temperature, 3.2 percent for strength, and 1.6 percent for hardness. Fresh trial checks confirmed generalization. The frame backs data-driven welding tuning, process watch, and quality control toward Industry 4.0, while wider alloy and parameter checks stay ahead.
pmc-13408478:
Salif Komi, August Winther, and colleagues propose in 2026 that the geography of the spinal cord, more than any single cell type, explains how walking rhythms arise. Central pattern generator circuits in the cord produce locomotion, yet linking their many neuron types to the rhythm has resisted decades of work. The team built a model mouse spinal cord wired by rules drawn from gene-expression maps.

Connections were sampled from measured projection patterns of each cell type, producing a network with nearby excitation, longer-range inhibition, and a lengthwise skew. Rhythmic, controllable locomotion emerged without heavy parameter tuning, and the model predicts waves of activity travelling along the cord during movement. The authors argue these spatial principles may be universal, offering neuroscientists testable predictions about how descending commands find the right spinal targets.
pmc-13411278:
Worapong Kosaruk, Patcharapa Towiboon, and Sarisa Klinhom review in 2026 whether dung samples can reveal immune health in zoo and wild mammals. Catching and bleeding wild animals disturbs them and skews results, so non-invasive markers are prized. An antibody called IgA, active at gut surfaces, washes out in feces and can be measured there.

Twenty-one studies across many species showed fecal IgA is measurable and shifts with real biology. In wild animals it tracked parasites, breeding effort, season, and gut microbe patterns. In captivity it moved with management and individual differences, and matched stress hormones only loosely. Differing lab methods block tidy cross-study comparison, so IgA reads best as a context-sensitive signal.
pmc-13411578:
Xiudong Guan and colleagues develop in 2026 a spinal fluid test for lung cancer that has spread to the membranes around the brain and cord. Scans and cell hunts in spinal fluid often miss this dangerous spread. Tumor DNA in spinal fluid is scarce, which defeats deep sequencing, yet rich in chromosome-scale changes.

Their shallow genome method reads copy-number changes from trace amounts of fluid DNA. Samples from 57 patients showed stronger tumor signals in spinal fluid than in matched blood. A genome amplification score separated membrane spread from brain-only spread with high sensitivity and no false alarms in this group. Repeat sampling also tracked treatment-driven shifts, which supports use in monitoring.
pmc-13414178:
Gulseren Dinc and colleagues test in 2026 whether oridonin, a plant compound, can shield rat ovaries from the chemo drug cisplatin. The drug saves lives yet burns through egg stores, a threat to young patients who want children. Thirty female rats formed three groups. One group stayed clean. One got cisplatin alone. One got cisplatin plus a daily dose of oridonin. After four weeks, ovaries and blood were checked for eggs, a reserve hormone, and harm signals.

Cisplatin cut egg counts at each growth stage and raised scarring in the ovary. Oridonin lifted egg counts back up and cut the scarring by a clear margin. The reserve hormone, pushed down by cisplatin, moved back toward normal. Harm and swelling signals fell too. The team credits a calmer TGF-beta and Smad3 path.
pmc-13415178:
Gadah Ali Alshahrany and co-authors combine a ginger compound with a licensed drug in a mouse model of multiple sclerosis, in 2026. Mice drank cuprizone, a toxin that strips myelin from brain nerves, for five weeks. Four weeks of recovery followed, with no treatment, 6-shogaol from ginger, ibudilast, or both.

Combined treatment improved movement, muscle strength, and memory more than either agent alone during recovery. Brain tissue showed lower activity in genes that drive inflammation and higher activity in calming pathways. Multiple sclerosis damages myelin and axons with no cure at present. A two-pronged pairing like this may support repair once the toxin stops, the authors suggest.
pmc-13415478:
Luis León-Mateos and co-authors present a 2026 real-world study meant as a benchmark for a targeted lung cancer drug. The cancer type carries a RET gene fusion, and a selective RET blocker showed strong results in a single-arm trial. Without a control group, doctors need outside data on how patients fare on standard first-line therapy.

The RECALIB-RET study pooled chart reviews from four European countries. Adults with advanced RET fusion-positive lung cancer had received at least one line of non-targeted systemic therapy. The team logged patient traits, biomarker testing, and treatment patterns in routine care. A small sample blocked the planned head-to-head comparison, so the paper reports benchmark outcomes instead. Trials without controls lean on such real-world yardsticks.
pmc-13415678:
Si-Zu Lin leads a very large team presenting the genome of Chinese fir, an important timber conifer, in 2026. The assembled genome spans about 11.24 billion letters, bloated by ancient repetitive DNA that the species clears slowly. Chinese fir belongs to the cypress family, whose place in gymnosperm family trees has been disputed.

Family analysis refined how cycads and ginkgo relate to gnetophytes and the pine family. No extra whole genome doubling appeared in the Chinese fir line beyond one shared by all seed plants. Population history clues point to glacial refuges and spread centers. A revised model of cone organ development may apply across gymnosperms.
pmc-13415978:
Ferdinand Medard Shilikale and colleagues describe team based care for a baby girl with Currarino syndrome, in a 2026 case report with a literature review. Currarino syndrome is a rare birth fault with three marks: a gut end made wrong, a bent sacrum bone, and a lump in front of the sacrum. Long term stool blocks plus sacrum faults should raise doubt in infants.

Scans confirmed the pattern in this child, and child surgeons, scan experts, and gene experts planned staged care as one team. The gene MNX1 drives many cases passed down in families, though how it shows varies widely. Early spotting guards against bowel blocks, infection, and nerve harm, the authors stress.
pmc-13416078:
Florian Sommer and colleagues track natural killer cells in colorectal cancer patients whose tumors carry the SARIFA pattern, in 2026. SARIFA marks tumors touching fat directly at the invasion front and predicts worse outcomes. Blood was sampled before surgery, a week or so after, and six months later in forty patients plus twenty-seven healthy controls.

Before surgery, SARIFA positive patients already had fewer natural killer cells. After surgery, counts dipped in SARIFA negative patients, then recovered by six months. Low counts persisted in SARIFA positive patients at six months. Inflammatory mediators rose after surgery equally in both groups. A built in immune trait may help these aggressive tumors arise.
pmc-13417478:
Junhee Lee and colleagues feed a blend of amaranth protein hydrolysate and Korean mint extract to mice with cancer related wasting, in a 2026 study. Wasting, called cachexia, drains muscle and fat and weakens patients. Tumour bearing mice received the blend by mouth for 14 days at two dose levels.

Weight loss eased, muscle and fat stores were partly preserved, and grip strength improved. Blood inflammation signals fell, muscle breakdown genes quieted, and a growth pathway switched back on. Fat tissue also shifted away from wasteful browning toward storage. The blend is proposed as a nutrition strategy, pending human study.
pmc-13418478:
Song Hu and co-authors trace a drug resistant Klebsiella strain carrying a rare resistance gene in a newborn intensive care unit, in a 2026 study. Three critically ill infants yielded isolates resistant to carbapenems, last line antibiotics. Genome sequencing, drug testing, and clinical timelines were combined to judge relatedness and spread.

All three isolates shared sequence type 35 and carried the gene on the same plasmid type. pmc-13418778:

pmc-13418878:

pmc-13419678:

pmc-13420278:

pmc-13420378:

pmc-13421378:

pmc-13421478:

pmc-13422878:

pmc-13423478: Advanced Science published this 2026 correction to a paper by Xia and co-authors on how the protein POU2F1 drives chemotherapy resistance in colorectal cancer cells. pmc-13423878:

pmc-13425078:

pmc-13425778:

pmc-13425878:

pmc-13426078:

pmc-13426478:

pmc-13426878:

pmc-13427578:

pmc-13427678:

pmc-13427778:

pmc-13427878:

pmc-13428078:

pmc-13429578:

pmc-13430478:

pmc-13433178:

pmc-13433978:

pmc-13434378:

pmc-13434578:

pmc-13435478:

pmc-13435578:

pmc-13435678:

pmc-13436078:

pmc-13436378:

pmc-13436678:

pmc-13437078:

pmc-13437278:

pmc-13437578:

pmc-13437678:

pmc-13439278:

pmc-13439478:

pmc-13439978:

pmc-13440178:

pmc-13440578:

pmc-13441378:

pmc-13441778:

pmc-13442678:

Patients rated all 18 movement items at least somewhat tied to daily life. Twelve items earned a high-meaning tag from patient views. More than 90 percent of experts backed four items as core for early disease checks. Experts backed six items as strong tools for tracking decline over time. Six named items, from stiffness to toe taps, won joint praise. The authors urge trial teams to weight those items first when they judge new drugs.
pmc-13445378:
Dainis Krievins and colleagues ask whether heart artery plaque load, measured before leg artery surgery, predicts death over five years in patients with no known heart disease, in a 2026 study. Blocked leg arteries often travel with silent heart disease, a main driver of poor survival. Scans gave both plaque volume and a flow measure for each heart lesion.

The group held 124 patients cleared for planned leg surgery, most of them men near age sixty-seven. More than half had silent flow-limiting heart disease, and plaque load ran high overall. Over five years, thirty-two patients died. Those who died carried near twice the plaque volume of survivors, and high plaque load marked a far worse outlook, which supports heart checks before leg surgery.
pmc-13445478:
Sophie-Anne Savard and colleagues report a 2026 chart review of necrobiosis lipoidica in children, a rare skin disorder far better described in adults. The team reviewed cases from 1980 to 2025 at a Montreal children's hospital, including only patients diagnosed before age 18 with clinical, histology, or photographic support.

Of 10 children, 8 were girls and 9 had type 1 diabetes, typically poorly controlled, with skin disease lasting 3.8 years on average and still active in 9 at last follow-up. Topical treatments eased symptoms more than appearance, and painful intralesional steroid shots gave the best, though partial, results. Pediatric disease looks more diabetes-linked than adult disease, the authors argue, with no validated treatment yet.
pmc-13446078:
Veit-Lorenz Heuthe and colleagues turn a swarm of tiny active beads into a computer that learns from motion itself, in a 2026 physics study. In reservoir computing, a lively physical system transforms inputs, and only a simple readout layer needs training, which saves energy. Most such systems cannot tune how their parts interact.

Hundreds of swimming beads, coupled through the fluid around them, form the reservoir here, and their coupling and memory can be tuned in place. The swarm forecast chaotic series with skill, working in parallel without time-slicing tricks. It also caught hidden anomalies in real time, flaws so subtle that the signal's plain statistics never changed. The work casts interacting beads as a flexible base for smart sensing.
pmc-13447178:
Alexander Yahanda and colleagues describe a 2026 operation to remove a rare bone tumour from the upper neck in one piece. Chordomas grow slowly yet invade nearby tissue, so leaving no tumour at the edges gives the best chance of control. Growths near the skull base and top spine vertebrae are among the hardest to remove safely.

A sixty-six-year-old man had a tumour starting at the second neck vertebra and reaching neighbours above and below. Surgeons worked in three stages from back, front and back again under one anaesthetic, lasting about twenty-nine hours. Breathing support took time to withdraw afterwards, yet he stayed free of recurrence with full strength beyond two years. The report also applies a new scoring frame to grade how complex such surgery is.
pmc-13447378:
Matthew Baugh leads a team building three-dimensional anomaly spotting for medical scans in 2026 work. A common strategy trains a model only on healthy scans, then flags anything the model cannot rebuild in a healthy-looking way. Older versions worked slice by slice, losing depth context, and ran slowly in full image space, while rebuild errors also produced false alarms.

The new method restores images inside a compressed three-dimensional space learned by a separate encoder, using a flow-based generator guided by the input scan. Comparing the restoration with the encoder's own rebuild, rather than the raw scan, cuts false alarms from compression. Models trained on fake faults in both image and compressed space performed best as a team across brain scan benchmarks. Speed rose roughly tenfold, though the newest benchmark remains far from solved.
pmc-13447478:
Shi Han and colleagues integrate a 2026 genomic study of survival outlook for patients in China with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma. After R-CHOP therapy, 30 to 40 percent relapse or resist treatment. The team sequenced tumor tissue and matching mouth DNA from 147 cases, testing mutation risk scores plus clinical factors against the standard prognostic index.

Mutations in TP53, SRP72, MYC, BCL2, and ASXL2 each predicted worse progression-free survival, and a five-gene score plus lactate dehydrogenase and marrow status beat the standard index. A three-gene score plus lactate dehydrogenase also beat the index for relapse prediction. Early risk sorting could steer high-risk patients toward stem cell or cellular therapy.
pmc-13447578:
Tianyu Wang and co-authors frame eye melanoma as a stress-dependent cancer in a 2026 review. Uveal melanoma is the most common primary eye cancer in adults, and it spreads to the liver in most fatal cases, where survival drops below a year. Drugs that work on skin melanoma largely fail here, pointing to distinct survival machinery worth mapping.

Tumour cells must survive two harsh homes, the sheltered eye and the demanding liver, by rewiring oxygen sensing, metabolism and internal clean-up under stress. Oxidative stress is cast as both shield and weakness, since pushing it past a threshold can trigger iron-driven or immune-visible cell death. Clean-up pathways sustain spread and drug resistance in the account. Named stress nodes, from redox balance to clean-up control, are proposed as drug targets to break adaptation.
pmc-13447978:
Takashi Miida writes in 2026 about standardising measurement of lipoprotein(a), the cholesterol-carrying particle tied to heart disease, in molar units. Levels of the particle vary by assay because its attached protein comes in many sizes, confusing doctors for decades. A mass spectrometry reference method endorsed in 2023 and a certification programme launched in 2026 now anchor global values.

A multicentre Japanese study covered here converted results from different assays for over six thousand patients onto the standard scale. High standardised levels tracked with more coronary disease, kidney disease and inherited high cholesterol. Two decision cut-offs were proposed to sort patients into low, middle and high risk bands, a first for globally standardised values. New drugs that slash the particle by up to ninety percent sharpen the need for trustworthy numbers.
pmc-13448078:
Tan and colleagues test whether an inflammation protein called pentraxin 3 drives harmful heart thickening under hormone stress. Angiotensin II, a hormone that raises blood pressure, was infused into mice for four weeks to force the heart wall to thicken. Their 2026 study compares normal mice with mice bred to lack pentraxin 3, and pairs the animal work with heart cells from newborn rats stressed the same way in dishes.

The hormone raised pentraxin 3 levels in both mouse hearts and rat cells. Mice without the protein developed far less thickening and scarring, and their heart stress markers, including two natriuretic peptides, stayed lower. Inflammatory signals such as tumor necrosis factor alpha also rose less, and chemical stress damage in heart tissue eased. Blocking this protein, the authors propose, could become a route to treat thickened heart muscle driven by inflammation.
pmc-13448178:
Zheng-qin Gao and Rui Fu test a 2026 pre-human safety study of the HIV entry blocker peptide 2P23 as a vaginal-rectal germ killer hope. Rats got acute high-dose vaginal-rectal treatment plus 90-day repeat dosing at three levels, with checks spanning weight, blood, organs, tissue, gut germs, baby-making, and embryo growth.

No deaths, odd signs, weight or blood changes, or organ or tissue damage showed. Gut germ shifts and baby-making effects also stayed absent, backing a no-seen-bad-effect level of 300 mg. The peptide looks safe for repeat vaginal-rectal use in animals, giving a hopeful stopping tool pending human trials.
pmc-13448478:
Kim and colleagues review in 2026 how brain imaging can reveal what non-invasive brain stimulation does after stroke, and why patients respond so unevenly. Stimulation aims to boost the brain's rewiring, but clinics lack objective markers of the changes it causes. The review unifies evidence from EEG, which records brain waves, and functional MRI, which maps activity through blood flow.

EEG measures such as wave patterns, stimulation-evoked responses, and balance between the two brain halves track excitability changes from treatment. MRI studies show altered activation and connectivity, especially in motor networks. Combining both scans, and adding computer models of the electric field, sharpened the picture and improved prediction of recovery. The authors propose biomarker-guided, adaptive stimulation tailored to each patient's brain state.
pmc-13448678:
Dongwoo Ki and colleagues describe in 2026 a structural feature that slows enzymes able to break down PET plastic. In one such enzyme from Cryptosporangium aurantiacum, a loop sticking out from the surface limits how well the plastic can reach the working site. The loop sits far from the active center, about 25 angstroms away.

Swapping that protruding loop for a flatter version sped up PET breakdown in the team's tests. Kinetic and adsorption studies showed the change eased productive access without altering how tightly the enzyme binds plastic. Similar swaps in other PET-cutting enzymes support a design strategy based on access, not only on the catalytic site itself.
pmc-13448878:
Ryan Perkins and co-authors test in 2026 whether twelve weeks of supervised aerobic exercise changes two blood markers tied to inflammation in type 2 diabetes. Thirty-three sedentary adults were randomized, twenty to training and thirteen to standard care. The training group exercised sixty minutes a day, five days a week, at about 70 percent of peak oxygen capacity.

Blood levels of sRAGE, a soluble decoy receptor thought to soak up harmful sugar-damaged molecules, rose across the training period, while a related marker, sTLR4, stayed unchanged. Trained participants also gained fitness, lost body fat, and improved insulin sensitivity on a standard index. Muscle samples showed shifts in ratios of tissue-remodeling enzymes, though not in the receptor protein itself. The authors say the pathways behind the sRAGE rise remain unclear and need more study.
pmc-13449078:
Mohammed Barghash and a large team pool in 2026 the results on endoscopic sleeve gastroplasty, a stomach-shrinking procedure done through the mouth without external cuts. Their systematic review gathered 33 studies with 8,880 patients, searching the literature to September 2025. Weight outcomes were split into short follow-up, up to six months, and long follow-up of a year or more.

Total body weight loss rose from 8.66 percent at one month to 16.13 percent at six months and 17.88 percent at one year. Longer horizons showed gentle fading, to 15.67 percent at three years, and only 6 percent of patients regained weight. Remission reached 62 percent for type 2 diabetes and 43 percent each for high blood pressure and abnormal blood lipids. Higher starting body mass predicted greater percentage weight loss, supporting the procedure's place in multidisciplinary obesity care.
pmc-13449178:
Lv and colleagues ask whether lymphoma that has spread into the bone marrow at diagnosis later blocks stem cell collection for transplant. Collection requires coaxing blood stem cells out of the marrow, and success means gathering at least a set minimum dose. Their 2026 study reviews 669 patients at four Chinese centers who had a first collection attempt between 2017 and 2023, and uses matching to balance the groups on other traits.

Of the patients, 138 had marrow involvement at diagnosis. Success rates barely differed: about 79 percent with marrow involvement against about 81 percent without, and the gap stayed small after matching. The amount of stem cells gathered per kilo of body weight was also like in both groups. Marrow involvement at diagnosis, the authors conclude, does not in itself spoil collection, so it should not by itself deter a transplant plan.
pmc-13449378:
Fatima Sharif and colleagues catalog in 2026 the gene mutations behind drug resistance in Pakistani patients with chronic myeloid leukemia. The study ran from January to June 2025 at the Armed Forces Institute of Pathology and enrolled 133 adults whose leukemia no longer responded to tyrosine kinase inhibitors. Targeted genetic tests hunted four known mutations in the BCR::ABL1 kinase domain, the engine of the disease.

Mutations turned up in 57 patients, 42.9 percent of the group. E255K dominated at 33.8 percent of all patients, followed by E255V at 8.3 percent, while the notorious T315I and Y253H appeared once each. Carrying any mutation came with significantly higher white cell counts. E255K specifically was tied to blast crisis, the dangerous advanced phase, at a significance level of 0.048. The authors press for routine molecular testing so resistant patients can be switched to fitting drugs sooner.
pmc-13449478:
Rafael Sala and colleagues propose in 2026 that ordinary blood tests, watched over time, can flag colorectal cancers headed for early spread long before the diagnosis lands. Stage decides survival in this cancer, falling from 93 percent at stage one to roughly ten percent at stage four, and most treatment advances still react to disease found late. Their concept, haematological pre-staging, reads complete blood count trajectories in the twenty-four months before diagnosis.

The study's highlights report that these pre-diagnostic blood paths separate metastatic from non-metastatic cases. Progressive anemia and rising inflammation, in particular, appear ahead of cancers that present already spread to distant sites. Dynamic trajectories carried more signal than any single measurement. The authors suggest such patterns could one day steer who gets imaging sooner and who enters closer surveillance, shifting part of cancer detection from reacting to established tumors toward anticipating them.
pmc-13449678:
Jordi Gumà-Lao and colleagues examined how gender and social class together shape self-rated health in Spain, publishing in 2026. Health gaps are often read along one axis at a time, yet a person's combined position may create distinct risk patterns. The team used decision trees to trace which conditions best predict poor self-rated health in each group.

Data came from the 2023 Spanish Health Survey, covering 10,210 adults aged thirty to sixty. Six groups were formed by crossing gender with social class, and a tree was grown for each. Trees for less skilled groups were more complex, reflecting faster accumulation of chronic illness at younger ages. Policy makers gain a finer map of where ill health clusters and which conditions drive it.
pmc-13449778:
Hosein Rostamian and colleagues publish in 2026 a faster protocol for editing the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae genome with CRISPR. The usual bottleneck is not the cutting enzyme but building the plasmid that carries each new guide RNA. That job is traditionally done with restriction enzymes and ligation steps that fail in fiddly ways. Their workflow swaps that cloning for whole-plasmid PCR: primers write the new guide straight into the plasmid, and seamless assembly closes the circle again.

The protocol covers guide and repair-donor design. It details insertion into a drug-selectable Cas9 plasmid with a redesigned guide site and extended scaffold, verification in bacteria, and delivery into yeast by a standard chemical method. The run typically takes ten days. Because the backbone works in strain backgrounds common in research, the authors pitch it for laboratories that iterate through many guides, from deletions to point mutations and protein tagging.
pmc-13449878:
Buytenhuijs, Schröder, and Textor apply an old immunology idea, shape space, to T cell recognition in this 2026 theoretical paper. Shape space pictures antibodies and antigens as shapes that fit or fail to fit, and it underlies maps used to track virus evolution. The authors ask what the equivalent landscape looks like for T cell receptors facing peptide-MHC complexes, the displayed protein fragments that T cells inspect.

Binding depends on several structural constraints, they propose. Those constraints can conflict. So the fragments one receptor recognizes form several separate, non-convex islands, rather than one tidy region. That model predicts small structural changes can sharply alter whether a fragment provokes immunity, and that two recognized fragments can look very different. Published mutation experiments offer some support, and the authors discuss consequences for predicting immune responses in cancer therapy.
pmc-13450578:
Sara Buchmuller and co-authors follow in 2026 how Swiss adults who had cancer as children rate their first long-term check-up visits. Late health harms are common in this group, so ongoing care matters. The study took in 145 survivors at two Swiss clinics and asked them to rate visits before and three months after.

Ratings were very high for care that felt centered on the person and for how well facts were shared. Worry levels sat near the middle of the scale. Covering more of the topics a survivor wished to raise lifted the care rating, while weaker mental health tracked with more worry. The authors suggest added mind care for survivors who arrive with low mood.
pmc-13451178:
Yiliminuer Abulajiang and others took stock of tumor DNA in blood for ovarian cancer in 2026, weighing its use as a liquid biopsy. Ovarian cancer is one of the deadliest female cancers, and early finds are hard. Tumor DNA shed in blood might flag disease, track small leftovers, foretell relapse, and steer bespoke care.

The review covers early screening, leftover tracking, relapse foretelling, and care choice, setting tumor DNA next to old markers on hit rate and true rate. It also weighs live limits: weak finds in early disease and no set test norms. Next work should hone test methods and join tumor DNA with other markers. Doctors gain a fair view of a bright but not yet routine tool.
pmc-13451278:
Wu and colleagues built a staged robot framework for inserting metal valve parts into holes with precision. It is a classic assembly task. Shiny surfaces, lost depth cues, and occlusion blind the cameras exactly when accuracy matters most. Their design treats insertion as a handover. Vision shrinks the error to a small neighborhood, then touch takes command.

Three phases follow in sequence: camera-guided coarse alignment, force-guided correction of the remaining offset, and compliant insertion with stiffness tuned live to the contact state. During correction the gripper traces a tiny spiral. The system watches lateral forces and torques settle toward a convergence criterion for centering. Experiments on clearance-fit and interference-fit tasks beat baseline methods on success rate, insertion time, and peak contact force in the reported comparisons. The authors argue explicitly coordinating vision-dominant and force-dominant stages is the key advantage.
pmc-13451878:
Jiangquan Zeng and co-authors build in 2026 a vision model that counts rubber trees from drone photos across all seasons. Exact counts guide yield guesses and farm care, yet crowns overlap and wild growth muddies the view. Their model, CSAF, stacks three parts: one that sharpens crown edges, one that enforces crown-like shapes, and one that adapts across seasons.

The team also released a data set of over 5,000 sharp drone images that span the full leaf cycle, from bud to leaf fall. On that set the model beat rival methods on crown spotting scores. Tests on three public sets checked that the gains travel beyond rubber farms.
pmc-13452178:
Ebba Elofsson, Magdalena Johansson, and Marcus Lind ask in 2026 whether how people rate their own health foretells a later heart rhythm disorder. Their cohort held over 100,000 middle-aged adults in north Sweden, free of the disorder at entry between 1988 and 2014. Health ratings came from a visit form, and new cases of atrial fibrillation were tracked for years.

Near 4,800 people later got the disorder. Each step down the self-rating scale, from very good toward poor, came with a higher risk, even with classic heart risks counted. The link also split by sex. The authors offer a one-line self-rating as a cheap early flag for rhythm risk in clinic visits.
pmc-13452278:
Alireza Sazmand and co-authors report in 2026 a tick-borne blood germ found for the first time in a striped hyena in west Iran. The germ, Cytauxzoon banethi, was known only from two European wildcats in Romania. The team read two genes from the hyena's blood and set them against known kinds.

One gene matched a kin species too closely to settle the name. The second gene sat near identical to the reference for this species and grouped with its line on the family tree. The find is the first in the hyena family, the first outside Europe, and the first in Asia. The authors urge wider wildlife checks with more than one gene.
pmc-13452778:
Maxime Remy and seven co-authors test whether gene sequencing of pancreas growths changes what doctors decide to do. The growths, called branch duct IPMNs, are fluid filled sacs that may turn to cancer, and rule books often leave doctors unsure. Their 2026 study gave 132 doctors in France four hard cases, each judged once before and once after gene results were shown.

Gene results swung choices hard in every case. When no risky mutation showed, plans for surgery flipped to watchful waiting in 43 to 61 percent of cases. When a risky mutation showed, waiting flipped to surgery in 72 to 90 percent of cases. Doctors also felt surer of their calls, and agreement between doctors jumped from near none to a solid level. The authors present sequencing as a strong aid for these borderline calls.
pmc-13453778:
Burcu Senkalfa and six co-authors chart the long course of pseudohypoparathyroidism, a rare disorder where the body resists its own hormones. Their 2026 study follows 19 children from 17 families at one center, with diagnoses from 1992 to 2025. Cases split into forms called PHP1A, PHP1B, and a milder relative, sorted by gene and clinical signs tied to the GNAS gene.

Nearly all children in the two main forms resisted parathyroid hormone, with resistance arriving near age 6 in PHP1A and age 11.2 in PHP1B. Thyroid underactivity showed in every PHP1A case and most PHP1B cases. Three children showed a rarer pattern that points to resistance in the brain's own thyroid control path. Half the PHP1A children had intellectual disability, and the same gene change gave varied pictures in different children.
pmc-13454278:
Xiaoli Huang, Tao Xu, and Min Du published a 2026 commentary on a case of liver cancer that had spread to the duodenum and caused severe bleeding. The case, reported by Zhang and colleagues, involved a patient whose tumor had also grown into the portal vein. Treatment combined a procedure to block the bleeding vessel with immune-based drug therapy, and the cancer shrank for a lasting period.

The commentary asks why spread to the gut is so often missed, noting that fewer than one in a hundred cases of liver cancer reach the digestive tract. The authors point to warning signs such as tumor growth in the vein and tumors near the duodenum. They also ask whether long-term survivors with high-risk features need closer checks for rare spread sites, while noting that one case cannot settle how care should change.
pmc-13454478:
Amos J. Nissley and five colleagues identify, in a 2026 study, a family of proteins that park and protect ribosomes in dormant archaeal cells. When food runs short, microbes shut down their protein factories for safety, yet the archaeal version of this hibernation was poorly mapped. The team worked with a methane-making archaeon and named the four proteins SriA through SriD.

All four genes sit together in one cluster, and each protein blocked protein making in test tubes. Cells missing the genes recovered poorly after long rest and lost part of their small ribosome stock. Frozen microscope images showed the proteins binding the ribosome in pairs, sharing neat contact surfaces. The family turns up across many archaeal branches. The authors say these guardians explain how archaea keep ribosomes intact through dormancy.
pmc-13455278:
Modanloo and an Iranian team co-built a program for anxiety in women facing gynecological surgery under spinal anesthesia. They used joint action research at a referral center from 2020 to 2023. Sixteen expert and planning sessions shaped steps aimed at providers, the ward, and patients across three action cycles.

Patient anxiety scored 6.1 on the visual scale before any step in the program's first evaluation round. After the provider-focused cycle it fell to 4.66, after ward changes to 2.86, and after patient-focused work to 2.64, each step statistically significant in paired testing. Early interviews and observations had generated 20 subcategories and six main categories of anxiety sources that the program design targeted. The authors conclude that involving patients and staff in designing the fixes, not just receiving them, drove the stepwise reductions achieved.
pmc-13455478:
Wei Zhang and colleagues build a three-factor chart to flag poor outcomes in drug-resistant lung tuberculosis in a 2026 study. Drug-resistant TB still cures too few patients, and doctors lack a simple admission check for who may fail, die or drop out. The team reviewed 184 patients treated in Fuyang City between 2021 and 2023, sorting 143 with good outcomes from 41 with poor ones, and testing 30 admission variables with a selection method.

Age, body mass index and albumin survived selection, with older age raising risk and higher weight and albumin protecting. The resulting nomogram discriminated well, with an area under the curve of 0.833, calibrated satisfactorily and showed value across risk thresholds from 0.1 to 0.8. Age mattered most in explanations of the model. Clinics gain a bedside chart from routine admission data, though it needs testing beyond one hospital before wider use.
pmc-13455778:
Linnea B. Linde-Krieger leads a twelve-author study, from 2026, of the people who staff opioid treatment programs and the toll the work takes. These programs are the only United States settings allowed to dispense methadone, and their counselors absorb clients' trauma stories daily. The team surveyed 44 administrators across 21 states and 83 staff members, with 30 counselors reporting on supervision.

Training about trauma and burnout was widely on offer, and most leaders and staff wanted reflective supervision tailored to their setting. A surprise split appeared in the numbers. Staff with clinical supervision reported lower vicarious trauma and burnout. Staff at sites merely offering training reported more of both. The authors read this as a warning that information alone does not protect workers, while a steady, relational supervisor does. They urge programs to expand supervision first.
pmc-13458578:
Hui Wang and colleagues test whether a simple insulin-resistance score predicts death in critically ill brain-vessel patients, and whether diabetes changes the answer. The triglyceride-glucose, or TyG, index comes free from admission labs. Their 2026 retrospective study pulls 2,584 adults with cerebrovascular disease from the MIMIC-IV intensive care database spanning 2008 to 2019 and models mortality out to a year.

Across everyone, the index looked useless: hazard ratios hovered near 1.1 to 1.15 and mostly missed significance. Diabetes status split the story open, with interaction tests significant at 30, 90, and 365 days. In patients without diabetes, each TyG unit raised the death hazard by roughly a quarter at every horizon. In patients with diabetes, no association appeared at all. The authors propose diabetes-stratified use of the index in neurocritical care, a reminder that a biomarker can be informative in one metabolic context and mute in another.
pmc-13459278:
Xumao Deng and co-authors built a new heart risk index for middle aged and older Chinese adults by combining a fatty cholesterol measure with blood sugar and belly fat. Standard indices capture how much fat circulates but miss small dense LDL cholesterol, an artery damaging particle type. Their 2026 study followed 3,969 adults aged forty five or older from a national aging cohort, none with cardiovascular disease at the start. It compared candidate indices on how well they forecast new heart disease and stroke.

During follow up, 1,029 participants developed cardiovascular disease. The new sdLG index beat the standard triglyceride glucose index at long term discrimination. Pairing it with a Chinese visceral fat measure, forming sdLG-cVAI, discriminated and reclassified risk best of all. People in the highest quarter of that combined index faced a hazard ratio of 1.77 for new disease versus the lowest quarter. Persistently high readings raised risk further.
pmc-13459678:
Iqbal and colleagues wrote a letter to the editor in 2026 about bias in artificial intelligence tools for Alzheimer's disease. These tools read brain scans and mix them with gene data, blood markers, and behaviour scores. The authors warn that training data lean heavily toward people of European ancestry. 

In one cohort of 1,730 people, the models missed more true cases among Hispanic patients than among non-Hispanic patients. Gaps also appeared for Black and Asian patients when set against White patients. Tools that scored very well inside the main data set scored lower on outside hospital data. The authors call for training sets that include more regions and ethnic groups. They also want routine fairness checks before such tools guide real diagnosis in clinics.
pmc-13461478:
Xu Yang and colleagues traced how a tiny RNA, miR-140-3p, restrains osteosarcoma, the commonest primary bone cancer of the young. The RNA runs low in osteosarcoma cells, and patients with low levels survive more poorly, the team found.

Single-cell data and database survival analyses guided the experiments. Boosting the RNA in dish and mouse tests slowed tumour growth and spread, stalled the cell cycle, and pushed cancer cells to die. Cutting it had the opposite effect, speeding growth and lung spread in mice. The RNA works by silencing a gene called UBE2C, which feeds a growth pathway named PI3K-Akt. Yang proposes this three-part axis as a treatment target for osteosarcoma.
pmc-13462278:
Bouketta and colleagues tested in 2026 whether common farm chemicals can be sprayed together with pest-killing fungi, a pairing that could cut costs in biological control. Two fungal strains that attack the olive fruit fly were challenged with five fungicides and four herbicides. The standard check mixes chemicals into the fungi's growth medium. Field spraying coats the fungal spores directly, so the team compared the standard method with a direct spore-mixture method and with live fly tests.

The methods disagreed. For one fungus, the standard check passed only one of four herbicides, while the direct method passed all four, and fungicide verdicts shifted from toxic to moderately toxic. The direct method's calls matched the live fly results more closely for both fungi, though the second fungus was weaker and less tolerant overall. The authors recommend the direct test as the more realistic gate for mixing fungi into spray programs.
pmc-13462678:
Fabio Pelle and colleagues report, in a 2026 case report with a literature review, a single-stage operation for a 40-year-old woman found to have two cancers at once. She had a thymoma in the chest and HER2-positive breast cancer. Two cancers together usually mean staged operations in separate sessions, which can delay cancer care. A multi-team evaluation planned one combined operation.

Robotic chest surgery removed the thymus tumor first, from the left side, with the specimen taken out below the breastbone to keep breast cuts untouched. Breast removal preserving the nipples, armpit node removal, and reconstruction followed through scar-sparing cuts. The breast cancer showed a complete response in the removed tissue, the chest tumor came out with clean margins, and the cosmetic result pleased the team. The authors frame combined cases as planning challenges, solvable when chest, breast, and reconstruction teams coordinate early.
pmc-13463478:
Asal Yunusova and co-authors follow low mood across the first year of college and link it to grades and sleep, in this 2026 study. The move to college is a known danger point for depression in young adults. The team used data from two spring terms at a private university, with wrist trackers recording sleep across the term.

The 271 first year students fell into four paths: low and steady, rising, falling, and high and steady symptoms. The low and falling groups earned higher spring grades than the rising and high groups. The low group also kept earlier bed and wake times and slept longer overall. The pattern ties steady low mood to both better marks and healthier sleep habits during a hard transition year.
pmc-13463578:
Xingyu Wang and five co-authors ask whether two amino acids, leucine and valine, can make pork more tender. Amino acids are the building blocks of protein. The group first compared pork of high and low tenderness, then fed the two acids to pigs and checked the meat.

Tender pork held more leucine and valine than tough pork did. Pigs fed both acids gave meat that cut more softly, held a larger share of unsaturated fats, and resisted spoilage by oxidation for longer. Gene reads tied the gains to shifts in fiber type, fat handling, and defense against cell damage. Meat producers gain a feed-based route to softer, sound pork.
pmc-13464278:
Lai, Lee, and Yang comment on a case reported by Gitte and colleagues, where imaging steered rescue of a blocked mechanical heart valve. The patient, a young adult on a weak blood thinner dose, had a stuck artificial mitral valve. The question was what blocked it: a clot, which drugs can dissolve, or pannus, scar tissue drugs cannot remove. Their 2026 piece uses the case to argue that imaging should answer the treatment question, not just confirm the block.

Four dimensional ultrasound from inside the food pipe showed a moving mass and a fixed layer, letting the team judge the clot as the blocker. They chose clot dissolving drugs, and later scans showed the valve leaflets moving freely again while the harmless pannus layer stayed. Lai and coauthors lay out a stepwise plan that pairs standard ultrasound, X-ray motion checks, and the four dimensional view to guide such calls.
pmc-13464378:
Giffin and colleagues studied in 2026 how early amyloid deposits, the protein clumps linked to Alzheimer's disease, change the brain's response to sepsis, a severe body-wide infection. They induced sepsis in young adult mice bred to develop amyloid early, then tested behavior and brain tissue after recovery.

Mice with amyloid showed a generalized fear response and worse performance on a puzzle box problem-solving task after sepsis. Brain gene activity showed inflammation pathways still switched on long after the infection cleared, more strongly in the amyloid mice. Immune cells in the brain called microglia also ate more synapses, the connections between nerve cells, three weeks after infection. The authors argue amyloid acts as a hidden risk factor that amplifies post-sepsis brain harm.
pmc-13465178:
Sinan Mutlu and three co-authors test neck ultrasound measures for spotting hard airways in 713 adults expected to be easy cases.
