Five regression methods, from a traditional linear approach to boosted trees and a neural network, were tuned to predict total acidity and vitamin C content.

Nonlinear models clearly beat the traditional method, with the neural network reaching the highest accuracy on both measures. Performance scores indicated the predictions were strong enough for practical sorting use. The authors present the combined method as a fast, non-destructive option for quality control, supply chain decisions, and breeding programs that need reliable measures of fruit chemistry.
pmc-13523378:
Huihong Shi and collaborators compare magnesium handling in the two founding sugarcane species in a 2026 study. Magnesium is central to chlorophyll and photosynthesis, yet how the two species regulate it was unknown. The transporter gene family for the mineral was listed in both species, activity was tracked across leaf development and daily cycles, and one carrier gene was tested in bacteria and in rice.

The two species responded differently to mineral supply, and their versions of the transporter gene followed distinct expression patterns. Both versions restored mineral uptake in a deficient bacterial strain, confirming shared transport ability. Boosting the wild species version in rice raised growth under low mineral levels and tolerance of excess. Promoter analysis pointed to different control factors in each species, suggesting distinct strategies for mineral balance.
pmc-13523478:
Nur Efşan Aydın and Sedat Çetiner test, in a 2026 animal experiment, whether melatonin or vitamin E helps bone heal after grafting in weakened bone. Healing in osteoporotic bone is a known difficulty in oral and facial surgery. The team created skull defects under induced osteoporotic conditions and filled most of them with a synthetic graft material.

Thirty-five male Wistar rats were split into five groups. One group received no graft, one received graft alone, and the rest received melatonin, vitamin E, or both given systemically. No healing appeared without a graft, while graft alone produced mild to moderate new bone. Melatonin produced pronounced, high-grade formation. Vitamin E gave no clear gain over graft alone, on its own or combined. The authors present melatonin as the more promising support agent.
pmc-13523578:
Ioannis Doundoulakis and colleagues asked whether a brief nerve block can predict lasting benefit from a heart denervation operation. Published in 2026, the study reviewed patients with stubborn ventricular arrhythmias at a single high-volume European center. Cardiac sympathetic denervation cuts overactive nerve drive to the heart, while a stellate ganglion block offers a temporary version of the same idea.

Three fifths of the sample stayed free of ventricular arrhythmias after denervation. In the small subgroup with nonischemic dilated cardiomyopathy, block response matched denervation benefit perfectly, suggesting the block can spot cases driven by nerve overactivity. Nonresponders, by contrast, may carry other mechanisms less likely to gain from surgery. The authors pitch the block as a low-risk selection tool, with larger studies needed.
pmc-13524878:
Angela Yee-Moon Wang leads an international expert group in a 2026 consensus statement on putting nutritional supplementation into practice for patients on dialysis. Guidelines suggest treating protein-energy wasting with oral or tube-delivered nutrition in this group, yet practical implementation guidance was missing. The panel aimed to bridge evidence and daily care across health systems.

Eight nephrologists and three dietitians drafted 46 statements, discussed them at meetings in Kuala Lumpur and Frankfurt in November 2024, then refined and voted anonymously following an established European nutrition society method. The final document carries twenty consensus statements and thirty-four practice points. Themes include screening and regular review for every patient, respect for patient preference in oral support, attention to kidney-specific formulas, and a defined place for nutrition delivered during dialysis when wasting persists.
pmc-13525878:
Muhammad Umar Farooq and others set out, in a 2026 paper, a protocol for rebuilding complex defects at the side of the skull base. The protocol distills over two decades of work at a busy United Kingdom tertiary center. This region packs fine nerves and vessels between the cranium and face, so tumors there challenge both removal and reconstruction.

The account looks back over practice across benign and malignant disease. Care is built around a team spanning ear surgery, neurosurgery, plastic surgery, anesthesia, radiology, oncology, and nursing. Planning, choices during surgery, care around it, and long-term rehabilitation are shown as one pathway. The authors report high complete removal and repair rates with modest harm rates, and they offer the refined protocol as a reference for centers set up the same way.
pmc-13526478:
Baayoud and colleagues report a 2026 case, with a review of past reports, of a 30-year-old man whose bulging left eye revealed IgG4-related disease. He had nine months of painless eye protrusion and eyelid swelling, and scans showed an orbital growth reaching back into the skull.

Doctors relieved the pressure through a small eyebrow incision and examined the tissue. The biopsy confirmed IgG4-related disease, an immune condition where certain antibody-carrying cells invade and scar tissue. Steroid treatment then gave a good clinical outcome. The authors stress that scans alone cannot separate this condition from tumors or other orbital disease, so tissue testing is essential before choosing treatment for unexplained eye protrusion.
pmc-13527478:
Wu and colleagues present a 2026 case report linking an outbreak of gouty panniculitis, urate crystals inflaming the fat under the skin, with a rare immune disorder. The patient, a 42-year-old Pacific Islander man, developed the skin eruption as idiopathic multicentric Castleman disease began, . A lymph node biopsy confirmed the diagnosis.

He responded well to siltuximab, a drug that blocks the immune signal interleukin-6, a known driver of this disease. Gout in fat tissue is rare on its own; an eruptive case arriving with systemic illness should prompt a search for a hidden blood or immune disorder, the authors argue. The exact link between the two conditions remains unclear. The case adds a visible skin clue to the early picture of a dangerous, hard-to-spot disease.
pmc-13527978:
Yi Gao and four colleagues investigate a gene called FBXW7 in intervertebral disc degeneration, a common cause of back pain. The work, published in 2026, began with a bioinformatics screen comparing normal and degenerated disc tissue. FBXW7 stood out as raised in badly degenerated samples. Lab checks on patient tissue confirmed higher levels of both FBXW7 and a signaling protein named JNK.

In cell experiments, silencing FBXW7 reduced the death of nucleus pulposus cells, the cells that cushion the disc center. Forcing extra FBXW7 raised JNK and pushed cells toward death. Silencing JNK cancelled that effect. In live animals, reducing FBXW7 eased disc degeneration. The authors conclude the FBXW7 to JNK route is a candidate target for future treatment.
pmc-13528078:
Suprapto and seven colleagues explore how to lift health service quality in Indonesia in a 2026 qualitative study. Interviews were held with providers, facility managers, policymakers, and community voices. Settings ranged from primary centers to district hospitals. Transcripts were coded for themes, with peer checks and member feedback for rigor.

Workforce strain stood at the center. Staff faced scarce ongoing training, heavy loads, and mixed clinical and management skills. Digital tools varied wildly between sites. Weak internet, low digital skill, and unlinked systems blocked progress. Policies often stalled at facility level under red tape. Community input channels were rare and thin. The authors call for joined-up strategies. Training, digital readiness, governance, and community voice must move together, they argue, for gains to last.
pmc-13528278:
Gizem Erdem, Nilüfer Kafescioğlu, and Gökçenay Başer put a chatbot therapist on trial in a 2026 study. A model tuned for family therapy methods held a session with a volunteer client. The client raised a relationship concern. Twelve seasoned supervisors then graded the transcript with standard scales. They did not know the therapist was an AI.

Ratings landed at moderate competence for systemic thinking and technique. Weak spots included pacing, joining with the client, and culture and context. Supervisors guessed the therapist was a beginner with under five hundred hours of practice. Erdem and colleagues say the gaps show what human therapists add. Judgment, attunement, and intuition remain hard to automate. They urge caution as AI advice tools spread among young users.
pmc-13529578: Peter and colleagues published a correction in 2026 in the European Stroke Journal to their article on calibrated non-inferiority margins. That method sets fair comparison thresholds in stroke trials when patient populations shift. The correction fixes panel B of Figure 3, whose graph did not match the data in Table 1. It supplies the corrected figure caption describing how prognostic factors were distributed across the historical meta-analysis and the new trial datasets.
pmc-13529778:
Shilin Yin and five colleagues tie a body clock gene to cholesterol making in mouth cancer in a 2026 study. The gene, PER2, runs daily rhythms. It was scarce in oral squamous cancers. Low PER2 let cells make more cholesterol and grow faster. Restoring it did the reverse. The team traced the chain link by link.

PER2 grabs a structural protein, MYH9, and recruits a disposal tagger. MYH9 then gets destroyed, which throttles the rate-limiting cholesterol enzyme. In mouse tumors, extra PER2 or the statin simvastatin each slowed growth. Together they worked far better. Daily rhythms in the pathway differed by sex in mice. The statin's power swung up to two and a half fold by dosing hour. Timed dosing windows were wider in females. The authors propose clock-aware statin pairing.
pmc-13529878:
Sun and five co-authors test whether a blood protein called sLRP-1 relates to obstructive sleep apnea in people who snore. The study enrolled 180 adults who had overnight sleep recordings. One hundred had sleep apnea and 80 did not. The team measured the protein with a standard lab test.

Protein levels were clearly lower in the apnea group. After full adjustment, higher levels meant lower odds of apnea. The link held across age and inflammation subgroups. Machine learning models separated the two groups well, and the protein ranked among the top signals. The authors say outside validation is needed before any clinical use.
pmc-13532778:
Luis García-Marcos and colleagues asked how development and inequality shape asthma and allergy rates worldwide. Published in 2026, the ecological study drew on the Global Asthma Network Phase I survey of children, adolescents, and parents across 16, 25, and 17 countries respectively. Lower-income countries report less asthma, yet the roles of development and inequality were unclear.

Human development and Gini inequality scores explained part of the variation, most for asthma in children, up to about seven tenths, and least for rhinoconjunctivitis. Eczema fell between, with stronger explanation in children than adolescents. Heat maps showed the highest rates where high inequality met high development. The authors warn that poorer communities inside rich countries face the greatest hazard, especially for asthma.
pmc-13534378:
Hadi Kooshiar and colleagues review in 2026 how well a balance confidence scale works for adults aged 50 and older living in the community. The scale asks people how sure they feel doing daily tasks without falling, a factor often missed by physical tests alone. Five databases were searched through July 2025 under a standard quality framework.

Twenty-two studies covered three scale versions in 11 languages. Consistency and repeat scores were strong, and most validity checks passed. Gaps remained in error measures, cross-cultural checks, and response to change over time, so some versions still need local testing before firm use.
pmc-13534878:
Makena P McLean and colleagues test in 2026 radio frequency tags for tracking human remains during disaster victim identification. Paper tags can rot or fail, which slows return of bodies to families. Nine tag types were buried, inserted, or attached to pig carcasses as human stand-ins across four studies.

All but two tag types stayed readable through decomposition and burial. Tags tended to shift position, so bone attachment is advised for keeping them in place. Handwriting survived best when done dry and shielded from fluids, and two tag types stood out as most useful for field teams.
pmc-13536678:
Maria-Jose Fernandez-Cotarelo and colleagues chart Clostridioides difficile infection in Spanish hospitals from 2016 through 2022 in a 2026 report. Using national discharge records, the team counted 66,864 cases and tracked age, other illnesses, intensive care use, length of stay, and deaths in hospital. Rates per admission nearly doubled across the period, prompting a closer look at which patients fared worst.

Most infections were recorded as secondary diagnoses, and those patients stayed longer, needed intensive care more often, and died more often than primary cases. Overall, about one in nine patients died in hospital, with the highest share in 2020. Older age, more prior illness, greater overall severity, and intensive care admission each raised the risk of death. The authors call for stronger prevention to cut the growing burden.
pmc-13536778:
Hao Wang and co-authors review how daily body clocks shape tumor immunity in a 2026 synthesis. Clocks in the brain, in single cells, and in daily habits such as sleep and meals jointly time cell growth, energy use, and immune activity. Disrupted clocks have been linked to higher cancer risk and poorer outcomes. The review connects clock disruption to changes in the tissue around tumors.

Disruption weakens immune watchfulness and reshapes both innate and adaptive defenses, helping tumors start and grow. Clock signals govern how killer cells, helper cells, and suppressor cells develop, move, and act. Proposed responses include timing treatments to the clock and pairing clock-targeted steps with immunotherapy. The authors present clock-aware care as a route to sharper, stronger cancer treatment.
pmc-13536878:
Garoma Desa and colleagues check vaccine protection against peste des petits ruminants in sheep and goats in southern Ethiopia in a 2026 monitoring study. The viral disease spreads fast among small farm animals and causes heavy losses. Blood samples from 901 vaccinated animals across three districts of Borana Zone were tested with a standard lab assay. Protection rates were compared by age, species, district, movement history, and sampling timing.

Overall protection ran high, with more than nine in ten animals showing conversion after vaccination. Older animals converted more often than younger ones, and animals without a movement history converted more often than movers. Species, sex, district, and sampling timing showed no clear gaps. The authors judge the campaign effective and recommend tracking animal movement to limit entry of unvaccinated stock.
pmc-13537378:
Pengruofeng Liu, Zimo Zhang, Minhan Li, Hairui Li, Guang Chu, Xiaoqian Du, Jun Lin, and Weiming Guo published this study in 2026. It designs a nanoparticle treatment for osteoporosis, the bone-thinning disease. Weak bones suffer a sour, stressed local setting where bone-eating cells run wild and bone-building cells falter.

Their particles blend selenium into calcium hydroxide. In dish tests, the particles raised a protective enzyme, mopped up harmful oxygen radicals, and neutralized acid. Bone-eating cells slowed, while stem cells built bone faster and laid down more mineral. Gene scans showed shifts in membrane signaling and matrix building. In mice made osteoporotic by ovary removal, local injections rebuilt bone density and fine structure. Blood markers improved and no organ harm appeared. The authors offer the particles as a setting-fixing therapy.
pmc-13537478:
Emilie Even Dencker and colleagues tested whether language software can spot surgical complications in health records. Published in 2026, the look-back Danish study covered 17,486 cases across 18 hospitals over six years. Problems after surgery guide quality checks, yet cheap, exact tracking methods were lacking.

The models scored from just over 0.9 to near perfect on a standard accuracy curve and beat diagnosis-code tracking by a wide margin. Sensitivity ran from seven tenths to full marks except for heart attacks at one half, while true-hit rates varied widely. Pairing software with human review of just over sixteen percent of cases reached a perfect true-hit rate. The authors present the software as a support for, not a swap for, manual checks, offering wider tracking.
pmc-13538378:
Zoran Kovacevic and Christoph Stadtfeld study how people recall positive ties inside a student community in a 2026 analysis of repeated surveys with 820 participants. Remembering who counts as a friend or positive contact guides help seeking and invitations, yet searching memory for ties is demanding. Recall order was modeled to detect which cues steer each next name, covering likeness, shared settings, tie quality, and visibility.

Recall runs followed several cues at once, tied both to the link between rememberer and nominee and to links between names recalled back to back. Patterns held steady across people and network types, while shifting within each recall run and as the community matured. The authors present social memory as a structured search shaped by layered social cues.
pmc-13539278:
Esther Kim and four co-authors present a 2026 study of a new way to measure how people discount future rewards. Classic tasks force a choice between money now and more money later, but they miss how torn the person feels. That feeling of conflict, called ambivalence, may add real information.

In their task, 105 people rated each choice on a hundred point scale, giving both the pick and its strength. The method reproduced two known patterns: larger rewards are discounted less, and dated rewards are treated more kindly than delayed ones. Ambivalence scores then linked with discount rates across people. The authors frame the task as a tribute to a field pioneer.
pmc-13539878:
Ngwa Niba Rawlings and five co-authors publish a 2026 photographic atlas of sand flies collected in Belize, small biting insects that can carry the parasites behind leishmaniasis. Naming these flies has long depended on grey drawings and written keys that nonspecialists find hard to use.

Collections from north-west and central east Belize between 2023 and 2025 yielded twenty species, pictured in 65 colour microscope photographs. Two species had never been recorded in the country before. The guide shows the body parts that separate one species from another and adds a step-by-step identification key. Specimens are stored in a Brazilian reference collection for future checking.
pmc-13539978:
Feng He and seven colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether alien plants growing together usually help each other invade, an idea known as invasional meltdown. Field records and experiments from many countries were combined to count how co-invaders actually interact.

Surveys of 3,039 plots found several alien species together in forty percent of sites. Pooling 4,415 observations from 122 experiments showed co-invasion cut alien plant performance by about a fifth on average. Most pairings were neutral, with competition next and help least common. Outcomes shifted with how many alien species were present and whether native plants joined the mix, so the authors reject meltdown as the norm.
pmc-13540878:
Jia Haijiang and colleagues test altitude effects in a 2026 chamber study. They tracked body measures and mental response speed. The goal was a fatigue warning for high-altitude work. Thin air is the core stress at altitude. Volunteers sat in a chamber that mimics high places.

The team recorded blood pressure and blood oxygen. They also recorded heart rate and reaction performance. Younger volunteers adapted better to thin air. Reaction speed held up well at first. It fell once oxygen dropped below a set threshold. Heart rate climbing at the same time made things worse. The authors propose warning thresholds for rest and workload planning.
pmc-13541578:
Asuka Miyamae and eight colleagues report, in a 2026 case, a two-month-old boy with Noonan syndrome whose extra tricuspid valve tissue progressively blocked blood leaving his right heart. Accessory valve tissue is rare on the tricuspid side, and the authors believe this combination with thickened heart muscle is the first well documented example.

Ultrasound showed the spare tissue prolapsing during each beat and choking the outflow tract, while catheter tests found right-sided pressure above the body's main pressure. Surgeons removed the accessory tissue and the obstruction resolved immediately. Beta-blocker treatment followed, and the baby went home stable. The authors warn that this pairing can deteriorate fast enough to kill.
pmc-13543378:
Ryozo Ishida and colleagues published a 2026 paper introducing PAVSAT, an automated tool for measuring blood vessel networks in microscope images. Imaging now captures tangled vascular structures faster than analysts can trace them, and older software struggles with curved vessels of changing width. The system pairs a YOLOv8 deep-learning segmenter, trained on stained vessel images, with skeleton extraction and a new branch-point finder. It takes repeated width measurements along each vessel, then converts the network into a graph for analysis.

A boundary-aware tiling scheme, which processes overlapping image tiles and merges the results, cut missed vessels sharply in test samples while adding few false alarms. Against expert hand measurements, the tool detected 91 to 98 percent of vessels and measured widths with 89 to 93 percent accuracy. Freely automating this work could speed studies of how vessels develop and how disease distorts them.
pmc-13543478:
Chukwuma Okoye's team published a 2026 protocol for OPTIMAge-IT, a trial testing whether a many-sided programme can prevent hospital-acquired disability in frail older Italians. Hospital stays often cost older adults muscle and freedom they never regain. Eight acute geriatric units are randomised as clusters to usual care or to a structured programme. It serves patients aged seventy and over with mild-to-moderate frailty, beginning once patients settle and running twelve weeks after discharge with a tracker and tablet for support.

The programme bundles guided physical exercise, computer cognitive training, nutrition advice, health teaching, drug review, and social company. The main outcome is change in a standard physical performance battery at discharge; other aims cover whether the programme, and its home phase, get used. As a protocol, the paper reports no results yet, but it lays out a repeatable design for tech-supported, whole-person hospital care.
pmc-13543578:
Sara Claes and colleagues published a 2026 evaluation of an unguided online well-being programme offered to Belgian adults. Participants could pick activities such as mindfulness, breathing exercises, walking, and cycling without any coach. Two hundred and eight people chose either the programme or a control condition by preference, and outcomes were tracked over eight months, with statistical weighting to balance the self-selected groups.

Real-world performance was sobering. Only about a third of those offered the programme took it up, nearly two thirds of starters dropped out, and many completers barely engaged, though most completers judged it acceptable. One outcome did improve significantly: a sense of meaningfulness, while broader well-being and peace of mind did not. Competing commitments were the main barrier to starting. Scalable wellbeing tools, the authors warn, fail quietly when nobody is helped to keep using them.
pmc-13543678:
Aida Feu Masdemont and co-authors report a rescue balloon procedure for early clotting of a prosthetic mitral valve during heart-lung machine support, in a case report from 2026. Clots on a new valve can block it within days of surgery, a rare but deadly event. Care is harder when shock needs external circulation support, since low flow aids clotting.

A man aged seventy-four had valve surgery plus aorta repair, then needed the support machine for severe shock. On day two, scans showed the new valve blocked by clot with stuck leaflets. More surgery and clot-busting drugs were judged too risky. A catheter balloon route through the heart wall was used as rescue.
pmc-13544278:
Melissa Villegas-Albo and co-authors report a chest tumor that looked like a different growth at first, in a 2026 case study. The patient, a woman aged forty-one, had two years of right sided chest pain and growing numbness in her right arm. Scans showed a large mass on the lung lining that reached into the chest wall.

A first sample pointed to a mild growth type, but surgery and full tissue tests showed a desmoid tumor instead. Thirty months later, scans showed the growth pressing on key structures at the top of the chest. The case stresses matching scan and tissue proof before settling on a diagnosis.
pmc-13545078:
Wenbiao Xiao, Dongmei Xia, and Ju Mao published a 2026 study of why university teachers keep using AI content tools after the novelty fades. Most uptake research stops at first use. Their model merged a continuance model, centred on whether expectations were confirmed and users feel pleased, with a tech-acceptance model. Survey data from 310 Chinese higher-learning teachers were run through structural equation modelling and a neural network ranking exercise.

Usefulness, satisfaction, ease, and expected performance each fed the intention to continue, while social pressure and risk did not. Satisfaction carried the effect of confirmed expectations and usefulness onward. The network ranked performance expectancy first among the drivers, satisfaction second. For tool makers and colleges, the message is that keeping teachers depends on proven performance and a pleasing experience, not hype or fear.
pmc-13546678:
Jie Wang, Ying Peng, and seven co-authors review how chromosome ends choose their upkeep path in cancer. Their review, from twenty twenty-six, covers telomeres, the caps that guard chromosome tips. Each cell split shortens the caps, a built-in limit on growth. Most cancer cells revive an enzyme that rebuilds the caps.

About a fifth instead stretch caps by copying from other DNA. Once set, each path stays stable, but what picks the path is murky. The review shows how the caps' chemical wrapping sways that choice. It walks through the main players that tend the caps. The insight may open new ways to block cancer growth at its roots.
pmc-13547678:
Jonghu Shin and Young-Won Yoon bring renal denervation up to date, in this review from twenty twenty-six. Zapping the kidney's sympathetic nerves to lower blood pressure crashed a decade ago when a big sham-controlled trial came back neutral. Better devices, better trial design, and better patient selection revived it.

Radiofrequency, ultrasound, and alcohol-based versions each show modest but real reductions against sham, on and off background medication, with effects holding to three years and no late safety alarm in follow-up. What is missing is the crown jewel: proof that strokes and heart attacks fall. Guidelines therefore seat denervation as an adjunct for carefully chosen patients with uncontrolled or resistant hypertension, never a replacement for pills. The authors close on response prediction as the field's next problem.
pmc-13548478:
Iva Burešová and colleagues followed 75 women with breast cancer in 2026 from diagnosis to the end of added drug and radiation treatment, tracking how body and mind changed together. Questionnaires captured fatigue, quality of life, mood, sleep, and motivation to move, while body mass index and a six-minute walk test gave objective readings. Average age was about 52.

Physical and general fatigue rose clearly, the physical side of quality of life fell, and weight crept up. Walking capacity, the objective measure, did not significantly change, and depressive symptoms actually eased, suggesting mental adaptation amid physical decline. Younger women lost more sleep quality, while older women lost more physical quality of life. The authors argue for age-sensitive supportive care.
pmc-13548578:
Saja Karanbash, Claude Daou, and Christelle F. Iskandar study eighteen E. coli strains gathered from irrigation water, farm soil, and lettuce, in a 2026 investigation of how farm bacteria endure. Such bacteria can ride water and soil onto fresh produce, where traits that help them persist may defeat washing and other controls. The team measured slime-layer biofilm building, tolerance of acid, and drug resistance, then read the genomes for matching machinery.

Most strains stayed sensitive to most antibiotics, and only a small share resisted several drugs at once. Biofilm building was widespread, and several strains shrugged off vinegar-strength acid similar to home washing. The three survival traits tended to appear together, suggesting shared pressure favors them as a package. The authors argue prevention must start before harvest, at water and soil, rather than relying on cleaning produce later.
pmc-13549178:
Lu and five co-authors checked in twenty twenty-six if thyroid hormone levels track kidney disease in folks with type two diabetes. All folks in the check had a normal thyroid gland by standard tests. They split near three thousand cases into those with and those without kidney disease.

One hormone, FT3, was lower in the kidney group, while two kin marks were alike. Folks in the top three bands of FT3 had far less kidney disease than the low band. The link bent in an L shape, with a turn near a set level. Below that turn, more FT3 meant less disease in a clear way.
pmc-13549978:
Wesley J. Wang and Evelina T. Akimova ask when in childhood hardship leaves its deepest mark on the body's aging clock, in a 2026 longitudinal study. Adversity in early life is tied to faster epigenetic aging, measured by chemical tags on DNA, but whether timing, total load, or recency matters most stayed open. Using a long-running American family study of nearly two thousand children, the team modeled poverty, instability, deprivation, and maltreatment across developmental windows.

Adversity during specific sensitive periods linked most strongly to faster epigenetic aging by late childhood. What mattered was timing, not the total count or the most recent exposure. The explained share was small, though, and directions differed by adversity type. The accelerated aging in turn related to higher body mass, depression odds, and more pregnancies and births in young adulthood, carrying part of the path from early hardship to later outcomes.
pmc-13550278:
Yujun Lin and colleagues map the young research field around a rare, aggressive chest tumor defined by loss of the SMARCA4 gene, in a 2026 bibliometric analysis. This undifferentiated cancer, formally recognized only in the 2021 classification, kills quickly and has no standard therapy. Searching two major databases from 2000 to 2025, the team kept 132 papers and charted who publishes, where, with whom, and on what themes.

Output grew at roughly thirty-two percent a year, with papers heavily cited. China and Japan led production, and a China and United States pairing formed the collaboration core. Studies of the gene's machinery are mature, while treatment research lags, and attention shifted toward diagnostic standards after formal recognition. Immunotherapy combined with chemotherapy currently anchors care. The authors urge biomarker-driven trials and bigger international teamwork.
pmc-13551378:
Mounir Yaâkoubi, Norbertus A Ipenburg, Anton C de Groot, and Thomas Rustemeyer published a 2026 survey of alkyl glucosides in cosmetics sold in the Netherlands. These mild cleansers and emulsifiers, made from glucose and fatty alcohols, are increasingly tied to contact allergy, with positive patch tests reported in Europe and North America. Data on their presence in products came mostly from the United States, so the team checked ingredient lists at the largest Dutch online retailer.

They examined 350 leave-on and 300 rinse-off products. About a quarter of sunscreens and a fifth of day creams contained at least one alkyl glucoside, while only one of fifty lip salves did. Across leave-on products the share was 16.9 percent in the reported count, giving clinicians local exposure figures.
pmc-13551778:
Huang and co-authors identify a tiny RNA shipped between cells that restrains a head and neck cancer. Their 2026 paper studies miR-7111-3p in nasopharyngeal carcinoma, where the molecule was scarce in patient serum and tumour cell lines. The team adjusted its levels in cells and mouse tumours, traced its delivery inside extracellular vesicles, the membrane parcels cells use to exchange cargo, and hunted its gene targets.

Raising the microRNA suppressed proliferation, migration, invasion, and the shape-shifting transition that helps cancers spread, while lowering it did the reverse. Its direct target proved to be amyloid precursor protein, better known from brain disease; restoring that protein cancelled the microRNA's benefits. Vesicles from microRNA-poor tumour cells raised the target and growth in recipient cells. In mice, extra microRNA shrank grafted tumours. The authors name the axis a therapeutic target.
pmc-13551978:
Ran Zhao, with nine colleagues, published a 2026 study of internet addiction in teens with depression and self-injury. The sample held 92 outpatients aged twelve to seventeen. Standard tests scored internet addiction, depression, and anxiety. A survey scale scored bullying by peers. Teens were split into low and moderate-to-severe addiction groups at a set test score.

Just over half the teens fell in the higher addiction group. Addiction severity rose with depression, anxiety, and bullying in simple links. In adjusted models, bullying stayed tied to addiction in both the depression and anxiety models. Depression also held on its own. Anxiety lost its link once bullying entered the model. A check using girls only addressed the skewed sex mix.
pmc-13553778:
Thiyagarajan V and Vidhyapathi CM build a system to spot road signs in poor weather, in a 2026 paper. Self driving cars need to read signs fast and well, yet fog, glare, and blocks in view can foil them. The authors add a cleaning step that clears haze from images before detection.

Cleaned images pass to a detection network built on a recent YOLO model, tuned by a new search method. The network blends features at several scales and weighs the most telling ones. On two large road data sets the system scored in the high ninety percent range for accuracy. Such gains could help driver aid tools in bad weather.
pmc-13554278:
Emelin Leandro Rodrigues leads a five-author team testing a yeast that fights a toxin-making mould on apples in a 2026 study. The mould Aspergillus clavatus makes patulin, a poison that can taint fruit and juice. Thirteen strains of one yeast species were screened against the mould. A common baker's yeast, tried for comparison, gave no protection at all.

Every strain of the test yeast slowed the mould, four of them strongly. The best strain also cleared patulin from apple juice fully within two days. Sprayed on apples before infection, it suppressed the mould well, while late spraying failed. Toxin removal worked by binding to cell walls and by inner cell action, not by juices the yeast released. Timing, the authors stress, decides success.
pmc-13554578:
Muhammed Oğuz and colleagues give clinicians a three-step ultrasound method for finding a key tendon band inside a deep neck muscle, publishing the note in 2026. The back of the neck packs muscles, nerves, and fascia into a tight space, and that crowding makes injections harder to aim and slower to learn. The semispinalis capitis muscle matters because it guides nerve blocks, facet injections, and botulinum treatment for neck dystonia.

Its tendinous septum, dividing the muscle's two heads, marks the boundary that separates important nerve branches, so injections on one side do not reliably reach the other. The proposed sequence starts by feeling the C7 spine, then placing the probe across it and sliding outward until the septum appears. The method should help trainees aim more safely and plan needle paths with confidence.
pmc-13554778:
Tse-Min Lu and co-authors evaluate a paclitaxel-coated balloon for treating coronary arteries in Chinese patients, covering both re-narrowed stents and newly diseased vessels. Their 2026 report describes a prospective registry run at nine sites in Taiwan, Hong Kong, and Singapore.

Five hundred patients received the balloon, which delivers a drug that limits tissue regrowth without leaving a permanent implant. At one year, 13.9 percent had a major adverse cardiac event, a combined outcome of cardiac death, heart attack, or repeat vessel treatment. Rates were higher for re-narrowed stents than for new disease, at 16.3 percent versus 10.5 percent respectively. Patients who received follow-up angiography had far more repeat procedures, which the authors say shows how surveillance imaging itself drives treatment decisions.
pmc-13555078:
David C. Lees's team presents the first chromosome-level genome of the Common Quaker moth, Orthosia cerasi, in a 2026 assembly. This medium-sized nocturnal moth is widespread across Britain, Ireland, Europe, and western Asia, with caterpillars feeding on oak, elm, hawthorn, and birch. The work belongs to the Darwin Tree of Life effort, which sequences eukaryotes found in Britain and Ireland.

The assembly spans about 1,022 megabases, with nearly all of it placed on 29 chromosomal scaffolds including the Z sex chromosome, plus a complete mitochondrial genome. Annotation found 15,702 protein-coding genes. The resource should support studies of moth evolution, ecology, and the species' recent decline, which researchers link to warming and mismatches between caterpillar growth and food plants.
pmc-13555878:
Michaela Sklenárová leads an twelve-author team testing a cannabis compound against rheumatoid arthritis in cells and rats in a 2026 study. The compound, cannabichromene, does not cause a high and may calm inflammation. In vessel cells stirred by a bacterial toxin, it lowered a key inflammatory signal at low doses. Rats with induced joint disease then received the compound, a steroid, or salt water.

Treated rats scored better on arthritis measures and lost less weight, though paw swelling barely budged. Tissue tests showed a whole inflammatory chain turned down, from signal proteins to helper cell drivers. Parts of the cell's alarm assembly were also suppressed. Joint damage markers, though, did not move, so the authors call for more work.
pmc-13557078:
Haque and co-authors report in 2026 a large chirality driven magnetoresistance effect in hybrid perovskite semiconductors. Chiral metal halide materials pair semiconducting traits with tunable handedness, which opens room temperature spin control. Spin valves built from them showed resistance swings above one hundred percent.

The effect is credited to an interface tunneling barrier shaped by chirality and spin. Current dissymmetry passed the limit a classic model sets from contact polarization alone. The response also shifted with material composition, which maps structure to spin behavior. A weaker proximity effect appears without the barrier, by contrast. The team offers design rules to strengthen the effect for devices.
pmc-13557378:
Hung-Chun Huang and six co-authors build a field test score to flag college athletes who need care for low back, pelvis, and hip problems. Such problems often come before back pain, but full exams take time. The team tested 864 athletes from ten schools with standard checks and history questions. Experts judged which athletes needed prompt care; just over half did.

A fourteen-point score built from the results sorted athletes well, holding up under repeat testing. Pain in the area, weak muscles, and higher body mass raised the score. The paper offers coaches a quick sideline tool for early referral.
pmc-13557478:
Jason M. Baron and Denise LaMarche Heaney measured real-world testing for chlamydia and gonorrhoea in the United States, in a 2026 claims-based study. Rules call for screening sexually active women under 25 and testing patients with symptoms, yet uptake in practice was poorly mapped. The authors analysed 2023 insurance claims from two million people with commercial or Medicaid cover.

Only about 24 percent of females aged 16 to 24 were tested, against 7 percent of males the same age. Even among young women seeing a gynaecologist the rate reached just 56 percent. Testing varied sharply by state and by provider, and companion tests for other infections were ordered unevenly. The authors read the gap between testing and likely sexual activity as rules not being followed, and call for better testing systems.
pmc-13558578:
Barış Reşitoğlu and nine colleagues worked in 2026 on squeezing the most medicinal chemistry from a wild mint of eastern Turkey. Mentha longifolia subspecies typhoides is rich in two triterpene acids valued by drug and supplement makers. The team collected seventeen samples from fourteen localities, macerated them in seven solvents of differing strength, and profiled the extracts with two kinds of mass spectrometry.

Alcohol extraction won on overall yield and carried the target acids well, alongside a strong load of rosmarinic acid and other protective plant compounds. The richest chemistry concentrated in leaves and flowers rather than roots or stems. Fine-tuning settled on mild warmth and neutral conditions for the extraction. Later sampling across the growing season let the authors say when and where the plant is worth harvesting, a practical guide for growers and processors.
pmc-13558878:
Pocut Astari, Dewi F. Suniarti, and Erik Idrus reviewed in 2026 the laboratory evidence that herbal products can prevent or soften mouth sores caused by the chemotherapy drug 5-fluorouracil. These sores are painful and often force dose cuts. Following standard review guidelines, the team searched five databases to March 2026. They sought cell studies and combined cell and animal studies of plant preparations in this injury model. Each study's reliability was graded with a toxicology tool.

Seven studies qualified, testing seven different products from a Japanese herbal formula and sage extract to cannabidiol and tea saponin. Across them, the preparations kept cells alive, quenched damaging oxygen radicals, calmed inflammatory signals, blocked cell suicide pathways, and sped surface repair, through a handful of named molecular routes. Every study passed the reliability check without restrictions. The authors stress that all evidence is preclinical, a map for trials rather than a treatment claim.
pmc-13559978:
Andrew Fenelon argues that a renewed public housing programme could improve population health, publishing the essay in 2026. Housing shapes health across life, yet the affordability crisis and a policy drift toward tenant vouchers have narrowed public housing's reach, even though it now serves nearly a million low-income families. Comparing American housing programmes, the author finds public housing an unexpected success story.

Children in public housing show better mental health, fewer emergency visits, and steadier housing, while adults report better health, lower diabetes risk, and stronger food security. Fenelon proposes serving a broader income range, integrating levels of government, keeping the social supports of project-based housing, improving management, and securing funding less exposed to political swings.
pmc-13560178:
Gu Li and three colleagues model how heterosexual people in China react when a sexual minority man comes out to them. Their 2026 study screened nearly fifty-five thousand people on a crowdsourcing platform and recruited 650 heterosexual adults who had lived through such a disclosure. Participants gave eighty-five factors covering the person, the setting, and what was done.

Background traits of the recipient, such as sex, age, and relationship to the man disclosing, predicted reactions most strongly. Context added smaller effects: when the news came wrapped in a love confession, assault, or substance use, reactions turned more negative. Reactions warmed when recipients had anticipated the news or when the disclosure mentioned a same-sex relationship. Machine learning caught tangled links among factors with fair hit rates. The authors argue that better coming-out experiences depend on recipient-side processes, especially in high-stigma settings.
pmc-13560478:
Kellee White Whilby and colleagues assessed whether racial equity impact assessments actually change local lawmaking, publishing the descriptive study in 2026. These assessments give legislators advance evidence on how a bill might affect racial equity, yet little was known about how their findings are rated or used. The team analysed all 296 assessments produced in the District of Columbia from 2021 to 2024, covering 409 bill-level ratings.

Nearly half the ratings predicted positive equity effects, 9 percent warned of harm, 10 percent were neutral, and about a third were inconclusive. Positive findings clustered in health and economic policy, adverse ones in criminal justice, environment, and infrastructure. Even among bills flagged harmful, most passed, often with changes. The authors conclude assessments help only where accountability structures force lawmakers to act on them.
pmc-13560578:
Joanna Darmos and colleagues report a pilot study, published in 2026. It was an operational pilot of a phone app. The app lets travellers pre-register for the European Union's new Entry/Exit System. This system records biometric border crossings. The App4EES project tested the app in real operations. The site was Stockholm Arlanda Airport. Travellers submitted face and document data before reaching the border desk.

Over 1,600 travellers completed the enrolment steps. They gave feedback afterwards. The app sped the border process. It met data protection and cybersecurity standards. Users had a positive experience. The design was intuitive. Travellers finished pre-registration easily. This supports wider rollout of such pre-registration tools.
pmc-13561078:
Stav Subach and co-authors published this behavioral study in 2026. It uses computer games to study foraging choices in people, borrowing designs from animal research. Foragers must balance food gains against the risk of being eaten, and update their choices as conditions change. One game had players gather resources in an open field under safe and risky conditions. A second game tested spatial learning in a maze.

Simulated danger made players forage less and hide more. Order mattered: players who met risk first adjusted less when conditions later changed, suggesting their sense of the environment lagged behind reality. Spatial skill carried over between the two games in both safe and risky settings. Maze performance improved across trials in the classic slowing curve of learning. The authors offer games as a controlled way to study human decisions under ecological pressure.
pmc-13561378:
Maialen Zabalza-Zudaire and colleagues published a study protocol in 2026 for the VOICE-DEP project on depression. Major depression is severe and often returns, yet diagnosis and follow-up still rest mainly on interviews and rating scales. Voice and speech might add useful clues, but past work has been uneven, mostly one-time, and rarely done with Spanish-speaking patients.

Under the protocol, speech during medical interviews, including a free-speech opening section, will be recorded in a standard way. Pitch, loudness, speed, word choice, and sentiment will be compared with clinician ratings and patient reports over time. The expected result is a Spanish-language longitudinal speech collection and a clear method for testing speech markers.
pmc-13561778:
Yang Liu and Jiesen Yin compare sports programs across five schools to learn why quality differs. Their study, from twenty twenty-six, treats youth sports as a health and education goal. Schools vary a lot in how well they run these programs. The team weighs policy, resources, staff, lessons, and student experience as a combined set.

A set-based method finds mixes of traits that lead to high or low quality. Strong leadership looks near-required but not enough on its own. Eight paths lead to high quality and eight to low. Rich schools win by using their edge well. Poorer schools can still win through smart organization. Student experience plays a middle role in several paths.
pmc-13562078:
Yan He and colleagues map how depression, anxiety, decision-making, and health habits lock together in prostate cancer survivors living with urinary incontinence. Their 2026 cross-sectional network study surveys 251 survivors at a large Chinese referral hospital between October 2025 and February 2026. Online forms fed both scale-level and symptom-level network models.

Anxiety and depression sat at the network's center, forming a tight mental cluster with loneliness. Shared decision making linked strongly to decisional conflict, while incontinence strain tied in a middling way to workout habits and weakly to mood. Inside the depression network, thoughts of self-harm and low energy were the most central symptoms. Hard-to-control worry anchored the anxiety side. The authors argue these core nodes deserve first attention in follow-up checks, and they call for long-term work to test whether central symptoms drive the rest.
pmc-13562478:
Fatema, Bahar, and Megharaj hunted cellulose-digesting bacteria in Australian marsupials in twenty twenty-six. Cellulose is Earth's most plentiful renewable plant material and a promising biofuel source, but it resists breakdown. Animals that eat tough plants host microbes that can crack it.

The team isolated bacteria from feces of koalas and common wombats. Ten isolates were screened on a cellulose medium; four showed strong clearing zones and high enzyme output in broth. Gene sequencing named three as Streptomyces species and one as Enterobacter. Each strain had its own best conditions for making the enzyme, differing in temperature, acidity, and timing. The authors present these marsupial-derived strains as candidates for breaking down plant biomass in industry.
pmc-13562678:
R. Gopi and five colleagues design a safer way to elect cluster heads in wireless sensor networks, the relay nodes that gather each group's data. Classic election schemes pick heads by chance or by search heuristics, ignoring whether a node can be trusted, so energy drains unevenly and attackers slip in. Their 2026 algorithm, ED-CHSS, scores each candidate on leftover energy, communication cost, and a trust index fed by past behaviour. Lightweight encryption then guards traffic inside each cluster.

Simulations showed the scheme cutting average energy use by 28 to 32 percent and stretching network lifetime by roughly 38 to 42 percent. Resistance improved against two named attacks: selective forwarding, where a node silently drops packets, and sinkhole attacks that lure traffic into a trap. Election odds also adapt to local node density and link steadiness. The authors pitch the design for mission-critical sensing where battery life and honest relays both matter.
pmc-13562878:
Bryan Khoo and six colleagues published a biomechanics study in two thousand twenty-six on kneecap ligament repair in children. Rebuilding the ligament that holds the kneecap in place uses either suture anchors or bone tunnels in the kneecap. Adult data existed, but child bone may behave differently.

The team tested ten kneecaps from child donors aged nine to eleven. Bone tunnel constructs held about one hundred seventy newtons before failing. Anchor constructs failed near fifty-five newtons, far weaker. Stiffness was about the same in both. Anchors failed by pulling out, while tunnels failed by the suture slicing through. The authors give surgeons child-specific numbers for choosing a technique.
pmc-13563678:
When a transplanted tissue flap loses its blood supply, surgeons rush back to the operating room, and every delay is blamed for failures. Alexander Fiedler and co-authors timed 113 such rescue operations at one center. They split the wait into ward-to-theater travel, anesthesia lead time, and room preparation.

The surprise: total waits matched between saved and lost flaps, about seventy-eight minutes each. No single delay segment predicted failure. Lost flaps trended toward longer anesthesia and longer operations, hints of harder cases rather than slower logistics. Weekend operations failed somewhat more often. The authors advise improving recognition and decision speed, plus anesthesia-surgery coordination, over shaving transport minutes.
pmc-13563778:
Meijiao Zhou and five colleagues track what happens in real clinics when dialysis patients start patiromer, a powder that binds potassium in the gut. High potassium threatens the hearts of people on haemodialysis, yet proof for this drug in that group was thin. Their 2026 study followed 10,860 adults at Fresenius clinics who began the drug between 2016 and 2022, comparing the three months before starting with a year after. Most took the lowest dose once daily, and dose changes were rare.

Control improved markedly: the share of patients below the 5.5 safety line rose from 35.6 to 69.9 percent, and average potassium settled from 5.60 down near 5.21 units by the fourth quarter. Use of the lowest-potassium dialysis fluid fell away as the drug took over. Hospital visits dipped for all causes and more for potassium crises. With no comparison group, the authors read the hospital trend cautiously, while calling the potassium control solid.
pmc-13563878:
Khushboo Yadav and three colleagues publish the complete genome of a bacterium that lives inside a medicinal plant and makes compounds able to kill priority drug-resistant germs. The strain, Streptomyces californicus ADR1, was isolated from Datura metel and had already shown antibacterial, anti-biofilm, and antioxidant powers in the dish. Its chemistry hinted at rich biosynthetic machinery. Their 2026 data report sequences that machinery end to end, so the genes behind the effects can be found and mined.

The genome spans 8.4 million bases across 262 scaffolds, with a high G+C content of 72.5 percent and 7,427 protein-coding genes. Mining software flagged 39 biosynthetic gene clusters, spanning non-ribosomal peptide makers, polyketide assembly lines, terpenes, and melanin pathways. Those clusters line up with the compound families earlier chemical profiling had detected. The authors present the sequence as a working map for turning a plant-dwelling microbe's hidden chemistry into candidate medicines.
pmc-13564478:
Magdalena Quepuy-Izarra and co-authors test an offline digital app for vaccination brigades in the Peruvian Amazon, in this 2026 study. Paper records are slow and error-prone in remote indigenous communities with no internet. The team timed 758 records, split between app and paper, and surveyed thirty brigade workers. Statistical models compared speed, while open comments fed a thematic review.

The app cut record time by about thirty percent, from roughly 4.6 to 3.2 minutes each. Built-in checks lifted data quality, a gain every surveyed user praised. Workers sorted into receptive, hybrid, and cautious profiles, shaped by tech familiarity, training, and location. The authors say tailored training and hybrid systems could carry the app nationwide.
pmc-13564578:
Haleema Qamar and four co-authors review drug targets for a stubborn form of heart failure in this two thousand twenty-six paper. In this form, the heart still pumps out a normal share of blood but fills poorly. It is a huge and growing burden with few good drugs. Its drivers span inflammation, oxidative stress, and failing cell power plants. Non-coding RNAs and epigenetic marks also steer the disease.

The review maps the target landscape across these pathways. It judges the animal and cell models used to test new drugs, noting where they mislead. It also covers fresh strategies now in reach. Translational researchers who move drugs from bench to bedside are the readers. The paper is a field guide to a hard target.
pmc-13565278:
Filipa Pinheiro, Maria Amaral, and Ana Loureiro study how whole families manage type 2 diabetes, in a paper dated 2026. The disease demands daily self-care, and in many homes relatives share the work informally. The family's grasp of health information and its general functioning may decide whether that care succeeds.

Four families in a Portuguese primary care unit were followed as individual cases. Structured interviews, guided by a family assessment model, supplied the qualitative strand. Standard questionnaires and a diabetes self-care scale supplied numbers. The team then watched what changed after nursing interventions tailored to each family. Comparing across cases links family literacy and dynamics to self-management habits, pointing nurses toward the household, not just the patient, as the unit of care.
pmc-13565478:
Binchen Wang and six co-authors redesign an enzyme that eats a carcinogen in fermented drinks, in a 2026 study. Ethyl carbamate forms during fermentation and appears in foods and liquors, including Chinese baijiu. An enzyme from a soil bacterium can destroy it, but the liquor's own flavor esters compete for the enzyme, wasting its effort. The team mapped how the enzyme grips its targets using docking, motion simulation, binding tests, and aroma analysis.

One redesigned variant, F157G, recognized the carcinogen better than the natural enzyme. Its breakdown rate for a rival flavor ester shifted in the desired direction as well. The goal is a treatment that strips the harmful compound while leaving the drink's prized flavor intact, a balance brewers have long wanted.
pmc-13566178:
Daebong Moon and co-authors analyze in 2026 sugar attachments on an engineered interferon protein using mass spectrometry. Sugar coating affects how therapeutic proteins work and last. The variant protein has two attachment sites, which doubles the analysis challenge for quality control in drug making.

They profile total sugars with a bright labeling method that improves sensitivity. Site-specific profiling used protein mapping after digestion, with one enzyme proving best for separating the two sites. The two sites carried distinct sugar distributions. Modeling suggests the extra sugar may boost stability and receptor binding. Combined methods give a fuller quality picture.
pmc-13569578:
Atopic dermatitis is a common, lasting skin disease marked by a weak skin barrier, a skewed type 2 immune response, and an uneven microbiome. Live probiotics can calm the gut-skin link, but results vary and safety worries remain. The four authors review a cell-free option: tiny vesicles shed by probiotic bacteria. These keep much of the microbes' effect without the risks of live cells. The review compares both kinds.

Gram-negative outer membrane vesicles carry lipopolysaccharide and signal mainly through TLR4, shaping innate defense and inflammation. Gram-positive ones carry other wall parts and favor TLR2 paths. Those paths support tolerance, regulatory T cells, and barrier repair. Both kinds eased inflammation and restored barrier and microbiome balance in early models. Clinical use still needs standard isolation, scalable production, strict safety testing, and regulatory agreement, though engineered ones may one day give targeted therapy.
pmc-13570978:
Keren Gueta and Carmit Klar-Chalamish study, in a 2026 online qualitative survey, how the October 7 war affected Israeli survivors of earlier sexual violence. In these lives, collective war trauma lands on top of personal trauma. One hundred twenty-six survivors described their mental and physical state, what made things worse, and how they coped.

Many described reliving the earlier trauma, with worsened post-traumatic symptoms and disruption to sleep, eating, and relationships. Feeling pushed to the bottom of social priorities deepened the harm, while some participants named protective resources and offered advice for health services during wartime. The exploratory account warns responders that war planning must include people carrying earlier sexual trauma.
pmc-13571378:
Chhayroud Heng and colleagues describe, in a 2026 multicenter Asian case series, five patients whose fast heart rhythms ran through nodoventricular accessory pathways. These are rare leftover connections between the heart's relay node and its lower chamber. Careful stimulation tests proved the ventricle took part in each circuit while the atrium did not.

Two patients also had Ebstein anomaly, a malformed tricuspid valve, supporting a developmental link the authors explain through displaced valve and node anatomy. Ablation targets differed widely by patient, succeeding at several distinct sites guided by tiny pathway signals. The series warns electrophysiologists to map the exact signal rather than burn a standard region.
pmc-13572178:
Mengxin Hu and colleagues test, in a 2026 study, whether tiny RNAs from two medicinal herbs can fight duck viral hepatitis across the species barrier. Such cross-kingdom effects are proposed for plant molecules in herbal decoctions. Sequencing found fourteen abundant candidate RNAs, which were synthesized and screened in duck embryo liver cells for protection against the hepatitis virus.

Two winners emerged, one from each herb. Both stayed stable under heat, cut virus replication, cell death, and oxidative damage in dishes, and improved survival when fed to infected ducklings, with calmer liver enzymes and less liver damage. One mainly curbed cell death while the other mainly curbed inflammation. The pair gives herbal medicine a concrete molecular story to test further.
pmc-13572378:
Bavani Gunasegaran, with three colleagues, reports a 2026 study that hunts for virus proteins inside glioblastoma, a fast and deadly brain tumour. Whether viruses play a role in this cancer has long been unclear. Tests in past work gave mixed results, in part due to the limits of each tool.

The team ran a protein-wide scan on tumour and control tissue from a public data set of 192 samples. A second group of 81 samples served as a check. Virus proteins from many species turned up, and human herpesviruses 1, 2, and 8 showed up more often in tumours than in controls. Host proteins tied to gene control, RNA handling, and energy use in cells also shifted. Links between virus and host proteins hint at paths for later work.
pmc-13572478:
Adrianna Wielgopolan, with two colleagues, reports a 2026 investigation of how mixed-feeling words affect a memory task. Most words feel clearly good or bad, yet some feel both at once. The team asked whether that mix, and mixes on two other scales, change how people hold letters in mind and where their eyes rest.

Two experiments used the N-back task, where people flag when a letter matches one seen steps back. Words mixed on good-bad tone or on how the feeling arises helped accuracy, while mixes on arousal did not. Eye tracking showed more and longer fixations for all mixed word groups than for clear words. The results suggest mixed feelings reach beyond tone alone and shape both thought and gaze. The work adds origin as a scale that matters.
pmc-13573378:
Sijia Huang, with six colleagues, presents a 2026 wound patch that treats infection and shows its own drug release by colour. Infected wounds heal slowly, with lasting swelling and weak new vessel growth, and carers cannot see how much drug a dressing has left. The patch answers with microneedles made of a crystal gel.

Near-infrared light heats copper sulfide particles in the needles, which kills germs and frees a second drug load on demand. That load pairs tannic acid with berberine for germ killing and damage control. The crystal structure shifts colour as drug leaves, so staff can read release by eye. Lab tests killed over 95 percent of two common bacteria and mopped up reactive damage near fully. In infected rats, the lit patch closed wounds to 94 percent by day ten.
pmc-13573478:
Yuko Tsurumi, with six colleagues, reports a 2026 case where an ultrasound probe inside a neck artery caught a problem the X-ray missed. Stenting a narrowed carotid artery can leave plaque or clot poking through the stent, a source of stroke during the procedure. Dye-based angiography is the standard final check, yet it can overlook such pokes.

The patient was a 92-year-old Japanese man with two tight spots in his right carotid artery. After stenting under balloon protection, the dye check looked clean. The ultrasound probe, though, showed a marked poke inside the far stent. A second overlapping stent, placed at once under renewed blockage, flattened the poke on a repeat probe check. The man recovered well and went home on day four. The authors back probe checks to guide rescue.
pmc-13574278:
Mackenzie Fernandez, with five colleagues, presents a 2026 lab protocol that clears mouse rib bone for imaging while keeping fluorescent tags bright. Clearing turns tissue transparent so whole organs can be viewed without slicing. Bone and cartilage resist most recipes, and harsh ones dim the glow that genetic tags provide.

The method adapts a water-based clearing family, Scale CUBIC, for adult rib bone and needs no decalcification step. Transparency arrives in about 48 hours. In transgenic mice bred to glow in set cells, both the glow and the tissue's natural shape survived the bath. Growth plate and repair zones in the rib stayed readable. The authors offer the recipe as a dependable route for hard tissue imaging in mouse models.
pmc-13575978:
Cynthia Picard and colleagues published a genetics study in 2026. They studied a lysosomal enzyme in Alzheimer's disease. Faulty protein clearance in lysosomes contributes to Alzheimer's. The enzyme cathepsin H recently emerged as protective. The team asked how the gene is regulated. Data came from spinal fluid and brain tissue. Three independent patient and postmortem cohorts were analyzed. A gene variant changed enzyme levels in the body. That variant also tracked with better cognition.

People with the protective form had fewer amyloid plaques. Spinal fluid levels tracked tau and neuron markers closely. Links to glial and immune proteins also appeared. Gene networks tied the enzyme to immune metabolism. The enzyme looks like an active disease contributor. It may offer a new biomarker or drug angle.
pmc-13576578:
Evy Á Lakjuni Guttesen, Hugin Reistrup, Anders Gram-Hanssen, Jacob Rosenberg and Jason Joe Baker published this 2026 nationwide Danish study on how badly reoperation statistics understate hernia recurrence. After ventral hernia repair, studies often count only patients who return for another operation as recurrences. The authors instead linked national registers with an electronic survey of patients who had primary ventral or incisional hernia repair between 2014 and 2024, counting self-reported recurrences too.

The study included 20,703 patients with a median follow-up of 5.5 years and an 80 percent survey response rate. After primary ventral repair, total recurrence was 15.5 percent, yet only 3.3 percent had been reoperated, a roughly fivefold underestimate. After incisional repair, recurrence reached 27.2 percent against 7.0 percent reoperations, about a fourfold gap. The authors conclude that reoperation alone badly biases studies of repair success, and that patient-reported recurrence deserves a place in outcome measurement.
pmc-13577578:
Gabriele Rossi, Rachel Creighton, Patricia Ayebazibwe, and five colleagues ask whether malnutrition labels capture different children in this two thousand twenty-six cohort study. Severe acute malnutrition is diagnosed by arm circumference, weight-for-height score, or swelling, but the criteria overlap and may select different children. In Aweil, South Sudan, the team followed children aged six to fifty-nine months in outpatient treatment by arm circumference only, weight-for-height only, or both. Body composition was measured by impedance and skinfolds at admission and discharge.

One hundred ninety-four children entered; one hundred twenty-seven reached discharge. The arm and combined groups were younger and more stunted, with the combined group most depleted in fat-free mass and phase angle. During treatment the weight group recovered fastest, gaining fat-free mass, eighty-two percent of weight gained. The authors argue admission criteria mark distinct recovery paths, informing later care.
pmc-13578278:
Ahmed and Ebid bake orange peel waste into clay bricks and measure what the fruit does to the building material. Construction needs greener inputs, and peel burned out during firing leaves pores behind. Their formulations replaced up to ten percent of the clay, fired at three peak temperatures.

More peel meant lighter, more porous, more absorbent bricks, because the organic matter combusts away. Compressive strength fell as pores grew, yet bricks with five to ten percent peel fired at the highest temperature still passed thresholds for non-load-bearing use. Thermal conductivity dropped substantially, reaching its best value at the highest peel content. The authors recommend that mid-range recipe as the balance point between strength and insulation.
pmc-13578478:
Mingyu Wang and colleagues joined gene data, gut germ data, and blood chemistry data from 348 Yorkshire sows to grasp backfat and birth results. They tied 37 germ groups to thick backfat and found a few germ types that pass from parent to young, such as Ezakiella and Corynebacterium. Host genes such as MED17 and VSTM5 seemed to shape the germs, while MC4R and MEDAG tied straight to backfat.

Acetate, a short fatty acid made by gut germs, stood out as a key go-between in fat growth. Extra acetate in test models changed fat use and gave better birth results. The chain from host genes through germs to acetate gives breeders clear aims for leaner sows that bear more young.
pmc-13579878:
Belinda Garth and colleagues set out a national plan to move women into healthcare leadership in Australia, in a 2026 protocol paper. Women form over seventy percent of the health workforce yet hold a small share of top posts, a gap that drags on care quality. Past fixes mostly coached single women, leaving the systems that block them untouched. This plan targets rules, culture, and structures across hospitals, colleges, and agencies at once.

The mixed methods design pairs records and policy reviews with interviews and surveys, all built with the people who must live with the changes. Set frameworks guide rollout and judge reach, uptake, and staying power. Findings will feed a shared toolkit, refined in learning cycles. No results are claimed yet; the paper's value is the blueprint and its built in checks.
pmc-13580678:
Alajeyan and colleagues examined whether solasodine, a plant compound from nightshade-family foods that is being studied against cancer, also harms healthy red blood cells. Their 2026 laboratory study used red cells from healthy volunteers and tested for eryptosis, the programmed death of red blood cells that can contribute to anemia during chemotherapy.

Alajeyan found that solasodine triggered modest red cell rupture alongside clear death signals, including surface changes that flag cells for removal, cell swelling, and spiky cell shapes. Supplying energy fuels such as ATP reversed much of the damage, as did removing calcium from the fluid around the cells. Several targeted blockers also protected the cells, and the death process needed three signaling proteins working together. The results warn that solasodine's cell-killing power is not cancer-specific and suggest protective add-ons for future drug development.
pmc-13581478:
Livia Perles and co-authors describe how two injured giant anteaters were fed during hospital care, in a 2026 paper. Both animals were wild and arrived after accidents that injured their brains. Almost nothing has been written about tube or vein feeding in this species. One anteater had a skull fracture and bleeding in the brain and could not eat on its own.

That animal was fed through a nose tube for seven days, with no choking or nose problems. It later ate on its own and went home after two months. The second anteater arrived in a coma and, after four days without eating, received partial feeding through a vein. Its blood sugar rose and was managed by slowing the drip. It began eating on day two but died two weeks after arrival from the head injury. The authors show both feeding routes can work in this species.
pmc-13582178:
Bassem Gerges, Allie Eathorne, and George Condous published a 2026 survey study on scanning for endometriosis before surgery. In that condition, tissue like the womb lining grows outside the womb and can cause pain. A 2024 expert statement urged scans as a first step in finding deep disease. An ultrasound scan through the vagina was named the first choice.

pmc-13582478:

pmc-13589678:

pmc-13589978:

pmc-13590778:

pmc-13591178:
Laura Longo and colleagues tell of a child with acute disseminated encephalomyelitis, a rare brain and cord illness that strips nerve coats, who lost leg use and bladder control. pmc-13591278:

pmc-13591378:

pmc-13591878:

pmc-13592478:

pmc-13592878:

pmc-13593678:

pmc-13594978:

pmc-13598578:

pmc-13607978:

pmc-13611978:

pmc-13612878:

pmc-13614178:

pmc-13615678:

pmc-13618378:

pmc-13619078:

pmc-13619178:

pmc-13619478:

pmc-13619678:

pmc-13621578:
Tatjana Adzić-Vukicevic and co-authors report a lung fungus invasion that mimicked cancer return in a man treated for early lung cancer, in a case report from two thousand twenty-six. pmc-13623078:

Full GLIM scoring used body measures plus a disease burden criterion. Malnutrition rates came out near forty seven percent by the classic method and forty nine by GLIM. Agreement statistics were computed with the classic score as reference. The study also hunted factors tied to GLIM diagnosed cases. Standardized diagnosis may steady nutrition care in kidney clinics.
pmc-13623378:

pmc-13623678:

pmc-13626978:

Both retrievals succeeded without surgery. pmc-13627778:

pmc-13628678:

Airway symptoms were common in both places but clearly higher near industry, in upper and lower airways alike. Breathing tests showed reduced function in the exposed group. The study gives local authorities hard numbers where previously there were mostly complaints.
pmc-13628978:

pmc-13629278:

pmc-13630278:

pmc-13631278:

pmc-13632078:

pmc-13632678:

pmc-13633878:

pmc-13635778:

pmc-13637278:

pmc-13637578:

pmc-13638778:

pmc-13639078:

pmc-13642378:

pmc-13643278:

pmc-13644778:

pmc-13645478:

pmc-13646178:

pmc-13646278:

pmc-13646878:

pmc-13648778:

pmc-13649078:

pmc-13649278:

pmc-13649978:

pmc-13654678:

pmc-13658378:

pmc-13669278:

pmc-13669978:

pmc-13672478:

pmc-13676178:

pmc-13676678:

pmc-13677078:

pmc-13677978:

pmc-13679678:
